01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.name: Roman Catholic Parish Church and Monastery of St. Ignatius of Loyola
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.alternate_name: Jesuit Church and Monastery of Győr
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.description:
According to certain experts, the layout and architectural character of the Jesuit Church in Győr – besides the Italian patterns of Jesuit church architecture and the first church of the Order in Hungary in Nagyszombat (Trnava) – was influenced by the Jesuit Church in Vienna. Its layout (a nave with three adjoining closed chapels on both sides) later became an emblematic element in Hungarian Jesuit church architecture. On the side walls of the nave topped by a barrel vault, there is a tabernacle. The sanctuary has a rectangular end, and is the same width as the nave.  
Besides traditional Jesuit iconography, specific features of Hungarian iconography from the period can also be seen relating to the Ottoman wars and the closely related theme of the *Regnum Marianum/Patrona Hungariae* (St. Stephen offering the country to the Virgin Mary). All the saints, kings and bishops lined up on the decorative programme were founders and supporters of the Catholic Hungarian Kingdom, and defenders against the infidels or non-believers (images of Turks and Protestants appear on the altars).  
The Tyrolean painter, Paul Troger, painted the main altarpiece (*Apotheosis of St. Ignatius*) and also the ceiling mural in the sanctuary (*Ascension of St. Ignatius*) in 1744; the ceiling of the nave (*Annunciation*) in 1747 and the murals of the vault pendentives of four Prophets and four Evangelists (dated with Troger's signature beneath *St. Luke the Evangelist*) in 1744. The *trompe-l'œil* architectural wall painting and the ceiling of the sanctuary are by Gaetano Fanti.    
The main façade, completed by Martin (Athanasius) Wittwer a Carmelite architect around 1726, is articulated by statues in niches (St. John of Nepomuk, St. John the Evangelist, St. Andrew, St. Francis Borgia, the Virgin Mary and St. Ignatius of Loyola), by windows and volutes, two towers and the main stone gate (1641).  
Between 1743 and 1744, János Götzelmayer from Győr created the main altarpiece adorned by two columns and sculptures representing St. Peter, St. Joseph, St. John of Nepomuk and St. Paul (made by Josef Rössler \[Ressler\]) and the coat of arms of the patron, Prebendary Ádám Acsády.   
Acsády's coat of arms also appears on the triumphal arch. János Burghar(d)t from Győrsziget made the organ (1755–1757) and Mihály János Crines from Győr made the altar cross (c. 1710). The embossed pulpit was donated by Bishop Márton Padányi Bíró and made by Lajos Gode, a disciple of G. R. Donner, in 1748–1749.  József Ullydeszki made the *ciborium* in the mid-1780s. The furniture is by local craftsmen. Both the monastery refectory and the former Jesuit apothecary are decorated with stuccoes.
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.short_description: The Jesuit Order settled in Győr in 1627 and played an important role in the Catholic spiritual renaissance (rooted in the Counter-Reformation movement) and the spread of Baroque art in Hungary. Building of the Jesuit Church dedicated to St. Ignatius of Loyola began in 1634/1635. The church was consecrated in 1641, but the interior decoration was not complete until the mid-18th century.
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.method_for_datation: Based on written sources, signed artworks and stylistic research.

01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.history:
The Episcopate of Győr, founded by King Stephen I, flourished until the Turkish occupation of Hungary diminished its prosperity. Győr, where the bishop resided, was only under Turkish rule for a short period, but the army of Suleiman the Magnificent ravaged the Episcopate on its way to and from Vienna (1529; 1532). Following liberation from Turkish rule, the city, an important link in the chain of Hungarian strongholds, was unable to return to normalcy as its infrastructure was in a state of decay. During this period, the bishop resided in Győr for short periods only.  
Apart from nurturing and supporting the spiritual life of Catholics, the renaissance of Catholicism in the 17th century also fostered the reconstruction of the city's infrastructure. The Jesuit order settled in Győr in 1627 establishing the church (dedicated to the founder, St. Ignatius of Loyola), monastery and school. The Jesuits played a central role in the infrastructural restoration of Győr, as well as the spiritual, cultural and scientific life of the city, until the order was dissolved in 1733.  
The financial difficulties that beset the Jesuits meant that the construction and interior decoration of the church was largely financed by patrons, among which, Archbishop György Szelepcsényi, Prebendary Ádám Acsády, Bishop of Győr, other members of the chapter and the families of children that attended the Jesuit school.  
Scholars tend to attribute the plans of the church to an Italian master, Baccio del Bianco. The construction was supervised by the Italian Bartolomeo Torre (from 1634/1635 to 1641). After the church was consecrated in 1641, local benefactors helped to install the first altars in 1642. The second era of construction extended into the 18th century: the main altar, ceiling murals of the bay, the sanctuary, general interior decoration and decoration of the towers of the main façade. The nave took on its current form after reconstruction of the church in 1738.  
After the Jesuit order was dissolved in 1733, the Benedictines obtained the building complex in 1802. Today the church is a Roman Catholic parish church. In place of the former Jesuit school stands a Benedictine high school built in 1888. The former Jesuit pharmacy houses an Apothecary Museum.

02bcbece-df7a-5e97-b5f8-fcadef79ac38.name:
Rein Abbey  
Rein Abbey Church and Monastery
02bcbece-df7a-5e97-b5f8-fcadef79ac38.alternate_name: Cistercians' Abbey and Church in Rein
02bcbece-df7a-5e97-b5f8-fcadef79ac38.description:
What all buildings – monastery and church – have in common is the fact that they contain Romanesque and Gothic remains. Most of the architecture around the cloister in the South, the agricultural buildings in the West, the wings in the East and in the North are originally old building stock. Some are visible, others are not because most of them got a baroque coat overlaid. The church was the latest – in the 1730s – to be baroquized. The building floor plan of the monastery complex is irregular, another relict of the medieval epoch.  
Approaching the abbey from the East, from where the course of the street leads directly to it, one would consider this aisle as the main façade. Noticing the irregularly arranged components of the building, four of them protruding, one understands that this side has many medieval parts. The main entrance is round the corner, on the abbey´s North side and utterly evokes the impression of a baroque monastery. The slightly protruding part of the building with entrance amid three floors and seven axes has been welcoming arriving guests for three centuries in the typically baroque way.
02bcbece-df7a-5e97-b5f8-fcadef79ac38.short_description: From the abbey´s foundation in the year 1129 until the erection of the new convent building, the renovations and baroquization from the beginning of the 17th century until the late 1770s, there was almost no change in the abbey´s architecture. Only after the Turkish invasion the damages to the buildings were being repaired and the fortifications expanded. From the beginning of the 17th century, the Cistercians started with structural changes of the Medieval buildings. The members of the convent got new apartments, and the Eastern part of the monastery complex was renovated. The new church was built on the site of the Medieval one, reusing the walls, the presbytery and the entrance to the former convent building. After removing the Romanesque pillars the new Baroque room – with side chapels and galleries above - became spacious and light.

02bcbece-df7a-5e97-b5f8-fcadef79ac38.history: After a split had occurred among the Benedictines – because of different interpretation of the order´s rules – three friars founded the new Cistercian order in Cîteaux. When the charismatic, (later saint) Bernhard joined them with friends and relatives, the religious community underwent a major upswing. Soon there were Cistercian abbeys all over Europe. Two were in Germany, one was Ebrach in Upper Franconia from where monks set off to Rein on Margrave Leopold´s the Strong order. On 25th March 1129 they arrived there and founded a new monastery on the very place. The sovereign donated the land. Gerlach, one of the friars, was elected the first abbot. The monks from Ebrach erected a first oratory and a monastery building from wood. A few years later they built a church (this time made of stone), a new monastery building and a protective wall enclosing the complex. From the Baroque epoch on, most of the buildings were renewed or stylistically adapted. They stayed almost untouched until our present day.
02bcbece-df7a-5e97-b5f8-fcadef79ac38.patrons: Monks from the Cistercian Abbey Ebrach in Bavaria settled in Rein (Styria) and founded a new monastery. The Traungauer margrave Leopold I donated the land.

Monastery complex, new convent building: Bartolomeo di Bosio (n.d.); baroquization North wing and Eastern part of the monastery´s building complex: probably Johann Georg Stengg (1689–1753) Homage Hall and library fresco paintings: Joseph Amonte (1703–53)

03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.name: Former endowment for ladies of rank (today Sacred Heart Convent) with collegiate church (today Sacred Heart Church)
03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.description: The irregular ground plan of the convent is shaped by the foundations, i.e. the architectural elements incorporated from the former princely castle of Sparberegg. At the centre is a two-storey Renaissance cloister on a virtually quadratic ground plan, with the convent church adjoining to the west, a longitudinal building, and to the east the irregular architectural elements of the endowment building adopted from the castle. The three-storey complex forms the perimeter of the convent square, also bordered by the church façade facing southeast.
03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.short_description: The endowment for ladies of rank, an important four-winged complex of the late Renaissance built on the foundations of a medieval castle, was founded by Archduke Ferdinand II (1529–95). The collegiate church, a hall building with retracted choir, originates from this first period (1567–70), however its original stuccowork was later replaced by rich Early Baroque forms.
03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.type: Secular architecture (endowment, convent building) and ecclesiastical architecture (former collegiate church)
03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.bibliography:
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 30.  
Grass, N., “Das Damenstift und seine Kunstdenkmäler”, in: *Haller Buch. Festschrift zur 650-Jahrfeier der Stadterhebung* (Schlern-Schriften 106), Innsbruck 1953, pp. 337–94.
03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.history: For the endowment for ladies of rank Archduchess Magdalena, a sister of Archduke Ferdinand II, erected the endowment building and church of Hall on the site of a princely castle and mint between 1567 and 1569. The consecration took place in 1560. The collegiate church, built between 1567 and 1570 by Giovanni Lucchese, acquired new stuccowork, executed by Onofrius Weigl of the Munich school, between 1629 and 1636, which was subsequently renewed following the earthquake of 1670. The spire dates from 1681. The façade stucco was added in 1691/92. In 1783 followed the annulment and in 1912 the building was bequeathed to the Convent of the Sisters of the Sacred Heart.
03024cb7-5500-585a-a978-a5263e16b1f2.patrons: Archduchess Magdalena of Austria (1532–1590, founder and first Princess Abbess) / Noble Convent of Hall

Summerhouse, architecture: Simon Gremblich \[n.d.\]; frescos: Kaspar Waldmann (1657–1720)

03b3fa81-12f0-534d-917e-8491471550e8.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Peter and Paul, former Augustinian Canons convent church
03b3fa81-12f0-534d-917e-8491471550e8.description:
The nave of the abbey church displays a conventional but preciously proportioned wall-pillar architecture. It is equipped with windows on the right-hand side only which fosters a bilaterally well-lit choir. The choir itself is framed by a pilaster arcade functioning as a dignified motive. Due to these instalments, the eye is captivated immediately. The high altar formally follows the model of its equivalent in the Theatine Court Church in Munich. The overlaid stucco shell ornament of the apse calotte, on the other hand, derives from the Freising Cathedral. Both presumably to demonstrate solidarity with the secular and clerical supremacy. The Rococo tabernacle from Ignaz Günther and the High Baroque main altar with its statues of the Church Fathers, St. Augustine and St. Ambrose, form a highly-contrasted union.  
The vaults are moderately decorated with coloured ornaments and arabesques in the Regency Style. In the nave, the theme of the ceiling frescoes is the religious order. Whereas in the choir, they depict the martyrdom of the patrons, St. Peter and St. Paul, and iconographically refer to the high altarpiece, which thematises “The Delivery of the Keys to St. Peter” (Johann Untersteiner, 1693). This propagates the leadership claim of the Catholic Confession.
03b3fa81-12f0-534d-917e-8491471550e8.short_description: The Augustinian Canons Convent Church is famous for its high-quality decorative elements that were added in the 18th century: delicate stucco and colourful ceiling frescoes carried out by Munich court artist Johann Baptist Zimmermann. Furthermore, it contains numerous sculptural works created by Ignaz Günther, one of the best German sculptors of the Rococo era. His major works include two fantastic processional carvings specifically created for Weyarn.
03b3fa81-12f0-534d-917e-8491471550e8.dates:
1687–93: construction of the abbey church including the high altar  
1729: stuccowork and ceiling frescoes of the church  
1763–65: reworking of the sculptures of the altars
03b3fa81-12f0-534d-917e-8491471550e8.method_for_datation: Archival documents and chronicle notes; inscriptions in the ceiling fresco.

03b3fa81-12f0-534d-917e-8491471550e8.history: The medieval monastery was founded in 1133 in the castle of a local count’s family. The castle chapel of St. James is still intact. Between 1687 and 1693, Lorenzo Sciasca, from Graubünden, built the construction in its present state on top of the remains of the former abbey church which had been destroyed by a fire. In preparation for the monastery’s 800th anniversary, Munich court artist and stuccoer, Johann Baptist Zimmermann, who was born in Wessobrunn, started implementing the stuccowork and ceiling frescoes in 1729. Appointing sculptor Ignaz Günther in 1763 indicates the continuing close affiliations with the Bavarian capital, Munich.

0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.name: Teleki Palace
0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.alternate_name: Roth Palace; Teleki-Degenfeld Palace; Palace-Hotel Szirák
0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.description:
The designer of the palace is unknown (some scholars attribute it to Giovanni Battista Carlone who worked in Eger, others to an unknown Italian architect). The two-storey palace was probably built using the remains of an older fortress-like building from 1690. The square-shaped main building is extended by two projecting side-wings on the garden side. On the two corners of the main façade facing the *cour d'honneur*, small corner-towers are mounted above semi-circular, closed balconies. The main façade is also articulated with a tympanum that crowns the central risalit. The tympanum is decorated with urns on the top and two corners, with an indented frieze below; small, round windows are visible in the mid-section. The lower part of the main façade was revealed during restoration, and today its arcades indicate the location of the top-floor of the two-storey cellar. The sail-vaulted cellar is accessible via a staircase inside; its upper floor serves as a supporting wall on the garden façade.  On top of the arcades, a terrace with wrought-iron railings (1860s) runs in front of the main façade, which can be approached from the ground floor by walking up a two-flight stairwell with an intermediate landing. Above the opulently decorated entrance, opening on the first floor of the central risalit, the *chronosticonos* (Latin inscription) bears witness to the fact that the palace was reconstructed by Tamás Királyfalvi Roth and his wife, Borbála Wattay, in 1748. On the ground floor there is a less opulent entrance.  
The lower part of the main façade is articulated with arcades. The windows are square-shaped, with horizontal drip mouldings on the first floor, and triangular-arched ones on the second. In the central risalit all the windows bear triangular-arched drip-mouldings that embrace festoon decorations. The palace is crowned with high gables and an attic; the side facades are less articulated.  
The rooms of the main building open up from a central hallway, which follows the layout of the relatively narrow entrance hall. The stairwell was formed throughout several reconstructions. A carved stone fireplace niche can be seen on the first floor. Except for the back rooms of the central risalit and the stairwell, all the rooms in the palace are vaulted and many of them are stuccoed.  
The Ceremonial (central) Banqueting Hall is located on the first floor of the central risalit. Painted at the request of József Teleki, sections of the side walls are framed with richly decorated, cannelured Composite columns decorated with urns and six scenes from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*. The latter are the works of an unknown local master, based on the engravings of the German engraver and miniature painter, Johann Wilhelm Baur (Joan Guiliam Bouwer or Bauer; 1600–1640), a follower of Stefano della Bella. Baur painted 151 illustrations for *Metamorphoses* in the 17th and 18th centuries, which were published several times (according to S. Somorjay the illustrations of the 1709 Augsburg edition were direct precedents of those at Szirák).
0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.short_description: The Ceremonial (Central) Banqueting Hall of Teleki Palace is decorated with Baroque wall paintings from the second half of the 18th century. The wall sections, richly articulated with visual architectural features, are decorated with six *grisaille* paintings depicting scenes from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.
0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, stylistic research and research into the local site.
0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.bibliography:
Kelényi, Gy., “Kastélyok, kúriák, villák” (“Castles, Manors, Villas”), *Architectural Traditions* (Épitészeti hagyományok), Budapest, 1974, p. 127.  
Somorjay, S., “A sziráki Roth-Teleki kastély és falképei” (“The Roth-Teleki Palace in Szirák and its Frescoes”*)*, *Teleki József (1738–1796) és kora* *(József Teleki and his Time (1738–1796)*. Discussiones Nogradiensis, 3, (Edited by M. Praznovszky, A. Rozsnyói), Salgótarján, 1987, pp. 157–161.
0478524a-1eaf-5e14-9e75-cd78015e45a8.history:
From the Middle Ages, Teleki Palace in Szirák exchanged owners many times, until, after the Turkish occupation, it was obtained by János Roth in 1692.  János Roth invited 27 Slovakian families from the *Felvidék* (“Upper Hungary”) to Szirák. The palace was constructed at the request of Tamás Királyfalvi Roth and his wife Borbála Wattay, as detailed in the Latin inscription above the palace entrance. Not long after it was completed, the palace burned down and was rebuilt by Tamás Roth. Today's palace was completed by 1748. When Tamás Roth's daughter, Johanna, married Count József Teleki, a member of one of the most significant Protestant aristocratic families in Hungary in 1762, the palace became the property of the Teleki family.  
Teleki's mother was the daughter of Pál Ráday, owner of Ráday Palace in Pécel. Teleki's uncle, Count Sámuel Teleki, was the Chancellor of Transylvania who founded a library in Marosvásárhely (Târgu Mureş). At the time, count József Teleki was one of Hungary's most erudite aristocrats.  
Teleki was a Protestant author, art collector, crown guard, *comes*, and from 1772, chief curator of the Protestant Lyceum in Marosvásárhely as well. Teleki and his Evangelist wife were great patrons of the arts and science:  their homes in Szirák and Pest were favoured meeting points of the Hungarian Protestant community. Teleki studied at the universities of Leyden and Basel, travelled throughout Europe, and was acquainted with notions of the Enlightenment. He also knew Voltaire and Rousseau personally.  
Teleki and his wife reconstructed the palace twice: once immediately after their marriage and then in the middle of the 1780s when, presumably, the paintings for the Ceremonial Banqueting Hall were commissioned.  
Teleki's grandson, József Teleki (1790–1855), and József's stepbrother, László Teleki (1811–1861), were also born in the palace. József became the first president of what is today the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and founded a library to which he donated generously. László became a notable politician during the Hungarian Reform era, and was appointed Hungarian Ambassador to Paris during the Hungarian Revolution of 1848–1849. After his suicide, he was buried in the Teleki crypt in Szirák, which was built in 1784.  
The palace was reconstructed and modernised in the 19th century; towards the end of the century it was acquired by the Dégenfeld family. In 1945 it was nationalised and became the property of Szirák State Farm. The palace, which was by now in a dilapidated state, was restored by the Hungarian Hydrocarbon Research & Development Institute in 1985. Today the palace is a four-star spa hotel of the Forever Resorts hotel franchise.

0485305f-5812-53a0-a3a3-161922e70b35.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Peter and St. Paul
0485305f-5812-53a0-a3a3-161922e70b35.description: The south-facing building is composed of a sequence of three centralised spatial units, commencing with an ante-bay with choir loft. The sequence, with shallow dome vaulting, becomes progressively narrower as it extends to the choir, whereby rounded projecting pilasters establish a smooth transition between the sections. Thus the overall view is one of a magnificent graduated prospect, within which it is the sequence of five altars that take pride of place. The frescos, framed by delicate rocaille stucco, are a late work of the Director of the Augsburg Academy, Matthäus Günther, executed in especially clear, luminous colours.
0485305f-5812-53a0-a3a3-161922e70b35.short_description: Götzens is the high point of Tyrol’s late Rococo-period parish churches. The building and its interior work were largely executed according to the design of the master builder Franz Singer and were completed in a short space of time, “all of a piece” so to speak. The coulisse-like “theatre prospect” combines architecture, stucco, altars, and the excellent frescos of Matthäus Günther into a harmonious whole.
0485305f-5812-53a0-a3a3-161922e70b35.method_for_datation: Through archives and the inscription on the spire “FS 1775 PM” (meaning: Franz Singer and Peter Mayr, the carpenter)

0485305f-5812-53a0-a3a3-161922e70b35.history: In the 18th century, efforts were made to establish independence from the Parish of Axams, and in 1736, a parish priest was appointed. In 1772 a new parish church was erected in the centre of the town according to plans from the “countryman, master mason and stucco mason” Franz Singer. The consecration, conducted by the Prince-Bishop of Brixen, Joseph Graf Spaur, took place on 24 June 24 1780. In 1786 Götzens became an independent parish.

05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.name: Reliquary of St. Stephen the King
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.description:
The reliquary bust of St. Stephen the King, on a base, shows the saint in royal dress. Characteristics of the Baroque style come to the fore in the saint’s head shown in the round and almost imperceptibly turned sideways, with striking features and a soft wavy beard and moustache.  
The bust was probably made by a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is the work of a contemporary Central European goldsmith.  
The Latin inscription in a cartouche nailed to the front of the base records that Cardinal Francesco Barberini, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, had this bust made in 1635 out of piety for St. Stephen. He commissioned the bust to hold the saint’s skull, endowing the relic with the reverence it deserved. Today it is still in Zagreb Cathedral dedicated to St. Stephen the King.  
St. Stephen, King of Hungary, converted the Hungarians to Christianity and in the early 11th century founded an archbishopric in his hometown Esztergom where he died. He was canonised in 1087 and his cult spread from Hungary to Croatia where it was especially widespread after the Middle Ages. At the time, Hungary and Croatia were in a union and known as the lands of the Crown of St. Stephen after the crown he wore.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.short_description: The reliquary of St. Stephen in the form of a bust shows him dressed as a king with a crown on his head. The bust was probably the work of a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is attributed to a goldsmith from the Central European circle. The Latin inscription in a cartouche on the front of the base verifies that the reliquary was commissioned by Cardinal Barberini in 1635, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, a member of a powerful and wealthy Roman family that died out in the male line in 1736.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.method_for_datation:
The 1915 Inventory of Zagreb Cathedral mentions the reliquary.  
A Latin inscription with the year of origin is on a cartouche on the front of the base.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.obtention: Cardinal Francesco Barberini gifted the reliquary to Zagreb Cathedral.

056fab85-863d-5746-9108-31105c02bedc.name: *The Judgement of Solomon*
056fab85-863d-5746-9108-31105c02bedc.description:
The Biblical episode tells the story of two prostitutes who give birth in the same house, but one of the newborns dies. Both claim to be the mother of the surviving baby and call on King Solomon to adjudicate. When he decides to split the newborn child in two with his sword, in tears the real mother renounces the child in order to save it, an astute strategy used by the wise king to identify her. This shows the capacity the Lord gave Solomon to distinguish Good from Evil, not as a gift, but as a readiness to listen through which the wisdom of God can be found. It is also a celebration of the wisdom of those who reign in the name of God.  
Over the centuries in the absence of any documents to verify the actual artist, the work has been variously attributed. One of the most notable theories is that an unknown follower of Caravaggio known as the Master of the Judgement of Solomon, on account of his strong personality (Longhi, 1943) painted it.  
The strong affinities to a non-Italian follower of Caravaggio have led some to attribute the painting to the Roman period of the young Jusepe de Ribera, when he had not fully assimilated the naturalism of his master although this is present in his later paintings (Papi, 2005).  
The essence of the painting is its compositional structure. The source of light outside the painting makes the scene a truly theatrical event. The rhythm is marked by the gestures of the figures in the scene arranged in a rigidly orthogonal progression.  
The king sits on a chair that rests on a step decorated with an ancient bas­‑relief, in front of a column acting as a perspective wing.  
The exasperation of the drama is not only evoked by the light and style, but by the atmosphere, a real stage on which the main player, Solomon, stands; the dark tones adding to the dramatic effect. These elements are consistent, notwithstanding the peculiarities of each artist, in what is known as the baroque language.
056fab85-863d-5746-9108-31105c02bedc.short_description: The biblical subject matter of this work is expressed through the dramatic use of gesture and light. Believed to be by an unknown follower of Caravaggio called the Master of the Judgement of Solomon, it is in a style similar to van Baburen and Neapolitan artists. Some scholars have identified the painter as the young Jusepe de Ribera.

05e251d9-e064-5378-ba65-e2eb92541ba9.name: Villa Aldobrandini, Water Theatre
05e251d9-e064-5378-ba65-e2eb92541ba9.description:
The downward-facing, luminous, continuous façade of the villa is characterised by a series of terraces, along a central axis, with symmetrical ramps and pathways that interrupt the steep hillside. Although it was only built later by Maderno and Fontana, the majestic *nymphaeum* located to the rear was part of Della Porta's initial design, and as such Aldobrandini had acquired all of the available water in the area and channelled it through an aqueduct.  
The long front of the *nimphaeum* is divided up architecturally by columns, pilaster strips, herms, and tympana, niches of varying depth, capitals, vases and framed busts. At the centre is a flight of steps over which water cascades, channelling the water into the large central- and side-niches, and flanked by two pillars known as the Columns of Hercules. In the side-niches, set against the backdrop of a cave partially painted with landscapes and decorated with mosaics, stand statues of a Cyclops and a Centaur with musical instruments (pan-pipes and bugle respectively), which once contained water-activated mechanisms that would have generated sound but which are now, unfortunately, no longer in operation. In the central niche, Atlas, originally standing beside Hercules (now lost), supports the celestial globe above the head of Tantalus (also interpreted as Enceladus), reconstructed and buried by rocks. The entire frontage is surmounted by a long inscribed commemorative dedication above which is a columned balustrade bearing statues and vases of flowers. The side wings lead on the left to the Parnassus or Apollo Room and the chapel decorated with gilded stuccowork and dedicated to St. Sebastian, the family's patron saint, and on the right-hand side to the "Ogliara", used as an oil store in recent times. The Parnassus Room originally had frescoed walls interspersed with mosaics and gilded stuccowork, with the *Stories of Apollo* by Domenico Zampieri, also known as Domenichino (1581–1641), now in the National Gallery, London. At the far end of the room is a grotto structure representing Parnassus, with the statues of *Apollo* accompanied by the *Muses* carrying instruments, which were initially activated by the air generated by a hydraulic system constructed according to the designs of the master organist Giovanni Guglielmi. The ceiling is painted as if the room were a pergola.
05e251d9-e064-5378-ba65-e2eb92541ba9.short_description: The water theatre, also known as the *nymphaeum*, was designed in the classical Roman tradition and has an extremely wide front—as wide as the building—that curves in a large exedra between two straight wings. Located behind the villa against the slope of the hill, almost acting as an embankment, it forms the boundary between the constructed space and nature, and was conceived, with its playful combination of water and sounds, as a scenic crown for the gardens as a whole.
05e251d9-e064-5378-ba65-e2eb92541ba9.type: Secular architecture, villa with water theatre (*nymphaeum*)

05e251d9-e064-5378-ba65-e2eb92541ba9.history: This, the most original and sumptuous of the villa Tuscolana, was built to the design of Giacomo Della Porta (Porlezza, Como 1532–Rome 1629) for Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, nephew of Clement VIII (1592–1606), from 1598, on the site of a demolished country retreat known as Belvedere that belonged to Antonio Contugi, doctor to Pius IV Medici.

06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.name: *The Holy Family and Relatives*
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.description:
This small, sketch-like picture represents the Holy Family with the Virgin Mary and child Jesus in the centre. St. Elizabeth presents young St. John the Baptist, who is handing Jesus an apple, symbol of rule over the world. St. Anne kneels before Jesus. Male family members occupy the background: St. Joseph with a palm branch absorbed in a book, and Zachariah and Joachim, Anne’s husband and Mary’s father.  
The scene is not derived from the Bible but is a story from the Pseudo-Bonaventura. about the Holy Family. The story relates that on their return from Egypt the Holy Family visited a relative, Elizabeth, whose small son, John, we are told, showed great respect for Jesus. Sadler approaches the story in genre fashion, exploiting the individual gestures of all the characters and the evening atmosphere. The painter fully exploits the effects of light and colour, using chiaroscuro to accentuate the family group that spans three generations: Anne, Mary and Jesus. Green, blue, yellow and red tones merge into an almost monochromatic background. The mode of painting on a non-absorbent copper base demonstrates Sadler’s brushwork, along with his trademark facial expressions for the figures.  
The devotional subject, a symbolic triangular composition, and the emotional effects of the scene indicate that the piece may have been designed for private worship. It is worthy of note that in the final phase of his studies at the Academia di St. Luca in Rome, Sadler took part in a painting competition which he won with a picture of the Holy Family. The painting corresponds with the Academia’s style, applying approaches associated with Pietro da Cortona, Corrado Giaquinto and Carlo Marrati.  
Sadler’s work, influenced by his studies in Rome, was unique in Moravia. His oeuvre, comprising ceiling and easel paintings, was chiefly associated with central and north Moravia. He was a son of the Olomouc sculptor Filip Sattler and son-in-law of the painter Jan Kryštof Handke.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.short_description: The devotional subject, symbolic triangular composition, and emotional effects of the scene indicate that the piece might have been designed for private worship. The painting is typical of Sadler, a leading Olomouc artist influenced by studying at the Rome Academy.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.method_for_datation: The picture was previously considered the work of Paul Troger. However, the figure types and brushwork confirm that Josef Ignaz Sadler, a prominent Olomouc artist, is author of the work as determined by Vlasta Kratinová.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.obtention: The picture comes from the Municipal (Gomperz) Gallery, which passed into the administration of the Provincial Museum in 1922. The Provincial Museum Picture Gallery became part of the Moravian Gallery, Brno in 1961.

06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.name: Royal Brigantine
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.description:
Responsible for the construction and design, Torquato José Clavina was the foreman ship's carpenter at the Naval Arsenal, much admired for his skill and competence. The brigantine is a magnificent work in gilded wood, crafted by the artist Manuel Vieira, while on the broadside is a panel of zoomorphic elements over darkened gold. In the Queen Maria I style, the barge is painstakingly decorated with pinnacles, friezes, caryatides, flower-like ornaments and tile panels depicting vases of flowers in frames. On the posterior panel of the quarterdeck cabin, there is a painting of Pedro Alexandrino de Carvalho, who was responsible for painting the sovereign's private cabin. The quarterdeck cabin stands out from all the others for its richness and beauty, notably for the framed Venetian mirrors. The lower poop panel has complex and beautiful ornamentation: Amphitrite and Neptune are represented in two bas-reliefs surrounded by gilded-wood floral borders.  
On board were 78 paddlers with 40 oars, which made the barge glide through the water with the help of the boss and the bow oarsman. Throughout its history, the barge transported several monarchs and heads of state.  
With the first French invasion of November of 1807, the barge was assigned to take Queen Maria I and the rest of the royal family to the *Príncipe Real*, the ship on which they would escape to Brazil. Likewise, it was from this galley that King João VI disembarked in Lisbon following this turbulent period.  
Later, on his first State visit in 1903, King Edward VII of England chose his oldest ally: Portugal. The Royal Brigantine headed for the British ship HMS *Victoria and Albert* to receive the monarch. This visit was followed by series of other State visits, amongst which were the visits of Kaiser William II of Germany, Émille Loubet, President of the Republic of France, and King Albert I of Belgium. The brigantine was always present.  
During the Republic, the brigantine was neglected and did not glide over the river for 40 years. In 1957, on the occasion of the official visit of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the barge crossed the waters of the Tagus for the last time.  
In 1963 it became part of the collection of the Museu de Marinha (Naval Museum) where it underwent restoration. The quality of the restoration saw the museum receive several honourable distinctions including that given by the World Ship Trust.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.short_description:
In 1780 Queen Maria I ordered the construction of a grand royal barge: the Royal Brigantine of Queen Maria I. Its construction was destined to celebrate the betrothal of Prince João (future King João VI) to the Spanish Princess Carlota Joaquina, in 1784.  
Symbol of power and a jewel of naval archeology, the brigantine represents more than 200 years of historical pageantry.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.method_for_datation: Technical and historical royal documentation in the Portuguese Naval Archives.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.obtention: In 1963 the Royal Brigantine and other royal barges were taken to the Naval Museum by order of the Naval Ministry of the time.

070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.name: *The Assumption of the Virgin*
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.description: This altarpiece was made for the chapel of the Bonasoni family in the church of San Francesco in Bologna. In 1798, following the Napoleonic suppression of the Franciscan convent, the painting became the property of the Italian State. The date “1592” is inscribed in the lower middle of the sarcophagus. Therefore, it is believed the picture was created in the early stage of Annibale Carracci's career. At that stage the painter was working in Bologna and was strongly influenced by Venetian models, especially Tintoretto. The figures of the Apostles are inspired by Raphael's *Transfiguration*, which is now in the Pinacoteca Vaticana. Great sixteenth-century models are combined with a detailed realism, thus making miraculous events credible because of their tangible appearance. There is an emphasis on the wonder of the Apostles, the naturalism of their bodies, including the Virgin and the absence of complex symbolic structures typical of sixteenth-century art. This becomes an efficacious religious teaching which involves people of every social and cultural status. The solid mass of the clouds under the Virgin and the angels as well as the landscape underneath are significant stylistic elements and anticipate the Baroque style to come.
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.short_description: This painting, dated 1592, was made for the chapel of the Bonasoni family in the church of San Francesco in Bologna. It became part of the Pinacoteca collections after the Napoleonic suppressions (1798). It is one of the masterpieces of Annibale's youth, influenced by Tintoretto and Raphael as well as real life experiences.
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.method_for_datation: The date is inscribed on the sarcophagus. The painting is mentioned in the Bonasoni chapel in San Frencesco by all the local guide books starting from Francesco Cavazzoni's manuscript *Pitture et Sculture* (1603).
070b42af-0546-59a3-b779-ec6bcb7dc5ca.obtention: Confiscated in 1798 after the Napoleonic suppressions.

07ac9ce1-f5e9-5c45-8c0c-b25875e68e94.name: *Six Episodes from the Life of Luigi Ferdinando Marsili*
07ac9ce1-f5e9-5c45-8c0c-b25875e68e94.description:
The peace of Carlowitz between the Habsburg Empire, Venice, Poland and Russia on one side and Turkey on the other was negotiated in 1698–99. Bolognese Count Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, a representative of Emperor Leopold I of Austria, was among the diplomats involved. After his return to Bologna he founded the Istituto delle Scienze (Institute of Sciences) (1711). This series is composed of six paintings: five depicting military camps, travelling armies and trains and one representing the discussion about the borders of the Habsburg empire. The paintings describe the negotiations and the following operations in order to define the borders of Venice, the Empire and Turkey in Bosnia and Dalmatia. All paintings are described in the *Instrumentum Donationis*, housed in the Istituto delle Scienze (first half XVIII century). Each painting originally bore a wooden caption explaining the scene depicted in it, today only one survives. This sort of documentary painting was new for Bolognese culture, and has been connected with the astronomical scenes commissioned from Donato Creti in 1711 by Marsili himself (now in the Pinacoteca Vaticana).  
In scene n. 291, painted with a rich brushstroke showing the influence of Giuseppe Maria Crespi, is depicted an episode of the negotiations for the peace: under a camp tent three diplomats sit next to their respective generals. In the foreground we are able to identify, thanks to the sealed letters they are holding in their hands, from the left the representative of Austria (Leopold Slink von Wischkirken or maybe Marsili himself, even if he was not the head of the diplomatic expedition), the representatives of Turkey (Reys Mohamed Effendi) and Venice (Carlo Ruzzini). We cannot say which exact moment of the negotiations is depicted here because the caption has been lost. The persons depicted are each identified with a letter which was further explained in a caption beneath the painting. However, the caption is now lost. It is a sort of birds-eye view of the military camp where the meeting took place, with a tent housing the diplomats and their respective armies. The paintings, dating to Marsili's most significant period of cultural and scientific zeal, employ a precise topographical description. They are a thorough representation of people, rather than focused on the epic and rhetorical meaning of the episodes.

In n. 291 is depicted a scene of the peace negotiations: under a camp tent three diplomats sit next to their respective generals.

0840a72d-a66d-5787-a529-19af7e729a18.name: Benedictine Abbey and Parish Church of St. Joseph
0840a72d-a66d-5787-a529-19af7e729a18.description: The monastery church is one of the earliest buildings in the Tyrol exhibiting the style of the early Rococo. The architecture is derived from that of St. Jacob’s in Innsbruck. The domed choir crossing, as the centre of the building, is adjoined by three apses and the tri-axial nave with shallow pilasters and lunette windows. A rudimentary transept has been inserted between the choir and the nave. The overall spatial impression is strongly influenced by the large-format ceiling pictures and the filigree rocaille stucco.
0840a72d-a66d-5787-a529-19af7e729a18.short_description: Together with Stams and Wilten, St. Georgenberg is one of Tyrol’s three large monasteries. Construction of the new church for the monastery, which was destroyed by fire in 1705, was conducted under Abbot Lambert Höllerer from Wessobrunn who attracted important southern German artists responsible for the exquisite Rococo interior work. The clearly structured architecture, with its distant echoes of Innsbruck Cathedral, is the work of Jakob Singer, a member of the most famous family of Tyrolian master builders of the mid-18th century.
0840a72d-a66d-5787-a529-19af7e729a18.dates: 1741–1743: first building phase; 1749/50: second building phase following collapse of the vault; 1778–1781: construction of the tower; 1743- c. 1775: interior
0840a72d-a66d-5787-a529-19af7e729a18.bibliography:
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 45f.  
*250 Jahre Stiftskirche Benediktinerabtei St. Georgenberg-Fiecht/Tirol*, Passau 2000.  
Hösch, K., *Stiftskirche St. Josef, Benediktinerabtei St. Georgenberg-Fiecht/Tirol*, Passau 2001 (Peda-Kunstführer 526).
0840a72d-a66d-5787-a529-19af7e729a18.history: The origins of the monastery can be traced back to Blessed Rathold in the 10th century. St. Georgenberg was elevated to the status of a Benedictine Abbey in 1138. Following a fire in 1705 the monastery was transferred from Georgenberg, which remained a site of pilgrimage, to Inntal. The simple, four-winged monastery complex was followed by the construction of the abbey church beginning in 1741 and which was consecrated in 1750. The stuccowork was carried out between 1743 and 1751; the frescos were painted by Matthäus Günther between 1744 and 1755. Work on the interior continued until 1775, the church tower was completed in 1781. Comprehensive restoration work carried out in stages since 1948 has restored the original spatial impression which was significantly altered in the 19th century.

0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.name: *St. Francis Xavier Preaching in Goa*
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.description:
The set of 20 paintings portraying the life of St. Francis Xavier (1506–1552) form the back-piece to a large chest-of-drawers in the sacristy of the 16th-century Church of St. Roque, and are the work of the Portuguese proto-Baroque painter André Reinoso and collaborators. Installed in 1619, three years before the official canonisation of St. Francis Xavier on the 12th March 1622, the set of paintings form part of a religious “propaganda” exercise to highlight the life and work of the great Jesuit missionary, which it was hoped, would speed up the process of his canonisation by the Catholic Church. The paintings were inspired by the first Portuguese biography of the saint written by Father João de Lucena (*Histórica da Vida do Padre Francisco Xavier, e do que fizerão na Índia os mais religiosos da Companhia de Jesus*) published in Lisbon in 1600.  
The scene featured here shows the saint ardently preaching in the cosmopolitan city of Goa shortly after his arrival there in 1542. The picture has particular interest from an ethnographic viewpoint in that it shows the variety of oriental customs as well as recording different social classes. In the picture a crowd of new converts: men, women and children, as well as Portuguese noblemen watching on horseback, surround the saint. The background scene features a landscape fashioned in the Italian style.
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.short_description: This oil on canvas painting, part of a set of 20, is attributed to the Portuguese proto-Baroque painter André Reinoso (c. 1590-1641). Commissioned by the Society of Jesus for the sacristy of the Jesuit Church of St. Roque, this and other paintings of the set form the back-piece to a large chest-of-drawers installed in 1619, three years before the canonisation of the great missionary of the Far-East, St. Francis Xavier.
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.holder: Lisbon's Holy House of mercy / Museum of São Roque
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.owner: Santa Casa da Misericórdia de Lisboa / Museum of São Roque
0843a6e8-14f1-5005-a1be-69139c9e1a4b.method_for_datation: This painting, as well as the other ones that make up the painted cycle dedicated to the life of St. Francis Xavier, was attributed to André Reinoso by the Art Historian, Prof. Vitor Serrão, after a thorough research on Reinoso’s life and his works, in the decade of 1990.

08c3d674-5ed7-54bf-8c13-bc9442f6ddaf.name: Spanish Steps
08c3d674-5ed7-54bf-8c13-bc9442f6ddaf.description: The stairway is dynamically structured, fragmented into a series of curvilinear segments, and paused by a large central square. The fluidity of the lines, totally devoid of angles, aim at recalling a waterfall: indeed, it almost simulates the fall of the water along the slopes of the Pincio, ideally ending in the Fontana della Barcaccia by Pietro Bernini, at the centre of the square. Intended as a pleasant place to stop and have a break, as De Sanctis himself stated, the stairway has low walls to allow one to sit on them, stone benches placed every twelve steps and landings large enough to induce a pause during the effort of the ascent. Through the curvilinear movement of the ramps, De Sanctis was also able to correct the visual irregularity of the site, characterized by pre-existing buildings placed on the sides of the stairway which were not aligned along parallel axes; by doing so, he managed to suggest the idea of a pre-existing visual axis between the facade of the church and the city below. In this complex architectural organism, two main sections can be distinguished: one at the top and characterized by a protruding circular volume flanked by two lateral stairs and an underlying ramp in axis with it, and a lower one (separated from the other by a large central widening) which repeats the same compositional scheme, but with a livelier articulation of the ramp that one encounters when going up from Piazza di Spagna.
08c3d674-5ed7-54bf-8c13-bc9442f6ddaf.short_description: The Spanish Steps were built to link piazza di Spagna with Via Felice, the first great street planned by Sixtus V (1585). Several projects were made between 1717 and 1720, also by Alessandro Specchi. “A protruding volume is flanked by convex stairs and a straight flight in front. The upper unit presents the theme in its basic form; the lower constitutes an articulate and lively variation” (C. Norberg-Schulz. Late Baroque and Rococo Architecture.).
08c3d674-5ed7-54bf-8c13-bc9442f6ddaf.bibliography:
Grundmann, S., “Spanish Steps”, in Grundmann S. (ed), *The Architecture of Rome,* Stuttgart/London: Edition Axel Menges: 2007: 259–260.  
Rolfi, S., “Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti”, *I principi della chiesa,* Milan: Edizioni Charta, 1998: 237–238.
08c3d674-5ed7-54bf-8c13-bc9442f6ddaf.history:
Until the beginning of the 18th century, the Santissima Trinità dei Monti, the church of the French nation located on the top of the Pincio hill, was connected through steep paths to the lively district below that had flourished around Piazza di Spagna. In the 1660s the French Crown had allocated 10,000 scudi, later raised to 20,000 at the beginning of the following century, for the construction of a stairway between the church and Piazza di Spagna. In 1660, at the time of Cardinal Mazarin, Gian Lorenzo Bernini proposed a project that introduced for the first time the idea of a stairway articulated in a series of curvilinear ramps interrupted by resting areas in place of a rectilinear and rectangular stairway (such as those of the Basilica of St. Mary of the Altar of Heaven known as Aracoeli or at the Capitoline Hill cordonata). However, the project was set aside by Pope Alexander VII, who did not like the idea of the French occupying such a large portion of land. It was only at the beginning of the 18th century, under Clement XI, that a competition was launched. The competitors were Alessandro Specchi (who held the title of Architect of the Roman People and was known for having designed the now the lost Port of Ripetta, which deployed a similar articulation in curvilinear ramps), Francesco De Sanctis (architect of the Minims of the Trinità dei Monti) and Alessandro Gaulli.  
On the death of Clement XI, the new Pope Innocent XIII and the friars of Trinità dei Monti chose De Sanctis’s project, which was carried out between 1723 and 1726 and was partly inspired, though with some variations, to the Berninian design. One of the main reasons why De Sanctis’s stairway was chosen was its being perfectly visible in all its parts (allowing therefore to be properly controlled) both from below and from above, thus guaranteeing respect for public order.
08c3d674-5ed7-54bf-8c13-bc9442f6ddaf.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.name: *Thronus Pietatis*
08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.description:
The crucified Christ is at the centre of the painting; the Holy Father hovers in the clouds holding up the cross, supported in the lower part by two *putti*. Above His head the Holy Ghost – a dove radiating light – is surrounded by cherubs.  
*Thronus Pietatis* is by the Bavarian painter, Johann Michael Rottmayr, who later moved to Austria and made his name working for the Austrian Monarchy. His first works in Vienna were frescoes in Lichtenstein Palace. He then worked in Melk Abbey and in the Viennese Church of St Charles, Borromeo.  
One of the best-known painters of late Austrian Baroque, his work is characterised by voluptuous figures, strong colours and Baroque gesture. His later works stand apart with calmer movement and paler colours.  
The painting was a commission for the chapel at Valpovo Castle owned by the Hilleprand-Prandau family, by origin from Tyrol. The Prandaus were one of the four most important foreign aristocratic families in Slavonia. The Habsburg Crown granted estates to foreign nobles in Slavonia after the retreat of the Ottoman Turks.
08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.short_description: The painting is by Johann Michael Rottmayr, one of the best- known Austrian painters of the late Baroque. The painting was a commission for the chapel at Valpovo Castle owned by the Hilleprand-Prandau family, by origin from Tyrol. The Prandaus were one of the four most important foreign aristocratic families in Slavonia. The Habsburg Crown granted estates to foreign nobles in Slavonia after the retreat of the Ottoman Turks.

08e1d8a5-b865-58e1-9955-912069643d70.name: Altar of the Holy Cross (Church of the Holy Cross)
08e1d8a5-b865-58e1-9955-912069643d70.description:
This is the final work of the sculptor, Francesco Robba, the most proficient marble sculptor of the Baroque period in northern Croatia. Robba trained in the workshop of the Venetian sculptor, Pietro Baratta, and in 1720 arrived in Ljubljana (Slovenia), where in 1727, he took over the workshop of his father-in-law, the Ljubljana altar builder Luka Mislej. Apart from the Slovene works, there are also known works by Robba in Klagenfurt, and several altars and statues made for clients from Croatia, primarily for the Jesuit Church of St Catherine and Zagreb Cathedral. His works represent High Baroque marble sculpture and altar making at their peak in Croatia.  
By reducing the architectural elements, the decorative parts benefit through sublimation into simple and yet powerful curved motifs. Robba achieves in the Altar of the Holy Cross a monumental altar, a composition both emphatic and dynamic. The diagonal axes of the sculptural groups *Moses with the Bronze Serpent* and *Abraham Sacrificing Isaac* on the side-ends of the altar, direct the viewer's attention to the central figure of the Crucified Christ, which, made prominent with a frame of yellowish marble, stands out against a background of drapery carved in black marble. With the repetition of oval motifs and segments of ovals in the ground plan and elevation of the altar (the framework of the central sculpture), and on its surfaces (the frame of the relief of the stipes and the ornaments on the sculptures' pedestals), a suggestive pulsating rhythm is achieved that corresponds to the marked dynamism of the altar sculpture. The Altar of the Holy Cross recognisably developed from the principles of the Italian High Baroque, with clearly marked features of the mature phase of Robba's individual style. There are clear compositional similarities between the figural groups and some Italian sculptures from the last quarter of the 17th century. For example, G. Le Court's, high altar in Sant'Andrea della Zirada of 1678 and A. Pozzo's Altar of St Ignatius in the Roman Church Il Gesù, as well as that seen 20 years later in the Dorfmeister approach to the altar in the Church of Maria Taferl in Vienna.
08e1d8a5-b865-58e1-9955-912069643d70.short_description: The Altar of the Holy Cross is the final and most mature achievement of the sculptor, Franceso Robba, who by his artistic achievements is a notable figure in European Baroque sculpture and altar making. The great suggestiveness and dynamism of his work is achieved by a successful synthesis of the sculptural, architectural and decorative elements of the altar, along with a well-considered application of various coloured marbles.
08e1d8a5-b865-58e1-9955-912069643d70.method_for_datation: Archival sources, data concerning the contract and consecration of the altar.

Horvat-Levaj, K., "Crkva sv. Križa" in *Križevci: Grad i okolica*, Zagreb, 1993, pp. 135–159.  
Klemenčič, M., *Francesco Robba in beneško baročno kiparstvo v Ljubljani*, Ljubljana, 1998.  
Klemenčič, M., "Francesco Robba" in *La scultura a Venezia da Sansovino a Canova*, Milan, 2000, pp. 776–747.

08e1d8a5-b865-58e1-9955-912069643d70.history: The altar, which was originally in the nave of Zagreb Cathedral, was moved to Križevci as the result of the Neo-Gothic renovation that took place after the great earthquake of 1880. At the beginning of 1748, Robba signed a contract with the Zagreb chapter to make the altar for the sum of 1600 florins, provided from the estate of Canon Georg Rees. However, the altar was only completed and consecrated in 1756.

09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.name: Colle Ameno Hamlet
09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.description: The hamlet was conceived to be a self-sufficient and rational structural space. It included the Ghisilieri Villa with its own courtyard separated from the hamlet where the patron spent most of his time. The workshops and houses for the craftsmen formed the heart of the hamlet and were intended to function as a small town. The hamlet had its own hospital (1738-1768) built for all the nearby peasants living in poor conditions without any social assistance. It was totally financed by Filippo Ghisilieri who supplied doctors, nurses and medicines. There was also a small church, consecrated in 1747. In addition, the china factory (1758-1768) was producing characteristic blue monochrome ceramics which are well known in the area. China manufacturing had great success in the eighteenth-century and many china factories developed in Bologna and its surroundings.
09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.short_description:
The so called Colle Ameno Hamlet was built after the will of the nobleman Filippo Ghisilieri and it is an interesting example of local aristocracy philanthropic spirit, a typical feature of the age of enlightenment  
This complex included many different buildings, besides the patron villa: an oratory, a hospital, and the village with workshops for craftsmen and china manufacturers. The name Colle Ameno, meaning “pleasant hill”, was chosen by the patron himself who was particularly fond of this residence and used to spend here most of his time.
09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.bibliography: Guidotti, P., *Colle Ameno: centro di cultura ed arte di sperimentazione scientifica e di attività artigiane di assistenza religiosa ed ospedaliera nel quadro dell'Illuminismo settecentesco bolognese*, Bologna, 1986.
09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.history:
Filippo Carlo Ghisilieri began building this hamlet from a small building with a chapel and a farmer-house on one of his family properties in the countryside a few kilometres from Bologna.  
The philanthropic purpose of the nobleman was to encourage commercial and artistic activities in his properties. At the same time the goal was to provide religious and sanitary assistance to people working there.  
Examples of small industrial organisations combining work and social assistance were quite common during the age of enlightenment, in part because of the presence of a still powerful land aristocracy. During the same time period, the Bourbons in Naples celebrated the creation of a silk factory next to a modern village in order to house the craftsmen.
09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.copyright: Copyright images: Comune di Bologna, Musei Civici d'Arte Antica – Provincia di Bologna.
keywords: Age of enlightenment; Commerce; Rural architecture; Villa
09dfb5c0-b836-54a3-89b4-d7c89cddca1c.author: Marta Forlai

0a87e99a-302d-505c-8b99-7925f335db12.name: Church of Our Lady in Szentgotthárd
0a87e99a-302d-505c-8b99-7925f335db12.description:
The sanctuary of the one-nave church closes in an arch. The church also houses a wide triumphal arch and a narrow entrance hall. The concave western façade, crowned by a tower with a clock and richly articulated with wall columns, mouldings and a tympanon, is decorated with statues of saints.  
Today's church is a simplified version of Pilgram's third design, which was altered due to financial difficulties. In his original plans, Pilgram also articulated the monastery with corner pavilions.  
The interior decoration of the church, especially the paintings, focus on the triumph of the Christian faith, and include paintings of Christian armies defeating the Turks at Szentgotthárd (i.e. the ceiling fresco in the nave by István Dorffmeister Senior and Junior from 1784) and the *Triumph of the Cross* (the work of Matthias Gusner, a Cistercian lay-brother from Heiligenkreuz). There are also illustrations of pious Christian life and “Happy Death” (*Buona mors*); the *Assumption of the Virgin Mary*; the *Resurrection of the Body* (on the vault above the sanctuary by István Dorffmaister) and the *Heavenly Altar of God's Lamb* (also by Dorffmeister).  
On the main altar is the *Assumption of the Virgin Mary* by Matthias Gusner, whose works are seen on the side altars also. (1) Either side of the Altar of St. Bernard of Clairvaux are angels bearing aloft the Instruments of the Passion (*arma Christi*). The oval painting in the middle is the *Pietà*, while St. Peter and Mary Magdalene are shown in high relief. (2) On the Altarpiece of St. Gotthard is the painting, the *Miracle of St. Gotthard*; either side are statues of St. Barbara and St. Catherine of Alexandria. The oval painting illustrates St. Sebastian and St. Roch, while the Saints Margit and Dorothy are in high relief. (3) The Altar of the Hungarian Saint King shows St. Stephen, St. Ladislaus, St. Imre (Emeric) and an angel holding a sword in defence of Hungary. Either side are statues of St. Agnes and St. Apollonia, and the oval painting depicts the Roman martyrs, St. John and St. Paul. St. Adalbert and St. Jadwiga are in high relief. (4) On the Altar of St. Joseph is the painting, the *Death of St. Joseph*. Angels stand on either side of the altar; the oval painting shows a Guardian Angel; St. Franca (abbottess) and St. Wendelin are in high relief.  
There are exquisite pieces of furniture: the engraved pulpit, choir, pews, and in the vestry, dressing cabinets. All the furniture was carved by Gáspár Schretzenmayer, a lay brother from Heiligenkreuz. The statues were carved by Joseph Schnitzer, a Cistercian master carver from Heiligenkreuz. The organ of the church was created by Ferdinand Schwartz in Graz in 1764. Today the Baroque organ case contains an organ from the 20th century.
0a87e99a-302d-505c-8b99-7925f335db12.short_description: The Cistercian Church and Monastery of Szentgotthárd are outstanding examples of 18th-century Hungarian religious architecture. Designed by Franz Anton Pilgram, construction began in 1740 and continued to 1769. The one-nave church with a frontal tower was consecrated in the honour of Our Lady. It is richly decorated with paintings, sculptures and carved furniture; the fresco was painted by Stefan Dorffmeister and his son, and the main altarpiece is the work of Matthias Gusner. The opulently carved and gilded furniture, the pews, pulpit and the organ in the church, are the work of the Cistercian monk Gáspár Schretzenmayer.
0a87e99a-302d-505c-8b99-7925f335db12.method_for_datation: Based on the general plan of Franz Anton Pilgram (1738–1740), layouts and designs, written sources and local research.

Szabó, Szombathely, 1981, pp. 365–540, 771.
0a87e99a-302d-505c-8b99-7925f335db12.history:
The Cistercian Monastery of Szentgotthárd was founded by King Béla III of the Árpád dynasty in 1183. French monks led by the abbot, arrived at the monastery from Trois Fontaines and commenced construction of the abbey in 1184. The church was consecrated to Our Lady. The abbey, which began to flourish soon after it was built, was donated by King Sigismund of Luxemburg to Palatine Miklós Széchy and his son. In the early 16th century, exercising their noble rights, the Széchy family relocated the monks from the monastery and converted the building into a family castle that served as a stronghold to protect them against the Turks. In 1556 the monks wanted to return, but Margit Széchy drove them away. Not long after this incident, the city commander, Wolfgang Tieffenbach a general of Emperor Rudolf, blew up the monastery.  
In 1675 Bishop György Széchenyi obtained the right of possession over the abbey from Emperor Leopold, and began construction of a new church between  
1676 and 1677, using the remains of the medieval church. The one-nave church with three altars was converted into a granary under King Joseph II in 1787. In 1988 it became a theatre and in 2007 it was transformed into a tourist centre.  
It was Emperor Charles VI who donated Szentgotthárd Abbey to the Cistercian Abbey of Heiligenkreuz in 1734. Robert Leeb, Abbot of Heiligenkreuz, decided to rebuild the church and entrusted Franz Anton Pilgram with drawing up plans for both the church and monastery. Pilgram's initial plans transformed the existing buildings but – probably at the request of Leeb – at first he altered these plans and then drew up another design for a completely new building. Construction of the monastery commenced in 1740 and by 1746 the monks were able to move into the half-complete building.  
The foundation stone of the church was laid in 1748, and in 1764, the new abbot, Fritz Alberik, blessed the almost complete building. However, it was not until 1779 that János Szily, first bishop of Szombathely, consecrated the building.  
The layout designed by Pilgram, follows South German traditions in its use of the so called lyre-shaped church layout. With sail vaults separated by cross-bracings that rest on pillars, the church has no side chapels; instead fairly shallow chapels have been inserted into the niches between the pillars. Due to these shallow chapels, the nave and the western façade are narrow and there is one tower in the middle of the western façade instead of two.  
During construction, the Abbey of Heiligenkreuz faced financial difficulties, and this is why Pilgram's plans were not fully implemented: his third set of designs foresaw the monastery with two additional wings that would have embraced the church from both sides. In the end, only the south wing was built. Of the north wing, only the foundation was completed, and this was another reason for the continued use of the old, so-called, granary-church.

0add5409-b394-5bfa-bd30-f8a38dd5179f.name: *The Martyrdom of St. Ursula*
0add5409-b394-5bfa-bd30-f8a38dd5179f.description: The altarpiece is hanging on the main altar of the church San Nicola e San Domenico, in Imola. It was originally painted for the left side chapel, patronised by the Vendini family. The painting survived many attempts of confiscation, including the Napoleonic suppression at the end of the eighteenth-century, thanks to the determination of the Vendini family. It is an example of Ludovico's full mature style, painted after his exposure to Venetian influence. This work testifies to the adoption of a new expressive language, a baroque rhetoric, which melds Venetian colour and mannerist composition. The chaotic bundle of victims and villains, theatrically exhibited, stand in contrast with the hieratic figure of the saint who is absorbed in prayer and clearly deriving from the *St. Cecilia* by Raphael. The colours are mostly dark, emphasised by a cloudy dawn; the background is the colour of blood, the same shade as Ursula's dress. This painting was a turning point for painting in Imola, not only in a positive way: patrons turned completely to Bologna and the local school of painting was blocked and made sterile by the impossible competition with the Carraccis Academy.
0add5409-b394-5bfa-bd30-f8a38dd5179f.short_description: The painting was commissioned by the Vandini family for the church where it hangs today. It is a great altarpiece which ties together Baroque language and Counter-reformation liturgy: Venetian colours combine with the rhetoric of gestures and feelings in a strongly emotional painting.

0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.name: *Holy Sepulchre*
0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.description:
The golden thread relief embroidery for the sarcophagus-shaped *Holy Sepulchre* covers eight panels and contains 16 oval medallions bordered by gold cartouches. Within the medallions is an iconographic programme based on juxtaposing Old Testament scenes, announcing the Sacrifice of Christ, with corresponding scenes from the New Testament.  
Within the lower oval cartouches are four embroidered scenes from the Old Testament: Abraham sacrificing Isaac, Moses with the brass serpent, Moses fighting the Amalekites, and the legend of the prophet Jonah and the sea monster.  
In the triangular gables of the roof are scenes showing The Last Supper and the Resurrection  
The longer sloping sides of the roof contain five scenes from the Passion of Christ: Christ on the Mount of Olives; Seizure of Christ or the Kiss of Judas; Christ before Caiaphas; the Scourging of Christ and the Crowning with thorns, on one side, and on the other, Pilate Revealing Christ (*Ecce Homo*); Christ Falling under the weight of the Cross; Crucifixion on Golgotha; the Deposition and the Burial.  
The *Holy Sepulchre* is the work of Wolfang Jakob Stoll, commissioned from him by the Bishop of Zagreb, Petar Petretić, whom Stoll served from 1650 to 1667. Petretić was a great patron of the arts and actively promoted Croatian art heritage.  
Stoll made many superb vestments most of which are stored in the Treasury in Zagreb Cathedral. The *Holy Sepulchre* is his greatest and most complex work and probably the only preserved example of an embroidered *Christ's Sepulchre* in Europe.  
Stoll based his rendition of the biblical scenes on copperplate prints, which were at that time widespread in Europe. He worked mainly from the prints of Jan and Egidius Sadeler who found their inspiration in the paintings of Marten de Vos, Theodor Barendsz and Jacopo Tintoretto.  
The decorative elements, such as festoons, genii, baskets of fruit and flowers, belong to the ornamental repertoire of Mannerism.  
The *Holy Sepulchre* was first placed in the Cathedral in Passion Week before Easter on 13 April 1659
0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.short_description:
The golden thread relief embroidery of the *Holy Sepulchre* covers eight panels and contains 16 oval medallions bordered by gold cartouches containing scenes from the Old and New Testaments.  
The Bishop of Zagreb, Petar Petretić, commissioned it from the German embroiderer, Wolfgang Jakob Stoll.

0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.name: Raio Palace
0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.description:
A two-storey palace with an irregular quadrangular plan; an internal staircase leads to what is known as the “noble” floor, the main ceremonial floor and where guests were accommodated and the owner slept. There is also an attic. The façade is covered with plain blue *azulejos* (tile panels). The main façade is predominantly horizontal; four windows alternate with three doors at ground level. On the first floor there are six windows and a bay window in the centre, which defines the axis, and has a balcony. On each side of the bay there are two exotic figures.  
The ornamentation on the window frames extends to the main door on the ground floor. Ornamentation of the lintels and door posts, as well as on the curved gables, is typical of André Soares's work.  
The theme is further developed in the façade axis, the ground-floor door having two console motifs, one on each side. The wood carvings and the furniture mirror the console motif.  
The building was part of the program for urban improvement in Braga carried out during the reign of João V in 1760.  
Worth mentioning in the context of Raio Palace, is another work by André Soares that shows the same transitional language between the Baroque and the *Rocaille*, the Malheiros Reimão House.
0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.short_description: Urban palace with a trapezoidal plan, two floors and a magnificent Rococo façade.
0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.location: Parish of S. Lázaro, S. José, Braga, Braga

0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.name: *Apollo and Daphne*
0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.description:
This sculpture is considered one of the masterpieces in the history of art.  
Bernini began sculpting it in 1622 after he finished *The Rape of Proserpina.* He stopped working on it from 1623 to 1624 to sculpt *David*, before completing it in 1625.  
With notable technical accuracy, the natural agility of this work shows the astonishing moment when the nymph turns into a laurel tree. The artist uses his exceptional technical skill to turn the marble into roots, leaves and windswept hair. Psychological research, combined with typically Baroque expressiveness, renders the emotion of Daphne's terror, caught by the god in her desperate journey, still ignorant of her ongoing transformation. Apollo, thinking he has achieved his objective, is caught in the moment he becomes aware of the metamorphosis, before he is able to react, watching astonished as his victim turns into a laurel tree. For Apollo's head, Bernini looked to *Apollo Belvedere*, which was in the Vatican at the time.  
The base includes two scrolls, the first containing the lines of the distich by Maffeo Barberini, a friend of Cardinal Scipione Borghese and future Pope Urban VIII. It explores the theme of *vanitas* in beauty and pleasure, rendered as a Christian moralisation of a profane theme. The second scroll was added in the mid-1700s.  
The group, like others created by Bernini in the Villa, was backed on to a wall, setting a mandatory point of view for the visitor entering the room, to fulfil the pictorial objectives and provide the surprising scenery, key components of the baroque style. As with other sculptures, it was placed in the centre of the room during the renovations of 1700. Bernini worked with the sculptor Giuliano Finelli, who provided the delicate detailing on the base, rocks and part of the leaves and tree.
0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.short_description: Bernini executed the group between 1622 and 1625. Such a pagan myth (by Ovid in *Metamorphosis*) in the cardinal's house is explained by a moral distich by Maffeo Barberini (Urbano VIII, 1623–1644) on the theme of *vanitas* “those who love to pursue fleeting forms of pleasure, in the end find only leaves and bitter berries in their hands.”

0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.name: *Boy with a Basket of Fruit*
0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.description:
The canvas is one of the first works Merisi undertook in Rome, having joined the workshops of Giuseppe Cesari, known as the Cavalièr d'Arpino, shortly after his arrival in the city in 1592. He stayed there for several months, exercising his abilities as a painter of still-life. In this painting, the artist represents different qualities of fruit, some of which are very ripe, with extreme realism. The extraordinary realism of the boy showing us the basket, illuminated by a source of light behind his back, can be attributed to the young painter's Lombard influence, his sensitivity so similar to that of the Flemish school.  
The Borghese painting should be compared to the famous *Basket* from the same period in the Pinacoteca Ambrosiana in Milan, belonging to Cardinal Federico Borromeo and executed in Rome on recovered canvas in the mid-1590s. At the time, Caravaggio, unknown and in financial straits, used second-hand canvases to save money.  
This work was one of the pieces that Scipione Borghese had confiscated from the Cavalièr d'Arpino in 1607. The famous painter personally owned a valuable collection of paintings, which ended up in the hands of the greedy cardinal. They became the core of the splendid Borghese Collection.  
The technical ability that Caravaggio shows in the work exemplifies the artist's idea that the same method is required to paint people and objects.  
The subject has been interpreted in different ways. Fruit is used as an allegory for abundance, but on account of its natural tendency to perish, is also a metaphor for the transience of life.
0bf3b5f9-5630-5af5-a852-fb4d0db276ec.short_description: This painting dates from the first Caravaggio period in Rome. The canvas is painted with a strong realism that gives the still-life the same importance as the figure. The Lombard, Venetian, and Flemish influences do not prevent the painting from representing a new artistic expression.
