178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.name: Processional Altar of St. John the Evangelist
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.description:
A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, which belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception, and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies. Traditionally, up until 1893, the altar was carried by farmers.  
Rectangular in shape, the *acroteria* (small bases placed at the four extremities) has a beaded edging, and four *albarradas* or ornamental vases, alternate with smaller jars in the middle. The entirety is covered with vegetable and scalloped-shell ornamentation, and St. James' crosses. The wooden carrying rods are also silver plated.  
The octagonal shaped pedestal stands over the main body, decorated with double scalloped-shell ornamentation, pear-shaped “tables” and St. James' crosses. There is also an octagonal platform with small jars placed at each corner of the pedestal.  
An iron column rises above the pedestal, covered with silk cloth embroidered with gold thread. It meets a gold and silver halo embellished with precious stones above which a gold and silver crown rests, also studded with precious stones. In the middle of the altarpiece, the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist is played out, the saint graphically shown immersed in boiling olive oil. The wooden effigy of the saint with clasped hands looks straight up at the sky. The silver boiler, standing on a silver tripod above the fire, is kept alight by two multicoloured wooden figures, kneeling at either side of the boiler. One of them is blowing and the other is using a solid-silver pitchfork.  
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist. There was another group of nuns in the same convent that devoted themselves to St. John the Baptist and commissioned a similar processional altar in honour of the saint. In fact, both altarpieces date from the beginning of the 18th century and were made in the same workshop. They both show the same crowned stamps of the city of Lisbon and the same maker's letter “M”.
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.short_description: A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, it portrays features typical of the Portuguese Baroque at the time of King João V. Designed to represent the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist, the piece belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception and was used in the procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja, on Corpus Christi Day.

17a09d9c-1607-5072-b048-d03e6a8f4a23.name: Church of St. Mary of Mercy: paintings by Gaspare della Vecchia
17a09d9c-1607-5072-b048-d03e6a8f4a23.description: Gaspare della Vecchia painted the cycle of eight scenes from the Life of Christ in the Church of St. Mary of Mercy in Buje – a little town in Istria – in 1711. In the style of the Venetian school, *Wedding at Cana* summarises the characteristic composition; developed diagonally receding into the depth of the picture, inhabited by figures in motion. The stereotypical postures and the typology of the characters show the influence of Gaspare's father, Pietro della Vecchia (1603–1678).

17e1db41-2961-5674-996c-df75d28862f4.name: Church of Santa Rosalia, funerary monuments to Prince Taddeo Barberini and Cardinal Antonio Barberini
17e1db41-2961-5674-996c-df75d28862f4.description:
The church of Santa Rosalia has a central plan with a continuous cornice, polychrome marble walls, double cross-vault and a presbytery, richly decorated with polychrome marble and monuments. The *Pietà group*, known as the Palestrina group, was added to a niche in the chapel behind the sacristy (the Depository of the Tombs); one of the later sculptures, attributed to Michelangelo, is now in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence.  
In the funerary monuments on the side-walls, of Taddeo Barberini (1603–47) to the right and his brother Cardinal Antonio (1607–71) to the left, the sculptor combines – using Berninian forms ­– the geometric shapes of the triangle (a kind of pyramid in *giallo antico* – golden antico ­– marble on lion’s paws) and the circle (the medallion in grey marble containing candid busts of the deceased) in a composition which, while centred on the two portraits and seemingly static, is animated by the figures of angels, intent on writing the epitaph on Antonio’s tomb or playing the trumpet on Taddeos, made using typically Baroque forms suspended at the moment of action: the rich draperies, the hair in locks dishevelled but harmonious, wings, plumage described in detail, and the soft modelled shapes of the figures, all of which are treated using light, such as to create highlights in the rigid geometric partitioning of multicoloured marble walls.
17e1db41-2961-5674-996c-df75d28862f4.short_description: In the funerary monuments of Taddeo Barberini and his brother Cardinal Antonio, the sculptor combines – using Berninian forms – the geometric shapes of the triangle (a kind of pyramid in *giallo antico* – golden antico – marble) and the circle (the medallion in grey marble containing candid busts of the deceased) in a composition which, while centred on the two portraits and seemingly static, is animated by the figures of angels, intent on writing the epitaph on Antonio’s tomb or playing the trumpet on Taddeos, made using typically Baroque forms suspended at the moment of action.
17e1db41-2961-5674-996c-df75d28862f4.method_for_datation: Inscription on the tomb of Antonio Barberini

17e1db41-2961-5674-996c-df75d28862f4.history: The Church of Santa Rosalia, commissioned by Taddeo Barberini (1603–47) from the architect Francesco Contini (1599–1669) as a family chapel, was completed by his son Maffeo (1630–85). Opened on 7 November 1660, it was dedicated to the saint who protected the Prenestini (people of Palestrina) during the plague of 1656. The church, with its twin towers, is integral to the scenographic backdrop made up of the sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia and the Palazzo Barberini. Inside the church, the funerary monuments of Taddeo and Antonio Barberini were placed on the side-walls at the beginning of the following century.

17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.name: *Firework Display Held in Brno on the Occasion of the Coronation of a Picture of the Virgin Mary of St. Thomas*
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.description:
In the 1730s Moravia hosted two festive events offsetting the largest religious festivals of the Czech baroque, the beatification and canonisation of St. John of Nepomuk in Prague (1729). As the capital of the Czech kingdom came into the spotlight for the whole country, so the celebrations of the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns in the Moravian margraviate. These occasions made the Holy Virgin the Queen of Moravia and the patron saint of the country. The festivities around the coronation of the picture of the Virgin Mary in Brno lasted a week. “The night turned into day and the town of Brno into a new heavenly Jerusalem full of scenes of adoration, praise and exultation”. The town's splendour was illuminated by 5,000 lights and plentiful firework displays. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with sculpted decoration and pyrotechnical effects. A detailed programme was issued to accompany the fireworks, explaining the display to viewers in 27 steps.  
After a fanfare of trumpets and tympani, the fireworks were set off by the firing of cannons, and an angel setting white and red fire to the chronogram “Mary the Gem and Patron Saint of the Town of Brno”. Rockets lit up six life-size figures: Emperor Charles IV, who donated the picture, his brother Jan Jindřich, founder of the Augustinian monastery, Pope Clement XII, protector of the adoration picture, the Bishop of Olomouc, who crowned the picture, the prior of the monastery, and the *genius loci* of Brno. The spectacle climaxed with Catherine Wheels at the tips of pyramids and six hearts burning under the figures. The fountain in the foreground started to spew a multitude of tiny stars and blue flowers, while the fire illuminated a flood of garlands. The final highlight of the show, to an overture of cannon fire, was the flight of a two-headed imperial eagle rising with an inscription within mighty flames.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.short_description: Celebrations for the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns of the Moravian margraviate. The Holy Virgin became Queen and patron saint of Moravia. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with pyrotechnical effects.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.method_for_datation: Marked bottom left: *F. A. Baran del;* bottom right: *F. A. Mayer Sculp: Brunae*. The little-known F. A. Baran was the artist and engraver of the fireworks print. František Antonín Mayer, a student of Jan Jiří Guttwein, was a bookbinder and engraver in Brno. He executed the engraving of the “silver altar” and the picture of the Brno Thaumaturga.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.obtention: Purchased in 1978 from an art shop in Brno.

1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.name: *Procession and* Auto de Fé
1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.description:
The Inquisition was established during the Verona Council of 1183 for the purposes of the judgment of heresy by the Roman Catholic Church. Necessitated by the emergence of various religious movements and the popularisation of different interpretations of Christian doctrine in opposition to the Roman Church, it was initially called the Episcopal Inquisition because it was administrated by the bishops. Later, in 1230, the Church tried to reform the role and actions of the Inquisition by recruiting professionals mainly from the Dominican Order.  
The new inquisitors judged heresy using local authorities under the Inquisition's procedures. In 1542, three years before the Council of Trent, Pope Paul III established a system of Courts as demanded by the "Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Roman and Universal Inquisition". The Inquisition was established in 1536 in Portugal following a request from King João III.  
Following judgment, defendants were submitted to punishment; a ritual of public penance of condemned heretics and apostates, the so called *Auto de Fé*. In these engravings two important moments of this theatrical religious scene are observed: the Procession taking place in Ribeira Square in Lisbon – close to the Royal Palace of King João V – and the condemned being burned alive at the stake wearing *sambenitos*, clothing with a red cross.  
The Portuguese Inquisition expanded to the colonies: Brazil, Cape Verde and Goa, where it continued as an activity of the religious courts until 1812. In Goa, the processes mostly concentrated on Jews, the Hindu communities and Indian Muslims. The violence of the Inquisition in Goa was so intense that Voltaire wrote: "Goa is sadly famous for its Inquisition, which is contrary to humanity as much as to commerce. The Portuguese monks deluded us into believing that the Indians were worshipping the Devil, while it was them who served him."
1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.short_description: The theme of these engravings is related to the brutality of the Inquisition. The Inquisition acted against those whom it deemed heretical and apostates. First they were humiliated and walked through the city in Procession. Then a mass would was said where the sermon preached the morality of the ceremony. Finally they were punished in public in the square.
1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.method_for_datation: The engraving is published in the *Annales d'Espagne et de Portugal, contenant tout ce qui s'est passé de plus important dans ces deux royaumes & dans les autres Parties de l'Europe, de même que dans les Indes Orientales & Occidentales, depuis l'établissement de ces deux Monarchies jusqu'á présent. Avec la Description de tout ce qu'il y a de plus remarquable en Espagne & en Portugal*, Amsterdam, 1741.

183b5543-14a1-5a82-b3dd-50b7597cdf96.name: *Father Martin Stredonius with a View of Brno from the East*
183b5543-14a1-5a82-b3dd-50b7597cdf96.description:
The scene glorifies the Jesuit priest and teacher Martin Středa (known as Stredonius, practicing in Gliwica in 1587; moving to Brno in 1649). Set in 1645, when the Swedish besieged the city of Brno during the Thirty Years' War, the painting depicts Středa's miraculous ascension to heaven at the very moment the attackers withdrew. The final and largest cannon ball aimed at Brno is said to have landed at Father Středa's feet where it remained, motionless. A besieger holding a cannon ball is shown in the bottom left-hand corner, while the focal point of the picture is the priest accepting holy wisdom through the Virgin Mary, expressed by a reflection of divine light. Středa is wearing a medallion with a portrait of the emperor, which accentuates his role as a defender not only of Brno but also of the whole Habsburg empire. In the top right-hand corner appear Jan Kapistrán (Capistranus) and another church father. Capistranus preached in Brno in 1451 and was also believed to possess supernatural powers. The *veduta* of Brno shows the fortified character of the city, with Špilberk castle.  
General Ludvík Raduit de Souches, commander of the Brno defense during the Swedish siege complies: “It appears that the bravery of the city defense was strengthened by fervent prayers and continuous fasting on the part of Father Středa, through which he transmuted power from heaven to defend and ensure the safety of the besieged. The enemy eventually saw that, having mobilised all their military efforts and set all kinds of traps, the spirit of the city was strong and unbreakable, and that it involved supernatural protection …”  Stredonius is said to have had the power of being in two places at once and of levitating during meditation. He wrote a biography of the martyred priest Jan Sarkander, a document that played a major part in the dissemination of the latter's cult and eventual canonisation as patron saint of Moravia and counterpart to St. John of Nepomuk.  
The cult of Martin Středa was promoted through prints of a similar composition. (Brno City Archive).
183b5543-14a1-5a82-b3dd-50b7597cdf96.short_description: The scene glorifies the Jesuit priest Martin Středa. It is set in 1645, when the Swedish besieged the city of Brno during the Thirty Years' War, depicting Středa's miraculous ascension to heaven at the very moment that the attackers withdrew. The *veduta* shows the fortified character of the city of Brno.
183b5543-14a1-5a82-b3dd-50b7597cdf96.method_for_datation: The picture is thought to have been commissioned by the Brno Jesuit Václav Škodovský. The authorship, originally ascribed to M. Willman, was determined by Dr. Vlasta Kratinová, curator of the Moravian Gallery collections. Lublinský produced several paintings for Brno clients at the time, such as *The* *Allegory of Justice* (Old Brno Abbey) and *The Guardian Angel* for Count Dietrichstein (Church of St. Thomas).
183b5543-14a1-5a82-b3dd-50b7597cdf96.obtention: The picture was donated to the Brno Picture Gallery – which came into existence as part of the Francis Museum, Brno – by Provincial Councillor Franz Georg Eberle in 1821, shortly after its establishment. The painting also featured in the museum’s first exhibition held in the Episcopal courtyard.

183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.name: *Adoration of the Painting of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo*
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.description:
The image within, praised by angels, is a painted reproduction of an adoration picture of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo which originated in the 1630s. Its subject is the miraculous transportation of the picture which, according to legend, was brought to its new location by angels. The gloomy landscape in the bottom section of the painting has, beyond doubt, an allegorical meaning, while the illuminated adoration image presents a reality higher than the earthly life, here represented by thistles, military fortresses and rocks. The artist accentuated the difference between the miraculous picture and mundane reality through quaint, rustic elements in the picture of the Virgin Mary, in terms appropriate to chronology and the taste of the period. On the other hand, the figures of the angels and the landscape are rendered in Herdt’s trademark warm red-brown and golden tones, revealing his Flemish training.  
This sizeable painting is an example of the then popular picture-within-a-picture type. The intention of such paintings was to visually enhance, or “update”, well-known and already worshipped miracle-inspiring pictures. These “miraculous” pictures were displayed on altars, like relics, and as such were to be venerated. At the same time, pictures-within-pictures were employed, by Counter-Reformation and missionary orders in particular, for more striking presentations of “miraculous” pictures among ordinary town and country people.  
The origination of the painting marks a key moment in the history of the worship of the miraculous Znojmo picture, since the burgeoning importance of the Znojmo Dominicans in South Moravia involved the cult of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo. One of the first mentions of a Marian brotherhood of the Holy Rosary, active in one of the chapels of the monastery complex, date to the same period. In 1734 the “miraculous picture” was festively crowned and placed on a new altar in the monastery church.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.short_description: The canvas is typical of the picture-within-a-picture approach of the time, intended to visually “update” miracle-inspiring pictures. Rustic elements used in the painting within the painting contrast the sacred with the mundane; the warmly rendered angels and landscape reveal the artist’s Flemish training.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and dated 1678. The Dominican monastery, established in Znojmo around the mid-13th century, suffered serious damage during the Thirty Years' War and was not substantially restored until several decades later. At that time, *The Invention of the Holy Cross*, a painting by Jan Daniel (de) Herdt a Dutch artist formerly active in Brescia, Italy, was obtained for the main altar. A year later, Herdt painted another canvas for the monastery, its subject being the adoration of a picture of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.obtention: The painting was probably found in one of the chapels of the Dominican monastery church in Znojmo which was pulled down in the late 19th century. The picture was transferred to Znojmo Castle chapel, administered by the Museum of Znojmo since the early 20th century.

198dcaff-0328-5a80-a4ea-d7ac0774b16b.name: *The Ancestral Gallery of the Eltz Family*
198dcaff-0328-5a80-a4ea-d7ac0774b16b.description:
The Eltz family were of ancient German nobility. They came originally from the town of Eltz in Moselland, their family lineage uninterrupted from the first decade of the 13th century. A branch of the counts of Eltz acquired estates in Slavonia in 1736, when Philipp Karl, archbishop and elected prince of Mainz, bought the Vukovar estate. Throughout the following decades, the family brought from Germany to Croatia family portraits and the *Ancestral Gallery*, consisting of 10 large paintings. The composition is the same for them all – four to six figures representing two generations of the family (father, mother, the eldest son and his wife) shown with the Eltz family's coats of arms combined with that of their wives. The lower areas of the paintings have long texts about the lives of those depicted. The elder generations of the family are sometimes dressed quite fantastically, while depictions of the later generations seen in the final painting in the Gallery (shown here) present a detailed study of the fashion of the period  
The *Gallery*, commissioned and painted during the second half of the 18th century, is probably the work of Georg Joseph Melber, a painter based in Mainz. In 1752, Melber painted portraits of Anselm Kasimir Eltz and his wife Maria Johanna (in the Gallery of Fine Arts in Osijek). These portraits are distinctly similar to the paintings of the Ancestral Gallery.
198dcaff-0328-5a80-a4ea-d7ac0774b16b.short_description: The Eltz family belonged to ancient German nobility. A branch of the counts of Eltz acquired estates in Slavonia in the 18th century bringing from Germany to Croatia the *Ancestral Gallery*. *The Gallery*, comprising 10 paintings, dates to the last quarter of the 18th century.
198dcaff-0328-5a80-a4ea-d7ac0774b16b.method_for_datation: The date and possible authorship of the painting was established by studying the inscriptions, and comparing the painting with other known works of Georg Joseph Melber.
198dcaff-0328-5a80-a4ea-d7ac0774b16b.obtention: Received from the Commission for the Collection and Preservation of Cultural Monuments and Antiquities in 1952.

19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.name: *Susanna and the Old Men*
19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.description:
According to historical sources, Rubens was one of the artists patronised by Scipione Borghese, who was a great admirer. This painting was probably done expressly for Cardinal Borghese, given that in 1622 it was fitted with a frame, now unfortunately lost. The commission, which lacks documentary support, could be understood to be a sign of recognition for the assistance that Borghese gave to the painter, who was already committed to Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, in asking him to consent to a longer stay in Rome.  
The painting relates to Rubens' second stay in Rome (1606–1608), when he was working on the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella – where Caravaggio had worked – in which he was decorating the high altar.  
The work depicts the story of Susanna as told in the Old Testament (Daniel 13, 1–64). This is a biblical theme that is particularly dear to the culture of the Counter Reformation, which saw in the heroine an example of truth and virtue as against lying, symbolised here by two old men who are trying in vain to seduce the maiden. To render the protagonist, Rubens, a passionate devotee of ancient art, drew on the famous bronze sculpture *Spinario* on the Capitoline Hill. It is an extremely harmonious figure in which the classical combines perfectly with the voluptuous and abundant forms, typical of the artist. There are also references to the great Venetians of the 16th century, especially Titian in his later style, Paolo Veronese and Tintoretto. These are evident in the use of a particular colour palette based on browns and golds, entirely different from the choices made by contemporary Caravaggesque painters, who focused on strong contrasts between light and shadow.
19b10be2-4026-59df-8bd7-f860cb379ee5.short_description: Rubens probably executed this work during his second stay in Rome (1606–1608). The pose of the central female nude shows knowledge of antique art (the *Spinario*) and appears from the darkness with the contrasting light of Caravaggio's tenebrism.

19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.name: *Adoration of the Shepherds*
19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.description:
The New Testament account of the shepherds' adoration of the infant Jesus is rendered as a genre picture. The landscape setting is not typical of Kremser-Schmidt's oeuvre which predominantly comprised sizeable altarpieces. The artist reduced the scene to primary figures and their attributes and based the picture on atmospheric use of colour and light. A contrasting motif of a forked tree receding into a dark cloud separates the main scene from the background. The light appears to emanate from within the picture itself, from the infant Jesus, and is reflected on the hay in the barn and tools in the foreground. These motifs are reminiscent of 17th-century Dutch painting, something that Kremser-Schmidt focused upon unlike his contemporaries. His interest in chiaroscuro and the relaxed brushstrokes pay tribute to Rembrandt's painting style. The colour scheme is, however, original. The scale of brown tones illuminated with various hues of golden ochre are offset by Mary's blue robe and accents of vermilion in the detail. The palette is complemented by a grey-blue background with light effects.  
The picture is one of only a few known examples of the artist's early work, that often appears to be inspired by northern Italian painting, and which he probably saw either during a journey to Venice in 1746 or through prints brought back from there for him. He later settled in Stein near Krems, and sent his paintings to Lower Austria, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia. In the last quarter of the 18th century his paintings were distributed in Moravia (Vranov, Bratrušov). His student, Franz Oesterreicher, worked in Jihlava. Schmidt's oeuvre spanned changes in style from the late baroque to classicism and this was accompanied by an extension of thematic scale: portrait, genre painting and ancient mythology.
19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.short_description: The shepherds’ adoration of the infant Jesus is rendered as a genre picture. The landscape setting is not typical of Kremser-Schmidt, whose work largely comprised altarpieces for the Habsburgian lands. The painter reduced the scene to primary figures and based the picture on the atmospheric use of colour and light.
19bd1476-0139-55f1-b234-c8d2e4fb2a12.method_for_datation: The picture was determined as a work by Kremser-Schmidt on the basis of a style analysis by Ivo Krsek.

1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.name: *The Beggar*
1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.description:
This painting has only recently (2002) been attributed to Jusepe de Ribera, despite the fact that it was ascribed to him in an old inventory of the Scipione Borghese collection.  
The painting is considered to be a reference point in the Roman phase of the Spanish painter (1612–1616), which some scholars identify with the work of another artist known as the Master of the Judgement of Solomon.  
The work is recognised as one of the first completed by a young de Ribera, when his style was still strongly dependent on Caravaggesque naturalism. With this painting, the composition and voluminous construction of his early career begins to blend with the more compact and tangible brushstrokes for which he is renowned in his successive Neapolitan phase.  
Also, the innovative nature of the canvas is evident in the choice of subject: the beggar, despite being poor and dressed in rags, is treated with the same dignity as an eminent figure, launching a trend for the depiction of paupers that evolved extensively in Rome in the following decades.  
The fragmented brushstrokes, the threads of colour that freely define the dense highlights, the shadows that add drama to the scene: it is the chromatic elements that emphasise the heightened humanity of the character. Through his close attention to reality, even on the very margins of society, de Ribera focuses on the profound and human gaze of the beggar, the results of an effort to transform the idea of Christian compassion into a tangible expression of pathetic suffering.
1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.short_description: The painting has recently been attributed to Ribera from a Borghese inventory from 1615–1630. Ribera stayed in Rome from 1612 to 1616 and this work probably dates from this first period of Caravaggio's influence. The work initiates the “*pittura pauperistica*” that developed in later years.
1af71b1a-176d-523c-9450-398ddc005fc7.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.name: *Annunciation*
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.description:
This painting was made for the altar of the church of the Santissima Annunziata (Blessed Annunciate) in Pieve di Cento, a small town near Bologna. The church was part of a recently built college held by the Scolopian Fathers, whose mission was the free education of poor children.  
The simple and clear structure of the painting is perfect for religious instruction. It follows the tenets of religious and profane painting as described in a 1582 book by Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti the Bishop of Bologna.  
Guercino depicts God the Father explaining his mission to the archangel Gabriel rather than depicting the Annunciation. The beautiful angel is a set on a diagonal cutting the picture in two, thus separating heaven from earth. In the lower half of the painting the kneeling Virgin is reading in a bare room, unaware of what is happening above her.  
Thanks to the Scolopian father Giacomo Bottini the painting “Intangible Dowry for the Instruction of the Poor” was saved from the French requisitions, in 1798.

The beautiful angel is placed on a diagonal cutting the picture in two, separating heaven from earth. In the lower half of the painting the kneeling Virgin is reading in a bare room, unaware of what is happening above her.
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.method_for_datation: The commission of the painting for the Church of the Santissima Annunziata (Blessed Annunciate) in Pieve di Cento as well as a series of payments were registered by Paolo Antonio Barbieri, Guercino's brother in the painter's Account Book in 1646.
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.provenance: Church of the Blessed Annunciate Santissima Annunziata (Pieve di Cento)
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.obtention: The painting was moved to the council room of the City Hall Municipal Palace of Pieve di Cento in 1924. At that time the church was closed, deconsecrated and converted into a store. Later the painting was moved along with its altar to the church of Santa Maria Maggiore.

1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.name: *Adoring Angel*
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.description:
Georg Raphael Donner was one of the most prominent and influential Central European sculptors of the first half of the 18th century. He developed his individual Neo-Classical style at a distance from the Baroque tradition, relying on models from antiquity and 16th-century Italian sculpture. His first monumental works were made for Pozsony (Bratislava) Cathedral, commissioned by Prince Primate Imre Esterházy.  
First of all he worked on the decoration for the Chapel of St. John the Almsgiver, executing the archbishop's sepulchral statue (1729–32). Later, he created the sculptural group of St. Martin and the beggar, as well as two adoring angels for the new high altar in the cathedral (1733–1735). This significant work is characterised by the perfect harmony between the sculpture and architecture; the idea and the form. The crowned canopy of the altar was originally carried by enormous free-standing fluted columns. The central figural group featured St. Martin seated on the back of a rearing horse. He shares his flowing cloak with the beggar lying on the ground. St. Martin is wearing a Hungarian noblemen's outfit and has the facial features of the archbishop. The beggar of heroic stature is looking at the saint with Christ's face, but the saint does not recognise him immediately. An external viewer of the altarpiece cannot recognise Christ's face either, because it is seen in semi-profile. Two huge kneeling angels join the scene on either side, their adoration directed towards the disguised Redeemer. Despite minor differences in movement, hand gesture and in the arrangement of drapery, the adoring angels are practically symmetrical; they are dignified celestial creatures, although their finely modelled, strong bodies are very real. Their pose expresses intimate and perfect veneration.  
The beauty of the modelling is enhanced by the subtle grey hue and silken lustre of lead, which also lends an earnest, reserved and elegant appearance to the statues. With these statues, Donner reached an initial peak of his oeuvre. The altar was dismantled in the 1860s when the cathedral was rebuilt in the Neo-Gothic style. The main group of the equestrian statue today is in the side aisle of Bratislava Cathedral, and the two adoring angels are part of the permanent collection at the Hungarian National Gallery.
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.short_description: The most important patron of the Viennese sculptor was Primate Imre Esterházy in Pozsony (Bratislava). The high altar of Pozsony (Bratislava) Cathedral was one of Donner's most significant works, but after it was demolished in the 19th century, the group of St. Martin and the beggar can be seen in the nave today, while the two huge angels were taken to Budapest in the 19th century.

1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.name: *Glorification of Emperor Charles VI*
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.description:
Sitting in his ceremonial tent on the right, the ruler is receiving a report. Surrounded by angels and wearing a crown, the Virgin Mary – in a cloud over the tent – reaches out towards the Emperor with an olive branch. To the right of the tent there is a column decorated with portraits of Habsburg rulers in roundels: emperors Ferdinand III, Leopold I, Joseph I and Charles VI. The dates inscribed on the column, 1740 and 1745, may refer to the emperorship of Charles Albert Elector of Bavaria and the Peace of Dresden Treaty, which resulted in the election of Maria Theresia's husband, Francis of Lorraine, as emperor. This is why it is likely that Francis of Lorraine commissioned the picture as a monument to his father-in-law's Ottoman campaigns. In the foreground on the left, a battle scene probably depicts the Siege of Belgrade, displaying the recognisable figure of Prince Eugene von Savoy.  
The fresco and altarpiece painter, Joseph Adam Mölck, studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and records mention that he was there in 1733. Mölck worked for 15 years in Bavaria and Tyrol. In 1764, he painted frescos and altarpieces for churches in Steiermark. He worked in Lower Austria for the final 12 years of his career. His oeuvre was extensive and he worked with collaborators to achieve large commissions. The art and theory of the Italian architect and painter, Andrea Pozzo, influenced Mölck's frescos.  
Mölck visited Vienna in 1754, but why he did so remains a mystery; there is possibly a connection between the commission of this painting and Mölck's appointment as Tyrolean court painter in 1755.
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.short_description: An allegorical composition of an emperor's military deeds is a special subject and this is a unique example of it. The dates on the column (1740 and 1745) may refer to the Peace of Dresden Treaty, which resulted in the election of Maria Theresia's husband, Francis of Lorraine, as emperor. It is likely that Francis of Lorraine commissioned the picture to commemorate his father-in-law's Ottoman campaigns.
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and dated.
1d94a91f-144d-5ad8-8788-222b25813e63.provenance: Probably commissioned by Emperor Francis of Lorraine

1de5d379-77f2-53f5-8b74-1effd8f999f9.name: Saint Mary Magdalene renouncing worldly vanities
1de5d379-77f2-53f5-8b74-1effd8f999f9.description:
Under the cover of a daily feminine toilette scene depicting a lady magnificently dressed taking off her jewellery in a luxuriously furnished room, this oil-on-copper allegory has both moral and apologetic purposes in line with the Counter Reformation. The painting records the first steps of St. Mary Magdalene towards her religious conversion, to renounce worldly belongings, retreat to the desert and her penitence, meditation and mystic encounter with Christ. St. Mary Magdalene was the embodiment of one who had abandoned a life of riches and ephemeral pleasures, and replaced it with a frugal contemplative way of life, thereby disdaining all worldly vanities.  
Several details in the painting carefully describe the circumstances of her retreat: the characterisation of St. Mary, and the room in which we see her, enhance the contrast between the luxury she is about to leave behind and the redemption she will achieve through a simple life and penitence in the desert.  
Within these details one can point out the furniture, the richness of the fabrics, and the detail of the lute on the arch – music is included within the worldly pleasures – and even the cat under the table, a symbol of domestic comfort. Yet the central topic of the action, vanitas, is represented by the gold, pearls and precious gems and jewels, which she is gradually scattering on the table, supreme emblems of vanity, beauty and worldly matters.  
In fact, therefore, this oil-on-copper painting is a precious iconographic document of the epoch, depicting both furnishing and sartorial fashion, but most importantly recording the jewellery in vogue at the time.  
Lastly it is also worth mentioning that this image was not painted by a professional painter. Sister Joana Baptista's biography is almost unknown; she was a nun from the Maltesas Convent of S. João of Estremoz, a small town in Alentejo. Her charming and naïve painting style is a fine example among other similar works made in Franciscan and Benedictine convents, painted by nuns to be seen by nuns, it presents St. Mary Magdalene as an example of good behaviour and devotion.
1de5d379-77f2-53f5-8b74-1effd8f999f9.short_description: Mary Magdalene strips off her jewels as symbols of vanity, thereby renouncing worldly luxury before embracing a life of penitence in the desert. As an iconographic document, the painting is a good example of the religious and moral ethics of the Counter-Reformation, while offering a window onto the daily life of the aristocracy.

1e902b54-02bc-52d4-a41f-4b3abe60ea34.name: *Sybil*
1e902b54-02bc-52d4-a41f-4b3abe60ea34.description:
The work was obtained by Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1617, and may originally have been commissioned from Domenichino by Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, although this is not certain. It is the first known piece having this subject (there is another original from 1622 in Rome at the Pinacoteca Capitolina).  
It shows one of the famous 'ideal figures' created by the painter through a progressive selection of forms until a studied, classical equilibrium between nature and perfection, beauty and expression of emotion is achieved: the representation of moods that is a central theme in the language of the Baroque.  
The figure assumes a singing pose. Numerous details refer to the musical background of the artist, who was a frequent visitor to the *Kapellmeisters* of Bologna. In this context Domenichino started to research a musical form that was entirely new at the time and that would become the style of instrumental Baroque music par excellence: the *trio sonata*. The maiden sits beside a beautifully carved viol and is holding a musical score in her hands. The laurel bushes allude allegorically to Apollo, to whom the sibyls were devoted, while the vine refers to the god, Bacchus, who is associated with poetic inspiration.  
The 11 pagan sibyls communicate the responses of the god Apollo through the oracles. Christian doctrine interpreted these maidens, who were dedicated to divinity, as forerunners of Christianity, attributing them the role of prophets of the coming of Christ. The female figure with her head bound in a turban alludes to the martyr Cecilia, whose body was miraculously found intact at the beginning of the 17th century, and whose story was painted as a fresco by Domenichino in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi. The painting shows an extraordinary synthesis between the colours of Bolognese painting and the drawing of Raphael and Leonardo's theories on aerial perspective, established at around the same time.
1e902b54-02bc-52d4-a41f-4b3abe60ea34.short_description:
The Sybil, holding a musical score in her hand, is portrayed as the revelator of the Divine Word. The figure is connected to the discovery of the body of Saint Cecilia, patron saint of music, in Trastevere, from whom it borrows the image of the turban as worn by the martyr, who was found near to the basilica of the same name in Trastevere.  
Through a selection of forms the painter reaches a refined and classical balance between nature and perfection; between beauty and the expression of feelings.

1eba92c3-546a-5f12-9712-a0103f836320.name: Catholic Subsidiary Church of the Holy Cross, former Jesuit Church
1eba92c3-546a-5f12-9712-a0103f836320.description: According to the origin of its architect, the Church of the Holy Cross was built after a specific model: the church of the Jesuit University (so-called Study Church), existing since 1617 in the Swabian town of Dillingen on the Danube. Comparable to that archetype, a hall of wall pillars leads to a recessed, deep and apsidal chancel. Only some unique details such as the ornamentalised windows and doorways as well as the Rococo-stucco betray the period of origin which is about 150 years later. Equally characteristic of this period and deviating from the archetype, extensive ceiling frescoes which illustrate the patrocinium cover the nave and chancel vaults. The appearance of the interior space  is characterised by the altars which are stylistically uniform and arranged according to scenographic perspectives.
1eba92c3-546a-5f12-9712-a0103f836320.short_description: Situated high above the old town, the Jesuit Church with its two-towered façade constructed in un-plastered tuff masonry characterises the historical visage of the former old Bavarian border town. Constructed according to the building tradition of southern German Jesuits as a wall pillar church, it is an especially late representation of its building type and therefore exhibits features in the magnificent Rococo style. Multi-figured ceiling frescoes, painted by Christoph Thomas Scheffler, student of Cosmas Damian Asam, dominate the interior space and tell the legend of the cross in dramatic compositions.
1eba92c3-546a-5f12-9712-a0103f836320.method_for_datation: Through archival sources; inscription on the ceiling fresco.

1eba92c3-546a-5f12-9712-a0103f836320.history: In 1575, the second Jesuit College after Munich was founded in the Electorate of Bavaria and also included a noviciate. When the latter was in need of extension and renovation around 1750, this was taken as an occasion to also replace the collegiate church. As of 1752, under the direction of the Jesuit architect Joseph Ignaz Merani of Dillingen, a large-scale new building was erected for this purpose. Merani was obviously given a hand with the doorways and windows by the famous Rococo architect based in Landsberg, Dominikus Zimmermann. By 1756, the church building completed two years before was already largely furnished. The ceiling frescoes were the last work of Augsburg’s painter Christoph Thomas Scheffler, trained by Cosmas Damian Asam, and are considered as his most significant creations.

1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.name: *Saint Michael Archangel with Four Saints*
1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.alternate_name: *Saint Michael Archangel with the Saints John the Baptist, Benedict, Francis and Jerome*
1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.description: This painting once on the high altar of the church of San Michele, St. Michael is described by the Bolognese art historian Malvasia as “of peculiar invention and of such a pictorial good taste”. The five saints, rarely associated, are crowded in the narrow space without being in emotional contact with each other: Benedict, Francis and Jerome are absorbed in their meditations, only the Baptist seems to notice the presence of the archangel. He points to the scale that will be used on the day of the Last Judgement to weigh merits and sins. The painting can be dated around the half of the second decade of the seventeenth-century based on the pictorial language maturity clearly visible in the monumental scale of the figures and the skilled brilliant use of colour.
1edf2644-7dd2-5ff4-84c5-5718c7698f11.short_description: The five saints, rarely associated, are crowded in the narrow space without seeming to be in emotional contact with each other.

1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.name: Coat of Arms of the Erdödy Counts
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.description:
The coat of arms has an elongated triangular composition. In the middle is a a horse-head-shaped shield quartered with a heart in the centre: (1) on gold, a black, displayed, crowned eagle; (2) and (3) a blue bar with two six-pointed gold stars one beside the other; (4) on gold, a crenellated castle with a window and a door, in the heart of the shield: on red a stag rearing to the right from a halved gold wheel. Crest: above the shield, a gold crown from which grows gold acanthus leaves and an angel. Bearers of the arms: on each side is an angel with gold wings and one foot stepping sideways. The “background” is richly decorated with acanthus leaves, which in this case take over the function of the mantle.  
The Croatian aristocratic family of Hungarian origin, known as the Bakochs, came from the village of Erdöd. From the 16th to the 19th centuries, the Erdödy family played a leading role in Croatian history, acquiring many estates, bestowing five Croatian *bans* (viceroys) and one bishop, and playing an influential part in Croatian political life. They were particularly famous for fighting against the Ottomans.  
Among their many estates, Klanjec castle – built in 1603 and locally known as Novi Dvori Klanječki – is worthy of special mention.  
The Erdödy coat of arms was produced in the sculpture workshop of the Ljubljana, later the Zagreb master sculptor and woodcarver, Ivan Komersteiner, whose arrival in Croatia marked the final advent of Baroque art.  
In the south apse of Zagreb cathedral there is a similar memorial arms by Ivan Komersteiner produced in 1693 for *Ban* Nikola Erdödy who liberated much of Croatia from the Turks.  
Nikola Erdödy built a chapel in the west wing of Klanjec castle dedicated to St Francis Xavier, which he decorated with wall paintings. It is possible that the family arms shown here is from the castle, or perhaps even that it was on an altar commissioned by the Erdödys, who were known to be great donors.  
The Erdödy arms, probably the work of an unknown sculptor from Ivan Komersteiner's workshops, has retained the basic characteristics of Ivan's style, seen particularly in the use of luscious and fleshy acanthus leaves and angel figures as ornamentation.
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.short_description:
Coat of arms of the Erdödy Counts, it comprises a shaped triangular composition around a crowned, quartered shield in gold-blue, with a red heart at the centre, and the family’s symbols. Two guardian angels support it, while there is a third, smaller, angel above the crown. Behind the shield and above the crown are gold acanthus leaves.  
The Erdödys were Croatian aristocrats of Hungarian origin, a family of high nobility that were influential in Croatian political life. The coat of arms is probably the work of the unknown sculptor from the Ivan Komersteiner's workshop. Komersteiner was one of the most important sculptors of continental Croatia at the end of the 17th century.
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.method_for_datation: From characteristics of morphology, style and typology, and comparison with other works by the unknown master from the Ivan Komersteiner workshop.
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.obtention: In 1946, following World War II, the artwork was secured by the Commission for Collecting and Preserving Cultural Monuments, Antiquities and Libraries (KOMZA). In 1952, following the proposal of the Commission for the Liquidation of KOMZA founded by the Ministry of Education, it became the property of the History Museum of Croatia (today the Croatian History Museum).

1f6d4b53-a43a-5b04-b151-93591d3db1a7.name: Sant’Andrea della Valle, Glory of the Virgin fresco
1f6d4b53-a43a-5b04-b151-93591d3db1a7.description:
The fresco, which is spread over a surface of 622 m2, represents the Assumption of the Virgin in the glory of Paradise. At the centre, in the lower register above the altar, the Virgin is ascending. Thanks to her red robe and blue mantle she strikes out from the swirling mass of clouds where saints, prophets, apostles, patriarchs and biblical heroines come together. Two putti are about to crown her with a wreath of roses. Proceeding upwards in the second circle, a celestial concert of angel musicians is depicted, while at the base of the lantern seven little angels support garlands and festoons of flowers and fruit.  
Christ, in a white robe, descends from the top of the lantern to welcome his mother to Heaven.  
A precise and orderly hierarchy is therefore established from top to bottom in which the light that radiates from the figure of Christ plays a structural, as well as symbolic role: golden and dazzling at the top, it dematerializes the angelic figures closest to the lantern, while it becomes more ‘concrete’ towards the bottom, especially in the clouds at the base, producing light-toned colours on the garments of the characters based on very refined accords of pink, yellow, gray, orange, green and purple.  
Among the saints in the lower circle, St. Andrew, with the cross of his martyrdom, can be seen holding the hand of the Theatine Andrea Avellino (canonized just a year before the beginning of the works) as he welcomes him to Paradise, while St. Peter is doing the same with Saint Cajetan.  
The inspiring models for Lanfranco are the domes that Correggio had frescoed in Parma Cathedral and in the San Giovanni Evangelista Church, in the same city. However, Lanfranco also refers to Rubens (who was in Rome at the beginning of the century), especially in the drapery, to Bernini in the gestures in movement of the figures, to the ancient models in the positions of some figures.  
The dome sparked great amazement in Rome, constituting the beginning of a new, fertile season in the decoration of vaults and domes: Baroque illusionism.
1f6d4b53-a43a-5b04-b151-93591d3db1a7.short_description: The dome, with its vortex of figures (strongly influenced by the art of Corregio in Parma) can be considered the birth of the tendency for the search of illusionist effects of the art of Seicento’s Rome.
1f6d4b53-a43a-5b04-b151-93591d3db1a7.bibliography: Costamagna, A., "... l'aria dipingeva per lui": Giovanni Lanfranco e la Gloria del Paradiso a Sant'Andrea della Valle, in Costamagna, A., Ferrara, D. and Grilli, C. (eds) *Sant'Andrea della Valle,* Milan: Skira 2003: 195–235.
1f6d4b53-a43a-5b04-b151-93591d3db1a7.history:
The construction of the church of the Clerics Regular (also known as Theatines), an order founded in 1524 by Gian Pietro Carafa (the future Pope Paul IV), began in 1591 on commission of Cardinal Alfonso Gesualdo, protector of the Congregation. After his death, he was succeeded by Sixtus V’s nephew, Cardinal Alessandro Peretti Montalto who, starting from 1608, entrusted the completion of the building to Carlo Maderno, while the initial project had been designed by the Theatine Francesco Grimaldi and Giacomo Della Porta.  
This majestic dome, second in size in Rome only to that of St. Peter’s in the Vatican, was completed in 1623.  
Cardinal Ludovisi, nephew of the newly elected Gregory XV, had pushed for the tribune and dome to be painted by his favourite artist, Domenichino, but Cardinal Montalto opted for a compromise by entrusting the dome to Giovanni Lanfranco (who had already proved his value in the magnificent illusionistic fresco of the Council of the gods in the Casino Borghese) while the pendentives and the vault of the apse were still commissioned to Domenichino. The two artists were both Emilian and pupils of Annibale Carracci. To the dizzying whirlwind of Lanfranco’s figures, Domenichino responded with his classic compositions marked by monumentality and calmness.

1f6d4b53-a43a-5b04-b151-93591d3db1a7.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

1f803c2c-5108-54ea-bfed-5c226d537a0e.name: Mirror
1f803c2c-5108-54ea-bfed-5c226d537a0e.description:
The mirror, which has a gilded wooden frame and ground-glass edges with flower and plant ornaments, is probably the work of one of the numerous glass workshops on the island of Murano, near Venice. Its form most probably suited the sophisticated taste of the European nobility. There are similar mirrors in many manors and museum collections today.  
Unfortunately, the original owner is unknown.  
Exhibited in the Baroque salon of the permanent collection of Varaždin’s Gothic-Renaissance castle, the mirror, together with other items of the collection, present the visitor with the most representative trends and refined atmosphere of the Baroque period in Varaždin.

It is representative of the trends and refined atmosphere of the Baroque period in Varaždin.

1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.name: Cistercian Abbey of Zirc
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.alternate_name: Roman Catholic Church of the Virgin Mary
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.description:
The one-nave church, which was probably designed by Martin Wittwer (and according to some scholars, also Mátyás Kayr), is extended by side chapels and has a sanctuary that closes horizontally. The two western towers of the one-nave church were later extended. The western facade, which boasts both Baroque and Classical features, is richly articulated with pillars, statue-niches and windows, and decorated with coats of arms. In the gable niche of the facade is a statue of the Virgin Mary, while in the niches above the doors that lead to the towers, are the statues of St. Benedict and St. Bernard of Clairvaux. The three frescoes in the entrance hall are the work of József Wagenmeister from Pest, painted between 1744 and 1748. The main altar, donated by István Dubniczay, Prebendary of Veszprém, is sumptuously gilded and decorated with columns and statues. The main altarpiece painting, *Assumption of the Virgin Mary*, is by Franz Anton Maulbertsch of 1754. The oval painting on the Altar of the Holy Cross, *Mary Magdalene at the Cross*, is also probably by Maulbertsch.  
The opulently decorated furniture was carved mainly by Pauline masters from Pápa. The pulpit balustrade (the work of an unknown master) is decorated with scenes from the New Testament, including the *Nativity of Jesus*, the *Resurrection of Christ* and the *Coming of the Holy Spirit*. The richly carved organ case was painted and gilded by György Seidler, the last lay-brother artist.  
The internationally renowned 20-hectare Cistercian *arboretum*, which lies to south of the church and monastery, is a nature reserve.
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.short_description:
The Cistercian Abbey of Zirc, founded by King Béla III in the 12th century, was rebuilt between 1732 and 1752 using spolia from the medieval abbey. The 18th-century monastery was designed by Martin Wittwer, and probably the church as well. The two western towers of the one-nave church were later extended. The church is augmented with chapels and bears a sanctuary that closes horizontally. Franz Anton Maulbertsch painted the main altarpiece, and the frescoes are by József Wagenmeister. The opulently decorated furniture was carved mainly by Pauline masters from Pápa.  
The monastery houses an internationally renowned library.
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.type: Religious architecture, abbey, church and monastery
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, and local research.
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.bibliography:
Horvát, K., *Zirc története.* (History of Zirc) Zirci könyvek I., Veszprém, 1930.  
Aggházy, M., *A zirci apátság templomépítkezései a XVIII. században (The Construction of Zirc Abbey in the 18th century),* Veszprém, 1937.  
Hervay, F., *Zirc, apátsági templom*. (Zirc, abbey church), Tájak-Korok-Múzeumok Kiskönyvtára 681, Budapest, 2001.  
*A ciszterci rend Magyarországon és Közép-Európában. Művelődéstörténeti Műhely* (*The Cistercian Order in Hungary and in Central Europe: History of Civilization Workshop*) Rendtörténeti Konferenciák 5 (Conferences about the History of Order), Szerk. (ed. B. Guitman), Piliscsaba, 2009.
1fce59b9-d0b0-54a7-8ffa-375dc1810d52.history:
The Cistercian Abbey of Zirc was founded by King Béla III of the Árpád dynasty in the heart of the forests of Bakony in 1182. Construction of the monastery lasted several decades. The founding monks came to Zirc from Clairvaux, one of the most renowned mother monasteries of the Cistercian order.  
The Cistercian order, which had flourished in earlier times, began to wane from the 14th century in Hungary as well as elsewhere. After a brief recovery under the rule of King Mátyás Hunyadi, the order continued to decline during the wars against the Turks and Ottoman rule in Hungary. The deserted abbey of Zirc was requisitioned by the Abbey of Lilienfeld in 1659, which appointed Márton Ujfalussy a Lilienfeld monk of Hungarian origin, as the Abbot of Zirc in 1660. Following the assassination of Ujfalussy in 1678, the abbots of Lilienfeld bore the title of Abbot of Zirc as well, and Hungarian members of the order only attended Zirc as “administrators”.  
In 1699, the Cistercian Abbey of Heinrichau in Silesia (Henryków, Poland) was requisitioned by Zirc Abbey. Silesian settlers built houses in the village, and the monks from Heinrichau raised a small chapel, which was demolished during the Rákóczi uprising of the Hungarians against the Habsburgs (1703–1711). Between 1715 and 1718 a new wave of settlers arrived in Zirc. During this time the monks from Heinrichau were situated in nearby Pápa and, in 1723, built a temporary monastery in Zirc from where they supervised the construction of the Baroque building complex that began in 1726 on the basis of plans by Martin (Athanasius) Wittwer.  
The one-storey monastery was complete by 1732 and in the same year the foundation stone of the church was laid. The church, which was also probably designed by Martin Wittwer (and according to some scholars also Mátyás Kayr), was built using spolia from the medieval church. The walls, pillars, window traceries and the vaults of the east-side transept chapels were still standing at the time; the west gable was blown up in the winter of 1738. A Baroque statue of St. Emeric stands today on what remains of the lower section of one of the medieval pillars. The church was consecrated in honour of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary by Bishop Márton Padányi Bíró in 1752.  
The western towers of the church were extended in 1854, and the stone spires placed on top of them in 1858. The altarpieces and the furniture were finished in the 1750s. The interior frescoes, completed in the 1740s, were heavily repainted in the 19th century; they only regained their original 18th-century appearance during the restoration of 1997–2005.  
At first the church organ – made in Pozsony (Bratislava) in 1752 – was probably located in the sanctuary; then a second organ was designed for the organ-loft. In 1770 the organ-maker, Péter Peking, created a new organ for the sanctuary, which was repaired once in the 19th century and again in the 20th century. The organ has since been replaced several times and its lower structure restored under professional supervision.  
The 18th-century monastery was rebuilt and extended in the Classical style in the 19th century. Another storey was added to the west wing between 1844 and 1847.  At the same time, the two-storey east wing, the abbot's residence, library and the “Red Tower” were built. The Baroque library used to be located in the room above the vestry.  
Silesia fell under Prussian control in 1742; the Abbey of Heinrichau was dissolved by the Prussian government in 1810, and Zirc Abbey regained its independence in 1814. In 1923, Pope Pius XI founded the Zirc Congregation of the Cistercian Order. In 1948, all five schools run by the order were nationalised, and the monasteries dissolved in 1950. Since 1982, the church has borne the title “basilica minor”. In 1989, the monastic orders were reinstated in Hungary, and from 1990, monastic duties were also revived in Zirc. Between 1993 and 1997 the order began to reinstate their schools; in 1994 they had repossessed one-third of Zirc Abbey and by 2002 almost the whole building was once again used by the Cistercian order.

2043c44f-e8e2-56f7-8fad-60beada641c2.name: Cattedrale di San Pietro
2043c44f-e8e2-56f7-8fad-60beada641c2.description:
The façade has red bricks which emphasize the decorations in white Istrian stone. It is divided into two levels employing two gigantic Corinthian columns. The front of the building is crowned by a triangular pediment with three entrances. There is a large central window, flanked by the statues of Saints Peter and Paul on both sides.  
The bell tower, positioned on the southern side, was completed in the fifteenth century and incorporates the cylindrical tower of a former basilica, dating back to the end of the tenth century.  
The plan for the church follows the Jesuit outline: a hallway lined with chapels that open out onto the nave. Also lining the nave is a series of arches that alternate with wide pillars culminating in an eighteenth century choir in the middle. A barrel vault, flanked by buttresses, is supported by a rich entablature. The wide upper windows create a luminous atmosphere within the church.  
The richly decorated 16th century presbiterium is constructed on a Greek cross plan with three apses and a rectangular space proceeds the choir. It is covered by a groin vault supported by four large Corinthian columns. On the ceiling of the groin vault, above the main altar, is a fresco depicting *La Dimora Celeste* (“Paradise”) painted by Prospero Fontana in 1579. In the lunette above the altar is the *Annunciation* (1618) by Ludovico Carracci. The semi-dome above the apse has a painting of *Christ Handing the keys to Peter* by Cesare Aretusi and Giovanni Battista Fiorini (1579). The Bolognese artists Donato Creti, Marcantonio Franceschini, Vittorio Bigari, Antonio Rossi, Giuseppe Marchesi known as Sansone and Ercole Graziani painted the eighteenth century altarpieces.
2043c44f-e8e2-56f7-8fad-60beada641c2.short_description: St. Peter's cathedral, whose original nucleus dates back to the 11th century, was remodeled and rebuilt between the second half of the 16th century and the 18th century. The imposing interior, nearly as high as that of St. Peter's in Rome is richly decorated with stuccoes, marbles, gold, frescoes and other works of art. The church holds pictures by Prospero Fontana, Ludovico Carracci, Marcantonio Franceschini and Donato Creti, and a terracotta group of depicting the Mourning over the dead Christ by Alfonso Lombardi.

2043c44f-e8e2-56f7-8fad-60beada641c2.history:
The original Romanesque cathedral was most likely dated from the beginning of the eleventh century. It was destroyed by a fire in 1014 and rebuilt in the second half of the twelveth century. Work continued until the fifteenth century. In the second half of the sixteenth century the Archbishop Gabriele Paleotti began a new ambitious program of works beginning with the apse. In 1575, the architect Domenico Tibaldi built a new presbiterium. This was decorated a few years later by several painters: Cesare Aretusi, Giovan Battista Fiorini, Bartolomeo Cesi, Camillo Procaccini and Prospero Fontana.  
Later, Archbishop Alfonso Paleotti commissioned architect Pietro Fiorini to create a simplification of the original plan by Tibaldi by eliminating the number of columns and pilasters in the naves. Unfortunately, the structuring may have been faulty as the vaults of the church collapsed in 1599. In 1605, work started again following the plan of Giovanni Ambrogio Magenta, under the supervision of Floriano Ambrosini. In 1612, the work continued by master builder Nicolò Donati, who partly modified Magenta's ideas.  
Work stopped for ten years, from 1613 until 1731. In 1734, Cardinal Prospero Lambertini, later Pope Benedict XIV, asked the architect Alfonso Torreggiani to complete the church and to build its façade: the façade was finally finished in 1776 by the architect Francesco Tadolini.

204d3403-6441-5819-b1d0-984860476398.name: Rimanóczy Mansion
204d3403-6441-5819-b1d0-984860476398.description:
The mansion has two levels, the central bay of which is complete with a mansard. The central bay is only slightly abutting in the middle on the main (courtyard) façade, but the side pavilions on the garden facade explicitly jut out, thus making the base of the building slightly U-shaped. The mansard roof is covered with wooden shingle. The levels are separated with dividing cornices. The windows are rectangular except for the first-floor windows of the central risalit; the middle windows of the side pavilions on the main and garden façades are crowned by linear hood mouldings (curved). The space between the upper-level windows and their hood moulds is decorated with plaster-panel adornments.  
The building is entranced on the ground floor – in the central bay of the courtyard façade – through a basket-arched, stone-framed gate decorated with the coat of arms of the Esterházy family (which had owned the mansion since the 19th century). Next to the gate there is a large terrace upheld on columns with a balustrade, decorated with *putti* and vases. From the terrace, through French windows, the banqueting hall is accessible.  
Three high, half-circle arched windows break up the façade of the central bay divided up by pilasters with composite-headed capitals that reach up to the mansard over the gate. Above them are panels (two blind windows on the sides and a high relief *Madonna and Child* in the middle.  
The central bay, like the main façade, is divided up by composite-headed pilasters. Three openings divide the upper floor with wall panels above them (within the middle panel is the Rimanóczy coat of arms held by lions, and three rectangular fanlights to the mansard). The year of construction is inscribed in Roman numerals on the wall panel above the windows, and above this there is a segmented pediment that has another window mid-field, decorated with a vase adorned with a Sun motif and held by *putti* either side.  
A *sala terrena* is located on the ground floor of the central bay. A staircase decorated with stuccoes with a wrought-iron banister leads to the upper floor, where some rooms have stucco decorations, and a ceiling fresco can be found in the corner room of the northwest wing (*Pallas Athene/Minerva as Patron of the Arts and Sciences*).  
Most spectacular, however, is the banqueting hall with its ceiling fresco of the *Triumph of Apollo* and a representation of the *Four Continents* by an unknown artist. A series of oil-on-canvas portraits over the wooden panelling at door height on the side walls, praise the Habsburg dynasty and the Esterházy family: *Queen Maria Theresia*, *Roman Emperor Francis I*, *Emperor Joseph II*, *Marie Antoinette* and P*rince Nikolaus Esterházy*. According to some scholars, these are by Franz Anton Palko. The Pejacsevich family later had the portraits repainted to represent their own family members, but these were restored in the 1980s with their original iconography.  
The manor buildings further away from the main building have been extensively reconstructed.
204d3403-6441-5819-b1d0-984860476398.short_description: The Baroque Rimanóczy Mansion was commissioned for Antal Rimanóczy between 1739 and 1758. The ceiling of the banqueting hall is decorated with an exquisite fresco, *Apollo Riding His Chariot Across the Sky*.

204d3403-6441-5819-b1d0-984860476398.history:
(Zsira-) Gyüleviz became the property of the Rimanóczy family – who built the mansion – in the middle of the 17th century when a local landowner's daughter, Katalin Rátky, married István Rimanóczy. They had no children, therefore the estate and the small mansion standing on it was inherited by the Rimanóczy's children from his second marriage with Krisztina Chernel: by Boldizsár, and after his death in 1730, by Antal.  
The Rimanóczy family achieved nobility in 1646, and received the *prenom* “Rimanóczy” from Charles VI Emperor in 1734. The mansion was commissioned by Antal Rimanóczy, a councillor of the Hungarian Court Chancellery. Building probably began in 1739 as indicated below the pediment on the garden façade.  
The identity of the architect is still a matter for debate. Endre Csatkai (1939) searched for the architect among the pupils of Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt or Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach.  
The grandiose construction was beyond Rimanóczy's financial capability and the mansion was maintained only by mortgaging his estates. After his death in 1758, his heirs inherited so much debt they had to rent out a part of the estate in 1760 and mortgage the rest; in 1771 they even had to sell a part of it to Count János Draskovich. Count Antal Jankovich bought the mansion from the Draskovich family in 1776. It was then inherited by the Pejacsevich family, on the distaff side, through the marriage of Katalin Jankovich and Count János Pejacsevich in 1800. In 1806, Katalin Jankovich commissioned József Hild to prepare designs for reconstruction of the mansion, but work never began. The mansion was then sold by the Pejacsevich family to József János Ruston in 1890, and exchanged owners and lessees frequently until, finally, Princess Margit Esterházy bought it in 1922. She had it renovated along the lines of plans submitted by István Möller between 1923 and 1925, and also had the garden redesigned. In 1929, the princess married János Almásy. László Almásy, János's brother, was a good friend and hunting companion of the princess's brother Antal Esterházy. László Almásy was the real “English patient”: a famous Africanist, cartographer, hunter and pilot, and a frequent guest of the Esterházy family.  
In 1934, the Esterházy family sold the mansion to the Congregation of the Daughters of the Holiest Saviour (*Legszentebb Üdvözítő Leányai Kongregáció*) who instigated social institutions in the building beside their provincial centre. They transformed the ground floor *sala terrena* into a chapel. After the Dissolution of the Monasteries in 1950, the estate was nationalised. The Council of the capital took over management of it in 1951, first hosting a social centre and then a home for the mentally ill from 1975. The building was renovated between 1984 and 1987, and has been managed by The National Trust of Monuments for Hungary since 2008. The garden is a nature reserve.

20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.name: Zelená Hora, Church of St. John of Nepomuk
20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.description: The church construction combines two chief motifs, a tongue, and a five-pointed star, creating a unique building. The expansive intertwining shapes and movement of light provide it with a striking dynamism. Here, V. Vejmluva established a “spiritual mausoleum” for John of Nepomuk, a saint canonised in 1729, and whose cult became one of the most widespread in Central Europe.
20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.short_description: This pilgrimage church is one of the most remarkable buildings in Czech lands. It combines two main motifs: a tongue, and a five-pointed star. The expansive, intertwining shapes and movement of light provide the geometrical central building with a striking dynamism. The building mythologizes in visual form a previously insignificant place and presents its origin as a divine miracle. It was here that a learned abbot of the Cistercian Monastery established a “spiritual mausoleum” for John of Nepomuk, a saint canonised in 1729, and whose cult became one of the most widespread in Central Europe.

20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.history: The establishment of the church was associated with the upcoming beatification and canonisation of John of Nepomuk after his miraculously intact tongue had been found in his grave in St. Vitus Cathedral, Prague. The construction was initiated by V. Vejmluva, abbot of the nearby Cistercian Monastery, who named the hill above it after Zelená Hora, near Nepomuk, the martyr’s birthplace and the place from which the first Cistercians came to Žďár. In 1722 the church was consecrated and construction work continued with cloisters with five chapels and five gates. After the architect’s death, the complex was completed by F. B. Klíčník who was, like Santini, a member of the Penitent Brotherhood in the monastery which was founded in 1722.

20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.name: *Still-Life*
20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.description:
Baltazar Gomes Figueira was born and worked in Óbidos, although he studied in Seville where he worked with the great 17th-century Spanish painters Francisco Herrera, Zurbaran and Juan de Castillo. There he probably learned how to paint *bodegones*, a Spanish term given to both still-life and domestic interiors, and sometimes featuring kitchen scenes. This type of still-life painting was very much appreciated in the 16th century as a result of the growing artistic interest in scenes from daily life as well as an increased curiosity in the natural sciences. In the framework of the Baroque aesthetic, the still-life genre conveys transcendental values through the depiction of inanimate objects.  
The painting is composed of three elemental groups: on the left-hand side the fish lying on the bare table represent the four cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, strength and temperance. The fish, separated from the other parts of the painting, are immersed in an intense penumbra and illuminated with a luminous white.  
Lying on a light-green tablecloth are the other two groups: four dead birds – a sparrow, green woodpecker, duck and partridge – represent disrespect, human fragility and vice, lust and temptation. The grapes lying within this ensemble represent redemption of all these sins through the Eucharist.  
Finally, on the right-hand side on the tablecloth, are a silver plate and some regional pottery beside the confectionery and fruit, these elements are symbolic of abundance, sensual desire, prosperity and immortality. The combinations of the four elements in each group are inked with the Four Seasons, the Four Elements (Earth, Air, Water, Fire) and with the Four Principles of Human Existence (Mind, Body, Spirit and Soul).  
The vivid detail, seen in the realistic drops of water near the fish for example, draw attention to the magical *chiaroscuro* accentuated by thin, transparent layers of paint.
20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.short_description: This still-life depicting fish, birds, fruit, confectionery, silverware and pottery was probably painted by Baltazar Gomes Figueira. It reveals two opposing realities: the spiritual world symbolised by four fish and a bunch of grapes, and the earthly reality and its dangers embodied in four dead birds, fruit and confectionery.
20d7a54a-622f-5e96-bb49-b5ebfbee73fc.provenance: Has long been part of the permanent collection of Grão Vasco Museum

2187568a-30fb-56b8-a477-3f4a26e1478c.name: *Saint Philip Benizi in Glory*
2187568a-30fb-56b8-a477-3f4a26e1478c.description: In 1697 Domenico Maria Viani was summoned to Imola by the Servite fathers in order to paint three pictures for their church. One of them, depicting “the Virgin Mary and the patron saints of Imola” is no more extant, however we still have the “Saint Philip Benizi in Glory” and “the Saint Pellegrino Laziosi Healed by the Crucifix.” Viani worked in Imola for a year and a half on these paintings. With his saint Philip Benizi, the Bolognese painter entered his mature phase, combining the style of Guido Reni learned in his father’s workshop with the baroque language of another Bolognese painter, Domenico Maria Canuti and employing a Venetian palette with warm colours. The group of the saint with the angels is seen from below and it gives the impression of the image continuing outside of the frame. The painting has always been mentioned by guides and art historians as very beautiful. The sumptuous gilded frame was carved in 1710 by the Imolese sculptor Giuseppe Giuliani.
2187568a-30fb-56b8-a477-3f4a26e1478c.short_description: The painting was made in 1697 by the Bolognese painter Domenico Maria Viani for the Servite fathers of Imola. It is a mixture of classical academic culture and a fully baroque style. The carved frame was made by the Imolese sculptor Giuseppe Giuliani.
