22194311-6d0c-5e2e-9f09-3fbdfff9f68d.name: Blagovestenska (Annunciation) Church of the Blessed Virgin
22194311-6d0c-5e2e-9f09-3fbdfff9f68d.description:
The main facade of the one-nave church – articulated with wall columns and emphatic mouldings – is crowned with a tower. The main gate, framed by garlands and topped with a heavily projected drip moulding, is embraced by columns decorated with leaves and spirals that support a stone balcony. Behind the balcony, the blind, oval choir window with an arched moulding is visible, both sides of which there are two blind windows with staggered mouldings. Above its shoulder, the facade is decorated with volutes, vases and obelisks. In front of the bell windows, arched and *ajouré* stone balconies can be seen.  
The side facades of the church are articulated by pairs of wall columns and oval, arched and square-shape windows.  
To the left of the main gate is the red marmor tomb (with an inscription in Greek) of Demeter Tolojanne, a Greek merchant from Vác, who came to Szentendre from Macedonia and died in 1759 at the age of 48. Above the entrance are portraits of *St. Constantine* and *St. Helena* in an arch-shaped frame.  
The three vaulted sections of the church are covered by net-vaults, and the stone choir is covered by a sail vault.  The arcade under the choir is topped by a barrel vault. The walls of the nave are articulated by semi-columns, and decorated with frescoes of the *Life of Jesus*. The gilded pulpit of the bishop is decorated with a portrait of St. Nicholas.  
The Rococo iconostasis (icon screen), which separates the nave and the sanctuary and rises as high as the nave, is a painted oak structure. It is the work of Mihailo Živković (Mihály Zsivkovics), a Serbian painter from Buda and protégé of Dionisziosz Popović Bishop of Buda. The iconostasis dates to the 1790s (or c. 1802–1804 according to some scholars), and is separated in the middle by a moulding which creates two main parts. The lower part is further separated by columns into five fields, each holding a painting by Zsivkovics in a richly gilded frame. In the middle, on the Gate of the Tsars, are scenes from the *Annunciation*, and above the gate is a painting of the *Last Supper*. On the left-hand side above the Gate of the Tsars is the *Virgin Mary with the Infant Jesus*. At the bottom are scenes from the *Life of Jesus*. To the right, above the Gate of the Tsars, is *Jesus Giving Blessings* and at the bottom are more scenes from the *Life of Jesus*. On other sections of the iconostasis are *St. Stephen the Deacon*, the *Annunciation*, and *St. John the Golden Mouth*. In the upper section (above the moulding) are paintings of the *Holy Trinity* and *Virgin Mary*, framed by volutes. Portraits of the 12 Apostles are contained in gilt and *ajouré* medallions.  
The altar table in the sanctuary, which closes off three sides of a trapezium, is made from red marble; the preparatory table for receiving the sacrament is of coloured stone (1754). The gilt *Zopfstil* candleholder, the painted cross of the altar table and the church Evangeliary (the work of a goldsmith from Moscow) are outstanding works.  
The Neo-Classical (1797) Serbian Orthodox school building adjoins the northern side of the church. The building used to serve as a teacher-training school between 1812 and 1816, but was then converted into a museum.
22194311-6d0c-5e2e-9f09-3fbdfff9f68d.short_description: The Blagovestenska (Annunciation) Church of the Blessed Virgin was built between 1752 and 1754, and represents an outstanding example of Serbian Orthodox architecture in Hungary. Featuring elements of the Baroque and Rococo styles with a one-tower western façade, the church has an interior appropriate for Byzantine liturgy. The paintings of the richly carved and gilded iconostasis (icon screen) are the works of Mihailo Živković (Mihály Zsivkovics), a Serbian painter from Buda.

22194311-6d0c-5e2e-9f09-3fbdfff9f68d.history:
The expansion of Turkish influence in the Balkans propelled waves of Greek, Dalmatian, Bosnian and Serbian refugees to the Hungarian Kingdom. In 1691, King Leopold I issued a “letters patent” for the sake of the Serbs who fled and settled in Hungary. King Leopold wished them to settle only temporarily in Hungary while their country was under Turkish rule, but the occupation dragged on for an unexpectedly long period. By the end of the 18th century the number of Serbs began to decrease both in terms of the population and the magistracy of Szentendre, while at the same time, the proportion of Hungarians and Germans increased, so a Catholic town magistrate was selected for a year and replaced by an orthodox magistrate the following year.  
In the 17th century some 800 fugitive families, including several merchants, sought refuge in Szentendre. They constructed a church in 1690 under the supervision of Arsen Crnojević Patriarch of Ipek. The iconostasis of the simple wooden church paid homage to the *Blagovestenska* (Annunciation) and was painted by masters from the Balkans in 1721. The iconostasis was later transferred to the Church of Izbég.  
The foundation stone of today's church was laid in 1752 and was consecrated in honour of the Annunciation by Dionisije Novaković Bishop of Buda in 1754. The design of the church is attributed to András Mayerhoffer, on account of its similarity to the Serbian Church of Pest and the Cathedral of Kalocsa, both of which were designed by him. The iconostasis was completed between 1802 and 1804.  
The 1787 decree of King Joseph II made German the compulsory language in schools, and thus the town council of Szentendre had to provide German language education for both Catholic and Greek Orthodox schools. Construction of the schools was slow, however, and there was a suggestion that Blagovestenska Church be converted into a school, but King Joseph II rescinded his language decree before he died rendering the conversion unnecessary.

2262494d-b37b-5d68-a4ee-4d60e60fde10.name: Parish and Pilgrimage Church of the Assumption
2262494d-b37b-5d68-a4ee-4d60e60fde10.description: The Pilgrimage Church of the Assumption is essentially a work of local Tyrolean craftsmen, which brought with them a certain folk art influence, for example in the ceiling pictures. The original Late Gothic hall church with retracted choir can still be seen in a number of pointed arches. In contrast, the interior work is characterised by the beginnings of the Late Baroque style. The delicate ceiling stucco, influenced by the Wessobrunn school, frames relatively small fresco panels which are painted in bright colours. The ensemble of altars is also of striking quality, in particular the painting of the left hand-side altar from Peter Candid from Munich (c. 1610/20).
2262494d-b37b-5d68-a4ee-4d60e60fde10.short_description: The Kaltenbrunn Pilgrimage Church in Kaunertal, delightfully situated on a steep incline, is an especially beautiful example of a medieval site of pilgrimage which was given a new face in the Late Baroque period, largely by local artists. The Late Gothic building received a Baroque vault with a multi-part cycle of frescos and strapwork stucco. A chapel was specially built for the miraculous picture in the centre of the nave.
2262494d-b37b-5d68-a4ee-4d60e60fde10.bibliography:
Jäger, J., *Der marianische Wallfahrtsort Kaltenbrunn im Oberinntal. Ursprung und Geschichte der Wallfahrt*, 3rd edition, Innsbruck \[n.d.\].  
Gauss, U., *Andreas Thamasch 1639–1697*, Weißenhorn 1973, p. 22f.  
Rietzler, H., *Wallfahrtskirche Kaltenbrunn. Pfarrkirche Feichten*, Salzburg 2003 (= Christliche Kunststätten Österreichs, vol. 396).
2262494d-b37b-5d68-a4ee-4d60e60fde10.history: The origins of the pilgrimage, which is recounted in a legend, presumably date back to the 12th century. A knight from Schenkenberg is purported to have consecrated a stone church on the site in 1285 which burnt down in 1438. At the end of the 15th century, work on a new building was started and consecrated in 1502 (choir), i.e. 1582 (nave). The tower was completed in 1668. A Baroque redesign was carried out in the 17th and 18th century, the interior is essentially characterised by the fittings from about 1720/30. Elevated to the status of a parish in 1891, it was restored between 1977 and 1982.
2262494d-b37b-5d68-a4ee-4d60e60fde10.architects: Architecture (Chapel of Mercy): Gallus Gratl (1684–1751); stuccowork, attributed to: Anton Gigl (1700–1769), Augustin Gigl (dates unknown, active in the first half of the 18th century); ceiling and altar paintings: Franz Laukas (1690–1765); high altar figures: Andreas Kölle (1680–1755); crucifix: attributed to Andreas Thamasch (1639–1697)

22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.name: House of the Holy Body (Museum of Baroque)
22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.description:
The 17th/18th-century palace, of which Casa do Corpo Santo is part, is a fine example of Portuguese civil architecture.  
Casa do Corpo Santo has a patio – a space mediating between the outdoors and the indoors – with stairs to the first floor. The walls are covered with cobalt-blue *azulejos,* which continue up the staircase to the first floor. On the stairs a tile-painted welcoming figure features.  
There are two rooms decorated with cobalt-blue *azulejos* representing hunting scenes, aristocratic leisure scenes and examples of labour, inspired by European engravings.  
Both rooms have painted ceilings. In the larger, first room, the tempera painted wooden ceiling depicts a Portuguese Vessel (Nau) at its centre, a potent symbol of the activities of the Brotherhood. The second room is a chapel, within the first room. It too has a painted wooden ceiling depicting scenes from the Life of Saint Elmo. It has gold-leaf carvings that create the impression of a Portuguese Baroque church interior in miniature.
22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.short_description: Casa do Corpo Santo is a fine example of Baroque architecture, covered with *azulejos* (tile panels) thought to have been painted by the Tile-Painting Master P.M.P. The brick floor aligns with the figuratively painted *azulejos*, which are complemented by the painted ceiling and, in the small chapel, gold-leaf carvings that enhance the shrines inserted within the walls. The monument is an excellent example of space management during the Baroque era.
22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.method_for_datation: At the entrance to the monument the date, 1714, is recorded. The original 16th-century palace was dated by archaeological excavations.

22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.history:
The palace of the Cabedo Family dates to the 17th/18th centuries. It was built on the site of an existing palace erected during the 16th century, as recent archaeological excavations have revealed. The Cabedo family offered part of the palace built in the 17th century, known as Casa do Corpo Santo, to the Confraria do Corpo Santo as accommodation. When the Brotherhood was disbanded in the 19th century this building continued to accommodate nautical organisations. In the second half of 19th century it was linked to the Setúbal Franciscan Fishermen's Society and the House of the Holy Body Maritime Corporation Fund.  
The House of the Holy Body belongs to the City Hall and hosts a Museum.
22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.patrons: Setúbal’s Brotherhood of Fishermen, Navigators and Ship Owners was born in the 14th century; its Book of Pledges dates to 1340. The Confraria do Corpo Santo (Brotherhood of the Holy Body) is another name for St. Elmo, or St. Pedro Gonçalves, the patron saint of the shipwrecked, and the protector of sailors. The house has two paintings depicting St. Elmo, one of which is oil on canvas and the other oil on copper.
22f1f5f5-f8b6-5763-8b6f-64f59694c51d.architects: Architect unknown. Tiles signed by “P.M.P.” probably the signature of the Tile-Painting Master Padre Manuel Pereira (Father Manuel Pereira) whose dates are unknown.

23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.name:
Kremsmünster Abbey and Abbey Church  
Kremsmünster Abbey and Abbey Church Divine Saviour and Redeemer
23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.alternate_name:
Kremsmünster Abbey and Abbey Church Salvator Mundi  
Kremsmünster Abbey and Abbey Church St Agapitus
23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.description:
During the Baroque epoch there was a brisk construction activity in Kremsmünster. One started without overall plans, step by step, at the end of the 17th century. The abbey wing and the guest wing were the first to be built. In the former there are the two most representative rooms: the Imperial Hall (the stucco work and the emperors’ portraits were added later) and the Library. Even the fish pools and the pavilion (the Mosque) were built at the end of the 17th century. During this time they also began to baroquise the Roman church. It was enlarged and coated with a new interior shell, while the Western front was a totally new addition. The church’s completion lasted until the first decades of the 18th century.  
It was in the middle of the 18th century when for a long time the most remarkable building in Upper Austria arose: the observatory, a typical Age of Enlightenment institution.
23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.short_description: Unlike other monasteries where the abbots built huge abbey complexes in the Baroque era, the Benedictines from Kremsmünster erected new buildings only step by step. It began at the end of the 17th century with the abbey wing, the fish pools, the garden pavilion (Mosque) and the baroquisation of the Roman church. The building was enlarged and the outside and inside were coated with a new shell. The completion lasted until the first decades of the 18th century. As a typical building project of this era, the Age of Enlightenment, whose people started to take a big interest in natural science, the observatory arose.
23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.dates:
777: foundation of the monastery by Tassilo III, last Duke of Bavaria  
1232 until 14th century: erection of the church and monastery buildings  
beginning 17th century: construction of the new monastery buildings and baroquisation until about 1700  
1638–40: erection of the greenhouse for figs  
1640–41: construction of the so-called Mosque (pavilion)  
1680/1681: church’s West façade, stucco work in the church  
1682–86: most statues on the church’s altars  
1690–92: construction of the fish pools  
1696: fresco painting in the Imperial Hall  
1700–12: painting at high altar  
1712: high altar  
1717: extension of the fish pools  
1719: stucco work in the Imperial Hall  
1721: emperors’ portraits in the Imperial Hall  
1748–59: construction of the observatory

23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.history:
Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria, to whose empire the Traungau (= the region around Kremsmünster) belonged, gained victory over the Slavs at the end of the 8th century. His wish to christianise them was the reason for founding the monastery. But there is another version of the story. According to a popular legend, Tassilo’s son Gunther was killed when hunting. The father came to guard his son's corpse in the night when a stag appeared and requested him to build a church and a monastery on the very place.  
This was followed by years of economic prosperity but also by raids, fire, loss and again by economic upswing. Like in many other religious communities, the epoch of the Reformation brought a decline. With the help of the emperor new and strong abbots were appointed, the monastic community increased, and a flourishing Baroque era could begin. Two abbots started the baroquisation of the monastery complex and added buildings such as the fig house and the pavilion, the fish pools and an observatory, Kremsmünster´s widely visible landmark. The Reform-Kaiser Josef II tried, of course, to close the community, but that was successfully averted by the abbot. During the Second World War the abbey was confiscated by the Gestapo. This didn’t dissuade the monks having their daily choral prayer in the church.
23195b9e-4d5c-54a6-af53-182de36033e4.patrons: Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria founded the monastery in 777 following the defeat of the Slavs.

23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.name: *St. Augustine*
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.description:
The monumentally proportioned, diagonally placed figure of Bishop St. Augustine dominates the work taking up almost two-thirds of the canvas. St. Augustine is sitting back, with one leg stretched out and the other bent at the knee. The Bishop is dressed in luxurious vestments and holds a burning heart in one hand, while with the other, he is writing in an open book. His bishop's mitre is also on the table. Behind his back there is a bookshelf, while on the other side, like a vision, is a rendering of the Holy Trinity.  
St. Augustine, a Bishop and Doctor of the Church, one of the four Latin Doctors, played a very important iconographic role in the Pauline order. Although the Paulines existed in the Middle Ages, they were formerly organised as an order in the High Middle Ages, living under the rules of St. Augustine. The choice of saints in Pauline iconography are not random, each figure symbolises a particular Pauline characteristic.  
This painting is by one of the greatest Pauline painters, Ivan Ranger. Born in Tyrol he joined the Pauline order as a trained lay brother-painter.
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.short_description: In this painting by the Pauline painter, Ivan Ranger, the Bishop St. Augustine is shown with his attributes of a burning heart, a book and a mitre. *St. Augustine* was painted for the Pauline Monastery in Lepoglava.
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.holder: Diocese Museum of the Zagreb Archdiocese
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.initial_owner: Pauline monastery in Lepoglava, Hrvatsko zagorje
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.method_for_datation: Research of the work of the Pauline painter, Ivan Ranger.
23450be7-55b2-508c-9b67-5501474d0bde.obtention: Founded in Zagreb in 1939, the Diocesan Museum’s remit was to preserve the country’s movable religious heritage that had become redundant. Gifted to the museum in 1940, prior to this, the work was in the sacristy of Lepoglava Parish Church, formerly the church of the Pauline Monastery, until the abolition of the order by decree of the Habsburg Emperor Joseph II in 1786.

2361bbd4-12bf-5fe1-a175-763b13784a3d.name: Chapel of Bones in the Old Convent of St. Francis, Évora
2361bbd4-12bf-5fe1-a175-763b13784a3d.description: In spite of its scarce artistic value this chapel remains a popular tourist attraction for visitors to Évora. The setting prevails: a room full of bones geometrically arranged on the walls, vaults and columns with hardly a vacant space. Meticulously arranged, the bones – mostly tibias and fibulas as well as series of skulls, are wainscoting the walls. This fact allows the building to acquire a look of a cave or a forbidden space, and offer visitors an unexpected proximity to the evidence of DEATH, which, thus, is, offered as a spectacle. Even at an international level, the Chapel of Bones is the most visible face of a popular reality throughout all the catholic countries – namely in Italy and Spain with some similarities or replicas in Portugal – as in Monforte, Campo Maior, Faro and Alcantarilha.
2361bbd4-12bf-5fe1-a175-763b13784a3d.short_description: A room with a quadrangular plan, square columns and a vaulted ceiling, located next to the old Chapter Room in the Convent of St. Francis in Évora. From the 17th century onwards the room was decorated completely – on the columns, vaults and walls – with bones in a fashion similar to “shell-work”.
2361bbd4-12bf-5fe1-a175-763b13784a3d.bibliography:
Esperança, Frei M. da, , *Historia Seráfica da Ordem dos Frades Menores de São Francisco na Provincia de Portugal*, Lisbon, Officina Craesbeeckiana, 1656.

Louro, Pe. Henrique da Silva, *Capelas de Ossos na Arquidiocese de Évora*, Évora, 1992.

2361bbd4-12bf-5fe1-a175-763b13784a3d.history: Taking advantage of the room behind the Chapter House in the enormous St. Francis Convent (partially destroyed in the 19th century), the friars decided to set up an iconographic programme displaying the values of Death by way of an organic shell-work like decoration. There is a dry, mummified corpse hanging on one wall possibly to add momentum to the macabre setting. According to anthropological analysis, around 5000 individual remains are recorded here. These were all removed from the graveyard of the convent which once also served the people of Évora.
2361bbd4-12bf-5fe1-a175-763b13784a3d.patrons: Religious Order of St. Francis (17th–18th centuries)

237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.name: Church of St. Lourenço de Almancil
237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.description:
The Pilgrimage Church of St. Lourenço de Almancil is built on pure geometric volumes. Its sober façades with simple, shaped openings are bordered with local limestone. The roof is covered with clay tiles. The exterior, like the cupola, is painted white, influenced by Arab models. There are some cobalt-blue *azulejos* on the exterior walls. The baroque design of the churchyard and doorway are surprisingly elaborate.  
Inside, the gilt, carved wood altar structure of the retable, with its characteristic Solomon temple columns, was built by Manuel Martins, who also carved the arch of the sacristy. Cobalt-blue tiles cover the interior walls, ceiling and cupola, submerging the visitor immediately in their ambiance on entering the church.  
It is probable that Policarpo de Oliveira Bernardes of Lisbon signed the tile panels, indicating his pride in this unique work. Bernardes belonged to a family of painters that specialised in perspective paintings on walls and ceilings. Rather than fresco, tile painting techniques are used here, the designs taken from Andrea Pozzo's book of perspective designs. The architectural *trompe l'œil* was intended to create a fantastic spectacle of Italianate buildings and landscapes which allowed the viewer to forget the earthly space they were in.  
The subject of the tile painting is the Life, Death and Coronation of St. Laurence. Born in Spain, St. Laurence was a martyr in Rome.  
Cobalt blue on a white background shows the European taste in Chinese porcelain at the time. It was first traded in Europe by the Portuguese, and influenced the colours of Portuguese Baroque tile work known as *azulejos*.
237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.short_description: The Church of St. Lourenço (Laurence) of Almancil is an example of Portuguese vernacular architecture. Inside, the walls, ceiling and cupola are covered with cobalt-blue painted and glazed tiles. The walls are adorned with *azulejos* depicting the story of the Life and Death of St. Laurence. The ceiling and cupola are decorated with *azulejos* with Italianate architectural themes in perspective. The carved, gilt- wood high altar retable, in the shape of a pyramidal throne, has massive columns decorated with *putti*, angels, foliage and birds.

237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.history: In the 18th century, the Algarve Bishops felt it necessary to increase the religious faith of the locals of Almancil. When water was discovered near a pilgrimage chapel dedicated to St. Laurence, it was seen as a miracle and a sign to rebuild the chapel. The patron of the church was the General Vicar of the Algarve Bishopric District, who also had responsibility for the Brotherhood of St. Lourenço dos Matos, his name and date (1730) are inscribed on the cupola tiles.

24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.name: *Annunciation*
24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.description:
The painting, a *bozzetto* (study), was acquired by the Italian State in 1915 as the work of Giaquinto. Over the years, it was attributed variously to different artists in the Neapolitan area, but in 1958 the small canvas was deemed definitively to be the work of the Puglian artist. After a stay of several years in Naples, Giaquinto moved between Rome, Turin and Madrid, where he worked as the head painter to the court of Ferdinand VI, becoming an outstanding exponent of the European Rococo style. In Rome, the artist had developed the Baroque tradition, adopting the magnificence and refinery of its forms and the colours of that artistic language, using it to reveal the truth behind feelings.  
The study is generally dated between 1753 and 1762 (the years he was working in Spain) on account of his artistic characteristics of that period, when the artist was using rapid, highly fluid brushstrokes to paint luminous, elegant and at times iridescent colours. These forms and colours made the painter one of the best known in the world, and even had an influence on the young Goya.  
The artist builds a scene that resembles a theatre: in the background, beneath the dove of the Holy Spirit, the cherubs observe from on high, as if from a box. Beneath the clouds, a large green cloth forms one wing of the obliquely set architecture. Beneath the rays of divine light, the Virgin Mary lifts her face towards the Angel Gabriel who appears on high, wrapped in a soft swirl of yellow cape, clouds and cherubs.  
The few domestic objects elegantly arranged around the “stage” relate the divine intervention to a simple, recognisable scene from daily life, bringing the believer closer and making him more involved.  
The canvas was thought to be the study for the painting showing the Archangel Gabriel that is part of an *Annunciation* kept at the Szépmuűvészeti Múzeum in Budapest. It has also been linked with the altarpiece in the Annunciata Church in Todi, and with that in the Church of the Hospital of the Brothers of Mercy in Graz.
24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.short_description: This is a decorative *bozzetto* for the Royal Palace in Madrid (Giaquinto moved to Spain in 1753). The dramatic arrangement of the figures is typical of the Neapolitan school. Giaquinto moved to Rome in 1723 and stayed there for 30 years. During this time he was close contact with the Italian painters Sebastiano Conca, Pietro da Cortona and Giovanni Battistta Gaulli.
24150312-4b63-5263-a2a6-f674be030d7d.obtention: Acquired by the Italian State in 1915.

2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.name: *Taking of Christ*
2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.description: The painting is one of a group of works confiscated from the workshops of the painter in 1607 on the orders of Paul V, and subsequently transferred to the collection of cardinal-nephew Scipione Borghese as a gift from the Pope. It is one of the most famous paintings of the Cavalier d'Arpino because of the chromatic quality and the complexity of the composition. It shows Christ being taken to the Garden of Gethsemane according to evangelical accounts, which also describe some peripheral episodes. At the centre of the scene is the figure of Christ, who stands out in the luminous glow of the torches and appears to emit his own light. In the bottom right, Peter holds his knife aloft, about to cut off the ear of the high priest's servant Malchus. On the left-hand side we see a perfect diagonal line traced between the figures running after the naked boy in the foreground. Notably, this latter was taken by the painter from a lost painting by Correggio (c. 1489–1534), which he may have seen first-hand during a trip to Parma. The composition and the attitudes of the figures express the taste of late Roman Mannerism, of which the artist was the best exponent during the 16th and 17th centuries. Beneficiary of the major commissions of the time, including primarily those placed by Pope Clement VIII Aldobrandini, Arpino headed the most important workshop in Rome, where a young Caravaggio worked having recently arrived from Lombardy. The high drama imparted by the sense of isolation around the figure of Christ, highlighted by flashes of light, was an essential focus of study and inspiration for Caravaggio's *Martyrdom of St. Matthew* produced a few years later for the Contarelli Chapel of the Church of San Luigi dei Francesi (1599–1602).
2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.short_description: This painting was considered “the most beautiful work by the Cavalier” (Bellori). Giuseppe Cesari was involved in some of the most important commissions of the time, including for Pope Clement VIII Aldobrandini. He owned the most important workshop in Rome in the late 16th century, where a young Caravaggio also worked soon after his arrival from Lombardy. Here he developed the still lives of his formative years, studying the issue of light in great depth. This work inspired Caravaggio's *Martyrdom of St. Matthew*.
2419c403-644a-5025-b2b0-f52545267a7a.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

24a6db52-11e5-5732-80c1-3183d123cf55.name: Academy Church of St. Catherine
24a6db52-11e5-5732-80c1-3183d123cf55.description:
The construction of the Jesuit Church of St. Catherine, Zagreb, marked the start of the Baroque period in inland Croatia. It was erected as part of a much larger complex on a prominent site alongside the city walls, and in its very positioning in the town plan heralded a new age. More relevant than that, however, for the development of Baroque architecture, are its architectural features.  
Like the home church of the Society – Il Gesù in Rome – St. Catherine's was a longitudinal, barrel-vaulted nave church with side chapels and lofts. However, the design for the chapels between the wall columns is connected to the Central European Late Gothic tradition of interior buttresses – *Wandpfeiler* – that at the beginning of the 17th century underwent an Early Baroque transformation thanks to the master builder Hans Alberthal. As in the paradigmatic Alberthal church in Dilingen, in St. Catherine's Zagreb, the wall columns are the main element of internal articulation (with Corinthian capitals and sections of architrave), the walls being used for the altars, which, setting the stage towards the sanctuary, give the hall-church interior its Early Baroque dynamic.  
It was in accordance with this stylistic and typological determination that the first facade was designed (it was replaced after the 1880 earthquake with a historicist facade). But along with the Early Baroque articulation of the surface with superimposed Tuscan pilasters and cornices, and with an effective stone portal (the portal re-incorporated into today's façade), the structure of the building along with evidence from historical sources, shows that that the original design included two *campanile*s, which were, however, abandoned during construction. Thus the Jesuit church in Zagreb, with its primarily south German spatial organisation, also corresponded with other churches of the Habsburg monarchy, which during the 17th century were characterised precisely by facades with two *campanile*s. Indeed St. Catherine's preceded the most important of these churches: the Jesuit church in Vienna, as well as that to which it is most related, the Jesuit church in Trnava.  
With its organisation of volume and space, St. Catherine's was the model for a number of Croatian churches, which placed Croatian Early Baroque architecture in the top-ranking Central European constructions of the time.
24a6db52-11e5-5732-80c1-3183d123cf55.short_description: The Academy Church of St. Catherine in Zagreb was the first religious Jesuit building in Croatia. The design has an international character: the Early Baroque spatial arrangement derived from a distinctive south German hall-type of church with internal buttresses and side chapels on which, at the time, the master builder, Hans Alberthal elaborated. By contrast, the Early Baroque façade, originally designed with two *campanile*s or bell towers, would have allowed St. Catherine's an elevated position within the hierarchy of Jesuit religious buildings of the Habsburg monarchy, preceding even the most important of them in Vienna and Trnava.

24a6db52-11e5-5732-80c1-3183d123cf55.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents, archival plans and stylistic features.

The foundation stone was laid in 1620, and the completed building was consecrated in 1632. St. Catherine obtained the status of an Academy Church when the Society was dissolved in 1773.

255d46e7-702d-567d-a268-09af7f2f4b6d.name:
Former Monastery Church Spital am Pyhrn  
Parish Church dedicated to the Ascension of Maria Spital am Pyhrn
255d46e7-702d-567d-a268-09af7f2f4b6d.alternate_name: Dom am Pyhrn/Dome located on the Pyhrn
255d46e7-702d-567d-a268-09af7f2f4b6d.description:
It is not surprising that Provost Heinrich Fürsten who was a typical baroque (ecclesiastical) prince replaced the Gothic church with a new one. Johann Michael Prunner built the edifice with the stone-faced façade, (almost) unique in Austria, and with two high and narrow towers, crowned by onion-shaped roofs and patriarchal crosses.  
The church´s interior was planned by Domenico Antonio Carlone. He did the stucco work and the colouring in the nave (white walls, white pilasters with grey capitals, fields in soft colours on balustrade and in the vault). The whole concept may go back to Provost Fürsten as everything in the nave is working up to a climax in the sanctuary: the slight convex balustrades in the gallery that look like theatre boxes are swinging towards, the pilasters are marbled there, the capitals gilded and the walls painted. The sanctuary is likewise a stage (Jesuit theatre was very popular then) with the huge fresco as stage design.  
Under Provost Fürsten´s successors the artistic decoration was carried on. Andreas Ferdinand Lindemayr made the polychrome separating grid, Martin Johann Schmidt and Michelangelo Unterberger did the paintings on the six side-altars and Veit Königer created the high-altar as well as the statue of St John of Nepomuk (opposite the richly decorated pulpit).  
The church´s artistic highlights are the fresco paintings in the sanctuary by Bartolomeo Altomonte (figural painting) and Francesco Messenta (illusionistic painting) as well as those on the Schutzengelkapelle´s (Chapel dedicated to the Guardian Angels) and sacristy´s ceiling by Wolfgang Andreas Heindl.
255d46e7-702d-567d-a268-09af7f2f4b6d.short_description:
The former monastery church was built and decorated in the baroque era under three provosts. Every builder commissioned well-known artists who achieved together an acknowledged work of art: Johann Michael Prunner, the architect, erected one of the few stone-faced buildings in Austria (most are plastered and coloured) and created a dynamic interior with curvilinear galleries and huge recessed windows above.  
Bartolomeo Altomonte and Francesco Messenta did the fresco painting in the choir that is considered to be one of the most important illusionistic paintings in Austria. The expressive ceiling frescoes in the Schutzengelkapelle (=Chapel dedicated to the Guardian Angels) and in the sacristy were painted by Wolfgang Andreas Heindl. Veit Königer, who was proven an important representative sculptor, created the marble high altar and the statue of John of Nepomuk opposite the pulpit.

255d46e7-702d-567d-a268-09af7f2f4b6d.history:
Emperor Henry II founded the diocese Bamberg in 1007, made it a territorial principality and appointed it to a free German bishopric. The prince-bishops were given the land on the Pyhrn under the condition to secure the road and to build a hospice/hostel there. The travellers, in particular the pilgrims, on the then-frequent route from German lands to the Adriatic Sea needed a rest in winter before crossing the Pyhrn Pass.  
About 200 years later the hostel became a collegiate monastery for secular canons. In the Baroque era it was appointed provostry. The provosts built then a new abbey edifice and a new church.  
Another 200 years later, the monastery was dissolved by Emperor Franz II/I. The former monastery church became the parish church. For some reason the emperor passed the property into the ownership of Benedictines from Baden-Württemberg whose monastery had been dissolved three years earlier. The religious stayed for two years and then moved on to Carinthia. The Spital manor was incorporated into the religious fund´s property and has served thenceforth until 2015 as office and administrative building and accommodation. After almost 1000 years it houses a ho(s)tel again.

26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.name: Bottle
26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.description:
In 1580 Portugal came under the rule of the Spanish Kings, giving rise to a new political situation that altered the traditional commercial relationship with both Portugal's European trading neighbours and the Far East. A deep political and economic crisis emerged and the pottery workshops of Lisbon searched for new markets. Blue Chinese porcelain, common during the Wanli period (1573–1619), was an inspiration for Portuguese faience. The wares were then exported via existing Portuguese trade routes to overseas colonies and north and north-western Europe.  
This bottle – with a flattened circular body – has a cylindrical neck and a trapezoidal foot. The neck is finished in copper. It has a lid, indicating that it would have been used as a drinking vessel. The shape, which was rare in China, is probably based on a metal model from western Asia.  
Painted in several shades of blue, the front bears the coat of arms of Philip II of Spain: a medallion with flowers sprouting out from a border of dots. On the reverse are more blooms and insects. Both sides have a blue border with dots in a darker shade, probably imitating the nails used in the metal models that inspired it.  
According to Howard and Ayers (1978), the coat of arms of King Philip II was copied from a coin. It is not clear how the piece was commissioned, however, because Spain had limited access to China via the Philippines through Formosa in the 1570s and, in around 1580 for a year, via some land granted in Pinal near Macao. Michel Beurdeley (1962) believes that Philip II had a collection of almost 3,000 Chinese porcelain objects.
26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.short_description: A porcelain bottle with the coat of arms of King Philip II of Spain. It was inspired in both shape and decoration by a pilgrim’s flask, a precious and much coveted object of the 16th century that was used to hold drinking water when on pilgrimage.

269581cb-ed2d-5f80-9d11-a0df2cebbab8.name: Saint Mary and Corbinian Cathedral
269581cb-ed2d-5f80-9d11-a0df2cebbab8.description: Situated on a hill above the town, the cathedral with its two towers is widely visible. From the outside, nothing indicates the Baroque splendour of the interior – the simple Romanesque exterior remains intact to this day. On the other hand, the interior unites all phases of construction and style to create a unique composition, which accounts for Freising Cathedral’s fame: the two arcades, forming the wall of the middle nave, are united my means of colossal pilasters. An entablature separates the wall from the vault, and, on the other hand, offers a stylistic bridge to the ribs of the vault, where finally, the Asam’s Rococo stuccowork unfolds in full splendour.
269581cb-ed2d-5f80-9d11-a0df2cebbab8.short_description: In two major phases, the medieval substance of the venerable cathedral of the Bavarian diocese Freising was transformed into one of the most splendid Baroque churches in Bavaria. The result is an outstanding unification of various levels of style, mainly due to the lush, all-embracing decorations of the brothers Cosmas Damian and Egid Quirin Asam.
269581cb-ed2d-5f80-9d11-a0df2cebbab8.dates: 1621–1626: first Baroque modernisation; 1723/24: second Baroque modernisation

Jahn, P. H., “Hans Krumppers Kuppelprojekt für den Freisinger Dom und die venezianischen Wurzeln der Münchner Architektur um 1600”, *Münchner Jahrbuch der Bildenden Kunst* 53, Munich 2002, pp. 175–222.  
Elsen, A., Höck, M., Benker, S., *Der Mariendom zu Freising. Konkathedrale des Erzbistums München und Freising* (Kleine Kunstführer 200, 10. Auflage), Regensburg 1994.  
Götz, U., *Kunst in Freising unter Fürstbischof Johann Franz Eckher 1696–1727, Ausdrucksformen geistlicher Herrschaft*, Munich/Zürich 1992, pp. 81–203, 260–8, 279–83.  
*1250 Jahre geistliche Stadt*, vols. I–II (Diözesanmuseum für christliche Kunst des Erzbistums München und Freising, Kataloge und Schriften 9 and 12), Munich 1989/94; vol. I, pp. 16–25, 30–40, 97, 210–12; vol II, pp. 282–99.
269581cb-ed2d-5f80-9d11-a0df2cebbab8.history: The history of the Cathedral of Freising goes back far into the Middle Ages – even the current structure is based on the five-nave, originally flat-roofed (1481–83 the nave was vaulted) Romanesque basilica. In 1621 the interior was modernised for the first time according to plans of Hans Krumpper. The wall structure still dates from this time. The final shape was given to the cathedral in 1724, when Bishop Johann Franz Eckher assigned the brothers Cosmas Damian and Egid Quirin Asam with the renewal of the presumably dilapidated church, on the occasion of the 1000th anniversary of the foundation of the diocese by St. Corbinian. This anniversary coincided with two personal jubilees for Bishop Eckher: He celebrated his 30th anniversary as bishop and his 50th as priest. The rebuilding of the cathedral can therefore be seen as a project for the personal prestige of a minor Bavarian noble whose intention was to confirm his claim to power and standing.

26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.name: Helblinghaus
26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.description: The five-storey corner building, prominently located at the junction of the upper and lower city squares, is an especially splendid example of the Baroque redesign of older Tyrolean buildings. The decorative elements of the Late Gothic townhouse, of which there are remnants, were largely replaced by the contemporary strapwork stucco which is to be found nowhere else in Innsbruck. The narrow side, framed by two corner bay widows, is the main façade and encompasses three window axes as opposed to five on the side façade.
26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.short_description: Essentially a typical Innsbruck townhouse of the late Middle Ages, whose magnificent Late Baroque façades were designed by the stucco mason Anton Gigl of the Wessobrunn school. The opulent vegetative and figurative ornamentation form a rich decor extending across the storeys and window axes.
26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.dates: Built in the 15th century, baroque redesign with stuccowork façade: c. 1730
26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.bibliography:
*Österreichische Kunsttopographie* vol. 38, 1, edited by Johanna Felmayer, Vienna 1972, pp. 163–72.  
Schnell, H., Schedler, U., *Lexikon der Wessobrunner*, Munich, Zurich 1988, p. 125.
26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.history: The original builder of the residential building, whose substance essentially originates from the 15th to 16th century, is unknown. There were numerous changes of ownership during the 16th and 17th centuries until it was purchased in 1725 by Johann Fischer, cashier of the mint in Hall. Baroque redesign took place in around 1730, and the residence remained in the possession of the Fischer family until 1777. At the start of the 19th century the property was in the hands of the family Helbing (or Hölbing), who ran a cafe on the premises.
26c1489b-c2e7-5be3-a2bf-7cb92673ce68.patrons: Johann Fischer, cashier of the mint in Hall

26c5f036-09c9-5bc4-82eb-9d7937324a0d.name: Galleria del Legato
26c5f036-09c9-5bc4-82eb-9d7937324a0d.description: The decorations of the vault are comprised of painted, illusionistic columns and pillars that stand on false parapets or balustrades. These decorations give the impression of resting on a genuine plaster cornice. They support a coffered ceiling with vaults, arches and false windows over a high pediment. On the walls large painted frames, designed to hold paintings, are interposed by monochrome niches with false statues, representing allegorical female figures. Above the doors are large oculi with decorated frames, flanked by monochrome putti. Ancient style busts are depicted inside. Some stylistic discordances suggest that this was the work of more than one artist as can also be deduced from the archival sources.
26c5f036-09c9-5bc4-82eb-9d7937324a0d.short_description: The room is located on the ground floor of the Palace, in the wing which was formerly the summer residence of the Papal Legates. Although not very well-known to the public it is a fundamental example of  Bolognese prospective “quadratura”. According to stylistic analysis and archival sources the attribution to Girolamo Curti known as “Il Dentone” (1575-1632) and to Angelo Michele Colonna (1604-1687) seems the most plausible.
26c5f036-09c9-5bc4-82eb-9d7937324a0d.method_for_datation: The architectural perspective of the ceiling recalls the style of Dentone, although Angelo Michele Colonna, in his self-written list of works, records working in a gallery for the Cardinal Santacroce on the ground floor of the Public Palace. Stylistic differences in the decorations lead us to hypothesize that several separate artists worked on the room over a long period of time. For example, a partially erased fresco depicting the bees of the Barberini could refer to the time when Cardinal Maffeo Barberini was Legate of Bologna (1611–1614).
26c5f036-09c9-5bc4-82eb-9d7937324a0d.bibliography:
Feinblatt, E., “Contributions to Girolamo Curti”, *The Burlington Magazine*, CXVII, 1975, pp. 342-353.  
Sjostrom, J., *Quadratura. Studies in italian ceiling painting*, Stockholm, 1978, p. 53.
26c5f036-09c9-5bc4-82eb-9d7937324a0d.history:
The north wing of the Palace dates to the 15th century. It was completed during the next century by various architects including: J. Barozzi da Vignola and G. Alessi. Ancient guide books attribute the decoration of this room to Girolamo Curti known as “Il Dentone” (1575–1632) whereas other sources mention Angelo Michele Colonna together with Agostino Mitelli. It seems plausible that Colonna and Mitelli contributed to this work after Curti's death (1632), following his preparatory designs. The decorations on the walls probably date to after the vault itself. The “Sala Urbana”, located on the second floor, was created in 1630 by Colonna with the help of “Il Dentone” himself. It was commissioned by Cardinal Bernardino Spada in honour of Pope Urban VIII.  
Forty years later the aged Colonna collaborated with the young Gioacchino Pizzoli to create the Galleria del Senato.

270888be-383f-5228-8d60-8d3b17284391.name: *View of the Monastery and Riverbank in Belém*
270888be-383f-5228-8d60-8d3b17284391.alternate_name: *View of the Beach and the Monastery in Belém*
270888be-383f-5228-8d60-8d3b17284391.description:
This painting is an admirable *veduta*, showing two outstanding building projects undertaken during the reign of King D. Manuel I (r.1495–1521): the Belém Tower and the Jerónimos Monastery.  
The *veduta* is in the mid-17th century genre style. The scene depicts the “da Bola” fountain in Lisbon, the meeting point for these picturesque figures.  
The Monastery's surroundings have changed considerably: the riverbank was much closer to the monastery and the beachside palace was where nowadays the Cultural Centre of Belém stands. Visible on the horizon is the Tower of Belém.  
The painting is historically significant, documenting the architectural changes to the monastery, such as the new façade of the monks' dormitory which had just been re-designed. Moreover, between the church and the dormitory, it is possible to see the now absent Kings' Room (*Sala dos Reis*). Contrarily, the cupola of the 1870s, still extant today, had not yet been built.  
A member of the St. Lucas Brotherhood until 1675, Filipe Lobo was active in the first half of the century. The similarity between his work and the *vedute* of the Dutchman, Dirk Stoop (the Hague, Mauritshuis), is noted. Dirk Stoop was a court painter and lived in Portugal for several years (1659–1662). He accompanied the Portuguese Princess D. Catarina of Braganza on her voyage to England to marry Charles II.
270888be-383f-5228-8d60-8d3b17284391.short_description: This painting is an admirable *veduta*, showing two outstanding building projects carried out during the reign of King D. Manuel (1495–1521): the Belém Tower and the Jerónimos Monastery.

27a151e4-bd94-52f6-b538-2f4bcdf9c778.name: *Madonna and Child with St. Anne (dei Palafrenieri)*
27a151e4-bd94-52f6-b538-2f4bcdf9c778.description:
The painting was conceived as an altarpiece for the Chapel of the Confraternity of the Papal Grooms (who following the abolition of horseback retinues had the privilege of accompanying the Pope during ceremonies) located in Saint Peter's Basilica. Commissioned in 1605, it was delivered shortly afterward and placed on the altar, before being immediately removed and transferred to the nearby Church of St. Anne, protector of the Confraternity.  
Caravaggio was paid a meagre sum, which was increased by Cardinal Scipione Borghese, who purchased the canvas for his city residence. This masterpiece was famously refused by the Confraternity, which disapproved of the realism used in the portrayal of their patron, whose name (“Anne”) means “Grace” in Hebrew, her daughter Mary and the Baby Jesus, all in a simple background barely illuminated by a single ray of light.  
The painting highlights the role of Anne as the creator; she who destroys “evil” and the role of the Virgin Mary who, with Jesus, crushes the head of the serpent, the symbol of sin. The subject also touched on the debate of the Immaculate Conception, in relation to Mary as a person, conceived without original sin (the dogma was not settled until 8 December 1854) and was therefore central to the dispute that split Catholics and Protestants at the time. The combination of these elements, in particular the extreme humanisation with which Caravaggio depicted the Holy Family, resulted in the judgement that the work was not sufficiently decorous for a representation of holy subjects, particularly at the time of the Counter-Reformation.  
A recent restoration has thrown new light on the technique used by the artist, who did no preparatory drawings. Indeed, the analyses carried out have shown some limited traces of incisions around the figures.
27a151e4-bd94-52f6-b538-2f4bcdf9c778.short_description: This painting was commissioned by the Confraternity of the Papal Grooms for the Sant’Anna Chapel located in Saint Peter’s Basilica. Considered to be lacking in decorum, it was removed after a month to the nearby Church of St. Anne in the Vatican, and later displayed in Cardinal Scipione Borghese’s collection. The religious theme is dealt with in an innovative, strongly humanised way. Caravaggio’s use of light greatly influenced his contemporaries, even the more classical painters. This work is an example of the contrast between the artistic views of the Counter-Reformation and uninhibited taste of the collector.

27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.name: *Magnificent Atrium with Figures*
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.description:
The growing influence and interaction between communications, especially the printing press and foreign travel, reinforced the cosmopolitan culture that came to characterise the processes of the European courts. Lisbon took the lead, when, under the reign of the King João V, Absolutism gave the Portuguese monarchy a renewed lease of life. Sacred and profane music, heard either at the Patriarch or at court, had a strong political meaning and reinforced the king's aura of majesty. King João V, therefore, commissioned artists such as Domenico Scarlatti; built the monumental Opera House next to the Royal Palace in 1754 (destroyed during the earthquake of 1755), and enlarged the Royal Orchestra with new foreign soloists.  
The theatrical scenery drawings of the Galli Bibiena family were not made on durable material. Due to the fact that the theatre sets they designed for court functions were temporary, few of their creations have survived. The richness and splendour of their stage sets can however still be judged from contemporary drawings, preserved in great numbers, and found mainly in collections in [Vienna](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), [Munich](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich") and [Dresden](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden "Dresden").  
This drawing by Francesco Galli Bibiena is a study for an unknown stage set. It is possible that it was brought to Portugal in 1750–1751 by his son, Giovanni Carlo Sicino Bibiena (1717–1760), who was charged by King José I to modernise both the theatres themselves and their services.  
The drawing shows an interior space with large arcades seen from a diagonal perspective. The composition is dominated by two large arches leading up to corridors at the top of a staircase. The vaults are richly decorated and the balconies bear several medallions with mythological figures at the centre supported by little angels. Bound by columns and female sculptures, the central area is occupied by women with children. Two dogs can be seen on the left. Through the main arcade a young crowned ruler makes his entrance surrounded by soldiers carrying banners, attracting everyone's attention.
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.short_description: This drawing by Francesco Galli Bibiena is a study for an unknown stage set. It represents an interior space with large arcades seen from a diagonal perspective. The vaults are richly decorated and the balconies bare several medallions with mythological figures at the centre supported by angels.

There is little information about the whereabouts of these drawings during the second half of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th. In around 1845 the drawing was in the collection of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Lisbon and then transferred to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in 1884, the date of its establishment.

27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.name: *The Adoration of the Shepherds*
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.description:
This bas-relief is part of a series which includes four horizontal and four oval scenes, all are in their original frames.  
Three shepherds approach to adore the Child. The Madonna, St. Joseph and the angels, occupying the middle of the scene, point to the object of interest, Jesus. Piò moulds the tender scene to create a soft and delicate three-dimensional picture, similar to his contemporary painters.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.short_description: This sculpture is a good example of the baroque technique of Bolognese terracotta. Terracotta bas-reliefs were intended as proper paintings, framed and hanging from the walls, but lacking colours. The figures are scattered on different planes; in the foreground they are nearly three dimensional while the background figures are drawn more two dimensionally.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.holder: Museo Diocesano di Arte Sacra di San Giovanni in Persiceto

27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.method_for_datation: The date is inscribed on the surface of the bas relief. The origin is described by the biographer of the artist, Zanotti.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.obtention: The bas-relief was originally made for the oratory of the Suffragio in San Giovanni in Persiceto. It was moved to the oratory of the Holy Sacrament and later to the church of the Madonna della Cintura. In 1948 it was moved again to the Collegiata (the main church) of San Giovanni in Persiceto. The museum of the church was opened to the public and it was exhibited there.

28584f5a-5266-5d2e-bd90-2752af7c1016.name: Palazzo Davia Bargellini
28584f5a-5266-5d2e-bd90-2752af7c1016.description: Engaged by Camillo Bargellini, the architect Bartolomeo Provaglia provided three different versions of the project for the ambitious family residence. Two of the more traditional designs were not executed. The internal organisation of the spaces corresponds to the Bolognese typical ‘senatorial’ residence. The sequence of entrance, atrium, monumental staircase (built in 1730) and great hall was intended as a ‘public’ route inside the walls of the private residence during events of political city life (in particular the appointment of the magistrate known as ‘gonfalonierato’). The noble apartments displayed a rich collection of paintings which are now in the collection of the Opera Pia and open to the public.
28584f5a-5266-5d2e-bd90-2752af7c1016.short_description: The palace is an example of the will of the Bolognese senatorial class to represent its own politic power and social role through art and architecture. Together with that of the Pepoli family, the Bargellini palace is the most representative example of local baroque residential architecture. Severe and impressive, the edifice is a huge and monumental building in its monolithic shape, erected over a high base (the so-called *scarp*), an element possibly deriving from medieval and fortified tradition. Very modern instead are the lacking of the portico and the superimposition of three main floors, granting it an emerging position in the city urban texture.
28584f5a-5266-5d2e-bd90-2752af7c1016.bibliography:
Matteucci, A.M., “Contributo alla storia dell'architettura tardobarocca bolognese”, *Atti e memorie della Deputazione di Storia patria per le Province di Romagna*, XXIV, pp. 225-252, tavv. 1-35.  
Cuppini, G., *Palazzi senatorii a Bologna. Architettura come immagine del potere*, Bologna, 1974, pp. 111-118, pp. 283-284.
28584f5a-5266-5d2e-bd90-2752af7c1016.history:
Around 1631 Camillo Bargellini, a member of the important lineage Bargellini (whose name maybe derives from the public office of the ‘bargello’ or ‘bergellino’), decided to build a new modern residence. He chose a site in Bologna, along the central Strada Maggiore, where the houses of the Budrioli and Desideri families stood. This land was purchased by his predecessor Ermes Bargellini in 1610. The building was designed by the architect Bartolomeo Provaglia and realised under the direction of the master builder Antonio Uri. Once the façade was complete, around 1638, the senator was allowed to acquire common soil, specifying his aim; the edifice was to be finished only many years later, in 1658. The monumental staircase was built in the first half of the eighteenth-century. The apartment in the right wing of the ground floor was decorated in the second half of the eighteenth century.  
Property of the Bargellini family until 1839, the palace was inherited by Marquis Virgilio Davia. He intended the palace to house the charitable foundation he instituted at the moment of his death (1876) which still exists today.

289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.name: *Aeneas’ Flight from Troy*
289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.description: A painting of the same subject, now sadly lost, was made for Emperor Rudolph II of Austria (1586–89). Given its immediate success, Barocci made a copy in 1589. According to tradition, it was Cardinal Giuliano Della Rovere of Urbino who later gave it to Scipione Borghese. Scipione was so pleased with the painting that in 1618 he commissioned Gian Lorenzo Bernini to produce a sculptural group (the first by the famous sculptor) showing the same subject. The work demonstrates the exceptional technique of the Urbino painter, who worked continuously on religious subjects and portraits, this being one of his few secular pieces. The scenery through which the protagonists move – bold imagery that did not escape Rubens – is highly dramatic: flames chase them, and the smoke and darkness of the night emphasise the imminent tragedy. The foreshortening of the stairway in the foreground, light reflecting off the balusters, creates a highly scenic element serving the theatricality of the episode, and presages future solutions employed in Baroque art. In the background, in addition to the Antonine column, there are clear references to the work of Raphael and Donato Bramante, who, like Barocci, came from Urbino. The monuments shown appear to compare Rome to Troy in flames, almost wishing to recall the terrible Sack of Rome by the Landsknechts in 1527.
289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.short_description: Barocci was a predecessor of Baroque art. The complex division of space, the spontaneity and naturalness of the figures' movements, the colours, all had a strong influence on 17th-century art, particularly that of Rubens. His anti-rhetorical figures were not appreciated in Rome and considered remote from classical art. Cardinal Scipione was inspired by this work when he commissioned Bernini to sculpt a statue of subject. This canvas is a replica of Rudolf II of Austria's painting (1586–89).
289e0b91-391c-5f31-815c-4363fea69bfe.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

28b857f3-2101-565b-a2b0-139be4166d04.name: Part of an 'Angel’s concert'
28b857f3-2101-565b-a2b0-139be4166d04.description: The coloured relief 'Angel’s concert' was created as an object of worship. The outer shape follows an erratic course, very likely caused by a missing part of the relief, and with the representation of a swelling cloudscape. Two dressed angels emerge out of the clouds that form the background. One of them is playing the lute and both are singing to the music, accompanied by a winged cherub. The angels are carved out to knee-length while only the cherub’s winged head is shown. Eye-catching, showing chubby and rosy cheeks and an unusual tufty hairstyle with some hair standing up, this relief may be regarded as typical of Hans Krumpper’s style. The relief stands as a very early example for the cheerfulness of the Baroque era, with flocks of church angels marking the climax after 1650.
28b857f3-2101-565b-a2b0-139be4166d04.short_description: The precious Early Baroque relief of a cheerful angel’s concert within a cloudscape was obviously created as an object of worship. One of the two angels plays the lute, while the other beneath holds the song book.

28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.name: *St. Jerome*
28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.description:
St. Jerome, Father of the Western Church, is shown translating the texts of the Old and New Testaments (*Vulgate*) into Latin. The scene is rendered suggestively with a neutral background from which the light-bathed figure emerges. On a table, near the books, there is a skull, signifying the penitential aspect of the saint, and his meditation on the Passion and death of Christ.  
The composition, executed with high realism, is synonymous with the artist's style, giving the subjects a very particular theatricality that focuses solely on the actions or expressions of the characters without using monumental scenery or artifice, typical of Baroque art. St. Jerome was one of the most commonly represented figures of the Counter-Reformation. His active and contemplative life was held up as a model for the faithful, who saw in him a route to salvation, in addition to the importance placed on studying and translating the scriptures from Greek and Hebrew. The *Vulgate* was in fact the first Latin transcription of the Bible and therefore became a key tool for the dissemination of the sacred texts. The painting, according to tradition, was carried out expressly for Scipione Borghese, having recently been elected cardinal with the help of his uncle Camillo, who had become Pope Paul V on 16 May 1605. The cardinal, who helped the artist escape a prison sentence related to problems involving women in 1605, the year the piece is dated, was one of Caravaggio's great admirers, and procured 12 of the artist's pieces for his collection.
28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.short_description: The artwork was given as a gift by the artist to Cardinal Scipione Borghese, who had helped him get out of a Roman prison. It represents St. Jerome, one of the Fathers of the Church, in the act of translating the *Vulgate*. For this reason, he is considered the patron saint of archaeologists, librarians, translators and students in general. The canvas dates from 1605, the year in which Borghese was made cardinal, making this painting even dearer to the newly appointed prince of the Church.
28f28da1-db6e-593f-a4b0-5bb45ac24d47.obtention: Acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

29d6d877-4212-55cf-9cef-7a3a0dcef44e.name: Augustinian Canons’ Convent of the Holy Saviour / Convent of Augustinian Canons
29d6d877-4212-55cf-9cef-7a3a0dcef44e.description: The powerful, but not completed tower designed by Hans Krumpper displays a blind frame-structure in its three storeys. The entrance hall, which looks like a triumphal arch in front of the sober façade, dates to the 18th century. The interior of the three-nave Late Gothic hall-church on octagon pillars appears light and broad due to the large distances between the pillars; on the sides, side-chapels are attached. Noteworthy is the light-coloured stucco decoration designed by Krumpper, with plastered applications such as blossoms, pearl strings, foliage, cherubs and rosettes accenting a basic framework. In the newly constructed two-storey chior area the sacristy lies to the left. Above the sacristy, the choir of the canons can be found as well as, on both sides, oratories for the nobility. The area of the high altar is kept intentionally free to great effect, allowing it to be submerged in light.
29d6d877-4212-55cf-9cef-7a3a0dcef44e.short_description: The church of the former Augustinian Canons in Polling, essentially a building of the Late-Gothic hall-type, served at the same time as a pilgrimage destination for the so-called Pollinger Kreuz (the Polling Cross). Significantly decorated with the important Early Baroque stuccowork of the Wessobrunn master Georg Schmuzer, it also contains a magnificent Rococo tabernacle by Johann Baptist Straub. Artistically notable 18th-century rooms include the attractive relic chapel with its intimate Rococo furnishings as well as the monastery library, whose ceiling frescos depict Enlightenment thought.
29d6d877-4212-55cf-9cef-7a3a0dcef44e.dates: 1605–1611: construction of the church tower; 1621–1626: Counter-Reformation re-design of the church; 1761–1765: partial renovation of the church interior including the relic chapel; 1755–1779: construction and furnishing of the library hall

Pörnbacher, H., *Kirche des ehemaligen Augustinerchorherrenstiftes Polling*, Lindenberg 1999.  
Zohner, W., *Bartholomäus Steinle (um 1580–1628/29). Bildhauer und 'Director über den Kirchenbau zu Weilheim'*, Weißenhorn 1993, pp. 90–4, 349–73.  
Volk, P., *Johann Baptist Straub 1704–1784*, Munich 1984, p. 201, passim.  
Simon-Schlagberger, A., *Johann Baptist Baader 1717–1780. Ein schwäbisch- bayerischer Maler zwischen Barock und Klassizismus*, Weißenhorn 1983, pp. 126–42.
29d6d877-4212-55cf-9cef-7a3a0dcef44e.history: According to legend the monastery was founded by Duke Thassilo III in 750 after a crucifix was revealed. Emperor Heinrich II is known as the second founder for having rebuilt the monastery as a convent for Augustinian canons in 1010 after its devastation by the Hungarians. From 1621 to 1628 many parts of the Late Gothic hall-church were adapted to the Counter-Reformation zeitgeist according to the designs of Hans Krumpper, which were then realised by Georg Schmuzer and Bartholomäus Steinle. Under the enlightened and scientifically engaged provost Franziskus Töpsl, the 18th-century brought about rich artistic development of the monastery buildings, but as a result of secularisation after 1803, large parts of these embellishments were destroyed. Therefore, only the Baroque library hall and the former collegiate church can be appreciated today.
29d6d877-4212-55cf-9cef-7a3a0dcef44e.architects: Design for remodeling and interior decoration of the collegiate church: Hans Krumpper (1570–1634); stucco: Georg (“Jörg”) Schmuzer (c. 1565–1645); altar sculpture: Bartholomäus Steinle (1580–1628/29); tabernacle: Johann Baptist Straub (1704–1784); ceiling paintings in the relic chapel and library: Johann Baptist Baader (1717–1780); altar wall and stucco in the relic chapel and stucco in the library: Thassilo Zöpf (1723–1807)

29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.name: *Allegory of the Fortunate Reign of Moravia*
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.alternate_name: *Homage of Olympus to the Moravian Land*
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.description:
The composition is executed in depth. Under a Zodiac indicating eternity at the top edge, flies Fame, trumpeting the glory of Moravia. The top section features the symbol of Moravia, an obelisk with a chequered eagle, towards which *putti* fly with a laurel wreath and a crown. On the left, a female figure with a palm frond symbolises monarchical virtue while on the other side sits *Potestas*, who personifies power, and to whom the *putti* hand the field emblems of the Roman legions. Next to monarchical virtue is Victoria, with a laurel wreath on her head and a statue of the goddess Nike in her hand. Below are Mercury, the god of trade, Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, and *Cognitio*, the personification of knowledge. Their opposite on the right is *Religio*, accompanied by the Old and New Testaments. The group is observed by Diana, goddess of hunting, and Fortune with a wheel. The central motif is *Abundantia* with a cornucopia. At the bottom are Hercules, the war gods Mars and Bellona, an allegory of eternal fame, a water god and a *putto* with weapons. Below the group is an allegorical female figure with a helmet and a palm frond, possibly symbolising strength and competence.  
In the early 1730s, the proprietors of the Moravian Estates decided to commission decorative artwork to finish off the reconstruction of the Provincial House in Brno. Provincial Governor Maxmilián Oldřich Count Kounic assigned the job to the academic painter Daniel Gran and the quadraturist Gaetano Fanti. *Allegory of the Fortunate Reign of Moravia* was executed above the assembly hall benches, while *Apotheosis of the Rule of Justice*, an allegory of a “good government”, was placed above the governor's seat. Three preparatory sketches (Albertina, Vienna; Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg) and two designs in oil (Akademie der bildenden Künste, Österreichische Galerie Belvedere) have survived for the first scene. A mirror image of Gran's painting from the Moravian Gallery was created as a template for a print.
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.short_description: This workshop image of Gran’s mural from the Assembly Hall of the Moravian Estates was created as a template for a print. The top section of the composition – a world of allegorical figures and ancient gods - features the symbol of Moravia, an obelisk with the country’s coat of arms.
29e8d7c4-4afa-510c-a674-f8b5ff0e817f.obtention: Acquired from private property in Brno, 1865.

2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.name: Caesar Fountain
2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.description: A series of fountains and columns, symbolising the rebirth of the city, demonstrates both its historical significance and its affiliation to Christianity. This idea reached its peak with Holy Trinity Column. Reducing history to myth was typical of both the aristocracy and town organisations in the period of the restoration of the country, ravaged by the Thirty Years’ War and devastated by religious conflicts in the second half of the 17th century.
2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.short_description: A series of fountains and columns, symbolising the rebirth of the city, demonstrates both its historical significance and its affiliation to Christianity. The central motif is the figure of G. J. Caesar considered from the 15th century onwards as the founder of the city. History turned to myth was typical of the restoration of the Czech and Moravian lands in the wake of the Thirty Years’ War and religious conflicts. The sculptor J. J. Schauberger, chiefly active in Olomouc and Brno, created his masterpiece, this equestrian statue, which was possibly inspired by Bernini’s Constantine the Great in the Vatican.
2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.method_for_datation: The construction of the fountains is documented by contracts, receipts and records from the Town Council. For example, J. J. Schauberger was paid 1,200 gold pieces for the statue of Caesar.
2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.bibliography:
Pavel Zatloukal (ed), *Horní náměstí v Olomouci*, Olomouc, 1995.  
Ivo Krsek –­­ Zdeněk Kudělka (ed), –­­ Miloš Stehlík –­­ Josef Válka, *Umění baroka na Moravě a ve Slezsku*, Prague, 1996, pp. 365, 369, cat. 120.  
Jiří Kroupa (ed), in *Dans le miroir des ombres. Moravie a la age baroque 1670*–­­*1790*, Paris–­­Rennes–­­Brno, 2002, p. 51.
2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.history: Olomouc was the capital of Moravia until the mid-17th century, seat of bishops and later archbishops. In 1642 it was taken by the Swedish army and occupied for eight years, and thus lost its former position. Of 30,000 inhabitants, only 1,765 survived in the devastated town. In 1655 Olomouc was proclaimed one of four Moravian fortified towns and its restoration was launched. The first builders were commissioned by religious institutions, with the Town Council joining in later. Although there were enough wells in Olomouc, fountains provided a major source of water, supplying the town until the late 19th century. The original number of seven fountains was concluded with the construction in Hlavní námestí Square of a new fountain, which replaced one with a child and dolphin that once stood outside the town gate.
2a461ed8-a056-5b1f-93df-891058b990b5.architects: Jan Jiří Schauberger (?, before 1725 Vienna, active in Olomouc – 1744 Brno), Michael Mandík, Václav Schüler, Václav Render (1669–1733 Olomouc), Filip Sattler (1695 Wenns, Tyrol – 1738 Olomouc)

2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.name: *Nativity*
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.alternate_name: Sketch for the altarpiece of the Voss Orphanage, Sopron
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.description:
Dorffmaister was a student at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1751 to 1759. In 1762 he settled in Sopron and worked until his death almost exclusively for Hungarian patrons as a fresco and altarpiece painter. He took commissions from everyone – bishops, various monastic orders and town or village communities.  
Being childless Charles Voss von Ehrenfels (d.1761) and his wife, Anna Dorothea Lanius (d.1770), made a pact that following the death of either one of them the one that survived should found an orphanage. Having survived her husband Anna Dorothea bought the Kisfaludy house in Sopron seeing it as a suitable building for an orphanage. The foundation charter of the institution was signed in 1768 and confirmed in the same year by Empress Maria Theresia.  
Following the death of Anna Dorothea, György Primes the vicar of Sopron, finished the construction and decoration of the orphanage whose chapel was opened in 1772, and decorated with an altarpiece by Dorffmaister accomplished in the same year.  
To the right of the altar, which takes up the entire main wall, there is a contemporary sculpture of the Guardian Angel. The commission for the altarpiece painting went to Dorffmaister who made an oil sketch, which has remained in the town to this day, and is illustrated here. In the building with its chapel that was newly consecrated in 2009 after a restoration, there is a community centre for Christian communities, courses, lectures, and various charitable activities.  
For the composition of the altarpiece for the Holy Trinity Chapel, the artist chose an unusual depiction of the Holy Trinity: he painted the figure of God the Father and the dove of the Holy Spirit among a choir of angels over a scene of the Nativity, gazing down at the stable in Bethlehem. In this representation, Dorffmaister merges three different types of picture: the Nativity, the Adoration of the Shepherds and the Adoration of the Magi. The result is one of Dorffmaister's most balanced and harmonious altarpieces. Beyond the motif of Mary's raised, shining white kerchief taken from northern Italian painting, the artist appears to follow the example of a mature Adoration of the Magi. The figures unfold from a dark background emphasised by strongly coloured drapery, sharp light cast on their faces, and light patches of folds in some of the garments.  
With this altarpiece, Dorffmaister's first major ecclesiastical undertaking in the town of Sopron, the artist reveals not only the rigour of his training but also shows how accomplished he is regards composition as well as style, depicting his figures in a confident and elegant manner.
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.short_description: A member of a Viennese artistic dynasty working solely from the Transdanubian region, Dorffmaister was an accomplished fresco painter, living from 1762 until his death in Sopron. The Voss Orphanage altarpiece, influenced by Viennese academic style, is one of his best studies.
2adedceb-8648-52a0-ae26-9e49a8fb53de.method_for_datation: The altarpiece after this sketch is signed and dated and still in situ
