370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.name: *Feast of St. Anthony of Padua*
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.description:
The subject is a relatively scarcely represented scene from the life of St. Anthony of Padua, priest, preacher and disciple of St. Francis of Assisi. The Franciscan saint sits at the table in the house of a wealthy man, blessing goblets of wine. On the left, a *putto* brings a lily, symbol of purity and one of the saint's attributes. On the right, precious tableware is displayed, as was customary at feasts from the 16th century onwards. Although the scene is illuminated at the centre, the picture features two pictorial sections: the left symbolising austerity and humbleness and the right, luxury and superiority. The artist also draws attention to the two sections by use of character types: the face of St. Anthony with his halo reflecting spiritual delight, while the gross face of the rich man shows sensual pleasure, greed and a boorish approach to the situation. The listening man on the right points out his gluttony, one of the seven deadly sins. The painter highlights the scene with a contrasting motif of deep-red drapery, which sets the colour tone for the whole picture. The painting stands out among Kracker's altarpieces and ceiling frescos because of its genre-painting atmosphere and use of chiaroscuro. It also manifests the artist's bold monogram *JK*, but not as distinctively as on some of his more sizeable compositions.  
The picture was part of the decoration of the refectory in the Franciscan Monastery in Moravská Třebová, together with *The Feast of the Holy Family* and *The Feast of St. Wenceslas*.  
Kracker was a leading exponent of the Vienna Academy style represented by Paul Troger and Michelangelo Unterberger. After studying in Vienna Kracker was active in the workshop of Josef Tadeáš Rotter in Brno, and later settled in Znojmo. His best-known works include ceiling paintings and altarpieces in the Church of St. Nicholas in Prague and in Nová Říše. His later work was associated with Hungary, where he joined the service of Bishop K. Esterházy in Jager.
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.short_description: The subject is a relatively scarcely represented scene from the life of St. Anthony of Padua. The canvas formed part of the decoration in the refectory of the Franciscan Monastery in Moravská Třebová. It is an early piece by the artist, J. L. Kracker who was active in Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary.
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.method_for_datation: The picture is marked with the artist's monogram *JK* bottom left, on a vessel.

387a8cd6-9d72-5dac-9a2c-95552d3ac478.name: *The Adoration of the Shepherds*
387a8cd6-9d72-5dac-9a2c-95552d3ac478.description:
This painting was executed by the Neapolitan painter during his stay in Bologna, for the Chartusian church of San Gerolamo. It is part of a series of eight, commissioned to different local painters, narrating episodes of the life of Christ.  
There is a strong naturalism inspired by Caravaggio and Ribera, but combined with the features of Neapolitan baroque such as dynamic movement, vivid colours, quick brush strokes and a lively composition. Nunzio Rossi shows some of the characters of the art in Naples around 1630–1650, when the local masters were working together with famous foreigners such as Van Dyck and Rubens. A touch of the style of Guido Reni, an artist that Rossi met while working in Bologna, is evident in the group of the Madonna with Child, reminiscent two pictures of the same subject (Naples, the Chartreuse, and Feldsberg castle), painted by Reni when the young Neapolitan came to Bologna.  
The focal centre of the composition is Madonna adoring the Child. Surrounding them are the shepherds and peasants with their animals and humble presents for the new born baby. The upper part of the painting is full of lively singing angels.
387a8cd6-9d72-5dac-9a2c-95552d3ac478.short_description: This painting was painted in Bologna for the Carthusian church of San Gerolamo. The strong colours and swift movements are indebted to the city of Naples with its paintings by foreign artists like Rubens and Van Dick and those by the member of the local school. In the Madonna with Child, note the influence of Guido Reni, the master of Rossi during his stay in Bologna.

3a5cad73-4f48-56b7-b114-82c0d7aa0b7a.name: Villa Albergati
3a5cad73-4f48-56b7-b114-82c0d7aa0b7a.description:
The vast building stands in the countryside. It is impressive for its remarkable size and the severe, massive aspect of the exterior which is quite unusual for a Villa. We know that the original plan for the exterior decoration with stairs, statues and freezes was not realised. Its exceptional extension in height, 4 floors plus the clock tower, is exceptional.  
In the middle of the building stands the magnificent white triple volume ballroom, with stucco decoration.  
The complex decorative cycle of painted ceilings includes two main halls and several rooms, each of them shows different original illusionist architectural paintings (quadratura). Allegories and episodes from mythology are the subjects of the painted ceilings. This is a common theme in spaces intended to host feasts and leisure events, such as this villa.  
The most important artists working in Bologna at the time were employed in this vast enterprise: Angelo Michele Colonna and Giacomo Alboresi, Giovanni Antonio Burrini and Marcantonio Chiarini, Vittorio Maria Bigari and Stefano Orlandi.  
The decorations date from 1665 to the second half of the eighteenth-century.  
On the ground floor one can admire an original example of the so-called “boschereccia” decoration. This is a room painted entirely with trees and vineyards, to simulate a landscape surrounding the visitor. It was originally used as a dining room. It was painted around 1776-1778 by Prospero and Gaetano Pesci.
3a5cad73-4f48-56b7-b114-82c0d7aa0b7a.short_description:
The monumental and sumptuous villa of the noble Albergati family stands in the fertile countryside around Bologna and can be considered one of the most significant examples of Italian seventeenth-century residential architecture.  
The uniqueness of this building is due to the magnificent ballroom occupying the centre of it: a sort of translation in architectural language and white stuccoes of the illusory painted perspectives known as “quadratura” that can be admired on the ceilings of the other rooms.
3a5cad73-4f48-56b7-b114-82c0d7aa0b7a.bibliography: *Le Magnifiche stanze. Paesaggio, architettura, decorazione e vita nella villa palazzo degli Albergati a Zola*, Bergamo, 1995.
3a5cad73-4f48-56b7-b114-82c0d7aa0b7a.history:
The patron, Marquis Girolamo Albergati Capacelli, was a representative of one of the most important and admired Bolognese Families.  
Little is known about his life but it is known that he was successful in completing two great architectural enterprises: the long porticoes to the shrine of San Luca in Bologna and his villa in the country. This villa was known as “Regio Palazzo”, “royal Palace”, because of its splendour and grandeur. It has been called the most complex and ambitious enterprise of the time: it took almost 30 years to be completed.  
During the eighteenth-century, the palace was a lively centre for cultural and social activities, hosting popes, kings, princes, musicians, men and women of letters, and even famous adventurers. The theatre within the villa was famous for the representations of plays written by the patron Marquis Francesco Albergati Capacelli. He was a theatre lover and friend of some famous playwrights of the time including Voltaire, Alfieri and Goldoni.

3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.name: *The Seven Saints Founders of the Servite Order*
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.description:
The whole series consisted of ten oval pictures. Two smaller paintings which were hanging near the apse, were lost at the end of the eighteenth-century, when the high chapel was refurbished. They were originally in the church of the Servites in Budrio, a small town near Bologna.  
The seven saints which are the founders of the Servite order are represented in three-quarters and move with eloquent gestures. In the background are depicted episodes of their lives and the saints’ attributes.  
Antonio Gionima, born in Venice, was one of the favourite pupils of Giuseppe Maria Crespi. The art historian Luigi Crespi praises his simple and free style and the freshness of his palette. His main features are quick brush strokes, the use of light and rich colours. He worked for a long time for the Servites of Bologna as well. For them he painted a similar series of portraits which were unfortunately lost. He died of tuberculosis when he was 35 years old.
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.short_description: The eight oval pictures decorating the nave of the church of San Lorenzo in Budrio represent the founders’ saints of the Servite order. They were made by the Venetian painter Antonio Gionima, one of the favourite pupils of Giuseppe Maria Crespi. In Bologna he developed a personal style, mixing his master’s features with a sort of expressive movement possibly derived from Aureliano Milani.
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.method_for_datation: The Servite fathers of Budrio decided to order ten oval pictures to hang over the arches of the chapels. The prior of the convent was Giovanni Antonio Cavalli (1719-1720), and the State Archive of Bologna still retains the receipt of payment signed by Antonio Gionima, dated 29th December 1720.
3b6dc052-9700-508f-9427-f498bf964545.obtention: Moved from the church of the Servite fathers to the church of San Lorenzo.

3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.name: Vranov nad Dyjí Chateau
3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.description: The chateau towers over the valley from a rocky promontory above the River Dyje in the Podyjí National Park. Of the original castle two prismatic towers, part of the ramparts and buildings in the outer bailey, have been preserved. Its well-devised fortification system became part of the reconstruction concept to glorify an ancient dynasty by means of a “*via triumphalis*”, the principal feature of which is the unique Hall of the Ancestors perched upon the promontory.
3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.short_description: This spectacular chateau above a meander of the River Dyje is one of the most remarkable buildings of mid-European Baroque. A well-devised fortification system became part of the reconstruction concept to glorify an ancient dynasty by means of “*via triumphalis*”, the principal feature of which is the unique Hall of the Ancestors perched on a rocky promontory. The design of the chateau is typical of the Habsburg Empire style. The decoration is the work of major Viennese artists with Italian leanings.
3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.method_for_datation: The fresco in the Hall of the Ancestors is signed and dated; further information follows from correspondence and archive documents.

3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.history: The chateau came into existence through the reconstruction of an old Romanesque-Gothic castle situated above a meander of the River Dyje. After a fire in 1665, Michael Jan II of Althann erected the impressive Hall of the Ancestors and a chapel to the design of imperial architect, Fischer von Erlach. Under Countess Marie Felicita and Michael Josef the chateau interiors were rebuilt in the classicist style. The provincial barrister, J. Hilgartner of Lilienborn, who acquired the demesne through bankruptcy proceedings, took up the original concept and put much effort into the completion of a landscaped park, which bears traces of pre-Romanticism and a Rousseauesque relationship with nature. Major building changes occurred in the 19th century when the demesne was owned by the Mniszeks, an aristocratic family from Poland. In 1938 Vranov became part of Hitler’s Third Reich; the chateau was confiscated and sold to Baron Gebhard von der Wense-Mörse. It has been state property since 1945.

3bdac2c6-586e-5e07-83d5-3032abb55d35.name: Triumphal Arch, Vác
3bdac2c6-586e-5e07-83d5-3032abb55d35.description: A Triumphal Arch with a single archway that rests on simple pillars, and which was designed using pure geometrical shapes. An attic can be seen above the indented cornice, and eagles on the frieze are depicted holding a festoon. The use of the eagle, a symbol of the Roman emperors, refers to both Queen Maria Theresia and her family, and her husband German Emperor Francis I of the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty (1745–1765). On the south side of the triumphal arch that faces the city, the inscription reads: “AETERNAE DOMUI” (“To the Eternal \[Habsburg\] House”). On the attic the portraits of the Queen and her husband are visible in *tondo*s (circular engravings in high relief). The inscription on the northern side of the triumphal arch, which faces in the direction of arrival into the city, reads: “FRANCISCO I. ROM. IMP. M. THERESIAE / AUG. HUNG. BOH. REGI PIIS FELICIBUS INVICTIS / JOSEPHO ROM. REGI NOBILISSIMO CAESARI LEOPOL- / DO / M. ANNAE M. CHRISTINAE REGIIS PRINCIPIBUS OB / VACII PRAESENTI EORUM MAJESTATE TRIDUUM BEA- / TUM CHRISTOPHORUS S.R.E. CARDINALIS A MIGAZZI / EPISCOP. VAC. SECUNDO ARCUM HUNC IMAGINIBUS / AUGUSTAE DOMUS INSIGNEM DICAVIT ANNO / MDCCLXIV.” (“Frances I. Rom\[an\] Emp\[eror\] M. Theresia \[Her\] Majesty Queen \[of\] *Hungariae Bohamie* \[Czech\] Pious and Fortunate Conqueror Joseph King \[of\] the Romans most celebrated Caesar Leopold / M\[aria\] Anna \[and\] M\[aria\] Christina Royal Princesses / to pay honour for the three days of lasting happiness while staying in Vác of their Highnesses / Cardinal \[of\] S\[acrae\] R\[omanae\]. E\[cclesiae\] Christoph Migazzi Bishop of Vác dedicated \[this\] \[triumphal\] arch decorated with the images of their Highnesses in the year \[of\] MDCCLXIV \[1764\].”) The *tondo*s on this side contain portraits of archdukes Joseph and Leopold as well as the portraits of archdukes Ferdinand and Maximillian.
3bdac2c6-586e-5e07-83d5-3032abb55d35.short_description: The Triumphal Arch in Vác is a unique edifice in the corpus of 18th-century Hungarian architecture of this type, and the first such arch to be built from stone in Central Europe. The second was built in Innsbruck a year later at the request of Queen Maria Theresia (1740–1780). It was based on the “Roman style” of the Triumphal Arch in Vác, which differed from the Late Baroque style on account of the direct influence of Antique forms and features.
3bdac2c6-586e-5e07-83d5-3032abb55d35.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources.

3bdac2c6-586e-5e07-83d5-3032abb55d35.history: Queen Maria Theresia (1740–1780) and her family visited Pest and Vác in 1764. For the occasion and to pay homage, Christoph Anton Migazzi Bishop of Vác and Archbishop of Vienna (1756–1757; 1761–1785), ordered the construction of the triumphal arch. It was designed by Isidore Ganneval – a student of Niccolò Servandoni – who introduced early Classical architecture to Migazzi’s court and subsequently to Hungary. His architecture, which was directly influenced by Antique forms and features and based on pure geometrical shapes, was one of the most modern styles in contemporary Europe. Master builders in Central Europe, many of whom held onto local traditions, did not even react to the new style for several decades. Stonemason, Matthias Chmelik, and sculptor, Joseph Bechert, worked on the construction.

3bdad233-bb58-5e5a-b8af-3018c4aa6440.name: Catholic Benedictine Abbey and Pilgrimage Church of St. Mary
3bdad233-bb58-5e5a-b8af-3018c4aa6440.description: The two-storey facade is a paraphrase of Bernini's Louvre-project and was designed by Enrico Zuccalli, the electoral court architect and Bernini scholar. The niche-figures of the apostles are by Ägid Verhelst, these are enclosed within voluminous Baroque curves and a fenestrated and lantern-crowned dome construction which soars mightily above them. The dodecagonal central-plan building and the easterly attached new chancel have a two-storey ambulatory, which originates partly from the era of the Gothic construction. On the inside, a lavishly stucco-decorated organ loft is located over the entrance portal. The wall spaces have in each case a shallow niche with an altar, crowned with *rocaille*\-cartouches, above which high windows lead the eye to the dome. Luxuriant stucco decorations with capricious *rocaille*, *coquillage* and foliage are ascribed to Johann Georg Üblher and Franz Xaver Schmuzer. The elliptical-shaped Louis XVI chancel, with its rational-coolish marble work, forms a contrast to the main room and includes the three-part high altar with the medieval miraculous picture. Installed at the basement-level of the chancel rotunda, four gilded, wood carved reliefs by the Roman Anton Boos illustrate scenes of the Life of Christ.
3bdad233-bb58-5e5a-b8af-3018c4aa6440.short_description: The Baroque architecture of the pilgrimage church of St. Mary and its splendid Rococo decoration add up to a complex masterpiece, created by the architects Enrico Zuccalli and Joseph Schmuzer, and based on an existent medieval central-plan building. Carved altarpieces of Johann Baptist Straub and the large ceiling fresco by Johann Jakob Zeiller crown the interior decoration which contrasts with the coolish Louis XVI style of the chancel.

3bdad233-bb58-5e5a-b8af-3018c4aa6440.history: The Benedictine Abbey was founded as votive by Emperor Ludwig (Louis) the Bavarian in 1330 and was consecrated in 1370. Under Abbot Placidus II Seitz large scale changes to the monastery buildings were initiated, and in 1710, the ceremonial laying of the cornerstone for the church’s reconstruction based on the existent medieval central-plan building took place. Enrico Zuccalli prepared the architectural plans and set to work on the construction of the new facade with its to-date unfinished towers. The high altar was consecrated in 1726. After a disastrous fire in 1744, which destroyed the greater part of the alterations, as of 1745, construction continued under the direction of the Wessobrunn master builder Joseph Schmuzer.

3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.name: *Visitation*
3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.description:
After studying locally in Langenargen, Maulbertsch went to Vienna where he was a pupil of Peter van Roy at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and where, in 1750, he won first prize in the academic painting competition. In 1758, he became an ordinary member of the Academy and was later a counsellor. Although both his home and workshop were in Vienna, his activities covered the entire Habsburg empire extending beyond its boundaries. Primarily a fresco painter, he was constantly overburdened with commissions from churches and secular patrons. His oeuvre includes several altarpieces, sketches and panel paintings, historical-mythological pictures, genre paintings and portraits, but also graphic works and etchings. In the course of his rich career, he traced a great arch of development from Late Baroque through Rococo to Neo-Classicism. He died in Vienna on 8 August 1796, while preparing his last great work, the fresco for Szombathely Cathedral.  
János Szily, the Bishop of the newly founded Szombathely diocese, commissioned Maulbertsch to decorate the salon of his personal residence in 1782. Almost 10 years later in 1791, he turned to Maulbertsch again for the altarpieces of Szombathely Cathedral. For the high altar, the Bishop ordered a picture representing the Visitation of Mary by Elizabeth, on the side altars the patron saints of Szombathely, St. Martin and St. Quirinus. In accordance with the pictorial practice at the time, the painter made some sketches which reflected his employer's requests and concepts, and sent them to Szombathely for approval. Some of these sketches have survived. The composition of the Pannonhalma sketch shows differences from the final version. On the altarpiece – executed in 1792 and gravely damaged during the World War II – Mary stands on the left, while in this sketch she stands on the right at the top of a stairway. Maulbertsch mentioned this modification in a letter he wrote to Bishop Szily in April 1792.
3c550833-69a7-533d-a88c-2cec359eede6.short_description: Maulbertsch's later works clearly show the influence of Neo-Classicism, as seen here and in several other of the painter's major works in Hungary (for example in Vác, Győr, Pozsony (Bratislava), Pápa, Eger and Szombathely). This sketch is a version of the recently restored, large-size, Szombathely High Altar painting, which was torn to pieces at the end of the Second World War.

3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.name: *Crucifixion*
3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.description:
The Dominican Monastery of St. Domingos de Benfica, founded in 1399 on the outskirts of Lisbon, was rebuilt in the second quarter of the 17th century during the government of Friar João de Vasconcelos (1624–1632). During this period Manuel Pereira was commissioned to make a series of sculptural devotional images among which were the *Crucifixion* and *Our Lady of the Rosary* – both located over the aisle altars – and *Saint Dominique of Gusmão* and *St. Peter the Martyr* in the main arch niches.  
Portuguese Manuel Pereira studied in Rome and lived in Spain where he received important commissions from the Madrid court, which at the time was the capital of the Iberian monarchy (1580–1640). Pereira worked in stone, wood and alabaster, and using these materials he conceived mainly devotional sculptures that visually imparted the values inherited from the Trent Council through the dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight), aimed at heightening the inner conversion of the Christian. Manuel Pereira's sculptures are characterised by their dynamic composition, combined with the delicate treatment of the surfaces, which in their smallest details irradiate light, delivering a deep and intense psychology. These aesthetic values are present in the polychrome wooden sculptures of the *Immaculate Conception* in Toledo, *St. Ignatius of Loyola*, *St. Francis Xavier*, *St. Aloysus Gonzaga* and *St. Francis of Borja* commissioned by the Church of São Roque in Lisbon. One can include the *Crucifixions* in Cartuja de Miraflores in Burgos and St. Domingos de Benfica in Lisbon, where the realism and inner drama are remarkably intense. In the São Roque Benfica *Crucifixion,* based on an engraving by Pontius from a painting by Peter Paul Rubens, Pereira's Christ hangs lifeless and heavy from the cross, His face contorted, exhaling His last breath and His eyes closing slowly in agony.
3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.short_description: The epitome of Manuel Pereira's sculpture lies in his Crucifixions among which this one, in the Church of St. Domingos de Benfica, is remarkably intense. Based on a composition by Rubens, Christ's heavy, lifeless body hangs from the cross, creating a deep and intense psychological tension that visually imparts the values inherited from the Trent Council through the dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight), which in this context suggests that the body is elevated to eternity through the inner drama of the Passion.

3cf90739-09e0-5aa5-94ec-9216852e94c4.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Vitus
3cf90739-09e0-5aa5-94ec-9216852e94c4.description: Overall, the church in Fulpmes, the first complete building from Penz, appears extremely conservative, with the strict form of a barrel-vaulted, architecturally rigid and uniformly structured hall together with small fresco panels. The discreet, by all means delicate stucco is maintained in the form of the Early Rococo, with few pronounced rocailles, and is the work of Anton Gigl, a member of a family of stucco masons of the Wessobrun school. Bergmüller’s frescos illustrate the triumph of Catholicism as a confession of faith. In the choir, the Worship of the Lamb and the Eucharist, in the transept the Triumph of the Holy Cross, and in the nave the Worship of the name of Jesus. Only parts of the Baroque altar décor are original and were largely replaced in the 20th century.
3cf90739-09e0-5aa5-94ec-9216852e94c4.short_description: The central hall, which appears broad and monumental for a parish church, is of the barrel-vaulted pilaster church type, with transept-like extended aisles before the choir. The main motif, continued throughout, is the pilaster arcade with pristine semi-circular arches. The stucco, in discreet colours, occupies a wide area, while the frescos in bold colours are situated in relatively small panels giving the impression of openings in the vault providing intermittent views of heaven.
3cf90739-09e0-5aa5-94ec-9216852e94c4.method_for_datation: Archives and signature on the choir fresco (1747)
3cf90739-09e0-5aa5-94ec-9216852e94c4.bibliography:
Bayer, K., *Franz de Paula Penz*, Vienna 1991, p. 12, p. 47f.  
Ammann, G., *Die Kirchen von Fulpmes, Stubaital/Tirol*. Munich, Zurich 1980 (= Schnell und Steiner, Kleine Kunstführer, No. 1239).  
Epple, A., *Johann Georg Bergmüller (1688-1762)*. Weißenhorn 1988, p. 19.  
Schnell, H., Schedler, U., *Lexikon der Wessobrunner*. Munich, Zurich 1988, p. 125f. (however, the register of Anton Gigl's works does not mention Fulpmes).
3cf90739-09e0-5aa5-94ec-9216852e94c4.history: Fulpmes originally belonged to the parish of Telfe in Stubaital. The first church in Fulpmes is considered to be the late medieval Sagererkapelle (today the Totenkapelle in Oberdorf). With the establishment of a beneficiary in 1745, the construction of the new Church of St. Vitus was instituted. Built in 1746/47 under the direction of the ecclesiastical building director Franz de Paula Penz, the building was consecrated as early as 1748. The plans originate from Josef Staph (as at Wilten); the execution was in the hands of the master mason Umhauser from Innsbruck. In the same year, 1748, it was elevated to the status of a parish district. The interior work was largely completed between 1747 and 1750.

3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.name: Church of the Gesù, painted architecture of the high altar
3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.description:
The church, based on a design in the Counter-Reformist style, has a wide nave with chapels that are intended to harmoniously combine the practical needs of preaching (larger spaces) with a sober, strict feel.  
Also for practical—as well as didactic—ends, the Jesuit Padre Andrea Pozzo created an illusory extension to the church, creating a prolongation of the choir behind the altar that contains a mock shrine modelled on Bernini's baldachin in St Peter's, and behind which there is a scene from the *Circumcision of Jesus*. The central space in front of the altar is covered by a mock cupola painted in perspective. It employs the solution used in Rome at Sant'Ignazio, but with greater sobriety in its architectural simplicity, and entirely free of figures. The artist's great skill and masterful perspective work are evident in the transitions, apparently forming a harmonious whole, between the real architecture of the nave and the mock pilasters and columns surmounted by capitals and trabeations in the painted area behind the altar. It should be noted that this use of painted perspective – undoubtedly dictated by economic need – at the time also assumed a symbolic significance inasmuch as true spiritual reality was sought beyond sometimes misleading appearances, to such an extent that the focal point enabling the illusion to be best appreciated is marked on the floor by a black disk, stressing—as confirmed by Padre Pozzo himself in his treatise *Perspectiva pictorum et architectorum* (1693)—that there is only "one position to which the believer should strive".
3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.short_description: For practical—as well as didactic—ends, the Jesuit Padre Andrea Pozzo painted a decorative scene that is one of the masterpieces of Baroque illusionistic art. A shortage of economic resources prompted the artist to create an illusory extension of the space in the church, creating a prolongation of the choir behind the high altar that contains a mock shrine, which stands before a representation of the *Circumcision of Jesus*.
3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.method_for_datation: Tantillo, A.M., "Chiesa del Gesù", *I principi della chiesa*, Milan, 1998.
3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.bibliography:
Pipita, G., *La chiesa del Gesù a Frascati: pitture di Andrea Pozzo*, Frascati 1995.  
Tantillo, A. M., "Chiesa del Gesù", *I principi della chiesa*, Milan 1998, pp. 100–101.  
"Colli Antonio", *SAUR Allgemeines Kuenstler-Lexikon*, 20, Munich-Leipzig 1998, p. 296.
3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.history: The Church of the Gesù, now found right in the centre of the city on account of gradual urban expansion, dates back to the late 16th–17th/early 17th­–18th centuries, although there were Jesuits in the city from 1559. The church was expanded to its current form with the support of Olimpia Aldobrandini Pamphili, after her death in 1681 (between 1696 and 1700), according to the traditional Jesuit model already used in the Roman churches of the Gesù, Sant’Ignazio and Vallicella.
3cf9cf20-5e20-5b72-b421-b8139a1cfb95.architects: Andrea Pozzo (1642, Trento – 1709, Vienna) with the help of his Jesuit pupil, Antonio Colli (died, Rome, 1723)
keywords: Perspective painting, *trompe-l'oeil,* illusionistic, fresco, Jesuit

3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.name: Villa Falconieri, fresco decoration in the Spring Room
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.description:
The interior was decorated immediately after the architectural extension, and was executed between 1668 and 1680 (possibly 1672–77), according to a single plan inspired by the cycle of the seasons and the ancient outline provided by Ovid's *Fasti*. The *trompe l'oeils* decoration is by Grimaldi, who after the death of Pietro da Cortona in 1669 directed some of the artwork using Cortona's pupils. The works harmoniously incorporate a range of different elements: the image of a garden in which the trees act as theatre wings, giving depth to the space and reflecting Grimaldi's scenographic culture; the rich vegetation surrounding the space in a sort of idealised isolation; the statues with garlands of flowers and the painted fountains and architecture – the whole marked by classical references and flights of fancy, filled with springtime symbols of flowers and fruits.  
The vault—painted by Ferri, Pietro da Cortona's principal pupil—shows *Flora* intent on scattering flowers and accompanied by the winds, in line with traditional iconography, stylistically characterised by graceful rhythms in polished forms with a classical style, a precursor to the shift towards Rococo.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.short_description: The Spring Room is part of a decorative cycle dedicated to the four seasons. Different elements representing the seasons merge harmoniously in *trompe-l'oeils* painted on the walls filled with springtime symbols of fruits and flowers. The vault depicts *Flora*, intent on scattering flowers and accompanied by the winds.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.method_for_datation: Guerrieri Borsoi, M. B., *Villa Rufina Falconieri*, Rome 2008.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.bibliography: Guerrieri Borsoi, M. B., *Villa Rufina Falconieri: la rinascita di Frascati e la più antica villa tuscolana*, Rome 2008 (with bibliography).
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.history: Villa Falconieri was erected on terracing originally created for a building from the Roman era. Built for Alessandro Rufini, a *Cameriere Segreto* (secret manservant) to Pope Paul III Farnese (1534–49), the villa originally had a square, fortified appearance with angular towers. Some decoration remains from this period, including the unicorn from the *impresa* of the Farnese family. It then passed to the Sforza family – related by marriage to the Boncompagni family – where it became a favourite meeting place for the papal court of Pope Gregory XIII Boncompagni (1572–85). It was at this time that Frascati became the holiday destination for the papal court and Roman nobility, reviving a tradition of *otia* (combining rest with meditation) thanks to its wholesome surroundings, abundance of water and the vicinity to nature. In 1628, ownership of the villa passed to the Falconieri family, which later—probably using a design by the architect Francesco Borromini (1559–1667)—entrusted Camilo Arcucci (1617/8–67), in partnership with Francesco Massari (1665–1705), with the task of expanding and converting it. The architect included the existing structure—a porticoed façade between two *avant-corps*—into an entirely new spatial concept, creating in the upper storey an ample concave *exedra*, which enabled optimum use to be made of the light, both in the contrast between voids and in-filled sections and of the alternating concave and convex forms, highlighted by the blind arches that frame the windows and decorate the entire façade, as was his preference.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.architects: Giovanni Francesco Grimaldi (1606, Bologna – 1680, Rome), painter and project leader; Ciro Ferri (1633, Rome – 1689, Rome) pupil of Pietro da Cortona (1596, Cortona ­– 1669, Rome)
keywords: Perspective painting, *trompe-l'oeil,* illusionistic, floral, fresco
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.author: Laura Indrio

3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.name: Church of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.description:
The church of Beja (1672) has a quadrangular nave covered by a tunnel vault; a narrower and lower chancel, a semi-circular apse – finished with a cupola and louvre – and a quadrangular addorsed sacristy, also covered with a vault.  
The church is an excellent example of a “total work of art” or *gesamtkunstwerk*, a sensibility often associated with Baroque interiors. The interior, a *theatrum* *sacrum*, holds within it the wood carvings of Manuel João da Fonseca and Francisco da Silva, which reflect the dialogue between the artistic schools of Lisbon and Évora. The ceiling compositions by Pedro Figueira, António de Oliveira Bernardes and João Pereira Pegado, who were influenced by the Beja masters, continue the artistic dialogue. Oliveira Bernardes' canvases and Gabriel del Barco's tile work represent the Mysteries of the Life of the Virgin, enhancing the theme of the Immaculate Conception.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.short_description: The church of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres in Beja lies close to the medieval city wall. Built in veneration of Our Lady, its importance was intensified by a miracle said to have taken place on a farm in Lisbon in the 16th century. Later, during the reign of King Pedro II, the church underwent renovation, turning it into one of the best examples of “plain” architecture and interior decoration in the Lower Alentejo. A remarkable example of a “Golden Church”, it is enriched with *azulejos*, gilded woodcarving, wall painting and canvases devoted to the Mysteries of the Life of Virgin, focusing on the co-existence of the Seven Sorrows and the Seven Joys of the Mother of God.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.bibliography: Serrão, V., Lameira, F., Falcão, J. A., *A Igreja de Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres em Beja, Arte e História de um Espaço Barroco (1672–1698),* Lisbon, 2007.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.history: During the 16th century a door was opened in the medieval wall of Beja allowing access to the main square, near the *Corredoura* (a road used for horse racing). Our Lady of Pleasures Church was built in veneration of the Miracle of Our Lady and to eulogise the Seven Sorrows and the Seven Joys of the Mother of God, the importance of which was further intensified by a miracle said to have taken place on a farm near Lisbon. According to tradition, the Virgin appeared to a girl and asked her to tell her parents and neighbours that a chapel should be built close by. Thereafter, a series of other miracles aroused intense devotional outbreaks in the country and overseas territories, and these accelerated the construction of even more places of worship.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.patrons: Brotherhood of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres

3f7f1a1e-4c4f-5c0d-bf56-e994790e9bdf.name: Benedictine Monastery, Rajhrad
3f7f1a1e-4c4f-5c0d-bf56-e994790e9bdf.description:
The monastery church was surrounded by four courtyards. In front of the west front is the prelature, in the south section the monastery, and opposite are two farmsteads. Unfinished west spires from the late 17th century were later incorporated into the church building. Structural engineers faced problems with the swampy terrain. Santini’s design was executed by the Brno builder F. B. Klíčník who reduced the number of neo-Gothic motifs, especially at the front. The niches contain statues of St. Vojtěch and the hermit, St. Vintíř. The gable between the spires features a mosaic of the Immaculate Conception (1895). The church, of a triplicate ground plan with a central octagon, is 79.5 m long. Triumphal arches accentuate the depth of the longitudinal space, endowing it with rhythm and monumentality. Santini’s design emphasised the optical effects relying largely on subsequent painting components. J. J. Etgens’s (1726–1729) frescos celebrate the Benedictine order and its spread throughout Europe, Asia and Africa in the first three centuries of its existence. Frescoes above the gallery represent the glorification of the Lord through singing and music.  
Above the sacristy, the church presbytery is adjoined by an oratory with an altar to St. Benedict. It was decorated with pictures by J. Zelený, a native of Rajhrad and the first teacher of the artist Alfons Mucha.
3f7f1a1e-4c4f-5c0d-bf56-e994790e9bdf.short_description: The monastery is one of the largest in South Moravia and the only one owned by the Benedictine order. It played a key role in local education and in the development of the economy. The frescos in the church, by the architect Santini, celebrate the Benedictine order and its spread throughout Europe, Asia and Africa in the first three centuries of its existence. The monastery is famous for its picture gallery. It also houses the Museum of Literature in Moravia.
3f7f1a1e-4c4f-5c0d-bf56-e994790e9bdf.method_for_datation: The construction of the monastery is documented by ample sources (correspondence and designs), as well as by records in the monastery chronicle. The original state of the complex is also captured in several engravings.

3f7f1a1e-4c4f-5c0d-bf56-e994790e9bdf.history: The monastery is one of the largest in South Moravia and the only one owned by the Benedictine order. It was established in around 1025 as a branch of a monastery in Prague-Břevnov, on a site of an old settlement. Until the 17th century it maintained a largely Romanesque appearance (reconstructed to a design by A. Erna in 1670). The reconstruction, triggered by efforts to promote the monastery to an abbey, started in 1721. The majority of the original buildings were demolished and the restoration was only completed in 1840. From 1540 onwards Rajhrad provosts held seats in the Provincial Assembly. The monastery played a key role in local education and in the development of the economy establishing the tradition of winemaking and beer brewing, and facilitating the construction of hospitals, workhouses and orphanages. After 1623 the monastery housed a prestigious school. It is famous for its large picture gallery which acquired art works from dissolved monasteries and chateau collections. Among the monastery’s valuable collection is the Rajhrad Altar (c. 1420).

3fa7c158-f2ad-5e29-985d-61f528ba2a1e.name: *The Rape of Helen*
3fa7c158-f2ad-5e29-985d-61f528ba2a1e.description:
Paris's kidnap of Helen, the beautiful wife of the king of Sparta, opens Homer's *Iliad*, an epic of the Trojan War. For artists, it provided a frequent source of moral, historical and entertaining scenes from the renaissance onwards.  
The drama of the event that led to the destruction of Troy is conveyed in detailed rendering of multiple figures moving through the picture area. Brutal, gory scenes are omitted; the artist presents the event as a theatrical spectacle. The suspense of the scene is enhanced by the presence of the elements: the wind blowing the flags, Helen's vermilion-red attire and pushing the sails of fleeing ships, and the sea. The ancient architecture of the harbour, with Tuscan columns and obelisks, was standard in the repertoire of 18th-century decorative painting. The warrior with erect shield on the left paraphrases Lysippus's “Borghese Warrior”, a staple object of study at art academies. The counterpart picture of *The Rape of Helen* was *The Rape of the Sabines*, a legend associated with the foundation of Rome and, according to Virgil, the continuation of Troy.  
Detailed narrative cabinet pictures with a host of figures are typical of the oeuvre of this academic Viennese painter who, together with Franz Janneck, specialised in the kind of decorative paintings favoured by art collectors. Inspired by Dutch 17th-century painting and, in particular, by Rudolphine mannerism, Platzer coined an original style, highlighting the sensory qualities of surfaces and things with scattered light and contrasting colours.
3fa7c158-f2ad-5e29-985d-61f528ba2a1e.short_description: A detailed narrative cabinet picture, typical of this academic Viennese painter. Inspired by Dutch 17th-century painting, in particular by Rudolphine mannerism, he coined an original style highlighting the sensory qualities of surfaces and things with scattered light and contrasting colours.

40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.name: National Palace of Mafra
40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.description:
Symmetrically organised, the building evolves from a central axis: the basilica flanked by the palace façades, the king's apartments at the north end, and the queen's on the south. At the back there is a convent, originally intended for the Order of St. Francis, which has at its nucleus a uniquely well-preserved 18th-century hospital.  
Altogether the palace occupies 38,000 m2 and has 1,200 rooms and 4,700 doors and windows. The high points of the Basilica are the ensemble of statues made by Italian masters, part of The Royal Commission that also comprises an important collection of 18th-century Italian and Portuguese paintings, two Flemish-made carillons with 92 bells, retables from the Mafra school of sculpture, and a set of six organs.
40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.short_description: The National Palace of Mafra is Portugal’s most important Baroque building, comprising a royal palace, a basilica and a Franciscan convent within which is a well-preserved 18th-century hospital. The palace houses the remarkable Royal Commission, a collection of Italian sculptures and Portuguese and Italian paintings, two carillons and six historical organs as well as precious gold artefacts and church ornaments.

40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.history:
Taking advantage of the prosperity granted by the Brazilian gold afflux, King D. João V ordered construction of the Palace in the hope that this initiative would bless him with the birth of a male heir to the throne. The first stone was set in 1717, under the direction of the architect Johan Frederich Ludwig.  
The so-called “Real Obra” was the first Portuguese school of Fine Arts, particularly for architects, stonemasons, carpenters, cabinetmakers and painters; in 1753, King D. João V’s son, King D. José I, implemented a School of Sculpture there under the direction of the Italian Alessandro Giusti.  
Mafra was King D. João V’s favourite palace, and at the end of the 18th century, he commissioned the mural paintings and a new ensemble of six organs for the Basilica. Although the palace was never a permanent royal residence, it was frequently visited by royalty for hunting in the extensive park or to attend religious festivities.  
In the aftermath of the monarchy’s last days, it was from Mafra that the last Portuguese sovereign, D. Manuel II, left to go into exile in 1910.

40212b79-f658-57bd-80ad-e8fd0a514a98.name: Old Federal State Parliament
40212b79-f658-57bd-80ad-e8fd0a514a98.description: The building, arranged around a rectangular inner courtyard, consists of a wide main wing with a street façade, vestibule, staircase and assembly hall on the second floor. Two narrower and lower wings adjoin it at right angles and enclose the courtyard to the north and south. The fourth side is composed of the parliament chapel of St George, built by Gumpp between 1725 and 1728 with entrances connecting it to the wings. In addition to the parliament hall with the Asam frescos, the congress hall in the north wing is a magnificent festive hall designed for the purpose of political representation.
40212b79-f658-57bd-80ad-e8fd0a514a98.short_description: The House of the Estates of Tyrol is the most monumental of Innsbruck’s Baroque palaces as well as the largest and most important secular building of the court master builder Georg Anton Gumpp. As a symbol of the self confident representation of the estates, the architecture and furnishings are of a special grandeur and artistic quality. Together with the Hofburg, the three-wing complex with connected chapel forms the representative centre of the state capital.
40212b79-f658-57bd-80ad-e8fd0a514a98.bibliography:
Bushart, B., Rupprecht, B., *Cosmas Damian Asam 1686-1739*, Munich 1986, pp. 261–2.  
Lorenz, H., *Barock*, Munich, London, New York 1999 (= Geschichte der bildenden Kunst in Österreich, Vol. 4), p. 290f.  
Öhler, H., *Ingenuin Lechleitner (1676–1731)*, Innsbruck 2008.  
Wieser, H., Öhler, H., Fischler, R., *Das Tiroler Landhaus*, Innsbruck 2009.
40212b79-f658-57bd-80ad-e8fd0a514a98.history: Since 1613 the estates convened in the “Haus zum goldenen Engel” (House of the Golden Angel), however its assembly room was too small for the full parliament. In 1666 it was moved to the “Hofplattnerei”, but the building was in poor condition. With the growing importance of the estates of Tyrol in the early 18th century a new building was constructed between 1725 and 1728 by Georg Anton Gumpp under the patronage of the prince-bishop of Brixen and the governor of Tyrol. The first period of interior design work ended in 1734, stucco was applied to the congress hall in 1758. Today the Landhaus is the seat of the Tyrolean parliament.

4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.name: *The Annunciation*
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.alternate_name: *La Madonna del Bell’Angelo* (*The Madonna with the Beautiful Angel*)
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.description:
This altarpiece was originally commissioned for the Fioravanti chapel in the former St. Bartholomew church. It was inaugurated in 1632. In 1647 the Barnabites fathers commissioned the same painter to complete two smaller side paintings with episodes of the life of the Virgin (the *Adoration of the Child* and the *Dream of St. Joseph*) and asked for some retouches to the *Annunciation*. In 1685 the church was inaugurated and the three pictures were moved to the fourth chapel in the right side aisle, where they remain today.  
The altarpiece soon became renown as the *Madonna del Bell'Angelo* (the Madonna with the beautiful angel) for the beauty of the announcing angel.  
Albani builds the picture by juxtaposing the standing Madonna, nearly indifferent to the annunciation, against the Angel that is bursting from the dark closed room with luminous shades of yellow. Following the angel, a cloud of cherubs and putti rolls from heaven in a chaotic but lively invasion. The picture mixes the naturalistic lesson of the Carraccis with the round lines and the vivacious movement of full Baroque style.
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.short_description: This painting was made by Francesco Albani, one of the pupils of the celebrated Carraccis. These three cousins strongly contributed to the Baroque revolution in Bologna and throughout Europe. Albani is a very pleasant painter. He tells the story of the *Annunciation* in a captivating way, showing the Madonna as a princess full of grace and self-control and the heavenly court bursting with enthusiastic life.
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.holder: Church of Saint Bartholomew and Gaetano
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.obtention: The object is still preserved in the original location.

43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.name: Church of St. Blaise, Dubrovnik
43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.description: In line with the Venetian origins of the architect, Marino Gropelli, the organisation of the ground plan and space of St. Blaise consists of a Greek cross inscribed into a square nave, which develops into a square sanctuary and concludes with an inscribed apse flanked by two sacristies. Apart from the traditional Venetian features in the choice of ground plan, Gropelli used the same model for the elevation and the vaulting: the central Corinthian columns bear the tambour of the high dome and lantern, and in the corners of the nave, there are lower blind cupolas. Barrel vaults cover the vertical “legs” of the Greek cross and the sanctuary, on the axis of which there are large thermal windows. Such articulation of the interior reveals direct models in classical Venetian architecture, for example, Sansovino's San Maurizio, while some details such as the dark-grey columns and arches, are inspired by Andrea Palladio. On the exterior, in addition to the sources mentioned above, Gropelli exploits the achievements reached by contemporary Venetian Baroque architecture. The plasticity of the vertical “legs” of the Greek cross – which by their height are prominent – are surmounted by a central cupola and placed in an oblique base of rustic stone (*bugnato*), with stairs and balustrades, while the three-part facade with a round gable is decoratively articulated in a similar way to Baltasare Longhena's Church of S. Lorenzo Giustiniani. The skilful architectural sculpting (*masqueron*s), along with the freestanding statues of the patron, the angels and personifications of Faith and Hope, tell of the primary vocation of the architect: sculpture. Thus with these characteristics, the Church of St. Blaise shows an architectural approach unique in Dubrovnik, one which influenced local architecture, primarily at the level of the enrichment of architectural embellishment.
43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.short_description: Badly damage by fire, the church was rebuilt between 1707 an 1715. For the reconstruction of the church dedicated to the city's patron saint, St. Blaise, the people of Dubrovnik (the Senate) chose a Venetian architect, Marino Gropelli who used the traditional Venetian ground plan with an inscribed Greek cross and domes in the central and corner fields. The exterior of the church is distinctive for its oblique base with stairs and a balustrade, and for the high quality architectural and figurative sculptures of the patron, angels and distinctive Venetian *masquerons*.
43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.type: Religious architecture, Baroque central church with a ground plan in the form of an inscribed Greek cross and dome
43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents and stylistic features.
43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.bibliography:
Prijatelj, K., “Barok u Dalmaciji”, in Horvat, A., (ed), *Barok u Hrvatskoj*, Zagreb, 1982, pp. 649–916.  
Marković, V., “Ljetnikovac Bozdari u Rijeci dubrovačkoj i Marino Gropelli” in *Prilozi povijesti umjetnosti u Dalmaciji* 30 (1990), pp. 95–114.  
Tomić, R., *Barokni oltari i skulptura u Dalmaciji*, Zagreb, 1995, pp.117–119.
43f9ab1d-8bff-5e93-86f0-37fefef1b1b8.history: Although spared in the earthquake of 1667, a fire in 1706 devastated the medieval church dedicated to the patron saint of the town, St. Blaise. The new church, built on the foundations of the old one, was re-orientated so that the entrance facade faced the main city street (*Placa*). Chosen by the people of Dubrovnik (the Senate), the architect of this highly demanding brief was the Venetian architect and sculptor, Marino Gropelli.
keywords: Dubrovnik, church of the patron saint of the city, Baroque, Marino Gropelli, ground plan in the form of an inscribed Greek cross, high altar

440083e7-d0c2-582e-be68-2e0366d38ec9.name: *Mythological Scene* (the Forge of Vulcan?)
440083e7-d0c2-582e-be68-2e0366d38ec9.description:
A painting that was part of a series which was once part of the Royal Palace Collection in Buda. In the inventory the painting is described together with the other pieces as: “school of Rubens, unknown figural composition in richly carved gilt wooden frame”.  
It is on the basis of this description, together with the size, that the four pieces have been identified. The paintings, all purchased by members of the Habsburg family over the centuries, were preserved in the Royal Collection but little is known about the method by which the works were selected, or the family’s preferences concerning the artists. It is only a few years ago that the list of works held in the Royal Collection could be investigated and some of the paintings were identified. The works arrived at the Budapest History Museum in poor condition and it is only thanks to exhibitions in recent years that a few of them have been restored.
440083e7-d0c2-582e-be68-2e0366d38ec9.short_description: A Baroque mythological scene, part of a series that originally decorated the Royal Palace in Buda.
440083e7-d0c2-582e-be68-2e0366d38ec9.obtention: Transferred to the Museum in 1945 along with other pieces from the Royal Collection.

44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.name: Processional cross
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.alternate_name: Processional standard of the brotherhood of the Tears of the Virgin Mary or of the Ponte del Borgo, later del Borgo, later Company of the Holy Sacrament
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.description:
This solemn gilded cross bears a rich decoration of vine leaves and vine-shoots made with a drill. There are interspersed with cherub heads and angels carved in the round, crowned with polychrome flowers and holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ.  
The branches resemble tree trunks with bark and knots. They end with two small knobs. The dead Christ in the middle is carved in the round, polychrome with an ample gilded cloth around his hips. On the upper part of the longitudinal arm hangs a cartouche with the writing \`INRI\` held by three small angels.  
Along the lower sides, stand on shelves four small statues carved in the round. They represent the Mourning Madonna, St. Bartholomew and two angels with gilded clothes and polychrome features.  
The stylistic features are late seventeenth-century and the delicate carving is associated with a skilled use of a drill.  
After the suppressions of 1798 that affected all religious companies and brotherhoods by the confiscation of their property, many of these processional items got lost. Thanks to a decree by the viceroy of Italy Eugenio Beauharnais in 1807 which stated for each parish church the presence of just one company of the Holy sacrament many processional crosses were preserved as properties of these companies. This happened in Budrio, where even the name of the company was changed.
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.short_description:
This solemn gilded cross bears a rich decoration with vine leaves and vine-shoots made with the drill. It is interspersed with angels carved in the round holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ.  
In the middle is the dead Christ surrounded by the Mourning Madonna, St. Bartholomew and two angels.  
The elaborate design is reminiscent of the local artistic taste of the end of the seventeenth century.

44f1f594-2aaa-5494-a299-c58ee9d66b02.name: Cistercian Monastery of Stams
44f1f594-2aaa-5494-a299-c58ee9d66b02.description: The exterior of the monastery building, in parts of compact proportions, is primarily characterised by the work of the family of master builders Gumpp. The elongated west wing, which terminates to the north in two massive corner towers, is composed of the sequence of monastery wing and sovereign’s wing with the festive hall of the Bernhardi wing as an intervening projection. Adjoining to the south is the two-storey church façade structured by columns. The monastery church, redesigned along Late Baroque lines and incorporating the medieval building fabric, still bears witness to the original form of a transept-less, flat-roofed Romanesque pier basilica. The hall is extended by transept-like chapels. Its uniform character is generated by the extensive stuccowork and the cycle of large format ceiling paintings.
44f1f594-2aaa-5494-a299-c58ee9d66b02.short_description: The Cistercian Monastery of Stams, founded in the late Staufer era, is one of Tyrol’s most important monasteries. The medieval complex was gradually replaced by new building in the Baroque period and the monastery church was refurbished with Early Baroque features before the comprehensive renovation of the 18th century. The appearance of the ensemble, despite a number of medieval architectural elements, is in the Baroque style.
44f1f594-2aaa-5494-a299-c58ee9d66b02.dates: 1615–1620: construction of the monastery building; 1631–1635; 1692–1724: Baroque redesign of the monastery church; 1729–1732
44f1f594-2aaa-5494-a299-c58ee9d66b02.bibliography:
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 39f.  
*Stift Stams/Tirol*, 11th edition, Munich, Zurich 1978 (= Schnell, Kleine Kunstführer, No. 289).  
Zohner, W., *Bartholomäus Steinle*. Weißenhorn 1993, pp. 37–51.  
Lebersorg, W., *Chronik des Klosters Stams*, Innsbruck 2000.
44f1f594-2aaa-5494-a299-c58ee9d66b02.history: The monastery, founded by the Prince of Görz-Tyrol in 1273, was settled by monks from the Cistercian monastery of Kaisheim in Swabia. The Romanesque monastery church was consecrated in 1284. Subject to damage in the 16th century, repair work begun in the early 17th century, i.e. its replacement by new buildings. Features of the monastery church from the first period of interior design work include the high altar (1609–13). Redesign of the royal crypt began in 1677. Comprehensive Baroque redesign of the monastery church was carried out between 1729 and 1734.

456f9027-f659-5ba1-9d14-abf84e696796.name: Parish Church of St. Stephen the Protomartyr
456f9027-f659-5ba1-9d14-abf84e696796.description:
The Parish Church of Pápa, with its façade bearing Classicist features and its two emphatic front towers, is a Late Baroque creation that reflects the refined taste of the Bishop of Eger, Károly Esterházy. The entirely flat façade is articulated by smooth pillars with Ionic capitals. Above the pillars, on the simple main moulding, is a tympanum that frames the Bishop's coat of arms. Two towers are mounted above the attic the highest tops of which are held by columns and pillars, the latter angled by 45 degrees on the façade, which brings to mind the monumentality of Roman Baroque. On the gables in between the towers, and surrounded by decorative vases, is a statue group of St. Stephen the Protomartyr and two angels.  
Inside, the nave is composed of an entrance hall, two sections covered by flat “cupolas”, and the sanctuary topped by a cupola. There are no side chapels along the nave as the aim of the designer was to create a space that could easily be taken in at a glance from any standpoint.  
The painted decorations of the church include the colourful scenes in the frame of the *quadratura* (painted perspectives of architecture) on the cupolas, and the *grisaille* paintings on the pendentives that Maulbertsch termed “high reliefs” and which follow the frescoes of the Church of Santo Stefano Rotondo in Rome.  
Further paintings include the *Twenty-Four elders Praising the Lord* from the Book of Revelation above the organ-loft by the entrance; *St. Stephen and his Followers Being Ordained as Deacons* on the first section of the cupola and the *Martyrdom of the Followers of St. Stephen* on the pendentives; *St. Stephen Preaching in a Church* on the second section of the cupola, and the *Miraculous Deeds of St. Stephen* on the pendentives; *St. Stephen Being Dragged to the Synagogue and his Heavenly Revelation* on the sanctuary cupola, and depictions of the *Miracles after the Death of St. Stephen* on the pendentives.  
In his program from 1779 the Bishop emphasised one scene in particular from the latter depictions – also seen in the Church of Santo Stefano Rotondo in Rome – in which St. Stephen the Protomartyr appears to Sarolta wife of Géza, Grand Prince of the Magyars, and prophesies the birth of her son, King St. Stephen (Szent István).  
There are other works by Maulbertsch in the vestry and chapel. The main altar holds a statue of two angels with the figures of St. Stephen and St. Andrew, made of Carrara marble either side, and a painting, *The Stoning of St. Stephen*, in the middle. On the instructions of the Bishop, four side-altars were built (consecrated to the Deaths of St. Joseph, St. Anne and St. Mary, St. John of Nepomuk, and St. Charles Borromeo).
456f9027-f659-5ba1-9d14-abf84e696796.short_description: Count Károly Esterházy (Bishop of Eger and an outstanding benefactor of his time) ordered construction of the parish church in Pápa. The Bishop, who was a follower of the more modern spiritual trends of the Catholic church, defined the details of the construction and the decoration in several programs. He found the most suitable practitioners for the job: the architect Jakab Fellner, the family's architect, and the painter Franz Anton Maulbertsch. The completed church, along with all its architectural forms and mural formations, reflect the Bishop's rational intellectuality, or in Maulbertsch's words [the building is] “bright, quietly ordered and easily recognisable in terms of [the character's] clothing and clarity of the stories”.
456f9027-f659-5ba1-9d14-abf84e696796.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, and stylistic research.

Pigler, A., *A pápai plébániatemplom és mennyezetképei (The Parish Church of Pápa and its Murals)*, Budapest, 1922.  
Garas, K., *Magyarországi festészet a XVIII. században (Painting in Hungary in the 18th century)*, Budapest, 1955, pp. 85–89.  
Aggházy, M., *A barokk szobrászat Magyarországon* *(Baroque Sculpture in Hungary),* Vols. 1–3, Budapest, 1959, Vol.  2, p. 207.  
Gerő, L., Sedlmayr, J., *Pápa*, Budapest, 1959, pp. 160—167.
456f9027-f659-5ba1-9d14-abf84e696796.history:
In 1771 Bishop of Eger Károly Esterházy, decided to demolish the Medieval Church of Pápa dedicated to St. Stephen the Protomartyr, and build a new church on the same site. He entrusted Jakab Fellner, the family's architect, to design the plans and oversee the construction. Fellner worked on the project between 1774 and 1780 and, after his death, József Grossman continued the work until 1785. The interior decoration of the church was created by the Viennese painter, Franz Anton Maulbertsch and his team of architectural painters, between 1782 and 1783.  
The Bishop decided that the *grisaille* scenes of the pendentives under the three cupola murals, should be similar in terms of theme (and sometimes even in terms of the figures used) to the murals portraying the story of St. Stephen the Protomartyr in the Church of Santo Stefano Rotondo in Rome (the “Hungarian Church”), painted by Niccolò Circignani in 1582, and of which the Bishop had made colourful sketches as a reference from which Maulbertsch and his team worked.  
Other elements of the church decoration were the work of several masters: Johann Messerschmidt created the statue group on the façade; other stone decorations were made by Johann Georg Mess and Martin Rumpelmayer. The main and side altars were built by József Grossman, and the marble decorations of the main altar are by Carlo and Giacomo Adami, two masters from Süttő. The figures in Carrara marble are by Philipp Jakob Prokop. On the main altarpiece, the painting, *The Stoning of Saint Stephen*, is by Hubert Maurer from Vienna in 1785, and those on the side altars by János Zickler from Eger between 1783 and 1786. Károly Esterházy also appears in an altarpiece painting accompanied by St. Charles Borromeo, who was a personal *beau ideal* for the Bishop. The Church was consecrated in 1795.

45d23113-bc1c-526b-981b-9433784c79c5.name: Palazzo Fantuzzi
45d23113-bc1c-526b-981b-9433784c79c5.description:
The impressive façade goes back to the Tosco-Roman tradition of sixteenth-century's buildings. It is decorated with elephants, alluding to the Fantuzzis' coat of arms.  
Inside, the celebrated staircase by Pietro Canali is sober, decorated with statues of Hercules and Atlas.  
On the second floor it is possible to visit the great hall, with frescoes painted by Francesco Galli Bibiena between 1678 and 1684. The artist abandoned the traditional frontal view and started a new way of painting architectural buildings by employing a corner perspective.  
On the wall there is a false double asymmetrical open gallery with gods and other mythological figures. Francesco was a very good figure painter, probably more skillful than his elder brother Ferdinando. Colonnades and wings increase the illusion, fooling the observer and appearing to enlarge the room.  
Opposite the windows a painted green garden opens the view onto theatrical suggestions.
45d23113-bc1c-526b-981b-9433784c79c5.short_description: Thanks to its façade without arcades, unusual in Bologna, it’s easy to recognise Palazzo Fantuzzi in via S. Vitale. Inside the palace, besides the ballroom illusionistically painted by Francesco Galli Bibiena (1659-1739) in a second time, Carlo Ridolfo Fantuzzi ordered Pietro Canali (1618-1680) to build a monumental staircase, one of the first late-baroque examples in Bologna.

45d23113-bc1c-526b-981b-9433784c79c5.history:
Built in 1517, in place of the previous medieval houses. This was the residence of the Fantuzzi family, whose members were part of the Bolognese Senate.  
The palace façade, possibly based on a project by Formigine and Bartolomeo Triachini, has not a portico, a frequent feature of Bolognese palatial architecture.  
The building was finished in 1680 when Carlo Ridolfo Fantuzzi was elected Gonfalonier. To celebrate himself, he decided to inaugurate a new staircase inside the building based on a project by Pietro Canali. This staircase was to lead the guests to the ballroom on the noble floor.

468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.name: Pilgrimage Church of the Scourged Saviour, Dyje
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.alternate_name: Church of St. John of Nepomuk, Dyje (Milfroň, Mülfraun)
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.description: The austere single-nave building is typical of the architecture in the Danube Basin during the second half of the 18th century. It poses a contrast to the colourful, mystical and complex paintings for which a printed programme has survived probably put together by the artist himself. Individual sections represent the scenes Ecce Homo, Adoration of the Shepherds, Allegory of Salvation and Allegory of the Church.
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.short_description: This pilgrimage church was part of a broad residential network attached to a major Premonstratensian Monastery in Znojmo-Louka. When the monastery was dissolved, the church became increasingly dilapidated. After the displacement of the Czech-German population in 1945 and the sealing of the Czech-Austrian border, the church, situated in the border region, lost its importance. Restoration of the church only began in 2004 as part of the international project, Culture 2000. The paintings with their intricate iconographic programme are by F. A. Maulbertsch and his closest associates.
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.method_for_datation: The chronogram in Abbot Lambeck’s consecration inscription over the entrance vault gives the year 1774. A record gives the date of the church’s consecration as 6 September 1778. In addition, the progress of the building work is recorded in correspondence between the abbot of the Premonstratensian Monastery in Louka and the Bishop of Győr, where Maulbertsch also worked at the time.

468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.history: The pilgrimage church was built after the demolition of the medieval Church of St. Lawrence in a village belonging to the Znojmo-Louka Premonstratensian Monastery. The monastery hospital was located in the village. The Znojmo-Louka Monastery, one of the oldest and richest in the country, created a unique series of buildings and pilgrimage sites in south Moravia associated with the main religious festivals of the year. When the monastery was dissolved by Emperor Joseph II in 1784 the church started to fall into disrepair. It was plundered during the Napoleonic Wars and used as stables and minor repairs did not rectify the structural problems of the building. After the expulsion of the Czech-German population in 1945 and the sealing of the Czech-Austrian border, the church situated in the inaccessible border region, lost its importance. Restoration of the church only began in 2004 as part of the international project, Culture 2000.

4741a810-33a7-588d-a74e-9f4b95e2c325.name: Gmunden Parish Church
4741a810-33a7-588d-a74e-9f4b95e2c325.alternate_name: Parish Church of the Virgin or Parish Church of the Assumption of the Virgin / Parish Church of the Epiphany
4741a810-33a7-588d-a74e-9f4b95e2c325.description:
Right in the city, the medieval (parish) church is situated on an elevation and since then has dominated Gmunden’s skyline. In the 15th/16th century it became surrounded by a graveyard, in the 17th and 18th century baroquisation in the form of additions, fittings and decoration took place. The high altar got in the 17th century its famous statues and other artworks, such as the baptismal font. An extensive baroquisation took place in the 18th century. The tower and the entrance hall were added and the interior was overworked in the style of the epoch.  
As a rare example of a place of worship, the church was not only dedicated to *one* holy person or *one* historic religious event, but to two: it was in the Middle Ages consecrated to the Holy Virgin and later to the Epiphany (in the 17th century). This probably happened when the high altar got the magnificent group of statues, the Adoration of the Magi.
4741a810-33a7-588d-a74e-9f4b95e2c325.short_description:
Typically Austrian, the Gmunden parish church was built in the Middle Ages and extended and decoratively overworked in the Baroque era. The up-and-coming princely city of Gmunden went through the same architectural development: initially there were mighty buildings from the Middle Ages, in the 17th and 18th century new edifices were added or old buildings were baroquized.  
In the course of baroquization, one of the most popular sculptors was commissioned in the 17th century to create statues for the high altar. About forty years later a well-known architect added the tower with onion-shaped roof and lantern. Like many baroque church towers in Austria, this became the landmark of the town.
4741a810-33a7-588d-a74e-9f4b95e2c325.dates:
1270: first documentary mention  
First half of the 14th century: construction of church  
Second half of the 17th century: start of baroquisation (exterior and interior)  
First third of the 17th century: Holy Virgin statue  
17th century: baptismal font  
1678: Epiphany statues  
1679: high altar (modified about 1860)  
1685: Anna altar  
About 1690: St Elizabeth and St Zachariah statues  
End 17th century: St Barbara and St Margaretha statues  
1713–18: construction of tower  
1723: entrance hall  
First half of 18th century: St Peter and St Paul statues

4741a810-33a7-588d-a74e-9f4b95e2c325.history:
Simultaneously with the region’s economic development, the city of Gmunden was growing and developing since the Middle Ages. There was only one obstacle to overcome: one had to open it for the road traffic. The town is situated on the North end of the long and narrow Traunsee which is surrounded by partially steep mountains, and it was because of this over the centuries without a land route. Transport took place by ship through the lake. Unaffected by this, city and citizens lived in prosperity as there had always been profitable (salt) mining.  
When the golden era of salt trade ended, the citizens changed direction – the salt’s healing power was discovered and a new branch of industry was born. Gmunden became popular as a brine spa and consequently as a summer retreat for the noble and wealthy from Vienna.

476338a6-6cae-5f4e-abd0-66a0360a466a.name: Monastery of San Michele in Bosco, Library
476338a6-6cae-5f4e-abd0-66a0360a466a.description:
The library is composed of three rooms in a row, lluminated by side windows. The central room is large and square, with three domed vaults separated by arches. The other rooms, the vestibule and the room dedicated to mathematical and scientific instruments, have vaulted ceilings.  
All the rooms are completely decorated with illusive architectural features which frame the figures. This homogenous decoration endows the small space with a magnificent and new face.  
The subject painted by Domenico Maria Canuti is that of Wisdom, a combination of science and religion. The complex meaning of the theological allegories is explained in a booklet specially published in 1681, to explain their significance after the work was finished.  
The ceiling of the main room, while separated by arches, shows the same decorative theme. Wisdom is celebrated: in the centre Divine Wisdom dominates Human Wisdom, at the sides allegorical figures warn against a daring use of knowledge and demonstrate how study and research must have Good as their main aim. The decoration is completed by painted telamones supporting the vaults on their shoulders, the Allegories of the Four Continents and of the main Doctrines in the lunettes.  
In the Vestibule of the library, the “sfondato” shows the Four Human Temperaments symbolically linked with the allegories of the Four Elements painted in the pendentives.  
In the last room are depicted the Cardinal Virtues in the pendentives and the Four Fathers of the Church as monochromes on the walls; in the middle of the ceiling the archangel Michael pleads with God to help the sciences and virtues.  
The Paintings in the three rooms are connected by the painted architecture by Enrico Haffner. The style emphasizes the figures without oppressing them and creates a homogeneous texture rich of inventions.
476338a6-6cae-5f4e-abd0-66a0360a466a.short_description: The church and monastery of San Michele in Bosco were built on a hill above Bologna in place of a former church dedicated to St. Michael dating to the 12th century. The first shrine on this site dates back to the 4th century. The Olivetan Fathers, living here since 1364, rebuilt the church and the monastery between 1437 and 1447; the buildings were refurbished again in 1517-23. The works were finished by 1660: the baroque library, painted by Domenico Maria Canuti and Enrico Haffner, is a significant example of Baroque painted decoration. The octagonal cloister painted by the Carracci and the refectory decorated by Vasari and his pupils are also some of the highlights of the architectural complex. Since 1896 the former monastery has housed the Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, a hospital.
476338a6-6cae-5f4e-abd0-66a0360a466a.bibliography:
*Il monastero di San Michele in Bosco e l’Istituto ortopedico Rizzoli. Guida storico artistica*, Bologna, 2006.

476338a6-6cae-5f4e-abd0-66a0360a466a.history: The Library was commissioned by abbot Taddeus Pepoli, an intellectual and patron of the arts. In 1627 he entrusted the architect Giovan Giacomo Monti with rebuilding the former 16th century library, in order to create a grander and newer edifice. The architect amplified the space with new vaulted ceilings seven feet high. In 1677 the rooms were covered with frescoes by Domenico Maria Canuti. He was assisted by Enrico Haffner, a painter specialized in illusionistic painting (quadrature). The decorations follow a complex and intellectual iconographic program which was most likely created by Pepoli who patronized the work. The library was inaugurated in 1681. After the suppression of the Olivetan order the monastery was first converted into a prison and later became the summer residence of the Papal representative. The library was stripped of its furniture, bookcases and instruments and used for rehearsals. In 1922, when the monastery was being used as a hospital, the library was restored. Today it holds a precious collection of books concerning orthopaedics.

47e8c461-ce20-5bec-a573-acc2559b5674.name: Dominican Church of St. Michael, Brno
47e8c461-ce20-5bec-a573-acc2559b5674.description: The two-spire frontage which is segmented with pilasters and lesenes culminates in a triangular gable on top of which is the patron saint of the church. In 1728, in order to break up the flat façade, statues by A. Riga were set in niches. The mock-Gothic Chapel of the Holy Grave was added in 1701. The single-nave church adjoining the monastery buildings is flanked by side chapels furnished by blocks of richly carved pews decorated with acanthus leafs.
47e8c461-ce20-5bec-a573-acc2559b5674.short_description: The church was frequented by Moravian estate-holders who held their sessions in the adjacent monastery. City development incorporated the new church into what was the fish market, so that its disposition was reversed and the building was entered from the east. Setting the church into a mild slope quickly caused problems; repairs included the construction of a terrace lined with statues. The church altars were decorated by leading Brno artists. The pulpit with sculpted fallen angels is particularly noteworthy. Sketches for some parts of the decoration have been preserved.
47e8c461-ce20-5bec-a573-acc2559b5674.method_for_datation: The laying of the church foundation stone and its consecration are recorded in the archives. The dating of artworks by individual artists may be derived from their biographies and by chronologies of their work.

47e8c461-ce20-5bec-a573-acc2559b5674.history: The church was frequented by Moravian estate holders who held their sessions in the adjacent monastery. The complete refurbishment of the original medieval church was financed by the legacy of the provincial judge, Lev of Kounice, who had established the Kounic family tomb there. City development incorporated the new church into what was the fish market, so its disposition was reversed and the building was entered from the east. Setting the church into a mild slope proved a problem shortly after its completion by J. K. Erna. Old views of the square, which also featured the margrave’s house and a mint, show the monumental effect of the church amidst the surrounding buildings.
