695fe7b5-976e-59d7-837c-a6310d21319f.history: Situated in the Barberini estate, on the Via dell’Olmata, probably originally placed centrally on the plot, it is located in the orchard behind the house and was commissioned by Maffeo Barberini from the architect Francesco Contini as a tribute to his wife, Olimpia Giustiniani, whom he married in 1653 and whose family coat of arms includes a triangular tower.

6b3fb735-8b90-551a-a89a-34d891bd5f48.name: Pilgrimage Church of the Name of the Virgin Mary, Křtiny
6b3fb735-8b90-551a-a89a-34d891bd5f48.alternate_name: Pearl of Moravia, The First Ave, Kiritein
6b3fb735-8b90-551a-a89a-34d891bd5f48.description: The white frontage, inventively set into its environment, is decorated with statues by I. Lengelacher, installed in 1740. The unique architectural concept of the church lends a certain magic to the whole area. Santini was acquainted with the numerical symbolism of the Jewish Cabbala, which was also developed by prominent Catholic scholars, and applied its principles in his extraordinary compositions. The ground-plan layout is a circle with internal and external pentagons symbolising the Marian star. The partial merging of the central and side spaces turns a cross-shaped schema into a monumental four-conch whole.
6b3fb735-8b90-551a-a89a-34d891bd5f48.short_description: Legend has it that Saint Cyril and Saint Methodius once baptised pagans in the Křtiny Valley. The significance of the pilgrimage site grew during the Thirty Years’ War. The architect, Santini, was acquainted with the numerical symbolism of the Jewish Cabbala, which was also developed by prominent Catholic scholars, and he applied its principles in his extraordinary compositions. The ground plan symbolises the Marian star. The ceiling painting is a metaphorical celebration of the Virgin Mary as the embodiment of Divine Wisdom.
6b3fb735-8b90-551a-a89a-34d891bd5f48.method_for_datation: With the dissolution of the Zábrdovice Monastery the written records and plans disappeared and only chronicles from 1650–1710 have survived. Individual construction phases are known from prints. Records of pilgrimages are kept in the Křtiny Parish Archive; several pilgrimage books originate in the late 17th century.

Mojmír Horyna, *Jan Blažej Santini-Aichl*, Prague, 1998, pp. 331–337.  
Jiří Kroupa, in Jiří Kroupa (ed), *Dans le miroir des ombres. La Moravie a la age baroque 1670*–­­*1790*, Paris–­­Rennes–­­Brno, 2002, pp. 90–92, cat. 5.  
Jiří Kroupa, *Umělci, objednavatelé a styl. Studie z dějin umění*, Brno, 2006, pp. 137–195.
6b3fb735-8b90-551a-a89a-34d891bd5f48.history: Legend has it that Saint Cyril and Saint Methodius once baptised pagans in the Křtiny Valley, hence its old name, *Vallis baptismi*. One of the oldest pilgrimage sites, oral tradition further credits the place with an appearance of the Virgin Mary of Křtiny in 1210 among the blossom from a horse chestnut tree in nearby Bukovinka. The first written record is in a papal decree of 1237. The statue of the Virgin Mary dates from the first half of the 14th century and was probably donated by Jindřich of Lipá. The significance of the pilgrimage site grew during the Thirty Years' War, when it became a destination for two major thanksgiving pilgrimages to the Virgin Mary, Protectoress of the country. The foundation stone for the present church was laid in 1728. When the Premonstratensian order was dissolved in 1784 the incomplete residence was converted into an aristocratic palace (it became state property in 1948). The pilgrimage tradition has survived and Křtiny is among the most visited of its kind in Moravia.

6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.name: *King Béla III founding the Cistercian Monastery at Szentgotthárd in 1183*
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.description:
Originally, the painting hung in the abbot's reception hall in the Cistercian Monastery of Szentgotthárd, as one of a representative series of six *panneaux*. The six paintings perpetuate important events in the history of the Szentgotthárd Abbey as well as two moments of Hungarian history – the battles of Mohács and Szentgotthárd – believed by many to have had a direct influence on the fate of the abbey. The large canvases covered the walls of the room like wall hangings, with the uncovered sections of wall painted with landscapes to complete the historical compositions. Both the *panneaux* and ceiling decoration are by István Dorffmaister, and were commissioned by Abbot Marian Reutter. The programme follows the work of the scholarly Cistercian monk, Theophil Heimb's history of the Szentgotthárd Abbey, published in 1764. The book contains detailed accounts of events that are faithfully translated into visual images by Dorffmaister. The main episodes from the history of the Cistercian order in Hungary provided the theme for the series, beginning with the foundation of the order. It captures the moment the French monks were received by the king and his escorts – who are wearing colourful Hungarian costumes – in front of an antique *porticus*. In the background there is a distant view of 18th-century Pest-Buda with a few medieval details added. Behind the monks there is an imaginary view of the Romanesque Church and Abbey of Szentgotthárd. The pure forms, simple light effects and the light-coloured palette – the stylistic marks of the Late Baroque mixed with the elements of Neo-Classicism so appropriate at the end of the 18th century – suggest an optimistic view of history, which is a rarity in Hungarian art.  
While Dorffmaister's historical paintings were born in ecclesiastical surroundings and according to the traditional artist-patron relationship, they still bore fresh, modern meaning and became representative works of the new European tendencies of the era.
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.short_description: The *panneaux* series from Szentgotthárd depicts Hungarian historical subjects; one section of it is kept in Heiligenkreuz. The *panneaux* is a very special Neo-Classical series of paintings, in this one a *veduta* of Buda Castle can be seen in the background.
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.method_for_datation: One painting of the series is signed. Origin and date verified by historical documents.
6b6ea556-21c1-572c-a50b-ec86e51487da.obtention: Cistercian Monastery in Szentgotthárd transferred from the former Cistercian Monastery in Szentgotthárd. Transferred to the Museum of Fine Arts in 1950–51 where it remained until 1974 before being transferred to the Hungarian National Gallery.

6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.name: *Namban* Folding Screen (*Namban Byobu*)
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.description:
The *Namban Byobu*, of which there are more than 70 extant, are some of the most impressive visual testimonies to the way Japanese painters perceived the first Europeans to arrive in Japan. The arrival of the Portuguese in 1543 and their expulsion almost a century later in 1639, gave rise to the so called *Namban Bijutsu* artwork, a result of the meeting of the Japanese and European cultures.  
A pair of six-fold painted screens, they both follow the most current theme of the *Namban Byobu*, depicting the arrival of the Portuguese in Japan. On the left, the screen depicts a great ship from Macao, or *kurofune* (“the black ship”), and on the right a procession, or *Namban Gyoretsu*, passing a Japanese street observed by curious inhabitants. Waiting for them are the Jesuits, whose church is built in the Japanese style with interior rooms that largely follow local models, such as the use of *tatami* to cover the floor or of *shoji* to divide the inner space. The daily life of the Jesuit mission is depicted in these *byobu* (*biombo* in Portuguese). The works convey their approach to “accommodation”, according to which special attention was paid to the European priests' and brothers' integration into Japanese society.  
The procession is composed of a Captain-Major, standing underneath a state parasol surrounded by other officers, as well as sailors, African slaves, Indians and Malays. The ornaments worn by the aristocrats and rich merchants are visible and notable: gold chains, crucifixes and daggers. While the majority of the characters wear *bombacha* – large baggy trousers used in the East to protect them from mosquitoes, their doublets have buttons, which were unknown to the Japanese, who called them *botan* from the Portuguese *botão.* This in itself is an interesting example of linguistic appropriation as a result of newly acquired cultural habits.  
These exotic objects, of which much care was taken, included Chinese folding-chairs, lacquered boxes, porcelain, bundles and bales of silk, Persian horses and caged animals. Their different places of origin were the result of Portuguese trade. By the 16th and 17th centuries Portugal had established trade routes along the coastline of the Indian Ocean, the Southern Seas and the China Sea. Some of the traders were born in Asia and many of them were the result of the progressive hybridism that characterised the lives of the Europeans in Asia during the period.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.short_description: In around 1543, the Portuguese (or *Namban-jin*) arrived in Japan, and so began a period of rich cultural exchange. Similar to several other *Namban* objects, this pair of folding screens – made by artists from Nippon – is a unique visual document that relates to the Portuguese presence in Japan.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.type: Furnishing that can be included in the *Shoheiga* category, meaning a large painted architectural surface, including folding screens. In this case, it is more specifically *Byobu*, meaning a painted folding screen.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.initial_owner: Tadao Takamisawa, António da Costa Carneiro, Portuguese ambassador in Japan
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.dimensions: H: 172.8 cm; l: 380.8 cm; depth 2 cm
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.method_for_datation: Tadao Takamisawa attributed the paintings to Kano Domi based on stylistic grounds, and thematic and pictorial parallels with other folding screens and works executed by the Kano school of painting, including Kano Naizen's *Namban Byobu*, also in the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.obtention: Acquired in the 1930s by Tadao Takamisawa from a *daimyo*'s (Great Lord) castle near Osaka, and later purchased by the Portuguese ambassador –António da Costa Carneiro – in Tokyo. Having belonged to the Ministry of Finance since 1952 it has been on permanent loan to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in Lisbon ever since.

6bedde02-9b3d-5029-bda9-ab2075c48438.name: Catholic Deanery Parish Church of the Assumption and St. Martin
6bedde02-9b3d-5029-bda9-ab2075c48438.description: The style and form of the parish church are shaped by the intertwining of conservative and more modern conceptions: the Classicism of the Salzburg school, as planned for both the building and its interior work, received a Late Baroque modification at the hands of local artisans. Competition between the artists ensued, Hueber changed the longitudinal building into a centralised space, Schöpf ousted Nesselthaler as the painter of the large main cupola. Despite many Classicist forms, above all in the stucco decoration, the spatial impression is dominated by the Late Baroque style. Rococo forms are completely absent, and thus the elated, sanguine expression of this stylistic phase.
6bedde02-9b3d-5029-bda9-ab2075c48438.short_description: One of the few important Early Classicist buildings in Tyrol, the Deanery Church is largely the work of artists from Salzburg, which is to be explained by the subsumption of the valley of Brixen under the archbishopric at that time. The plans of the Royal Building Commissioner, Hagenauer, were executed in the style of the Late Baroque by the acting master builder Hueber. Together with the stylistically somewhat conservative interior work, the spatial impression tends to be that of the Late Baroque tradition rather than the Louis XVI style.
6bedde02-9b3d-5029-bda9-ab2075c48438.bibliography:
Frodl-Kraft, E., “Wolfgang Hagenauer und eine Gruppe nordosttiroler Kirchenräume”, in: *Wiener Jahrbuch für Kunstgeschichte*, 14 (=18), 1950, pp. 131–94 (p. 167ff.).  
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*. Innsbruck 1955, p. 51f.  
*Brixen im Thale: 788-1988. Ein Heimatbuch*, Sebastian Posch (ed.).       Innsbruck 1988 (= Schlern-Schriften, vol. 281).  
Hahnl, A., “Der Salzburger Hofbauverwalter Wolfgang IV. Hagenauer (1726-1801)”, in: *Barockberichte*, 44/45, 2006, pp. 883–900.
6bedde02-9b3d-5029-bda9-ab2075c48438.history: Records of a parish church in Brixen date back to the 9th century, originally dedicated to St. Martin alone. In the 14th century the patronage of Mary was added. The new building was constructed between 1789 and 1795 according to plans from Wolfgang Hagenauer from Salzburg. Frescos and altarpieces are the work of Andreas Nesselthaler and Joseph Schöpf 1795/96, the high altar is from Peter Pflauder according to a sketch from Hagenauer and Nesselthaler, as is the pulpit (1795).

6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.name:
Emperor Ferdinand´s II Mausoleum  
Burial Place of Emperor Ferdinand II and his family
6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.alternate_name: Church of St Catherine of Alexandria and Mausoleum
6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.description:
Pietro de Pomis was commissioned by the later emperor Ferdinand II to build the Mausoleum in the South of the cathedral. It is a two part complex with the church, dedicated to St Catherine of Alexandria, and the chapel with the crypt. Saint Catherine was the patron of the Jesuit University. This, her statue on the roof and the façade allude to the Habsburgs´ affinity to the Jesuit order. The triangular gable framed by a segment gable was firstly used at the façade of *Il Gesù,* the Jesuits’ mother church in Rome.  
The oval-shaped floor plan of the Mausoleum is remarkable since the astronomer and mathematician Johannes Kepler had shortly before succeeded in calculating the ellipse shape correctly.  
When de Pomis died in 1633 Pietro Valnegro took over the construction management. He finished the roofs, built the tower and added a lantern to it. On top of the church´s cupola and of the mausoleum´s lantern are – at the same height – ecclesiastical and imperial symbols, the cross and the eagle sitting on the orb. On top of the highest part of the building complex, the tower´s lantern, the imperial sceptre rose high into the sky (it was later replaced) to claim the Habsburgs’ supremacy.  
The building’s art historical highlight: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach had been entrusted with the interior design which is said to be his earliest documented art work.
6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.short_description: When archduke Ferdinand from Inner Austria, the later emperor Ferdinand II, had finished his studies with the Jesuits in Ingolstadt he lived for some years in the family´s residence in Graz. There, the protestants had gained enormous power for what reason he started to take counter-reformatory steps. To achieve his goals he elevated art and architecture to an important matter. He began to build the Mausoleum, taking Italian architecture as a role model, such as Il Gesù, the church of the Jesuits in Rome. The three-quarter columns and the huge crowning gables on the west façade, building two triumphal arches, are supposed to symbolise the Catholic restoration.
6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.dates:
1608: red marble sarcophagus  
1614: start of the complex´s building on the site of a former cemetery chapel  
after 1619/20: addition of the façade´s two segment gables  
1622–37: roofing work  
1635–36: building of the tower  
about 1635/36: statues on the roof  
1640: stucco work and altar consecration in the crypt

6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.history: On the territory of the Holy Roman Empire life in this epoch was characterised by the Thirty Years War. It had started as a political conflict, became a religious war and ended with the triumph of the Catholic church. As a result, the church dignitaries eagerly started to build and to rebuild churches and monasteries. The Catholic Habsburg emperors, being strictly religious, fought the burgeoning Protestantism in the area. The protestants had to convert to the Catholic faith or to leave the country. Archduke Ferdinand, the later emperor Ferdinand II, was an eager counter-reformer and advanced the Catholic restoration. In this atmosphere many new buildings arose to symbolise the supremacy of the Catholic church. The Mausoleum was one of the first to be erected, many others followed. It was a prosperous time for art and architecture, as the wealthy and the noblemen followed the example of the church as builders. Baroque became the era´s artistic expression.
6c0b15f5-1758-54c6-8bd8-1fb02ba5d2bc.patrons: The future Emperor Ferdinand II of the Holy Roman Empire had built the Mausoleum as a crypt for his family and for himself.

Interior of the two storey mausoleum, burial chapel: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach (1656–1723); putti above the cornice and other stucco work: Joseph Antonio Serenio (ca. 1650–after 1702); ceiling’s fresco paintings: Matthias Echter (1653–94); figures in the niches: Marx Schokotnigg (1661–1731)  
Crypt: red marble sarcophagus: probably Sebastiano Carlone the elder (before 1570–after 1612); stucco work: Mattia Camin (n.d.), later replaced by Josef Antonio Serenio (ca. 1650–after 1702)

6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.name: *St. John the Evangelist*
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.description:
St. John the Evangelist, gospel author and apocalyptic visionary, holds the Book of Revelations, with seals. At his feet is an eagle, one of his attributes. The eagle's mighty flight and the ancient belief that the bird could shade (or stop) the sun contributed to its coming to symbolise the soul and a mystic vision of God. Much of the animal symbolism of the Evangelists is derived from the Old Testament vision of Ezekiel (Ez 1:10). The eagle was attributed to John by the Church Father Hieronymus.  
The slender figure in an elegant, balanced posture with one foot forward is wrapped in a decorative cloak. The cloak, running from the left shoulder around the right hip opens into a mighty relief train that fills the space between the book and a pedestal on the right, the outline of the figure thus appearing compact. Schweigl ornamented the soft surface of the statue with folds and incisions in the hem of the cloak. The soulful face corresponds with traditional representations of St. John the Evangelist, his fine facial features off-set with locks of wavy hair. The visual effect of the sculpture is enhanced by the treatment of its surfaces: gold plate combined with matt and gloss finishes.  
The artist's development included being apprenticed to his father who came from Tyrol. After studying at the Vienna Academy and following his father's death, Schweigl took over the family workshop in Brno. The workshop, which also functioned as a private art academy, produced sculptures for the whole of Moravia, part of Silesia. A series of sculptures for the Church of St. James was one of Schweigl's first independent commissions. He wrote several manuscripts on art and artists in Moravia intended for pedagogical schools, which laid the foundations of art history research in Moravia.  
In a later phase, Schweigl employed the St. John figure in a statue of the saint for a side altar in Vranov Church near Brno.
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.short_description: The slender figure in an elegant, balanced posture with one foot placed forward is wrapped in a decorative cloak. It was one of Schweigl’s first independent commissions. His writing on art laid foundations for art history in Moravia and his workshop’s output covered Moravia and parts of Silesia.

6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.method_for_datation: The authorship of Andreas Schweigl is recorded in written sources regarding the contents of the Church of St. James (Brno City Archive).

During Re-Gothicization in 1865, the sculpture along with the rest of the contents, were transferred to the parsonage. It has been museum property since 1947.

6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.name: *Lamentation of Christ*
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.description:
The canvas dates from the Flemish painter's first trip to Rome (1602), and is contemporaneous with his first Roman commission: the paintings for the Sant' Elena Chapel in the Church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.  
The work was probably done for Cardinal Montalto and did not become part of the Borghese collection until 1827.  
The scene shows the Lamentation of Christ according to the Gospels. In the centre of the picture, conforming to the dramatic style typical of Baroque art is the body of Christ in a bold foreshortened position, stretched out on an ancient sarcophagus and surrounded by different characters. Mary supports him with the shroud (in which he is wrapped) while looking to the heavens, where beams of light pierce dark clouds, accentuating the almost nocturnal setting of the subject. John the Evangelist, the young apostle loved by Jesus, stands opposite the elderly Joseph of Arimathea. The right side of the painting shows two female figures: one the pious woman, almost hidden, and Magdalene, in full light, in the act of drying her tears. The high drama of the composition and the richness of the colours perhaps come from the famous *Deposition* that Caravaggio completed for the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella (1602–1604). The painting nonetheless reveals clear references to Dutch Mannerism, combined in this case with classical models copied by the artist in Rome, with brilliant colours and diagonal compositions taken from Venetian and Emilian painting.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.short_description: This work was painted by Rubens during his first stay in Rome (1602). He matched Barocci's colours, the dense brushwork of the late Titian, and the roman statuary and the light and shadow of Caravaggio. The Baroque genius had blended, in an absolutely original way, this tradition with new experimentation.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

6e6f8f63-bda4-54b4-97b7-a669957462fe.name: Parish Church of St. Peter and Paul
6e6f8f63-bda4-54b4-97b7-a669957462fe.description: Visible from a distance, the steeple of St. Peter and Paul was also designed by Josef Schmuzer. It is largely decorated with artistic illusionistic façade paintings by the Augsburgian fresco-painter Matthäus Günther. These frescos display the patrons of the church, St. Peter and St. Paul, framed within triumphal arches. A hall-shaped nave is attached to the late Gothic-style chancel, situated behind the steeple. The transept-like extension on the east bay terminates in side chapels, bearing remarkable similarities to the parish church of St. Martin in Garmisch  which had been built by Schmuzer a decade earlier. He produced a simple, yet ideal spatial design for the more complex liturgical functions of a civic parish church, such as the rites of baptism and burial. The permanent repository of the Eucharist is not only where daily mass, including homilies, is  performed but also special liturgies such as those at Holy week, Easter, the beginning of Lent, the feast of Corpus Christi, the Ascension of Christ, All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day. The functional separation of altars, such as the division between the three main altars and additional cults like the veneration of the Cross and St. John of Nepomuk, has also been solved in the church’s design.
6e6f8f63-bda4-54b4-97b7-a669957462fe.method_for_datation: From documentation of the church’s founding; inscription on the steeple.

6e6f8f63-bda4-54b4-97b7-a669957462fe.history: Josef Schmuzer, a member of the Wessobrunn school of master builders and stuccoworkers, extended the Mittenwalder parish church while retaining the chancel walls and a chapel in order to do justice to the growing population of this prosperous market town. Most notably, the Veronese red marble used for the high altar made its way over the Alps following the Roman “Via Claudia Augusta”. This trade route, which would later lead from Nuremburg to Venice via Augsburg, passed through Mittenwald and made the city an important trans-shipment point for marble and other goods. The construction of the church was sponsored by the prince-bishop of Freising, who was the sovereign of the region at this time.

6e86658a-4fe2-52c2-916e-c3e6d84d0114.name: Votive church of St. Mary of Jerusalem, Trški Vrh, near Krapina
6e86658a-4fe2-52c2-916e-c3e6d84d0114.description:
The legend of the Franciscan lay brother, Joachim, who found a small statue of the Virgin Mary under some ruins in Jerusalem, is the central subject of the ceiling painting on the apse vault, surrounded by four medallions depicting scenes from the Life of the Virgin Mary: *Birth of the Virgin Mary*, the *Visitation*, the *Annunciation*, and the *Immaculate Conception*. On the surfaces of the rather flat dome pendentives, the four evangelists are accompanied by their traditional attributes; further in, the paintings of the central nave become both compositionally and thematically more complex. The dominant position in the centre of the flat dome-like ceiling is dedicated to the *Assumption of the Virgin* painted in the tradition of illusionist painting but with *quadratura* that is decorative more than functioning as an extension to the architecture. Surrounded by four scenes from the Old Testament, on the triumphal arch is a depiction of the Original Sin. Eden is presented in deep perspective; a timid landscape shaded by the tree holding the forbidden fruit. Next is *Judith Decapitating Holofernes*, after a painting by Rubens. *Ester and King Ahasver* and the *Judgment of* *Solomon* follow, painted with similar attention to movement and expression. The Old Testament repertoire is accompanied by depictions of the Four Fathers of the Church; four scenes in *grisaille* depict more scenes from the Old Testament – *Moses Releasing Water from a Rock, Noah's Ark, Jacob's Dream* and the symbolic image of the Virgin Mary inspired by the Song of Songs: “*Sub umbra illius, quem desideraveram, sedi et fructus eius dulcis gutturi me”.* \[“I sat down under his shadow, whom I desired: and his fruit was sweet to my palate”\].  
Lerchinger's characteristic style as seen in Trški Vrh is best described by Anica Cevc: “In adornment, he has developed a distinct personal Rococo language. He is playful and pliable in forming his depicted stucco *rocaille* imitations, which he uses to densely line vaults. He places flowers between or inside, a permanent decorative element from his earliest to last works. In that instance, his church interiors are visually changed into blossoming summerhouses, or he fills them up in a strip cartoon fashion with a series of images in rich frames hanging from a wall. His frescoes represent a regional variation of Central European Rococo.”
6e86658a-4fe2-52c2-916e-c3e6d84d0114.short_description: The Votive Church of St Mary of Jerusalem is one of the most beautiful Baroque pilgrim churches of North Croatia. Built on a hill in Trški Vrh near Krapina, and surrounded by a circle of vaulted arcades, the church dominates the scenery. Built according to the architectonic features of the Baroque, it is a central-quatrefoil church with a long, wide sanctuary. Building finished in 1752 and in 1772 the illusionist painter Anton Joseph Lerchinger and his workshop decorated the entire interior with illusionist paintings. The dedication of the church of St. Mary of Jerusalem relates to a legend according to which in 1669 a Franciscan lay brother, Joachim, found a small statue of the Virgin Mary under some ruins in Jerusalem. A depiction of the scene is on the apse vault.

6eb2ee09-8be4-5e2d-b37a-ac0f60e77977.name: L’Huillier-Coburg Mansion
6eb2ee09-8be4-5e2d-b37a-ac0f60e77977.description:
The Mansion-house in Edelény has a U-shaped layout, a typical feature of European and Hungarian Baroque architecture. Also in line with the traditions of Baroque architecture, two parallel rows of rooms are arranged around an axis. The most representative rooms are located on the first floor, the so-called *piano nobile* (noble floor). The two wings have two floors while the main, mid-section building consists of three floors. The exterior design of the mansion is articulated with richly decorated windows, and its central risalit with monumental pilasters. The north façade develops into two massive corner towers, which bear typical features of late 17th- and early 18th-century architecture. The towers presumably signify the social status and military career of the owner. The L'Huillier and Santa Croce coats of arms are located in the centre of the fourth tier of the north façade. The inscription on the plaquette on the south facade records the names of the owners and the year when construction was completed. The main hall with its stucco decorations is situated on the first floor of the main, mid-section building.  
Seven rooms on the first floor of the mansion wings are decorated with frescoes illustrating symbolic mythological figures and Rococo scenes depicting a rendition of an aristocratic lifestyle. (One of these rooms – painted in impressive green tones – is located in the west wing and the other rooms are located in the east wing). The decoration in Room 103 consists of two scenes of courtship in the background of which there is a woman on a swing; on the wall in front of this another scene depicts a carriage pulled by swans. Other paintings illustrate hunting scenes and some other smaller works of *putti*. The paintings in Room 104 are allegories of the Four Seasons and the Four Elements. Room 105 is decorated with ornamental flower pieces, and the ceiling fresco depicts a *putto* and a winged figure, presumably Hermes. Room 106 also has ornamental flower pieces, and the walls of the door and window niches are decorated with emblems that follow the *Idea Sapiensis* (1725), a work by Antonio Vanossi. Also, the frescoes and paintings in this room illustrate a rendition of an aristocratic lifestyle according to the era, and there are depictions of mythological figures such as Jupiter, Narcissus and Andromeda. The fresco in Room 110 depicts Fame (*Fama*) in the Company of Minerva, and Virtue Crowning the Female Figure of Royal Wisdom. The walls are decorated with cartouches illustrating scenes from the myth of Pyramus and Thisbe. In Room 112 the paintings depict allegories of the Four Continents.
6eb2ee09-8be4-5e2d-b37a-ac0f60e77977.short_description: The 18th-century L'Huillier-Coburg Mansion in Edelény is one of Hungary's most impressive aristocratic buildings. The owner, Jean-Francios L'Huillier from Lotharingia, served in the emperor's army, was captain of Eger Castle and ennobled in 1715. The mansion was inherited by his daughter. Count István Esterházy, who was the second husband of L'Huiller's granddaughter Ludmilla Forgách, decorated the house with elegant Rococo wall-paintings illustrating the aristocratic lifestyle of the era.
6eb2ee09-8be4-5e2d-b37a-ac0f60e77977.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual research, stylistic research, wall and mural restoration analysis, and archaeological findings.

Pazár, M., Joó, T., “Új adatok az edelényi kastély építéstörténetéhez” (“Additional Data on the Construction History of the Edelény Palace”), *Műemlékvédelem (Monument Trust)*, 1963, pp. 138–144.  
Joó, T., “Az edelényi kastély” (“The Edelény Palace”), *Művészettörténeti Értesítő,* 17:3–4, 1968, pp. 189–207.  
Jávor, A., “Lieb Ferenc, az edelényi festő” (“Ferenc Lieb, Painter of Edelény”), *Művészettörténeti Értesítő*, 49:3–4, 2000, pp. 167–186.
6eb2ee09-8be4-5e2d-b37a-ac0f60e77977.history:
The mansion-house was built between 1727 and 1730 by General Jean-François L'Huillier, captain of Eger Castle. L'Huillier was ennobled in 1715, and obtained the land on which the property was built in 1727. After his death in 1728, construction was completed under the supervision of his wife, Maria Magdalena Santa Croce. The architect was thought to have been Giovanni Battista Carlone – who at the time lived in Eger – however, no conclusive evidence to support this assumption has been found to date.  
The house was inherited through the female line by L'Huiller's daughter. Count István Esterházy, who was the second husband of L'Huiller's granddaughter Ludmilla Forgách, entrusted Franciscus Lieb from Igló (Spišská Nová Ves) with painting the allegories and Rocco scenes seen in several rooms.  
After the death of L'Huillier's last descendant, Count Ferenc Dessewffy in 1820, the mansion was acquired by the Prince of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha who leased it out to various institutions. In the 1920s the mansion was sold to the State and used by the County Court. After the Second World War it was used by the police, and after that it was divided into several flats. Today the mansion is managed by the National Trust of Monuments for Hungary, under whose auspices a restoration programme began in 2009.

6ecdbd5d-f71a-5358-b6f8-723236965edc.name: Provincial House
6ecdbd5d-f71a-5358-b6f8-723236965edc.description:
The Provincial Assembly held sessions in the monastery refectory. Not much survives of the original decoration, only a record of the decoration by J. Spillenberger, a canvas by M. A. Lublinský and the 35 coats of arms of the lords supervising the construction of the Assembly Hall in the 1580s. The hall was reconstructed in 1733 by M. Grimm. The decorative subject matter in the Assembly Hall is encompassed by the slogan “Civil Virtue Makes the Moravian Land Happy”, a saying defined by the Provincial Governor M. O. Kounic in accordance with his policies, which included acknowledgement of the right to rule in the female line and the guarantee of Moravian virtue and wealth through affiliation with the Danube states.  
The original architecture determined the division of the paintings on the ceiling into two sections. The main part is the *Allegory of the Virtues and Wealth of Moravia*. The walls are covered with “statues” of emperors painted in an illusionary manner, while medallions feature Marobud, the mythical founder of the Moravian empire and Anna of Jagellon, heiress of the Moravian Margraviate.
6ecdbd5d-f71a-5358-b6f8-723236965edc.short_description:
The Moravian Provincial Assembly held sessions in the Dominican Monastery. The decorative subject matter in the Assembly Hall is encompassed by the slogan “Civil Virtue Makes the Moravian Land Happy”, a saying defined by the Provincial Governor M. O. Kounic in accordance with his policies, which included acknowledgement of the right to rule in the female line and the guarantee of Moravian virtue and wealth through affiliation with the Danube states.  
D. Gran’s mural in the Assembly Hall sealed his reputation as one of the most sought-after fresco artists of the first half of the 18th century.
6ecdbd5d-f71a-5358-b6f8-723236965edc.method_for_datation: The building is dated 1692, F. Ř. I. Eckstein’s painting is signed and dated. Receipts and correspondence for individual phases of the construction survive.

6ecdbd5d-f71a-5358-b6f8-723236965edc.history: The construction of the New Town Hall complex took place in the early 13th century and the late 18th century. From 1297 onwards a section of the Dominican Monastery was used for sessions of the Provincial Court and Assembly. In 1783, both Court and Assembly were transferred to the Augustinian Monastery and the premises of the dissolved Dominican order served military purposes. After reconstruction in 1934–5, the premises became the headquarters of the city administration. The courtyard contains Renaissance and Baroque portals from houses demolished during the course of Brno’s redevelopment in the late 19th century.

6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.name: *The Suicide of Lucretia*
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.description:
The *Suicide of Lucretia* is the work of the Baroque artist, Carlo Francesco Nuvolone, or Nuvoloni (as he is known to some authors) whose work belongs to the Milanese Baroque school. The painting, done in the latter part of Nuvoloni's career when he achieved work of a higher quality, is less cloying and has less pathos than earlier works. Taught by the Mannerist painter, his father, Panfilo Nuvolone (1581–1651) at the Ambrosiana Academy in Milan, he went on to study there with the well-known painter G. B. Crespi aka *il Cerano* (1557–1632). Influenced by Guido Reni, Francesco was nicknamed Guido di Lombardia. His work is characterised by pleasing colour, expression, sensuality and composed pathos. Francesco painted portraits, religious compositions and historical subjects. Other works by him are found in Milan (the Pinacoteca Ambrosiana and the Pinacoteca Brera), in churches in Pavia and Varese, in Piacenza (Museo Civico), in the Dresden Alte Pinakothek and in some chapels in Lombardy.  
The subject of the painting is Lucretia, daughter of the Roman senator, Lucretius Tricipitinus, and wife of the Roman consul, Tarquinius Collatinus. Following her rape by Sestus Tarquinius, son of King Tarquinius Superbus, she committed suicide in 510 BC, which spurred Roman discontent with tyrannical rule and led them to proclaim a Republic.  
The dying Lucretia lies diagonally in the foreground. Her torso unclad, she has a mortal wound to her breast. Her greyish flesh colour is in contrast to the rich folds of red drapery that cover her knees, and in harmony with the white and green fabric of her clothing. An older woman bends over her curved body wrapped in a dark cloak, from which her lit face and the palm of one hand poke out. Lucretia and the older woman create a simple, closed composition with characteristic composed Baroque ardour and exaltation. Lucretia, symbol of chastity and of tragedy at the same time, is the victim of her own beauty. In the mid-ground on the left-hand side of the picture, from the deep shadow alongside a pillar, peer the faces of three old men. On the opposite side, the composition opens out to a landscape, bounded with clouds, within which are two Roman soldiers. The painting is composed of light and cold tones, with a silvery range.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.short_description:
*The Suicide of Lucretia* is the work of the Baroque painter from Lombardy C. F. Nuvoloni, known by some as Nuvolone, who was born in Cremona. Taught at the Ambrosiana Academy by his father, Panfilo, he went on to study with G. B. Crespi. Inspired by the painter Guido Reni, he was nicknamed Guido di Lombardia, living and working in Milan, painting portraits, religious and historical subjects.  
The theme of this painting is the suicide of Lucretia. Lucretia was the daughter of the senator, Tricipitinus, and the wife of the Roman consul, Tarquinius Collatinus. In 510 BC, following Lucretia's rape by Sestus Tarquinius, son of King Tarquinius Superbus, the Romans ousted the king and declared a Republic.  
The painting shows the half-naked body of Lucretia in her death throes. Leaning over her is an older woman, while in the background three old men peer out. In the background landscape, Roman soldiers are barely discernable. In this painting, the artist depicts the tragedy of a beautiful woman with a composed ardour characteristic of the Baroque. He painted Lucretia in a cold and light tonality, richly lit with a silvery light; in the dark mid-ground, in contrast, are barely discernable figures.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.method_for_datation: The attribution to Nuvoloni by Dr. Grgo Gamulin in 1961 was through stylistic analysis and comparative material, as well as by comparison with the other established works of the painter.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.

6f440b91-1d47-595b-811b-e240f0b3282e.name: Abbey Church dedicated to the Ascension of Maria and to Saint Jacob/James the Elder
6f440b91-1d47-595b-811b-e240f0b3282e.description:
In the third quarter of the 17th century new parts and wings of Stift Schlierbach/Schlierbach Abbey were erected on the place of the medieval fortress and the later convent edifices. Vischer’s engraving in the Topographia Austriae Superioris gives an idea of how it possibly looked in this time. The data acquisition had stopped before start of building, with ancient buildings remaining on the place and planned abbey wings included on the view.  
The abbey’s extended west front with thirty windows axes, three floors and plain facade is enthroned over the valley, unpretentious in its exterior, according to Cistercian order rules that demand a simple lifestyle. Only the north front has later received a delicate decoration – either to welcome guests who drove straight towards it or for the monks’ own pleasure who could see it from the then-existing extensive park area opposite.  
As it was the baroque era and the abbots were above all ecclesiastical princes, the interior was furnished in a most splendid way. The members of the well-known Carlone family with their many architects, artists and artisans were the preoccupied performers and created what many art historians evaluate as one of the most important baroque interiors in Austria, particularly the quality of the stucco work and interior decoration.
6f440b91-1d47-595b-811b-e240f0b3282e.short_description: The abbey with its several magnificent baroque halls such as the Bernhardisaal (hall dedicated to St Bernard) and the library, is best known for its richly decorated church. One would call the interior “double-baroque” as a first baroque builder began to decorate what the second completed and multiplied some years later. South German/Austrian stucco work, carving and gilding work culminated in this building which has a unique look and is therefore outstanding under Austria’s baroque churches.

6f440b91-1d47-595b-811b-e240f0b3282e.history: After 300 years of changing ownerships, Eberhard von Wallsee V acquired dominion of Schlierbach, including the fortress (1353). Some months later he founded a Cistercian convent with the first prioress (later abbess) Elisabeth von Gundelfingen and twelve nuns to whom he donated the property. Under the 17th and 18th abbesses the doctrine of Protestantism spread rapidly in the region, the convent secularised, declined and was left by the nuns. During the following years it was administrated by different religious organisations until emperor Ferdinand II (1578–1637) decided that Cistercians should take over the place. In 1620 three monks who came from Stift Rein in Styria started rebuilding the monastery and re-catholisation. Since that time the abbey has stayed under the ownership and responsibility of Cistercians.
6f440b91-1d47-595b-811b-e240f0b3282e.patrons: Eberhard von Wallsee V founded a Cistercian convent (1355) on the place of a former medieval castle that existed until 1556. 1620 resettlement by Cistercian monks who came from Stift Rein/Abbey Rein in Styria, Austria.

6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.name: *Aeneas and Anchises*
6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.description:
This is the first work that a young Bernini completed for Scipione Borghese, who already owned a Barocci painting of the same theme. The subject, taken from Virgil's *Aeneid*, was potent for the Cardinal because it confirmed a dynastic celebration, Aeneas being considered an ancestor of the Borghese family, while simultaneously representing the birth of Rome. Aeneas, fleeing Troy with his father Anchises and his son Ascanius, arrived in Lazio and founded the eternal city. As a result, this subject acquired by analogy an historical and theological value: Ancient Rome and the Roman Church. The flight of Aeneas was also related to the Christian idea of *pietas romana*, while the figure of the hero symbolised the political role assumed by Scipione during the papacy of his aging uncle (in Latin, *scipio*, the staff that bears, as Aeneas supports Anchises).  
The sculpture retains the compactness of the block shape on a vertical axis into which the contrasting movement of the figures is woven, taken from the previous late-Mannerist period in Tuscany. On account of its transitional style, it has long been assumed to be the joint work of Pietro Bernini, the famous sculptor of Pope Paul V, and his young son. However, recently discovered documents unequivocally ascribe the work to Gian Lorenzo.  
The definition of the muscles and the plasticity of the shapes demonstrate Bernini's awareness of Hellenistic art, as well as Raffaello and the Carraccis. The sculptor is undertaking a study of ancient art, integrating it into the new language of art, with its psychology and drama, which would later be known as the Baroque.  
Bernini paid attention to the tactile quality of the marble, finishing the surface with different tools. This allowed him to create contrasts between finishes, achieving the illusion of colour and assimilating the sculpture to a painting.
6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.short_description: The artist pays attention to the tactile quality of the marble surface to obtain the illusion of colour. Aeneas's escape from Troy had an historical-theological meaning: the concept of *imperium* is moved to the Roman Church. The theme symbolises the *pietas romana* and Scipione's political role.
6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.name: Franciscan Monastery, Votive and Pilgrimage Church of St. Anthony of Padua
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.alternate_name: Monastery  Church of St. Anthony, Pilgrimage Church of St. Anthony
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.description: The complex, consisting of the votive and the pilgrimage sanctuary, is accentuated by three dome-shaped roofs and harmonically nestles on the slope of Mount Wank. The nave is surrounded on three sides by an arcade that had to channel the processions. On the inside, the nave turns out to be an oval structure. Behind a triple arcature, it connects to the older octagonal votive chapel with the foursquare presbytery and the newer circular side chapels.
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.short_description: The votive and pilgrimage church, crowned with three domed helmets and harmonically nestling on the hillside of Mount Wank, has to offer exceptional art experiences: The capriccio-like, yet atmospheric ceiling fresco of the prematurely deceased  Augsburg-born painter Johann Evangelist Holzer flags the high point of Late Baroque ceiling painting in Bavaria, while the high-quality altarpiece of the Venetian painter Bartholomeo Litterini shows the extensive trade relations of the former market town Partenkirchen.
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.dates:
1704–08: construction of the octagonal votive chapel;  
1734–47: construction of the oval nave and the whole interior decoration
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.location: Garmisch-Partenkirchen, part of town Partenkirchen, Upper Bavaria
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.method_for_datation: Chronicle sources, memorial plaques, and the signature dated from 1736 in the ceiling fresco.
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.bibliography:
Bauer, H. and Rupprecht, B. (eds), *Corpus der barocken Deckenmalerei in Deutschland, Bd. 2: Freistaat Bayern, Regierungsbezirk Oberbayern. Die Landkreise Bad Tölz-Wolfratshausen – Garmisch-Partenkirchen – Miesbach*, München: Süddeutscher Verlag, 1981: 405–421.

Hitchcock, Henry-Russell, *Rococo Architecture in Southern Germany*, London/New York: Phaidon, 1968: 144.  
Jocher, N., *Partenkirchen, Votiv- und Wallfahrtskirche St. Anton (Kleine Kunstführer 128)*, 10. völlig neu bearbeitete Auflage, Regensburg: Schnell & Steiner, 2001.  
Mick, E. W., *Johann Evangelist Holzer (1709–1740): Ein frühvollendetes Malergenie des 18. Jahrhunderts* (Schnell & Steiner Künstlerbibliothek), München/Zürich: Schnell & Steiner, 1984: 64–74, 102.
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.history: In honour of St. Anthony, wealthy citizens donated a votive gift of gratitude in 1704, as the market town of Partenkirchen was spared from a pillage during the War of the Spanish Succession. The octagonal chapel was consecrated in 1708. The devoted local parson, Matthias Samweber, initiated the extension of the structure by adding the nave between 1734–36. The designs were delivered by the Wessobrunn master builder, Joseph Schmuzer. The young fresco artist, Johann Evangelist Holzer, accepted the task of implementing the paintings. After his sudden death in 1740, a colleague from Augsburg undertook the task of painting the still missing ceiling fresco in the presbytery. The final consecration took place on 29 October 1747.
6f6ce19b-9a97-5bde-a364-24c17801ef40.patrons: Founders of the octagonal votive chapel: Christoph Perwein, Elias Gröber, Johann Schmauntz, and Jacob Lidl, citizens of Partenkirchen; Patron of the oval extension: Matthias Samweber, parson  of Partenkirchen (in office 1720–42)

6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.name: *Stove*
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.description:
This stove once adorned the interior of the former Dietrichstein Palace next to the Franciscan Monastery, Brno. The palace, pulled down in a street development in 1906, was said to be one of the most beautiful in Brno.  
The bottom section features a scene in relief from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Venus and Adonis, with *putti* carrying a vase. The upper ledge bears the Dietrichstein coat of arms; the decoration climaxes in the figure of Ganymede kidnapped by Jupiter in the form of an eagle, another scene from Ovid. These myths frequently provided subject matter for the decoration of residences both secular and religious. They usually appeared as ceiling paintings and sculpted garden ornamentation, as well as on utility objects such as table crockery.  
The richly decorated stove manifests the span of work assigned to the sculptor employed by the imperial court. In the final phase of palace reconstruction by František Antonín Grimm, carried out from the early 1740s, Ignaz Lengelacher also created the ornamental stone vases on the entrance frontage. The stove is similar to those found in Klosterneuburg, near Vienna, designed by Donato Felice d'Alio, in whose studio Grimm worked.  
After the mid-18th century the Dietrichstein Palace was a major centre for the social life of Brno. Under the next owner, Count Salm-Reifferscheidt, it became a meeting place of the oldest Brno freemasonic lodge.
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.short_description: The richly decorated stove manifests the span of work assigned to the sculptor employed by the imperial court. Legends from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* were frequent subjects for decoration in residences both secular and religious. They often appeared in ceiling paintings, as well as in applied arts.
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.location: Museum of Applied Arts, Brno, Moravia
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.method_for_datation: The authorship of the image is defined by the work’s origin and the participation of Ignaz Lengelacher in the sculpted decoration of the Dietrichstein Palace.
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.obtention: The Stove was acquired by the Museum of Applied Arts (Moravian Gallery, Brno since 1961) before 1928.

6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.name: *Sleep*
6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.description:
According to the payments made, the sculpture was commissioned between 1635 and 1636 by the nephew of Paul V, Marcantonio Borghese, with the mediation of Marcello Provenzale. It shows a *putto* with light, butterfly wings sleeping deeply. On his head, beside his arm and along his body are opium poppies, which allude symbolically to sleep, as does the small dormouse curled up on the rock. The subject relates to the literary description in Cesare Ripa's *Iconology* (1603), essential reading for artists in the 17th and 18th centuries, who drew on it constantly to compose allegorical subjects. The dormouse was considered to represent sleep or the “third phase” of the night, the “black” phase.  
The choice of the valuable and extremely hard Belgian marble (or “touchstone”) was probably due both to iconographic considerations and the artist's desire to show his skill in rendering soft flesh and the limp abandon of the limbs. The work, highly inspired by ancient sculpture, was thought to be an archaeological find in the early 18th century. Placed in Villa Pinciana and extolled by contemporary sources, the room housing it was given the name “sleep room”. It was accompanied by two vases with handles formed by entwined snakes, also in black marble, made in 1638 by Silvio Calci of Viterbo (active in Rome in the first half of the 17th century), possibly also alluding to sleep. Therefore the whole composition can be interpreted as an allegory for sleep, or maybe death.  
Compared to Bernini's grandiose and theatrical style, which characterised the entire Roman Baroque period, Algardi's style is marked by a greater classicism and a more lyrical tone, attributes that were particularly appreciated in the final years of the 17th century.
6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.short_description: The sculpture is an allegorical representation. Black marble was chosen because it is a colour associated with the idea of night and sleep. The work shows an attention to antique art and the work of Bernini.
6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.name: Ponte Sant’Angelo
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.description: At the time of Bernini's interventions, the statue of St. Peter (by Lorenzo Lotti, called Lorenzetto) and that of St. Paul (by Paolo Romano) were already there, guarding the bridge towards the southern side. Coming from Campo Marzio, the beholder first encounters the *Angel with the Column,* by Antonio Raggi, to symbolize the Flagellation as the beginning of the Passion of Christ, while at the end of the path the *Angel with the Lance of Longinus* appears, sculpted by Domenico Guidi, the final event of the Crucifixion, when Longinus pierced the side of Christ. Between these two extremities there are, in order, the *Angel with the Scourges* by Lazzaro Morelli, the *Angel with the Crown of Thorns* by Paolo Naldini (copy of the Bernian original in Sant'Andrea delle Fratte), the *Angel with the Holy Face* by Cosimo Fancelli, the *Angel with the Robe and the Dices* by Paolo Naldini, the *Angel with the Nails* by Gerolamo Lucenti, the *Angel with the Cross* by Ercole Ferrata, the *Angel with the Subscription* by Giulio Cartari (or by Bernini himself) and the *Angel with the Sponge* by Antonio Giorgetti. The angels, located in accordance with the chronological sequence of the events of the Passion as indicated by the objects they carry, underline with great dramatic force the processional role the bridge had. The bridge in fact played as an obligatory point of passage between the secular city and the holy city of the Vatican, in line with contemporary Counter-Reformation dictates on devotional practices connected to meditation on the Passion of Christ. Such practices were strongly encouraged and supported by the Catholic Church in the 17th century. Bernini replaced the previous travertine parapets with elegant, grated balustrades so as to allow the view of the river. Placed between the transient elements of the water and the sky, the angels are also characterized by an accentuated dynamism. The frescoes by Anastasio Fontebuoni in the church of Santa Prisca (early 17th century) and those in the church of Santa Prassede (1594–96) have been identified as possible referents for Bernini's iconography: the church of Santa Prassede, moreover, supposedly hosted a relic of the column of the Flagellation, which Antonio Raggi faithfully reproduced for his *Angel with the Column*.
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.short_description: The statues of the Angels on the bridge commissioned by pope Clement IX were designed by Bernini in 1669. A scenografical fix route created for pilgrims and travellers heading for Saint Peter’s.
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.method_for_datation: Literature of the time, archival documentation.
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.bibliography:
Minozzi, M., “La decorazione di Ponte S. Angelo”, in Strinati, C. and Bernardini, M.G. (eds), *Gian Lorenzo Bernini: regista del Barocco,* Milan: Skira, 1999: 77–83.  
Tolomeo M.G., *Ponte Sant'Angelo,* Rome: Fratelli Palombi, 1990.
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.history:
The ancient Aelian Bridge was built by Hadrian in the 2nd century AD to connect the ancient *Campus Martius* with his mausoleum. It underwent structural changes under Alexander VI (late 15th century) and was decorated to celebrate the triumphal procession of Charles V (1536). On that occasion Lorenzetto and Raffaello da Montelupo had created stucco statues of patriarchs and evangelists. It is very likely that, for the realization of his own project for the bridge, Bernini had gathered information, through prints, about the older decorative apparatus.  
The project to redecorate the bridge was resumed in 1669 by Pope Clement IX Rospigliosi, who commissioned Bernini to repair the structure, to enlarge it with an arch and to decorate it with a double row of angels bearing the symbols of the Passion of Christ, to be placed on the parapets. To ensure a degree of uniformity, Bernini provided a series of terracotta drawings and models to his collaborators, reserving for himself the execution of the *Angel with the Crown of Thorns* and the *Angel with the Subscription.* Clement IX, who saw the two sculptures in the artist’s studio, was deeply impressed and had copies made for the bridge, while donating the originals to Cardinal Rospigliosi for his palace. They remained there until 1729, when they were transferred to S. Andrea delle Fratte, Bernini’s parish church. Paolo Naldini made the copy of the *Angel with the Crown of Thorns* while Giulio Cartari (but according to other sources it was actually Bernini himself) that of the *Angel with the Subscription*.
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.architects: Gian Lorenzo Bernini; Lazzaro Morelli; Antonio Raggi; Cosimo Fancelli; Girolamo Lucenti; Giulio Cartari; Ercole Ferrata; Antonio Giorgetti; Domenico Guidi; Paolo Naldini
keywords: Saint Peter’s
7010dd9f-1c48-5d61-8274-d1798c1f774b.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.name: Amalienburg
702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.description: The exterior of the broad, single-storey construction has a pale pink and white stucco facade. Its architectural centre is the round Hall of Mirrors, which curves towards the otherwise straight garden front and is vaulted by a flattened dome. On its roof, a circular platform with a skilfully forged balustrade served as a shooting stand for the Electress’s   pheasant hunt. Two equally sized wings adjoin to the Hall of Mirrors. They house hunting rooms, resting chambers, a kitchen and other rooms for the court society to enjoy their distractions . The stylistically homogeneous interior decoration of the Amalienburg is attributed to a cohesive concept of construction and décor.
702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.short_description: Located in the Nymphenburg Palace Park, the elegant hunting pavilion was built in the style of a French maison de plaisance and is one of the greatest exponents of its kind, due to its prominent artful interior decoration. Starting in 1734, Charles Albert, Prince-Elector of Bavaria, assigned famous architect, François de Cuvilliés the Elder, to plan and build the Amalienburg for his wife Maria Amalia. The capriccio-like stucco décor of the interior in the late Régence  style is regarded as the magnum opus of Munich court stuccoer Johann Baptist Zimmermann.

Hitchcock, Henry-Russell, *German Rococo: The Zimmermann Brothers*, London: Allen Lane, 1968: 58–62, 89.  
Hojer, G., *Die Amalienburg: Rokokojuwel im Nymphenburger Schlosspark*, München: Schnell & Steiner, 1986.

702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.history: During the reign of Charles Albert’s father, Prince-Elector Maximilian Emanuel, a garden pavilion existed at the location that would later become the Amalienburg. In 1734, Charles Albert tasked his court artist, François de Cuvilliés the Elder, with the construction of a hunting pavilion for his wife, Maria Amalia of Austria, daughter of Emperor Joseph I. Just five years later, the Amalienburg was completed and decorated with Johann Baptist Zimmermann's stuccowork and ornamental carvings from Johann Joachim Dietrich. The style and decorations of the Amalienburg were supposed to resemble a maison de plaisance, thereby following a trend from France where these hunting and summer estates had come into fashion in the 18th century. In accordance with the new living trend at the time, called "commodité" (intimate rooms and retreats for informal relaxation), they were designed to escape the strict court etiquette and indulge in hunting, celebrating and other kinds of leisure distractions in an intimate setting.
702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.patrons: Prince-Elector Charles Albert of Bavaria (gov. 1726–45; 1742–45 as Charles VII, Holy Roman Emperor)

71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.name: *Susanna and the Old Men*
71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.description:
The painting, signed and dated, was acquired by Marcantonio IV Borghese in 1783 along with other works of the Flemish school. No details are known about the commissioning of the canvas, which, like the Rubens' example (inv.277), handles a subject common to painting of the Counter-Reformation. The account is taken from the Old Testament, specifically the Book of the Prophet Daniel (13, 1–64), and illustrates well the defeat of deception, expressed by the two old men – shown with lustful eyes and faces – and the victory of truth, represented by the naked Susanna.  
Van Honthorst, known in Italy as Gherardo delle Notti, manages to transmit the feelings of surprise, indignation and shame in the Biblical heroine by the fountain, through her open mouth and terrified look. The study of mood is related to experimentation of Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Guido Reni, who rendered it first in marble and then on canvas.  
Although the composition follows a diagonal arrangement, possibly inspired by Emilian painting that he encountered on his long trip to Italy in the 1620s, the canvas belongs to the final productive phase of the artist. He was better known as a painter of “genre scenes” particularly renowned for the extraordinary lighting effects inspired by the Caravaggesque school of Bartolomeo Manfredi, which he frequented when in Rome. Despite connections to a secular theme and culture, van Honthorst, the leader of the Dutch Caravaggists, captures the instrument of Divine Will in the figure of Susanna, who is entirely surrounded by light, and who triumphs only after suffering cruel injustices.
71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.short_description: The subject is connected to the representation of the emotions according to the experimentation of Bernini and Reni among others. The theme of the painting relates to the concept of deception being defeated by divine truth.
71e28132-f25f-5443-be2a-e44193609556.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.name: Jesuit Church of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, Brno
72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.description: The triple-nave building was among the first Baroque constructions in Moravia (1602). The monumental altar (1734–1737) has, over a silver tabernacle, a replica of a Madonna painting from the largest Marian church, Sta. Maria Maggiore in Rome. The altarpieces and ceiling paintings are by F. A. Scheffler. The sculptures are by J. J. Schauberger. The gallery pews (1602–1605), and the sides of the pews in the main nave (1660s), are particularly remarkable. The organ with figurative decoration in an organ-loft supported by angels is by A. Riga (1728). The sacristy vault is decorated with stucco featuring garlands and heads of *putti*.
72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.short_description: Established in 1578 the college is the second oldest in Moravia. The construction of the complex took place with the support of the Cardinal and Count František of Dietrichstein, the prime mover of the Re-Catholicization of Moravia, and his brother, Provincial Vice-Chamberlain Zikmund. Both are buried in front of the high altar. The college ceased to exist with the dissolution of the Jesuit order in 1773. Only the college portal and the church of the original complex have survived. The monumental high altar features a replica of a Madonna painting from Sta. Maria Maggiore, Rome.
72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.method_for_datation: The construction of the church is mentioned by Pietro Gabri in his testament. Paintings by B. di Anna are signed as is the ceiling painting, which is also dated 1744. Several contracts have been preserved, for example that of J. K. Pröbstl, as well as a contract for the supply of stone. Activities in the Jesuit monastery are also recorded in the books of the Town Council particularly during the religious conflicts of around 1600.
72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.bibliography:
Eugen Dostál, *Umělecké památky Brna*, Prague, 1928, pp. 92–100.  
Bohumil Samek, *Umělecké památky Moravy a Slezska I, A-J*, Prague, 1994, pp. 199–204.  
Josef Koláček, *200 let jezuitů v Brně*, Velehrad, 2002.
72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.history: Established in 1578 on the site of a medieval convent, the college is the sixth oldest in Czech lands and the second oldest in Moravia. The construction of the complex took place with the support of Cardinal and Count František of Dietrichstein, the prime mover of the Re-Catholicization of Moravia, and his brother, Provincial Vice-Chamberlain Zikmund. Both are buried in front of the high altar. The college ceased to exist with the dissolution of the Jesuit order in 1773. The buildings housed an academy and later a barracks. The church sustained serious damage in the bombing of Brno in 1944.
72ba5e39-e72c-5bad-9793-0ee02e82a133.patrons: Cardinal and Count František of Dietrichstein, provincial vice-chamberlain Zikmund, the Jesuits order

737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.name: *St. Florian*
737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.description:
The wooden statue of *St. Florian* has a counterpart, *St. Donatus*, both of which are one and a-half times life-size. Both pieces were transferred to the National Museum in Budapest on permanent loan from the town of Körmöcbánya (Kremnica) in 1892. There is documentary data to confirm that *St. Florian* was part of the interior furnishing of the Parish Church of Our Lady, on which Stanetti worked between 1763 and 1764.  
In 1880 a landslide meant that the church was demolished and that the furnishing was taken out of the church and scattered among various locations. Most of the statues are now in Slovakian museums.  
It is known that the two gilded statues *St. Donatus* and *St. Florian* were originally placed independently in the nave. The two saints, which belong to the age of imperial Rome, had been revered since the Middle Ages as protectors from lightning, hailstorms and fire.  
The sculptures portray both saints as sturdy athletic men with reserved gestures, and their heroic poses are borrowed from stone sculpture similar to those erected near to vineyards and wheat fields. *St. Donatus* wears a wreath of leaves on his head and holds a bundle of lightning bolts to his chest; the sheaf of wheat that he originally held in his left hand is lost. Helmeted *St. Florian* has a burning house at his feet and a pail in his right hand. The flag from his left hand is lost.  
Dionysius Ignatius Stanetti, who made both sculptures, was a descendant of a noted Silesian dynasty of sculptors. His uncle, Johann (Giovanni) Stanetti perhaps toured Italy and was employed by the court circle in Vienna. Dionysius Stanetti moved to Hungary in the 1740s. He was married in Körmöcbánya (Kremnica) and was a burgher of the town until his death. Apart from the Late Baroque furnishings in the churches of the neighbourhood, he also created monumental public memorials: the Holy Trinity columns in Besztercebánya (Banská Štiavnica) and Körmöcbánya (Kremnica).
737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.short_description: The Silesian, Dionysius Ignatius Stanetti, settled in Hungary. His sculptures from Upper Hungarian mining towns are well known. The church of Körmöcbánya (Kremnica) was demolished in the 1880s after a landslide and consequently the Baroque furnishings were scattered throughout the region. The two quality sculptures of *St. Donatus* and *St. Florian* were both deposited by Kremnica town in trust to Budapest.
737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.obtention: Originally from the Roman Catholic Parish Church of Körmöcbánya (Kremnica), the two sculptural saints were initially deposited in 1892 at the National Museum in Budapest in perpetuity; in 1950 the sculptures were transferred to the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest, and in 1974 to the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest.

73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.name: Villa Montalto Grazioli, fresco decoration in the gallery
73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.description:
The long sides of the room — measuring approximately 20 x 5 metres — are richly decorated with alternating *trompe-l'oeil* architectural elements (columns, niches, pilasters and balusters) and simulated sculptures (statues, candelabra, vases and herms). In an apparently never-ending play of illusory space, the room showcases the technical ability and inventiveness of the painter, who uses light to reproduce the polychromy of the different materials painted (marble, bronze, wood and stone).  
On the shorter sides, the space appears to extend through a row of columns painted in perspective, holding up small vaults, beneath which stand the statues of Apollo and Diana, ending in a theatre curtain revealing a sort of *nymphaeum* surmounted by a balustrade, over which treetops and blue sky can be glimpsed. The doors depict the female allegories of the *Continents* and the *Seasons*, symbolised by pairs of children playing with bunches of grapes in the autumn, water in winter, flowers in spring and ears of corn in summer.  
The vault is divided into four parts showing the four elements: *water, air, earth and fire*, recognisable through the motifs painted between the male figures holding up the cornices: aquatic plants, shells and corals for water; creepers and birds for air; vegetables and flowers for the earth; and burning braziers for fire.  
The rich and complex decorative repertoire typical of the painter—whose initials I.P.P. can be seen in several different places—is even more recognisable in the vaulting cells, where winged sphinxes with women's heads sit beside elements of the Odescalchi family coat of arms: the eagle, lion and incense boat. It is a painting full of references to nature: representations of flowers and fruits, foliage and sky, complete with exotic elements revealing knowledge acquired from travel; framed within a single, perspective-based composition made even more magnificent and brilliant by the gouache technique with gold highlighting that harmoniously combines a masterful use of perspective, illusionistic scenography drawn from experience of the theatre, the latest geographic and scientific knowledge and rich inventiveness.
73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.short_description: The long sides of the gallery are richly decorated with alternating mock architectural elements and simulated sculptures in an apparently never-ending play of illusory space. The technical ability and inventiveness of the painter – who uses light to reproduce the polychromy of the different materials painted ­– is showcased within the gallery, in which on the shorter sides, the space appears to extend through a row of columns painted in perspective, holding up small vaults, beneath which stand the statues of Apollo (on one side) and Diana (on the other).
73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.method_for_datation: In the catalogue edited by A. M. Tantillo, “Villa Grazioli”, *Villa e paese*, Rome 1980, p. 160.
73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.bibliography:
Tantillo, A. M., (ed) "Villa Grazioli", *Villa e paese*, Rome 1980, pp. 156–60.  
Tantillo, A. M., "Villa Montalto Grazioli", *I principi della chiesa*, Milan 1998, p. 102.
73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.history: The villa was built at the end of the 16th century by Cardinal Antonio Carafa (1538, Naples – 1591, Rome), a librarian linked to Pope Gregory XIII Boncompagni (1572–85). Designed along the lines of a typical villa Tuscolana on raised foundations, it has one side facing Rome and the other overlooking a garden enclosed by two avant-corps. Having passed through the hands of several owners over the centuries (Acquaviva, Borghese, Peretti Montalto, Savelli, Odescalchi and Grazioli) and now used as a hotel, its interior retains interesting decorative features dating from a period stretching from the early 17th century to the first half of the 18th century. Most notably, in the first half of the 18th century, Baldassarre Erba Odescalchi—nephew of Innocent XI—significantly restored and expanded the villa with the construction of a fully decorated gallery on the southern portico.
73986917-1bf1-5ab7-ba8a-a2cdccc6fd71.patrons: Baldassarre Erba Odescalchi, nephew of Pope Innocent XI (1676–89)

739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.name: Scene showing a squadron of Hussars
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.description: At the time of Count Kazimir Drašković (1716–1765) part of his *banderium* was barracked in Trakošćan. His military biography during the reign of Empress Maria Theresia still decorates the rooms and inventory of Trakošćan Castle. He began his service in the Austrian army in 1734, and fought on the battlefields of Europe. His courage was notable on both the Italian and German battlefields in the war of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) and in the Seven Years' War (1756–1763). In 1763, promoted to artillery general, he then became a commanding general in Transylvania. He was decorated with the highest military order of the Austrian Empire – the Commander Cross of Maria Theresia. There are many items from his time in Trakošćan Castle: portraits of army officers, family members, flags and other material, and particularly wall paintings in the military cabinet on the second floor. The room has canvas wall coverings that give a complete picture of Count Drašković’s military units in the mid-18th century. The large painting consists of 11 parts; the eight larger ones show the *banderium* on parade, composed of 821 people; and the three smaller ones show military symbols, cannon, lances, drums and flags. The paintings are realistic and show in detail the soldiers' uniforms, weapons and the distribution of the units and their parts. A schematic presentation, the soldiers have no personal characteristics, but are portrayed according to type with dark moustaches and red cheeks while the infantry units are faithfully rendered; the soldiers distributed in two companies of fusiliers and one of grenadiers. The staff includes hunters, musicians, guards and a canteen, a surgeon and NCOs. Especially interesting is the small band: the first painting of a military band in Croatia. This was the count's own professional band, which played at his castle during peacetime. It consisted of eight wind instrumentalists: four oboists, two fagottists and two horn players. It also had a tambour major. The cavalry has two squadrons of Dragons and three squadrons of Hussars. The scene shown here is the light cavalry of the Hussars, three troops placed one behind the other in two rows each. They are dressed in blue dolmans, red trousers, brown cloaks and light-brown boots. On their heads, they have busbies.
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.short_description: In a landscape are three double rows of cavalry in blue uniforms led by officers mounted on white horses. There are several houses above the units. This scene, painted on canvas wall hangings, is part of a series depicting military units, which covered one of the rooms of Trakošćan Castle. Croatia's most important aristocratic family, the Counts Drašković, owned the castle. General Count Kazimir Drašković, from whose time these hangings date, had a distinguished military career and was decorated with the highest military order of the Austrian Empire – the Commander Cross of Maria Theresia.
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.type: Canvas wall covering; part of a wall painting
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.method_for_datation: Analysis of style and comparison with the Small Genealogy of the Drašković family.
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.provenance: Found in Trakošćan Castle when it became a museum in 1953
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.obtention: The wall painting was made either to fit the wall of another room in Trakošćan Castle or some other building that belonged to the Counts Drašković, and was later adapted to fit the cabinet, probably when Trakošćan Castle was renovated in the second half of the 19th century.

73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.name: Sugar bowl
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.description:
The master, Domokos Kuny’s father, founded a pottery in Buda producing faience and ceramics in what is today Christina Boulevard. Three masters and eight apprentices worked in his manufactory in the 1780s. The products of the workshop were extremely popular among the bourgeoisie and aristocracy of Buda and Pest in the late 18th century.  
The white glazed sugar bowl is decorated with floral motifs and on the base is the sign “OF” (Ofen=Buda). Domokos Kuny’s (1754–1822) father was Dominique Cuny who mastered the craft of ceramics in a Strasbourg manufactory before arriving from Baden-Durlach to Holics in Upper Northern Hungary. The commercial and economic development of Buda attracted him and he settled down in the city in 1784–85 and founded a manufactory. In the surrounding countryside were clay mines, perfect for the production of ceramics.
