Ivo Krsek –­­ Zdeněk Kudělka (ed) –­­ Miloš Stehlík –­­ Josef Válka, *Umění baroka na Moravě a ve Slezsku,* Prague, 1996, pp. 51, 68, 206, 207, 267, 269, 360.  
Michal Altrichter – Milan Togner – Vladimír Hyhlík, *Olomouc. Univerzitní kostel Panny Marie Sněžné*, Velehrad, 2000.  
Martin Pavlíček, Šalamounův chrám v české barokní architektuře, in *Historická Olomouc XIII. Konec švédské okupace a poválečná obnova ve 2. polovině 17. století*, Olomouc, 2002, pp. 253–272.  
Martin Pavlíček, “A tak postavil ty sloupy v sínici chrámové”. Nerealizovaný projekt sloupu jezuitských světců před kostelem Panny Marie Sněžné v Olomouci, *Studia Moravica. Acta Universitatis Palackianae Olomucensis Facultas Philosophica – Moravica* 2/2004, pp. 265–272.
846382be-ca5f-5bdc-b8e9-6f11b341886e.history: The church was built on the site of a former Minorite Monastery, part of the oldest Jesuit college in Moravia. The original church was destroyed by the Swedish army but was not restored as it was not big enough. The new church was constructed following the design and a wooden model by M. Klein under the guidance of L. Klöckel. During a visit by Cardinal Aldobrandini, later Pope Clement VIII, or on state visits by emperors, the church could hold as many as 2,500 people. In 1773, when the Jesuit order was dissolved, the complex passed to the local military garrison and served as a warehouse. Today it is once again accommodates the university established in 1576, renowned in the 18th century for its graphic theses, carved in Czech and German (Augsburg) workshops.

84c37b00-8c97-5129-b86c-59196b9c0933.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Andrew
84c37b00-8c97-5129-b86c-59196b9c0933.description: The elongated two-bayed choir, refurbished in the Baroque style, adjoins the spacious, virtually quadratic Late Gothic nave in the form of a three-aisled basilica. The Late Gothic construction can be seen on the typical 5/8 polygon termination and the outer buttresses. As the east bay is somewhat wider than the west bay the spatial boundaries become obscured when viewed from the nave so that the light-flooded choir behind the triumphal arch acquires a detached, almost visionary appearance. The centre is occupied by the high altar whose superstructure incorporates the upper east window, an effect modelled on Bernini’s Chair of St. Peter in Rome. The altar crown with its stucco draperies forms the transition to the vault zone with ceiling frescos in sweeping cartouches.
84c37b00-8c97-5129-b86c-59196b9c0933.short_description: The Late Gothic city parish church of Lienz is an important example of the Baroque redesign of a medieval ecclesiastical building in Tyrol. The contrast between the triumphal Baroque forms in the choir and the austerity of the nave is consciously set in scene and the choir, site of the Holy Communion, is staged as a vision of heaven.
84c37b00-8c97-5129-b86c-59196b9c0933.dates: 1457: consecration of the Gothic building; 1737: Baroque redesign begins; c. 1760–c. 1765: choir
84c37b00-8c97-5129-b86c-59196b9c0933.bibliography:
Maister, K., *Unterkircher, Franz, Die Stadtpfarrkirche zum Hl. Andreas Lienz Osttirol*, 2nd revised edition. Munich, Zurich 1956.  
Beinsteiner-Krall, G., *Anton und Joseph Anton Zoller. Ein Beitrag zur Barockmalerei in Tirol*, Innsbruck 1978.  
Pizzinini, M., *Stadtpfarrkirche St. Andrä in Lienz, Diözese Innsbruck, Bundesland Tirol*, Passau 2004.  
*Österreichische Kunsttopographie*, vol. 57,1, Bezirkshauptstadt Lienz und Lienzer Talboden. Horn 2007.
84c37b00-8c97-5129-b86c-59196b9c0933.history: Lienz was under the jurisdiction of the Archbishopric of Salzburg since 811 and the parish had existed since the Early Middle Ages. The first building on the site and immediate predecessor was consecrated in 1204 and subsequently destroyed by fire. The remains were integrated into the present building which was consecrated in 1457. In 1737 the choir and the tower adjoining to the north were damaged in a fire. The reconstruction of the choir was carried out between c. 1760/65. The tower, also restored, was crowned by a Baroque capped-roof which was replaced by a Neo-Gothic pointed helm-roof in 1907.

85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.name: Franciscan Church and Monastery of St. Roch, Virovitica
85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.description:
The spatial organisation of the four-winged, two-storey Franciscan complex is based on a classical monastic solution of cross-vaulted corridors in the cloister opened up with arcades, and a sequence of similarly vaulted rooms alongside the external facade. Against this model, the monumental Franciscan Church of St. Roch is characterised by carefully planned Late Baroque features. Although it too is in line with the Franciscan tradition, it is characterised by a nave hall-church with a somewhat narrow straight-ended chancel. The articulation of both walls and ceilings show the presence of a well-informed Central European architect. Alongside the walls, articulated columns rise with elegant Ionic pilasters forming shallow concave side-chapels. The columns and pilasters support the arched architraves and the ceiling strips, in the nave the calottes, and in the sanctuary, the ellipsoidal domes.  
Appropriate Late Baroque transformation of Early Baroque wall columns (*Wandpfeiler*) and side chapels was carried out in the Church of St. Veit am Vogau by the famed Styrian architect, Josef Hueber, from Graz. In 1745, Hueber put forward a prototype solution for a religious space similar to St. Roch for the chapel of Batthyhány Palace in Ludbreg, therefore, it is plausible that he had a very direct impact on the Franciscan church in Virovitica. The argument is more solid when considering St. Roch's grand façade, flanked with a side bell-tower, as this corresponds with the aforementioned Hueber church in Vogau. With markedly similar stylistic and typological characteristics, St. Roch is notable within the body of Franciscan churches of inland Croatia and is echoed during the second half of the 18th century, mainly in the architecture of parish churches.
85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.short_description: The Franciscan Church of St. Roch in Virovitica relates to Early Baroque, Central European hall churches with wall columns and side chapels but in its rounded chapels, it also demonstrates the introduction of Late Baroque spatial dynamics. In 1745, the architect Josef Hueber of Graz was engaged in renovations to Batthyhány Palace chapel in Ludbreg, where he appropriately centralised the longitudinal chapel in the Late Baroque manner. In light of this, therefore, it is fair to assume that he influenced the appearance of St. Rochus whose façade articulation is similar to some other Hueber churches in Styria.
85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.type: Religious, Baroque four-winged monastery; Late Baroque nave church with ellipsoidal side chapels
85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.history: Written sources tell of the existence of a Franciscan monastery and church in Virovitica as early as 1280, but after the Ottoman siege of 1552, nothing remained of the medieval complex. It was only after the Franciscans had returned to Virovitica in 1684, and the Turks expelled, that the first wooden monastery and church were constructed. Today’s four-winged masonry-built monastery was erected between 1726 and 1751 (by 1730 the Franciscan theological school was active). The foundation stone of the new church was in place by 1746, and by 1752, the monumental High Baroque building was completed. Following damage by an earthquake in 1757, the church was reconstructed by Italian craftsmen.
85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.architects: Master builders: Giovanni Bérta (known work c. 1770),  Giulio Zérone (known work c. 1770); sculptors: Josip Holzinger  (1735–797), Stjepan Severin (c. 1700–1760); painters: Josef Anton Cusetti (1750–1793), Damian Bittner (1733–1768); cabinetmaker: Timotej Schwab (known works c. 1770)
85df3bed-0c03-5101-8ebd-9303881f7f36.author: Katarina Horvat-Levaj, Mirjana Repanić-Braun

85ea18f4-df5c-5e4b-ac52-cad7c455e015.name: *The Apotheosis of Emperor Joseph II*
85ea18f4-df5c-5e4b-ac52-cad7c455e015.description:
This small allegorical composition is a rare example of a piece that might have been planned originally purely as a decorative piece. The execution of the painting is finely detailed, and contrary to its small size, it is of exceptional quality. The painting is also unusual in its representation of the emperor, which is not at all in keeping with the normal iconography associated with him.  
The Holy Roman Emperor Joseph II (1765–1790) was King of Hungary from 1780 to 1790. The eldest son of Maria Theresia and Francis von Lorraine, having succeeded to the throne, he tried to organise a unified empire with reforms of Enlightened Absolutism. Both his political and religious policies served the emperor's overall ideal of the strong central power of the state. His reform policies were named after him and are known in Hungary as Josephinism. A limited guarantee of freedom of worship was seen with the Patent of Tolerance in 1781, and he abolished serfdom and the death penalty. Like many of the enlightened monarchs of the time, he was a prolific patron of the arts, commissioning an opera from Mozart and a funeral cantata from the young Beethoven.
85ea18f4-df5c-5e4b-ac52-cad7c455e015.short_description: Because of its small size and compositional form, this painting is a rare example of Baroque allegory associated with the Holy Roman Emperor Joseph II (1765–1790). The painting glorifies the Habsburg emperor and Hungarian king during whose reign Enlightened Absolutism was born. Because of his reforms and the laws he passed, the era is known in Hungary as Josephinism.
85ea18f4-df5c-5e4b-ac52-cad7c455e015.provenance: From the Royal Collection, Royal Palace, Buda
85ea18f4-df5c-5e4b-ac52-cad7c455e015.obtention: Transferred from the Royal Collection, Royal Palace in Buda in 1945
keywords: Enlightenment; Josephinism; allegory; Joseph II Habsburg; Maria Theresia; Franz von Lorraine; panel
85ea18f4-df5c-5e4b-ac52-cad7c455e015.author: Beatrix Basics

86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.name: *St. Augustine*
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.alternate_name: *St. Augustine Stepping On the Head of Heresy*
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.description:
*St. Augustine* furnished the entrance of the *Nossa Senhora* *da* *Graça* Convent in Lisbon ruled by the order of St. Augustine. Built around 1271, important reforms of 1565 followed by others in the 17th and 18th centuries, transformed the convent into one of the most sumptuous in Lisbon. After the earthquake of 1755 the convent collapsed and was rebuilt. The grand Italianate late Baroque painting, *St. Augustine,* was probably a gift from King José I to the friars, given that Lusitano was the king's first official court painter.  
The Saint, dressed in Episcopal robes, is writing while he steps on the head of Heresy. At his side a *putto* encourages some dogs to attack Heresy while another, in the lower part of the painting, is burning heretic books. An allegorical figure of The Church sits at the upper left-hand side as, rendered in dark ochre, it emerges statue-like out of the shadow. On the right-hand side a classical building in daylight sweeps into the background. Behind St. Augustine are ruined monumental columns. The realism, upheld by the depth of the landscape, contrasts with the crowded, chaotic interior of the St. Augustine's *scriptorium*.  
The painting, signed and dated by Vieira Lusitano, emphasises his nomination as *accademico di merito*, an honour bestowed on him in 1727 by the St. Lucas Academy in Rome. No other Portuguese artist had previously received this honour. Lusitano was influenced by Roman, late Baroque and Rococo art; his teachers included Benedetto Lutti (1666–1724) and Francesco Trevisani (1656–1746), a disciple of Carlo Maratta (1625–1713).  
*St. Augustine,* a large-scale geometric composition with calculated asymmetry and movement, has theatrical appeal. Its characters are set among solid architectural components and a naturalistic background. The *putti,* characteristics from the Roman tradition, enable the artist to play with symbolic elements while the sumptuous use of colour: ochre, red, various blues and white; the flesh tones and gold and silver details in the bishop's robes, is also notable. Vieira Lusitano had many sophisticated patrons. He often made use of allegory to introduce complex ideas into the works he was commissioned to paint.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.short_description: A late Baroque masterpiece influenced by Roman Painting. The scene, a contrast between the crowded, chaotic *scriptorium* of St. Augustine and the open classical cityscape, celebrates the author, bishop and Father of the Church St. Augustine stepping on the head of Heresy.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.initial_owner: Convent of Nossa Senhora da Graça, Lisbon
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.method_for_datation: Francisco Vieira Lusitano has signed and dated the picture.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.provenance: Convent of Nossa Senhora da Graça, Lisbon
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.obtention: The convent and the order of St Augustine were extinguished and their assets confiscated by the Portuguese state in 1834. This painting was included among the objects that were confiscated and taken to the Fine Arts Academy Museum in Lisbon. When the museum closed, the collection transferred to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in Alvor Palace, Lisbon.

86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.name: *Death of St. Joseph*
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.description:
St. Joseph, the patron saint of a happy death and of Austria, became a principal subject of altarpieces around 1700. Many 18th-century artists embraced the subject, for instance Carlo Maratta in 1676, and it was adopted in around 1730 by Francesco Solimena, Giambattista Pittoni, Giambattista Piazzetta and Francesco Trevisani (Rome, S. Ignazio). Trevisani's work became a template for a number of pictures around the theme of St. Joseph, including Paul Troger's *Death of St. Joseph*. Korompay's Christ is very close to Troger's figure of Christ in the painting mentioned, especially in his mirror-image gesture. While in Troger's picture (and in the majority of the examples given) St. Joseph is lying on a bed, Korompay depicts him kneeling, supported by an angel. The motif was probably not the artist's own; he might have come across it in a reproduction print of an artwork from the Italian *Settecento*, a period that favoured motifs of drooping figures – whether they were saints or Christ himself – supported by angels. Pittoni employed this relationship between two figures in his *Ecstasy of St. Theresa*, Ricci in *Landscape with St. Mary Magdalene and an Angel*, and Trevisani in *Christ on the Mount of Olives*. The motif, however, can also be found in Troger's and Franz Anton Maulbertsch's early oeuvres.  
Korompay developed the composition of the main figures in a shallow foreground, placing them within a group of appealing gesticulating figures that provide a link with the second figurative layer represented by an angel and *putti*.  
The artist's segmented brushwork accentuates the illusion of the scene's ascending tendency. The palette features a rich scale of subtle warm shades blending into one another – from deep red to pale pink and mauve – making up the colour base of the picture. Korompay off-set this colour scheme with the pasty tones of lemon yellow and yellow-green seen in Joseph's gown, and the cold blue of Jesus' cloak, contrasting with his red undergarment.  
The painting was a template for the side altar altarpiece at the Parish Church of St. James, Brno, which is preserved there to this day.
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.short_description: St. Joseph, patron saint of a happy death, became a principal subject of altarpieces around 1700. The composition, based on paintings by F. Trevisiani and P. Troger, is the template for the side altar altarpiece at the Parish Church of St. James, Brno, preserved to this day.
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.method_for_datation: Korompay created seven pictures for the Church of St. James, a fact recorded in the sources and reflected in the paintings of Franz Anton Palko – a painter of altarpieces and a distinguished portraitist active in Brno and south Moravia.
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.obtention: Acquired from the collection of the Brno based historian Ernst Hawlik in 1826.

87a1dd6a-9de9-541b-8e2c-4db747def725.name: Church of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary and Calvary, Moravská Třebová
87a1dd6a-9de9-541b-8e2c-4db747def725.description: The concave-segmented frontage with prominent volute consoles opens into a single-nave space with side chapels. The church encloses a small square.
87a1dd6a-9de9-541b-8e2c-4db747def725.short_description: The building and furnishing of the church, together with its Stations of the Cross and Calvary, are fine examples of architecture in what is only a minor cultural centre in Moravia. The decoration, including remarkably expressive carvings, was targeted at a Czech audience. The church was designed by A. Beduzzi, a Viennese theatre engineer, who frequently worked for the Liechtensteins.
87a1dd6a-9de9-541b-8e2c-4db747def725.method_for_datation: The church fresco is signed and dated. Records relevant to the sculpture work have survived in the parish chronicle. A sketch for the Celebration of St. Aloysius is preserved in the collections of the Moravian Gallery in Brno.

87a1dd6a-9de9-541b-8e2c-4db747def725.history: The origins of the town go back to the mid-13th century. During the reign of the Lords of Boskovice and Žerotín (1486–1622), Moravská Třebová was a centre of humanist education, dubbed by some as “the Moravian Athens”. A Gothic church burnt down in 1726 and the new church was designed by A. Beduzzi, a Viennese theatre engineer, who frequently worked for the Liechtensteins. The church contains remarkably expressive carvings by J. Pacák.

8882d0e5-57fa-5c65-adef-21bc617bd242.name: *Portrait of a Laughing Youth*
8882d0e5-57fa-5c65-adef-21bc617bd242.description:
The painting is mentioned for the first time as part of the collection in the 1693 inventory. It has been attributed variously to different artists in the past, but was confirmed as a “Carracci Caricature” in an 1833 *fideicommissum* (a deed forbidding the heirs to the Borghese estate from splitting up the collection). In the 20th century, it was deemed to be an early work of the Bolognese artist, at a time when Carracci made numerous attempts at “genre works”, leaving some superb examples, such as the famous canvas , *The Beaneater* in the Galleria Colonna, Rome (c. 1583–1584).  
The portrait of the jester has always been thought to be a character from the *Commedia dell'Arte*. This small sketch shows a smiling, mocking youth dressed in a dark suit, ruff and light hat, awkward and upside-down. The supposed jester, with his grotesque red nose, cannot be identified entirely with the theatrical comic tradition and, although the severe and sober clothes resemble the Bolognese mask of “Dottor Graziano”, the unusual hat is perhaps an invention of Carracci himself.  
The light comes from the right, creating a *chiaroscuro* effect on the folds of the hat, emphasising the satisfied look and ambiguous smile of the character, the focal point of the portrait.  
It is the complicit look and smile of a comic actor that, between fiction and reality, skilfully establishes a relationship with the viewer.  
The portrait stands against a simple yellow background, which helps to focus attention on the burlesque face, whose keen, realistic expression is rendered with a sombre palette of colours.  
Free charcoal lines quickly define the sketch, combined with fast, fluid brush strokes. Given the medium (paper on canvas) the use of these tools seems to suggest a desire to capture the immediacy of a live portrait, rather than a caricature, which has been suggested, although this area was of interest to the painter.  
The modernity of expression in the sketch anticipates by half a century the portraits of Velazquez and Bernini and appears to be the beginning of the study of emotions and character types that characterises 18th-century artistic innovation.  
The work is one of Carracci's “small portraits” painted after 1582, where his search for reality was based on simple lines and not precise reproductions of faces.
8882d0e5-57fa-5c65-adef-21bc617bd242.short_description: This piece is an interesting example of the artistic re-invention pursued by Carracci. In his sketchy *Portrait of a Laughing Youth*, dating to around1584, the young artist captures a moment of the youth's laughter. With its spontaneity, it is extraordinarily modern, anticipating the portraits by Bernini and Velázquez 50 years later. It may be the portrait of an actor, the Bolognese mask of the “Dottor Graziano”.

894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.name: *Geometrical Elevation of the Building of the Chemical Laboratory* Azulejos
894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.description:
In 1772, under the educational reforms of King Jose I's Prime Minister the Marquis of Pombal, a new statute for Coimbra University emerged. The views of the Marquis and other Enlightenment figures replaced the Aristotelian school of thought previously taught by the Jesuits, who were expelled in 1759. The aim was to modernise teaching by basing it on practical experience and observation.  
In addition to hiring foreign teachers, buying new textbooks and the acquisition of specialised didactic teaching aids, the university replaced the Jesuit-built college with new buildings, one where the former College of the Jesus Society had been and another where the Paço das Escolas (School Hall) once stood.  
The buildings followed the designs of the English Engineer William Elsden, who was also responsible for the construction. The tile panel *Geometrical Elevation of the Building of the Chemical Laboratory* is one of nine panels decorating the Bishop’s palace.  
The building shown here was used by the science department, which had been newly created through Pombaline reform. Today the building hosts the Museum of Science, part of the University of Coimbra.  
The decoration of the Bishop's palace (today the Museu Nacional de Machado de Castro) was commissioned by the Bishop, formerly the Rector of the University. The panels were designed to celebrate the Pombaline reform of the University of Coimbra (1772–1777), and to mark the important role played by D. Francisco de Lemos de Faria Pereira Coutinho, known as “Reformer and Rector of the University of Coimbra”. He was picked out to lead local reform by the Marquis of Pombal.  
The panels were made at Nova Fábrica da Telha Vidrada, a factory founded in 1773 to meet the demands of (*azulejos*) required for the construction and renovation of the University buildings.  
The production of *azulejos* with repetitive patterns, single figures and ornamental and figurative panels are part of the second phase of the Rococo period (or Pombaline style) that occurred after the earthquake of 1755. In Coimbra this period was extended until the end of the century, whereas in Lisbon, *azulejos* from 1790 onwards had been designed in the Neo-classical style leaving the Rococo for the minor panels.  
The frames of bulky shell forms, similar to those present in some paintings of the period, probably belong to Salvador de Sousa Carvalho (1727–1810), who alternated with Manuel da Costa Brioso (1752–1776) as the director of the Nova Fábrica da Telha Vidrada.
894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.short_description: The panel is an excellent example of 18th-century quality ceramics produced in Coimbra. It represents a memorial of Pombaline reforms at the University of Coimbra depicting the façade of the Chemical Laboratory.

894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.name: Church of Worship and Basilian Monastery of Máriapócs
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.alternate_name: Greek Catholic Church of Worship and Monastery
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.description:
The Church of Worship of Máriapócs has a transept and two towers on the west façade; the sanctuary is oriented east. It has three ridged turrets on the roof and the vestry is on the south side.  
The date of construction and the names of the builders are commemorated on a chronosticon above the main gate, above which there is a mosaic representing the Madonna (*Theotokosz*). Beside bishops, many of the church’s patrons are lying in the crypt.  
The main red marble altar was a gift from Count Pál Forgách Bishop of Nagyvárad (Oradea) in 1750; the two preparation altars (in the sanctuary with the main altar); its pulpit (carved and gilded with the statue of St. Michael the archangel above); the painting of the Apostle Paul below the baldachin, with paintings, *Christ and the Samaritan Woman* and the *Seed-Sower*, and the structure of its iconostasis (with a Rococo balustrade and crowned with a cross; the pictures of which date to 1896) are also 18th century.  
There are two side altars: on the north side, the Altar of the Virgin Mary (1943–1944) designed by the Franciscan monks of Pécs, now houses the the miraculous “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs”. The south altar, known as the Altar of the Heart of Jesus, holds a cross relic. The Great Altar of St. Basil is at the same side of the church.  
The sanctuary wall paintings, by Manó Petrasovszky, depict King St. Stephen (Szent István) I offering Hungary to the Virgin Mary with the first martyr St. Stephen, patron saint of the Diocese of Hajdúdorog, and Hungarian saints and pilgrims. The stained-glass windows were made after designs by Petrasovszky between 1944 and 1945. Other wall paintings are by József Boksay (1943).  
The two-storey rectangular Baroque monastery is connected to the church via a suspended corridor.
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.short_description: The Church of Worship in Máriapócs is one of Hungary's most important places of worship particularly for the Greek Catholic community living mostly in eastern Hungary. Up until 1950, the church was maintained by monks from the next-door Basilian Monastery, which was consecrated in 1756. The interior of the church along with the furnishing, much of which dates to the 1780s, has been renovated several times during the 19th and 20th centuries. A copy of the miraculous “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs” was placed in the church in 1707. Since then, this miraculous image has wept twice, attracting numerous other miraculous events to Máriapócs.
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, stylistic and field research.

894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.history:
The Church of Worship and Monastery of Máriapócs is a highly significant place for the Greek Catholic Church. Pócs first gained significance in 1696 when in a small, wooden Greek Catholic church in Pócs a group of soldiers witnessed a devotional image, painted in 1676, weeping.  
The original “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs” was commissioned by László Csigri judge of Máriapócs as a votive painting in gratitude for his release from Turkish captivity. István Papp, the younger brother of the local Greek Catholic pastor Dániel Papp, painted the picture but the judge could not pay him on completion. Lőrinc Hurta and his family subsequently purchased the painting and donated it to the church. Following the first act of weeping, Emperor Leopold I had the painting transferred to Vienna, where it was finally placed in St. Stephen's Dome on 11 September 1697, the day the troops of Prince Eugene of Savoy defeated the Turkish armies at Zenta (Senta). The people of Vienna related the triumph to the miraculous power of the “Mary of Pócs”, which Leopold I confirmed in his bull issued to Pócs in 1701.  
Belief in the power of the painting led Leopold I to support the people of Pócs in their fundraising efforts to erect a new church in 1701. Later, Charles VI Emperor gave permission for construction of a church, and the settlement of Greek Catholic Basilian monks in Pócs; Count Ferenc Károlyi donated a large sum of money towards construction as well as his entire Pócs estate.  
Construction began in 1731 at the personal expense of Bishop and Apostolic Vicar György Bizáncy Gennadius, but was halted when the bishop died in 1733.  
István Simon Olsavszky and Gábor Blazsovszky renovated the deteriorating walls before Bishop Mihály Mánuel Olsavszky continued the building programme and consecrated the church in 1749. The foundations were laid and the sanctuary walls erected by 1748.  
In 1749, Bishop Olsavszky received permission from Queen Maria Theresia to establish the Basilian Monastery and the independent bishopric of Munkács (Mukachevo). By 1751, the foundation stone was laid and part of the monastery was complete, so the monks from Munkács (Mukachevo) moved in. The whole building was consecrated in 1753.  
By 1756, the church was complete.  
The Greek Catholic Vicar of Pócs addressed a petition to the emperor requesting that the “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs” be returned. Leopold I promised that a replica would be donated to the church in his written transcript addressed to István Telekessy Bishop of Eger, but in the end, Telekessy commissioned an Austrian artist to paint the copy in 1707, which arrived to Pócs in the same year.  
The paintings of the iconostasis (replaced in 1896) are by Mihály and Tádé Spalinszky (Tádé was also a Basilian monk) of Polish origin between 1785 and 1788. Its gold-plated wooden structure was probably made by a craftsman from Eperjes (Prešov).  
In 1943, the miraculous “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs”, which hung above the Royal Door of the iconostasis, was moved to a side altar in the north wing, then in 1946, on the 250th anniversary of the first weeping, it   was moved to its present location.  
The marble main altar was made in the 18th century; the towers of the church in 1856, and the new bronze gate of the church completed in 1991 for the visit and mass of Pope John Paul II. Pope Pius XII gave the Church of Worship of Máriapócs the title Basilica Minor in 1948.  
The church was cared for by Basilian monks until the dissolution of the order in 1950. The monastery then became a care home, and 10,000 volumes from the library were removed, along with valuable furnishings and items of worship from the church and monastery, which were scattered among various locations. Renovation of the church and monastery began in 2008.

89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.name: *All Saints*
89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.description:
A gathering of saints opens up into a view of the heavens, symbolising the Church Triumphant. The ancient festival of All Hallows dates to as early as 609. Saints of all nations glorify the Holy Trinity, together with angels. In the left foreground is St. Francis of Assisi, above him St. Anthony of Padua and St Florian with a flag. At the bottom in the centre is the patron saint of the country, St. John of Nepomuk, with a palm leaf, and two Moravian martyrs, Jan Sarkander and Jan Capistranus. At the bottom on the right is St. Norbert, a Premonstratensian saint, with a monstrance. Above him are St. Lawrence and St. Stephen holding stones, St. Andrew carrying a cross, St. Peter with a set of keys and St. John the Baptist with a cross and an inscribed ribbon. The central space is occupied by the Church Fathers St. Hieronymus, St. Augustine with a burning heart, and St. Gregory. Below Christ and God the Father on the left, are the Old Testament prophets, King David with a harp and Moses with the Decalogue. On the right is the Virgin Mary – model for the Church Triumphant – absorbed in prayer, and New Testament figures. Chains of figurative groups create several layers in infinite space, the illusion of which is enhanced by the contrasting foreground, the scale of colour and light effects, and the drapery by which the artist rhythmically joins the figures into a single spiral flow.  
This sketch-type painting was a study for a high altar painting in Milotice Parish Church near Kyjov. It is generally thought to be one of the best works of Josef Stern, an artist from Brno who came to Moravia from Graz having studied at the Vienna Academy and journeyed to Italy. He was court painter to the Dietrichsteins and was said to be among the most learned artists in Moravia. During his work in Kroměříž he met F. A. Maulbertsch, whose expressive style had a significant impact upon him.
89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.short_description: This sketch-type painting was a study for the high altar painting in Milotice Parish Church. The gathering of saints opens up into a view of the heavens, while chains of figurative groups make up several layers in infinite space to create an illusion that is enhanced by a contrasting foreground and the scale of colour and light.
89e2bfdb-bfe0-596f-8f06-5bde0062915b.method_for_datation: Josef Stern’s authorship of the Milotice picture is upheld by 19th-century written sources; these references have been confirmed by modern style analysis.

8a50a95e-def1-531c-840c-040f6cf8a2f3.name: Marionette of Hamlet
8a50a95e-def1-531c-840c-040f6cf8a2f3.description:
William Shakespeare wrote his tragedy *Hamlet* around 1600–1601. The protagonist of this work is one of the most famous characters in world literature. The success of the play was very quick and Pietro Resoniero made this marionette, still wearing the original clothes, after moving to Vienna, in 1667. Resoniero, originally from Venice, founded in Vienna an Italian marionettes theatre by the "JUVEN MARKT" and a school for puppet-masters. He probably introduced the character of Pulcinella in Austria and Germany, where he was called Casperl or Hanswurt (John Sausage). From Italy came the Rezzonieri (the Resonieri family) and the Griffi, who were the first in Germany to make plays with the "Puppenspielen" (Yorik, *La storia dei burattini*, 1884).  
The marionette's head is made of pine wood. Its hair is made of silk thread, the mouth is finely formed and the eyes are made of glass, probably Murano. The precious garments he is wearing declare the character's social state. Turned down eyebrows and wrinkles at the sides of the mouth express desperation giving the face a heart-rending expression and foretelling the future tragedy. A very sophisticated device endows the marionette with an ample chance of movement, it can move its feet, walk and bend its knees.
8a50a95e-def1-531c-840c-040f6cf8a2f3.short_description: This marionette represents Hamlet, the world famous Shakespearean character. It is still wearing the original clothes and thanks to a sophisticated device can walk and bend its knees. It was made by an Italian puppet-master, Pietro Resonieri, in the second half of the seventeenth-century.
8a50a95e-def1-531c-840c-040f6cf8a2f3.dates: Second half of the sixteenth century
8a50a95e-def1-531c-840c-040f6cf8a2f3.bibliography: Guarino, M., Fabbri, I. *Chi è di scena! Burattini e Marionette in Emilia Romagna,* Regione Emilia Romagna, Istituto per i beni artistici culturali e naturali, Bologna, 2009 (DVD Rom).
materials: Wood carved and painted, silk, glass
keywords: Marionette; Theatre; Resoniero; Hamlet
8a50a95e-def1-531c-840c-040f6cf8a2f3.author: Vittorio Zanella

8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.name: Villa Zanchini-Garagnani
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.description:
The villa is formed by the superimposition of eighteenth-century elements on the original nucleus of the building, once crowned by a small covered terrace (altana) on the top of the roof.  
The scenographic solution of the front with lateral arcades forms an aedicule that covers the curved stairs. This elegant feature was used as an entrance for coaches. The two hexagonal aedicules can be dated to the seventeenth-century and were attributed to the local architect Giovan Giacomo Monti. The curved flight of stairs is similar to solutions employed in Bolognese buildings of the same age, so that this part of the villa can be considered the first to be built.  
Distributed around the central hall are several different rooms. The elegant and measured interiors can be dated to the latest transformation that involved the building, at the end of the nineteenth-century. The rooms are decorated with stucco in Neo-classic style and in some case they still hold their original “Venetian style” floors.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.short_description:
The originality of this villa is the scenographic structure of its front formed by different arcades that hide and, at he same time, introduce to the two-curved stair flights, bringing to the first floor.  
The dynamism and elegance of the space and the changing views that can be enjoyed through the arcades and columns from the small loggia on the top of the stairs, are typical of the local baroque architecture that owns most of its devices to the theatre tradition.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.dates: 1679; 1786; 1881 restoration of the building and decoration of the interiors in Neo-classic style
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.bibliography: Matteucci, A. M.,*Ville storiche di Zola Predosa*, Province of Bologna, Municipality of Zola Predosa, without date.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.history:
Not much is known about this villa and its architect remains unidentified. A Latin inscription, still visible on the building, tells us that it was built in 1679 by Edoardo Zanchini. At the beginning of the eighteenth-century the villa passed to the Zambeccari family and in 1786 it was restyled and enlarged by Marquis Vincenzo Zambeccari. In 1878 it was sold in a public auction to Raffaele Garagnani who promoted some restoration work and took the villa back to its original splendour.  
The whole building was seriously damaged during the Second World War. The private chapel next to the villa was destroyed and the roof was completely rebuilt by the Garagnani Family. They still own the villa and the surrounding land with vineyards and orchards.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.patrons: Edoardo Zanchini; Vincenzo Zambeccari; Raffaele Garagnani
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.copyright: Copyright images: Comune di Bologna, Musei Civici d'Arte Antica.
keywords: Residential architecture; Scenography; Villa; Monumental staircase; Loggia

8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.name: Console
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.description: From a base with four round feet springs the console resembling two vine branches, intertwined with vine-leaves and grapes. The carving is powerful as the volumes are full and in the round. The wood is gilded with silver leaf. The table is painted to look like a dark green false marble, with pale green veins. Formerly thought to be a nineteenth-century remake from a Tuscan workshop, today this console is considered an original piece dating to the eighteenth-century. The original provenance is unknown, but it was likely made in Tuscany. The console is part of the furniture of the baroque apartment, on the first floor of the building which was made between 1736 and 1738 for the wedding of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.short_description: This piece of furniture is very original; the base is made of vine-shoots and grapes realistically intertwined with a strongly naturalistic carving. We don’t know its original provenance. The console is housed in the red living room of the baroque apartment on the first floor of Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1736 and 1738 for the marriage of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.dates: First half of the eighteenth century
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.copyright: Copyright image: Archivio fotografico Musei Civici di Imola.
materials: Wood carved, painted as marble and covered with a silver leaf
keywords: Console; Woodwork; furnishing; wood carving; grape design; vine tendris decoration; workpshop
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.author: Oriana Orsi

8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.name: Catholic Pilgrimage Church of the Holy Cross
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.description: The church’s modest exterior with a tail gable on the front side betrays little of its rich interior, although the building design is already apparent: a cross with central-crossing cupola and three uniformly designed arms, supplemented by a transverse oblong vestibule to the north. The spatial impression of the interior is dominated by the crossing with slanting pilaster piers according to the Roman design, surmounted by the cupola with its large skylight turret. The symbolism of the cross informs the building design and is also present in pictorial form as a symbol of salvation in Christoph Anton Mayr’s cycle of frescos.
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.short_description: The only genuine centralised building of the great Tyrolean master church-builder Franz de Paula Penz was built on the ground plan of a Greek cross, here symbolising the crucifix. The interior is dominated by the crossing cupola with its main scenes of the Legend of the Cross in bold colours. The clear unity of form and expression, as typical for smaller Late Baroque centralised buildings, has reached a high degree of perfection here.
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.method_for_datation: Portal with date 1764, frescos inscribed 1767; archives
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.bibliography:
Walch, O., *Die Kreuzkirche in Pill/Tirol*, Innsbruck 1988.  
Bruckmann, E., “Verschiebung der Kreuzkirche in Pill, Tirol”, in: *architektur aktuell*, vol. 16, no. 88, 1982.  
Bayer, K., *Franz de Paula Penz*, Vienna 1991, p. 66.
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.history: The veneration of the holy cross of Pill dates back to the time of the War of the Spanish Succession as Bavarian troops invaded Tyrol. On 25 July 1703, during fighting, the bridge over the Inn at Zirl burnt down and the bridge cross fell into the river. It was recovered undamaged downstream from Pill, was soon held to be miraculous and was erected in a provisional wooden chapel. Increasing numbers of pilgrims occasioned curate Bernhard Kiechl to build the church in 1764, consecrated by the Bishop of Brixen Leopold Graf Spau on 25 July 1766. During the last renovation of 1981–5 it was moved five metres back from the main road passing directly in front of it.
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.architects: Architecture, plans: Franz de Paula Penz (1707–1772); building supervision, attributed to: Johann Michael Umhaus(er) (c. 1710–1784); ceiling frescos: Christoph Anton Mayr (c. 1720–1771); sculptural work, attributed to: Gregor Fritz (1693–1774)
keywords: Pilgrimage church; centralised building; ceiling frescoes
8b5631ba-9d56-54cf-bb44-b2f1586d62ac.author: Frank Purrmann

8b73574b-b242-5496-8220-49ca7d6386ab.name: *The Arrival of the Holy Crown at Buda*
8b73574b-b242-5496-8220-49ca7d6386ab.description: The history of the Holy Crown goes back a long way and tells a story full of dramatic event. During the reign of Queen Maria Theresia, the Holy Crown was preserved in Vienna. In 1780, when the Holy Roman Emperor Joseph II (1765–1790), son of Maria Theresia, ascended to the Hungarian throne, the Holy Crown was kept in Vienna but Joseph II refused to be crowned with it or take the coronation oath. For this reason he was named *Pál Ányos*, and this is why his nickname “king of Hut” was widespread all over in Hungary. Following his death, the Holy Crown was returned to Buda in a ceremonial procession to the Royal Castle. On the occasion the diet was summoned there, which had last happened in 1530. The engraving represents the ceremonial procession, and is well known as the first and only example of such a festive event in Hungary.
8b73574b-b242-5496-8220-49ca7d6386ab.short_description: An engraved representation of the return of the Holy Crown of Hungary from Vienna to Buda in 1790.
8b73574b-b242-5496-8220-49ca7d6386ab.method_for_datation: On the basis of the object itself
8b73574b-b242-5496-8220-49ca7d6386ab.obtention: Purchased from an art dealer between the two world wars in Budapest.

keywords: Ceremonial procession; festivity; Holy Crown; Joseph II Habsburg; Maria Theresia; Pál Ányos; Pest; Buda; engraving
8b73574b-b242-5496-8220-49ca7d6386ab.author: Beatrix Basics

8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.name: *Prince Livio Odescalchi*
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.description:
Prince Livio Odescalchi (1652–1713) belonged to the influential Italian Odescalchi family, a family that throughout history produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI.  
Emperor Leopold I Habsburg, in gratitude for the great financial aid granted him by Pope Innocent XI to meet the costs of the war against the Ottoman Turks, named his nephew Livio Duke of Srijem and granted him the Ilok estate as a fief and many other privileges. Livio himself had excelled in the battle to defend Vienna in 1683.  
He was a great collector and decorated his residences with fine artworks. He was also a patron of the arts.  
The marble *Prince Livio Odescalchi* by the Roman sculptor of French origin, Pierre-Etienne Monnot, is an outstanding work with realistic emphasis on individuality. Dramatic tension is achieved through the expression of the head turned to the right, and by the rich drapery enveloping the body falling in heavy semicircular folds.  
Monnot often worked for the Odescalchi family. He was an excellent master with a fine technique and a strong and characteristic expression reminiscent of Bernini.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.short_description: The marble *Prince Livio Odescalchi* by the Roman sculptor of French origin, Pierre-Etienne Monnot, shows Prince Livio Odescalchi, a member of the influential Italian family that throughout history produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI. The sculpture shows the influence of Bernini. Livio Odescalchi had links to Ilok and Slavonia by way of the deed of gift he received from Leopold I Habsburg, granting him the Ilok estate and surrounding lands and other privileges for merit in wars against the Ottomans.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.initial_owner: The Odescalchi family, owners of Ilok Manor
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.method_for_datation: Information about the work is due to the research of the Italian art historian, A. Bachi, an expert in Roman Baroque sculpture.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.provenance: Artworks including *Prince Livio Odescalchi* were moved to the newly formed Ilok City Museum in 1952, which transferred to Odescalchi Manor in 1968.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.obtention: Up until World War II, the Odescalchis owned Ilok Manor. As state property, it had several different uses but after refurbishment in 1968, it became a museum and this bust and other objects from the Odescalchi estate became part of the new permanent collection.

8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.author: Nela Tarbuk

8c4762e1-5805-5789-8cac-3fcdc7d7a021.name: *Portrait of a Sculptor – Gottfried Fritsch*
8c4762e1-5805-5789-8cac-3fcdc7d7a021.description:
A slightly stooped male half-figure emerges from a dark background, in which the viewer can make out roughly worked stones. While his expressive look scans the viewer, the man, holding a pair of compasses in his left hand, leans against a sculpture in progress representing a human figure. The clothes (a casually open shirt, fur hat), the statue and the tool are attributes that characterise the person depicted as an artist-sculptor. The lower section of the picture has probably been cut off at some point: the sculptor's fingers touch the canvas edge and the palm of the statue surfaces suddenly at the bottom-right of the trunk, without logical connection.  
The composition is diagonally balanced; the light accents of the white shirt and the body are supplemented by the colour contrast of the green coat and its pink lining.  
During the Baroque period artists were frequently represented as art connoisseurs, collectors of antiques and court artists with characteristic attributes, whereas before they had been regarded as mere craftsmen.  
Gottfried Fritsch (1706–1750), the last classical Baroque sculptor in Moravia, is depicted as a *virtuosus quondam statuarius*, a learned artist. The picture comes from the Tovačov chateau, owned by the Petřvaldskýs of Petřvald in the 18th century. Count Amand Antonín oversaw from Tovačov a demesne in which he initiated important artistic activities. Among other things, he enabled Fritsch to study sculpture in Vienna and Italy. The sculptor decorated the Petřvaldskýs' graveyard in Střílky.  
Franz Anton Palko, who also worked as a painter for the Bishop of Olomouc, stayed in Brno where he created the altarpiece for the parish Church of St. James. František Vavřinec Korompay, a renowned artist, was one of his students. Palko's benefactors and patrons included Count Wenzel Anton Kaunitz-Rietberg, State Chancellor of the Habsburg monarchy. The count particularly admired the artist's “French” portrait style.
8c4762e1-5805-5789-8cac-3fcdc7d7a021.short_description: The picture represents “a learned artist”, a sculptor-virtuoso. The “French-style” portrait was created for the Lord of Petřvald, a significant supporter of the arts. The painter was one of the most acknowledged portraitists of the period and was also active in the imperial court in Vienna.
8c4762e1-5805-5789-8cac-3fcdc7d7a021.initial_owner: Amand Anton Petřvaldský of Petřvald, Střílky
8c4762e1-5805-5789-8cac-3fcdc7d7a021.method_for_datation: The high quality of the picture, its colour scheme and layout invite comparison with *Portrait of Father* from 1746 (Belvedere, Wien), *Self-portrait with a Broad-brimmed Hat* and *Portrait of Count* *Unwerth* (Szépművészeti Múzeum, Budapest).
8c4762e1-5805-5789-8cac-3fcdc7d7a021.obtention: An inventory made after Amand Petřvaldský of Petřvald's death in 1762 contains and entry: *Porträt den Bildhauer Fritsch vorstellend, in einem Rahme*. The picture was originally found in Střílky Chateau and later in Tovačov Chateau; it then became the property of the Künburgs. In 1946 it became part of the picture collection at Brno Museum. It has been in the Moravian Gallery, Brno since 1961.

8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.name: Old Residence Theatre
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.description: Red and gold characterise the horseshoe-shaped theatre, whose sculptural decoration is an impressive abundance of shapes as well as floral and highly symbolic figural elements, as for example, the herms, which personify the seasons. The large Electors’ box, flanked in each case by 28 boxes on four tiers, soars above the entrance opposite the stage. The artistic design of the tiers reflects the respective class of the audience according to courtly absolutism. Therefore, the ground-floor boxes of the city nobility have simple ornamentation; the first tier of the high nobility, on the contrary, is decorated with splendid adornments such as carved red draperies on the balustrade and figural supports. Balustrade-reliefs and cartouches adorn the second tier for the lower nobility and the third tier for court officials. In accordance with contemporary taste the boundaries between the proscenium and the reality of the auditorium and the performance are blurred.
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.short_description: The opera house of the city residence of the Bavarian Electors, known as Cuvilliés Theatre, is considered to be exemplary among courtly Bavarian Rococo buildings. Construction began in 1751 to the plans of the Paris-trained architectect François Cuvilliés the Elder, on behalf of Elector Max III Joseph. The capricious wooden carved French-style rocaille adornments of the boxes deserve particular mention, as does the technical distinction of the former liftable orchestral pit.
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.location: Munich historic centre, Munich Residenz, Upper Bavaria
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.bibliography:
Heym, S., “Kurfürst Max III. Joseph”, *Die Münchner Residenz. Geschichte – Zerstörung – Wiederaufbau* (ed. K Faltlhauser), Ostfildern 2006, pp. 86–95.  
Meitinger, O., “Der Wiederaufbau des Cuvilliés-Theaters (Altes Residenztheater)”, *Die Münchner Residenz. Geschichte – Zerstörung – Wiederaufbau* (ed. K. Faltlhauser), Ostfildern 2006, pp. 215–23.  
Brunner, H., *Altes Residenztheater München. Amtlicher Führer*, Munich 1997.  
Heym, S., *Das Alte Residenztheater, Cuvilliés-Theater in München*, Munich 1995.
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.history: Following the fire at the Elector’s residence in 1750, François de Cuvilliés the Elder was put in charge of drawing up the plans for a “new opera house”. The cornerstone was laid in 1751, and in the presence of Elector Max III Joseph, the theatre opened in 1753. His successor, Elector Karl Theodor then had the opera house extended in accordance with contemporary concepts of theatre design, thereby making it accessible to larger audiences. As a protection measure during World War II the Rococo-furnishings were removed and put into storage until 1943. Both stage and auditorium were destroyed in 1944. The theatre was reconstructed by 1956 but not on the same site. It is now located at the so-called *Apothekenstock* (Apothecary block) of the residence.
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.patrons: Elector Max III Joseph of Bavaria (r. 1745–1777)
8d201913-9b63-5da3-b54b-6ea89a835960.architects: Architectural concept: François de Cuvilliés the Elder (1695–1786); head of construction: Leonhard Matthäus Gießl (1707–1785), François de Cuvilliés the Younger (1731–1777), Carl Albert von Lespilliez (1723–1796); stucco and former fresco: Johann Baptist Zimmermann (1680–1758); sculptures: Johann Baptist Straub (1704–1784) and workshop, Joachim Dietrich (1690–1735); joinery/ornamental carvings: Adam Pichler (c. 1690–1761); former stage construction: Giovanni Paolo Gaspari (1712–1775)

8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.name: St. Michael Archangel
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.description:
This statue was made for the library of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, near Bologna, and dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna but mainly worked in Rome after 1625. In the period of the full flourishing of baroque art he became the main interpreter of classicizing sculpture.  
In this bronze group depicting the struggle between St. Michael and the devil, Algardi leaves aside his usual stylistic moderation. The rhythm is frantic and agitated: the angel is tense as he strikes his final blow; the clothes hang to his legs, while his face and breast keep their beauty unchanged. The sculpture is influenced by the painting of the same subject painted by Guido Reni for the Roman church of S. Maria della Concezione. Compared with the airy elegance of the painting the sculpture appears more rhetoric and forced.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.short_description: This statue was made for the library of the convent of San Michele in Bosco, near Bologna. It dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna, but after 1625 he worked mostly in Rome. The struggle between the archangel and the devil compelled the artist to abandon his usual controlled style. He adopted a more complex and violent rhythm, while continuing to look for ideal elegance and beauty.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.initial_owner: Convent of St. Michael in the wood
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.method_for_datation: In his *Vite de pittori, scultori et architetti moderni*, published in Rome in 1672, Giovanni Pietro Bellori notes that Algardi made for Taddeo Pepoli, abbot of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, a statue depicting St. Michael Archangel trampling over the Devil. The statue was to be exhibited in the library, financed and promoted by the same abbot.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.obtention: In 1799, when religious orders were suppressed, the Accademia Clementina took care of the statue, once in the library of the convent; in 1871 it was moved to the Museo Civico and since 1985 it has been exhibited in the Museo Civico Medievale.

8df53ce3-81e5-5c23-89d6-2324283cfe08.name: *Portrait of Provost Augustinus Aurelius*
8df53ce3-81e5-5c23-89d6-2324283cfe08.description: The composition is typical of portraits of High Church representatives. The provost of the Augustinian monastery in Šternberk is portrayed at the age of 50 sitting in an upholstered armchair with gilded carving, against a background of a green curtain and a decorative vase with the monastery's emblem. The shape and colours of the drapery create a dynamic spiral movement adding to the portrait's effect. Augustinus Aurelius is dressed in ceremonial clothing, a white soutane, white surplice and blue almuca, holding a blue cap in his left hand. The attributes of his position in the church also appear: a mitre, sceptre and a crucifix around his neck. With his right hand, the provost points to the plans for the Výšovice residence which was, together with the completion and decoration of the Šternberk Church, among the provost's major building enterprises where he favoured a plain classical style. The provost's diary has survived containing an entry on a performance given by the young Mozart in Brno in December 1767. The provost may have met Korompay on this occasion and commissioned him with the portrait. Although Korompay was a renowned portraitist in his time only a handful of portraits of this type have survived. The provost's portrait was inspired by František Antonín Palko, said to have been the artist's teacher. Korompay's craftsmanship is evident in the finely rendered lace of the attire and its ornamentation. Colour harmony, fine, light, modelling of shapes, and the rendering of the provost's soulful expression, manifest the skill of an artist obviously influenced by Martin Meytens's court portraits and French models.
8df53ce3-81e5-5c23-89d6-2324283cfe08.short_description: The composition is typical of portraits of High Church representatives. Colour harmony, fine, light, modelling of shapes, and the rendering of the provost’s expression, manifest the skill of an artist obviously influenced by the court portraits of František Antonín Palko and Martin Meytens.
8df53ce3-81e5-5c23-89d6-2324283cfe08.method_for_datation: The picture is marked on the reverse: *Reverendissmus et amplissimus Dominus Aurelius Augustin, natus 18 Januari 1719, electus die 16. Nov. 1757. Pictus Brunae Franc: Korompay Ao 1768*. Within the painting: *Restitutio parochiae Veyschonvensis 1765* (on the sheet)*; Aet. 50* (on the vase).
8df53ce3-81e5-5c23-89d6-2324283cfe08.obtention: The picture, intended for the hall of an Augustinian residence in Výšovice, is on long-term loan to the Moravian Gallery, Brno.

8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.name: *Patrona Hungariae sending St. Michael to Fight Against the Turks*
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.description:
In 1739, the Catholic convent in Sopron commissioned Martino Altomonte – a first-generation member of the Austrian High Baroque – to paint a picture for the high altar in St. Michael's Church. He passed the commission onto his son and collaborator, Bartolomeo. The Altomontes, who specialised in large church paintings, historical and triumphal compositions and frescoes, worked in the Italian Baroque tradition. Martino, although of Tyrolean stock, was born in Naples. He used an Italian version of his real name, Hohenberg, and first used his assumed name at the Polish court, where he painted compositions about the hereditary rulers. Later he was active in Vienna. His son, Bartolomeo, was a pupil of Solimena in Naples for two years.  
The vast altarpiece for Sopron echoes one of Francesco Solimena's (d. 1747) most popular creations, the fresco he painted in the San Domenico Maggiore in Naples in 1709. Bartolomeo continued to make use of details from Solimena's repertoire in his other works representing the Holy Trinity, St. Dominic with other saints, and the defeated heretics.  
In this picture, he adapted the subject to meet the wishes of his employers. The Virgin is represented as the patron saint of Hungary (indicated by the Hungarian coat of arms below her right hand), and the defeated are depicted as Turks wearing clothes and arms painted with pedantic accuracy. The impressive multi-coloured altarpiece, painted in the last years of the so-called Balkan campaign, illustrated for the faithful their release from Turkish rule – by then gradually becoming a reality – a notion suggested in the lower part of the picture by a battle scene, in the upper part by celestial rejoicing.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.short_description: In 1739, the Catholic convent in Sopron commissioned Martino Altomonte to paint a picture for the high altar in St. Michael's Church. He gave the commission to his son, Bartolomeo. Although this large altarpiece borrows motifs from Bartolomeo's teacher, Francesco Solimena's, painting in Naples the subject matter has a Hungarian actuality.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.method_for_datation: Through archive data, the signature and analysis of motifs.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.obtention: On loan to the Hungarian National Gallery from the Roman Catholic Parish Church, Sopron.

8eae54be-a311-5baa-9827-cbd83ce0a66a.name: Court and Theatine Church of St. Cajetan
8eae54be-a311-5baa-9827-cbd83ce0a66a.description:
The Theatine church dominates Munich’s Old Town with its two towers and two-level facade. Various statues of saints relevant to the church stand in the façade niches: Cajetan, as founder of the Theatine order and the patron saints of the founding family of Maximilian, Ferdinand and Adelheid, all of which are designed by Ignaz Günther. Above the main portal there is a dedication inscription, and above this the triangular gable bears the coat-of-arms of the Bavarian–Saxon alliance crowned by the so-called Theatine Cross. Two towers with octagonal helm-roofs and volutes adorn the front of the church.  
Based on a relatively simple ground plan in crucifix form, the interior has an arrangement similar to the order’s Mater Ecclesia S. Andrea della Valle in Rome. The inner façade mirrors the younger outer one with coat-of-arms and dedication inscription. The impression of grandeur and vastness of space is created by the opulent, colossal columns which fit perfectly the courtly taste for splendour. White stucco dominates the interior of the church and shows an abundance of floral and figural forms. The three-bayed nave and the connected domed side-chapels are illuminated by light from the clerestory and the light that filters in through the large main dome, which, resting on a tambour above the crossing, is separated from the nave and transept by four arches. The highpoints of the interior are the three monumental main altars in the choir and transept, both of which are crowned by stucco figures. Pairs of torsional columns bring about conceptual unity while at the same time professing to the Catholic confession of St. Peter’s Church in Rome.
8eae54be-a311-5baa-9827-cbd83ce0a66a.short_description: The Theatine Church is a landmark of “Odeonsplatz” in Munich due to its unique yellow colour and monumental appearance. Built as a votive church by the Elector and his wife to celebrate the birth of crown prince Max II Emanuel, the white-stucco interior which is lavishly decorated and has splendorous columns, is overwhelming. With its tambour cupola pointing towards Rome the Theatine Church is an example of the Italian High Baroque in Bavaria, which really became established after the end of the Thirty Years’ War.
8eae54be-a311-5baa-9827-cbd83ce0a66a.method_for_datation: Inscriptions above the main portal and inside the church

8eae54be-a311-5baa-9827-cbd83ce0a66a.history:
The ruling couple of Bavaria commissioned the church in honour of the long-awaited birth of crown prince Max II Emanuel in 1662. Agostino Barelli was responsible for the design of the votive church and Enrico Zuccalli worked as construction supervisor.  
Bavarian Elector Ferdinand Maria attended the ceremony where the cornerstone was laid on 29 April 1663. Work on the main dome began in 1674, followed by consecration to celebrate the thirteenth birthday of the young crown prince in 1675; the dome was not completed until 1690.  
François de Cuvilliés the Elder designed the façade of 1765–68 on behalf of the Elector Max III. The Theatine Church got its current characteristic colouring in 1860.

8eb3dd19-e7f3-5304-999c-aa03dcd16789.name: Milotice Chateau
8eb3dd19-e7f3-5304-999c-aa03dcd16789.description: A four-wing, two-storey chateau with corner towers. A moat, a wall with bastions, arcades and vaults on the ground floor have survived from the former Renaissance chateau. Above the garden parterre is a terrace with a two-shouldered staircase and an entrance to the main rectangular hall – the large summer room – lit by the large bay windows. The *sala terrena* is below the staircase. Part of the original art collection is preserved in the chateau, chiefly paintings by J. F. Adolf, together with various items of furniture and porcelain from the 18th and 19th centuries. The countess's study, with original canvas wallpaper, is among a few rooms to survive intact. The chateau is adjoined by a “French Baroque garden” with a central pavilion (1766), an English park, two conservatories with a display of Moravian Baroque sculpture and a vast pheasantry.
8eb3dd19-e7f3-5304-999c-aa03dcd16789.short_description: The layout of the four-wing chateau with corner towers was dictated by a previous Renaissance building. Its reconstruction in the “Danubian style” was carried out by a local master builder, while its decoration involved artists from Brno and Vienna as well as Italian stucco specialists. The impressive entrance consists of sculpted decorations, introducing the main concept of the building: the celebration and mythologization of the investor’s family. The subject of the wall and the ceiling frescos is the triumph of the imperial army in the struggle against the Turks at the turn of the 17th century.
8eb3dd19-e7f3-5304-999c-aa03dcd16789.method_for_datation: The chateau was constructed between 1586 and 1596, when the demesne was owned by Bernard Ludvík Tovar of Enczesfeld. Designs for the garden (1716), chateau, the sculpted decoration and the paintings on the staircase are documented in contracts. The fresco in the main hall is signed and dated; dates are also found on the portal (1722) and the ledge of the balcony on the first floor (1743). Receipts for the interior decoration from 1744–1745 have also survived.

8eb3dd19-e7f3-5304-999c-aa03dcd16789.history: A late-medieval fortress surrounded by a moat, and a major Hussite centre during the Hussite wars, it was converted into a four-wing Renaissance chateau that dictated the layout of Milotice Chateau. The chateau has been owned by some prominent families: the Žerotíns, Zástřizlys, and Valdštejns. In 1648 the demesne was purchased by the provincial governor Gabriel Serényi. It has been subject to catastrophic fires twice, in 1663 and 1705. It was probably reconstructed, “Danubian style”, by F. B. Klíčník, a local master builder.

8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.name: *Portrait of Tommaso Campeggi and his Family*
8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.description:
This painting formerly credited to the Lombard painter Pier Francesco Cittadini, has been recently reattributed to the Bolognese painter Lorenzo Pasinelli (1998). The portrait is characterised by the presence of such Nordic elements as the dark background and the analytical description of the 12 people. Pasinelli probably painted the great canvas during his stay in Rome, as a present for his host Tommaso Campeggi, the ambassador of Bologna to the Holy See. In 1666 it was moved to the palace owned by Tommaso Campeggi in via San Mamolo, in Bologna. When the house was sold the picture was moved to the residence of “Strà San Donato” and finally to the castle of Dozza, the Campeggi country residence.  
It is one of the rare examples of group portraits in Bolognese baroque painting. The impression is that of an austere and somewhat provincial aristocracy. They are not concerned with being carefully examined by the painter and only interested in portraiture for its social implications. The family is sitting in the traditional scheme, following a hierarchical order and rigidly divided in two groups, males and females. The first born is given central position, next to his sisters who are holding his gloves. Tommaso is the most static and affected figure with rigid authoritarianism, whilst the elegance of the clothes is more emphasized in the female figures.
8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.short_description: The painting depicts the entire Campeggi family. The result is a perfectly balanced mixture of Bolognese and northern features combined with compositional and technical skill.

8f46d6d0-5d30-5f67-bdeb-b7f85e029705.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Cape Espichel
8f46d6d0-5d30-5f67-bdeb-b7f85e029705.alternate_name: Santuário de Nossa Senhora do Cabo; Santuário de Nossa Senhora da Pedra Mua
8f46d6d0-5d30-5f67-bdeb-b7f85e029705.description:
The sanctuary is located at the top of Cape Espichel. It has a U-shaped floor plan due to the pilgrim's lodging houses which formed a square. The houses are decked with continuous arcades and are very simply built, typical of the traditional architecture of the Lisbon and Setúbal Peninsulas. Centred at the far west-end of the square is Our Lady of the Cape Church.  
The church has a single, clear nave with two pulpits in the middle of it. Due to the design it can be attributed to João Antunes, architect of the Casa do Infantado nearby. The church was likely to have been commissioned by the Infant Francisco, King João V's brother and head of the brotherhood of Our Lady of the Cape. There is a large cross at the opposite end of the church, on the axis of the square. Continuing along this axis, the aqueduct meets the water house to supply the sanctuary with water. The water house is a hexagonal-shaped building with one door. It is equipped with an undulating dome and crowned with a lantern. Its construction dates to 1770, and was the initiative of King José I after he had stayed at the court of the sanctuary. At the same time, between 1760 and 1770, the sanctuary's infrastructure was improved with the construction of kitchens, an oven and wood store, stables, a water tank and an “opera house” – a small theatre with dressing rooms and a backstage area, which today is completely dilapidated.  
Separate from this group of buildings, is the Memory Hermitage, found near to where the sanctuary was founded. The building is cubic in form with a smooth reverse ogee dome. Despite not knowing the date of its construction it was probably rebuilt in the 17th century. It is decorated with 18th-century *azulejos,* depicting the legend of the Miraculous Finding of the Image of Our Lady at the site.
8f46d6d0-5d30-5f67-bdeb-b7f85e029705.short_description: The origins of the cult date to the 15th century; most of the buildings date to the 17th and 18th centuries. A pilgrimage sanctuary with a U-shaped floor plan, it was created around pilgrim’s lodging houses that formed a square. The respective church, to which the lodging houses belonged, was at the far end of the square.
8f46d6d0-5d30-5f67-bdeb-b7f85e029705.bibliography:
Romariz, C., Carvalho, A. M. Galopim de, “Formações margoglauconíticas do Miocénico superior a norte do Cabo Espichel”, *Boletim da Sociedade Geológica de Portugal*, Vol. XIV, Fasc. I. Lisbon, 1961.  
Carvalho, A. Ayres de, *D. João V e a arte do seu tempo*, 2, Lisbon, 1962.  
Ribeiro, O., *A Arrábida, Esboço Geográfico*, Câmara Municipal de Sesimbra, Sesimbra, 1986.  
Serrão, E. da Cunha, Serrão, V., *Sesimbra Monumental e Artística*, Sesimbra, 1986.
8f46d6d0-5d30-5f67-bdeb-b7f85e029705.history:
The origins of the cult performed at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Cape Espichel dates to the 15th century. Most of the buildings centre about the sanctuary, except for the Memory Hermitage, also known as Nossa Senhora da Pedra Mua Hermitage. The sanctuary and its associated buildings date to the 17th and 18th centuries, a period of pilgrimage which received royal attention and protection, especially during the reign of King José I.  
The origins of the sanctuary are connected to a legend, which relates that two elderly people – one from Caparica (on the south bank of the River Tagus) and another from Alcabideche (near Cascais) – dreamed about Our Lady appearing on top of the cliffs of Cape Pedra Mua riding a gigantic she-mule. Inspired by their dream they followed their calling and met at the top of the promontory where they found the miraculous image of Our Lady. The footprints of the she-mule left on the stones of the promontory continue to bear witness to the veracity of the legend, although in reality these are footprints of two types of dinosaur (one being the largest footprint of this type).

8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.name: Catholic Guild Church of St. Joseph
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.alternate_name: Church of the Brotherhood of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph for Craftsmen
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.description: The church is composed of two storeys. While the crypt is formed of two octagonal crypt chapels – a simplification of Herkomer’s plan for a holy sepulchre – the upper storey is composed of two simple quadratic spatial components for nave and choir. The centralised design is underlined by rounded corners. The powerfully built arcade-above-pilaster piers clearly divide the two sections, while reuniting the two in the overall prospect. Sweeping, erect proportions and bold accents lend the building qualities that clearly extend beyond that of a country chapel.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.short_description: St. Joseph’s in Bichlbach is the only surviving guild church in Austria. This is its primary significance, as opposed to its architectural and artistic qualities. The exterior of the church located on a hill above the village is plain, but however the interior of the centralised hall building with lightly slanted corners and adjoining choir, displays architectural ambition and charm. Here the spatial impression is completely dominated by the mighty high altar.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.method_for_datation: Founding charter of the guild from Emperor Leopold I with the plans from Herkomer, issued in 1694.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.bibliography: Dussler, H., *Der Allgäuer Barockbaumeister Johann Jakob Herkomer*, Kempten 1956, pp. 71–4.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.history: The origin of St. Joseph’s is directly connected to the social conditions in Außerfern. In summer there was virtually no work for the craftsmen who were thus forced to take to the road as journeymen. Church services, held on their departure and return, were celebrated together in the guild church. The brotherhood under the patronage of St. Joseph, the patron saint of craftsmen, was founded by the parish priest Lukas Egger in 1690 (certified by Emperor Leopold I in 1694). The founding charter already contained initial plans for the church building drawn up by Herkomer, master builder of Füssen, however their execution was delayed. The building was finally begun in 1710 according to new plans and was largely completed in the space of two years. The consecration did not take place until 1726.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.patrons: Parish Priest Lukas Egger/Guild of Masons and Carpenters

8f66553f-e1b0-520b-9337-b61ebdf1701d.name: *St. Gertrude*
8f66553f-e1b0-520b-9337-b61ebdf1701d.description:
St. Gertrude (626–659) was the daughter of Pepin I of Landen, the Prefect of the Palace of the Merovingian King Dagobert I of Austrasia. She was abbess of the Monastery of Nivelles (today in Belgium) founded by her mother Saint Itta of Aquitania. St. Gertrude is presented as a noble and independent woman who refused to marry because she wanted to be a nun. She devoted her life to the study of the Holy Scriptures and collaborated with the Irish saints Foillan and Ultan to assist the needy and promote Evangelisation.  
The Monastery of Arouca commissioned Jacinto Vieira to make a set of limestone sculptures of male Benedictine saints for the nave and a set of female saints for the choir, all of which were particularly venerated by the Cistercian Order. Almost unknown, Jacinto Vieira belonged to a group of Northern Portuguese sculptors, who, during the reign of King João V, sought to combine the national Portuguese aesthetics typical of the 17th century with the Italian aesthetic peculiar to the erudite Roman Baroque. Mainly an expert in sculpture in wood, Vieira managed to adapt his mastery in wood, acquired in the saint-making workshops, to stone sculpture.  
This image of St. Gertrude depicts her with an abbess' crosier and a medallion surrounded by a *gloria luminosa* filled with an inflamed heart with Baby Jesus, following the iconographic canons of the day and the austerity of the Cistercians. St. Gertrude stands out due to the elegance of her gesture, her contemplative facial expression and her mystical aura over the other nuns, all of them dressed with delicate pleated garments and habits with enormous sleeves, which are the main features of this set of sculptures.
8f66553f-e1b0-520b-9337-b61ebdf1701d.short_description: St. Gertrude was canonised in 1677 and is an emblematic character both of the Benedictine and Cistercian orders. *St. Gertrude* is one of a set of stone sculptures from the Monastery of Arouca depicting the saints worshipped by the Cistercian Order to enhance their role in promoting the Teachings of Christ according to the Counter-Reformation.
