90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.name: *The Kiss of Judas*
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.description:
The sculpture represents a scene from the Gospel of St. Matthew (26:49) when Judas, one of the apostles, marks Christ with a kiss as the man who should be arrested and tried. As in the sculptures featuring Christ parting with Mary in the Heiligenkreuz Monastery Museum, Austria, and in the Bratislava City Museum, Slovakia, in *The Kiss of Judas* Giuliani concentrates – in the encounter of two figures – on the motif of instant motion typical of the work of Giovanni Bernini, a key baroque sculptor. The dramatic subject of Judas's treason is conveyed by means of the medium as a contrast in the approach to both figures: the figure of Christ is self-absorbed, resigned to his fate, characterised by calm gestures and static drapery flowing in large forms, while Judas approaches Christ in an expressively captured haste which the sculptor has portrayed, aside from Judas's step forward, by a dramatic gesture extended into space, as well as by Judas's clothes floating around the body as if blowing in a wind.  
The sculpture is unique, in that no associates or assistants participated in its creation, as was the case with Giuliani's sizeable works.  
Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice, and later in Munich under Andreas II Faistenberger. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy, in Moravia for the Kounics (Slavkov) and many times for the Liechtensteins (Lednice).
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.short_description: The sculpture depicting a dramatic scene of treason from the Gospel of St. Matthew exemplifies a typical baroque motif of instant motion. Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice and later in Munich. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy in Austria and Moravia.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.method_for_datation: The overall approach to shape in the figures is classic Giuliani. His authorship is confirmed by the execution of the faces as well as by the softly modelled and finely executed drapery of both figures, which complement not only the form but also become major interpretational elements of the content.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.obtention: The sculpture became part of the museum’s collections before 1962; its provenance is unknown.

90e620af-4d11-5f42-a4a6-000de55134c6.name: Illusionist Collages to be deciphered obliquely
90e620af-4d11-5f42-a4a6-000de55134c6.description: Two pictures made from coloured paper strips, exactingly juxtaposed and glued in successive layers, and strategically placed to allow different images to appear from distinct angles. Both pictures, which once belonged to the Cabinet of Physics of the Colégio de Nobres were used to illustrate visual effects. A seated young boy playing cards and a man laughing can be seen in one picture. In the other picture one of three images can be observed in succession from different angles: a woman playing a fife, a boy sitting at a table feeding his dog and an old usurer. Both pictures are framed in black painted wood, ornamented with gold motifs and protected with a glass. The set can be removed from the frame by opening a side lock and pulling a ring-pull.
90e620af-4d11-5f42-a4a6-000de55134c6.short_description: Two pictures that when observed from different angles change to another image are an example of optical phenomena of 18th-century physics. In one of the pictures two images appear and in the other three images are discerned.

90e620af-4d11-5f42-a4a6-000de55134c6.method_for_datation: These two pictures are mentioned in an inventory of the Colégio de Nobres’, undated. They were probably executed between 1766 and 1768.
90e620af-4d11-5f42-a4a6-000de55134c6.obtention: These pictures once belonged to the Cabinet of Physics of the Colégio de Nobres in Lisbon and were transferred to the University of Coimbra in 1773.

90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.name: Catholic Collegiate Church of St. Lawrence and St. Stephen
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.description: The building is composed of three nave and two choir bays without transept. The space’s uniform appearance is largely due to the barrel vault extending along its entire length and the uniform sequence of aisles. Here, drawing on early North Alpine Jesuit buildings, the Italian scheme of a hall with side aisles has been executed in the form of a pilaster construction. During the course of the stuccowork the entablature, which originally extended over the side chapels, was restricted to the choir-loft parapets. Above this transverse, barrels cut into the main vault. As a result of the choir lofts at entablature height the interior still echoes with the closed atmosphere of an Italian-style hall with side aisles. Although the interior design originates from two phases, the overall impression is one of great uniformity.
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.short_description: The Wilten collegiate church is one of the first large longitudinal buildings built in the German-speaking region following the Thirty Years’ War. Although the architecture and fittings originate from two different periods, the interior presents a uniform appearance. The strict sequence of altars from the first Early Baroque period of interior design work, framed in gold and black, contrast with the fresco panels from the second phase with their bold colours, framed by heavy Italian ceiling stucco.
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.dates: 1651–1667: new Baroque building; 1713–1719: façade; 1702/03: stuccowork; 1702–1707: ceiling paintings; 1665: altars (1767/68 altered)
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.bibliography:
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 31f.

90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.history: According to records the first church in Wilten dedicated to St. Lawrence dates back to the 6th century. According to legend the monastery was founded in 878 by the giant Haymon. Conferred on the Premonstratensians in 1138, consecration of the collegiate church took place in 1201. Rebuilt in 1288 following a fire, the collapse of a tower in 1644, which severely damaged the church, resulted in the new Baroque building (1651–77). The façade as well as the frescos and stucco ornamentation originate from the early 18th century, further modifications took place in the mid-, i.e. second half of the 18th century. From 1946 to 1956 restoration work repaired war damage from 1944.

914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.name: *St. Jerome*
914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.description:
The painting is signed (FED.BAROCIUS/URB. as PING. at) and first appears in the inventory of the Scipione Borghese collection in 1693. No details of the commissioning and dating of the work are known, but stylistic considerations allow us to place it in the final decades of the 16th century. This dating is close to his other painting in the Borghese Collection, *Aeneas' Flight from Troy* (inv.68) of 1598. Indeed the figure of the aged Anchises appears to be the same as the figure of St. Jerome, here intent on beating his chest with a stone.  
Federico Barocci, a renowned portraitist, was one of the most esteemed painters in Counter-Reformation Rome, and worked for the new religious congregations such as the Congregation of the Oratory founded by St. Philip Neri at the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella, and older orders such as the Dominicans at the Church of Santa Maria Sopra Minerva.  
This small painting, probably for popular worship, shows the saint in a cave, barely illuminated by the light of a candle in his lantern, cleverly placed along the right edge of the painting so as to direct the ray of light only on to the figure of the protagonist. His gaze, full of the spirituality that was a key feature of the great Urbino artist's paintings, is directed towards the face of Jesus nailed to the cross that he holds in his hand. Beside him lie objects of study and meditation: book, skull and hourglass, as well as the cardinal's hat that, along with the red cape around his body, recall the important role the saint played in the Church: translator of the Biblical texts (the *Vulgate*).  
The most recent restoration work carried out reveals a lion, from whose paw Jerome removed a thorn, sleeping like a cat in the background, indicating its absolute submission. Behind an opening in the rock, barely illuminated by the moonlight, is the Ducal Palace of Urbino, the artist's city of birth and probably where the work was painted.
914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.short_description: The painting, which in the background has the Ducal Palace of Urbino, the birthplace of the artist, shows St. Jerome a protagonist of the first cardinals of the church. He strikes his chest with a stone. The saint is in the dark, the only light coming from a small lamp. Lighting is part of the repertoire of the great Baroque era.
914d504a-f1d9-547d-a104-0080ce3a5c65.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.name: *The Baptism of St. Augustine*
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.description:
The picture depicts the baptism of St. Augustine (354–430), together with his son Adeodat, by St. Ambrosius. Augustine, one of the Church Fathers and Bishop of Milan, influenced Christian doctrine from the Middle Ages to modern times with his writing.  
The base of the font is a beehive, a symbol of the church and an Augustine attribute. This picture was a template for a high altar painting in Jevíčko Church, commissioned by the Abbot of the Augustinian Monastery in Brno. It shares a number of motifs with *The Baptism of Prince Bořivoj* (Svatopluk?) by Josef Winterhalder Jr. (Silesian Provincial Museum, Opava). For example, drapery hangs in the foreground and columns form a vista into the temple space, with segmentation and illumination provided by a row of windows. The main light source in both pictures enters the scene through the vault to accentuate the central figurative motif, and although light is a unifying factor for both artists, for Havelka, it is assigned a different role. There are also similarities in the figurative aspects of both paintings, such as the standing and kneeling male figures in the foreground.  
These analogies may be explained either by a joint model (a print) from which both artists derived their motifs or by the fact that Havelka drew inspiration from J. Winterhalder Jr. The latter speculation is supported by the colour scheme of this design; silver-white and cold blue, colours that are not found in the rest of Havelka's oeuvre.  
The Museum of South Moravia in Znojmo holds another smaller version of Havelka's *Baptism of St. Augustine*. The Znojmo picture probably preceded the Brno design as its style appears more spontaneous and it is composed as a rectangle.  
Some of Havelka's pictures indicate that he was familiar with the work of F. A. Maulbertsch and J. W. Bergl, whose paintings were known in Havelka's native region. Similar compositions can be found in the work of C. Carlone and F. J. Spiegler (Merdingen).
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.short_description: St. Augustine, one of the Church Fathers, together with his son Adeodat, are baptised by St. Ambrosius. This is a template for a high altar piece in Jevíčko Church. Havelka’s style indicates that he was familiar with the work of both F.A. Maulbertsch and J.W. Bergl.
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.method_for_datation: J. I. Havelka’s authorship is illustrated by some of the figurative types, the light, sharp, segmented and vivid brushstrokes and the impasto application of white with a half-dry brush on the drapery crest. This attribution is confirmed by the transfer of the exhibited model into a larger format for the altar in the Jevíčko Church. The picture is ascribed to Havelka in both archive sources and in 19th-century literature.
91dd3f61-5c6d-56ac-a627-29e49ab8fc08.obtention: The picture is on long-term loan from the Augustinian Abbey, Old Brno, which between 1956 and 1993 was administered by the Moravian Gallery, Brno.

91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.name: Águas Livres Aqueduct
91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.description: The aqueduct has three main parts: the Mãe d'Água reservoirs located near the spring at the beginning of the course in the Carenque valley; the aqueduct and its secondary aqueducts spreading out around the city with a total length of 58.135 km. The system includes arches over the Alcântara valley. These are 941 m in length with an ensemble of 35 arches of which 14 are pointed and 21 are round. The ultimate destination of the Águas Livres aqueduct is the Mãe d'Água reservoir delivering water to the city. The reservoir is a wide, vaulted construction with an approximate capacity of 5,500 m3. The formal structure is perfectly justifiable for a work of this nature, which demands various materials and rational engineering. The incredible height of the rises of the Aqueduct's arches in the Alcântara valley is astonishing. The technical audacity is largely due to the Custódio Vieira's knowledge of engineering. The aqueduct pays homage to Roman models as it is imposingly “imperial” in its monumentality and even in its geographic position. The scarce ornamentation of Mãe d'Água das Amoreiras reservoir is compensated by the scale of the work and imposition of the vast stripped and solemn walls, as if the building was in fact a temple of the waters.
91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.short_description: An aqueduct using a classic system of gravity to capture, conduct and distribute water to the city of Lisbon. An open-air structure, it is mainly known for its monumental pointed arches over the Alcântara valley. There are also the underground galleries, the Mãe d'Água reservoir, and other springs dotted throughout its course. The main, oldest spring is located in the municipality of Sintra, which is endowed with adjacent works, canals and fountains.

91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.history: At the beginning of João V's reign, the water supply in Lisbon was at a critically low state so in 1723, in an attempt to overcome the problem, Claudio do Amaral (attorney of west Lisbon) proposed that a study should be carried out on the spring at the Belas Águas Livres. He hoped that the study would allow water from the Belas Águas Livres to be channelled via an aqueduct into Lisbon. The king supported this decision and granted the means necessary to fund the aqueduct such as, in 1729, imposing a tax on the sale of certain goods entering the city (meat, wine, straw, olive oil and salt). Work began on the aqueduct in 1731 and, although construction didn't finish until approximately 1799, water was first channelled by the structure to Lisbon in 1744.

92161025-78e1-5830-b62b-9297166e8c90.name: Santuario della Beata Vergine di San Luca
92161025-78e1-5830-b62b-9297166e8c90.description: Starting from the project made by Sacchi, Dotti’s drawings provided an elliptic plan, completed by a high chapel covered by a great dome. Most important Dotti thought of a very ingenious and startling connection of the body of the church and the last section of the portico accompanying the faithful from the city. The main façade is linked to the covered route through a sort of tribune while another one is symmetrically repeated on the other side of the front giving way to the exit. There is also a place for resting after the effort of climbing the hill which opens towards the sky, encouraging meditation and prayer before entering into the sacred space of the church.
92161025-78e1-5830-b62b-9297166e8c90.short_description: Located upon the so called hill ‘della Guardia’ (“of the guard”), in the outskirts of Bologna, the shrine is dedicated to the Virgin, in particular to a miraculous painting of a Madonna with child attributed to St. Luke’s brush. A place of special worship for the Bolognese people, this religious complex is characterised by the harmonious connection between architecture and landscape: the soft bends  seem to be inspired not only by the sinuosity (due to the site orography) of the covered route (a portico) leading to the place but are also in relation with the circular and linear structure of the main building.
92161025-78e1-5830-b62b-9297166e8c90.bibliography:
Matteucci, A.M., *Carlo Francesco Dotti e l'architettura bolognese del Settecento*, Bologna, 1969, pp. 73-99.

92161025-78e1-5830-b62b-9297166e8c90.history:
In 1680, Cardinal Lazzaro Pallavicino bequest some money to build a new altar for the miraculous painting of the Virgin still preserved in the old church. It was realised in 1696 in the shape of a modern chapel. In this same year, refurbishing work was made enlarging the church, so that when the new chapel was finished (1713) the church appeared too poor and indecorous. The architect G. Paolo Sacchi was charged to design a new building and his project was presented in 1717. Five years later the Swiss Carlo Francesco Dotti, a celebrated master builder, made a new project that was approved and finally built.  
The new shrine was consecrated in 1765.

9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.name: Blessing Christ Child
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.description: The Christ child giving his blessing might originally have been part of a Madonna with Child. Iconographically and with great certainty the polychrome figure can be identified as the Infant Jesus according to the effortless gesture of his right hand raised in blessing. The almost-nude child is apologetically dressed only with a gold-plated waistcloth across the right thigh, with his arms spread. Finest proportions and the effects from the flesh-tint result in one of the most brilliant small sculptures of Hans Degler and can be compared with his work *Mary and the Jesus Child* donated to the nearby village church of Weilheim-Unterhausen in 1621. Short curls of hair, some of them above the forehead, and the drapery of the waistcloth were typical of that time. The closed lips in the facial expression of the child underline the graveness with which he looks onto the world.
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.short_description: It is assumed that, originally, the sculpture was accompanied by the Virgin Mary on whose lap the Infant Jesus was once seated with his outstretched arms.
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis of Hans Degler’s work.

92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.name: Palazzo Poggi’s Observatory
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.description:
Built to easily view the entire night sky, the Observatory has an elevated and massive structure and is shaped like a tower. The upper part is located over a large terrace which is jutting out. On top, stands a large chamber with wide windows, rotated 90˚ from the axis of the tower below.  
It is known that the Observatory was modified by the architects with the help of many experts including learned scientists working at the Institute, such as Eustachio Manfredi.
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.short_description: Together with the anatomical theatre in the Palace of the Archiginnasio, the Observatory is the most important evidence of Bolognese scientific culture and activity during baroque age. Both were connected with places of learning: while the first was part of the so-called ‘studio’, the famous, local University, the second was created as part of the Eighteenth century Institute of Sciences and Arts, a very modern institution where, according with the project of the founder, the count and general Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, scientists and artists should have collaborated in researching and teaching.
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.bibliography:
Matteucci, A. M., *Carlo Francesco Dotti e l'architettura bolognese del Settecento*, Bologna, 1969, pp. 100-101.  
Lenzi, D., “Le trasformazioni settecentesche”, *Palazzo Poggi: da dimora aristocratica a sede dell'Università di Bologna* (ed. A. Ottani Cavina), Bologna, 1988, pp. 58-78.
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.history: The Observatory was created as part of the Institute of Sciences and Arts. The Institute, due to the farsighted outlook of its founder, Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, was composed of two academies. The first was devoted to scientific studies, while the second was intended for the teaching of the arts. At the beginning of the eighteenth century it became necessary to find an appropriate building to house the Institute. Among the requirements for a suitable building was the stability of the structure in order to erect an Observatory on the roof. The Academy purchased the sixteenth century palace owned by the cardinal Giovanni Poggi. The Observatory was started in 1712 under the direction of the architect Giovanni Battista Torri. After his death, the following year, Carlo Francesco Dotti, architect of the Observatory, modified the plan. The work was finished in 1725.

92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.name: *Still life with Fruits, Parrots and a White Cockatoo*
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.description: Jakab Bogdány left his native town, Eperjes (Prešov) in Upper Hungary, at a young age, going first to Vienna and then to Amsterdam where sources mention him in 1684, and where he may have pursued his studies. At any rate, Amsterdam, then the centre of middle-class genres, especially still life, was a perfect school for an artist just starting out. At first he painted flower and fruit pieces, which proved to be a lifelong experience for him, for the effect of the Dutch example remained discernible in this group of works throughout his life. Bogdány moved to London in 1688, and his technical expertise soon earned him fame among the English aristocracy. His most important clients were the royal family themselves. As a sign of both his artistic and social recognition, he gained English citizenship in 1700 and purchased an estate near London. He began to paint animal compositions, mainly exotic birds, designed for above doors or mantelpieces; most of these pictures are still in situ, found in their original settings in private collections in rural England. Influenced by the painter, Melchior de Hondecoeter, an outstanding Dutch master of bird paintings, Bogdány's are actually elegant genre pictures with exotic birds as actors against a background of elegant parks and classical buildings. He studied, and from the point of view of ornithology, accurately depicted, rare and colourful birds in the aviary at Windsor Park, which belonged to one of his main clients, Admiral George Churchill.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.short_description: Jakab Bogdány, born in Eperjes (Prešov), completed his studies in the Netherlands and became famous in England, becoming extremely popular with the English aristocracy. He was a master of the artistic form he practiced – still life paintings with birds – and worked for the royal family. The Hungarian state repurchased his splendid still life paintings with birds in the early 20th century.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and the date defined by stylistic analysis.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.obtention: Purchased from an English private collection in 1907; in the Museum of Fine Arts until 1974 and then transferred to the Hungarian National Gallery.

9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.name: *St. Onuphrius*
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.description:
José de Almeida, a highly important Portuguese sculptor of the Baroque period, made a qualitative leap that can be more easily explained by considering his career and his works that are extant. After studying in Rome under the patronage of King D. João V, he worked at Carlo Monaldi's atelier, and became a member of the St. Lucas Academy which awarded him several commissions. Returning to Lisbon he worked in stone but it was inconclusive due to qualitative irregularity. It is worth mentioning the following works: *St. John the Baptist* and *Queen St. Elizabeth* made for the Bemposta Palace chapel vestibule (finished by Barros Laborão); the *St. Paul* and the *St. Camillus de Lellis* for the porch and façades of the Necessidades Palace, together with his signed works, of which a fountain decorated by him is located in front of the Bemposta Palace chapel.  
His series of wooden Virgins include those at St. Mamede Church and the Old Church of Our Lady of Conception, and probably one at the Lady of the Rosary from the S. Domingo Church in Guimarães. Confusingly, they are attributed either to him or to Machado de Castro.  
Less known are the *The Steps of Passion* or *Processions*, a set of articulated and spindly figures from the brotherhood and the Church of Lady of Monte do Carmo in Lisbon. They exhibit remarkable modelling of the faces and hands, as well as perfect use of both plastic and luminous values, typical of someone with solid training. They represent the largest preserved sculptural cycle in wood made in the Almeida Workshop.  
*St. Onuphrius*, which aesthetically belongs to this group, is similar to sculptural representations of the previous century. The sculpture is made according to the aesthetic values of Roman sculpture while still retaining its Portuguese identity.
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.short_description: In his masterpiece, *St. Onuphrius*, José de Almeida demonstrates his skill in rendering human anatomy; his ability to manipulate light and imbue drama, seen in the clothing and in the details of the hair and beard.
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.initial_owner: Church of the Santíssima Trindade e Redenção dos Cativos, Lisbon
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.dimensions: H: 169 cm; l: 55 cm; w: 39 cm
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.method_for_datation: Cyrillo Volkmar Machado (1823) was the first author to refer to the *Saint Onuphrius*, and attributed it to José de Almeida. In 1914, Joaquim de Vasconcelos discarded this information and suggested it was the work of the sculptor Manuel Pereira. In 1950 and 1963, Reynaldo dos Santos returned to Cyrillo's attribution of José de Almeida which, since then, has been consecrated.
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.provenance: Church of the Santíssima Trindade e Redenção dos Cativos, Lisbon
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.obtention: *St. Onuphrius* was taken from the Sacramento Convent in Lisbon which was the depository for the objects taken from the extinct religious corporations. It was integrated into the sculpture collection of the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in 1913. According to a report dated 1833 it had been used in sculpture classes at the Academy of Fine Arts, having previously been removed from a chapel at the Holy Trinity Church and the Redemption of the Captives, in Lisbon.

938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.name: *Remembrance*
938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.description:
A young woman in a coat lined with fur gazes out of the picture lost in thought while knitting a stocking and no longer listening to the sound of a violin. It appears that the music has reminded her of a past situation probably of a romantic nature. The violinist, sensing the woman's mental absence, remains in the background. A richly decorated mirror, glossy box, knitting basket, a broken string of pearls and precious sheet in the right-hand corner, make up a sentimental still life. The emotional air of the picture is accentuated by a landscape on the wall of an otherwise austere interior.  
Genre painting was once considered low and its subjects trivial if picturesque and amusing. With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century the subject of the actions and relationships between people, originating in 17th century Dutch burgher culture, became increasingly important. Pictures typically combined landscape, genre painting and narrative, with conversation often providing a vehicle for the “action”. Conversation scenes between men and women were particularly popular. They were largely based on the Dutch “fine style” promoted by Rembrandt's student Gérard Dou in Leyden, and shaped by the Scandinavian tradition of attention to detail and close observation of reality. While Rembrandt arrived at expressive internal visions, painters of the Leyden school mastered the techniques of representing different materials – later taken up by the Biedermeier. Pictures by the “*Fijnschilders*” were highly valued and sought after in their time. The word *fijn* encompasses more than the obvious notion of something fine, holding connotations including nice, refined, elegant, apt, precise and sensitive. In 18th-century Central Europe the style found admirers among both art collectors and painters. Braun, a member of the Vienna Academy, often transformed moralist paintings by the Dutch painters Frans van Mieris and Dou into pleasant pictures. He was also a competent portraitist, restorer and art dealer.
938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.short_description: With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century the subject of the relationships between people, originating in 17th-century Dutch burgher culture, became important. Braun, a member of the Vienna Academy, often transformed moralist paintings by the Dutch painters F. Mieris and G. Doue into pleasant pictures.

940289de-5702-585e-a85b-f982cfbe67a4.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Stephen
940289de-5702-585e-a85b-f982cfbe67a4.description: The barrel-vaulted hall church with shallow pilasters has been erected on the ground plan of a Latin cross with a four-bayed nave and single-bayed choir with appended semi-circular apse, which, relative to the nave, is barely retracted. The nave bay before the choir has been extended with aisles in the manner of a transept, thus creating space for the two side altars. The system of walls with double pilasters in the nave and single pilasters in the choir, all supporting round arches, generates a circumferential wall arrangement composed of pilaster arcades. Simple lunette windows are inscribed in the arches, surmounted by the vaulting cells painted by Knoller. At the entrance to the choir the large, lightly projecting arcade forms a triumphal arch.
940289de-5702-585e-a85b-f982cfbe67a4.short_description: The church in Anras is a beautiful example of the sophisticated Tyrolean parish church architecture of the mid-18th century. The building is monumental and spacious, the interior work of exquisite taste. The traditional pilaster church scheme has been realised employing a very simple, rational formal language, establishing a dignified setting for the magnificent fittings and furnishings which succeed in generating an overall impression devoid of excess.
940289de-5702-585e-a85b-f982cfbe67a4.bibliography:
Bayer, K., *Franz de Paula Penz*, Vienna 1991, p. 54f.  
Baumgartl, E., *Martin Knoller 1725–1804*, Munich 2004.  
Kröll, K., *Die Kirchen, Kapellen und Bildstöcke der Pfarre Anras*, Salzburg 2006.
940289de-5702-585e-a85b-f982cfbe67a4.history: The building incorporates parts of the first, Gothic church of St. Stephen from the 13th century. Penz erected his new building at a right angle to the old building, transformed the choir into a sacristy and thus turned the nave of the old church into a connecting wing leading to the curate’s house to the west. In 1751 Penz was appointed “Building Director”, the foundation stone was laid in 1753 and the church was consecrated in 1756. Work on the interior continued until around 1760 and was concluded with the pulpit and confessional boxes.

945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.name: Villa Borghese
945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.description:
The building is inspired by the ancient suburban villas. From this model the villa also takes the whiteness of the external surfaces which used to be richly adorned with ancient statues and reliefs. In 1808 Napoleon, brother-in-law of the descendant of Scipione, Prince Camillo Borghese, forced Camillo to sell him over 300 pieces from the collection of antiquities to be allocated to the Musée Napoléon (now the Louvre). The architect of the Villa, Flaminio Ponzio, who was later replaced by the Flemish Giovanni Vasanzio (Jan van Santen), designed the facade of the villa with two bodies jutting out on the sides of the loggia, using as a model another famous Roman Renaissance suburban villa, the Farnesina by Baldassarre Peruzzi. The motif of the soaring turrets on the side wings in the back part of the building is taken from the Medici villa. The stairway with two parallel flights also has a precedent in Michelangelo’s stairway in the Senatorial Palace at the Capitoline Hill. The interior is divided in two levels: on the first floor one finds the reception hall, which solemnly welcomes the visitors as they enter from the loggia, and behind it a gallery parallel to the hall.  
Upstairs, above the gallery, a loggia used to be found, opening onto the secret garden, frescoed by Lanfranco and then walled up at the end of the 18th century. The interior, together with the park of the villa, underwent radical renovation at the time of Prince Marcantonio Borghese IV who, starting from 1775 and until about 1790, commissioned the architect Antonio Asprucci to coordinate the decoration of vaults and walls with frescoes, mosaics, and marble and stucco reliefs, an enterprise which saw the contribution of many renowned Italian and foreign artists. It was in that period that the art collection underwent a more organic arrangement by adopting modern museographic principles aimed at maximizing the beholder’s appreciation of the works.
945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.short_description: The Casino Pinciano – now Museo and Galleria Borghese –dating to the years 1608-1613 was built by Flaminio Ponzio, pope’s favourite architect. It was completed after Ponzio’s death in 1613-15 by Giovanni Vasanzio, his assistant. Between 1775 and 1790 prince Marcantonio IV Borghese ordered architect Antonio Asprucci to renovate the interior of the *casino*: Asprucci coordinated all the works executed by his workshop, including paintings, stucco works, mosaics etc.
945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.bibliography:
Moreno, P.- Stefani, C., *Galleria Borghese,* Milan: Touring Club, 2000.  
Rolfi, S., “Villa Borghese”, *I principi della chiesa,* Milan: Edizioni Charta, 1998: 144–146.
945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.history:
In 1608 Cardinal Scipione Borghese’s ecclesiastic career, favoured by his uncle Pope Paul V, was on the rise. It was under this positive circumstance that he started the construction of the Casino Nobile, which still today hosts the famous Borghese collection of art and antiquities, in the vineyard outside Porta Pinciana, purchased by the Borghese family in 1580. Starting from 1606 (one year after the election of Paul V) the property had started to grow thanks to the purchase of neighbouring land and the donation of a vineyard by Tommaso d'Avalos d'Aquino.  
The Casino was intended to house a real "theatre of the Universe", a microcosm made of the innumerable *naturalia* and *artificialia* that Cardinal Scipione had keenly collected. In line with the encyclopaedic taste of the time, the collection included ancient sculptures, contemporary and Renaissance works of art (among these the famous sculptures of young Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Caravaggio’s paintings and Raphael's Deposition) as well as minerals, fossils, watches, lenses with the most extravagant shapes, and automata. The creation of an aviary and the grafting of exotic plants in the garden is also due to the cardinal’s scientific interest. In 1633, shortly before his death, Cardinal Scipione instituted the *fideicommisum,* which established the unity of the collection as a whole, forcing the heirs to preserve it intact over the centuries.
945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.architects: Flaminio Ponzio; Giovanni Vasanzio; Antonio and Mario Asprucci
945a367a-70ed-5ad3-8637-a7e320c01f52.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

94e30f90-0e79-5e44-a2cc-93bce28a4337.name: Parish Church Birth of the Virgin Mary, St. Peter and Paul, former Convent Church of Augustine Canons
94e30f90-0e79-5e44-a2cc-93bce28a4337.description: The externally modest triple-naved late gothic Basilica with a free-standing bell tower surprisingly has a lavish Rococo style furnishing on the inside. Cheerfully designed and abundantly dense stucco extends over vaults and the high nave walls. Because the stucco was affixed in stages by the Schmuzer workshop, noticeable distinctions in style can be recognized, starting from the chancel via the nave up to the organ loft: while the foliage and strapwork décor of the chancel are still fashioned in the late Régence style, scalloped Rococo as a new ornamental motif appears in the nave. Matthäus Günther’s extensive fresco cycles with Augustinian scenes expand from west to east on the high nave walls. The circular painting in the crossing of Augustine in heavenly glory replaces a customary Baroque cupola. The parts of the fresco coming out of the framework connect the painting with the stucco works of the vault. With this they resemble frescoes by Cosmas Damian Asam, of whom Günther was a pupil. Franz Xaver Schmädl’s grandiose scenographic main altar and the projecting stage-like side altars in the central nave support the overall theatrical concept of the interior.
94e30f90-0e79-5e44-a2cc-93bce28a4337.short_description: The mediaeval Basilica of the Rottenbuch Augustine Canons received a luxurious Rococo furnishing in the 18th century by local artists. Exuberant stucco decorations of the Wessobrunn master craftsmen Joseph and Franz Xaver Schmuzer, a multipartite fresco cycle with scenes from the life of St. Augustine by Matthäus Günther and the scenographic main altar with a rare three dimensional representation of the birth of the Virgin Mary by Franz Xaver Schmädl, give the interior of the convent church an especially solemn effect.
94e30f90-0e79-5e44-a2cc-93bce28a4337.method_for_datation: Through archival sources and dated signatures on the frescoes.

Vollmer, E. C., *Der Wessobrunner Stukkator Franz Xaver Schmuzer. Ein Meister des süddeutschen Rokoko (Bodensee-Bibliothek 24)*, Sigmaringen: Thorbecke, 1979, 16–21.
94e30f90-0e79-5e44-a2cc-93bce28a4337.history: The history of the former Augustinian Convent Church of Rottenbuch can be traced back to the 11th century. After many fires and the collapse of the church tower, a new late gothic Basilica emerged with a transept that remained unchanged in essence after the remodelling of the interior and the refurnishing in Rococo style beginning in  1737 under the direction of Wessobrunn master builder and stucco worker, Joseph Schmuzer. In collaboration with his son, Franz Xaver, Joseph Schmuzer crafted the lavish stucco decorations up to 1744. Immediately following the adorning of the chancel and transept, the famous Augsburg frescoer, Matthäus Günther, began painting throughout the church.
94e30f90-0e79-5e44-a2cc-93bce28a4337.patrons: Provosts Patrizius Oswald (gov. 1700–40) and Clemens Prasser (gov. 1740–70)

957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.name: *St. John of Nepomuk*
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.description:
The Czech martyr John of Nepomuk became one of the major Moravian saints at the turn of the 17th century. The general vicar of the Archbishop of Prague was murdered in 1393. As a saint, his cult spread all over the Czech lands and Roman Catholic Europe and even overseas. John of Nepomuk was worshipped even before his canonisation and beatification in Rome in 1729. Today, one still encounters pilgrimage sites, pictures and statues erected in his honour in many places in Moravia.  
Ignaz Lengelacher, sculptor to the Dietrichstein family, frequently devoted himself to St. John of Nepomuk as a subject for his work in Moravia, from the saint's figure on the Holy Trinity Column in Mikulov (1723–34) to his statue in Pouzdřany (1751).  
In terms of composition, the subject appears in Lengelacher's oeuvre in a number of versions, manifesting the artist's fertile imagination and the inventiveness of his approaches to a single saint. St. John is alone in Lengelacher's statues, standing or kneeling, or sometimes accompanied by the standing figures of angels holding characteristic attributes.  
Lengelacher paid particular attention to interpretation of the saint's mental state in the adoration of the cross which, as shown by the position of hands, he had initially been clasping in quiet, self-absorbed contemplation. The seriousness of the subject is accentuated by the strict emphasis placed on the plain physique of the statue. The cloud pedestal provides the figure with a compositional base and indicates a connection with the transcendent, as the figure is an apotheosis of a martyr, a patron saint of the Czech lands.  
After 1750, Lengelacher left for Bavaria and then went to Bruchsal in the Baden region, where he entered the service of the Bishop of Styria. In 1758 he is recorded as the sculptor to the enlightened and art-loving Margrave Karl Friedrich of Baden (c. 1811) in Karlsruhe, whose court also hosted, among others, Voltaire, Lavater and Goethe.
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.short_description: John of Nepomuk became one of major Moravian saints at the turn of the 17th century. His cult spread all over Catholic Europe and even reached overseas. Today one still encounters pilgrimage sites, pictures and statues erected in his honour in many places in Moravia.
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.method_for_datation: Style analysis is supported by the sculpture’s origins as private property in South Moravia.
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.obtention: Purchased in 1974 from a private owner.

9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.name: Benedictine Abbey of St. Mang/Magnus
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.alternate_name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Mang and Town Hall/Town Museum
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.description: Herkomer's monastery – inevitably tiered and intricate, due to its narrow hillside location – surprises with original ideas, specifically the library. Created as an oval rotunda, it corresponds, through an oculus, with the refectory beneath. The ceremonial hall is crowned with a scrolled gable and dominates the large courtyard facing the town. Also used for parish service, the abbey church flaunts its precious marble and rightfully qualifies as an import of Venetian architecture. The local tradition of wall pillar construction creates the layout, but is formatively combined with elements of Benedictine churches which can be found in the Venetian realm: the domed vaults refer to Santa Giustina in Padua, whereas the choir and the crossing are linked to San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice. Another reference to Venetian models are single motifs such as the so-called Diocletian windows, an antique window type deriving from Roman baths which had been popular in Venice since Andrea Palladio.
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.short_description: Dedicated to the so-called Allgovian apostle, the Benedictine abbey resides on a scenic slope at the edge of the old town of Füssen, between the Lech's riverside and the castle named "Hohes Schloss", and is a rarity as an offshoot of Venetian ecclesiastical architecture. As a native to the Allgäu region, its versatilely-trained builder, Johann Jakob Herkomer, competently combined local traditions of art and architecture with his expertise achieved in Northern Italy. Particular mention should be made of the church's furnishing with marble altars, two altarpieces painted by the Venetian artist Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini and the splendid ceremonial hall decorated by stuccoer Andrea Maini.
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.method_for_datation: Archival documents; inscriptions on the crossing piers; medallions on the gateway containing dates of the foundation and construction.
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.bibliography:

Riedmüller, T., *Kloster St. Mang* (Kataloge des Museums der Stadt Füssen 1), Füssen: 1994.  
Seufert, I., *Johann Jakob Herkomer (1652–1717)*, Lindenberg im Allgäu: Kunstverlag Josef Fink, 2009: 25–40, 50, 52–60, 77, 80, 83–86.  
Seufert, I., *Kath. Stadtpfarrkirche St. Mang in Füssen*, Beuron/Lindenberg im Allgäu: Kunstverlag Josef Fink, 2004.
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.history: Founded around 850, the Benedictine abbey originated from a church that was built around 730 by the St. Gallen monk, Magnus of Füssen, whose final resting place lies in this very location. After his canonisation, the place of worship evolved into a destination for an increased number of pilgrimages. A Baroque renovation of the monastery was initiated by the cornerstone ceremony on 10 May 1701, which skilfully incorporated the medieval foundations of the structure. The construction and artistic management were assigned to Johann Jakob Herkomer, a universal artist born near Füssen, who had been trained in the Region of Veneto, including Venice. Before his death in 1717 – the year of the consecration – he was able to complete the structural work and started implementing the stucco and fresco decoration in the choir and the transept of the church. Maintaining Herkomer's style, his nephew, Johann Georg Fischer, finalised the church, including designs for the altars, while the task of decorating the ceremonial hall was given to the Ticino stuccoer, Andrea Maini.
9589f8d6-a852-5a6a-9183-c9a9681b93a0.patrons: Abbots Gerhard Oberleitner (gov. 1696–1714) and Dominikus Dierling (gov. 1714–38)

958f68a4-0c25-54c7-908c-2464cacbbedd.name: St. Florian Abbey and Abbey Basilica
958f68a4-0c25-54c7-908c-2464cacbbedd.alternate_name: Augustinian Canons´ Abbey and Abbey Basilica in St. Florian
958f68a4-0c25-54c7-908c-2464cacbbedd.description:
After the end of the Wars Against the Ottoman Empire the Augustinian Canons commissioned an architect to erect a new church on the place of an earlier one. Next, the enormously long west wing was built. Another architect who slightly changed and finished the representative staircase added the magnificent portal extending over the three floors.  
The south wing with the pavilionlike Marble Hall became St. Florian´s landmark. The court was completed by adding the east wing with the Library in its centre. There is another, almost unseen wing, protruding from the abbey building in the Northeast, the Summer Refectory. It bespeaks an unexecuted scenic project that would have been completed with a twin building opposite (a theatre) and a spacious connecting French garden.
958f68a4-0c25-54c7-908c-2464cacbbedd.short_description: Like most people of this era, the five Baroque prelates and provosts loved building. They started to erect a new church in 1686, re-using Romanesque and Gothic walls from an earlier building, and new monastery wings at the beginning of the 18th century. It took 65 years and three architects to complete the ensemble. So St. Florian abbey has become a very good example to understand how Baroque art and architecture developed within two thirds of a century.

1706–31 paintings, stucco, stoves, fittings guest rooms

958f68a4-0c25-54c7-908c-2464cacbbedd.history:
Under Roman rule, (the later saint) Florian(us) confessed being Christian, and was therefore tortured and thrown bound into the river Enns where he died. He was probably buried somewhere under the abbey church; for that reason St. Florian soon became known as “place above the saint´s grave”.  
The monastery was probably founded by nearby residents and not like many other abbeys by a prince or by a nobleman. Nevertheless, the Augustinian Canons acquired property and made profits over the centuries and erected new buildings during the Baroque era. Under Emperor Joseph II they had to put up with expropriation and loss. Anyway, St. Florian has economically recovered and is still known for its magnificent Baroque architecture.

95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Nicholas
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.description: The parish church of Elbigenalp is built according to the simple parish church scheme of a hall nave and retracted choir. The rounding of the eastern nave corners and boldly curved choir arches enrich the prospect of the choir. The ceiling frescos and side altars, as well as the pulpit (c. 1770) which originates from the parish church of Mayrhofen in Zillertal, lend the space a magnificent overall impression, hardly to be suspected from the outside.
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.short_description: The outwardly unimposing hall building, whose interior architecture is also decidedly plain, is famous for its ceiling frescos painted in lucid colours, late works of Johann Jakob Zeiller from Reutte. Thanks to the stucco framing of the fresco panels, also painted, the artist succeeded in creating a uniform Late Baroque system of decoration which lends the church the character of a festive hall.
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.dates: 1661–1674: Baroque modification; c. 1770–1776: Rococo interior work
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.method_for_datation: Archives and inscriptions on the north wall of the nave (parish priest J. Rormoser and master builder Georg Falger, 1674) as well as the ceiling picture (1776).
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.bibliography: Geisler-Moroder, R., *Kath. Pfarrkirche St. Nikolaus, Elbigenalp - Lechtal/Tirol*, 2nd edition, Regensburg 1985.
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.history: The original church building was erected in around 1300, and the ancient parish of Lechtal is first documented in 1312. The church was enlarged in the 15th century and once again between 1661 and 1674 together with a modification (consecration 1685) and finally in 1774 when the flat wooden ceiling was replaced by a vault. This was painted by Johann Jakob Zeiller and completed in 1776 (signed and dated). The majority of the additional interior work also originates from this period.
95bc3bec-8854-560d-8e97-c743653554a8.architects: Master builder, modification: Georg Falger (1661–1674); sculptor of side altars: Maximilian Hitzelsberger (1743–1780); ceiling frescos: Johann Jakob Zeiller (1708–1783)

963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.name: *Samson Imprisoned*
963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.description:
The painting is first mentioned as being part of the Scipione Borghese Collection in 1650, but no details of the date of its commission have survived. The date given (1590–1595) relates to the period in which Annibale, one of the founders of the *Accademia degli Incamminati*, was active in Bologna working on the decoration of the Palazzo Fava. It is possible that the naked figure of Samson is a draft, possibly a trial-run for one of the many monochrome nudes, often used as telamons, in the fresco decoration of noble Bolognese residences. Annibale continued his decorative work in Rome, where he worked on the famous Galleria di Palazzo Farnese. It was here, abandoned by his family, that he suffered from the depression that eventually killed him.  
The subject covers the biblical passage in the Old Testament (Judges 15, 12) in which Samson, imprisoned by Judas' men and about to be taken by the Philistines, is about to fulfil the Will of God. Invested with the Holy Spirit, he manages to free himself from his ropes and uses the jawbone of an ass to kill more than 1000 men. The painting does not show the action, but depicts the splendid, monumental muscular figure emerging from a dark background. We cannot even see his face, which thanks to its foreshortened position is hidden by shadow. All our attention is focused on the figure of the hero: the bent leg and the hands behind his back demonstrate the careful anatomical study undertaken by one of the greatest Baroque painters of the early 17th century.
963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.short_description: This work was probably painted in Bologna, a year before Annibale moved to Rome. It is actually more advanced than the decorations of Fava Palace in Bologna (the monochrome gods and frieze) and is closer to the classical forms of Palazzo Farnese. This painting is an example of the Carracci Academy.
963a62ad-af06-501c-b4d1-95dcf8be84c1.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

96a0b74f-0971-56c3-8154-0b603d6d4116.name: *Portrait of Emperor Joseph II and His Second Wife Marie Josepha of Bavaria and Counts Esterházy, Bathiany and Liechtenstein*
96a0b74f-0971-56c3-8154-0b603d6d4116.alternate_name: *Joseph II with Wife Maria Josepha of Bavaria, Close Courtiers and Ladies-in-Waiting*
96a0b74f-0971-56c3-8154-0b603d6d4116.description:
A counterpart to this sizeable canvas is the picture *Maria Theresa with Sons Below the Bust of Her Deceased Husband Franz Stephan of Lorraine and Chancellor Kounic-Rietberg*. This painting represents the hierarchy of both the dynasty and the monarchy. After the death of his father, Joseph II ruled side-by-side with Maria Theresa. In the background, Josef Wenzl of Liechtenstein indicates a medallion bearing a portrait of Isabela of Parma, Joseph II's first wife. On the right, behind the throne, Joseph's two unmarried sisters, Marie Elisabeth and Marie Anna, are engaged in conversation. In the foreground stands Franz Esterházy with a tiger skin, while Count Karl Josef Batthyány, High Steward, is located at the edge of the canvas. The festive air is enhanced by the arrangement of a drapery with golden tassels together with the seating of the figures on the steps. The landscape in the background features an obelisk topped with a globe upon which an eagle perches holding in its beak a curled serpent biting its own tail a symbol of eternity. The eagle, a creature associated with Jupiter, was among the attributes of imperial iconography and refers to the sovereign's virtues. Another attribute and a symbol of wisdom is the shield with the head of Medusa at the bottom of the picture, on a stone vase. A group of *putti* taming a lion in the upper section of the vase symbolise the power of love and its victory over physical strength.  
The group portrait was commissioned by the abbot of the Premonstratensian Monastery in Louka near Znojmo as an expression of loyalty. The paintings come from the summer refectory, a key section of the monastery designed as a “Temple of Solomon”. The major decorative components were paintings by Franz Anton Maulbertsch depicting essential elements of the Premonstratensian order. These were accompanied by a series of portraits of monastery supporters and superiors.
96a0b74f-0971-56c3-8154-0b603d6d4116.short_description: The group allegorical portrait of the Habsbourg family was commissioned by the abbot of the Premonstratensian Monastery in Louka near Znojmo – one of the most important monasteries in the Danubian country – as an expression of loyalty. The painting represents the hierarchy of both the dynasty and the monarchy.
96a0b74f-0971-56c3-8154-0b603d6d4116.method_for_datation: Palko did a sketch for the picture of Maria Theresa known from a replica by Josef Winterhalder Jr. After Palko’s untimely death, the two paintings were finished by Anton Glunck, a graduate of the Vienna Academy. Glunck is also mentioned as the artist of the pictures in the inventory of the monastery collated by Josef Winterhalder Jr., who also supplemented it with drawn records. Glunck’s participation is confirmed by three receipts preserved in the Moravian Provincial Archive.
96a0b74f-0971-56c3-8154-0b603d6d4116.obtention: The picture comes from the summer refectory of the Premonstratensian Monastery in Louka near Znojmo. When the monastery was dissolved in 1784 the picture became the property of Count Waldorf in Sádek, near Třebíč, until 1904. It was then owned by Count Chorinský and found in the Veselí na Moravě Chateau. After the Second World War the picture came into the possession of the State Chateau, Valtice.

9709130f-3233-59f7-bcd0-0c3810a8a498.name: Palazzo Malvasia
9709130f-3233-59f7-bcd0-0c3810a8a498.description:
Initial contact began with the architect Alfonso Torreggiani in 1745. The following year, the Count engaged Giovanni Carlo Sicinio Galli Bibiena, son of Francesco and nephew of Ferdinando. The celebrated architects and stage designers worked for the most prestigious European courts. Giovanni Carlo left Bologna for Lisbon shortly after he projected the staircase of the Malvasia Palace.  
On a very small area (about 4x7 meters) the staircase is based on an oval plan. It is characterised by a single flight, which is very sinuous and dynamic, and by the presence of two mythological figures. The first one, representing Sisyphus is located on the right where the flight turns. The second figure, representing Athena, stands in a niche in the wall with two heraldic dragons at her sides. The statues are the works of the sculptor Filippo Scandellari, aided by Giovan Battista Canepa.  
The ceiling shows a particular solution, typical of Bolognese baroque architecture. Containing a ‘sfondato' or “chamber of light” (a space with windows not visible by the visitors), often painted, as in this case, and opened in its central part.
9709130f-3233-59f7-bcd0-0c3810a8a498.short_description: Very original in its shape, the staircase realised in the residence of the Malvasia family is one of the most representative creations of Bolognese late baroque architecture. It was designed by a member of the famous dynasty of theatrical architects and stage designers, Giovanni Carlo Sicinio Galli Bibiena; thanks to his ability in those fields the work is intended to astonish and involve the visitors, inviting them to start climbing the stairs and reaching the apartment of count Cesare Alberto.
9709130f-3233-59f7-bcd0-0c3810a8a498.bibliography:
Roversi, G., *Palazzi e Case Nobili del '500 a Bologna. La storia, le famiglie, le opere d'arte*, Bologna, 1986, pp. 300-307.  
Godinho Mendonça, I.M., “Precisazioni sullo scalone di palazzo Malvasia in Strada Maggiore a Bologna”, *Arti a confronto. Studi in onore di Anna Maria Matteucci* (ed. D. Lenzi ), Bologna, 2004, pp. 289-303, figg. 211-216, XC-XCI.
9709130f-3233-59f7-bcd0-0c3810a8a498.history: Acquired in 1535, Count Malvasia restored a palace originally made for the Fantuzzi family located in Strada Maggiore. The restoration kept the original portico and built a new façade for the upper floors. Important work was intended to renew the interiors of the palace, made – or begun – around the mid eighteenth-century. From 1756 Count Cesare Alberto Malvasia, a member of the Bolognese Senate, was a patron to the work. He lived in this palace until 1761, when he moved to another residence projected and built under his supervision. The new palace was in a new style, inspired by Italian and Bolognese sixteenth-century architecture. The palace of Strada Maggiore was sold to Filippo Savini in 1771.

97284ed3-c2ab-51af-8cd2-2ae8ea41f09e.name: *Portrait of the Beneficiary Faustino das Neves*
97284ed3-c2ab-51af-8cd2-2ae8ea41f09e.description:
Strongly influenced by her father, Baltazar Gomes Figueira, and by painters such as Francisco Zurbarán, Juan de Roelas and Daniel Seghers, Josefa de Ayala worked in a small provincial centre outside Lisbon. Away from the court, and in a place where the medieval lifestyle was preserved, she related to the politics opposed to the Spanish Habsburg dynasty, supporting the Restoration cause of the Royal House of Braganza. The social life of this micro-society revolved around social gatherings and meetings in convents and noble residences. The noblemen – members of the Municipal Senate – religious orders, brotherhood and charitable institutions with whom she fraternized, were well-read and had no economic restrictions. In their homes were many works of art some of which were commissioned from local provincial artists.  
From as early as the 17th century, Josefa had several biographies written about her. Costa Meesen (1696) referred to her “cleanliness and aptitude” upon imitating “things from nature”. Writer Damião Froes Perym (1736) also praises her “skill, beauty, honesty and charm” and her moral virtues. In the 19th century, José Silvestre Seabra and Almeida Garrett made reference to *Portrait of the Beneficiary Faustino das Neves*, considering it the genre which best revealed the sensitive side of Josefa d'Óbidos. The piece got lost in time and in 1957 it was identified by Reis-Santos as the work of Josefa d'Óbidos.  
The artist perfectly captures the psychology of this distinguished man from Óbidos. His dark clothing and his vigorous look contrast with the luminosity of the white and beige of his face, accentuating the Counter-Reformation features of the piece. The male figure, accompanied by an angel announcing his death, is purposely decentralised relative to the axis of the composition. This is a peculiarity which enhances the formal skills of Josefa de Ayala thus allowing her to be included within the ranks of the best 17th-century Portuguese painters.
97284ed3-c2ab-51af-8cd2-2ae8ea41f09e.short_description: Josefa de Ayala skilfully conveys the psychology through the glance, gesture and pose of this distinguished man from the town of Óbidos. His dark clothing and vigorous look contrast with the luminosity provided by the white and beige tones of his face. The figure is accompanied by an angel announcing his death.

97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.name: *Capture of Christ*
97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.description:
The canvas came to the Borghese collection due to the life annuity agreed in 1787 by Marcantonio Borghese with the sculptor Bartolomeo Cavaceppi, who gave a number of different pieces from his collection.  
The painting shows notable similarities to the *Capture of Christ* painted by Caravaggio (Dublin, National Gallery of Ireland), handling the same subject in a more balanced and composed manner. Bright armour that illuminates the scene contrasts with the central figure of Christ, dressed in red with his gaze lifted to the sky and his hands together, the only figure who is facing the viewer.  
The composition appears orchestrated with rhythm, suggesting a drama that is more theatrical than profound. The work shows the influence of the Caravaggesque language used by Bartolomeo Manfredi, focusing on a substantial simplification of the dramatic, artistic and moral implications of Merisi's painting. The Caravaggesque inventions thus became easier to spread and, reproduced in different contexts, they quickly became elements of “typical” painting, which in turn gave rise to the phenomenon of “Caravaggism”.  
This method, described as *Manfrediana methodus*, became widespread in Rome in the first decades of the 17th century, in particular among the ever-present colony of northern artists who came to new and prestigious commissions. Van Baburen, who worked with David de Haen on the decoration of a chapel in the Church of San Pietro in Montorio in Rome, was particularly able to mediate between the Caravaggesque lesson and the Baroque style of Rubens' work.
97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.short_description: The Dutch painter arrived in Rome around 1617 and assimilated the *chiaroscuro* of Caravaggio's style. He had an important role in establishing Utrecht as a stronghold of the Caravaggesque style.
97430dda-4f55-5d8c-8dbf-87ed5f7bc6a3.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

97e3480f-d7cd-56d6-b710-84eb08c01f73.name: Fronteira Palace and Gardens
97e3480f-d7cd-56d6-b710-84eb08c01f73.alternate_name: Palace of the Marquis of Fronteira
97e3480f-d7cd-56d6-b710-84eb08c01f73.description:
The main palace comprises a central two-floor building that is terminated on each side with small, quadrangular towers. The main façade has a Serlian porch, and a staircase leading to the forecourt. Above it is a loggia of the same design supported by Ionic columns. The lateral wings are decorated with Ionic pilasters.  The palace has the most important collection of azulejos *in situ*: polychrome *azulejos* (painted tile panels) depicting noblemen and women, mermaids and scenes of fishing in the gardens and Terrace; the sets of the Room of the Battles and of the Panel's room. The seventieth century grotto-work and the stucco from the 18th century are also remarkable.  
  
The interior is organised around a monumental double staircase that connects the forecourt with the “noble” or ceremonial floor, which in turn allows access to the gallery and terrace. A room in the east wing has a unique decorative cycle of figurative *azulejos* depicting hunting scenes, and ornamental stucco work with mythological themes from the 18th century.  
  
The palace complex includes an art gallery (also known as a terrace) a chapel, library, the Venus Garden, and the formal or grand garden.
97e3480f-d7cd-56d6-b710-84eb08c01f73.short_description: The Palace of the Marquis of Fronteira brings together both the splendour and refinement of the nobility's social life in the late 17th century. The combination of a main building with two storeys, a wing, sculptures and tile panels – which spread throughout the gardens with lakes – is a remarkable example of early Baroque architecture.

97e3480f-d7cd-56d6-b710-84eb08c01f73.history: João de Mascarenhas, the first Marquis of Fronteira, commissioned the palace in around 1665–1673 following loyal services to the Kings of Portugal during the Portuguese Restoration War against Spain. In 1672 Mascarenhas' Summer Palace was inaugurated in the presence of Prince Regent Pedro (future king Pedro II). When the earthquake of 1755 destroyed the family's permanent residence in Lisbon they moved permanently to the summer palace in Benfica. In the last quarter of the 18th century, major improvements, including the restoration of the rococo and neoclassical stucco, took place to the main body of the building and a new wing was added. Some further adaptations were undertaken in the 20th century as it keeps being the family residence.

97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.name: *St. Joseph Calasanctius before the Virgin with Hungarian Pupils*
97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.description:
Felix Ivo Leicher arrived in Vienna from the Silesian town, Bílovec, with the support of the Piarist Fathers. He enrolled as a pupil at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna (his presence is documented from 1751) and won second prize in the academic competition of 1754, which made him a supported member of the Academy known as *Schutzverwandte*. He worked for a long time with Franz Anton Maulbertsch who remained a lifelong friend. His compositions, loose modelling, effective lighting and the ability to portray characteristic types undoubtedly betray the influences and ideas of Maulbertsch, although Leicher's approach is softer, weaker and without the expressive power, dramatic vitality or pictorial virtuosity of his master.  
Allegedly, a burgher of Tata commissioned this picture in Vienna for the Tata Piarists in 1767. Leicher worked in Vienna and was a pupil and protégé of the Piarists for whom he carried out a lot of work, undertaking several altarpieces on which he represented St. Joseph of Calasanctius (1556–1648) the founder of the Piarist order, who was canonised in 1767. In the main, these pictures refer to the educational activity of the order, depicting the saint with a circle of students as he recommends them to the patronage of Mary and the Infant Jesus whose figures appear among the clouds. This is the theme of the devout Tata painting *St. Joseph Calasanctius before the Virgin with Hungarian Pupils* depicting boys, dressed in contemporary Hungarian fashion, accompanied by St. Joseph and their guardian angel. The light, which draws the viewer's eye upwards, together with the expressive gestures and the sweet mild faces, call to mind the art of Leicher's master, Franz Anton Maulbertsch. The Tata picture is one of Leicher's most harmonious. He repeated this theme, in a larger format and different composition, in the Piarist Church of Brezno and paintings for altarpieces in the Piarist churches of Mikulov, Benešov and Nagykároly (Carei).
97f72893-57de-5507-8d3c-253570b152a5.short_description: A pupil of Franz Anton Maulbertsch, Felix Ivo Leicher worked on several altarpieces in Hungary (Vác, Martonvásár, and Besztercebánya (Banská Bystrica). The subject of this painting, commissioned by a burgher of Tata in Vienna for the Tata Piarists in 1767, is especially popular in Hungary because of its representation of children.

982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.name: Monument to Luigi Ferdinando Marsili
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.description: This monument was commissioned by the Institute of Sciences of Bologna to commemorate one of its main founders, General Luigi Ferdinando Marsili in 1733, three years after his death. The monument is located in the right arm of the transept of the church of St. Dominic in Bologna which was refurbished a few years before by the architect Dotti. It is made of a very poor material, stucco, which is a mixture of marble powder and sand. Many Bolognese sculptors used stucco in the Baroque age to create true masterpieces for churches and noble residences. From the church wall hangs a great and rich curtain covering objects once beloved by the General; books, weapons, and artist tools. The upper portion is occupied by the slender figure of Fame, holding in her hand a trumpet and an oval medallion with Marsili’s profile. Under the diagonally projecting slab with its Latin inscription struggles Time, represented as an old man with a sickle. The baroque theme of Fame defeating Time is perfectly conveyed.
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.short_description: This monument represents the baroque spirit in the use of allegories, in the employment of many diagonals crossing in the composition and in the dynamic movement transmitted to the sculpted curtain.
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.method_for_datation: The monument date is established thanks to archive documents and to the Latin inscription.

986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.name: *St. Florian with a View of Jihlava*
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.description:
The picture is a typical example of a votive painting designed for a town environment. In their everyday prayers and pledges, people of the period turned to saints as protectors against the various perils of life. The promotion of saints in these roles was among the chief tools of re-Catholicisation in rural areas. St. Florian, protector from fire, was among the most worshipped. Here the saint is depicted as the protector of the town of Jihlava. Under Swedish siege during the Thirty Years' War the town suburbs were burnt down and the majority of the houses were destroyed. Only one-eighth of the Jihlava population survived.  
Jihlava is the oldest mining town of the Czech lands, renowned in the Middle Ages for its silver mines. Mining law was codified there for the first time in Central Europe, alongside municipal law. This formulary law became a template for a number of other mining towns. The economic development of Jihlava was facilitated by trade and crafts, especially weaving. In the mid-18th century, Jihlava was the second largest manufacturer of cloth in the Habsburg monarchy. This *veduta* is dominated by the Jesuit Church of St. Ignatius, with the parish Church of St. James in the background, on the right; the whole town is encircled by its walls. The square is lined with stone buildings, with arcades and a town hall that feature different types of vaulting. The regular ground plan of the right-angled network of streets with a square in the centre, the largest in Moravia, was defined by a building order made by King Přemysl Otakar II in 1270.  
The work of Václav Nosek has not yet been fully mapped as it has a relatively broad span. After settling in Jihlava in 1702, he worked for the town as well as for the Bishop of Olomouc (Kroměříž, 1711) and the Premonstratensian monastery in Louka u Znojma (*Education of the Virgin Mary*, side altar, 1712). In the 1720s, Nosek also produced templates for graphic illustrations of Episcopal prints.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.short_description: The picture is a typical example of a votive painting. The promotion of saints as protectors was among the chief tools of re-Catholicisation in rural areas. St. Florian, protector from fire, is represented here as the patron saint of Jihlava, one of the largest and wealthiest Moravian towns.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.initial_owner: Parish Church of St. James, Jihlava
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.method_for_datation: The archivist and historian Johann Peter Cerroni states that Nosek painted a picture of St. Florian with a *veduta* of Jihlava. By stylistic comparison the work may be associated with the painting in the Moravian Gallery.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.obtention: The painting from the Highlands Museum, Jihlava was transferred to the Moravian Gallery in Brno in 1962. It probably comes from the parish Church of St. James.

990ef20d-c9c1-58c2-9f59-b045aeba60f7.name: Abbey Church of the Benedictine Order St. Ulrich and St. Afra
990ef20d-c9c1-58c2-9f59-b045aeba60f7.description: The monumentality of the church soars above the cityscape of Augsburg, especially when seen from the Ulrichsplatz in the north. In particular, the onion dome, destined to be a model for countless later Bavarian churches, dominates the silhouette of Augsburg across a wide area. Unlike the multi-faceted exterior, the Late Gothic interior is a sober architectural piece, its highlight being the tripartite group of altars in the choir: This group comprises the high altar of 1604 (executed by Hans Degler, a representative of the Weilheim school, probably after designs by Hans Krumpper), the altar of St. Ulrich in the south, and the altar of St. Afra in the north. Seen from the middle nave, the three altars amalgamate into a coherent and splendid composition. Stylistically, the interior decoration achieves organic unity with the architecture, even though the interior is 150 years younger. The three carved altars are executed in a hybrid style typical of southern Germany in around 1600. This style adopts antique details while, overall, giving the impression of preserving the decorative richness of the Late Gothic. The main scenes of the altars are not, as would be expected, dedicated to their patrons, but instead show important scenes from the Life of Christ (Birth, Resurrection and Pentecost), therewith marking the most important religious holidays of the year. Scenes from the Life of St. Ulrich and, respectively, of St. Afra are shown in the predella and in a smaller frame at the top of each of the particular altars.
990ef20d-c9c1-58c2-9f59-b045aeba60f7.short_description: The Late Gothic basilica of St. Ulrich and St. Afra was updated in several phases with a splendid Baroque décor, resulting in spectacular plurality and combination of styles. The three altars in the choir, seen together from the middle nave, create an impressive effect. Their Baroque composition, divided into many small sections, corresponds surprisingly well with the cathedral-like medieval architecture. Altars and architecture respectively share the steeple-like silhouette that bridges the almost 150 years that separate them. The monumental bronze sculpture of the crucifixion by Hans Reichle is one of the most important German works in this genre, dating to around 1600.
990ef20d-c9c1-58c2-9f59-b045aeba60f7.dates: 1603–1608: vaulting and decoration of the altars in the choir; pulpit in the middle nave; 1698–1705: Chapel of All-Saints; 1714: renovation of the Chapel of St. Simpert; 1762–1765: renovation of the Crypt of St. Ulrich
990ef20d-c9c1-58c2-9f59-b045aeba60f7.method_for_datation: Archival documents and an inscription on the high altar: “MCIIII”

990ef20d-c9c1-58c2-9f59-b045aeba60f7.history: The church has been a place of worship since 1012, being associated with the late antique martyr Afra and then with its second patron, Bishop Ulrich, who was canonized in 993 and one of the heroes of the battle at Lechfeld in 955, at which time it was under the administration of the Benedictine Order. The monastery took a supra-regional role since the late medieval period. Since 1449 it was immediate to the Emperor. It was during that high point in its history, precisely 1467, that today’s Late Gothic building was begun, but never finished. In 1594 the spire was completed; on the occasion of the 1300th anniversary of the martyrdom of St. Afra, in 1604, the church was vaulted. Decoration of the choir followed in 1607. Several other interventions were undertaken with regard to the relics of local saints during the Baroque period: in 1698 a new Chapel of All Saints was built annexed to the sacristy; renovations include the Chapel of St. Simpert of 1714, and in 1762, the crypt, together with the tomb of St. Ulrich.

998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.name:
Engelszell Abbey Church  
Trappists' Abbey Church in Engelszell
998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.alternate_name: Engelszell Abbey Church dedicated to the Ascension of the Virgin
998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.description: After a hard time – in 1571 the abbot and all monks died of the black death, later the reformation caused a big loss of friars and in 1699 a big fire destroyed almost all the buildings – Leopold Reichl, then administrator, eventually succeeded in improving the monastery´s economic state. As abbot he had the abbey complex and the church rebuilt. The latter arose, similar to the Wilhering abbey church, with a classic baroque outer appearance and a fanciful Rococo interior. The main façade with pilasters, gables and tower follows the same architectural principles. The interior is characterised by a spacious, highly decorated nave which was done by many of the artists who had worked in Wilhering abbey previously. Nonetheless, Engelszell´s church architecture and fittings are unique and individual works on their own.
998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.short_description: Under abbot Leopold Reichl, the most important personality in Engelszell´s history, the monastery experienced a big boom. He won many Conventual friars for the cloister, ran the monastery´s business well and acquired important wealth. As builder he erected the Baroque church, added two cloister wings and baroquized the Engelhartszell parish church. The monastery´s church got a classic Baroque exterior, while the whole interior is Rococo – it reflects the artists´ enjoyment of the era as well as the glorification of the Ascension of Maria.
998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.dates:
1754—64: construction of church  
as of 1758: stucco work  
1759—62: paintings at high altar and at side altars  
about 1760: fresco paintings on the ceilings of the choir and antechoir  
1763: portal, choir stalls, organ case, antechoir statues
