998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.history:
Distinguishing between “Old Engelszell” and “New Engelszell” means to differ from two, if not three periods. The first period lasted from the foundation in 1293 until the year 1925. Dividing up into three eras, a first period would end in the year 1786 when the - then Cistercian - monastery was dissolved by the Reform-Kaiser Joseph II. Rise and decline of the monastery had taken place within 39 years, during abbot Leopold Reichl´s reign. He had made Engelszell a flourishing cloister. The day after Reichl’s death Joseph II had it closed.  
The second period starting in 1786 lasted 139 years during which time Engelszell was managed by the Cistercians from Wilhering, and later by different (secular) owners. The last and third period, “New Engelszell”, started in 1925 when Trappists, a later-founded branch of the Cistercians, moved in. It has remained in their custody up to the present day.
998e991a-2cc4-5639-8635-5be3bb4c0eb9.patrons: The abbey was founded 1293 by bishop Bernhard (Wernhart) von Prambach. In 1295 Cistercians settled in and Engelszell became a daughter monastery of Wilhering abbey.

999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.name: *The Prodigal Son*
999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.description:
The painting only became part of the Borghese collection in the 19th century, having earlier been mentioned in the collection of Prince Lancellotti, although the details of its commissioning are unknown. The canvas (1627–1628) reworks an earlier piece completed 10 years before for Cardinal Serra in Ferrara.  
The subject is taken from the parable of the prodigal son from the Gospel of St. Luke (15, 11–32). It tells of the forgiveness of a father who welcomes his youngest son after he has squandered his inheritance and been reduced to poverty and hunger. The scene in the canvas focuses on the moment when the aged father, shown in the centre of the composition, having found his son in such miserable conditions – rendered with marked realism in the rags tied around his waist – orders his servant to give him decent clothing. The boy is in fact busy putting on a clean shirt. The idea of a return to domestic intimacy is suggested by the closed window, in which the painter accurately renders the reflection of light.  
Guercino was able to portray this moment of family intimacy with great tenderness, in particular the detail of the dog resting his paws on the young man's lap, pleased that his master has returned home. The presence of the dog also enhances the symbolic idea of faithfulness often attributed to them, in accordance with allegorical custom in the Baroque tradition. This virtue is related to mercy according to the meaning given in the parable: the teaching that Christ imparted to his followers.  
Guercino, renowned as a painter of emotions, clearly shows here the father's forgiveness; he believed that his son was dead before he found him. From a stylistic point of view, we can see the influence of Venetian colourism, which Guercino had acquired on his trip to Venice in 1618, and which the artists blends together in a measured composition of classical inspiration.
999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.short_description:
In this painting, the colours are clearly influenced by Venetian art (Guercino stayed in Venice in 1618) combined with the more classical design of the figure.  
Guercino, renowned as a painter of “emotions” here clearly represents the forgiveness of a father who believing his son to be dead, is re-united with him.
999586a0-c924-50ff-946c-368f78217139.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

99f56792-6482-5cfa-83ad-cfea74567160.name: Garden of the Bishop’s Palace
99f56792-6482-5cfa-83ad-cfea74567160.description:
Gardens held a central place in 17th- and 18th- century European art. The Baroque garden sought to represent the universe, symbolically blending aesthetic values with philosophical ideals. Sometimes large in scale, usually complex, and rich in terms of decoration, they combined nature with ornamental elements such as in Portuguese statues and *azulejos* (tile panels), reflecting the social status and the customs of their patrons. The ecclesiastical garden was an excellent vehicle for the diversion, spiritual exaltation and social projection of both the resident and his visitors.  
The Garden of the Bishop's Palace was probably conceived as a space for the celebration of God through the allegories and examples of virtue it expounded. In the intermediate rectangular terrace divided into three longitudinal axes with a central lake and four others at the corners, granite sculptures depict the spiritual world (representing the Four Cardinal and Three Theological Virtues as well as the Apostles in the monumental Apostles' Stairway), the material world (signs of the Zodiac, the Four Continents, Seasons and Four Elements) and lastly the national reality (a monumental Kings' Stairway with images of the Portuguese kings). The several different levels of the garden are connected by stairways.  
The Lake of the Crowns and a curious overflow garden named *Jardim Alagado* occupy the same level, from which two monumental stairways lead to the upper level where the Water Tank and the Moses Cascade, a purely a decorative feature, are situated.
99f56792-6482-5cfa-83ad-cfea74567160.short_description: The Garden of the Bishop’s palace combines lakes, fountains, flowerbeds and stone sculptures representing religious themes, pagan personalities and the kings of Portugal.

99f56792-6482-5cfa-83ad-cfea74567160.history: The Garden of the Bishops of Castelo Branco was conceived in the first quarter of the 18th century by the Bishop of Guarda, João de Mendonça (1711–1736), who built it close to the Winter Palace which he used to avoid the freezing temperatures of winter in Guarda. In 1771, the Diocese of Castelo Branco was created, and the former Winter Palace became the Bishop's official residence. The Garden was completed at the end of the 18th century under the direction of D. Vicente Ferrer da Rocha, second Bishop of Castelo Branco, assisted by Fr. Daniel Joaquim do Rosário. At the beginning of the 20th century, a new level at the entrance of the main terrace was installed. It is decorated with flower beds surrounded by hedges and *azulejos* depicting the Bishops of Castelo Branco.

9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.name: *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian*
9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.description:
These splendidly colourful Rococo statues of *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* came to the museum from the parish church of Egervár in the county of Zala. The patron of the church, Count Ignác Széchényi, commissioned a new large tabernacle with six carved figures for the high altar of the church, made in around 1730, in 1757. The Széchényi family already had connections with artists in Graz, the area where Philipp Jakob Straub chose to settle and work.  
Both statues are of saints believed to be protectors from the plague, and both express pain and suffering. *St. Roch*, dressed in pilgrim's clothes, turns his eyes heavenward. His lips parted in pain, he points to the wound on his foot. Next to him is the dog that allegedly brought him bread when he was suffering from the plague. Bound to a tree and wounded by arrows, the young martyr, *St. Sebastian*, is resigned to his fate. His head rests on his shoulder and tears drip from his closed eyes. *St. Roch*'s garments flutter in deep folds, providing the contrast of light and shade, while light glides softly on the sensuously beautiful body of *St. Sebastian*.  
The statues are promoted into the vanguard of Rococo sculpture in Hungary by the outstanding quality of modelling, the subtle and reserved colouring and the empathic rendering of emotions.  
Philipp Jakob Straub was born into the Württenberg family of sculptors and moved to Vienna with his brother, Johann Baptist Straub (later court sculptor in Munich), in 1727. Philipp Jakob Straub studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1730 to 1733, at which time he settled in Graz. In Graz he worked on commissions for the church, the aristocracy and the middle class, both in wood and in stone. On stylistic grounds, research attributes to him an extensive oeuvre in Styria where he introduced the influence of Bavarian Rococo sculpture and the practices of stone sculpture from the court in Vienna.
9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.short_description: The high altar in the parish church of Egervár (c. 1730) contained tabernacle statues – two of which were *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* – and all of which were commissioned from Styria in 1757. Documents relating to count Széchenyi's relationship with the church and the artist helped to confirm the attribution of these works to Philipp Jakob Straub, a member of the South-German Straub family. Straub settled in Graz and brought fine Rococo sculpture to the Transdanubian region.

9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.name: *St. Donatus*
9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.description: At the end of the 17th century, the Imperial General Count Donat Heissler commissioned an altarpiece painting for the church of the Holy Virgin in Buda to commemorate his release from prison. Heissler was commander-in-chief of the imperial army fighting in Transylvania and died in 1696 in a battle against the Turks. He commissioned and donated this altarpiece painting dedicated to the patron saint of prisoners and of the city of Buda from 1724, St. Donatus, who appears as a Roman soldier. Angels floating above the clouds hold the signs of his martyrdom:  a knife and a vessel full of his blood. Below, Castle Hill in Buda is depicted, its tempestuous landscape hints at St. Donatus' role in protecting it.
9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.short_description: A Baroque altarpiece painting of St. Donatus against the stormy landscape backdrop of Castle Hill in Buda.

9ab90117-bb9a-5811-9c4c-57b0013aa1e6.obtention: Gifted to the Museum by the Church of the Holy Virgin in Buda.

9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.name: *Antependium with the Tribute of Continents and Imperial Countries to the Holy Family*
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.description: This colourful embroidery was executed as a “needle painting” and is set within an original gilded frame. An eventful scene opens out with a central motif of columned architecture with staircases and balustrades, and adoring female figures. At the bottom left, four girls kneel, with the coats of arms of the imperial Electors of the clergy who facilitated the foundation of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno. The Archbishops of Treves, Cologne and Mainz are represented by the coats of arms of Karel Kaspar von der Leyen (1652–1676), Maximilian Heinrich von Bayern (1650–1688) and Johann Philipp von Schönborn (1647–1673). Opposite, four girls kneel with the coats of arms of the imperial countries: Bavaria, Saxony, Brandenburg and Pfalz. In the centre are four female personifications of the continents, Asia, America, Africa and Europe, in precious attire. The women and a host of lay people of both sexes pay tribute to the Holy Family. The Virgin Mary is supervising the education of Jesus, while St. Joseph hands to the Pope – a personification of the Church – a sheet with the text *Ecclesiae Petenti Satisfiat*. The scene is crowned with the dove of the Holy Spirit. At the sides are monumental summerhouses with decorative vases and cartouches with the inscription *Ite ad Joseph* (Go to Joseph), while the Old Testament quotation (Gen 41:55) relates to the figure of St. Joseph of Nazareth. In combination with the text on the donated sheet, it elucidates the subject of the embroidered antependium emphasising the role of St. Joseph, patron saint of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno, as a righteous protector of the church and promoter of Divine will. Towards the horizon, various landscapes alternate on the antependium, valleys and hills dotted with dominant castles. The intricate layout of the embroidery may refer to a major event in the history of the Franciscan convent or it could commemorate the establishment and construction of the Convent Church of St. Joseph in 1651–1653.
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.short_description: The subject of the technically and artistically remarkable antependium is derived from the legends of St. Joseph, a popular saint of the Baroque period. It is one of only a few examples of the use of figurative embroidery in sacred art during the first half of the 18th century, and a specimen of monastery art.

9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.name: *Paulines at Prayer*
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.description:
Their hands clasped in prayer, the Pauline brothers kneel on a paved balustraded terrace in a garden in front of a row of vases on pedestals with flowers in them, with palm trees behind them arranged in shortened perspective. The perspective of the composition, based on two intersecting linear scenes, shows the vision of the patron of the Paulines and St Paul the Hermit in a cave on the lawn. The vision of the Patron of the Paulines depicts the Virgin Mary, St. John the Baptist and the *Agnus Dei* with His leg curved around a flag with a cross.  
The use of perspective, accentuated by the row of classical pedestals, evokes an earlier style. The foreshortening decreases the depth of the scene and emphasises the initial pair of brothers and the first pedestal, which brings them closer to the front of the painting. The morphology and typology of the Pauline brother figures, St Paul the Hermit and the ornamental motifs on the vases together with the flowers in them, suggest a date of around 1740, being elements of the Baroque style. The work is in the style of the lay brother and painter, Ivan Ranger. Ranger, regarded as one of Croatia's greatest Baroque painters is most famous for his frescoes, which he painted in enormous numbers. Ranger was already a trained artist when he arrived at the Lepoglava monastery from Tyrol. The Pauline Order accommodated a number of lay brothers in their monasteries, comprising painters, sculptors, cabinet-makers and other masters of the arts and crafts. They produced works for the interiors of churches and monasteries in the monastery workshops.  
Lepoglava was the largest and most important Pauline monastery in Croatia. It was the main centre for educational and cultural learning, with a Latin grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates. The Paulines, together with the Jesuits, played a key role in promoting Baroque art and culture in Croatia.
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.short_description: The altarpiece, depicting the Pauline brothers in a garden praying in front of flower vases, is probably the work of the lay brother and painter Ivan Ranger, a trained artist who came from Tyrol. Ranger – who joined the Pauline Order in Lepoglava and remained there until he died – is regarded as one of Croatia’s greatest Baroque painters. He is especially famous for his frescoes, which decorate many Pauline interiors as well as other churches and monasteries. The Lepoglava monastery was the main centre of the Pauline Order. It had a grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates. Together with the Jesuits, the Paulines played a key role in advancing Baroque art and culture in Croatia.

9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.obtention: The Diocesan Museum in Zagreb was founded in 1939 to safe-keep church artworks that for various reasons were in danger of devastation. This altarpiece was placed in the museum to preserve it.

9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.name: Sunflowers frame
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.description:
From an inventory of the properties of Vincenzo Bargellini, these pendant frames made in 1750 were originally made for holding mirrors, today they hold pictures. They were shown at an exhibition in Bologna in 1935 on Bolognese eighteenth-century art. At that time the frame was still holding a mirror.  
No mention is made of these frames in Vincenzo Bargellini's letters to Venice to commission furniture. Therefore, it is believed they were made in Bologna by local craftsmen following Roman and Venetian models.  
The high quality of the work is evident in the rich and naturalistic decoration. The sunflowers are an allusion to a particular destination.  
A frame similar to this pair is held in the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna; the evolution of this same style can be recognised in the frames made for the pictures by Marcantonio Franceschini exhibited in this same museum, made especially for the paintings in 1710–1711.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.short_description:
The extraordinary vivacity of this mirror frame testifies at a very early stage (1699) the great skill and the refined taste of Bolognese baroque carvers, who were looking at Rome and Venice for up to date ideas.  
The frame is dated and signed (JACINTO MONTEILTH FECIT1699). Unfortunately, there are no other occurrences of the carver’s name in objects or documents in Bologna. The style of the frame is similar to one in the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.holder: Museo di Arte Industriale e Galleria Davia Bargellini
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.method_for_datation: The frame is dated and signed (JACINTO MONTEILTH FECIT1699). Unfortunately, there are no other occurrences of the carver’s name in objects of documents in Bologna. The style of the frame is similar to that of one in the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.obtention: This frame together with its pendant is mentioned in the 1750 inventory of Vincenzo Bargellini, at that time it was holding a mirror. It is exhibited in the museum since 1924, after the convention between the Municipality of Bologna and the Opera pia Davia Bargellini (owner of the picture gallery and of some of the family furniture).

9dd60e86-bef2-5b84-bc64-d726595a61b1.name: Armillary sphere from the Grammar School, Varaždin
9dd60e86-bef2-5b84-bc64-d726595a61b1.description:
An armillary sphere used as an astrological instrument to teach the distances between planets and stars and to measure time in the Jesuit Grammar School in Varaždin. Engraved on the ring of the sphere are the signs of the Zodiac.  
The grammar school, founded by the Jesuit order in 1636, continued under the headship of the order until 1773 when Pope Clement XIV extinguished the order with his Bull of Suppression. The curriculum at the school was according to the Jesuit system and teaching was in Latin. Immediately after the suppression of the Jesuits, by decree of Empress Maria Theresia the Bishop of Zagreb, Josip Galjuf, took over the grammar school in Varaždin and other schools in Croatia and Slavonia. He appointed Anton Rajšp, former Jesuit and doctor of theology, as head of the grammar school. The Pauline order took over the school in 1776 but after suppression of the order by decree of Emperor Joseph II, Anton Rajšp became the head of the school again.

9de9a399-a1b2-585d-bb72-59083e988fb6.name: Franciscan Church and Monastery of Our Lady of Trsat
9de9a399-a1b2-585d-bb72-59083e988fb6.description:
The Baroque inventory of the Franciscan Church and Monastery of Our Lady of Trsat in Rijeka speaks eloquently of the milieus that influenced art and architecture in Croatia during the Baroque era:  the Central European artistic and cultural influence in the North, and Italian, mostly Venetian, in the South. Both influences met in Rijeka because of its close proximity to Italy and due to the fact that at the time the town was under the domain of the Habsburg Monarchy. The political connection between Rijeka and the capital of Styria, Graz, resulted in Giovanni Pietro de Pomis being commissioned by Stefano della Rovere (Captain of Rijeka between 1608 and 1638) to paint the altarpiece of St. Anne for a side-altar in the Church of Our Lady of Trsat. Stefano della Rovere played an important role in the revival of the city of Rijeka, strengthening its commercial links and settling military and political disputes between Venice and the court in Graz. The Altarpiece of St. Anne, commissioned to commemorate the death of Rovere's wife, is the work of Giovanni Pietro de Pomis, Ferdinand II's most respected artist and architect before the artist's transition to the Viennese court in 1633.  
In the 1630s and 40s, the Franciscan lay-brother painter from Switzerland, Serafin Schön, worked in the monastery in Trsat. The influence of 16th–17th-century Bavarian painting in Schön's characteristically brilliant colouring is clear, bearing a resemblance to that of Peter Candido or Antonio Maro Viani whose altarpiece paintings are in the Church of St. Michael the Archangel in Munich. Assumedly, therefore, prints were not Schön's only inspiration while he was painting the Trsat compositions.  
In the first decade of the 18th century, the Venetian painter, Cristoforo Tasca, appeared. Tasca, originally from Bergamo, was a pupil of Antonio Zanchi from whom he inherited the “*tenebroso*” style of painting. Between 1704 and 1714, he painted the Old Testament themes of *Manna from Heaven* and *Multiplication of the Loaves* for the monastery in Trsat, as well as a large ceiling painting the *Assumption of the Virgin* in the Summer Refectory. Above the triumphal arch in the church, Tasca painted the *Annunciation* and the *Transportation of the Holy House of Loreto to Trsat*.  
The three wooden side altars of around 1723 are by the Franciscan lay-brother sculptors of Tyrolean origin, Dionizije Hoffer and Ivo Schweiger. Their stylistic origins are discernable in the formal features of their works, which are markedly influenced by some of Tyrol's leading Baroque sculptors.
9de9a399-a1b2-585d-bb72-59083e988fb6.short_description: Founded initially in the 13th century, the Church and Monastery of Our Lady of Trsat is Croatia's oldest sanctuary. Dedicated to the Virgin Mary, it was built in 1291 in veneration of the legend of the transportation of the Holy House of Loreto from Jerusalem to Trsat in Rijeka. In the 15th century, the Church of Our Lady was built and the Franciscan Monastery alongside it; both were redesigned extensively during the following centuries. The inventory of the church demonstrates a development of style throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, revealing a wide range of different stylistic influences.
9de9a399-a1b2-585d-bb72-59083e988fb6.method_for_datation: The monument and its inventory are dated in archival sources and by the inscriptions.
9de9a399-a1b2-585d-bb72-59083e988fb6.bibliography:

Repanić-Braun, M., *Barokno slikarstvo u Hrvatskoj franjevačkoj provinciji sv*. *Ćirila i Metoda,* Zagreb, 2004.  
Baričević, D., *Barokno kiparstvo sjeverne Hrvatske*, Zagreb, 2008.
9de9a399-a1b2-585d-bb72-59083e988fb6.history: The founding of the Franciscan Church and Monastery on the hill of Trsat in Rijeka dates back to the 13th century, built in veneration of the legend of the transportation of the Holy House of Loreto from the Holy Land to Trsat in Rijeka. According to the legend, angels brought the Holy House to the Franciscan church and dedicated it to the Virgin Mary in 1291. Three years later, in 1294, the “Santa Casa” was again transported by angels to Recanati and, finally, in 1295, to Loreto. The church and monastery have both been renovated and extended several times since Count Martin Frankopan initiated the building of the Church of our Lady in the 15th century. In 1641, he had both church and monastery completely renovated in the Baroque style; the Baroque interior decoration spans the 17th and 18th centuries, with works of various stylistic origins.

9f186000-f429-588b-b1a7-58bcf82d6a8f.name: Queluz Royal Palace
9f186000-f429-588b-b1a7-58bcf82d6a8f.description: The original centre of the palace is located to the right of the square from where the palace expanded southwards. Mateus Vicente de Oliveira – the first architect to work on the new palace – began by designing a ceremonial façade on a receding rectangle; this opened up a second rectangular area. From here two concave and symmetrical wings form a Baroque square and a defining reception axis. As a result, despite its small dimensions, the building is a monumental ground-level palace. The façades are designed to be seen from the gardens.
9f186000-f429-588b-b1a7-58bcf82d6a8f.short_description: A summer palace belonging to the Portuguese court which developed around a former palace. From the outside, the main façade forms a semi-circular plan around a Neo-Classical statue of Queen Maria I by Joaquim José Aguiar. The interior has a U-shaped floor plan embracing a “French” style garden with other wings bordering the park.
9f186000-f429-588b-b1a7-58bcf82d6a8f.bibliography:
Ferro, I., O *Palácio de Queluz*, Lis­bon, 1997.  
Delaforce, A., Afonso, S. L., *Palácio de Queluz* – *jardins*, Lisbon, 1988.
9f186000-f429-588b-b1a7-58bcf82d6a8f.history: The fire at the Palace of the future King Pedro (the former palace of the Castelo Melhor family or “Corte Real” family) was providential in that the court had a self-interest in Queluz. Therefore, some time after 1747, building of the future Queluz Palace commenced. The configuration of the façades facing the Court of Honour and the Pênsil Garden date from this period. With a late Baroque and cosmopolitan style, the dimensions of the house are not large. When the young Pedro married Queen Maria I, the Palace assumed a state function and was adapted for court ceremonial use and as an occasional royal residence. In 1758, under the direction of Jean-Baptiste Robillion, the palace acquired a “French” ambiance. Jean François Cragnier, Pierre Larrie and Jacques Antoine Collin remodelled the “French-style” interior decoration of the ceremonial rooms assisted by great Portuguese masters, among whom the carver, Silvestre Faria Lobo, stands out. As a result, the building has no stylistic homogeneity, having taken on the Baroque and *Rocaille* styles with Neo-classical details.
9f186000-f429-588b-b1a7-58bcf82d6a8f.patrons: Casa do Infantado; Prince Pedro (future King Pedro III); King José I; Queen Maria I; King João VI

9f49f5dd-d459-5ea6-9096-89e2765a2369.name: Ospizio di San Michele
9f49f5dd-d459-5ea6-9096-89e2765a2369.description: The original nucleus, corresponding to the second block of the current building coming from Porta Portese, was developed on three floors with two lower side wings, where the refectory and workshops were located. Following the additions promoted by Innocent XII and his successors, the Hospice now has the shape of a very long parallelepiped aligned with the river Tiber, completely devoid of ornamentation. Inside, Carlo Fontana created a large central barrel-vaulted room overlooked by galleries with cells, arranged on different levels. Thanks to its articulation in three distinct parts, the separation between women, men and prisoners was guaranteed. The interventions carried out under Clement XI concerned the wing opposite the Tiber, towards the Church of Santa Maria dell’Orto, where the home for the elderly was established, divided into male and female sectors and provided with a large central courtyard.
9f49f5dd-d459-5ea6-9096-89e2765a2369.bibliography: Rolfi, S., “Ospizio di S. Michele”, *I principi della chiesa,* Milan: Edizioni Charta, 1998: 218–219.
9f49f5dd-d459-5ea6-9096-89e2765a2369.history:
The pontificate of Innocent XII (1691–1700) was characterized by a general moralizing tendency, like the abolition of papal nepotism and the fight against luxury and pomp that had pervaded the reign of his predecessors, especially that of Alexander VIII Ottoboni. The numerous social measures promoted by the pope and the push given to the creation of charitable institutions fit into this perspective. The new almshouse, the Hospice of St. Michael, had been already built at the time of Pope Innocent XI Odescalchi with the aim of offering a job to imprisoned or abandoned youth: indeed, in 1686, the so-called youth conservatory of San Michele a Ripa was built on the initiative of Carlo Tommaso Odescalchi on his own land near Porta Portese, in Trastevere, and the Port di Ripa Grande.  
In the workshops, located on the ground floor of the building, the youth learned and practiced the professions of shoemaker and carpenter. In 1695, under Innocent XII, wool mills were then created and, at the time of Clement XI (1700–21), the School of Tapestry.  
The original building, designed by Carlo Fontana and Mattia de’Rossi and completed in 1689, was smaller than the current one. In 1693 Innocent XII, having decided to also relocate the prisoners there, as well as the poor from the Hospice of St. Sixtus and the spinsters of the Lateran Hospice, raised the wings of the building.  
Further extensions took place between 1708 and 1709 and again in 1714 with Nicola Michetti, who took over from Fontana the direction of the works. Michetti raised the facade and modified the street level, lowering it to obtain shops and warehouses from what used to be the cellars. The hospice was extended again with Ferdinando Fuga (1734) and at the end of the century under Pius VI.

9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.name: *Pontifical Ceremonial Jug and Basin*
9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.description:
This oval basin, incised on its perimeter, is decorated with a strip of wrought ornamentation with festoons, grids, roses and a pair of *putti* heads. Its perimeter features a half-figure of St. John of Nepomuk, the patron saint of the person who commissioned the work. Opposite is a wrought oval label with a winged column representing the emblem of the Nová Říše Abbey, and engraved initials of the person who commissioned the piece, *N.A /W./P.N./C.G.* (*Nobilis Abbas \[Johannes Nepomucenus\] Wyminko, Praepositus Neureuschensis /C.G.*). Provost Jan Nepomuk Wyminko/Vejminko (c. 1683–1755) graduated from Hradisko, near Olomouc. He was provost of the Premonstratensian Abbey in Nová Říše from 1725 to 1732; in 1733 he was appointed the monastery's first abbot.  
The jug and basin are part of a luxurious set that included ceremonial cruets and a chalice (not preserved). The works, both in their shape and decoration, are derived from Augsburg models (for example, those created by masters of the Biller and Drentwett families). The jug serves for purification at the mass: the priest uses it to wash his hands before taking the blood and body of the Lord. Any spilt water is caught in the basin.  
Josef František Rossmayer probably took his apprenticeship in Prague and after journeyman's service abroad was appointed master in Olomouc in 1730. He made, among other things, candlesticks “in the Augsburg manner” for the main altar of the Sv. Kopeček Church, near Olomouc, a chalice with enamel figures of Christ's relatives for Brno cathedral and bindings for missals for the cathedral in Olomouc, in which he combined Augsburg and French models known from prints.
9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.short_description: The jug and basin are part of a luxurious set that included ceremonial cruets and a chalice. The pieces, from an Olomouc workshop, are derived from Augsburg models both in shape and decoration (compare, for example, those created by masters of the Biller and Drentwett families).

9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.name: Ship’s commode/oratory
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.description:
Oratories commonly belonged within a domestic context but an oratory desk was used either as a portable piece of furniture for religious purposes or as a cabinet-on-a-stand for reading. This particular oratory was used on board a ship and is the result of a cumulative commercial exchange among merchants who travelled via existing Portuguese trade routes to overseas colonies and ports or to north or north-western Europe. This is why it is probable that the ship's commode would have been influenced by several artistic styles: from Coromandel (the south-eastern coast of the Indian Peninsula), Chinese folding screens (*Henan*), or English Japanned furniture.  
Designed by Gaspar Ferreira and Manuel Silva, the commode was built to enable sailors and passengers to practice their religious routines on board ship. Probably commissioned by King D. João V, it is composed of two parts: the inferior part consists of three drawers and a desk with an oblique lid; while the superior section is shaped like a cupboard with a gabled segmental arch topped by the royal coat of arms.  
Carved and sculpted urns with flares decorate the top edges. Painted in bright red lacquer it has black decorative tablets and gilded iconographic motifs or *chinoiseries* – Chinese scenes. Both the design and ornamentation are characteristic of the so-called D. João V style. On the inside of the cupboard is an oratory with the following figures: St. Anthony of Lisbon on the right and St. Barbara on the left flanking Christ Crucified. The inside of the doors are painted with scenes of the Passion of Christ (Christ with the Cross; Lord of Cana Verde on the right; Christ tied to the Column and the Resurrection of Christ on the left).
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.short_description: A large commode/oratory with a cupboard, for use on board ship. The black decorative tablets are decorated with vegetal elements, while Chinese scenery – known as *chinoiserie* – decorates the larger panels.

9fdbb7de-267f-5e7e-bd02-0d31db272651.name: St. Martinho de Tibães Monastery
9fdbb7de-267f-5e7e-bd02-0d31db272651.description:
The Monastery is composed of a large building with a church, cloisters, courtyards and some monastic areas or adjoining wings. There is also a walled convent that includes gardens, an agricultural area and a forest. The church was built between 1628 and 1661 to the plans of Manuel Álvares and Friar João Turriano. “Plain” in style, its dimensions are huge. The interior decoration is notable for its decorative woodcarving designed and carved by Friar Cipriano da Cruz Sousa, André Soares and Friar José de Santo António Vilaça. The importance of Tibães Monastery is due also to its role as a “workshop-school” for a group of woodcarvers, sculptors, architects, master masons, carpenters, and other artists working in the north-west of the Peninsula.  
The monastic enclosure is unique because of the forest, large rural farm and Baroque garden. The garden has monumental fountains with a remarkable hagiographic and allegoric iconography and also has some important hydraulic pieces that are still in operation. It stands out as a unique example of Baroque monastic garden design.
9fdbb7de-267f-5e7e-bd02-0d31db272651.short_description: St. Martinho de Tibães Monastery is composed of four main parts: the church, monastery and adjoining ensemble, the ruins and enclosure. The church was rebuilt between 1628 and 1661 to the plans of Manuel Álvares and Friar João Turriano. The interior decoration is notable, mainly composed of gilt woodcarving, designed and carved by Friar Cipriano da Cruz Sousa, André Soares and Friar José de Santo António Vilaça.

9fdbb7de-267f-5e7e-bd02-0d31db272651.history: The monastery was founded in the 12th century and rebuilt between the 17th century and the 18th century, when important works of reconstruction were once again undertaken. With the dissolution of the religious orders in Portugal between 1833 and 1834, the monastery was abandoned and all its assets sold at public auction. In 1864 it was acquitted by the Portuguese state.

9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.name: *St. Peter Freed from Prison*
9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.description:
The work describes an episode in the life of Peter told in the Acts of the Apostles that took place during the unbridled persecution exercised by Herod. Imprisoned and guarded by two soldiers, the apostle is freed by an angel, who invites him to get up and guides him to safety outside the city walls without anyone seeing him. This miraculous feat is described using a basic but unusual composition, eliminating all characters other than the two protagonists. Foreshortening at the bottom of the painting brings the feet and the hand chained to the stump into the foreground, and the low viewpoint highlights the sudden appearance of the angel, who practically inspires in the viewer the same wonderment we see on the face of the saint, ragged and tired, on being woken so unexpectedly.  
In the 1790 inventory of the Borghese collection, the painting was described as the work of “Monsù Valentin”. The piece reworks some ideas typical of Caravaggism, such as realism based on a few details and the use of light as a tool for building the scene. The angel stretches out towards Peter and, rather than floating, appears to rest on a thick blanket of clouds, as if he is actually ready to lift up the old apostle. The Lombard artist's training was somewhat fragmented, taking him first to Rome, then to Venice, before joining Francesco Albani, one of the painters who best represents Bolognese classicism. Around the middle of the century, in 1656 and 1657, he also worked with Pietro da Cortona on the decoration of the Gallery of Alexander VII in the Quirinal Palace, becoming, along with Pietro Testa (“il Lucchesino”) and Nicolas Poussin, one of the main exponents of the Neo-Venetian styles of Roman Baroque painting.
9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.short_description: The painter – a follower of Caravaggio – was first influenced by Francesco Albani from Bologna and later by Pietro da Cortona. The lowered point of view highlights the sudden descent of the angel, inspiring in the viewer the same wonderment that can be seen on the face of the saint, who is ragged and exhausted in his sudden awakening.
9fdcf747-a0f7-5bde-8142-f71208183658.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.name: Vojković Palace
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.description: The Late Baroque palace occupied the sites of three older plots. Although the remains of the older houses bring about certain irregularities, the architect created a well-worked out spatial organisation within the framework of the three-winged, U-shaped ground plan. The covered passageway or entrance on the ground floor, and the hall that surmounts it in the same format on the top floor, placed the whole length of the entrance wing on the central axis, giving the building its particular quality. Two symmetrical stairways ascend to small vestibules either side of the entrance to the hall. The fact that here, unlike contemporary Croatian palaces, the characteristic passageway along the courtyard façade was omitted, the double sequences of rooms along the side-wings compensate for this anomaly. The palace achieves equal architectural value exteriorly. The central entranceway passage and hall on the façade are emphasised by their projections, and what is more, the hall achieves independence in the roof area too, emphasised by a scalloped, contoured gable. The elements of articulation, particularly on the window frames and the pilasters, are characterised by the plasticity and dynamics of the Late Baroque, and their enhanced grouping on the central projection – accented by the portal of the undulating gable – is in line with the entire architectural concept of the palace. In this context, an important part is played by the urban location of the palace, which has an entrance façade facing the street that leads to the main square of the Upper Town (that of St. Mark ), while it is also located at the city's edge so that it includes a spacious garden. Thus, the palace contributes to the Baroque opening up of medieval fortified cities and characterises the Baroque synthesis of urban and out-of-town residences and distinctive garden palaces.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.short_description: The Late Baroque Vojković Palace in Zagreb's Upper Town is characterised by a well-worked-out organisation of space and volume that can be described as one of the most opulent aristocratic residences of the time in inland Croatia. The characteristic Baroque three-wing ground plan is organised around a central axis, with an entrance passageway on the ground floor and a hall on the first floor. Particular architectural prominence is given to the hall externally with an intricate gable projection. When the surrounding parkland is included, the building presents a typically Baroque unification of city- and country-house, known as a garden palace.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.type: Secular, three-winged palace with a central hall
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents and stylistic features.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.bibliography:
Horvat, A., (ed) “Barok u kontinentalnoj Hrvatskoj” in *Barok u Hrvatskoj*, Zagreb, 1982, pp. 1–381.  
Dobronić, L., *Palača Hrvatskog povijesnog muzeja 1764–2004*, Zagreb, 2004.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.history: The Lieutenant Colonel of the cavalry troop at Banska Krajina (Border), Sigismund Volković, commissioned the palace in 1764. The Volković residence was the meeting place of the Zagreb elite and the venue for theatrical performances and concerts, particularly after the fire in Varaždin in 1776 when the *ban* (viceroy's) government returned to Zagreb's Upper Town and the nobility followed suit. Although the owner twice tried to sell the palace to the Zagreb County in the 19th century, the palace changed noble owners several times – the Oršićes, the Kulmers and finally the Rauch family. Today the palace houses the Croatian History Museum.
keywords: Zagreb, Vojković Palace, Late Baroque, three-winged ground plan, façade projection with prominent gable
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.author: Katarina Horvat-Levaj

a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.name: Church of St. Ignatius, *Triumph of St. Ignatius* ceiling fresco
a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.description: It is one of the largest frescoed vaults in the world, extending over a length of over forty meters. Inside the fake architectural framework, consisting of colonnades and arches supporting a broken frame that appears of the same height of the nave, the figure of Christ with the cross stands out in the dazzling central empty space. From him a ray of light stems, hitting St. Ignatius, the closest person to Christ and placed at the top of a pyramid of clouds and angelic figures. Four other light rays radiate from Ignatius, reaching the corners at the base of the fresco, below the false coupled columns, where the personifications of the four continents Europe, Asia, Africa and America are depicted. The goal of the fresco is thus clear: the exaltation of Ignatius and the missionary activity of the Jesuits, enlivened by the divine light which, starting from Christ and reflected by Ignatius, radiates to the whole world. The personifications of the then known continents are four young women who each have a different animal as their attribute, according to the tradition as formulated in the famous *Iconologia* by Cesare Ripa (1593): the horse for Europe, who holds the terrestrial globe to symbolize her dominion on the world; the camel for Asia, with her arms outstretched to the sky to signify that all religions originated there; the crocodile for Africa, a brunette queen holding elephant tusks; the puma for America, armed with a spear and with coloured feathers on her head. Under each of them the personifications of Vices and Errors are seen falling down or chained, defeated by the evangelizing mission of the Jesuits. In addition to Ignatius, other saints of the Order are depicted in the sky, such as Francis Xavier, Francis Borgia and Aloysius de Gonzaga. The influence of the brightness of Venetian painting, particularly Veronese’s, and of the monumental effects achieved by Pietro da Cortona in the vault of Palazzo Barberini are very tangible in this immense composition. Moreover, it is possible to recognize the influence of Roman painting of the late 17th century, such as the vault in the Galleria of Palazzo Colonna by Giovanni Coli and Filippo Gherardi.
a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.short_description: Masterpiece of illusionist Late Baroque painting: the multitude of figures which seem to be freely floating in the space is strictly ruled by the laws of perspective. Example of *quadratura* or perspective painting recently brought to Rome by Enrico Haffner.
a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.bibliography:
Strinati, C., “Gli affreschi della chiesa di Sant'Ignazio a Roma”, in De Feo V. and Martinelli V. (eds), *Andrea Pozzo,* Milan: 1996, 66–93.  
Fabrini N., *La chiesa di Sant'Ignazio in Roma,* Rome: 1952.
a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.history:
In 1626 Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi, nephew of Pope Gregory XV, sponsored the construction of a large church dedicated to Saint Ignatius, the founder of the Jesuit order (he had been canonized by Ludovisi’s uncle in 1622) and promoter of the adjacent Collegio Romano, an institution modelled after the University of Paris, where Gregory XV himself had studied.  
The works, directed in this phase by the Jesuit architect Orazio Grassi, continued until the end of the 17th century, when Andrea Pozzo, a Jesuit architect and painter from Trento, who had studied at the Collegio Romano, was commissioned in 1685 to paint a fake dome on canvas, since erecting a real one was considered impossible due to static and logistical problems. The perspective dome gained Pozzo success and fame, and thus he later received the commission for the frescoes of the presbytery and the vault of the nave too.
a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.copyright: Copyright images: Archivio fotografico Soprintendenza Speciale PSAE e Polo Museale della Città di Roma.
a11b2e57-9c11-512a-8371-c9788eb14109.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.name: *The Saints Mark, St. Anthony Abbot and St. Sebastian*
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.description: The painting was commissioned to Ubaldo for the church of St. Mark in Vigorso di Budrio (Bo). Saint Mark, clad in bright red is shown looking for inspiration for the Gospel, next to him is a lion, the emblem of the saint. In the foreground St. Sebastian is tied to a column, his body pierced by an arrow while an angel is handing him the palm of martyrdom. Nearby is St. Anthony Abbot with his classic attributes; the fire, the bell and the pig. The composition is very simple and clear. The light comes from one direction and symbolises the light of God to which the evangelist points. The painter is inspired by the great Bolognese school, in particular Guercino and Ludovico Carracci, and to the Venetian school.
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.short_description: The painting shows St. Mark writing the gospel, St. Sebastian tied to the column and St. Anthony the Abbot.
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.holder: Church of St. Gervasius and Protasius
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.method_for_datation: The step in the lower middle is inscribed “U.G.F. 1773” (Ubaldus Gandulfius fecit 1773).
a16290fe-5502-55e2-82db-8e2fe1c592e5.obtention: The painting has been moved from the original church to the present one for safety reasons.

a1adff22-8dc6-5b01-a64c-2281cef78bdf.name: Archbishop’s Palace of Veszprém (since 1993)
a1adff22-8dc6-5b01-a64c-2281cef78bdf.description:
The two-storey palace has a U-shaped layout. Its facade stands on the edge of a cliff on Castle Hill and faces east. Fellner incorporated the remains of the medieval palace and the 18th-century palace into the south wing of the new building, and built the north wing to match it. The two wings are linked by the east wing, which is actually the main wing of the palace. The U-shaped layout chosen by Fellner uses the limited space afforded by the narrow building plot on the edge of Castle Hill very effectively.  
A driveway leads to the central risalit of the main facade crowned with a broad balcony with wrought-iron railings. Above the balcony on the central axis of the middle risalit, there is a very high arched window embraced by pilasters and pillars, and crowned with a tympanum framing Bishop Ignác Koller's coat of arms. An urn is mounted on the attic above the tympanum in between two *putti* surrounded by decorative garlands. The two side-wings are heavily projected; their facades separated by mouldings and articulated by three square-shaped windows on the first floor, and three arched windows on the ground floor. Above the windows, in the middle, are tympanums with coats of arms in their mid-sections. The windows either side are decorated with garlands underneath their drip mouldings. On the eastern facade at the rear of the building, the central risalit juts out forcefully. The ground-floor risalit is articulated by an arcade, which has a broad balcony above it with wrought-iron railings. Above the three arched windows of the first floor, a tympanum can be seen.  
At the top of the Baroque central stairway leading from the entrance hall, there is a magnificent suite of rooms decorated with works of art. Some of the furniture, decorative and everyday objects are from the 18th century, others are late Renaissance or 19th century. The fresco, *Holy Trinity with Adam and Eve and the Ancient Fathers* in the bishop's private chapel, is the work of Johann Cimbal (1772); it is an Allegory of Salvation, Faith and Crucifixion that leads to the redemption of mankind. The main hall on the first floor (used as a dining hall, and today as a reception hall) has walls decorated with the paintings by Cimbal also (including the *Four Seasons* of 1772). As of 1768, Cimbal received several large-scale commissions in the Hungarian Kingdom, including altarpieces and frescoes for several churches, and the murals of the Bishop's Summer Residence in Sümeg (landscapes from 1769–1771).  
The walls in one of the reception rooms are decorated with a sequence of engravings covered with glass, purchased by Bishop Ignác Koller in Paris in 1772; the glass was produced at Bakony glass foundry. The walls of the bishop's private library are covered with 18th-century wood panelling and furnished with a series of portraits of the Bishops of Veszprém by various artists.  
The Episcopal Library, founded by Bishop Márton Padányi Bíró, was formerly housed in the Bishop's Palace in Sümeg. Ignác Koller continued to expand the library collection in Veszprém.
a1adff22-8dc6-5b01-a64c-2281cef78bdf.short_description: The Archbishop’s (former Bishop’s) Palace was designed by Jakab Fellner by order of Bishop Ignác Koller. The palace was built between 1765 and 1776. The chapel and the main hall of the building are decorated with frescoes by Johann Cimbal.
a1adff22-8dc6-5b01-a64c-2281cef78bdf.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources.

a1adff22-8dc6-5b01-a64c-2281cef78bdf.history:
The Diocese of Veszprém, the first and oldest diocese in Hungary, was founded by Géza, Grand Prince of the Magyars, between 966 and 1000. The *Comitatus* (administrative county) of Veszprém had maintained a bishop's residence since medieval times, but it was confiscated and used for military purposes during the Turkish wars. During this time the bishop resided mainly in Sümeg, but the building there was demolished in 1713 so, in 1733, Bishop Ádám Acsády built a new two-storey palace.  
The palace was never used by Bishop Acsády's successor, Ignác Koller Nagymányai, Bishop of Veszprém and *Comes* (Leader of) the *Comitatus* of Veszprém, for he considered it inadequate, and entrusted Jakab Fellner – recommended to him by his contemporary Bishop Károly Esterházy – with the design of a new and more fitting bishop's palace in 1763.  
At first, to cut costs, the bishop considered erecting the palace on the flat plot below the Castle and not on the site of the medieval bishop's palace on Castle Hill. In the end, though, he decided that Castle Hill was a more fitting and elegant site for the bishop's palace and so the building was erected there, with its eastern facade on the edge of a cliff. While Fellner supervised, the construction team was led by master stonemason, Vencel Hauensteiner. The foundation stone was laid in 1765, and the building was complete by 1772 except for the interior decoration.  
Bishop Ignác Koller lived long enough to move into the palace, but after his death, his brother, Ferenc, a counsellor of the court chamber, requested that Queen Maria Theresia grant him permission to continue construction at the bishop's expense. The palace was consecrated in 1776.  
In 1993 the Archdiocese of Veszprém received the Episcopal (Metropolitan) title, and the Bishop's Palace was renamed the Archbishop's Palace.

a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.name: Holy Trinity Column, Olomouc
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.description: The column, on a hexagonal ground plan, is 35 m tall and has a chapel on the ground floor. It celebrates the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. The sculpted decoration of the column consists of 12 sandstone statues of light-bearers, 12 reliefs with half-figures of the apostles, reliefs with allegories of Faith, Hope and Charity, a sculpture of the Assumption in the central part and, topmost, a sculpture of the Holy Trinity. There are 18 figures of the saints, including the patron saints of the country, preachers (John Capistranus was active in Olomouc) and martyrs. The Jesuit saint, Aloysius Gonzaga, was canonised at the time of the column’s construction (1726). Apart from gilding, the column was originally decorated with white marble.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.short_description: The column presents the largest grouping of Baroque statues within a single sculpture in Central Europe. In 2000 it was listed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site. The column celebrates the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. The top sculpture of Christ the Saviour and God the Father, the ruler of the world, opens with Archangel Michael, symbol of the eternal struggle with heresy. The work, by several Olomouc masters, is one of the last memorial columns to be built under the Habsburg monarchy in several towns from the second half of the 17th century onwards.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.method_for_datation: The construction of the column is recorded in Town Council minutes; contracts with individual craftsmen have also been preserved.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.bibliography:
Pavel Zatloukal (ed), *Horní náměstí v Olomouci*, Olomouc, 1995.  
Miloš Stehlík, Slohová podstata sochařského díla Ondřeje Zahnera, *Opuscula Historiae Artium*, F 42, 1998, pp. 7–26.  
Marek Perůtka (ed), *Sloup Nejsvětější Trojice v Olomouci*, Olomouc, 2001.  
Miloš Stehlík, in Lubomír Slavíček (ed), *Josef Winterhalder d. J. (1743 Vöhrenbach – 1807 Znojmo). Maulbertschs bester Schüler*, Langenargen–Brno, 2009.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.history: The Holy Trinity Column was built as a counterpart to the Plague Column of the Virgin Mary in an adjacent square on the initiative of V. Render, a local master stonemason. He oversaw the construction and also contributed preliminary finance. Before his death in 1733, Render built the first-floor chapel. The invasion of the Prussian army in 1741 delayed the construction for which several local masters had joined forces. F. Sattler was responsible for some of the sculpted decoration of the column, with the larger part executed by O. Zahner. It is one of the last memorial columns to be built under the Habsburg monarchy in several towns from the second half of the 17th century onwards. Consecration of the column by the Bishop of Olomouc and Cardinal Troyer was conducted in the presence of Empress Maria Theresa and her husband František I of Lorraine. In 2000 the column was listed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site.

Salzburg – 1773 Olomouc), Wolfgang Träger (1714 Pilsen – 1763 Olomouc), Jan Michael Scherhauf (1724 Wels – 1792 Olomouc)

a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.name: Chiesa dell'Assunzione
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.description:
The sober but elegant façade of the church overlooks a square and acts as a sort of scenographic wing for one of the main streets. It is a central plan church with an octagonal tiburium. The brickwork façade is made of two orders linked by two elegant volutes, a typical baroque feature.  
Thanks to the hemispherical apse the interior looks quite spacious and it is marked by white stucco columns; between them open small choirs with refined stucco frames.  
The altars date from the end of the eigtheenth to the beginning of the nineteenth century The apse is Neoclassic.
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.short_description:
This church was renovated by the architect Alfonso Torreggiani. It is one of the many churches in the diocese of Bologna located in the small towns outside the city and rebuilt or restyled during the XVIII century.  
Local late baroque church architecture is characterised by a sober style, lacking painted decorations, but enriched with some structural features, in this case, the small, elegant lateral choirs in the interior.
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.bibliography: Samoggia, L., *Veder lo dolce piano. Guida di Medicina e del suo territorio*, Medicina, 1994.
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.history: The small church was commissioned by the local Brotherhood of the Assumption. It was designed by Alfonso Torreggiani in 1748 and was built in the following years.
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.architects: Alfonso Torreggiani (Budrio, 1682 – Bologna, 1764) together with Carlo Francesco Dotti. He perfectly employs the so called Barocchetto style: the most elegant and brilliant artistic expression of the local late Baroque.
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.copyright: Copyright images: Ufficio Beni culturali ecclesiastici della diocesi di Bologna.
keywords: Religious architecture; stucco decorations; barocchetto
a3dbcd5e-444c-5eb7-b75a-b12e4e2d351c.author: Marta Forlai

a40d3450-a81b-50ab-977f-7fb4b482ca51.name: *Winter Landscape with Skaters, a Country Cottage and a Tower*
a40d3450-a81b-50ab-977f-7fb4b482ca51.description:
The picture was inspired by a 17th-century Dutch painting employing a motif of a tree contrasting with light effects. The magic of this cabinet, or study, image lies in the view from above and the elaborate rendering, facilitated by the base, a smooth copper plate. Epic, occasionally anecdotal motifs, idylls of village life, combine with the romantic representations of a tower and a village church. This combination of landscape and genre painting is rooted in the Scandinavian tradition of attention to detail and meticulous analysis of reality. Yet the realism and inherent rationalism of this picture may also be perceived as an “unattainable ideal”, adding refined descriptiveness to an inner emotional concept to achieve a perfect world that is far from reality.  
Dutch painting provided something of a template for technique, leading to a precise and fine style. In the mid-18th century, the Vienna Academy opened “Dutch-style” courses for landscape painting, and in 1768 the first landscape school was established in Vienna, typically enough at the Copperplate Engraving Academy, where emphasis was placed on technique and detailed study from nature.  
Dutch “Golden Age” painting is associated with the ostensible values of high 18th-century society: communality, morality, co-existence with nature, objectivity, and the beauty of the mundane. Dutch landscape art showed the countryside “true to life”; rural motifs were understood as images of human nature. Pictures reminiscent of Dutch 17th-century paintings were particularly sought-after for the decoration of “cabinets”, or studies, as they were deemed appropriate both to antique modes of room décor and period taste. The pictures were hung in such a way as to encourage close examination by the viewer, who should be immersed in the picture distinguishing even minutiae including brush strokes and the artist's technique, thereby discovering new details and reading the stories conveyed.
a40d3450-a81b-50ab-977f-7fb4b482ca51.short_description: The cabinet picture was inspired by 17th-century Dutch painting. Its magic lies in the view from above and the elaborate rendering facilitated by the base, a smooth copper plate. Transferring reality into a lyrical world, the painting creates an idyllic atmosphere.
a40d3450-a81b-50ab-977f-7fb4b482ca51.method_for_datation: The picture was determined by a style analysis carried out by Dr. Vlasta Kratinová. Ferg was first apprenticed to his father and later to J. Orient in Vienna. In 1718 he travelled to Germany, visiting Leipzig and Braunschweig. In 1724 the artist came to London, where he died in poverty.
a40d3450-a81b-50ab-977f-7fb4b482ca51.obtention: Acquired in 1949 from the Biskupice u Jevíčka Chateau.
keywords: Cabinet; landscape; art; genre painting
a40d3450-a81b-50ab-977f-7fb4b482ca51.author: Zora Wörgötter

a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.name: Oršić Palace
a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.description:
By way of its organisation of space and volume, and its relationship with the surrounding outlying parkland, Oršić Palace occupies a leading position in the Late Baroque architecture of inland Croatia. In its individual typological features, the palace bears the stamp of intimacy. Within the wider context of its geographic location and the period in which it was built the palace reflects a kind of Late Baroque revival, revealing innovations that were brought into Central European architecture by some of the great names of the High Baroque such as Fischer von Erlach and Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt.    
This is a palace with an oval-shaped, pavilion-concept central hall. These aesthetically articulated stylistic features are married with traditional elements of a centuries-old feudal tradition in Hrvatsko Zagorje.  
Built within extensive grounds, the two-storey palace features a three-winged, U-shaped ground plan, with a central zone and corner projections emphasised by their volume. In line with this axial concept is the formation of the central entranceway on the ground floor (flanked by a staircase), and the oval dome-ceilinged hall on the first floor, which rises up into the roof zone and forms a prominent, convex projection on the façade.  
Near the courtyard, the traditional passageway was retained but was opened up with arcades and, apart from the central hall, within the sequences of rooms along the external façade, only the private chapel at the end of the lateral wing stands out. The plastic articulation of the palace is in keeping with an accepted organisation of space and volume. Thus the convex façade projection is emphasised by a portal on the ground floor and a large row of pilasters on the first floor, while the same space inside is characterised by the articulation of *trompe l'œil* fresco windows within which are painted landscapes. How the surrounding landscape may have looked after the gradual devastation of the environment is calculable by studying the surviving plan of the park. In addition to a standard Baroque-style, axially placed avenue approach the palace grounds contain Romantic, organically designed plantations, walks and water features.  
These stylistic and typological features suggest a refined client and a knowing and sensitive architect at work, who were able as the Baroque era waned, to call once again on the supreme achievements of Viennese secular architecture: the well-known Imperial Library in the Hofburg (1722), a supreme example of an intricate Central European building with a central oval hall.
a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.short_description: Oršić Palace in Gornja Bistra represents Baroque palaces at the peak of their development in inland Croatia. Within the framework of three-winged complexes organised around a central axis, the concept of the Hildebrandt pavilion is expressed in the central zone of the palace where the roof of the main hall is not only raised higher but with its oval, convex form is made even more prominent on the facade. The rich plastic articulation and *trompe l'œil* window frescoes, together with the radial disposition of the fenestration, makes the palace the entire focus of the surrounding parkland.
a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents and stylistic features.
a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.bibliography:
Marković, V., *Barokni dvorci Hrvatskog zagorja*, Zagreb, 1975, pp. 31–35; 102–104.  
Obad-Šćitaroci, M., *Perivoji i dvorci Hrvatskog zagorja*, Zagreb, 1989, pp. 57–60.

a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.history: Vice-marshal Krsto Oršić II built the palace on his estate, which is on the western slopes of Medvednica not far from Zagreb.
a447deea-11d8-55f7-beea-e00f1a38c54f.architects: Unknown architect and fresco painter; painter: Franz Anton Maulbertsch (1724–1796)
