a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.name: Parish Church of Our Lady of the Snow
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.description:
The most valuable part of the church is its interior furnishing. The illusionist wall painting (1740–1743) is a highly accomplished work by the Paulist painter, Ivan Krstitelj Ranger, from Tyrol. Along with scenes relating to the titular saint, Mary, Ranger painted the ceilings and walls of the church with numerous saintly and allegorical figures as well as scenes from the Old and New Testaments. Although the pulpit has been identified as the work of the Graz sculptor Joseph Schokotnigg, it is stylistically reminiscent of Johann Baptist Straub's of 1730 in Schwarzspanierkirche in Vienna (today in Laxenburg Church). The same sculptor is ascribed the altars of St. Joseph and St. Barbara (1742–1743; gilded 1761), located alongside the triumphal arch of the church; an analogy is noted in the very distinctive compositional approach, similar to that seen in the Altar of the Immaculate Conception in Krakaudorf (Styria). The architecture and decoration of the high altar of 1743 is more traditional. With the exception of the earlier statue of *Mary the Immaculate* in the central intercolumniation (by the local sculptor, Ivan Pittner and derivative of the earlier high altar of 1729), the remaining sculpture is related stylistically to the work of Philipp Jakob Straub.  
The side chapel altars are more modest architecturally and hold works of the local sculptor, Ivan Adam Rosemberger, among others. There are some works connected with J. Schokotnigg's oeuvre (*St. John Nepomuk* and *St. Francis Xavier* on the Altar of the Holy Rosary of around 1743–1744), and some by F. J. Straub (*St. Andrew*, *St. Stephen* and *St. James* on the Altar of St. Stephen).  
Although more modest in terms of sculptural achievement, the interior of the Church of Our Lady of the Snow was completed with the addition of the choir rail in 1742. Here, sculptures of the Annunciation have been identified as the work of Zagreb sculptor, Joseph Weinacht. Finally, the *Pietà* group placed in a niche on the church façade (end of the 17th century) is by the Varaždin sculptor, Ivan Jakob Altenbach. All of which gives insight into the broad range and quality of Baroque sculpture in Croatia – comprising works that range from those created by top Central European artists to the more modest works of local and domestic sculptors.
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.short_description: The interior of the Pilgrimage Church of Our Lady of the Snow is among the most complete, representative and beautiful Baroque interiors in northern Croatia. With the harmony of the motifs, the wall painting and the church furnishing, it is an outstanding example of a Baroque *Gesamtkunstwerk*, or complete work of art. It was furnished and decorated in the 1740s, mainly due to donations from the Croatian aristocracy, who commissioned the region's leading artists.
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.type: Religious, monastic church and interior furnishing
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.method_for_datation: Archival sources, a description of the church in 1758, and a date on the high altar.
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.bibliography:
Vukičević-Samaržija, D., *Gotičke crkve Hrvatskog zagorja*, Zagreb, 1993.  
Mirković, M., "Zidno slikarstvo u kontinentalnoj Hrvatskoj", in *Hrvatska i Europa: kultura, znanost i umjetnost, sv. III.: Barok i prosvjetiteljstvo (XVII-XVIII stoljeće)*, Zagreb, 2003, pp. 663–674.  
Baričević, D., *Barokno kiparstvo sjeverne Hrvatske*, Zagreb, 2008.
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.history: Countess Elizabeta Keglević commissioned the church in around 1676 on the foundations of an older Gothic building. Probably with the help of donations from under-governor Adam Najšić, it was given the Baroque treatment in 1739 when the chapels and sacristy were added to it and the covered walkway was built. The wall painting and inventory of the church date to the 1740s. The pulpit, erected in 1742 with contributions from the parishioners and constructed under the auspices of parish priest, Pavel Kunek, has polychroming and gilding undertaken in 1743, thanks to a donation from Second Lieutenant Ignac Bedeković. While the local community financed the pulpit, representatives of the Croatian aristocracy were among the donors for the rest of the furnishing, as detailed above under “patrons”.
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.patrons: The parish priest, Pavao Kunek, and parishioners (pulpit); under-governor Baltazar Bedeković and Helena Rozalija Somogy (high altar), Count Ivan Franjo Čikulin (Altar of St. Joseph), Zagreb under-sheriff Nikola Vojković (Altar of St. Barbara), Archbishop of Kalocsa, Count Gabrijel Herman Patačić of Zajezda (Altar of the Holy Rosary), Bishop Stjepan Puc (Altar of St. Stephen Protomartyr)
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.architects: Painters: Ivan Krstitelj (Johann Baptist) Ranger (1700–1753); sculptors: Joseph Schokotnigg (active 1700–1755), Ivan Adam Rosemberger (d. 1758), Ivan Pittner (active c. 1721–1745), the circle of sculptor Filip (Philipp) Jakob Straub (1706–1774), Joseph Weinacht (active 1744–1750), Ivan Jakob Altenbach (active c. 1675–1678)
keywords: Belec, Ivan Krstitelj Ranger, Joseph Schokotnigg, Ivan Adam Rosemberger, Ivan Pittner, Filip (Philipp) Jakob Straub, Johann Baptist Straub, wall painting, sculpture, altar, pulpit
a4a60e43-6d75-5cd4-a151-56c32467ac05.author: Vlasta Zajec

a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Gall
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.description: The ground plan of the Weer church can largely be traced back to that of its Late Gothic predecessor, with a somewhat retracted choir and a 5/8 choir termination and hall nave. The interior is characterised by the systematically arranged pilaster walls with powerful entablature throughout. The vault above it is divided by high formerets (wall-ribs) resulting in four arches which appear to support the illusionistic painted cupolas above the choir and nave. The master builder, who long remained unknown, has now been identified as Michael Umlauf, a former employee of Franz de Paula Penz.
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.short_description: The extremely plain building with its gothic tower situated at the edge of the village holds a surprise in store with its splendid interior, most notably the large cupola frescos from Zeiller. The relatively austere architecture is moderated by the Rococo stuccowork, while the altar décor is executed in the rich style of the Late Baroque.
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.type: Ecclesiastical architecture (parish church), originally a succursal church
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.bibliography: Harb, R., *Pfarrkirche zum hl. Gallus in Weer*, Salzburg 1995 (= Christliche Kunststätten Österreichs, No. 264).
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.history: Weer, first elevated to the status of a parish in 1954, was originally a branch of the parish of Kolsass and was under the administration of Fiecht Monastery near Schwaz. The first church, belonging to a farm, dates from the 8th century. It is assumed that a new building was erected in the 13th century. In the last third of the 15th century a larger Late Gothic church was erected. The tower in the southern corner of the choir and the choir’s foundations were incorporated into the new Baroque building of 1778 which was consecrated on 5 July 1781.
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.architects: Architecture: Johann Michael Umhauser (1731–1784); frescos and altarpieces: Franz Anton Zeiller (1716–1794)
keywords: Late Baroque; Rococo; parish church; hall church; ceiling paintings
a4fa79fe-9566-5ada-9e76-a7cb473d338d.author: Frank Purrmann

a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.name: Church of San Girolamo della Carità, Spada Chapel
a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.description:
The most spectacular element of the chapel consists of its walls, entirely covered with intarsia alternated with marble slabs that imitate damask, in antique yellow for the vegetal decorations and for the emblems of the Spada (lilies, stars and swords, in the upper band) and in dark onyx for the mirrors, made by Giovan Battista Scala, known as il Napoletano (the Neapolitan), Giovanni Maria della Monaca and Giovanni Somazzi. The traditional balustrade is here replaced by two kneeling angels holding a jasper drape, imitating the Eucharistic tablecloth, a work of Antonio Giorgetti, pupil of Bernini. The wings of the angel on the left are made of wood and are mobile, so as to allow access to the chapel. The altar also has a fake damask altar frontal, made with marble inlays of flowering branches and lilies. The detached fresco of the Madonna and Child is framed by polychrome marble, namely a laurel wreath in antique green and two palm branches in light marble. On the sides there are two relief medallions with the faces of Saints Francis and Bonaventure by Paolo Naldini.  
On the side walls there are two sofas in black marble, with armrests in yellow marble, on which two sleeping figures lie between alabaster cushions and drapes: on the left Bernardino Lorenzo Spada, bishop of Calvi (died 1543), by Ercole Ferrata, and on the right Giovanni Spada (died 1247), chaplain of Innocent IV, sculpted by Cosimo Fancelli between 1656 and 1659. Above the two monuments, medallions with the effigies of the most illustrious members of the Spada family hang from bronze ropes: *Amadore I Spada and his brother Aleramo* by Paolo Naldini, *Pietro di Cecco and Serrone di Pietro Spada,* also by Naldini, *Amadore Spada and his son Mengo* by Antonio Raggi, *Amadore II Spada* by Francesco Baratta, *Mutio Spada and his nephew Antonello* by Ercole Ferrata and *Ghino di Mengo Spada* by Giuseppe Perone. The floor is also decorated with similar inlay motifs, while the barrel vault is frescoed with the dove of the Holy Spirit and the personification of Faith and Charity.
a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.short_description: Highly scenographical chapel: its inlaid marbles simulate damask. Two angels by Giorgetti (Bernini’s follower) bear the jasper cloth referring to the Eucharistic altar-cloth. The left angel has movable wooden-made wings to allow the entrance to the chapel. Tombs: Bernardino Lorenzo Spada (by  E. Ferrata) and G. Spada (C. Fancelli).
a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.bibliography: Papaldo, S., *San Girolamo della Carità,* Rome: Istituto di studi romani, 1978.
a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.history:
San Girolamo della Carità was the seat of the homonymous Confraternity, known for its charitable works which had been particularly encouraged under San Filippo Neri, who had lived there since 1551 for over thirty years and had established the Oratory.  
The chapel, dedicated to the Madonna as depicted in a late 15th century fresco, was granted on 17 October 1595 to Orazio Spada, but there is no information on how it originally looked. After the death of Paolo Spada, brother and heir of Orazio, embellishment works were carried out in the fourth decade of the 17th century. In 1654 Virgilio Spada, grandson of Orazio, Oratorian father and secret almsgiver of pope Innocent X and then of Alexander VII, had the work resumed with the aim of transforming the chapel into the family mausoleum, thus celebrating the most illustrious ancestors of his family. According to the sources, Francesco Righi designed the chapel, but Virgilio Spada, also an amateur architect, contributed with his original inputs. He personally followed the work, including the construction of the balustrade. Spada was also very close to Borromini, to whom he had also given advice for the symbolic and religious aspects of some of his projects, such as that of the Oratory of Santa Maria in Vallicella: for this reason, the Spada chapel was considered for a long time the work of the famous Ticino architect.
a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.architects: Francesco Righi (architect); Antonio Giorgetti; Paolo Naldini; Ercole Ferrata; Cosimo Fancelli; Giovan Battista Scala, called il Napoletano; Giovanni Maria della Monaca; Giovanni Somazzi
a51acff1-9c1c-5dbf-9dfe-0bd7de1b2bee.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.name: Parish Church of Our Lady of the Snow
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.description:
A network of elongated *rocaille* scrolls and cartouches, into which floral twigs and garlands are interwoven covers the walls of the church like lace to form a framework for the wall paintings. Due to the long construction period, the stucco decoration was created over a long period, but nonetheless is based on an extensive, uniform iconographic programme. The Marian topics include the *Legend of Our Lady of the Snow* and the *Foundation of the Roman Church of Santa Maria Maggiore* shown in a number of scenes in the sanctuary of the church (transposed into one of them is a contemporary depiction of the foundation of the church in Kutina). Considerable space on the walls and ceiling of the nave is devoted to the *Passion*. Accompanying these is a sequence of emblematic depictions based on the Old Testament as well as motifs relating to the Mysteries of the Joyful, Sorrowful and Glorious Rosaries.  
Authorship of the wall paintings has not been thoroughly elucidated yet, partly because in the forms the personal styles of three painters can be observed, while the only signatures to be identified are those of Franciscus Weitenhiller of 1776, and Joann Joseph Görner (probably a Varaždin painter) of 1779. While Görner painted the ceiling paintings in the nave, Franciscus Weitenhiller painted the figurative images on the walls of the sanctuary and nave (many of which were subsequently heavily retouched) integrated in the "lace" of the *rocaille* stuccowork. Because of the misspelled signature, the author was at first identified as Josep Weitenhiller (who it is recorded worked in Slovenia). There are also some excellent woodcarvings. The High altar (1739) is attributed stylistically to the Zagreb sculptor, Joseph Weinacht. Weinacht was one of the most accomplished local sculptors of the first half of the 18th century whose style shows the influence of contemporary Styrian sculpture, which suggests that he trained there. The pulpit (around 1761) is ascribed to the Zagreb sculptor, Franjo or Franz Straub (1726–before 1771), and is classified as among the most luxurious and opulent Baroque embodiments in north-west Croatia, as well as an outstanding specimen of dynamism aspiring towards the monumental, characteristics that define his work.
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.short_description: A church with a nave only and no aisles, it has a belfry on the facade and is surrounded by a covered walkway. The simplicity of the exterior is much at odds with the rich interior, which is among the most luxuriously fitted-out Baroque churches of northern Croatia. The integrity of the opulent Baroque interior is achieved above all through the rich stucco decoration that covers the walls like lacework, framing the wall paintings dedicated to Marian and Christological subjects.
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.dates: High altar: 1739; pulpit: c. 1761; stucco work and wall painting: 1765–1779
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.method_for_datation: Archival documents and inscriptions on the monument.
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.bibliography:
Karač, V., "Pregled urbanog razvoja i arhitektonske baštine Kutine" in *Kutina: povijesno-kulturni pregled s identitetom današnjice*, Kutina, 2002, pp. 398–429.  
Mirković, M., "Zidne i svodne slike u crkvi Marije Snježne u Kutini" in *Kutina: povijesno-kulturni pregled s identitetom današnjice*, Kutina, 2002, pp. 436–452. Repanić-Braun, M., "Franciscus Weittenhiller – novo ime kasnobaroknog zidnog slikarstva u sjevernoj Hrvatskoj" in *U služenju Božjemu narodu*, Požega, 2007, pp. 790–796.  
Baričević, D., *Barokno kiparstvo sjeverne Hrvatske*, Zagreb, 2008.
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.history: The Baroque church was built on the site of an older building. Construction took a long 40 years, with the sanctuary completed in 1729; the nave in 1748 and building concluded in 1769. Count Karlo Erdödy II and his wife, Countess Erdödy, financed the construction and fitting-out of the church from 1740.
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.patrons: Count Karlo II Erdödy and his wife Countess Erdödy, *née* Kohary
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.architects: Painters: J. Weitenhiller (active c. 1770), Joann Joseph Görner (active c. 1770), Ivan Krstitelj (Johann Baptist) Ranger (1700–1753); sculptors: Joseph Weinacht (active c. 1740–1750), Franjo (Franz) Straub (1726–before 1771)
keywords: Kutina, Joseph Weinacht, Franjo (Franz) Straub, wall painting, stucco decoration, sculpture, altar
a547eac4-472d-532a-8452-486859f4e916.author: Vlasta Zajec

a553f0d5-43fe-535b-9d07-0aff49e30b7f.name: *Portrait of Father António Vieira*
a553f0d5-43fe-535b-9d07-0aff49e30b7f.description:
In this engraving Arnold van Westerhout represents the humanist, António Vieira, as a man of knowledge and a father of the Society of Jesus. His gaze extends beyond the horizon: whether towards Brazil where he grew up or to Lisbon, the home he always defended with the staunchness he employed to preach the Christian faith. The Flemish artist concentrates on António Vieira's facial expression to heighten his altruistic character which is shown in constant reflection about the human condition and his own experience of it.  
This painting celebrates António Vieira's exemplary life dedicated to the defence of human rights, whether to those of Brazil's indigenous peoples or the Jews persecuted by the Inquisition.  
Born in Lisbon in 1608, António Vieira departed to S. Salvador da Bahia with his parents at the age of six. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1623 and become a priest 12 years later. He played a fundamental role in the relationship between Jesuits, coloniser and the indigenous peoples of Brazil, exhibiting in his sermons an anxiety about the socio-political conditions that would characterise his missionary activity. With knowledge of the languages and costumes of the Brazilian Indians he was a missionary and a preacher with a humanistic vision.  
Following independence from Spanish domination, Vieira returned to Lisbon where he became an important figure in the court of King João IV. He rapidly became a key player in state decisions and helped re-establish the Portuguese Empire's economic, political, diplomatic and religious profile in Lisbon and in the most important colony at the time, Brazil. In the latter, and at Vieira's advice, the Commercial Company of Brazil was instituted with two intentions: to resist Dutch invasion and to foment the recovery of local sugar production with the objective of export to Europe.  
In Lisbon he proposed economic reforms that would force a change in the doctrine of the Inquisition. He terminated the distinction between 'new-Christians' and 'old Christians' in order to attract the investments of Jews who had fled the Kingdom. The idea generated a conflict with the Society of Jesus and the Dominicans, which resulted in António Vieira being persecuted by the Inquisition.  
Later in his life he was one again accused of heresy. This was as a result of a letter he sent to the Bishop of Japan in which he outlined his *Theory of the Fifth Empire*. Here he predicted that Portugal was predestined to be the next grand empire following the Assyrian, Greek, Persian and Roman.
a553f0d5-43fe-535b-9d07-0aff49e30b7f.short_description: An engraving by Arnold van Westerhout of António Vieira, a Portuguese Jesuit Priest, writer and preacher. As a senior diplomat as well as a missionary in Brazil, he became both an influential figure in Portuguese culture and in the defence of human rights of indigenous peoples.

a553f0d5-43fe-535b-9d07-0aff49e30b7f.author: Rui Oliveira Lopes

a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.name: *Ecce Homo*
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.description:
The work may have been commissioned directly from the artist by Cardinal Scipione Borghese. It is first documented in his collection in 1613. In the canvas, the story of the Passion of Christ is transformed for the viewer into a subject of meditation. Light suffuses the body of Christ in a diagonal line high-lit by the hem of the red cloak held up by the executioner. We see the regal symbols that Christ was forced to wear, the crown of thorns, the reed sceptre and the red cloak as signs of mockery and derision, with which the Gospels tell us Pontius Pilate presented his prisoner to the crowd with the words “*Ecce homo*” (“Behold the man”). Along with the column (representing flagellation), and hammer and nails, which anticipate the crucifixion, the scene is transformed from a historical account into a meditative subject designed to inspire among the faithful feelings of compassion and shared pain with the martyr. The executioner, awkward and unrefined next to the beauty of Christ's face, is placed in the darkness – both literally and spiritually – as one who does not recognise the divinity of the Son of God. The capacity to inspire reflection on the dogma of faith while simultaneously engaging the viewer emotionally is the basis of the ethos of the Counter-Reformation. Communication of feelings and affections was also fundamental to the development of Baroque art.  
In this piece, Giovanni Baglione emphasises the dramatic sense of the scene through the use of *chiaroscuro* developed by Caravaggio and his followers from their experiments undertaken in Rome in the first years of the 17th century. On the other hand, Christ's face, gazing towards the heavens in a mood of total acceptance of divine will, reflects the more delicate and idealised style of the Carracci school, in particular Guido Reni.
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.short_description: The theme of derision is shown in comparison with those who don’t recognise Christ as the Son of God, sent to earth to save mankind. The scene sends a very clear message against the Reformation. Although the subject is intended for meditation, its theatrical style is a prelude to the drama expressed in Baroque art.
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.bibliography:
Della Pergola, P., *Galleria Borghese. I dipinti*, II, Rome, 1959, n.97, p. 66.  
Herrmann Fiore, K., in *Titian to Tiepolo: Three Centuries of Italian Art*, exhibition catalogue (Canberra, Melbourne), Milan, 2002, cat. 48, pp. 148–149.

keywords: Christian themes; Reformation; Counter-Reformation; symbolism
a5972045-60f7-5320-a28d-a171b75b6a68.author: Sofia Barchiesi, Marina Minozzi

a858e4fd-51fa-5212-b9c8-f9dc77b93dee.name: The Four Continents
a858e4fd-51fa-5212-b9c8-f9dc77b93dee.description: On a low scalloped base, with relief decoration, are four female figures – allegories of the four continents. Europe, presented as the Ruler, is on horseback and has one leg resting on a globe. At her feet are an open book, a lute, fasces and a scroll. Africa, seated on a lion, holds an elephant's tusk in her right hand with smaller tusks and snakes at her feet. Asia, seated on a camel, has one leg on a pumpkin; alongside the pumpkin is a vessel from which smoke is rising. America is an American Indian on the back of a crocodile. She holds an eagle in her left hand, her right foot resting on decapitated human head on the ground. All the figures are marked with the imprinted seal of the Viennese porcelain manufactory (the Austrian shield) and the mark *bossierer* (M).
a858e4fd-51fa-5212-b9c8-f9dc77b93dee.short_description: A group of unpainted porcelain female figures – allegories of the four continents – Europe, Africa, Asia and America.

a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.name: *Mourning over the Dead Christ*
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.description:
In 1592 the Metropolitan Chapter of the Cathedral of Milan contracted with Federico Barocci for an altarpiece. The *Mourning over the Dead Christ* was officially commissioned for the altar of Saint Giovanni Buono in 1600. Unfortunately, the painter was already quite old, ill and had many personal problems. When he died, in 1612, the work was left unfinished.  
The great picture was carried to Milan in 1628 to be completed by a different artist. This project was blocked by the plague of 1630, and in 1739 the painting was finally exhibited on the altar without any further intervention. In 1763 it was moved and sold to the abbot Antonio Magnani who donated it the Municipality of Bologna.  
Many surviving drawings document the long and careful work in the creation of this painting. The figures are all gathered around the dead body of Christ, who is lying in the lower portion of the painting. The wide architecture above, which was planned to have been occupied by two flying angels, is empty and barely sketched. The dead body of Christ is sometimes compared to the *Pietà* painted by Annibale Carracci. Shining colours are reminiscent of the mannerist style and the figures express a strong emotional tension that was intended to be felt by the faithful watching the picture. This is following the rules of Counter-reformation art policy.
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.short_description: This great piece was commissioned in 1600 by the Chapter of the Cathedral of Milan to Federico Barocci. He is known as one of the most significant Italian painters working between the movements of Mannerism and Counter-reformation. When he died, in 1612, the work was not finished. The architecture in the background is barely sketched, the figures gather around the body of the dead Christ in full light, the focus is on strong emotional turmoil.
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.initial_owner: Chapter of the Cathedral of Milan
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.method_for_datation: The complex story of this patronage is documented by the annals of the Cathedral of Milan; we learn that the artist received 200 scudi on the 22nd April 1600. However, in 1608 he had only made a preparatory cartoon and some sketches. When he died the work was left unfinished.
a88e90bf-7959-5aa6-a673-2e933380fad8.obtention: The painting was bequest to the library of the Archigimnasium in 1811 by the abbot Antonio Magnani; deposited in the Pinacoteca Nazionale it was returned to the Municipality of Bologna in 2002. It is now exhibited in the Collezioni Comunali d'Arte.

a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.name: *Virgin Mary with Jesus*
a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.description:
This standing Madonna with child is characterised by an S-shaped cloak encircling the figure from the left shoulder to the right knee, appearing blown by a sudden gust of wind. The cloak makes up a surprisingly rich yet compact outline for the carved statue. Madonna’s posture contrasts with the expressive air of the drapery. Her head slightly turned towards the child, she is only holding him with indicated touches of the hands, presenting Christ to the viewer in the manner of the Gothic Madonna and thereby emphasising the notion of the Eucharist. The motif of Baby Jesus playing with Madonna’s veil is of the same origin. With her physique, facial expression and plain clothes, the Madonna’s nature appears almost secular.  
Weber employed a similar compositional scheme, in a reduced form and mirror-like manner, in the figure of St. Rose of Lima on a side altar in the Dominican Church of the Holy Cross, Znojmo. The restrained expression of both figures is typical of Weber’s oeuvre, which found a relatively broad application in South Moravia (in Lechovice, Suchohrdly, Tasovice, Dyje, Znojmo). In the 1740s Weber worked for the Augustinian order in Brno (his son was a member of the order). Apart from his decoration of the Augustinian library (now to be found in Old Brno), an entrance portal with the figures of Moravian margraves has survived.  
Leonard Weber came from a large family of sculptors in Silesia and later settled in Slovakia. Sculptors of the same name, possibly a father and son, whose relationship has not yet been demonstrated, were also active in Budapest at the time.
a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.short_description: The standing Madonna with child is characterised by an S-shaped cloak encircling the figure from the left shoulder to the right knee, appearing blown by a gust of wind. The restrained expression of the figures is typical of Weber’s oeuvre, which became relatively widespread in South Moravia.
a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.obtention: Acquired before 1950 from a private collection, Budkov Chateau.

a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.name: *Maria Varasdiniensis*
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.description:
The figures of the Virgin Mary and Child Jesus are hieratically positioned front-on. Beneath a textile canopy edged with labrequin, the ends of the drapes lifted and knotted, both wear conical cloaks, white wigs and crowns. At the top of the canopy is a gold ring with rays, upon which is the dove of the Holy Spirit with outspread wings. The ornamentation on the cloaks of both Mary and Jesus are motifs from the beginning of the 18th century, mostly acanthus and other foliate scrolls. In the middle of each of their cloaks is a painted gold heart within which are their individual monograms. On the other hand, the faces and wigs of both Mary and Jesus already show Rococo characteristics.  
The representation of Mary and Jesus in conical cloaks is a votive scene that first appeared during the Baroque period. More usually stiff cloaks scattered with floral motifs and adorned with jewellery such as chains and pendants hang over the cloaks like garlands.  
One of the foremost characteristics of the Pauline order was its veneration of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which resulted in her central place in their iconography. In 1672 there were 80 churches dedicated to the Virgin Mary.  
This votive painting of Mary, which hung above the pulpit in the nave of Lepoglava church, was probably intended for Varaždin as the Virgin Mary was its patron.
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.short_description:
A crowned Mary and Child Jesus stand front-on under a textile canopy. They both wear white wigs and conical cloaks richly decorated with gold hearts within which are their monograms. This votive-type Virgin and Child first appeared during the Baroque period.  
The Pauline Order especially revered the cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary and her portrayal had a central place in their iconography.
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.holder: Diocese Museum of the Zagreb Archdiocese
a9e17673-d137-5b5c-89ad-8c71949fda7f.obtention: The painting came from the former Pauline Church in Lepoglava, Hrvatsko zagorje and gifted to the Diocesan Museum in Zagreb in 1940.

a9e83744-68da-5616-9775-18e9d9b4eb46.name: Svatý Kopeček (“Holy Hill”)
a9e83744-68da-5616-9775-18e9d9b4eb46.alternate_name: Basilica of the Annunciation at Svatý Kopecek – Basilica Minor
a9e83744-68da-5616-9775-18e9d9b4eb46.description: The church frontage, with wings for the two residences, lies at the top of a hill rising abruptly over the Olomouc flatlands and dominating the surrounding landscape. The segmented, three-axis frontage of the church protrudes into the surrounding space. The portal is crowned with statues of Generosity, Glory and Hope by J. Winterhalder Sr. (1731); the niches contain statues of St. Stephen (patron saint of the Hradisko Monastery), Sts Augustine and Norbert, patron saints of the Premonstratensian order, and the Virgin Mary of Svatý Kopeček with Child, in the upper section. The residential wings are lined with statues of the Apostles and two Protectors from the Plague. The church vault is covered with organically interconnected stuccos and frescos. In the window lunettes, the Four Ages of Man sing praises to the Virgin Mary. Two oval frescos depict Mary’s Devotion to God and Mary as Protectoress from the Onset of the Devil. The south wing houses several historical halls, such as the Chinese Hall and the festive Andrýsek Hall, with pictures by P. Troger. Behind the church complex are an open semi-circular cloister and a chapel, making up a spacious courtyard.
a9e83744-68da-5616-9775-18e9d9b4eb46.short_description: With a spatially segmented frontage opening onto the countryside, the pilgrimage complex is a typical example of Counter-Reformation architecture. The church vaulting, decorated with spectacular stuccos, is among the largest specimens of the style north of the Alps. The vaulting was created by Italian sculptors and decorators, whose further work had a profound influence on art in Moravia. The complex, equipped by leading artists from Vienna and Olomouc, includes a unique series of artworks from the second-half of 17th century, only a tiny proportion of which have survived in the Czech lands.
a9e83744-68da-5616-9775-18e9d9b4eb46.method_for_datation: Handke’s painting is dated. A print of the high altar, created on the occasion of the coronation of the Marian picture in 1733, gives Fontana as the (concept) artist. Archive sources regarding the building such as contracts, receipts and a chronicle of the Premonstratensian residence have survived.

a9e83744-68da-5616-9775-18e9d9b4eb46.history: Legend has it that the chapel on the hill was built by Andrýsek, an Olomouc burgher who had a vision of the Virgin Mary. In 1645 the chapel was plundered by the Swedish army. The abbot of the Premonstratensian Monastery in Hradisko asked Bishop Karel II of Lichtenstein for permission to build a new Church of the Annunciation. In 1684, two single-floor residences were added to the sides of the church, the one on the north for priests and that on the south reception halls. The pilgrimage site was visited by Empress Maria Theresa (1748). In 1784 the church was granted the status of “basilica minor”, meaning that pilgrims could receive the same indulgences there as in Sta. Maria Maggiore, Rome.

aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Aires
aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.description:
In the south-facing Rococo outline of this church, designed by Father João Baptista, the light and shadow contrasts created by the different coloured marble is notable, which together with the arches framed by colourful *scagliola*, is typical of the Alentejo tradition.  
The façade has a triangular pediment and is flanked by two bell towers with a carillon of 1955 and niches. The doorway is Rococo (1755). Above the right lateral arch of the portal is a small sundial made of white limestone, which dates from the late 18th century. The dome dominates and is illuminated by four large windows.  
The nave is divided into three spans separated by fake pilasters. It has two pulpits and two *loggia*s for parishioners that are raised in the central spans and closed off by railings. The interior *azulejos* are 19th century.  
The chancel, built between 1744 and 1750 on a slightly circular plan, is opened up by four round arches with projecting cornices and supported by white and blue marble columns. On four sides of the chancel on Rococo pedestals stand the gilded wooden figures of the Four Evangelists by the sculptor João Baptista.  
The gilt wood baldachin crowns a Gothic polychrome statue of Our Lady of Aires, (late15th century) made of limestone.  
Building of the octagonal sacristy began in October 1743. On the left-hand side are Pombaline (Marquis de Pombal, Prime Minister 1750–1777) Neo-Classical paintings.
aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.short_description: This old devotional Sanctuary in Alentejo is a remarkable example of a Baroque church built in a rural environment. The south-facing *rocaille* outline, designed by Father João Baptista, together with the contrasting light and shadow created by the different coloured marbles is notable, as are the arches framed by colourful *scagliola*, typical of the Alentejo tradition. The church, built on a Latin cross plan, has two symmetrical bell towers; the interior is decorated with stucco and mural paintings.
aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.location: Parish of Nossa Senhora da Anunciação, Viana do Alentejo, Évora
aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.bibliography:
Leal, P., *Portugal Antigo e Moderno*, Lisbon, 1893.  
Espanca, T., “Inventário Artístico de Portugal – Distrito de Évora” in *Santuário de Nossa Senhora de Aires*, Cidade de Évora, No. 60, Lisbon, 1978.
aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.history: The sanctuary of Our Lady of Aires had for a long, long time been a devotional meeting place for thousands of pilgrims during the religious festivals held annually in the Autumn. For this reason the Senate of Viana obtained a decree from King José I (dated 27 September 1751 and signed by the Marquis of Pombal) to create a tax-free Fair of Nossa Senhora de Aires. In light of this, the 16th-century church was replaced by a more impressive one, which was managed by Father José Peres. The plan was approved by Archbishop D. Fr. Miguel de Távora, and construction began in July 1743. The blessing and initial inauguration took place on 15 March 1760 while the church was still in an unfinished state. Work continued up until the second blessing of 13 May 1804.
aa140333-d6b3-5bef-ae43-a31bb8c0fd39.architects: Architect: Father João Baptista (active 1743); Oratoria by St. Philip Neri, Estremoz; master of construction: Manuel Antunes; master stonemason: Manuel Gomes co-ordinating several local artists: António Ferreira Esteves, Gonçalo António da Silva, Manuel Madeira, André Melro, António Monteiro [dates unknown]

aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.name: *Ecstasy of St. Catherine of Siena*
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.description:
The painting, which because of its small size was undoubtedly intended for private worship, is first listed in the Borghese Collection in 1790. The canvas shows St. Catherine of Siena, who belonged to the order founded by St. Dominic, who died in 1380 and was canonised in 1461.  
The saint is shown with her typical attributes: the crown of thorns, heart, crucifix and lily, plus a representation of the stigmata, which she received on 1 April 1375. The luminous background highlights the figure, which is arranged along a diagonal line inspired by the work of Correggio.  
The two angels that hold the saint emphasise the spirituality of her ecstasy, nonetheless returning her to reality. The work is rendered with great sensitivity by Agostino (who founded the renowned *Accademia degli Incamminati* in Bologna with his brother Annibale and cousin Ludovico).  
Agostino's work uses the natural world as a model. The canvas, usually dated to the final decade of the 16th century, is perfectly consistent with the dictates imposed on artistic production in the Counter-Reformation, stating that representations of saints must inspire compassion, the spirit of emulation and prayer among the faithful.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.short_description: The canvas shows the ecstasy of St. Catherine of Siena, who belonged to the Dominican order. Here the saint is shown with her usual attributes, similar to the Passion of Christ (crown of thorns, wounded heart, crucifix and – surprisingly – the stigmata that Catherine received in 1375). Agostino Carracci, who founded the renowned *Accademia degli Incamminati* in Bologna with his brother Annibale and cousin Ludovico, is one of the exponents of the naturalism movement, in place of the extreme realism of the art of Caravaggio and his followers.
aa71143e-7119-5bbe-91ff-c1d89f9994c6.obtention: Acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

aa9991a1-125f-59f7-ab98-3d002c581e07.name: Augustinian Monastery, Hermits of St. Thomas the Apostle, Brno
aa9991a1-125f-59f7-ab98-3d002c581e07.description: The horizontally spread frontage of the church, with its accentuated central axis, is an example of Italian mannerist architecture. The architects, O. Erna and J. K. Erna, were leading lights of Moravian architecture in the 17th century. Two-layered relief segmentation is supplemented by niches that hold statues by the itinerant Flemish sculptor, J. van der Furth who also created the statues for some of the side altars and worked for Brno Town Council. The original frontages differed according to the various functions of the monastery buildings, but these have been unified in modern times.
aa9991a1-125f-59f7-ab98-3d002c581e07.short_description: This medieval monastery, restored after damage sustained in the Thirty Years’ War, was reconstructed in the 18th century. It hosted religious festivals and also housed a grammar school and university. During the late 18th century, the buildings were used by the state administration. The late 17th-century appearance of the church is largely preserved. The high altar is adorned by a famous altarpiece by F. A. Maulbertsch. The contents of the monastery, partially the work of masters settled in Brno, were destroyed by bombing in 1945. Only the library (where later the geneticist J. G. Mendel studied) survived.
aa9991a1-125f-59f7-ab98-3d002c581e07.method_for_datation: Archive material (especially contracts, receipts and designs)

aa9991a1-125f-59f7-ab98-3d002c581e07.history: The monastery by the town walls was destroyed during the Hussite Wars and particularly during the siege of Brno by the Swedes in the 17th century. Its restoration was undertaken in 1665, when J. K. Erna started to build a new church nave. The reconstruction was completed in the first half of 18th century under the guidance of M. Grimm. In 1736 the monastery hosted one of the greatest religious festivities, the Coronation of the Miraculous Picture of the Virgin Mary (of Old Brno). After the dissolution of the Jesuit order locally, one of the monastery buildings became a grammar school, and became known among the best in the Habsburg monarchy. From 1778 the monastery also housed a university. In 1783 the monastery was transferred to Old Brno, the church became a parish church, and the monastery buildings were adapted for the state administration.

aaa25ff7-c27e-579e-8df1-c5585d0b9612.name: Jesuit Church Innsbruck
aaa25ff7-c27e-579e-8df1-c5585d0b9612.description: The Innsbruck Jesuit College was built with reference to the Salzburg Dome, to which it displays certain similarities. The two-bay nave is a hall with side aisles and galleries structured by double pilasters. In the centre there is a crossing with cross-arms extending into the nave aisles, vaulted by an octagonal dome resting on a drum. The choir terminates in a semi-circular apse. Some ungainly forms indicate that the main parts probably originate from the Jesuit priest Fontaner.
aaa25ff7-c27e-579e-8df1-c5585d0b9612.short_description: The Holy Trinity Church in Innsbruck, one of the few large ecclesiastical buildings constructed during the Thirty Years’ War, illustrates the high standing which the Jesuit order attained within state and society following its summons to Tyrol by Emperor Ferdinand I. The monumental construction with its double-tower façade and crossing dome were built under the patronage of Archduke Leopold V and his wife Claudia de’ Medici as the college’s spiritual centrepiece.
aaa25ff7-c27e-579e-8df1-c5585d0b9612.dates: 1619–1622/1627–1640 (Early Baroque building and interior work phases)

Keßler, D., *Der Dillinger Baumeister Hans Alberthal*, Dillingen 1949, pp. 99–106.  
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 32f.  
Skalecki, G., *Deutsche Architektur zur Zeit des Dreißigjährigen Krieges*, Regensburg 1989, p. 75f and p. 116f.  
Schnell, H., Schedler, U., *Lexikon der Wessobrunner*, Munich, Zurich 1988, p. 63.
aaa25ff7-c27e-579e-8df1-c5585d0b9612.history: The Jesuit College Innsbruck was founded in 1561. A Gothic chapel initially served as a church. A new building was constructed between 1619 and 1622 by the master mason Johan Alberthaler from Dillingen according to the plans of Matthias Karger, however, this collapsed in 1626. For the new construction executed between 1627 and 1640, the master builder Santino Solari, who was responsible for the Salzburg Dome, was appointed advisor. Up until 1635 the construction was supervised by the Jesuit priest Karl Fontaner. Christoph Gumpp was also involved in the planning. Consecrated in 1646, the façade was completed in 1900/01. The building was then reconstructed between 1946 and 1953 following severe bomb damage.

aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.name: *St. Francis of Assisi* Azulejos
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.alternate_name: *St. Francis of Assisi* Blue-and-white tile panel
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.description:
Our Lady of the Visitation Convent in Vila Verde dos Francos is a Franciscan Convent of the third order and, therefore, part of a noble residence where a few Franciscan friars lived a monastic life. D. António de Noronha, the owner of the residence, along with other nobles – both men and women – often went there to retreat.  
Society life necessarily followed strict social rules, which were taken very seriously. As part of the social mores was the struggle of the Christian soul against the Devil – Psychomachy – fundamental to salvation. Updated continuously up until the end of the Baroque period, the Hagiography (example of life) of St. Francis of Assisi was used as a didactic tale to explain to men, and especially to women, how to behave in society. As shown here, St. Francis was a sinner during his youth and, like him, people have the opportunity to resist temptation.  
The remarkable blue-and-white tile composition, by an artist from the Oliveira Bernardes' workshop circle, reveals a sophisticated technique and an artistic capacity to transform these moralising figurative *azulejos* into impressive iconographic themes.  
Handling the use of engravings in a most creative way, the artist adapted those compositions: pilasters with angels and *albarradas* (vases with flowers), to the wall covering as if it were a scenic architectural stage.  
This particular chancel panel recounts the episode of St. Francis converting Muslims in Syria during the Fifth Crusade. On this journey a woman with a lovely body but a "filthy soul" tried to tempt him. Feigning acceptance of her sinful offer, he took off his clothes and leaped into a fire, inviting her to follow him. He miraculously survived, having overcome the temptation and led the woman to salvation.
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.short_description: In this *azulejos* panel, St. Francis of Assisi is tempted by Evil, symbol of vanity and lust, one of the most regrettable sins of women. Evil Is conveyed here by a half-naked, half-devil woman.

aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.name: Altarpiece: The Builder Shows King Ladislav (St. Ladislaus) the Drawings of the Cathedral
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.description:
The large wooden winged altarpiece of St. Ladislav (St. Ladislaus) held a cycle of 12 paintings depicting the Life of St Ladislav; 10 of them are extant today. The winged doors, painted on both sides with eight surfaces, closed off the main niche of the retable.  
Hungarian-Croatian King Ladislav I of the Arpad dynasty (c.1040–1095) founded the Zagreb diocese in 1094.  
The iconographic programme of the paintings is outstanding, mixing traditional scenes from the history of Ladislav, with a post-Trent interpretation, reinterpreted by the painter who depicts the king as a saint; a merciful saint who was canonised in 1192.  
According to the wishes of the bishop who commissioned it, most of the cycle refers to the domestic milieu – referring to its history – contemporary aspirations relating to the unification of the country and the establishment of the diocese of Zagreb.  
The painting, *The Builder Shows King Ladislav the Drawings of the Cathedral* depicts King Ladislav wearing a crown, and the builder showing the king a drawing of the cathedral roof as it is being built. Two barely visible male figures also take part. A large cathedral (later demolished) was built in the 12th century on the site of a smaller one from Ladislav's time. A similar scene, *St. Ladislav Shows a Cathedral with Two Towers to the Virgin*, embellishes the Chapter's oldest seal dating to the 13th century.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.short_description: A painted scene from the Life of St. Ladislav cycle, which links the legend of King Ladislav I of the Arpad Dynasty (around 1040–1095) with Croatian history, and accentuates the foundation of the diocese of Zagreb in about 1094.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.type: Painting, part of a cycle for the winged altarpiece of St. Ladislav
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.initial_owner: Zagreb Cathedral; the altarpiece was commissioned by Bishop Aleksandar Ignacij Mikulić (1688–1694). The side altarpiece of St. Ladislav was originally housed in the northern apse of the cathedral.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.method_for_datation: Bishop Mikulić ordered gilding and painting for the altarpiece In 1690. The painting and sculptural parts were already finished, so the cycle of paintings can thus be dated to this year. The historical documents include the testament of Bishop Martin Borković (1667–1687). Among the notes of the executor, capitular curator and canon Ivan Znika, there is an item about a payment made to the “*pictori Ioanni*” for the bishop's portrait. Stylistic analysis: eminently comparable are the portrait of the bishop (after 1687) and in 1690, the Life of St. Ladislav cycle altarpiece paintings.
aaf8ceca-6748-56dc-9931-1bdfb87139eb.obtention: In 1882, following the earthquake of 1880, during the renovation and restoration of the cathedral in the Gothic-revival style by H. Bollé, the St. Ladislav (St. Ladislaus) altarpiece was removed from the cathedral. Parts of it were brought together for the Cultural and Historical Exhibition of Zagreb in 1925. After the exhibition closed on 31 December 1925, these pieces were given to the museum by the Committee of Zagreb Croatian Women for the Preparation of the Exhibition.

aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.name: Hellenbach Manor
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.description: Hellenbach Manor, known as the Marija Bistrica Castle, lies northwest of Marija Bistrica a famous shrine and place of pilgrimage dedicated to St. Mary. Built on a square plan, it has a central hall that is much higher than all the other rooms. The ground floor, the so-called *piano nobile*, is subordinate to the first floor. On the front façade, the porch is disposed of elegant Classical features: four columns connected by a baluster fence, which carries the high architrave and the triangular gable. A prominent central section defines the opposite façade. The first-floor rooms are elegantly decorated with stucco decoration in the Classical vocabulary of garlands, festoons, architraves and pilasters.
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.short_description: The last quarter of the 18th century in northern Croatia was marked by the powerful influence of Classicism, with manors in the Classical style built parallel to residencies of the late Baroque. One of these was so-called Hellenbach Manor in Marija Bistrica. Built before 1786 by the Sermage family, in the 19th century the Hellenbach family purchased it. Hellenbach Manor is in the International Classical style inspired by a renewed interest in Palladianism, which spread from France in around 1750, and which other European cultural centres embraced.
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.bibliography: Žmegač, A., “Dvorac Marija Bistrica” in *The Art topography of Krapinsko-zagorska County*, Zagreb, 2008, pp. 454–455.
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.history: Hellenbach Manor, probably built by the noble family Sermage, came into the possession of the Keglević family and then the Jelačić family. Finally, in 1851, the Hellenbach family purchased it.
keywords: Manor, domestic architecture, Classical architecture
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.author: Mirjana Repanić-Braun

aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.name: Szombathely Cathedral
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.description: The ground plan of Szombathely Cathedral merges the central and the longitudinal types. It commences with an organ-loft and an entrance hall, followed by three sections topped by sail vaults, and decorated with altar-niches. In the fourth section, the nave expands into a wide transept which, according to local tradition, it is not topped by a dome resting on a tholobate. A long, semi-circular sanctuary adjoins the transept, which opens into a vestry. The interior is articulated by monumental columns. The facade is framed by two towers. The details are moderate and linear, but the mouldings do not stand out emphatically. The two towers, capped by two pyramidal spires, embrace a two-level mid-section, closed by a triangular tympanum. The mid-section consists of a two-storey tetra-style portico, decorated with Tuscan columns on the lower level and Ionic columns on the upper. The classical column articulation, the indented cornices and the dramatic light and shade effects – all typical Baroque features – are missing. The inscription on the building reads: “JOAN. SZILY PRIMUS EPPVS SABAR. MDCCXCVII”. (“János Szily First Bishop of Szombathely [Savaria] 1797”). The building symbolises the genesis of Neo-Classicism in Hungary, but as the frescoes are irreparable and most of the original altarpieces have been destroyed, the interior does not reflect the original visual appearance of the cathedral.
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.short_description: Szombathely Cathedral is an outstanding example of the Hungarian Late Baroque style with Neo-Classical features. Queen Maria Theresia (1740–1780) founded a new diocese in 1777 and appointed János Szily as bishop, who was the patron for the construction of the Bishop’s Palace, Seminary and Cathedral. Of this building complex, the construction of the cathedral was completed last (1791–1814). The cultural and historical value of the cathedral lies in, among other things, that on one hand it is one of the last creations in the Late Baroque style, while on the other, it also symbolises the genesis of Neo-Classicism. The ceiling frescoes in the cathedral were destroyed during a Second World War bombing raid.
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, and stylistic research.
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.bibliography:
Galavics, G., “A szombathelyi püspökség mint műalkotás. Das Bistum von Szombathely als Kunstwerk” (“The Diocese of Szombathely as an Artwork”), *Melchior Hefele (1716—1794)* *építész emlékkiállítása. Gedenkausstellung des Architekten Melchior Hefele (1716–1794) (An Exhibition in Remembrance of Melchior Hefele (1716–1794) Master Architect)* (ed. Zsámbéky Mónika), Szombathely, 1994, pp. 111–113.  
Jávor, A., “Zu Maulbertschs Spätwerk in Ungarn (Eger, Pápa, Szombathely)”, *Franz Anton Maulbertsch und Mitteleuropa. Festschrift zum 30-jahrigen Bestehen des Museums Langenargen,* (eds) E. Hindelang, L. Slaviček, Langenargen–Brno, 2007, pp. 103–119.  
Sisa, J., Wiebenson D. (ed.), *Magyarország építészetének története (The History of Hungarian Architecture)*, Budapest, 1998, p. 154.
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.history:
Due to the oversized character of Hungarian dioceses, Queen Maria Theresia (1740–1780) decided to found new ones, including the diocese of Szombathely in 1777. János Szily (1777–1799) was appointed as Szombathely's first bishop. After the diocese was founded, it was felt that Szombathely required new public buildings to reflect the town's new-found status. Accordingly, Szily was the patron of the building complex comprising first the Bishop's Palace, then the Seminary and lastly the Cathedral (1791–1814). The architect of the cathedral was Melchior Hefele, one of the most significant masters of his time.  
The frescoes, which were destroyed during World War Two, once represented scenes from the Life of the Virgin Mary painted by Franz Anton Maulbertsch and finished by his assistants. The same fate befell the altarpieces and the paintings of the *Conversion of St. Paul* and the *Giving of the Keys*. The altarpiece paintings dating to 1791 of local saints, St. Quirinus and St. Martin were also destroyed, but the sketches that relate to these works can be seen in the Österreichische Galerie in Vienna and the Bishop's Palace in Szombathely. The main altarpiece painting (1791–1792) of the *Visitation* prevailed. A sketch for an unfinished painting of St. László (Ladislaus) King of Hungary striking water from a rocky outcrop can be seen in the Bishop's Palace. One of the side altars holds a painting by Stephan Dorffmaister of King St. István (Stephen) founding the Benedictine Abbey of Pannonhalma.
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.patrons: Bishop János Szily (1777–1799); Bishop Count Ferenc Herzan (1799–1806); Bishop Lipót Somogy (1806–1822)
aba86bb8-5f7f-5ca4-9864-ffab3b1afa2b.architects: Architect: Melchior Hefele (1716–1794); painters: Franz Anton Maulbertsch (1724–1796), Stephan Dorffmaister (1730–1797), J. Winterhantel, A. Spreng

ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.name: *The Illustrious Men of Budrio*
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.description: These paintings are good examples of the fashion of collecting and cataloguing local memories in a sort of Filopatria (love for one's home-town). This was typical of the baroque age and of the age of the Enlightenment. They are composed of several roundels that had to be filled from time to time with portraits of illustrious citizens. In the first painting are depicted doctors, soldiers, ecclesiastics and venerable men living between the Middle Ages and the Early Counter-reformation. Among them are Mercatello, a medical doctor in Bologna, Antonio Cossa, professor of Law, and Bartolomeo Garganelli, professor of Law and Astronomy. In the second painting, finished in 1799, we find especially ecclesiastics, diplomats and magistrates, philosophers, scientists, medical doctors and theologians: Francesco Muratori, professor of Anatomy, Vincenzo Menghini medical doctor and chemist, the local historian Domenico Golinelli and his son Ludovico, a clergy man; artists such as the follower of the Carracci Giacomo Lippi, the baroque painter Giovanni Battista Caccioli, the set designer Vincenzo Gotti; the architects Alfonso Torreggiani and Giuseppe Tubertini. In the third picture illustrious men not included in the first two are depicted, who were born before the end of the century, like the landscape painter Alberto Melonari, the “quadraturista” Giuseppe Carlo Gotti, the set designer and member of the Bolognese Accademia Clementina Alessandro della Nave, the illustrious chemist and pharmacist, Francesco Maria Coli, professor of the University of Bologna, Domenico Inzaghi and Don Giuseppe Benedetti from whose bequests to the town of Budrio were created the public library and the Pinacoteca.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.short_description: These paintings, hanging in the first room of the Pinacoteca, celebrate men born in Budrio who became famous in various fields including literature, politics, sciences and arts. Many of them are also part of the history of Bologna and its institutions because, given that they were born in Budrio, they are also Citizens of Bologna.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis; the tradition attributes them to the local painter Faustino Trebbi, for stylistic reasons it is thought he only painted the third one. The other two are probably the work of different artists.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.obtention: Public Library, then moved to the Pinacoteca (1989).

ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.name: Book Cover
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.description:
A Baroque book cover of embossed silver and richly decorated with volutes, shells and acanthus foliage. Both the front and back covers have a central crest of two important families: the Crest of the Gaos (Gaus?) family of Rijeka on the front, and the crest of the Brajković family of Senj on the back. Mentioned initially in Rijeka in 1614, The Gaos (Gaus?) family appear in a document of 1616, as “de Hahnberg”. The Brajkovićs of Senj are a prominent Croatian family, descendants of the Miroslavić family, first mentioned in Poljica in 1420. One of the best-known members of the family was Martin Brajković (Senj 1668–Vienna 1708), Bishop of Senj and Modruš from 1700 to 1703, and Bishop of Zagreb from 1703 until his death in 1708. Who ordered this book cover and why is unknown; similarly how these two families are connected in the first half of 18th century is also an unknown.  
There are two silver hallmarks on the object: one is a Venetian hallmark with St. Marcus, and the other is the control mark of Venetian mint “Zecca” that belongs to Zuanne Premuda who worked at assay control from 1712 to 1749.
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.short_description: A Baroque book cover of embossed silver richly decorated with volutes, shells and acanthus foliage. The Crest of the Gaos (Gaus?) family of Rijeka is on the front, and the crest of the Brajković family of Senj on the back. One of the best-known members of the Brajković family was Martin Brajković (1668–1708), Bishop of Senj and Modruš, and later Bishop of Zagreb.
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.initial_owner: Gaus (Gaos?) family of Rijeka, or the Brajković family of Senj

ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.method_for_datation: The date and origin of the object are according to the hallmarks.
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.obtention: Donated by Draga Butković, Gundulićeva 22a, Zagreb, in 1957.

ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.name: *Portrait of Count Miklós Zichy*
ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.description:
A male portrait set in front of a dark background. The artist has concentrated on the features and characteristics of the sitter, making this a rare example of family portraiture that differs from the traditional type of so-called Ancestors' Galleries.  
In 1740, Count Miklós (Nicolaus) Zichy (1710–1758) became landlord of different possessions in Buda (Budakeszi, Óbuda and Újlak among others). A patron of the arts, he financed the building of churches, public buildings and his own castle, built in 1745, in the centre of Óbuda. The Count became a well known and outstanding personality of the region. This type of portraiture does not make use of the traditional attributes and settings of the so-called Ancestors' Galleries but rather connects Baroque representative portraiture to bourgeois portraits of the early 18th century.
ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.short_description: A Baroque official portrait of Count Miklós (Nicolaus) Zichy (1710–1758), one of the richest landowners of the Buda area and a significant patron of the arts. Zichy financed the building and construction of churches and public buildings and constructed a family palace in Óbuda (Old Buda) in 1745.
ad69ad7a-9e01-515e-b676-3ad43b71d387.obtention: From the bequest of Count Jenő Zichy in 1903

ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.name: Biblioteca Joanina da Universidade de Coimbra
ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.description:
Outside, the royal coat of arms crowns the Baroque doorway as a memento of royal patronage. Inside, two identical triumphal arches link the three rooms and create a multiplicity of images that attract the eye to King João V's portrait overlooking the Library like an altar in a church.  
Competing with the Golden Libraries of central Europe, the *chinoiserie* motifs on the bookshelves, give the visitor a taste of exoticism, while the allegorical *trompe l'oeil* ceiling paintings recall Portuguese participation in globalisation.  
In this “noble” floor open to visitors, the shelves contain 28,943 books, but two more levels of shelving are in use today below this one where around 30,000 rare and antique books are stored.
ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.short_description:
The Library of the University of Coimbra is an important example of civil Baroque architecture during the reign of King João V, and one of the most beautiful libraries in Europe. The main façade, with its four huge monolithic columns and arches connecting three spacious interior rooms, underline the notion that these are *royal* entrances to knowledge stored away in the library bookcases that cover the walls.  
On the wall facing the door is a portrait of King João V by the royal painter G. D. Duprà. The allegorical *trompe l'oeil* ceiling paintings by Simões Ribeiro (1723) create the illusion of the library being larger than it really is.
ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.location: Parish of Sé Nova, Coimbra, Coimbra

ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.history: In 1716 the rector of the university requested of King João V some simple improvements to the university library in order to store new books on theology, philosophy and law acquired with the University’s new curricula. The King, however, saw this as an opportunity to aim higher and gave the university permission to construct a new, modern library.

adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.name: Palazzo Barberini (National Museum of Archaeology)
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.description:
The palace is characterised by the coexistence of ancient structures - the concave dual-ring terminal portico of the sanctuary whose column bases can be seen on the floor at the entrance - and the structures built between the late middle ages and the time of the Barberini tenure. The inscription of the main portal, dated 1498, and the coat of the arms of the Colonna family on the well are evidence of the significant work commissioned by the Colonna family. Two central flights of stairs in the *cavea* and the installation of the well give the palace the character of an urban development, enhanced by the axiality of the entire complex, and underlined by the fusion between the ancient and modern structures.  
The Barberini family (Taddeo and his son Maffeo) highlighted the penetration with antiquity scenically through the internal restructuring of the central hall, by the inclusion of the covered roof terrace to the front, and the addition of a cruciform *nymphaeum* to the rear (designed by Francesco Contini in 1660), as if intending to display symbolically – in a sort of ideal appropriation of antique and Roman history – the new status acquired by the family.  
This continuous dialogue with "reused" antiquity was further accentuated by some of the outstanding objects from the region that were housed within the palace by Taddeo's brother Cardinal Francesco Barberini (1597–1679). Most notable among these is the famous multicoloured mosaic of a Nile scene that was originally the floor of a basin, which was found in the apse-room of the lower temple. It remains one of the most interesting and peculiar items in the museum.  
The interior of the palace is richly decorated with frescos of mythological, biblical and historical scenes that are attributed to artists from Zuccari's circle and which date, therefore, to between the late 16th and first-half of the 17th century. The final urban development, undertaken by Maffeo Barberini in 1656, was the introduction of a road connecting the lower and upper sanctuaries, the palace and the church.
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.short_description: The palace is characterised by the coexistence of ancient structures of the 2nd-century BC Roman sanctuary and structures built on top of them between the late middle ages and the time of the Barberini family's tenure. It was this link with antiquity and Roman history that the Barberini family highlighted in their scenically penetrative plan for the palace, which was intended to display symbolically the new status acquired by the family, by means of a sort of ideal appropriation of antiquity and Roman history.

adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.history: The town and Palace of Palestrina had been owned by the ancient feudal family of Prince Francesco Colonna until it was acquired by Pope Urban VIII (1623–44) in 1630 as a gift for his brother Carlo Barberini. The Barberinis, originally from Barberino in Val d’Elsa, were based initially in Florence where they were landowners and then merchants. In the 16th century the first prelate, Francesco (1528–1600) moved to Rome, and it was Taddeo Barberini, son of Carlo who died in 1630, who was responsible for the reorganisation and elevation of the palace. The palace crowns the slopes where a 2nd-century BC sanctuary dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia – famous in antiquity for her oracles – once stood. Having suffered bomb damage during the last war, in 1956, some ancient structures were revealed beneath the palace, which was then given to the State and turned into the National Museum of Archaeology.

ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.name: Sanctuary and Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard
ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.description:
The Cistercian Monastery of Alcobaça was founded as a gift to St. Bernard of Clairvaux shortly before his death on an estate granted by King Afonso Henriques (the first King of Portugal) in 1153. Having just conquered the Arabs, Afonso Henriques wanted to commemorate his victory, and foundation of the monastery was part of his strategy to consolidate his authority in the new kingdom. The Monastery is considered to be one of the best preserved medieval monastery complexes in Europe besides being a bastion of the Portuguese nationality.  
Sanctuary: as part of the New Sacristy, this Chapel was called the “Mirror of Heaven” by the eminent Portuguese art historian, Reinaldo dos Santos, due to its supreme beauty and spirituality. Building began in 1670 when Frei Constantino Sampaio was Abbot of the Monastery (1669–1672).  
With an octagonal plan, the interior is fully covered with gilded wood and is lit by a ceiling lantern. This light, filtered and diffused, enhances the theatrical atmosphere of the gilded and polychrome Baroque octagonal structure, which includes six horizontal niches filled by 89 reliquary sculptures.  
Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard: the sculptural ensemble in terracotta represents the Transit of St. Bernard. It was built when Frei Sebastião de Sottomayor was the Abbot of the Monastery (1675–1678). The ensemble can be divided into two groups: at the lower level is a group of free-standing sculptures and another of high-relief figures inserted at the back of the altar. St. Bernard is shown in agony at the centre of the scene, while close to his feet Cistercian monks mourn his death. Close to St. Bernard’s head, the kneeling General Abbot and a group of musician angles glorify his death. At the top, surrounded by two musician-angels and cherubs, the Virgin welcomes the soul of St. Bernard with opened arms. The life-size sculptures are built in overlapping horizontal blocks.
ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.short_description: The Monastery of Alcobaça was founded as a gift to St. Bernard of Clairvaux shortly before his death on an estate granted by King Afonso Henriques in 1153. The monastery became powerful due to donations throughout the centuries and contains several treasures, namely the Baroque reliquary Sanctuary and the Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard.

ae5eb4e1-dec3-5bc8-8109-e2ff967a5580.name: Parish Church of St. John of Nepomuk and former Jesuit Monastery, Székesfehérvár
ae5eb4e1-dec3-5bc8-8109-e2ff967a5580.description:
The church consists of a nave, three adjoining side chapels on both sides, and a sanctuary. Its façade is articulated by wall pillars and a tympanum; the two towers are decorated by windows and clocks. Above the front entrance, which is decorated with volutes, are wall pillars and mouldings; the date 1751 can be seen. The Jesuit coat of arms is placed above the wrought-iron gate.  
The Jesuit working brethren (*fratres operarii*) also participated in the painting of the church under the instruction of renowned masters of the Austrian Baroque movement. Caspar Franz Sambach from Breslau (Wrocław), later the head of the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna (Vienna's Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture), painted the fresco in the nave. One part of the fresco on the side of the sanctuary, depicts one of the central themes of the Hungarian Baroque, the so called *Patrona Hungariae* (King St. Stephen offers Hungary to the Virgin Mary). The section of the fresco on the side of the main entrance and the choir, illustrates allegories of Faith, Hope and Love. The painting on the sanctuary wall shows the Apotheosis of St. John of Nepomuk, and, according to legend, the benefactors of the construction, P. Antal Vanossi SJ and Mrs. Antal Amadé, are also represented. The sanctuary fresco depicts the Holy Trinity.  
Michelangelo Unterberger created the side altarpiece paintings, *St. Ignatius of Loyola*, and those of *St. James*, *St. Aloysius Gonzaga* and *St. Francis Xavier*. The *Guardian Angel*, *Holy Cross* and the Loreto Chapel were painted by Jesuit *fratres operarii*, Antal Werle and János F. Magis. On the side wall of the choir, a portrait of Ignác P. Stocker can be seen. The vestry is to the right of the sanctuary, and the Loreto Chapel on the left. The amazingly beautiful church furniture was also carved by Jesuit *fratres operarii* between 1749 and 1760, under the instruction of Bernát F. Baumgartner, an outstanding master of Hungarian Jesuit fretwork and wood carving (the woodwork and wooden decorations of the altars were made in 1757; the pews in 1760; the furniture of the refectory, which disappeared in the 19th century, in 1759; he also made the furniture of the monastery and the apothecary). Of the *fratres operarii*, János Pál Koller and Fülöp Kratz (wood carvers) and József Cordelli, a painter and wood carver who trained in a joiner's workshop and was later naturalised in Fehérvár, are worth particular mention. The Rococo oak furniture of the vestry was made by the Pauline monk János Hyngeller between 1764 and 1767.
ae5eb4e1-dec3-5bc8-8109-e2ff967a5580.short_description: The Jesuit Church and Monastery of Székesfehérvár, built between 1745 and 1756, is a marvellous example of the workmanship of the Jesuit artists, masters and “working brethren” (*fratres operarii*) in Hungary. The masterful wooden decorations, carved in the Jesuit joiner's workshop of Bernát Baumgartner, are an outstanding feature of the church interior. Besides the Jesuit Masters, the painter Caspar Franz Sambach also participated in the decoration of the church. The church is dedicated to St. John of Nepomuk, patron saint of the Jesuit order. An icon of obedience, St. John maintained the secrecy of confessions. His good reputation meant that he was popular in countries that were under Austrian Habsburg rule.
ae5eb4e1-dec3-5bc8-8109-e2ff967a5580.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, and stylistic research.

ae5eb4e1-dec3-5bc8-8109-e2ff967a5580.history:
Until the Ottoman rule, Fehérvár was the sacral centre of the Hungarian Kingdom: it served as a venue for coronations and a place of burial for Hungarian kings. The city was occupied by the Ottomans in 1543 and remained under their rule until 1688. After the occupation, the Jesuit order, which settled in Fehérvár in 1688, was the driving force behind the re-introduction of Christianity in the city. The Jesuits built their Church (dedicated to St. John of Nepomuk), Monastery and School on the site of the former Church of St. Jacob, which had been turned into a mosque by the Turks. Jesuit artists and the working brethren (*fratres operarii*) played an important role in the design, financing and completion of the church, towards which P. Antal Vanossi SJ, head of the Jesuit province in Austria, was a major benefactor.  
The Church and Monastery were designed by the architect Paul Hartzinger, a disciple of Martin (Athanasius) Wittwer, a Carmelite monk, who was also naturalised in Fehérvár. The patron of the construction was Ignác P. Stocker SJ. Building of the complex began in 1742 but the foundation stone of the church was not laid until 1745. In 1747, the decoration of the interior and exterior of the church began; the pulpit was completed in 1749. Construction work continued until the 1750s (main altar 1750; entrance gate 1751 and consecration of the church in 1756).  
Following dissolution of the Jesuit order, the buildings were used by the Pauline order between 1773 and 1786, and by the Cistercians from 1813 to 1950. After that the church fell under the control of the diocese, and the monastery became the centre of the King St. Stephen Museum.

aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.name: *Pentecost*
aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.description:
Joseph Ignaz Mildorfer was born into a well-known Tyrolese painter-family and moved at an early date to the imperial city of Vienna to earn his living as did many of his contemporaries from Tyrol. Between 1740 and 1742 he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna where, in 1742, he won a competition and in 1751, following the example of his fellow painter, Paul Troger also from Tyrol, he became an academic professor. As a fresco and altarpiece painter, Mildorfer won fame and important commissions in Austria, Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary (Pápa, Sárvár, Fertőd, Holics (Holič) and Máriavölgy (Marianka). His skilfully executed early battle scenes bear witness to an almost unknown chapter in his oeuvre.  
Traditionally, the high altar painting in the Holy Spirit Church in Sopron along with the sketch made for it, were attributed to István Dorffmaister who was a graduate of the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and a resident of Sopron from 1782. However, recently, it has become clear that the execution of the high altar painting and the Pietà side-altarpiece are earlier: appearing to be the same age as the structure of the high altar, which together with its plastic decoration, dates to around 1750. The composition of the *Pentecost* altarpiece – the type of figures represented and their formation – are very close to the *Assumption* fresco painted by Mildorfer in the chapel of Castle Milotice in Moravia in the 1750s. Here similar character types swing into ecstasy; the same bearded characters, the use of very strong foreshortening close to caricature, and disproportioned, over-sized hands and feet. The strong light streaming into the picture from the dove of the Holy Spirit almost brightens the whole picture space: the figures of the apostles appearing before it almost as silhouettes.  
The Sopron altarpiece, along with the excellent *bozzetto* (sketch) both of which are attributed to Mildorfer, belong to a group of early Hungarian works from the generation of Viennese painters from the Paul Troger school.
aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.short_description: Recently attributed to the excellent Tyrolese painter, Joseph Ignaz Mildorfer, the high altarpiece in Sopron and its expressive *bozzetto* (sketch) belong to a group of early Hungarian works from the generation of Viennese painters from the Paul Troger school. Mildorfer was a master of several frescoes in Hungary (Pápa, Sárvár, Fertőd, Holics (Holič) and Máriavölgy (Marianka).
aef39b85-cdec-5249-98d0-e5cf50a42a36.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis of Mildorfer’s work
