af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.name: Black Eagle Pharmacy Museum
af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.description:
The three-axis facade of the 18th-century, L-shaped, two-level, saddle-back-roofed building of the Black Eagle Pharmacy Museum is in the Classical style. The ground floor is adorned with simple toothing and the upper floor is embellished with surface decoration. The upper-floor windows have curved top-planes. The door frame of the former pharmacy entrance (in the middle axis of the street facade), and the red limestone frames of the windows on the ground floor, are adorned with carved garlands.  
Inside, the pharmacy service area was in the arched, divided space on the ground floor. Four pieces of oak furniture made by Bernát Baumgartner (SJ) and his workshop are still in situ, including a carved and gilded unit with shelves of different lengths and widths, a worktop, cupboards and drawers; the names of medicines are written in Latin in white letters on the white surface of the cabinet drawers, which have handles of either brass or wood. The Empire table, made under Ferenc Braun the owner after 1811, is horseshoe shaped, and holds gilded wooden statues of Hygeia and Panacea, daughters of Asclepius, the god of healing. The pharmaceutical jars on the shelves are of various periods. About 160 wooden skillets, a dozen holders for powders and liquids with the initials “I.H.S.”, a brass mortar (with the inscription: “Apothecae S. J. Alba Regalensis Anno 1752”) and a tincture-press remain from the original mid-18th-century apothecary set.
af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.short_description: The history of the Black Eagle Pharmacy in Székesfehérvár is associated with the Jesuit order. The Society of Jesus (SJ) considered the professional healthcare of the community as an integral part of its duty and established pharmacies in several Hungarian towns. Granted the right to operate a pharmacy in Székesfehérvár in 1745, the first pharmacy was established in the refectory of the old Jesuit monastery from 1746, for which Bernát Baumgartner (SJ) and his workshop produced richly adorned wooden furniture in 1758. The furnishings were auctioned after the dissolution of the order in 1773, but did not go far, however, for Ferenc Walter purchased the furnishing for the Black Eagle Pharmacy that he opened across the street and which operated for 200 years.
af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, field work and restoration.

af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.history:
The Jesuit order settled in Székesfehérvár in 1688. The first pharmacy was opened in the town the same year and owned secularly up until 1745 with exclusive rights to run a pharmacy. The Jesuits then bought the rights, operating pharmacies in several Hungarian towns including Pozsony (Bratislava), Nagyszombat (Trnava), Trencsén (Trenčin), Eger, Győr and Kőszeg. Besides their devotion to providing healthcare in the local community, the order had extensive experience in pharmacy-management worldwide owing to their missionary activities in, for example, Europe and the Far East. The Jesuit Székesfehérvár pharmacy was established in the old monastery refectory in 1746, where Brother Joannes Maschner was apothecary until 1747. He was succeeded by Mathias Hyll who remained in the position from 1748 to 1774.  
The cabinetmaker, Bernát Baumgartner (SJ) and his workshop produced richly adorned wooden furniture for the Rococo-stuccoed pharmacy in the monastery refectory in 1758. In 1773, when the order was dissolved, the finely carved and gold encrusted apothecary’s unit, the table (since destroyed) and the pharmacy equipment were auctioned. The equipment did not go far, however, for Ferenc Walter purchased it for the Black Eagle Pharmacy that he opened across the street. After 1811, Ferenc Braun, the owner at that time, replaced the table with one in the Empire style. The secular pharmacy operated continuously until 1971 under several different owners. Recent restorations have revealed the original blue-green mottled surfaces of several wooden skillets with inscriptions in a Rococo cartouche frame. These, along with certain pieces of wooden furniture from the pharmacy laboratory, must have belonged to the furnishing of 1758 and are thought to be the works of József Codelli, a Jesuit convert and head of the furniture workshop between 1746 and 1747. A pharmacy museum was opened on the premises in 1973; since 1975 it has been known as the Black Eagle Pharmacy Museum.

af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.name: *The Immaculate Conception with the Saints Petronius and Dionysius*
af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.description:
This altarpiece is one of the most celebrated works of the young Giovanni Antonio Burrini. It was commissioned by the noble Ratta family at the end of the seventeenth-century. Two saints are surrounding the Virgin. They are Petronius the bishop and patron of Bologna, and Dionysius the martyr and bishop of Paris who is often confused with the Areopagite. Saint Dionysius was probably painted by request of the patrons. It is believed that one of the members of the Ratta family was a diplomat sent by the pope to France to persuade Louis XIV to abolish the edit of Nantes and restart the prosecution of the Huguenots.  
The altarpiece is built on a pyramidal composition and is dedicated to the Carraccis and to Guido Reni. The delicate features and the brush strokes are reflective of Lorenzo Pasinelli and Sebastiano Ricci as both artists were working in Bologna at that time.
af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.short_description: This celebrated altarpiece is one of the masterpieces of the young Burrini. Depicted at the feet of the Virgin, Saint Petronius, the patron of Bologna, and Saint Dionysius, the patron of France. The lively figures are reminiscent of Lorenzo Pasinelli, while the luminous colours and the quick brush strokes are an homage to the Venetian artist Sebastiano Ricci.
af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.provenance: Ratta Garganelli Chapel, San Giacomo Maggiore, Bologna
af7b7b45-598f-5e3c-8472-5d1ad570467e.obtention: This painting was originally made for the Ratta Garganelli chapel in the church of San Giacomo il Maggiore in Bologna. Later it was moved to the parish church of Monghidoro.

afbab4a5-e4c8-5be4-8822-1d88eb3b80a7.name: Zichy-Meskó Palace
afbab4a5-e4c8-5be4-8822-1d88eb3b80a7.description:
The palace is a three-storey building between Kolostor and Új streets with an internal courtyard. There are two closed balconies on the sides of the main facade upheld by stumpy pillars. The facade is moderately decorated: the ground floor is adorned with toothing, while the upper floors are connected with alettes. The second-floor windows with hood-mouldings bear Rosetta, tendril and volute motifs, while those on the third floor are twin windows with simple stone frames. The back facade is even simpler; the medieval-framed windows contrasting with the round-arched windows of the banqueting hall, which are two-storeys high. The main-entrance gate on Kolostor Street, through which the ground floor corridor is accessible, has an 18th-century lock and iron hoops. The gateway has a wrought-iron gate adorned with ornamental flowers that bear initials, probably those of the Meskó family. The three-armed staircase that leads up to the second floor is punctuated by four alcoves that hold life-sized allegorical female figures identified in the literature as Fortune, Power, Justice and Science. At each step, on the handrail, there are *putti* holding flower vases, which at one time held candelabras.  
There are two representative rooms in the *piano nobile* on the second floor:  the two storey-high banqueting hall with its walls divided up by double parastades, and an allegorical ceiling painting within a richly adorned architectonic frame depicting a fisherman cooking a meal in a marmite next to a tree with a woman on one side and a fishing *putto* on the other (according to scholars it is by Daniel Gran, c. 1734). The other, the so-called reception room, has a painted ceiling decorated with flowers, *volute*s and acanthuses, at the sides of which are human faces in shields. *Boiserie* (wood panelling) covers the side walls up to the ceiling, punctuated by figure-of-eight-shaped *boiserie* fields filled with carved flowers, garlands and grid motifs, contained within rectangular frames. The genre portraits of Baron Jakab Meskó and his wife – recalling French-Flemish paintings – are in two oval wooden planes on one of the walls. Between the portraits there is a Venetian mirror above a marble fireplace. Carved consoles abut from the plane of the *boiserie*, originally used to hold small porcelains and vases.
afbab4a5-e4c8-5be4-8822-1d88eb3b80a7.short_description: The Zichy-Meskó Palace, located in the heart of the city of Sopron, is an impressive Baroque edifice that reflects the former grandeur of city palaces of the Hungarian nobility. There are four allegorical life-sized female figures on the stairway and exquisite ceiling painting in the elegant banqueting hall on the upper floor. The elaborately carved *boiserie* (wood panelling) in one of the rooms was rare in 18th-century Hungary. In the reception room, the genre portraits of Baron Jakab Meskó and his wife – both drinking a hot beverage and the baron smoking a pipe good-humouredly – are by the Viennese painter Ludwig van Roy of around 1740.
afbab4a5-e4c8-5be4-8822-1d88eb3b80a7.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources.

afbab4a5-e4c8-5be4-8822-1d88eb3b80a7.history: There was probably an older building on the site of the present 18th-century three-storey Zichy-Meskó Palace as indicated by the medieval-framed windows on the back facade. There is no exact information available about the Baroque reconstruction, but the design of the present facade dates to around 1725. In 1734 the building was owned by Countess Bartalotti, and became the property of the Meskó family after her death in 1772. The four allegorical female statues on the stairway, the ceiling painting in the banqueting hall – formerly related to the Viennese artist István Dorffmaister – along with the ceiling painting in the *boiserie* (wood-panelled) reception room, originate from this period around 1770. The two oval wooden planes incorporated into the *boiserie,* representing Baron Jakab Meskó and his wife in relaxed poses, were painted by the Viennese artist Ludwig van Roy in 1740. Certain sections of the stairway handrail were replaced in the 19th century. The palace was bought by Lajos Niczky, sub-prefect of Sopron county in 1816. Niczky sold it to Miklós Zichy in 1828, who sold it to Mária Meskó in 1850. The Zichy-Meskó family, united in marriage, owned it until 1945.

b0926d7c-2c0b-52f5-9714-d64d818e9564.name: Cistercian Abbey of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary
b0926d7c-2c0b-52f5-9714-d64d818e9564.description: The marvelous obverse of the monastery impressively reveals its double function as a twin-façade: the eastern part of the building to the left serves as a monastery building and the western part, to the right, as a residence. The enormous pomp of the front pillars of the church proclaims visually the duality between spiritual and worldly power. Statues play the roles of Christ as Savior of the World and Saint Benedict and Bernhard of Clairvaux as the patrons of the Cistercian Order. The richly ornamented pillars of the church interior mirror those of the Theatine Church in Munich, while the monumental proportions of the barrel-vaulted wall-pillared hall mimic the Jesuit Church in the same city, expressing that the elector Maximilian II Emanuel is following the tradition of Counter-Reformist foundations of his forefathers. The church nave, flanked by high chapels, opens onto a long choir where numerous choir-stalls are a reminder that the convent once was rich in members. A great number of confessionals stress the idea of the atonement of the monastery’s founder.
b0926d7c-2c0b-52f5-9714-d64d818e9564.short_description: The Cistercian Abbey Fürstenfeld is also known as the “Bavarian Escorial” due to its function as a Baroque monastery residence. It contains possibly the most magnificent monastery church of Upper Bavaria, whose grandiose interior is laden with columns and contains, among other fine works, frescos and altars from the famous family of artists, Asam. The interior is abundantly furnished with white carved and stucco figures and a multitude of confessionals, all of which remind one that, at one time, this was the Wittelsbachian Monastery of Atonement.
b0926d7c-2c0b-52f5-9714-d64d818e9564.dates: 1691–1700: monastery and residence building; 1714–1741: church; 1752: church tower; 1760–1762: high altar

b0926d7c-2c0b-52f5-9714-d64d818e9564.history: The former Cistercian Abbey Fürstenfeld was founded in 1263 as an atonement monastery by Duke Ludwig (Louis) II in remembrance of his first wife Marie of Brabant whom he had executed on suspicion of adultery. Marie’s son Emperor Ludwig (Louis) the Bavarian further cultivated the abbey. In 1691 Abbot Balduin Helm laid the foundations for the monastery, the design for which was greatly influenced by the Bavarian Elector Maximilian II Emanuel’s wish to extend the monastery connected with his family as a residence. For this project the court architect Antonio Viscardi was contracted, who also began to erect the abbey church as well in 1700. In 1701, however, construction of the church ceased for financial reasons. Due to the occupation of Bavaria by Austria, which followed as a result of the War of the Spanish Succession, and Viscardi’s death, the foreman Johann Georg Ettenhofer was not able to complete the church until 1714 and it was not sanctified until 1741. The monastery itself financed all construction costs itself and did not receive any financial assistance from the reigning Wittelsbach family.
b0926d7c-2c0b-52f5-9714-d64d818e9564.patrons: Maximilian II Emanuel, elector of Bavaria (1680–1726); Abbots Balduin Helm (1690–1705), Liebhard Kellerer (1714–1736), Konstantin Haut (1734–1744), Alexander Pellhammer (1745–1761), Martin Hazi (1761–1779)

b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.name: *Portrait of Count Sámuel Teleki with Baron Sámuel Brukenthal’s half-length portrait*
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.description:
J. M. Stock was a Transylvanian Saxon portrait painter and engraver, who matriculated to the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna in 1763, where he was a pupil of Meytens. From 1771, he studied at the Academy of Engraving in Vienna and afterwards lived in Pozsony (Bratislava). As an art connoisseur in Vienna, he dealt with Sámuel Brukenthal, Governor of Transylvania, and carried out commissions for him. In 1786, the painter gave up his work in Bratislava and went with Brukenthal to Nagyszeben (Sibiu).  
The portrait of Sámuel Teleki with Sámuel Brukenthal in the background is a *Freundschaftsbild* or “friendship picture”. Although they had similar scientific interests, and were both art collectors and founders of a museum and library (Teleki in Marosvásárhely (Târgu Mureş) and Brukenthal in Nagyszeben (Sibiu), the intellectual basis of this “friendship painting” was their freemasonic relationship. Both were members of important lodges in Vienna and helped to initiate and then supervise methodical preparation of an encyclopaedia undertaken by the Masonic Lodge in Nagyszeben (Sibiu); the intention of the project was to cover the history and contemporary conditions of all three nations inhabiting the region.  
Stock portrayed both Teleki and Brukenthal at their desks. Teleki, in Hungarian national costume, poses in a way commonly adopted by scientists and is within a context suggestive of a study. In the background, Brukenthal is portrayed dressed in casual garments in the pose of a French encyclopaedist-philosopher; the portrait provides a fitting detail for the interior. In addition, the picture includes motifs relating to freemasonry for on the desk, among other objects suggesting scientific study, is a map of Háromszék county in Transylvania showing the names of cities particularly active in freemasonry. The bust of Joseph II, also on the desk, is significant in that the Edict of Tolerance issued by the Emperor in 1781, made Sámuel Teleki's public career possible permitting, amongst other things, his appointment as Vice Chancellor of Transylvania in 1787.
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.short_description: Johann Martin Stock was a well-educated portrait painter and graphic artist in Nagyszeben (Sibiu) and Pozsony (Bratislava). This portrait is a *Freundschaftsbild* or “friendship picture” of the library's founders, the Transylvanian count Sámuel Teleki and his friend, Baron Sámuel Brukenthal, whose portrait is in the background.
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.method_for_datation: The painting, both signed and dated, portrays two men whose identities have been confirmed with the help of engravings.
b10f4142-3c70-5d92-a683-74544a7543bd.obtention: Transferred from the City Art Gallery to the Museum of Fine Arts where it was up until 1974, when it was moved to the Hungarian National Gallery.

b2356556-a625-5737-b479-cc4ee36bec9e.name: Abbot’s House
b2356556-a625-5737-b479-cc4ee36bec9e.description:
A grand house surrounding a trapezoidal inner courtyard with four irregular wings, its seven-axial main façade has a shoulder between each level and garlands on the upper floor divided by alettes with Ionic capitals. It looks onto Széchenyi Square. Rectangular-framed windows with hood-moulding adorned with volutes and shell motifs, are repeated in the middle axis above the two windows of the enclosed balcony, which rests on abutting stone consoles over the main gate. Between the balcony windows there is a stone crucifix with a corpus and the coat of arms of the Benedictine order. On the two sides of the closed balcony there are two alcoves with the statues of *King St. Stephen* on the left and *St. Benedict* on the right. The crowning cornice over the balcony is significantly abutting. The main facade is crowned with a tympanum with a gilded motif of the Eye of God in the middle.  
The wide, round-arched main gate leads to a spacious entrance with three arched sections. The rooms are accessible from a quadripartite-vaulted corridor. On the ground floor to the left of the gate, there are arched rooms, a stairway and the service rooms (kitchen, lavatories); to the right is the refectory and other service rooms (storage room, bakery). The most representative rooms are on the upper floor: the exquisite dining room behind the main axis (now the museum banqueting hall) with rooms each side and the chapel. The monk's cells used to be in the left-hand wing. The wing at the furthest side of the courtyard was used as a carriage-stable, barn and storage rooms.  
The walls of the dining room are painted with a marbled finish; the ceiling is adorned with (signed) paintings by István Schaller, from Győr (other scholars say Tyrol). The programme for the paintings was probably the brainwave of Benedek Sajghó, Abbot of Pannonhalma: allegories of the *Church Triumphant over False Teachings* (entrance); the *Triumph of the Church* (in the middle, dated: 1756) and the *Annunciation* (front-facing wall). In the interim arch sections: the *Christening of the Pagan Hungarians*, the *Dream of Pope Sylvester II Sending a Crown to St. Stephen*, *Abbot Astricus Handing the Crown to St. Stephen*, the *Visit of St. Imre (Emeric) to Pannonhalma*, and on the walls between the closed balcony and the two windows, *grisaille* allegorical representations of the monks' daily lives. All the paintings are framed within elaborate stuccoes.
b2356556-a625-5737-b479-cc4ee36bec9e.short_description: A spectacular Baroque town palace built to accommodate the Benedictine monks of Pannonhalma. Surrounding a trapezoidal inner courtyard with four wings, Benedek Sajghó Abbot of Pannonhalma, began construction in the early 1740s. The most outstanding decorations – wall paintings and stuccoes – are in the dining room.
b2356556-a625-5737-b479-cc4ee36bec9e.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual resources, the signature and date and field research.

Velladics, M., *Magyar Épitészet. Barokk, rokokó és copf. (Hungarian Architecture. Baroque, Rococo and Zopf)*, Budapest, 2002, pp. 54–55.
b2356556-a625-5737-b479-cc4ee36bec9e.history:
In the medieval period there were several smaller residential buildings on the site in Győr where the Abbot's House now stands. According to the *cadastre* of 1617, one of the buildings was owned by Beccaria Virgil, a merchant of Italian origin who was town magistrate (1635 and 1636). By all accounts he was an influential and wealthy citizen; patron of the St. Rosalia Altar in the Church of St. Ignatius in 1642. Another resident was Mátyás Nyéki Vörös (a canon, a member of the Chapter of Győr and an accomplished writer); both of these men were significant citizens of Győr.  
In 1668, Abbot Egyed Gencsy purchased several houses in the street until all the houses where the building now stands were acquired by the Abbey of Pannonhalma. Abbot Benedek Sajghó bought the last house in 1733, and established the Abbot's House in the early 1740s as monk's accommodation (hence the name), as it was far more convenient for the abbot and monks to rest in Győr on their way to and from Pannonhalma.  
House building was strictly monitored in 18th-century Győr: because of the Turkish threat houses could be no taller than the ramparts, and as the abbot perceived the house with several storeys, the military council had to give their approval.  
During the Napoleonic Wars when the town was occupied by the French, the soldiers of the Napoleonic army held a ball in the beautifully decorated dining hall to celebrate Napoleon. The remains of their painted poems praising the emperor in pigeon French (because they were Italian) can still be discerned on the walls. Napoleon did not actually attend the ball, but the citizens of Győr were present.  
Joseph II dissolved the Benedictine order in 1786 and the building became the property of the Hungarian Chamber; first serving as barracks and later as an orphanage. In 1802, Francis II reinstated the order and their estates and five monasteries were returned to them (on condition they provided the teaching in 10 grammar schools, took over the Jesuit boarding and grammar school and the Academy of Győr) and the Abbot's House was given back to the Benedictine monks of Pannonhalma. By royal order in 1817, however, the monks handed the building over to the Chapter of Győr, and it became a seminary for priests up until 1857; from 1910 it was a residential training college. In 1949 the former Monk's House became the Xántus János Museum, which it still is today in addition to being the headquarters of the Museum Directorate of Győr-Moson-Sopron County.

b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.name: Monstrance of the Bemposta
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.alternate_name: Monstrance of the Chapel of the Palace of Bemposta or Palace of the Queen
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.description:
This magnificent monstrance in gilded silver and gold with a triangular base, sits on three volutes ornamented with floral motifs, ribbons and cartouches. On the three inferior angles of the base there are cherubs and three figures that symbolise Faith, Hope and Charity. On the top corners there are three full-bodied angels conveying Eucharistic motifs, while six cherubs and seraphs, overlap, ascending along the stem.  
On the three faces of the base oval bas-reliefs represent themes from the Eucharist: The Supper at Emmaus and the giant bunch of grapes, Fruit from the Promised Land and Christ at Calvary.  
The monstrance' sunburst is encircled by clouds. It has a radiant splendor with irregular rays, covered with precious stones. The monstrance's surface is entirely adorned with precious stones, some of them large and of excellent quality, creating a spectacular decorative and chromatic effect.  
The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metal and gemstones.  
It is likely the monstrance was commissioned by King Pedro III, husband of Queen Maria I. In Pedro III's Will of 1786 he foresees that his son, the future King João VI, should have the country house in Queluz, and urges him to care for the divine cult traditionally associated with the Bemposta Chapel, where he wished the precious monstrance to be kept.  
Attribution of this piece is controversial. Traditionally, researchers attributed it to J. F. Ludovice, the goldsmith and architect of the Convent of Mafra. Their theories were based on an existing drawing of the monstrance at the Museum, which also came from the Bemposta Palace.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.short_description: A majestic monstrance in gilded silver with precious stones that creates a spectacular chromatic effect. The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metals and gemstones.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.method_for_datation: Vassalo e Silva (2000) proposed that Adão Gottlieb Pollet both designed and made the monstrance. This is based on a specific analysis of the application of the gemstones. Although initially the  monstrance was dated to 1740–1750 the date is now thought to be later, 1775–1780.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.provenance: Chapel of the Palace of Bemposta
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.obtention: Given over to *Museu National de Arte Antiga* by the National Academy of Fine Arts in 1876

b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.name: *King João V of Portugal Drinking Coffee and Chocolate*
b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.description:
This interesting miniature, set within an ornate silver frame displaying the royal coat of arms, is one of only a few remaining objects from the Joanine court to have survived the Earthquake of 1755. According to the family of the Marquis of Foz, to whose collection this miniature belonged until 1901, this scene represents King João V being served drinking chocolate at home by the Duke of Lafões. However, in the corner of the miniature is the date 1720, making the Foz identification of the duke implausible given that the duke was born in 1718 and would have been two years old at the time this picture was painted. The most plausible hypothesis is that the person depicted is Prince Miguel of Braganza, the half-brother of the King and father of the future Duke of Lafões, who would, therefore, be the child represented. The Foz family also asserted that the Marquises of Angeja and Alegrete appear in the painting, as well as the painter himself and the house chaplain, however, firm identifications have been neither consistently contradicted nor confirmed.  
The objects depicted in this composition are noteworthy: the utensils associated with painting are in the foreground: a pallet, brushes and a sketch on a piece of paper. The objects related to drinking: a coffee pot, hot chocolate maker, tea cups and a bottle, alluding to the popularity of chocolate and coffee both of which became extremely fashionable among the Portuguese aristocracy and throughout the rest of Europe.  
Although the scene suggests a relaxed and jolly atmosphere, the strict etiquette and hierarchy of the Joanine court is present within the structure of the composition: the representational field is divided into two halves, with the higher ranking figures on the left-hand side.  
Nothing is known about the identity of the miniaturist, although his name suggests that he might be one of many Italian artists who, together with other foreigners, came to work in Portugal during the reign of João V. The frame presents plant-like decorations with acanthus, volutes and shell shapes in chiselled and embossed silver – a feature associated with the first quarter of the 1700s. The frame is surmounted by a shield and crowned with the Portuguese royal arms sustained by two lieutenant *putti.* A grotesque mask at the bottom centre is typical of this phase of the Baroque period. A chiselled frieze with laurel leaves serves as an internal frame for the miniature.
b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.short_description: A miniature painting representing King João V of Portugal with a group of courtesans being served coffee and chocolate, within an ornate silver frame bearing the royal coat of arms.
b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.dates: 1720 (miniature); first quarter of the 18th century (silver frame)

b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.name: Catholic Parish Church of St. Alban
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.description: The largest rural church in the Tyrol, under the patronage of St. Alban of Mainz since the Early Middle Ages, is an imposing Early Classicist building with Late Baroque elements. The latter were executed against the designs and directives of the Salzburg church administration, for example the frescos, which were not originally planned. The design of the Royal Building Commissioner Hagenauer was replaced by the working plan from Thomas Mayr of Lienz. This envisaged a pilaster church enriched with narrow choir lofts in a highly uniform, strict arrangement, however according to the Baroque scheme.
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.short_description: The parish church of Matrei is one of the largest rural churches in Austria as well as one of the most important buildings within the circle of Salzburg Early Classicism influenced by the Royal Building Commissioner Wolfgang Hagenauer. However in its planning and realisation it is largely the work of local artisans who mixed “enlightened Classicism” with Late Baroque traditions.
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.location: Matrei in East Tyrol, East Tyrol
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.bibliography: Brugger, A., Wörgötter, J., *Pfarrkirche St. Alban Matrei in Osttirol*, Matrei 1984.
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.history: The parish of Matrei had been under the jurisdiction of the Archbishopric of Salzburg since the Early Middle Ages. A church stood on the site of the Vordermarkt (front market) in the Late Middle Ages but was destroyed by fire in 1326. Its Gothic successor was consecrated in 1334. Due to disrepair and lack of space the decision to erect a new building was made in 1770 and work began in 1777. The church was completed in 1783 and consecrated in 1789. The high altar and side altars were not erected until 1805–1807.
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.architects:
Architectural plan: Thomas Mayr \[n.d.\], Christoph Anton Mayr (c. 1720–1771); ceiling frescos: Franz Anton Zeiller (1716–1794); altar superstructures: Anton Simeth \[n.d.\]; figures: Petrus Schmid \[n.d\]; paintings: Andreas Nesselthaler (1748–1821);  
Pulpit and baldachin, carpentry: Michael Hueber \[n.d.\], stuccowork: Franz Graßmayr \[n.d.\], sculpture: Johann Paterer (1712–1785)
keywords: Parish church; Early Classicism; ceiling frescoes
b460a85c-5f50-5ffc-9b0a-485d88e4ddaa.author: Frank Purrmann

b4b15f34-442c-5333-aad1-149ef41e40f4.name: Basilica di San Paolo Maggiore
b4b15f34-442c-5333-aad1-149ef41e40f4.description:
On a brick and sandstone façade, Ercole Fichi located the two upper statues, St. Charles Borromeo and St. Philip Neri, the lower ones, St. Peter and St. Paul, were carved by Domenico Mirandola and Giulio Cesare Conventi. The frieze is decorated with fleur-de-lis and swords, the Spadas' heraldic symbols.  
Magenta planned the church on a Latin cross scheme, with a single nave and side chapels. Several art works enrich the inside, together with the painted decorations that represent stories of St. Paul.  
In the 19th century Angelo Venturoli and Antonio Serra drew plans for the altars; the most famous local baroque artists (Guercino, Giacomo Cavedoni, Mastelletta, Giuseppe Maria Crespi) painted the altarpieces. Ludovico Carracci painted for this church his celebrated “Paradise”.  
Baroque frescoes on the counter façade and the vault representing the life of St. Paul's are by Giuseppe (1645–1727) and Antonio Rolli (1643–1696), who painted them in 1695: while Giuseppe was working on them, he fell from a scaffolding and died. The work was finished by his pupil Paolo Antonio Guidi (1675–1704).  
In the choir and the transept Giuseppe Antonio Caccioli (1672–1740) painted figures inside the quadratures by Pietro Farina: the two artists together decorated the dome with the “Ecstasis of St. Paul” and the pendentives with the four continents.  
A masterpiece is the *Beheading of St. Paul*, a sculpture by Alessandro Algardi, made between 1641 and 1647, and placed inside a ciborium behind the high altar. Local artisans, following the drawings of Francesco Borromini, made the tabernacle of the high altar.
b4b15f34-442c-5333-aad1-149ef41e40f4.short_description: Well known for hosting Algardi's masterpiece (the marble group of the *Beheading of St. Paul*), the church was built after a project by Giovanni Ambrogio Magenta, while the façade is thought to be by Ercole Fichi. Inside, the walls and vaults are decorated with frescos and the side chapels house paintings by celebrated artists of the seventeenth-century.
b4b15f34-442c-5333-aad1-149ef41e40f4.bibliography:
Fanti, M., Riccomini, E., Rubbi, P. E, Tassinari Clò, O., *Le chiese di Bologna*, Bologna, 1992.  
*Storia dell'architettura italiana,  Il Seicento* (ed. A. Scotti Tosini), II, Milan, 2003.  
Fanti, C., *Le chiese di Bologna*, Bologna, 1992.  
Fini, M., *Bologna sacra. Tutte le chiese in due millenni di storia*, Bologna, 2007.
b4b15f34-442c-5333-aad1-149ef41e40f4.history: The church construction began in 1607, following a project of the architect Giovanni Ambrogio Magenta which was financed by the Spada, a noble Bolognese family. The main building’s work was finished in 1611, but the façade was built in 1636, following a project by Ercole Fichi. The church was called “Maggiore” to distinguish it from the other two dedicated to St. Paul in Bologna (Osservanza and Ravone). From the Napoleonic Age the church was ruled by the diocesan clergy and in 1806 it became a parish church. The Barnabite fathers came back in 1959. Pope John XXIII attributed the title of basilica to the church two years after its construction. Antonio Maria Zaccaria, founder of the Barnabite order, was a medicine doctor and that is why St. Paul is the patron of medical doctors.

b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.name: *Gallery of Paintings*
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.description:
The *Gallery of Paintings* shows a large curtained hall, its walls covered with paintings and two mirrors. There are paintings everywhere, on the floor and table, leaning against chairs and resting on stands. There are groups of men and women, members of the nobility and the middle class talking together and viewing the exhibition. Shifted from the central axis of the composition, behind a group of women around an oval table, is a large open door through which there is a view of a garden with a round flowerbed, fountains and architecture. Bordering the *scotia* – the area above the cornice over which rises the half-circle moulding of the ceiling – hangs a cartouche with a two-headed eagle holding a sword and key in its talons.      
A companion painting shows another curtained hall with paintings and many viewers, with a large door opening into another exhibition hall. Bordering the *scotia* in this painting there is a cartouche with a family monogram in the centre, flanked by two allegorical female figures holding a ducal coronet with five tines.  
The Gallery of Paintings genre developed in the 16th and 17th centuries when the first private collectors, the French and Italian nobility, presented their paintings, sculptures and other artworks in their mansions. As the popularity of these “exhibitions” grew, paintings of this kind increasingly showed imaginary galleries that did not represent any particular collection, but a selection of the best-known paintings of the time. *Gallery of Paintings* is attributed to the Flemish painter, Balthasar van den Bossche, who played an extremely important role in the early 18th-century art world. Among other things, he was manager of the Antwerp art gallery. Strongly influenced by the Flemish painter, David Teniers the Younger (1610–1690), Bossche was born only years before Teniers' death. Teniers was court painter and keeper of the art collections in Brussels. He painted several versions of the *Gallery of Paintings* composition, showing Archduke Leopold Wilhelm's art collection. It was from these paintings that attribution of the works of Italian Renaissance painters Giorgione, Titian and Veronese was possible.         
In all probability, acquisition of the *Gallery of Paintings* was for the manor of a prominent noble Croatian family or maybe by an industrialist. This type of painting was characteristic of Flanders during the Baroque period.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.short_description:
The *Gallery of Paintings* shows a large curtained hall, its walls covered with paintings and two mirrors. Individuals and groups of people are viewing the artworks and talking to one another.  
The interior scene is typical of a humanist's or wealthy merchant's home, turned, as was the fashion, into a gallery for artworks and other treasures.  
The *Gallery of Paintings* and its companion are attributed to the Flemish painter, Balthasar van den Bossche, whose work was influenced by David Teniers the Younger. Teniers depicted several variants of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm's collection as a *Gallery* painting. Bossche probably found inspiration in Teniers' *Gallery* paintings for his own, painted almost 20 years after Teniers' death.    
In all probability, acquisition of the *Gallery of Paintings* was for the manor of a prominent noble Croatian family or maybe by an industrialist.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.method_for_datation: The attribution was made by Miroslav Gašparović, Director of the Museum of Arts and Crafts.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.obtention: A gift of the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb in 1909: when the Museum of Arts and Crafts was founded in 1880, suitable material for the newly founded museum was taken from the National Museum's archaeological department. Thus, the Archaeological Museum donated the above *Galleries* because it had nothing in common with archaeology.
b4c166af-6d62-5c17-b7f3-8f2e2ca40078.bibliography: *Muzej za umjetnost i obrt, 1880–1970. Katalog izabranih djela* (Museum of Arts and Crafts, 1880–1970: catalogue of selected works), Zagreb, 1970.
keywords: Gallery of Paintings; Flanders; Balthasar van den Bossche; collection; collector; eagles

b537e33e-fe1b-5a74-b20a-7d704ca4a6b4.name: Church of Santa Maria della Pace
b537e33e-fe1b-5a74-b20a-7d704ca4a6b4.description:
Alexander VII ordered the opening of the square in front of the church within the dense urban fabric of medieval Rome, thus producing a spectacular effect: when the beholder comes from Via della Pace, the facade suddenly appears in all its monumentality among the buildings that surround it.  
Two concave lateral wings constitute the backdrop of this real theatrical architecture. From this background, the convex body of the semi-circular portico of the church, supported by Doric columns, powerfully juts out. The architrave is Ionic instead, and is not divided into metopes and triglyphs as in the Bramante temple of San Pietro in Montorio. This generates a pleasant contrast between the plastic chiaroscuro of the Doric columns and the fluidity of the continuously horizontal architrave.  
The upper part of the facade is also plastically framed by a set of pilasters and semi-columns, re-proposing, in the central part, the convexity of the portico: moreover, the sense of spatial emptiness provided by the entrance between the columns at the centre of the portico corresponds, in the upper floor, to the emptiness of the window, aligned with the portal of the church. The motif of the paired columns is symmetrically repeated in the upper part of the facade.  
It is possible to access the square from the back of the church too, through two openings in the side wings of the facade. The side wings’ function is, moreover, to hide the two back streets from those looking at the church from the square.
b537e33e-fe1b-5a74-b20a-7d704ca4a6b4.short_description: The façade is one of the most perfect examples of Baroque theatricality applied on urban planning. Semicircular portico links up with the sides, like two theatrical wings.
b537e33e-fe1b-5a74-b20a-7d704ca4a6b4.bibliography:
Grundmann, S., “S. Maria della Pace: facade”, in Grundmann S. (ed), *The Architecture of Rome,* Stuttgart/London: Edition Axel Menges, 2007: 231–233.  
Rolfi, S., “S. Maria della Pace”, *I Principi della Chiesa,* Milan, 1998: 200.
b537e33e-fe1b-5a74-b20a-7d704ca4a6b4.history:
The pontificate of Alexander VII Chigi was characterized by the will of the pope to give a new face to Rome through large-scale urban interventions, such as the construction of straights, squares - such as that of St. Peter's Basilica, commissioned to Bernini - and scenic widenings. Having as goal the celebration of his own family name, Alexander VII promoted the restoration of many civil and ecclesiastical buildings that had been erected or decorated at the beginning of the 16th century by his famous ancestor, the Sienese banker and patron Agostino Chigi, such as the 15th-century church of Santa Maria del Popolo or the church Santa Maria della Pace, which was decorated with frescoes by Raphael.  
In particular, in the case of Santa Maria della Pace, the new facade, commissioned to Pietro da Cortona, followed a vote of the pontiff to the Virgin to avert the plague and the threats of Louis XIV king of France.
b537e33e-fe1b-5a74-b20a-7d704ca4a6b4.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.name: Pilgrimage Church of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.alternate_name: Pilgrimage Church St. Mary in the Pear Tree
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.description:
Westwards, the pietà-bearing pear tree was especially highlighted by its framing showcase architecture (now filled with an organ) . Located on the opposite side is the high altar. With their assigned bays, which are flanked by conches, both liturgical features originally formed two “sacred places” facing one another – a unique structure in Southern Germany. The domed structure in the centre serves as a meeting hall for the pilgrims. With its light-flooded lantern , which holds statues of the 12 apostles, it refers back to the Roman Pantheon and therefore functions as a universal symbol for the heavens and the Blessed Virgin Mary.  
The dedicated functions of the spatial sections are mirrored in the actual layout: It is composed of seven differently sized, interlinked circles. The curving of the lateral walls and the large arched openings combine the three spatial sections. Despite the room divisions, it creates a space continuum with the character of a centrally planned building. Attached is the sacristy, facing west behind the tree alcove, and an eastern tower surrounded by three conches behind the altar apsis. Besides the tall lantern of the central domed structure also the two conche-flanked bays were originally crowned with smaller lanterns, so that together with the three towers the building held a fantastic six-towered appearance. Altogether, the church represents one of the few ecclesiastical “fantasy concepts” that had truly been realised in the architectural history of Europe .
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.short_description: A pear tree bearing a miraculous pietà was the eponymous event for the construction of the Early Baroque pilgrimage church St. Mary in the Pear Tree. A richly turreted  exterior design is connected with a complex triplicity of circular rooms. Coherent echoes of the Roman Pantheon play an explicit role. Moulded stucco applied to the inner walls and vaults provides the splendour that is to be expected.
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.bibliography:
Schütz, B., *Maria Birnbaum: Deutschorden-Wallfahrtskirche*, Kleine Kunstführer 401, 13. neubearbeitete Auflage, Regensburg: Schnell & Steiner, 2004.  
Krins, H., *Barock in Süddeutschland*, Stuttgart: Theiss, 2001: 62–65.  
Schütz, B., *Die kirchliche Barockarchitektur in Bayern und Oberschwaben 1580–1780*, München: Hirmer, 2000: 96–98.  
Schütz, B., *Die Wallfahrtskirche Maria Birnbaum und ihre beiden Baumeister*, Kieler kunsthistorische Studien 4, Frankfurt am Main: Peter Lang, 1974.
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.history:
The eponymous event for the construction of a pilgrimage sanctuary, outside the village of Sielenbach in the Ecknachtal region, was a pear tree bearing a miraculous image in the form of a so-called pietà. Because the latter presumably performed divine healings, a church was built surrounding the tree in 1661. An early change of plans initiated the addition of three towers and the semicircular sacristy in the west, followed by a conch that harboured the pear tree until 1866. Along with its miraculous image, the tree had died in 1668, only three years after the consecration, which led to several liturgical changes. The church was mostly restored to its original state in 1866. In this process, a remnant of the memorable tree trunk was incorporated into the furnishing of the high altar.  
The architecture that was planned by the Munich Electoral Master Builder, Konstantin Pader, seemingly traced back to suggestions of Philipp Jakob von Kaltenthal, a patron who travelled widely and was highly educated in architecture. As commander of the Teutonic Order, von Kaltenthal resided at the nearby castle Blumenthal. He had spent a lot of time in Rome where he had become acquainted with the model for the architectural idea that was later to be authenticated by himself: the domed rotunda in the Pantheon – the most symbolic Marian Church of the Eternal City at the time.
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.patrons: Philipp Jakob von Kaltenthal, Commander of the Teutonic Order at Blumenthal (gov. 1658–69)
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.architects: Architectural designs, stucco, and decoration: Konstantin Pader (1605–81);  Stuccowork: Matthias II Schmuzer (1636–86)
b611d069-f267-5ab1-8a39-7ff245de0666.author: Peter Heinrich Jahn, Hanna Böhm

b6545e53-8929-5a75-82b4-3c17d868a214.name: Franciscan Church of St. John the Baptist
b6545e53-8929-5a75-82b4-3c17d868a214.description:
The model for the design of the nave-church of St. John the Baptist with its shallow side-chapels should be sought, judging all in all, in the Zagreb (chapter) Franciscan Church dating to the first decade of the 17th century, or in the Viennese church of the Franciscan Order (1603–1611). In the harmonious Early Baroque space of the Church of St. John the Baptist there are a number of valuable woodcarvings illustrating important phases of the art form in northern Croatia during the Baroque period. The pulpit (1675) – a long and richly articulated item with statues of Christ and the apostles in niches – is a consummate example of Late Mannerist wood carving and one of only a few preserved monumentally founded 17th-century pulpits in Croatia.  
The monumental three-part altar (1700–1702), built according to the designs of the Franciscan, Kristofor Zettl of Munich, fills the chancel completely. The skilled perspective foreshortening of the niches, concluded by coffered vaulting, complement the spaciousness of the altar architecture. The sculptures are by the Maribor sculptor, Franjo Kristof Reiss, and the polychrome and gilding the work of the Zagreb painter and gilder, Joakim Shidt. In the side-chapels there are five altars built during the 1740s, which by stylistic analysis, are attributable to Ivan or Johann Adam Rosemberger, Varaždin's principal sculptors at the time.  
The sculpture of the altars of St. Anthony of Padua (1725) and Our Lady of the Scapular (1735–1745), on the other hand, show a kinship with the work of Ivan Matija Leitner, a sculptor from Bavaria who had a workshop in Graz. The aforementioned altars are found within two chapels decorated by the Styrian stucco master, Joseph Antonio Quadrio. The Paulist painter, Ivan Krstitelj Ranger decorated the monastery apothecary in 1750 – the central scene of this work shows Mary as Queen of the Universe surrounded by allegorical depictions of the Four Continents and Four Elements.
b6545e53-8929-5a75-82b4-3c17d868a214.short_description: The Early Baroque interior of the church presents a kind of gallery of woodcarving spanning the second half of the 17th and mid-18th centuries. It tells of changes in style and taste, as well as demonstrating the Varaždin Franciscan community's range of commissions. Through the order's connections, the Franciscans were able to commission works by leading foreign artists (the high altar) and from local sculptors (five altars with sculptures by Ivan Adam Rosemberger from Varaždin).
b6545e53-8929-5a75-82b4-3c17d868a214.type: Religious, monastery church and interior furnishing
b6545e53-8929-5a75-82b4-3c17d868a214.dates: Church (1650–1655); pulpit (1675); high altar (1700–1702); altars of I. A. Rosemberger (1740s); stuccowork of J. A. Quadrio (1716–1717)

b6545e53-8929-5a75-82b4-3c17d868a214.history: Peter Rabba of Graz built the Early Baroque Church of St. John the Baptist on the foundations of an older church, on the site of the Franciscan Monastery in Varaždin, reconstructed in 1626. The monastery played an important role in Varaždin as the apothecary established there became a public municipal apothecary from 1679 to 1772; the monastery also had an important and active role in education from the early 18th century to the first decades of the 20th.

b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.name: Stove
b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.description: A stove on an iron pedestal and composed of two main parts, the lower has a scalloped design; the walls of the corpus are green and decorated with white sculptural and relief decoration (bunches of flowers, volutes and *Rocaille*). In the centre of the lower part are elongated cartouches with scenes in relief. In two of these cartouches ladies and gentlemen are ambling in the countryside with shepherds' crooks in their hands, while in the third there is an idyllic picture of music-making under a tree. The top of the stove ends with a three-dimensional figure of a female shepherd with a lamb in her arms. The firebox is at the rear.
b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.short_description: A white and green stove richly decorated in the lower part, with a three-dimensional figure of a female shepherd at the top.
b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.obtention: Acquired from the Vraniczany-Dobrinović family in 1936.

b6798fda-f618-5e17-b54f-4eeaaaee4956.name: Santa Maria di Galliera
b6798fda-f618-5e17-b54f-4eeaaaee4956.description: The church shows a single nave plan with side chapels, typical of Counterreformation churches. The interior space was intended as a theatre, devoted to preaching, and the attention of people had to be focused on the high altar as on a stage. The interior is a perfect blend of different arts and techniques. The colours of the frescoes harmonise perfectly with the white and gold stucco decorations and with the soft light coming from the windows.
b6798fda-f618-5e17-b54f-4eeaaaee4956.short_description: This church is a classical example of Bolognese High Baroque. The interior with single nave and side chapels emphases the counterreformation use of churches as places especially dedicated to preaching. The pictorial decoration showing three episodes of the life of St. Philip Neri, founder of the Oratorian congregation, covers the ceilings and the apse, conveying an impression of lively movement. The high altar is typically baroque, with its elegant curves and its open shape, embracing the visitor. It is a good example of the combination of different techniques (sculpture, architectural  and figural painting) and of the employ of different materials (stucco, painted and gilded wood, fresco, and oil on canvas).
b6798fda-f618-5e17-b54f-4eeaaaee4956.dates: In the fourteenth-century the first church dedicated to the Holy Spirit was built on this site, in the seventeenth-century the church was remodelled in the present form by Giovanni Battista Torri

Riccomini, E., *Ordine e Vaghezza*, Bologna, 1972, pp. 101-102.
b6798fda-f618-5e17-b54f-4eeaaaee4956.history: The church was originally built in the fourteenth-century and dedicated to the Holy Spirit. It became an important place of worship of the Madonna, today displayed on the high altar but originally painted on a wall outside the church. In the fifteenth-century the present sandstone façade was added in the Renaissance style. The interior was refurbished in the seventeenth-century by the architect Giovanni Battista Monti for the Oratorian Fathers. He was invited to Bologna and in charge of the church following the will of Pope Gregory XV Ludovisi (1621). The fresco decorations of vaults and walls were added in 1730 ca. by the Bolognese painter Giuseppe Marchesi known as  Sansone. The side chapels are home to several famous pictures by Bolognese masters (Albani, Guercino, Franceschini) framed by beautiful stucco or gilded wooden frames. In 1806 the Congregation of the Oratory was suppressed following Napoleonic dispositions and the church was temporarily closed. Today the church is owned and maintained by the Oratorian Fathers.
b6798fda-f618-5e17-b54f-4eeaaaee4956.architects: Architects: Giovanni Battista Torri, Francesco Galli Bibiena (1659–1739); sculptors: Giuseppe Maria Mazza (1653–1741), Silvestro Giannotti (1680–1750), Angelo Gabriello Piò (1690–1770); painters: Giuseppe Rolli (1645–1727), Giuseppe Marchesi known as Sansone (1699–17)

b70d09b4-b304-5766-96c2-44d09249f330.name: *Portrait of Carlo Broschi called Farinelli*
b70d09b4-b304-5766-96c2-44d09249f330.description: This painting is a portrait of the world famous soprano castrate singer Carlo Broschi whose stage name was Farinelli. He is wearing a cape of the order of Calatrava as in 1750 he was made a Knight of this important Spanish order by the king of Spain Ferdinand VI. The singer touches a page of music laid on the cembalo with his left hand. In the background, oval portraits of the King of Spain and his queen, Maria Barbara di Braganza, are surrounded by a tripudium of nymphs and cupids. There is also a self-portrait of the painter, Corrado Giaquinto. The portrait was part of Farinelli’s rich collection of paintings decorating his villa in Bologna, where he retired after a long stay at the court of Madrid (1737–1759).

b7235782-b04a-58a3-83e1-28d83ed8c19d.name: *Plan for the House of the Invalids in Pest*
b7235782-b04a-58a3-83e1-28d83ed8c19d.description:
The engraving and etching was made after the original drawing by the imperial architect, Anton Erhard Martinelli (1684–1747), for the largest Baroque building, the House of the Invalids in Pest. The building, which was never finished following Martinelli's original plans, is today the City Hall of Budapest.  
The building, which was originally used as a military hospital, has three gates, the central one leading to the former chapel where there are allegorical figures of *War* and *Peace* with a statue of *Atlas* above. The façade is decorated with reliefs commemorating Emperor Charles III and Eugene of Savoy. The foundation stone was laid in 1716, and the main façade was finished in 1731. With the death of the architect, Martinelli, construction of the building stopped in 1741. During the reign of King Joseph II it became a casern named after the founder, Charles III. It became the City Hall in 1894 and was transformed for the purposes of the central office by the architect Ármin Hegedűs.
b7235782-b04a-58a3-83e1-28d83ed8c19d.short_description: A printed *veduta* using a mixed technique showing the plan of the largest Baroque building in Budapest – the House of the Invalids in Pest – designed by Anton Erhard Martinelli (1684–1747). The building, which was never finished following Martinelli's original plans, was rebuilt at the end of the 19th century as the City Hall of Budapest, for which use it is still inhabited today.
b7235782-b04a-58a3-83e1-28d83ed8c19d.method_for_datation: On the basis of the signature

b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.name: *Maria Immaculata*
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.description: This marble figurine, signed by Schletterer, corresponds with the popular type of Immaculate Virgin that evolved during the Catholic revival: the Virgin is at prayer atop a globe and a crescent moon, while she stands on the head of a serpent that symbolises evil. The slender female figure is modelled in a slight S-curve; her compact silhouette determined by the cloak. This feature, along with her charming face and the picturesque details such as the *putto* hiding beneath the drapery, derive from a Viennese variant of the arsenal of Late Baroque Venetian sculpture. The most notable representative of this trend in the imperial city of Vienna was Lorenzo Mattielli, while the leading master of the classical style was Georg Raphael Donner. Both artists influenced the oeuvre of the Tyrolese sculptor, Jakob Christoph Schletterer, who passed down his increasingly sophisticated classicistic style to subsequent generations during his long tutorship at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. In the main, Schletterer made altar sculpture and reliefs for monastic churches in Lower Austria, but sepulchral monuments are also known to be by his hand. His documented works in Hungary – the Virgin Column in Sopron made after Andrea Altomonte's plans in 1745, and the garden statues at Darufalva (Drassburg) from 1758 – suggest that he probably delivered other works to Transdanubia. This signed, white marble *Immaculata* from Esterházy Castle, today at the Hungarian National Gallery in Budapest, is a more animated Rococo variant of the garden statue in Darufalva (Drassburg). In the collection of the Hungarian National Museum there is a similar Immaculata figurine, produced in Tata and transferred from the Cistercian abbey in Zirc, which also dates to the 1750s.
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.short_description: As a follower of Georg Raphael Donner and a professor at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, Schletterer’s monumental works are found throughout Hungary (Győr, Sopron and Drassburg). This small, signed sculpture belonged to the Esterházy family in Tata.
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.provenance: Count Ferenc Esterházy, Esterházy Castle, Tata
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.obtention: From the collection of Count Ferenc Esterházy at Esterházy Castle, Tata; Kuny Domokos Museum, Tata

b755f317-188a-5599-8821-1c6c3bb2c776.name: *The Anatomical Waxes of the Istituto delle Scienze*
b755f317-188a-5599-8821-1c6c3bb2c776.alternate_name: Wax statue representing a naked man (Adam); wax statue representing a naked woman (Eve); wax statue representing a skinned man (“scorticato”); wax statue of a man showing superficial and deep muscles; wax statue of a man showing deep muscles; wax skeleton of a woman showing deep skeleton muscles; wax male skeleton; 52 anatomical waxes
b755f317-188a-5599-8821-1c6c3bb2c776.description: The eighteenth-century was an especially lucky age for Bolognese wax artists thanks to the renovated intellectual life in town. Originally for the creation of ephemera as well as for long-lasting works. This art was generally employed for scientific purposes, by doctors, as they needed to study the delicate intricacies of the human body. In 1742 Pope Benedict XIV commissioned Ercole Lelli, a professor of the local Academy of Fine Arts, to create a group of anatomical waxes for study purposes for the room of Anatomy in the *Istituto delle Scienze*. Lelli had to mould eight statues on natural scale including a naked man and woman, and six skinned figures in order to emphasise the different muscular layers. The series is composed of more than 40 anatomical waxes representing muscles and bones. A century later professor Michele Medici wrote that Lelli used two human skeletons for his skinned men, arranged and modelled the different muscles with a mixture of hemp, wax, bran and turpentine then moulded the muscles in the right places, from life. Lelli said that the human body, known through the dissection of corpses, was the main interest of artistic anatomy. Every single detail was carefully studied and analysed; even the statues attitudes, especially in the nudes, were made to emphasise the superficial muscles.
b755f317-188a-5599-8821-1c6c3bb2c776.short_description: The eight anatomical statues realised by Ercole Lelli, include the 52 anatomical waxes (30 of them are about muscles and 20 about bones). Lelli planned the furnishings of the anatomy room; designing elegant cabinets with glass panes, perfect for housing the anatomical waxes, alternating with showcases where the statues could be easily studied from each point of view.

b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.name: Ivan V Drašković (about 1660–Varaždin, Croatia, 4.1.1733)
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.description:
For generations the Drašković family played an important part in the political and social life of Croatia. Counts from the 17th century (1631), numerous members of the family became *bans* (viceroys) and high-ranking military officers. The family's wealth comprised numerous estates, among which were Trakošćan and Klenovnik castles in northwest Croatia. Ivan V Drašković, son of vice-marshal Ivan IV and Marija Magdalena Nádasdy, studied in Varaždin, Vienna and Bologna before returning to Croatia in 1695. In 1699, he became Grand Sheriff of the Valpovo and Baranja County, and shortly after became a royal councillor. Having excelled militarily, promotion to General followed in 1708 and the Croatian parliament named him Commander of the Croatian National Troops. He actively supported the proposal to ensure the right of succession of the Habsburg female line (Croatian Pragmatic Sanction) in 1712. He fought as vice-marshal (*podmaršal*) on the Turkish border. Drašković was acting *ban* (viceroy) from 1718 to 1732 but only officially appointed to the post on 2 February 1732. He died suddenly the following year.  
The portrait, painted some time shortly after Drašković officially became *ban* in 1732, depicts the elderly count as a nobleman, his right hand holding a general's baton. On the right-hand side, the imperial eagle holds the coats of arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia, signifying his official status as *ban*. In the background to the left is Trakošćan castle, with tents and soldiers below.
b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.short_description: Count Ivan V Drašković was acting *ban* (viceroy) from 1718 to 1732. Officially appointed *ban* on 2 February 1732, he died suddenly the following year. Drašković actively supported the right of succession to the Habsurg female line (Croatian Pragmatic Sanction). The portrait, painted some time shortly after Drašković officially became *ban*, depicts the elderly count as a nobleman, his right hand holding a general's baton.

b76ae0c2-5d4f-563b-9c84-b8b5747b1e2f.method_for_datation: The imperial eagle holding the coats of arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia signifies the office of *ban* (viceroy), and enables the painting to be conclusively dated to 1732 or 1733.

b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.name: *Still Life with Fruit, Dead Birds and a Bowl of Morels*
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.description:
The area of the picture featuring a seasonal still life is packed with dead birds – coal tit, great tit, goldfinch, pigeon, woodpecker, woodcock – and fruit such as grapes, damsons and apples, the produce of the autumn harvest. As is common with similar decorative still life paintings, the fruits shown do not co-exist in nature: morels are among the earliest spring mushrooms. The composition axis is provided by a silver-plated gun in the diagonal. Attention is drawn to the centre of the painting by red tones, changing to olive-green towards the edges.  
Still life paintings made appealing decorations for chateau interiors as supraports, in dining halls, hunting rooms and studies. The Central European artists continued the tradition of Flemish still life established by Frans Snyders and Jan Fyt.  
This still life is the only known work by Coelestin Anctor Ximenes, a remarkable artist of Spanish origin. In 1698 he became a burgher of Brno and an active member of the painters' guild. He signed a proposal that painters and sculptors be articled, the first attempt to detach artists from the guild system, which was followed by efforts to establish an art academy in Brno by the artists Etgens and Eckstein. The majority of artworks to originate in Moravia in the second half of the 17th century were the work of foreign artists mainly Dutch and Italian, while work by Czech artists prevailed in the 18th century.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.short_description: The painting, reminiscent of 17th-century Dutch models, is the only known work by Coelestin Anctor Ximenes, an artist of Spanish origin who settled in Brno. The picture comes from the chateau of the High Steward of Archduchess Marie Isabela of Parma, in Brussels.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.location: Rájec nad Svitavou State Chateau, Moravia
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.method_for_datation: The picture is marked and dated *Ximenes fe. 1697*.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.provenance: Collection of Count Salm-Reifferscheidt at the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.obtention: The picture comes from the collection of Count Salm-Reifferscheidt at the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau, where it remains to this day. The origins of the collection, which is dominated by Dutch painting, was associated with Antonín Karl Salm-Reifferscheidt (1720–1769), High Steward of Archduchess Marie Isabela of Parma in Brussels. Salm-Reifferscheidt also built the Rájec chateau, designed by Isidore Canevale.

b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.name: Parish Church of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.alternate_name: The one-time Pauline church in Lepoglava
b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.description: During the 1770s, the sculptor, Alexius Königer and his assistants, made five altars and a pulpit. The co-operation between Alexius Königer and the painter and gilder, Franz Kochler from Vienna, is well documented. Königer's sculptural figures are characterised by their smooth theatrical gestures; they are playful and smiling as if dancing to distant music of their time. Along with the works of F. J. Straub and V. Königer, the sculptures of A. Königer constitute one of the very finest episodes of Rococo and Late Baroque sculpture in northern Croatia. Although created over a short period a gradual change is discernable in the Rococo expression of the pulpit, the Altar of St. Anne (completed 1777) and of the Holy Angels, to the increasingly obviously Classicist components of the Altar of the Holy Cross (1779) and St. Paul the Hermit. This holds particularly true for the high altar. Apart from Königer's two earlier altars in the side chapels of the same church, important phases in Late Mannerist altarpieces and sculpture in northern Croatia is evident. The Altar of the Holy Spirit, consecrated in 1657, is a splendid piece matched by the excellent Altar of the Mourning Mary (1676), with statues by the Varaždin sculptor Ivan Jakob Altenbach, whose stylistic expression belongs in the watershed between late Mannerism and early Baroque. Also worth mentioning are the sculptures in the niches of the church façade (1711). The author of these, Johannes Vedl, was a sculptor whose descent and oeuvre remains un-explicated to this day. He signed his name on the back of the figure of Christ. The end of the same decade (1718) saw the creation of the stucco decorations in the Patačić family chapel, by the Italian, Joseph Antonio Quadrio from Styria, who was also the author of the stuccowork in the monastic library (1710–1711). Several grand Baroque structures in northern Croatia hold Quadrio's works such as the one-time Jesuit churches in Zagreb and Varaždin and the Franciscan Church in Varaždin. The works of the Pauline painter, Ivan Ranger include wall paintings and the painted backs of the choir stalls (1735–1737) in the choir and in the sanctuary (1742). Ranger's work compliments the richness of the interior furnishing and constitutes one of the pinnacles of Baroque painting in northern Croatia in both the complexity of the iconographic programme and their painterly execution.
b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.short_description: The Pauline church in Lepoglava – a small town at the very heart of the north Croatian region of Hrvatsko Zagorje – played an important role in the cultural life of Croatia as did the entire monastery, which at one time belonged to Pauline monks. The chronological complexity of the furnishings in his Baroque-style Gothic church are seen in the unity of the five altars and a pulpit by the Pauline sculptor, Alexius Königer and his assistants in the 1770s, as well as by the paintings of the Pauline painter, Ivan Krstitelj Ranger (1733–1737; 1742).
b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.type: Religious, monastic church and interior furnishing
b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.method_for_datation: Archival sources and dates on the monuments themselves.

Baričević, D., *Barokno kiparstvo sjeverne Hrvatske*, Zagreb, 2008.
b7e5673f-ac22-50e2-93c9-7ef32d8a22c1.history: The Monastery and Church of St. Mary was founded at the beginning of the 15th century by Herman of Celje, and was modified and fortified to protect the town against the Ottomans at the end of the century during the time of the Hungarian-Croatian king and Croatian viceroy Ivaniš Korvin (1495–1497). From the end of the 17th century, the monastery was the seat of the Croatian Paulist province. During the 16th and 17th centuries, a Paulist high school operated there, and later a school of philosophy. After the dissolution of the order in 1786, the monastery and church came under the chapter of Čazman and, in 1854, it was converted for use as a correction facility. The facility occupied the monastery until 2001, at which time the complex was restored to a church.

b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.name: Santa Maria in Montesanto and Santa Maria dei Miracoli in Piazza del Popolo
b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.description: The two twin churches in Piazza del Popolo function as sacred propylaea that solemnly introduce the holy city. Both with a central plan, the two churches were designed using the Pantheon as a model, with a lowered dome and front portico surmounted by a triangular tympanum. Due to the presence of the domes, they also function as immediate visual reference to the dome of St. Peter's Basilica, the coveted final destination for pilgrims and travellers who have just arrived in Rome. However, there are differences in the floor plan, not perceptible from the outside: Santa Maria dei Miracoli is perfectly circular, while Santa Maria in Montesanto is elliptical. The bell towers were built in the 18th century and aimed at further emphasizing the central axis of Via del Corso. The symmetrical arrangement of the two churches on the same axis and at the entrance to three streets call to mind the so called ‘spyglass perspective’ typical of classical theatre, which Palladio, in the previous century, had brilliantly mastered in the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza. Palladio has in fact designed a fixed stage backdrop where two straight roads branch off from the front providing a sense of depth. The sense of movement generated by the perspective of the three streets is thus counterbalanced by the marked centrality and immobility of the two domed churches, providing a strong and impactful visual effect.
b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.short_description: Architect Carlo Rainaldi was commissioned to design two Churches facing the piazza, to give the city an inner gate that celebrated the beginning of the "goosefoot" of three major streets fanning toward the city. A sort of scenographical welcome to the travellers.
b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.bibliography:
Janowitz, E., “S. Maria di Montesanto e Santa Maria dei Miracoli”, in Grundmann S. (ed), *The Architecture of Rome,* Stuttgart/London: Edition Axel Menges, 2007: 239–241.  
Rossi Pinelli, O., “Piazza del Popolo”, *I principi della chiesa,* Milan: Edizioni Charta, 1998: 202–203.
b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.history: Since ancient times, the area which would become Piazza del Popolo was the first place within the Aurelian Walls that travellers coming from north encountered when entering the city through Porta Flaminia (later called Porta del Popolo), located at the end of the homonymous consular road.  At the time of Alexander VII, the square completely lacked the representativeness that one would have expected upon entering the Eternal City: it was a large irregular trapezoidal area with a single decorative element in the centre, the Egyptian obelisk from the Circus Maximus, erected by Sixtus V in 1589. The beginning of the three straight roads that together formed the so-called Tridente, namely Via del Babuino, Via del Corso (urban continuation of Via Flaminia) and Via di Ripetta were characterized by the presence of modest huts.  Bernini had already tried to embellish the square on the occasion of Christina of Sweden’s visit in Rome (1655), redesigning, however, only Porta del Popolo and part of the facade of the Church of Santa Maria del Popolo. When the Carmelites, in 1658, asked for permission to build a new church at the end of the block of houses located between Via del Corso and Via del Babuino, Pope Alexander VII sensed the strong visual and architectural impact that the new building would have had on the general appearance of this entrance to the city. He thus ordered that an identical church between Via del Corso and Via di Ripetta be erected to balance it. In 1661 Carlo Rainaldi was commissioned to design them, but he would eventually complete only the Church of Santa Maria in Montesanto: Santa Maria dei Miracoli would in fact be redesigned by Bernini and built by Carlo Fontana between 1673 and 1675.
b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.architects: Carlo Rainaldi; Gian Lorenzo Bernini; Carlo Fontana
b877d849-b748-5962-84ed-c9654876418b.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

b913c9c8-b526-5186-ba17-20f47cbdbdf1.name: Sé Catedral de Santarém
b913c9c8-b526-5186-ba17-20f47cbdbdf1.alternate_name: Jesuit Church and College of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception;  Patriarchal Seminary
b913c9c8-b526-5186-ba17-20f47cbdbdf1.description:
The building is situated in Marquês da Bandeira Square. The typically Jesuit facade consists of four levels and five vertical sections separated by wide pilasters. The façade is broken up by windows and four niches that contain the Jesuit saints, St. Ignatius Loyola, St. Francis Xavier, St. Francis Borgia and St. Aloysius Gonzaga.  
The two towers commonly seen in Jesuit church architecture have been replaced by the patron saint of the church, Our Lady of Conception, flanked by large volutes and pinnacles. Several other ornamental features reflect the Flemish and Manueline styles, breaking away from the austerity of Jesuit architecture. Above the principal door is the Jesuit symbol “IHS”.  
The plain, single-nave interior has eight side chapels, five of which have gilt-carved wood retables (Our Lady of Assistance; Chapel of St. Francis Xavier (the Sacred Heart of Jesus Chapel); Chapel of Our Lady of Glory and Chapel of Our Lady of Conception), one is of marble (Chapel of Our Lady of Good Death), another in marbled wood (Chapel of St. Aloysius Gonzaga) and two in stucco imitating marble (St. Anne's Chapel and the Chapel of St. Francis de Borgia). The simple wooden roof of the nave is decorated with *trompe l'œil* paintings: a central *Immaculate Conception* flanked by four Jesuit saints, four female figures from the Old Testament (Jahel, Esther, Deborah and Judith) and the Four Continents (America, Africa, Europe and Asia). It is also worth mentioning the magnificent polychrome stone inlay in the main chapel, surmounted by a frescoed dome depicting the *Coronation of Our Lady*.
b913c9c8-b526-5186-ba17-20f47cbdbdf1.short_description: Built within the Jesuit College of Santarém, the Church of Our Lady of Conception, now the Cathedral of the Diocese of Santarém, presents an imposing façade rich in the symbolism of the Company of Jesus. Inside, it consists of a single nave and eight side chapels with richly decorated *trompe l'œil* ceiling paintings, carved and altars and, within the Chancel, polychrome stone inlay work that breaks away from the architectural austerity of previous Jesuit projects.

b913c9c8-b526-5186-ba17-20f47cbdbdf1.history:
In 1609, D. Duarte da Costa, Armeiro Mor of the Kingdom (in charge of the weaponry) and a Jesuit priest, offered to finance the construction of a college for the Company of Jesus in Santarem. In 1647, King João IV gave the Company the estate of the ruined Royal Palace and appointed Mateus do Couto (“uncle”) as architect. The original project contract was signed by the Superior General, John Paul Olivia, in 1653, in Rome, and as with other Company projects, was obliged to follow specific rules. Construction of the church began in 1672 and approval for the facade was given in 1673. An inscription on the facade indicates that the work was probably finished by 1711. The Jesuits were expelled in 1759 and their assets were confiscated. In 1780, Queen Mary I offered the Santarém building to the Patriarchal Cardinal of Lisbon to accommodate the Patriarchal Seminary. Following the French invasions and the Civil War, the Seminary was closed in 1834. It was restored by Cardinal Guilherme Henriques de Carvalho in 1853.  
On 16 July 1975, the Papal Bull Apostolicae Sedis Consuetudine of Pope Paul VI created the Diocese of Santarém and the church became a cathedral.
