b950cb2a-23dc-5f18-98ea-549f9d27c81c.name: Holy Trinity Column
b950cb2a-23dc-5f18-98ea-549f9d27c81c.description:
An outdoor free-standing spiral column on a triple pedestal in the main square of Sopron, it represents Hungary's first outdoor-column spiral. The bottom level of the pedestal is curved with bevelled edges; its middle part is a curved-sided square with prisms at the edges; the top is decorated with offsets, serving as a pedestal for marginal figures.  
At the front on the second level of the pedestal, the double Löwenburg-Thököly coat of arms inscription in Hungarian reads: “This votive sculpture was erected by Count János Jakab Löwenburg and his wife in 1701, it was restored by the public of Sopron Free Royal City in 1797, 1847, 1883 and 1911”. Standing on the ledges of the mid-level pedestal-columns are ancillary figures of the Thököly-Löwenburg families' patron saints: St. James, St. Stephen King of Hungary and, at the corners, St. John of Nepomuk and St. Anthony of Padua. At each of the four corners are four figures of female saints (Barbara, Regina, Anne and Catherine – also the Thököly-Löwenburg families' patron saints; the *Immaculata* is at the bottom of the column. The patrons at the front are Count János Jakab Löwenburg half-kneeling and Countess Katalin Thököly kneeling on a pillow; both have their arms raised and look upwards towards the Holy Trinity at the top. Between them is an inscription in Latin with the *chronosticon* of the year 1701: *“VnI trInoqVe Deo patrI fILIo spIrItVI sanCto eX Voto posVIMVs sopronll.”* (“We the \[citizens\] of Sopron erected \[it\] in gratitude to the One God Holy Trinity, to the Father, to the Son to the Holy Spirit.”) There are further inscriptions on the other sides of the pedestal about the patrons.  
It is interesting that no other representation of Count Löwenburg remains from this era as far as we know.  
Above the mid-level pedestal there is a spiral column decorated with garlands and *putti* – its shape and garland decoration evoking the baldachin columns in St. Peter's Basilica, Rome – but, finally, the column is crowned with the Holy Trinity above the Corinthian column capital (the Father on the right and the Son on the left; above them the dove of the Holy Spirit among golden rays).
b950cb2a-23dc-5f18-98ea-549f9d27c81c.short_description: The Holy Trinity column in Sopron is one of Hungary’s most beautiful Baroque monuments with its pedestal decorated with figures of saints and patrons. Erected to commemorate the end of the plague epidemic, it was built between 1697 and 1701, out of a sentiment of plight and gratitude.
b950cb2a-23dc-5f18-98ea-549f9d27c81c.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, stylistic and iconographic examination.
b950cb2a-23dc-5f18-98ea-549f9d27c81c.bibliography:
Thirring, G., *Sopron*, Budapest, 1925.  
Heimler, K., *Topography of Sopron (Sopron topográfiája),* Sopron, 1936.  
Csatkai, E., *Sopron*, Budapest, 1954.
b950cb2a-23dc-5f18-98ea-549f9d27c81c.history:
Baroque Holy Trinity columns are sculptures representing the Holy Trinity placed on free-standing columns in public spaces, and are usually erected out of a sentiment of plight and gratitude after great epidemics. The richly sculpted Holy Trinity sculpture in Sopron was erected following a plague epidemic that raged there at the end of the 17th century. In April 1695, after the epidemic had come to an end, Count Lipót Kollonich Archbishop of Esztergom Cardinal and Primate, suggested to the city assembly that a Holy Trinity sculpture be erected out of plight and gratitude that the town had survived, and requested donations from the citizens to realise it. The assembly of a Protestant majority responded positively to the suggestion, and works probably began that year, although there is no written evidence to confirm that assumption. The sculpture is mentioned in 1697 in the protocols of the town council when a carpenter complained about the sculptor, Szervác Leitner, who (as the context suggests) took part in carrying the sculpture into the town.  
Debate is still ongoing as to who was responsible for the design and sculpting of the monument. Since Kollonich himself presented the design, some researchers are of the opinion that Leitner was not sufficiently proficient as an artist to design and sculpt the monument, so Kollonich had the design and the sculpture made in Vienna or Kismarton (Eisenstadt), close to the Esterházy court. Guild legislation did not allow sculptors to act as stonemasons.  
Stylistic and iconographic examinations distinguish between different masters and sessions on the sculpture (the qualities of female saint figures are different; the representation of St. John of Nepomuk is very early). Based on inscriptions and local chronicles the column was erected in 1701. The site was already an important one in Sopron in the 18th century.  
The inscription on the sculpture mentions Countess Katalin Thököly (the sister of Imre Thököly) and her third husband, Count János Jakab Löwenburg as patrons, and a council protocol reveals that Löwenburg established a foundation for its maintenance as well. But when the sculpture needed repairing and people turned to the foundation for finance it was no longer in existence. The city, however, felt duty bound to renovate the monument and in 1796 and 1797, at the city's expense, the sculptor János Mynch restored it.  
The monument was renovated on several occasions subsequently.

b9e5d59c-90cf-5a1d-80ec-21247c2e8944.name: *St. Francis Xavier and St. Ignatius of Loyola*
b9e5d59c-90cf-5a1d-80ec-21247c2e8944.description:
Saint Ignatius of Loyola was the main founder and the first Superior General of the Society of Jesus, a religious order of the Catholic Church professing directly to the Pope a vow of obedience, as far as missionary duties were concerned. The early Jesuits were sent by Ignatius to pagan lands where they could work on the propagation and strengthening of the Catholic faith. Among them was St. Francis Xavier. He had studied at the same college as St. Ignatius in Paris and helped him plan the foundation of the Society of Jesus. St Francis was sent to Lisbon in 1540 principally because King D. João III wanted him to serve in India.  
In a short period of 10 years (1542–1552) he converted people from Goa, Ceylon, Malacca and Moluccas, where he established several missionary centres; he also established some others in central and southern Japan. He was buried in Goa where is body is still enshrined at the Basilica of Bom Jesus. He continues to be considered the greatest missionary since the Apostles.  
Christianity was expanded by St. Francis Xavier's work as a missionary and by his apostolic zeal. He became a model of holiness and an instrument of evangelisation against other confessional denominations.  
The floral and vegetal motifs that adorn these two sculptures have their origins in oriental art. Commissioned during Portuguese rule in Asia the sculptures are the result of the exchange of knowledge and ideas, techniques and materials from both cultures. The technical expertise reached by both Chinese and Japanese artists allowed their elite cosmopolitan styles to be linked together, and their patrons and the merchants who dealt with their work, to discover new art markets.

baa63eae-aa4d-5b6b-ba04-a84fbdbf637b.name: Lyceum
baa63eae-aa4d-5b6b-ba04-a84fbdbf637b.alternate_name: Eszterházy Károly Főiskola (Eszterházy Károly High School)
baa63eae-aa4d-5b6b-ba04-a84fbdbf637b.description:
A three-storey building, its wings surround a rectangular inner courtyard with a mansard roof decorated with two vases, which sits over the abutting middle bay crowned with a tympanum. Above the three ground-floor round-arched gates of the central bay on the second floor, there is a balcony on stone consoles with wrought-iron railings in front of French windows. Above the windows are tympanum and garland motifs; the latter can be seen above the arched windows of the third storey as well. The middle bay is divided by two storey-high pilasters the corner bays of which are only slightly abutting. The connecting wings have a saddle roof.  
Inside the main entrance, an oval hall is accessed through barrel-roofed corridors.  A two-armed stairway with balustrades leads up to the second floor of the middle bay, where the exquisite two-storey-high library, Great Hall, chapel and theatre are located. The famous observatory is in the back axis of the building in the east wing.  
The Library ceiling painting in the south risalit is probably the Austrian Johann Lucas Kracker's most significant work in Hungary. The monumental, perspectival tabloid – an addition suggested by Esterházy – represents the Trident Synod in a huge Gothic temple (designed by Joseph Zach in 1782) in which self portraits of Kracker and Zach feature.  
The oak furniture was designed by Fellner and built by Thomas Lotter. The 24 gilded portrait medallions were made by Vencel Halblechner between 1778 and 1779.  
After the death of Kracker in 1779, Esterházy commissioned Franz Sigrist to complete the painting programme. Sigrist painted the ceiling in the Great Hall of the west bay where the four university faculties (1781–1782) are watched over by God. Beneath sunrays is Science, portrayed occupied in typical activities. Under Physics and Geography the date and signature of Sigrist (“Sigrist / pincit Ano 1781”) is discernable.  
The barrel-vaulted chapel is on the north side of the building. The painted ceiling is adorned with the allegorical *Saints of the Church* and the *Glory of All Saints with the Holy Trinity and Mary* in which the Hungarian saints: Stephen, Emeric, Margaret, Elizabeth and Ladislaus, are emphasised. The main altar in coloured marble sits in a basket-arched alcove beneath the Hungarian saints (Giovanni Adami, 1794). The altar painting (*St. Stephen offers Hungary to the Virgin Mother*) is the work of a local painter Mihály Hesz (1813).
baa63eae-aa4d-5b6b-ba04-a84fbdbf637b.short_description: Construction and decoration of the building, based on designs by Josef Ignaz Gerl and Jakab Fellner, lasted for more than two decades from 1762. The erudite and business-minded Bishop Károly Esterházy, who was educated in Rome, commissioned the building which was designed specifically as a university. However, with its exquisite wall paintings, huge library and modern, well-equipped observatory, the Lyceum never gained university status because of the resistance of Queen Maria Theresia, and later that of King Joseph II and Barkóczy Archbishop of Esztergom, during the *Ratio Educationis* era. Thus it was destined to remain a Lyceum. The building is a beautiful example of Hungarian Late Baroque-Rococo architecture with Neo-Classical features.
baa63eae-aa4d-5b6b-ba04-a84fbdbf637b.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources and field research.

baa63eae-aa4d-5b6b-ba04-a84fbdbf637b.history:
The bishops of Eger had long planned to establish an institution of higher education in the town. Bishop György Foglár founded an academic law faculty (*Foglarianum*) in around 1740, to which Bishop György Barkóczy added a liberal arts faculty in 1744. Barkóczy wanted a new building for his school and commissioned Josef Gerl, an architect from Vienna, to design it. His plan could not be fulfilled, however, until his appointment as Archbishop of Esztergom in 1761. Bishop Károly Esterházy succeeded Barkóczy as Bishop of Eger, and wanted to establish a university by adding a theology and a medical faculty to the academy. He also wanted to erect a new building and contracted Gerl in 1762 to design new plans. Following the ideas presented by Esterházy, Gerl reworked his plans and added an observatory and a library to the original drawings. Gerl received another request from the chapter to modify the plans so that students could move from the deteriorated *Collegium Juridicum Foglarianum* to the new building. This was accomplished by adding another floor. Esterházy received no state subsidies, so he lobbied priests to build up a construction fund.  
Work began in 1763 led by Jozef Francz, a foreman from Vienna. The stonework was supervised by József Hagen and János Miller from Demjén. As Esterházy had not raised sufficient funds to finance the entire construction, he sacrificed much of his private wealth to continue the building programme. He commissioned Jakab Fellner to modify the plans and to manage the building and construction. Fellner determined the final interior structure of the building, modified the facades (to accommodate the extra level) and increased the size of the windows. He designed *Zopf* decorative features (the wrought iron railings of the first-floor balcony for example) and furnishings for the library. Fellner delegated onsite supervision to János Povolni in 1764. After the death of Fellner in 1780, József Grossmann took charge of construction. The *Scola Medicinalis*, the first medical school in Hungary, opened in 1769.The Lyceum, which never gained university status, operated a philosophy and a justice faculty from 1777.   
The observatory dome was completed in 1778, for which the acknowledged Jesuit astronomer, Miksa Hell, directed the purchase and installation of the astronomical equipment. The *camera obscura* on the 10th floor of the observatory was designed by Hell, and Lénárd Fassola was responsible for the construction of many of the instruments. The furnaces were designed by the renowned stove-maker, Károly Magner from Győr, in the *Zopf* style.  
Construction of the Lyceum was complete by 1782 but the interior design was not finished until 1795. The ceiling painting in the library was executed by Johann Lucas Kracker and Joseph Zach; those in the Great Hall are by Franz Sigrist (1781). The chapel wall paintings are by Franz Anton Maulbertsch and his assistant, Márton Mich (1793).  
The famous Lyceum library opened in 1793, virtually the first public library in Hungary. Bishop Esterházy died in 1799 and bequeathed a great number of books to the library.  
The bishopric press founded in 1755, operated from the ground floor of the Lyceum. The museum and picture gallery on the third floor became part of the Dobó István Castle Museum in the 1950s after nationalisation. The theology and justice academies functioned until 1949, as did the art school, founded in 1828 by Archbishop János László Pryker, and the training and practice schools. The Lyceum was a pedagogical school from 1949 and a teacher training college from 1963. It was known as Ho Si Minh from 1970 to 1990, since when it was renamed Eszterházy Károly.

bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.name: *St. Thaddeus Jude*
bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.description:
This sculpture portrays the saint in a state of self-absorption and contemplation. With the head slightly tilted towards the right shoulder, the shape is defined by a picturesque cloak inventively arranged on the chest to cascade over a plain, low pedestal. The rich folds of the gown are partially obscured by a medallion with a profile of Christ, while the iconography identifies the bust as St. Jude Thaddeus, a close relative of Jesus and disciple to Him. Jude Thaddeus brought a portrait of Christ’s face to the king of Edessa (the Image of Edessa). Jude died a martyr’s death in Persia or Phoenicia and is often represented by the attribute of the club that killed him. St. Thaddeus Jude is patron saint of the desperate and of lost or forgotten causes. The silver surface of the bust accentuates its spiritual, melancholic aura.  
The Provincial Museum in Olomouc owns a similar sculpture of a female figure with a ribbon in her hair. Presumably both busts are fragments of a larger series, the remainder of which are missing. Their “distant” inspiration may have been Bernini’s prestigious portraits.  
Zahner probably came to Olomouc via Vienna, after an apprenticeship to his father in Würzburg. In the 1740s he was assigned a particularly significant task, taking up the sculpted decoration of the Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc.  
With more demanding commissions, Zahner was assisted by Jan Kammereit, Wofgang Träger and Jan Michael Scherhauf. The work of this Bavaria-trained sculptor was received with great acclaim in Moravia.
bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.short_description: This sculpture portrays the saint in a state of self-absorption and contemplation. The rich folds of the gown are partially obscured by a medallion with a profile of Christ and the iconography identifies the bust as St. Jude Thaddeus. A. Zahner also created the UNESCO monument, Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc.
bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.method_for_datation: The attribution of this originally anonymous carving to Zahner was determined, in particular, by the characteristics of the saint: chiselled nose and sunken eyes, which resemble Zahner’s earlier works. His work is typified by an effort to transcribe the mental disposition of his figures.

baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.name: Breast Ornament
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.description:
Jewellery reached its zenith in the 18th century. Monarchs throughout Europe – from Lisbon to Dresden; England to Naples – wore jewellery to reinforce their majesty and political power. High standards of craftsmanship together with up-to-date designs supplied the luxurious and ostentatious Portuguese court of Kings João V (1706–1750) , José I (1750–1777) and Queen D. Maria I.  
At this time of Portuguese Absolutism, the magnificence of Portuguese jewellery is closely linked with the colonisation of Brazil, with enormous quantities of gold pouring into the kingdom (from 1699) and diamonds (from 1729) onwards. Greater quantities of precious gems were mined in Brazil, in Rio das Velhas, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso and Bahía, further increasing the materials available.  
This particular ornamental breast jewellery – which would have adorned a lady's dress – is a remarkable example from the period. So many bejewelled women would have added to the splendour of court life, its balls and receptions. The naturalism of this piece together with the asymmetrical composition confirms that the fashions emanating from the French court of Louis XV were extremely popular, although from the late 1760s this gave way to the Rococo style exemplified by softer and more graceful shapes of exceptional beauty.  
This piece of jewellery was designed as a single piece with the exception of the garland topping it which was added later. Ornaments such as this one were often constructed in stand-alone parts so they could be worn separately. The silver structure is set with chrysoberyls, garnets, yellow topazes, colourless gem-stones quartz, beryl and topaz. The array of colourful gems includes green and blue doublets and, as usual then, a fair number of quartz and topaz backed with various shades of coloured foil to create striking variations of light and colour.
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.short_description: Costume jewellery of this kind was a magnificent addition to a lady’s dress. Typologically it relates to the fashionable aristocratic jewellery of the European courts from the second half of the 18th century. It is also a direct consequence of the Portuguese colonisation of Brazil.
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.method_for_datation: The piece was brought to the MNSR on 3 August 1945 from the Royal Treasury of Oporto by the goldsmith and researcher José Rosas Júnior.
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.obtention: The object was kept in the Necessidades Palace in Lisbon (inv. 13405). In the MNSR it was first kept in the “Deposit of the *Património Nacional*” (inv. 401/495), now known as the *Direcção Geral da Fazenda Pública*.

bbc7739e-3d42-5ce9-8c5c-bfb1ee694806.name: Oratorio della Santissima Trinità
bbc7739e-3d42-5ce9-8c5c-bfb1ee694806.description:
The Oratorio della Santissima Trinità has a square plan and a vaulted ceiling with lunettes. The interior is completely decorated. On the ceiling is depicted the Trinity. Figures of prophets are painted in the lunettes. The walls are decorated with biblical scenes framed by squares and separated by monochrome figures in a sort of frieze.  
The complex iconographic program is centred on the celebration of the Trinity and the Alliance between God and Man. All of the scenes depicted come from the Old Testament with the exception of the *Baptism of Christ*. Lionello Spada planned the general scheme of the cycle and painted it along with Francesco Brizio. Two of the scenes are attributed to Lucio Massari. It is very difficult to distinguish the different painters owing to their great technical and stylistic homogeneity. This testifies about their common will and technical preparation.  
The frescoes in this oratory are a good example of the renovation of painting created by the Carracci and developed by the Academy (Accademia dei desiderosi later the Accademia degli Incamminati), which was founded by the three Bolognese painters in 1582 in order to teach young artists. The perspective in the landscapes in the background of Francesco Brizio's paintings, where figures and landscape are equally important comes from the style of Ludovico Carracci. The painted illusionistic architecture of the ceiling shows Spada's apprenticeship as a Quadraturista (painter of illusionistic architectures).  
The imposing framing of the high altar and the wooden stalls of the choir, where the members of the brotherhood used to sit, carved and inlaid in oak, perfectly complete the decoration.
bbc7739e-3d42-5ce9-8c5c-bfb1ee694806.short_description: The Oratory of the Holy Trinity holds one of the most significant decorative cycles painted by the Bolognese school in the early 17th century. At the same time it is important evidence of the work of local brotherhoods assisting pilgrims. Its interior is completely decorated with beautiful frescoes painted by Lionello Spada, Lucio Massari and Francesco Brizio, pupils of the Carracci. The frescoes represent stories from the Old and New Testament. The wooden carved choir is among the finest works of Giacomo da Bergamo, called Venezian, a cabinet maker.

bbc7739e-3d42-5ce9-8c5c-bfb1ee694806.history:
The construction of the oratory linked to the the church and dedicated to the Holy Trinity and began in 1603. It was built by the Brotherhood of the Holy Trinity, whose task was to provide assistance for poor pilgrims and convalescent patients at the nearby hospital of St. Mary.  
Three well-known pupils of the Carraccis, Lionello Spada, Francesco Brizio and Lucio Massari began work on the painted decorations. The work began in 1605 and today these are considered one of the most significant fresco cycles of the early 17th century in Bologna. The beautiful carved wooden choir and the framing of the altar were commissioned in 1615 from Giacomo da Bergamo, known as 'Venezian'.  
The brotherhood of the Holy Trinity was suppressed in 1798, after the Napoleonic conquest, and all its properties passed to the Hospital of St. Mary.

bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.name: *Expulsion from Eden*
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.description:
The painting was until recently ascribed to Giovanni Antoni Pellegrini (1675–1741) but further study of comparative material and references by Visnja Bralic, an art historian from Zagreb, has led to a new attribution of the Venetian painter, Girolamo Brusaferro. Although little biographical information exists about the painter, his work is well known, and this knowledge is supported by other extant pieces by him. Brusaferro, who painted altarpieces for churches in Venice, and historical and mythological scenes for private collections, was a member of the Venetian painters' guild (1702–1722).  
The Expulsion from Eden theme was a popular subject for painters during the Baroque period. Here, the artist expressively shows the drama of Adam and Eve driven out of Paradise for their disobedience to God by an angry angel. The busts of the three actors almost fill up the whole surface of the canvas. The angel stands accented with flaming sword in hand, and according to the iconographic principle, in front of the gates of paradise, thus stopping Adam and Eve returning to their haven. The angel, powerfully illuminated, stands with outspread wings brandishing his sword, while the naked bodies of Adam and the hardly visible Eve are in penumbra. Their faces and movements reveal their fear and despair. While Adam is running from the glare of the flaming sword, Eve raises her hands and face to the sky, begging for Divine forgiveness. The colours are warm with a light hue. The figures, emphatically voluminous and in motion, heighten the dynamic nature of the composition.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.short_description: *Expulsion from Eden* is the work of the Venetian master, Girolamo Brusaferro, who painted numerous altarpieces for Venetian churches, along with other historical and mythological compositions. The Expulsion from Eden theme was a popular subject for painters during the Baroque period. The picture shows the moment when the angry angel, fiery sword in hand, drives Adam and Eve from their earthly paradise. The terrified and despairing exiles have committed the original sin, the shadow of which has fallen over the whole of mankind. While the powerful, naked Adam in painful spasm is bending over, Eve turns to heaven and begs for Divine assistance. The angel, with robust body and wide outstretched wings, brandishes the fiery sword at Adam. The impressive dynamic composition, marked, bright tonality and emphatic voluminousness of the figures distinguish this painting.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.method_for_datation: The attribution, made by Visnja Bralic, made use of existing literature, other comparative material and stylistic analysis.
bbe41557-7e8b-54e0-a258-e5856417bd55.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.

bc90e672-a635-5571-ab06-4dce45c85ddd.name:
Trinity Church  
Parish and Pilgrimage Church Stadl-Paura  
Paura Church
bc90e672-a635-5571-ab06-4dce45c85ddd.alternate_name: Pilgrimage Church dedicated to the Holy Trinity
bc90e672-a635-5571-ab06-4dce45c85ddd.description:
From the moment Maximilian Pagl was abbot he sincerely wished to build the Holy Trinity Church. However, he could not carry out the project until nine years later, referring to the vow. By then he pushed it, gathering all his strength.  
The abbot asked Johann Michael Prunner, the architect, to hurry up with the building in order to fulfil the oath. After only three years the shell of the church was complete and the artists started painting the cupola, the dome lantern and the walls. After a total of ten years Abbot Maximilian Pagl consecrated the altar of the Father and could say the first mass. Unfortunately, he soon became seriously ill and died before the building was completed. His successors concluded the church – according to the founder´s plans and ideas – which became a synthesis of arts.
bc90e672-a635-5571-ab06-4dce45c85ddd.short_description: Founder Abbot Maximilian Pagl who had worked out the theological program made the Holy Trinity the maxim of the church. Everything in and on the building refers to this idea. The church´s exterior ground plan is an equilateral triangle (to outwardly symbolise the Father, Son and Holy Spirit), while the interior ground plan is a circle (symbolising inwardly the one God). There are three equal towers, three equal portals, three equal facades and three altars opposite three doors and three organs (in the floor above), any of them – according to abbot Maximilian Pagl´s wish – singing the Holy Trinity´s praise.

bc90e672-a635-5571-ab06-4dce45c85ddd.history:
The baroque Stadl-Paura pilgrimage church elevates on a hill next to the right bank of the river Traun. A former chapel dedicated to St. Blasius stood at the same place and was still mentioned in the early Middle Ages.  
The village at the river became important in the 13th century for the salt trade and transport by water. Trade, transport and the fact that the near municipality of Lambach was an important traffic junction, brought enormous wealth to the region. Many edifices were built in the 17th and 18th centuries, still apparent, such as the architectural jewel of the Holy Trinity Church.
bc90e672-a635-5571-ab06-4dce45c85ddd.patrons: Benedictine Abbot Maximilian Pagl from Stift Lambach erected the church – referring to an oath he had made – to thank God that there were no victims of the black death in the area.

bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.name: *Josip Kazimir Drašković* (4.3.1716 – Klenovnik, Croatia, 9.10.1765)
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.description:
The Drašković family played an important role in the political and social life of Croatia throughout many generations. Counts from the 17th century (1631), numerous members of the family were Croatian *bans* (viceroys) and high-ranking military officers. The family's wealth included numerous estates, among them Trakošćan and Klenovnik castles in northwest Croatia. Josip Kazimir Drašković, son of viceroy Ivan V, was a prominent high-ranking officer, a colonel by the age of 30, and a general by 1750. He took part in quenching the peasants' and soldiers' uprising in Croatia in 1755. In 1758, Empress Maria Theresia awarded him her Military Order for outstanding bravery in the defence of Olomouc; in 1765, he was awarded the Commander's Cross of the same Order for defending Moravia. He was married to Suzana Malatinski with whom he had three sons and a daughter.  
The portrait, originally in Trakošćan, was probably part of the Gallery of Officers serving under Josip Kazimir, consisting of 50 portraits (the other portraits are in Trakošćan Castle Museum). The portrait is the work of the Viennese painter, Johann Michael Millitz. Between 1764 and 1778, he painted numerous members of the Croatian and Hungarian nobility, and painted Josip Kazimir's daughter Julijana (married to Count Erdödy). Drašković is shown wearing a Commander's Cross of Maria Theresia's Military Order. The portrait, modified probably in 1765, commemorates the higher order of Commander's Cross, over-painting the Military Order received by Drašković in 1758.
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.short_description: Count Josip Kazimir Drašković, son of viceroy Ivan V, was a prominent high-ranking officer promoted to general in 1750. He took part in quenching the peasants’ and soldiers’ uprising in Croatia in 1755. In 1758, Empress Maria Theresia awarded him the Military Order, and in 1765, he was awarded the Commander’s Cross of the same Order.
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.method_for_datation: The date and origin of the portrait were established through information known about Josip Kazimir Drašković as well as by stylistic analysis of the painting and other known works by Johann Michael Millitz.
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.provenance: Estate of the Drašković family from Trakošćan
bcbffbcf-b106-5603-ac6b-c0832f43b411.obtention: Received from the Commission for the Collection and Preservation of Cultural Monuments and Antiques in 1952.

bd0098d5-7fb6-5d0b-bb54-6f7f23563f71.name: Catholic Parish and Pilgrimage Church of the Sorrowful Mother
bd0098d5-7fb6-5d0b-bb54-6f7f23563f71.description: The exterior of the cruciform pilgrimage church with rotund arms does not have much in the way of sculptural decoration beside the niche over the west portal. In contrast, the interior of the church building, which shows a tendency to a central-plan, might overwhelm the visitor with its sumptuous decoration. Colossal pilasters structure the room and accentuate the wall-mounted niche figures of saints which refer to the Benedictine Order and the adoration of the Virgin Mary. Stuccowork on a coloured base covers the ceiling of the church displaying a large repertoire of forms: wide acanthus vines in the High Baroque style, angel figures and floral elements, including leaf- and shell-motifs. In between the stucco are numerous frescos, in many cases thematically related to the Sorrowful Mother, but also illustrating biblical scenes or allegories (the centre panel is a modern reconstruction). In the backmost conch above the portal there is a built-in organ loft. The side altars of the transept arms show significant stylistic differences: the overall impression and the twisted columns of the Altar of St. Ulrich relate to Baroque forms; the putti and more playful decorations of the Altar of St. Stephen, on the other hand, are rooted in Rococo designs. As a pilgrimage church the building has – as is characteristic for the region – a two-storey ambulatory with a double altar which offered separate oratories for monks and aristocratic pilgrims.
bd0098d5-7fb6-5d0b-bb54-6f7f23563f71.short_description: The appeal of the pilgrimage church built by Johann Schmuzer with, for the region, a typical two-floored ambulatory chancel and double altar, lies especially in its sumptuous High Baroque stuccowork on the ceiling. Numerous frescos, in many cases referring to the theme of the Sorrowful Mother, are also part of the stunning decorative programme. Another highlight is the virtuosic Rococo altar of the local plasterer, Tassilo Zöpf.
bd0098d5-7fb6-5d0b-bb54-6f7f23563f71.dates: 1688–1692: church building; 1721: high altar; 1751: altar of the southern transept arm
bd0098d5-7fb6-5d0b-bb54-6f7f23563f71.bibliography:

bd0098d5-7fb6-5d0b-bb54-6f7f23563f71.history:
In the 17th century, pilgrimage in Vilgertshofen underwent significant development due to the re-emergence of the cult of the Adoration of the Virgin Mary. To cope with the large number of pilgrims the Benedictine Abbey of Wessobrunn decided in favour of constructing a new church for which they chose the local master builder Johann Schmuzer as architect. The ceremonial laying of the cornerstone took place in 1687; Bishop Eustach Egolf Freiherr von Westernach conducted the consecration on 12 October 1692. The south tower was not built until 1732 because of the War of the Spanish Succession. The north tower was never built.  
The so-called *Stumme Passionsprozession* (Silent Passion Procession) which takes place on the Sunday after Assumption, in which villagers represent biblical figures, was instigated by the confraternity founded in 1708 and to this day is still only performed as a tradition in Vilgertshofen.

bd228d18-d160-5fd5-95ad-52e75e120f02.name: Welcoming Person (*Azulejos*)
bd228d18-d160-5fd5-95ad-52e75e120f02.description:
The Halberdier (here shown isolated) is the first of three welcoming halberdiers painted on tiles (*azulejos)*, which decorate the main staircase of the Mitra or Patriarch's Palace in St. Antão do Tojal (now Casa do Gaiato). The elaborately decorated *trompe l'oeil* *azulejos* were meant to transform an ordinary staircase into a magnificent one. Since the 16th century, tiles were used in Portugal to decorate churches, palaces and gardens; in the first half of the 18th century the most sophisticated colour used on tiles was cobalt blue. The artist used architectural drawing, ribbons of foliage and flowers, and little exotic pets such as monkeys and birds, to make visitors believe they were in a splendid garden guarded by halberdiers. To enhance the *trompe l'oeil* illusion, the halberdiers are drawn to natural scale, as if they were actors on the set of an opera.  
Designed to create the ambiance of a splendid welcoming ritual for those visiting the palace, all three characters exhibit magnificent Baroque outfits: the fabric of the jackets are embroidered with gold thread. These particular halberdiers display details that represent military dignity, such as the *écharpe* diagonally draped over the bust of one, or that used as if it were a belt, or a *cravat* attached to the button hole of a jacket (this one probably represents King João V's special German or *Tudesco* guard). Painted *azulejos* on staircases or patios, with welcoming personages such as personal guards, are characteristic of Palaces in Lisbon and are often seen in religious buildings such as, Setúbal, Corpo Santo Brotherhood or Évora University (Saint Spirit Convent).  
The artist who invented this iconography signed some of his works with the letters "P.M." or "P.M.P.", which is thought to be linked with Father Manuel Pereira, an amateur painter and architect who lived in the kingdom of Pedro II and his son João V.  
The Ancient Patriarch's Palace in Lisbon dates back to the 17th century and was renovated in the 18th century. The work is likely to be by the Italian Architect Antonio Cannevari, who constructed the new Palace Church, a nearby Fountain, the Aqueduct, and also a new small Palace with an exterior fountain. The patron responsible for all these new urban structures and the decoration of the old Palace was the Lisbon Patriarch Tomás de Almeida. These artworks were designed to receive King João V and his entourage when they were on their way to visit the most important project of his reign – the Mafra Convent and Palace – which was under construction at that time.
bd228d18-d160-5fd5-95ad-52e75e120f02.short_description: The first of the three welcoming halberdiers painted on a life-size scale on tiles, decorating the main staircase of Mitra or Patriarch's Palace in St. Antão do Tojal. The *azulejos*, painted in cobalt-blue with gold detail on the halberdier's outfits, were designed to transform a simple staircase into a magnificent one in order to receive guests such asliliguest King João V and his courtiers.

bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.name: Monstrance
bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.description:
The monstrance is by the Graz goldsmith, Hans Georg Pfisterer. The shaped oval base has enamel medallions showing scenes from the Passion of Christ and continues into a knob, shaped like a Baroque vase, from which rises the top part of the monstrance of the so-called sun type. Bands and foliate ornaments completely cover it intertwined with filigree and jewels. The opening of the ostensory has a six-sided moulded frame made up of wavy and angled sides and surrounded by airy filigree ornamentation of entwined scrolls and jewels that form flowers. Above the ostensory is a richly decorated canopy under which God the Father, holding the globe, hovers in clouds. Above the canopy is the dove of the Holy Ghost. At the foot of the frame, two adoring angels kneel on narrow decorated bases. The bottom edge of the monstrance has a lambrequin motif from which pearls hang.  
Bishop Juraj Branjug of Zagreb acquired the monstrance. He was one of Croatia’s most active bishops in 18th-century in the field of religious art building a new palace in Zagreb and renovating and building many churches. He had his own woodcarving workshop at Kaptol whose master craftsmen made altarpieces and pulpits adorned with the bishop’s arms for many churches. He bought and donated first-class liturgical objects to the cathedral.
bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.short_description: A so-called sun monstrance covered with filigree work, a series of bands and foliate ornaments, jewels and enamel medallions showing the Passion of Christ. Made by the Graz goldsmith, Georg Pfisterer, it was acquired by Bishop Juraj Branjug for Zagreb Cathedral.

bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.name: *Madonna and Child with St. John Nepomuk*
bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.description:
The painting is a *bozzetto* (study) for the altar piece commissioned by Benedict XIII for the canonisation of John Nepomuk on 11 March 1729, and intended for the Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano. The canvas shows John Nepomuk (named after his place of birth: Pomuk, the ancient name for the city of Nepomuk) kneeling before the Madonna and Child, surrounded by *putti* and angels.  
One in the foreground is showing the palm leaf of the martyr and has raised his finger to his mouth, a gesture that alludes to the virtue of the saint, renowned not only as protector of Bohemia, but also as the patron saint of confessors. John, confessor of the queen, aligned himself with the Archbishop of Prague against the claims of King Wenceslaus IV who imprisoned him for refusing to divulge the secrets of the confessional. He was tortured by the King before being flung from the Charles Bridge and drowned in the Vltava.  
The martyrdom is reproduced in the background behind the saint, who is dressed in his priestly robes and canonical cape. Beside Mary, another angel is giving the martyr the crown of stars that, according to tradition, surrounded his head as he floated in the river. The study, usually dated to the 1720s, was acquired by the Italian State in 1921, and is therefore not a part of the Borghese family collection.  
The painting is from Conca's early period when he was one of Rome's most fashionable artists. His painting style of grandiose and exuberant lines, similar to the style of Carlo Maratta, is characteristic of a later phase of Baroque painting, by then infused with the appealing and exuberant language of Rococo culture. As proof of the altarpiece's renown and the devotion of the Bohemian saint, prints were made of it, one of which was engraved by Gottlib Heiss in 1735 and is part of the Borghese collection.
bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.short_description:
The *bozzetto* (study) was made by Sebastiano Conca for an altarpiece in St. Giovanni in Laterano (now lost). Conca, from Naples, arrived in Rome in 1706 at which time his style was similar to that of Carlo Maratta.  
This is a typical example of a Baroque altarpiece, the *sacrum* appearing in a monumental internal space providing a clear perspective.  
Conca's painting, with its exuberant, grandiose lines, is characteristic of late Baroque art and its captivating and magniloquent language is taken from Rococo culture.
bddc17e1-fe8c-5d35-aa32-18312e773658.obtention: The work was acquired by the Italian State in 1921.

bddfa965-f0a5-5c48-ad19-ac2d02720ed9.name: Palazzo Pepoli Campogrande
bddfa965-f0a5-5c48-ad19-ac2d02720ed9.description: The façade overlooking via Castiglione opens in the middle, with a rich diamond portal. The ceiling of the staircase was decorated by Domenico Maria Canuti (1665) with two important episodes of the life of Taddeo Pepoli, inside oval frames. Taddeo is shown becoming the ruler of Bologna in 1337 and when he was appointed apostolic vicar by Pope Benedict XII in 1340. The ballroom ceiling is one of the most significant examples of Bolognese baroque. Canuti was aided by Mengazzino for the perspective painting. The middle of an opened ceiling with strong scenographic light shows the *Glorification of Hercules* (1669-1671). The eye of the viewer is attracted by the dynamic tension of the figures moving upwards and by the illusionistic architecture. In the following room the Rolli brothers painted the *Triumph of the Bolognese Aristocracy* which depicts the twinning of Bologna and Venice (1686). In the next rooms the anti-classical painter Giuseppe Maria Crespi painted between 1699 and 1700 *The Four Seasons* and *The Olympus*. The figures stand directly on the framing of the ceiling without employing an illusory perspective. The beautiful foreshortening seems to anticipate Tiepolo, Piazzetta and Goya. Donato Creti made the last room decoration in 1710 collaborating with Ercole Graziani senior who painted the quadratura. The representation of *Alexander Cutting the Gordian Knot* is whirling inside an impressing verticality culminating in a dome. The paintings housed in these rooms come from the Zambeccari collection. The palace is now property of the Council and houses a beautiful painting collection donated by Mons. Francesco Zambeccari, owned by the Italian State.
bddfa965-f0a5-5c48-ad19-ac2d02720ed9.short_description: This building, from the architectural point of view one of the most significant senatorial residences between seventeenth and eighteenth-century, was built starting from 1653. The rooms on the first floor were decorated from 1665 to 1710, by some of the main artists working in Bologna (Domenico Maria Canuti, Domenico Santi called Mengazzino, Giuseppe and Antonio Rolli, Giuseppe Maria Crespi, Donato Creti and Ercole Graziani senior). The pictures hanging to the walls date from the sixteenth- to the eighteenth-century.

bddfa965-f0a5-5c48-ad19-ac2d02720ed9.history: In 1653 Odoardo Pepoli was a freshly appointed Senator. He built a huge residence over former houses on his property to promote the elevated social prestige he and his family had recently gained in town. The work continued until 1665, when Domenico Maria Canuti took up the fresco decoration of the staircase. Fifty years later, in 1710, Odoardo and other members of the family, namely Ercole and Alessandro, commissioned the decorations of five rooms. Around 1710 the architect Giuseppe Antonio Torri built the façade overlooking via Clavature. The second name of the building, “Campogrande”, derives from its last owners.

bdff40ed-75c1-5545-b898-4ec10bbd906e.name: Spada Palace, The Perspective Corridor
bdff40ed-75c1-5545-b898-4ec10bbd906e.description: To allow the passage between the two courtyards, Borromini designed a gallery supported on both sides by coupled Tuscan columns with a coffered barrel vault, similar to the vestibule that Antonio da Sangallo had designed by for the courtyard of the nearby Palazzo Farnese a century earlier. Thanks to some skilful adjustments, the Borrominian colonnade, although measuring only 8.58 meters in length, appears much longer, about four times longer, so much so as to make the cast of a Roman warrior statuette at the end of the corridor (which, since 1861, has replaced an original and even more spectacular backdrop painted with plant motifs) and the courtyard beyond the portico appear very big. Indeed, the latter actually turns out to be nothing more than a skylight. Only by walking inside the perspective can one realize the deceptive optical effect that Borromini so intelligently designed: firstly, the mosaic floor is placed uphill; secondly, as you proceed towards the terminal part, the vault is lowered and the distance between the columns is reduced both in depth and in the sense of width. According to the rationalist theorist Francesco Milizia (1787) the Borrominian perspective intended to compete with the Vatican Royal Staircase created by his rival Bernini.
bdff40ed-75c1-5545-b898-4ec10bbd906e.short_description: Bought by Cardinal Spada, the palace was restored by Borromini. The architect shows his mastery of perspective laws by building a short corridor (9 meters) which seems much longer. It witnesses the taste of the patron for illusionist art; in 1635 he had already asked the Bolognese artists A. Mitelli and M. Colonna, to paint perspectives in the palace.
bdff40ed-75c1-5545-b898-4ec10bbd906e.bibliography: Cannatà, R., *Galleria di Palazzo Spada, Rome,* Rome: Istituto Poligrafico e Zecca dello Stato (Polygraphic Institute and State Mint), 1995.
bdff40ed-75c1-5545-b898-4ec10bbd906e.history:
Capodiferro-Spada Palace was built starting from 1549 on commission of Cardinal Girolamo Capodiferro, in the Regola rione, a few steps from the imposing Farnese Palace, which had been recently built. Unlike the latter, characterized by an almost medieval austerity, Capodiferro Palace was enriched by elaborate decorations on the facade, including niches with statues of emperors and heroes of ancient Rome. In 1632 the palace became the property of Cardinal Bernardino Spada (1594–1661) who commissioned Francesco Borromini to make some changes, including the spectacular modification of the stairwell and the creation of the connecting gallery between the two courtyards (the famous Perspective corridor), built between 1652 and 1653. Cardinal Spada originally had had a fake perspective frescoed on the left side of the courtyard, where Borromini’s Perspective would later be constructed. This original perspective was painted by Giovan Battista Magni, an expert quadraturist from Emilia. Only after the purchase of a very small plot of land from the neighbouring property of the Massari family could he transform that painted space into a real one, breaking through the frescoed wall and creating a real vaulted perspective corridor, which connected the courtyard with the land he had just acquired.  
Borromini had already shown his theatrical and illusionistic talent in the creation of the so called ‘Macchina delle Quarantore’ in St. Peter’s Basilica, which had greatly impressed Cardinal Spada. For this new project, the architect used the advice of the Augustinian Giovanni Maria da Bitonto, a famous mathematician.

bf3df40c-9dbc-5641-863e-11c7fa684ee3.name: *Mature Self-portrait*
bf3df40c-9dbc-5641-863e-11c7fa684ee3.description:
The exact date of the self-portrait is unknown, but the slightly greying temples suggest that the artist was about forty. This hypothesis is consistent with the style of the period, which many scholars have likened to the emotional sensitivity of his contemporary, Velázquez.  
Bernini painted only for himself, creating portraits, and in particular self-portraits, in private. He did not seek physiognomic detail or self-aggrandisement, focusing instead on researching psychology and the reality of the human condition. These features give painting back that immediacy which makes his paintings a precursor of the modern Borghese portrait.  
The brush strokes are fast and spontaneous, the shaking effects helping to humanise the subject. The background of the painting appears not to be finished, concentrating our attention on the expression of the face, whose features are rendered by deep chiaroscuro and colouring attributable to Annibale Carracci.  
The head is turned slightly away from the profiled bust. This arrangement suggests a slight movement of the face toward the viewer, accentuated by subtle movement of the hair caused by the twisting.  
Bernini uses strong combinations of light and shadow to add intensity to the eyes, which are almost sculptural in form.  
No documentation has ever been found to confirm the hypothesis that this canvas was taken from a diptych, whose pendant was the portrait of Costanza Bonarelli, the woman Bernini loved. The right-hand side of the canvas is frayed, hence the assumption that this is indeed part of that split work.  
The painting was donated to the Galleria Borghese in 1911 by Baron Otto Messinger, who owned a substantial body of works from the Chigi collection. It is, therefore, assumed that this famous self portrait came from the same place.
bf3df40c-9dbc-5641-863e-11c7fa684ee3.short_description:
This painting demonstrates the self-awareness of the artist, whose pose betrays his preoccupation with intellectual discovery.  
Bernini created many self-portraits during his career.

c03de3e5-cb58-583e-a3da-b1fc529f12c3.name: Pilgrimage Church of the Virgin Mary of Dolours, Sloup
c03de3e5-cb58-583e-a3da-b1fc529f12c3.description: The oval nave is closed with a presbytery and a simple column altar of local black and red marble. O. Schweigl’s construction frames the statue of the Pieta and Virgin Mary of Dolours Adored by Angels, which peaks in the figure of God the Father, the Dove of the Holy Spirit and a “lacework” baldachin.
c03de3e5-cb58-583e-a3da-b1fc529f12c3.short_description: Construction of the church was inspired by the miraculous recovery of a local miller’s daughter after praying to a statue of the Virgin Mary. The ceiling painting was executed by a later rector of the Vienna Academy C. F. Sambach. The Assumption scene, placed in an illusionary architectural frame, is supplemented with allegories of the Virtues in pendentives. Sambach also created the pictures for the side altars. This series of large paintings is among his best work. The festive atmosphere of the interior is enhanced by rich decoration and flower ornamentation by specialist artists.
c03de3e5-cb58-583e-a3da-b1fc529f12c3.method_for_datation: Preparatory sketches for the ceiling painting have been preserved in the Albertina Wien and Szépmüvészeti Múzeum in Budapest, the first of them is dated 1752.

c03de3e5-cb58-583e-a3da-b1fc529f12c3.history: Sloup was a summer retreat for the Counts of Rogendorf. The church in which its founder is buried was built next to a former homestead (now the parsonage). Construction of the church was inspired by the miraculous recovery of a local miller’s daughter after praying to a statue of the Virgin Mary that was said to have been brought from the Minorite Monastery in Brno. The furnishing of both church and the residence were completed under the subsequent owners, the Salm family, who held this sought-after pilgrimage site until 1945.

c10e7808-93b9-5026-9072-8a182fd026e7.name: Esterházy Palace
c10e7808-93b9-5026-9072-8a182fd026e7.description:
The main building of the palace complex is a complicated one, redesigned and modified in several periods. The middle part and the connecting sections of the side wings are three-storeys high; the horseshoe-shaped wings are one-storey high and, directed towards the main gate, rectangular side wings are connected to them. There is a belvedere over the middle bay. The main façade is decorated with pilasters, tympanum motifs, military trophies and a shield within which is the Esterházy coat of arms. There is a clock in the middle of the tympanum on the garden facade decorated with vases and *putti* and oval windows in the middle of the tympanums of the arched connecting wings. Balconies with wrought-iron balustrades on the second-floor level of the side wings, and a two-armed stairway with wrought-iron railings decorated with *putti* holding wrought-iron lamps, leads to a balcony from which the banqueting hall on the first floor is accessible. There are fountains in the courtyard and at the sides of the building.  
Among the most outstanding spaces are the *sala terrena* (with coloured stuccoes and wall paintings; the reconstruction of its 18th-century grotto with fountains whose porcelain animals spit water, began more recently); the summer dining area (with stuccoes); the ceremonial banqueting hall on the first floor of the middle bay with a ceiling painting, *Apollo's Triumph*, and allegorical statues of the Four Seasons in four corners of the hall.  
In the 18th century, the palace was famous for its exquisite furnishings and valuable artefacts, for example the *panneaux*, silk tapestries (e.g. those with the Esterházy design), *boiserie* with *panneaux* and wall-paintings in some rooms; chandeliers, clocks, ceramics, books, carpets, furniture and paintings; *chinoiserie* (furniture, ceramics \[also Japanese\], blue-and-white wall paintings, wallpapers and Chinese-lacquer panels in three rooms).  
In the garden (the first design by Anton Zinner) orange trees from the princely orangerie were planted in large buckets to furnish the *parterre* and chamber-gardens on both sides of the palace. The garden and park complex were organised around three main avenues, a *broiderie parterre* (large *parterre*) decorated with fountains and sculptures, *boskes,* and a garden for wild animals (*Lustgarden*). But the most valuable artefact of all was Franz Joseph Haydn, who lived in Eszterháza for 30 years and composed music to entertain Prince Nikolaus, his patron, and presented his operas in the then famous “great theatre” on the palace's west side (no longer extant).
c10e7808-93b9-5026-9072-8a182fd026e7.short_description: The Esterházy Palace complex in Fertőd-Eszterháza is an outstanding creation of 18th-century European and Hungarian palace architecture; a *maison de' plaisance* – “merry residence”, or *Lustschloss* in German – that was constantly reshaped, along with its garden, by its *Maecenas,* Nikolaus Esterházy, from the 1750s to the 1780s. In the period, it was the centre for Hungarian *chinoiserie*. The *opera* (great theatre) and the marionette theatre (small theatre) were exquisite parts of the complex. Franz Joseph Haydn was head of Prince Nikolaus's orchestra for 30 years and lived in the *Muzsikaház* (Music House) in the palace grounds.
c10e7808-93b9-5026-9072-8a182fd026e7.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, field research of the wall paintings and walls, and archaeological excavation.

c10e7808-93b9-5026-9072-8a182fd026e7.history:
The settlement in Eszterháza, now part of Fertőd, was connected to Süttör in the 18th century, along with the building complex and the estate. At the time Süttör was a Nádasdy estate, which was confiscated from the family as a result of the Wesselényi Conspiracy, and given to Palatine Pál I Esterházy. After the death of Prince Pál his youngest son, József I, inherited the estate. In 1720, József commissioned Anton Erhard Martinelli to design a hunting lodge, which according to some scholars made use of an old Renaissance hunting lodge built on the Süttör part of the estate, and for which Simon Mödlhammer created the palace roof.  
This building was inherited by József I's youngest son, Miklós II (Prince Nikolaus II Esterházy) in 1721, and in the early 1750s, Nikolaus moved there with his wife. The design of the building complex, the garden and the forest around it, were documented in a contemporary oil painting that went missing during the Second World War, but a photographic reproduction of the painting is extant.  
Nikolaus probably began reconstruction of the palace complex and enlargement of the main building in 1762, maybe to the designs of Nicolaus Jacoby an Alsatian *ingenieur*. According to recent research, the first phase of reconstruction took place between 1762 and 1764, and the second phase between 1765 and 1768. The expansion plan of Eszterháza – known as a “directive” – can probably be dated to 1762, and recent research connects it to Girolamo le Bon or Melchior Hefele.  
An important milestone in the reconstruction of the palace was Queen Maria Theresia's visit in 1773:  for the occasion, the marionette theatre was completed, and the marionette opera, *Philemon and Baucis* by Joseph Haydn, was presented as a tribute to her. Two guard's buildings were built at this time and were complete by 1776. In the garden boskets, the temples to Diana, Venus, the Sun and Fortuna were built, and the inner ”large *parterre*” was redesigned, or rather reformed, in the garden. A third, greater period of construction took place between 1775 and 1778: the building of the Belvedere as it is seen today. The *Ermitage* (hermitage) was complete by 1775, when Archduke Ferdinand Habsburg and Maria Beatrice d'Este visited Eszterháza. The so-called Bagatelle, a Chinese pavilion, was finished by 1783. Reconstruction of the garden was almost continuous until the 1780s. The fountain, with an artificial waterfall on the east side of the large *parterre*, was built between 1783 and 1784, based on designs by Franz Gruss.  
To the east of the palace, the prince built a separate row of houses for the masters and other personnel. On this side, near to the marionette theatre, were the administrative buildings (“small palace”) and the orangerie. Actors, musicians and the pharmacist lived in the *Muzsikaház* (Music House), built to the west of the palace, where the three-roomed apartment of Joseph Haydn was. The stables and the inn for travellers who were not accommodated in the palace were also located on the west side.  
The first *opera* burnt down in 1779, but the prince erected an even more exquisite building within two years of its demise, designed by Michael Stöger.  
As to the identity of the architect responsible for reconstruction of the palace, a scholarly debate rages even today as to whether it was Melchior Hefele, Nicolaus Jacoby or Ferdinand Mödlhammer.  
The blue-and-white wall paintings in some of the rooms relate to the early period of construction (1750s and 60s). The ceiling paintings in the banqueting hall, chapel and the *sala terrena* were painted by Josef Ignatz Mildorfer; the sculptures made by, among others, Josef Ressler/Rössler and Johann Friedrich Schrott; the wrought-iron work by, among others, Carl Franke.  
The Golden Age of the palace ended in 1790 with the death of Prince Nikolaus II Esterházy. The family left Eszterháza to live in their residences in Kismarton (Eisenstadt) and Vienna.  
Then, at the end of the 19th century, Prince Nikolaus IV and his wife Countess Margit Cziráky, moved in. They renovated, modernised and decorated the palace with Rococo, Neo-Rococo and other period furniture, and extensively redesigned the garden.  The interior decoration was accomplished by Miksa (Maximilian) Schmidt and the F. O. Schmidt company.  
After the death of Prince Nikolaus V his eldest son, Pál V Esterházy, became the next and last master of the property. After the Second World War the Soviet army established a military hospital there and some of the furnishing was destroyed, the rest salvaged by soldiers and locals. Later the palace was nationalised.  
Reconstruction of the main building began under Jenő Rados in 1957, and was completed by 1959 for the anniversary of Haydn's death when a palace museum was opened with a Haydn Memorial Exhibition. The University of Sopron was the guardian of the palace until 1996. Currently it is managed by the National Trust of Monuments for Hungary. The Trust is repurchasing artefacts from the palace that have been dispersed, and renovating the complex in the framework of an EU-funded project.

c12600d6-b0d6-53b9-bebc-3d8909f57339.name: Views with ruins
c12600d6-b0d6-53b9-bebc-3d8909f57339.description:
These pictures decorated one of the halls in Palazzo Aldrovandi, later called the Palazzo Montanari. They were moved to the Collezioni Comunali d'Arte in 2001 after they were purchased by the Municipality of Bologna.  
The series was painted between 1724 and 1733 by Pietro Paltronieri called Mirandolese (architectures) and Vittorio Maria Bigari (figures). Both artists worked for Pompeo Aldrovandi (1668-1752), a famous Bolognese prelate who was ordained cardinal in 1734. He transformed the family house in Via Galliera into a sumptuous residence, inspired to the most famous French models.  
Il Mirandolese was a very celebrated landscape and ruins painter. He was so celebrated that he participated in a series of the *Allegorical Tombs*, commissioned by Ms. Mac Swiny and dedicated to the Duke of Richmond. This patronage involved other painters, both Bolognese and Venetians including Pittoni, Cimaroli, Canaletto, and the Riccis.  
In this painting he freely combines ruins of imposing classic architecture, fragments of gothic churches, allegorical tombs, and simple wooden houses whilst using complex scenic perspectives.  
In this pre-romantic atmosphere Vittorio Maria Bigari places his slender and elegant figures. They are painted with a swift brushwork, which allows them to appear to move gracefully and indifferently, as they are walking, talking, and sitting on the ruins.  
The collaboration between the two artists is exceptionally good, as the high quality of Bigari's work emphasises the elegant scene created by Mirandolese.  
This cycle of paintings is part of a movement in archaeology, perspective and landscape which was starting to develop. The trend continued in France and England and can be seen in the paintings of Hubert Robert and Jean Honorè Fragonard. In Italy, the etchings by Giovanni Battista Piranesi were also a continuation of this movement.
c12600d6-b0d6-53b9-bebc-3d8909f57339.short_description:
This series was painted between 1724 and 1733 by Pietro Paltronieri called Mirandolese (architecture) and Vittorio Maria Bigari (figures). It was originally hanging in Palazzo Aldrovandi Montanari.  
This cycle of paintings reflects the taste for archaeology, perspective and landscapes made popular in England and France by the paintings of Hubert Robert and Jean Honorè Fragonard and in Italy by the etchings of Giovanni Battista Piranesi.

The name Vittorio M. Bigari and the date 1733 are written on the inscription held by the statue of a woman standing in the niche of the classical temple in the *View of Ruins with a River and a Gothic Church*. Using these dates, it is assumed the date of the execution of the whole series is between 1724 and 1733.

c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.name: Parish Church of Sümeg
c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.alternate_name: Church of the Ascension of Christ
c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.description: The church is a prototype of a simple, rural, Baroque single-tower church. On entering the church are the organ-loft and the entrance hall; the building then continues in three sections topped by a sail vault and ends with the sanctuary. The façade is furnished with statues of the Virgin Mary, and two Hungarian Holy kings, St. Stephen and St. Ladislaus. In the entrance hall are statues of the precursors of Christ, the prophets and sibyls. On the pillars are representations of David as an ancestor of the Family of Christ in front of King Saul and, later, as King David. In the Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre, accessible from the entrance hall, are frescoes depicting the *Limbo of the Fathers* (the *Bosom of Abraham*) and *Sacrifice of Abraham*. In the first section of the nave the ceiling frescoes depict *God Dispatches the Archangel Gabriel* and *Moses Receives the Tablets of the Law*. Underneath these scenes are the *Birth of Christ* and the *Annunciation* on the right, and the *Naming of Jesus* on the left. On the ceiling of the second section are the *Star of Bethlehem* and the *Road to Calvary*. To the right of this is the *Adoration of the Magi* and, to the left, the *Hill of Calvary*. The decoration on the ceiling of the third section portrays *Angels*, *Christ with the Apostles*, and the *Arrival of the Holy Spirit*. Underneath the image of *Christ* a depiction of the *Resurrection* can be seen; and beneath the *Arrival of the Holy Spirit* are the *Pentecost* and *St. Peter*. The main wall of the sanctuary is decorated with the *Transfiguration*, where the damned are seen on the right and the saved on the left. The ceiling frescoes portray the *Holy Trinity*, *St. Martin*, *St. Francis de Sales*, and the *Four Church Fathers* (St. George, St. Jerome, St. Ambrose and St. Augustine). *St. Michael* and the *Twenty-Four Elders of the Apocalypse* are pictured weighing souls in the fresco in the organ-loft, where there is also a portrait of Bishop Márton Padányi Bíró. There are two self-portraits of Maulbertsch in the church: one in the organ-loft among a crowd of nobles and another in the *Birth of Christ* where he is seen among the shepherds.
c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.short_description: The significance of the Church of the Ascension of Christ in Sümeg lies in its magnificent fresco cycle, painted by Franz Anton Maulbertsch in 1757. Born in Langenargen, Maulbertsch was a disciple of Peter van Roy and Paul Troger in Vienna. Following the Baroque tradition, the fresco cycle carries a complex theological message probably composed by the learned and rigid Márton Padányi Bíró Bishop of Veszprém, who also built for himself a mansion in the town.
c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual resources.
c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.bibliography:
Gerke, F., *Die Fresken des Franz Anton Maulbertsch in der Pfarrkirche zu Sümeg (The Frescoes of Franz Anton Maulbertsch in the Parish Church od Sümeg)*, Mainz, 1950.  
Garas, K., *Franz Anton Maulbertsch: Leben und Werk (Life and Work)*, Salzburg, 1974.  
Levárdy, F., *Sümeg, plébániatemplom (Süme, Parish Church)*, Budapest, 1981.
c14455aa-18e4-5464-a835-2f441f182d82.history: Bishop Márton Padányi Bíró inherited a diocese that was in financial ruin. A talented administrator, he managed to restore the economy of the Veszprém diocese and ordered the construction of several parish churches. The church in Sümeg was of course one of these, and its special significance was probably due to the fact that the bishop also built a mansion for himself in the town, which became his favourite residence. The church was built between 1756 and 1757 presumably under the auspices of Joseph Tiethart a master mason from Veszprém, who conducted the construction of the mansion as well. The bishop entrusted Franz Anton Maulbertsch with painting the fresco cycle that delivered a complex theological message. This proved to be Maultbertsch's most outstanding work in Hungary.

c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.name: Parts of the St. Mary and St. Ladislaus altarpieces from Zagreb Cathedral
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.alternate_name: St. Mary and St. Ladislaus altarpieces
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.description:
The museum's altarpiece composition comprises parts of two altarpieces, that of St. Mary and St. Ladislaus. It has a central niche from the altarpiece of St. Mary – decorated with acanthus leaves, putti and bunches of fruit – within which the statue of Mary with the Child Jesus in her arms is standing on a half-moon entwined by a serpent. In front of the niche stand the statues of St. Ladislaus, the King, and St. Emeric, the Duke, which belonged to the altarpiece of Ladislaus.      
The composition, flanked by carved consoles attached to the wall, has the same ornamental decoration as seen in the central niche of the altarpiece of St. Mary; the consoles used to support painted altarpiece wings. Above them are the statues of the four evangelists, which were originally in the niches of the predella panel of the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus.  
In a contract of 1686, the sculptor from Ljubljana, Ivan Komersteiner, agreed to make the altarpiece of St. Mary for the apse of the north aisle of Zagreb Cathedral. In another contract of 1688, he agreed to make its pair, the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus, for the apse on the south aisle. Komersteiner was already a citizen of Zagreb with a workshop in Zagreb's Kaptol.    
The two altarpieces were identical in design: winged altarpieces with painted panels showing scenes from the Life of Mary on the altarpiece dedicated to her, with statues distributed on two levels and in the attic. Painted panels depicting scenes from the Life of St. Ladislaus decorated the altarpiece dedicated to him, with appropriate statues. While the wings from the altarpiece of St. Mary were destroyed those from the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus are kept in Zagreb City Museum.     
St. Ladislaus, the King of Hungary, was responsible for the foundation of the Zagreb Diocese.  
Komersteiner was responsible for the statues and woodcarving. Ivan Eisenhort and Bernardo Bobić collaborated on the painting and gilding of the altarpieces, while Matijaž Erlman began the work on the architecture for the altarpiece of St. Mary.  
The arrival of the sculptor, Komersteiner, to Zagreb marked the final entrance of the Baroque in the sculpture of continental Croatia. He brought with him as a novelty the ornamental decorative motif of Baroque acanthus, so-called Italian leaves, and his statues anticipate a new style expressed in the mobility of the slender figures of saints in characteristic counterpoise, freeing them from dependence on altarpiece niches.      
Komersteine's expression in his work has no direct analogies either in Croatia or in neighbouring territories, but the indirect influence of Italian art in his work is undeniable.  
During renovations in 1882, both altarpieces were removed from Zagreb Cathedral.
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.short_description:
A “composite” altarpiece composition comprising parts from the Altarpieces of St. Mary and St. Ladislaus originally designed for the apses of the north and south aisles of Zagreb Cathedral.  
During renovation of the cathedral in 1882, both altarpieces were removed and partially destroyed in the process. They were made by Ivan Komersteiner, a sculptor who worked first in Ljubljana and then in Zagreb. His arrival in Zagreb marked the final entrance of the Baroque to continental Croatia.
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.method_for_datation: Contracts from 1686 and 1688 in Acta capituli antiqua fasc. 101
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.obtention: In 1921, the Commission for Education and Religion gave the order to transfer parts of the altarpieces to the Museum of Arts and Crafts to protect the cultural heritage.

c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.name: Catholic Parish and Pilgrimage Church of the Exaltation of the Cross and Our Lady of Sorrows
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.description:
The church is not only girded by cornices but also surrounded by a double series of large round-arched windows and four projections, each of them crowned by a tympanum. In the west – and very typically in the Baroque style – the main facade balloons out in a dish-shape manner from the exterior to the pulvinate middle part. Here it then rises, over a diadem-like curved cornice and a multi-scrolled ornamental gable, up into a squat looking turret with an onion-shaped roof.  
A centralised effect within the light-flooded galleries and four-bay aisle of the wall-pillar church is created through diagonally bent vaults, which allow the whole aisle to blend seamlessly with the richly decorated choir and its flat cupola vault. In addition to this effect, the two side altars also lead the viewer’s eye towards the high altar. The colorful and bright spatial impression is created through virtuoso stucco decoration in the Rococo style. This, together with the large ceiling frescos place the adoration of both the Cross and the Virgin Mary within the heavenly plan for salvation in accordance with the double patronage of the church. But, at first, the undersides of the galleries depict scenes from pilgrimage history directed towards pilgrims; the upper lateral barrel-vaults then show the suffering of the Virgin Mary. Finally, above these, one can find the oval ceiling fresco which echoes the paintings in the vault of the choir.
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.short_description: From 1749, under the auspices of the Premonstratensian monastery Rot an der Rot, the spacious pilgrimage church in Maria Steinbach was rebuilt and enlarged in order to do justice to the enormous inflow of pilgrims. The church is deemed to be one of the jewels of Bavarian Rococo. Its art historical fame originates from its overwhelmingly rich interior with its eloquent frescos rich in images, virtuosic use of stucco and whimsically designed altars.
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.method_for_datation: Archival evidence and also an inscription on the south portal. Above the main portal are placed the coats-of-arms of the abbots Hermann Vogler (gov. 1711–1739), and Mauritius Moritz (gov. 1760–1782) referring to the church’s elevation to a pilgrimage sanctuary, and respectively, completion of the church building.
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.bibliography:
Schütz, B., *Die kirchliche Barockarchitektur in Bayern und Oberschwaben 1580–1780*, Munich 2000, pp. 51, 155.  
Buck, I. A., *Katholische Pfarr- und Wallfahrtskirche Maria Steinbach*, Lindenberg 1998.  
Beck, O., *Katholische Pfarr- und Wallfahrtskirche Maria Steinbach* (Kleine Kunstführer 205, 7th revised edition), Regensburg 1992.
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.history: The pilgrimage to Maria Steinbach is incorporated in the Premonstratensian abbey Rot an der Rot which was founded in 1126. From 1723 onwards the former parish church was considered a pilgrimage centre due to Abbot Hermann Vogler's donation of a particle of the cross. For the purposes of adoration, a 100-year-old crucifix was restored and erected upon the high altar along with two assistant sculptural figures, a *Mater Dolorosa* and the *Apostle St John*. The steadily growing flow of pilgrims, supposedly due to the miraculous healing powers attributed to the sculpture of the Virgin Mary, was the reason that, in 1734, Maria Steinbach was elevated to a special place of pilgrimage dedicated to the Virgin Mary. To meet the demands of such a steadily growing number of pilgrims it was decided to rebuild the church according to the so-called “Vorarlberger Münster” scheme (named after the regional school of Austrian master builders). The architecturally trained local Premonstratensian monk, Father Benedict Stadelhofer was chosen as architect in 1746. After the transferral of the miraculous image of the Virgin in 1754, the church was then consecrated in 1755 although consecration of the high altar and thus the ultimate finish of the building process took place later, in 1770.
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.patrons: Abbots of the Premonstratensian Abbey Rot an der Rot, Ignatius Vetter (gov. 1739–1755), Benedict Stadelhofer (gov. 1755–1760), Mauritius Moritz (gov. 1760–1782)
c173e928-a469-521a-8d30-74c53fdeb588.architects: Design of architecture: Pater Benedikt Stadelhofer (1694–1760); master builder: Anton Lacher (1705–1777); stucco: Johann Georg Üblher (1703–1763), of the altar and ornamental niche: Franz Xaver Feichtmayr the Younger (1735–1803), Franz Xaver Schmuzer (1713–1775); frescos: Franz Georg Hermann the Younger (1692–1768)
