cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.name: Pair of Torchères
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.description:
These two grandiose torchères were ordered for the Chapel of Saint John the Baptist to be installed in São Roque church in Lisbon. With a triangular base, in gilt bronze, they form a pyramid held by titans. Above, a cornice developing into a dome is finished with Rocaille-inspired shells and a D. João V shield on each of the three surfaces of the torch holders. In niches below the dome, forming an oratory, the Doctors of the church are seated: St Jerome, St. Thomas Aquinas, Sr. Ambrose and St. Bonaventure, St. Augustine and St. Leo the Great. The hybrid ornamentation develops upwards in fluid volutes – wing, acroterion, cymatium – flowers in the shape of garlands, phytomorphic elements – rope, laurel and acanthus – and zoomorphic elements, as well as a variety of *putti* inspired by the Roman Baroque.  
They were conceived and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi with the cooperation of the metalworker Fellice Schiffone, the carpenter Lucano Celladini, Agostino Ancidoni another metalworker, and Lorenzo Morelli a silversmith and founder. Following the death of Giuseppe Gagliardi minor finishing and the lamination were concluded by his son, Leonardo Gagliardi, who like his father was a master silversmith.
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.short_description: A splendid pair of torch holders in gilt bronze and chiselled silver, they form part of a royal commission for the Chapel of St. John the Baptist. Designed and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi, the metalworkers Fellice Schiffone and Agostino Ancidoni collaborated with him on the project. Lucano Celladini was the carpenter and Luciano Morelli was the silversmith and founder.

cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.name: *Vizovice Chateau, Chapel*
cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.description:
The chapel in the south wing of the Vizovice Chateau in the Wallachia region is built into a central layout with three apses and crowned with a cupola. The drawing represents the chapel on a single level. On the left is a pulpit decorated with a relief of the Baptism of Christ, and the high altar with the Assumption of the Virgin Mary with a sarcophagus-shaped tabernacle, figures of Mary's parents, St. Joachim and St. Anne, and a Marian picture carried by angels, the top of which features a monogram of the name “Mary”. The second altar, decorated with consecration crosses, provides a framework for a picture of St. John of Nepomuk. The third field is a design for an oratory with illusionary drapery. In the place of the door is the last of the vaulting joints decorated with tetramorphs of the evangelists with angels carrying the gospels, from the left: Matthew, John (eagle), Mark (lion) and Luke (bull).  
Schweigl's design, with fine ornamentation in Louis XVI style, was executed with only minor changes (the latest of which was in 1777), in accordance with the requirements of the chateau's sponsor Heřman Hannibal of Blümegen (c. 1774), who also endowed the chapel with precious chasubles and liturgical objects that have survived to this day. A relief of the birth of Christ was created for the pulpit, replacing the original design. The decoration of the oratory is much more austere, without the theatre-like curtain.  
The Rococo interior with its relief decoration stands in contrast to the low-key classicist architecture of František Antonín Grimm who trained in Rome, in the studio of Nicolo di Salvi, in France and in Germany. The design bears witness to the versatility of the learned Brno sculptor, Andreas Schweigl. Schweigl did not underestimate the role of the decorator, something that gained in significance towards the end of the century.
cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.short_description: The design shows the versatility of the learned Brno sculptor Andreas Schweigl, who did not underestimate the decorator’s role. The chapel interior, with fine Louis XVI ornamentation, contrasts with the low-key classicist architecture of František Antonín Grimm, who trained in Rome, France and Germany.

cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.obtention: The drawing comes from the collection of Jan Petr Cerroni, Brno archivist and historian. Date of acquisition is not given.

ce47157c-f9a0-5662-9c5f-3c7280fea2d6.name: Quirinale Palace, Frieze of the Sala Regia
ce47157c-f9a0-5662-9c5f-3c7280fea2d6.description:
The frescoed frieze is located ten metres above the walking floor and just above the windows. The short side walls show a decoration with allegorical figures inside niches, biblical representations, coats of arms and the heraldic animals of the Borghese family (dragon and eagle).  
The frieze of the long walls, on the other hand, depict a loggia framed by Ionic pilasters resting on painted corbels, from which various groups of exotic characters peek over. Between the arches of the loggia there are also square windows and under them the monochrome images of the several buildings erected by Paul V during his pontificate (the Quirinale Palace, the facade of San Pietro, the Mostra dell’Acqua Paola, the Pauline Chapel in Santa Maria Maggiore) accompanied by allegorical figures and Borghese emblems. Between the square windows one can see the ovals with episodes from the *Stories of Moses,* who, as the legislator of the Old Testament, prefigures the role assumed by Christ and therefore by Peter and the Roman pontiffs as guides of the Christian world. Among the Oriental delegations that look out from the loggia we can recognize the Japanese, led by Hasekura Tsunenaga, which visited Rome in 1615, the two Persian embassies (in Rome in 1609), the Congolese delegation (1608), that of the Armenian Patriarch (1610) and the Ethiopian one sent by the Negus Seltan Sagued. The short sides of the room and the long wall facing Via del Quirinale were almost entirely executed by Giovanni Lanfranco, Carlo Saraceni and assistants; the other long wall is by Agostino Tassi and collaborators. The magnificence of the whole fresco is due to the perfect fusion of allegorical images and symbols with the portraits of representatives of foreign delegations, with their exotic costumes rendered with great accuracy. The psychological analysis of the individual figures is also very remarkable, showing diverse attitudes such as surprise, haughtiness, amusement and lively curiosity.
ce47157c-f9a0-5662-9c5f-3c7280fea2d6.short_description: The exotic characters at the false *loggia* in the main hall of the papal palace refer to the important eastern legations visiting Rome at the beginning of the 17th century. They celebrate the relationships with the East and the missionary activity promoted by Pope Paulus V.
ce47157c-f9a0-5662-9c5f-3c7280fea2d6.bibliography: Terzani, L.,“Sala Regia”, in Briganti, G., Laureati, L., Terzani, L. (eds), *Il patrimonio artistico del Quirinale. Pittura antica. La decorazione murale,* vol. 1, Milan: Electa – BNL, 1993: 76–123.
ce47157c-f9a0-5662-9c5f-3c7280fea2d6.history: The Sala Regia (Royal Hall) was built by Carlo Maderno during the renovation works promoted by Paolo V Borghese along this wing of the Quirinale Palace, which had been used as papal seat since the end of the 16th century. It was the room where the pope’s public audiences and meetings with foreign ambassadors and delegations visiting Rome were held. The frieze, alluding precisely to those functions and exalting Paul V’s foreign policy – especially with the East and Africa – as well as his missionary activity, was frescoed between 1616 and 1617 by a workshop directed by Agostino Tassi and Giovanni Lanfranco. The first project involved covering the whole wall surface with frescoes, and only at a later time was it decided to limit it only to the upper part, while the lower part would host drapes and tapestries.
ce47157c-f9a0-5662-9c5f-3c7280fea2d6.architects: Giovanni Lanfranco and his workshop; Agostino Tassi and his workshop

cee9abc9-7697-5210-9e9a-510d6ec672a0.name: Model for a male saint (St. Paul?)
cee9abc9-7697-5210-9e9a-510d6ec672a0.description: The small sculpture without a colour setting was originally used as a model for an assistant figure on an altar which is still unknown. Its strong impression, influenced by the sculptor J. B. Straub, resembles the laterally reversed large figure of *St. Joachim* which is part of the high altar of the monastery church of Fürstenfeld. The sculpture is considered to resemble the Apostle Paul, which iconographically is typified by the full beard and the large folio held on the left thigh. The dressed figure with a greatcoat has been placed in a standing position, with bare feet, right leg on the ground, and the left foot gaining a foothold on a rock. While the left arm is stretched out ahead and to the side with (the now lost) hand in an instructive attitude, the head is slightly raised and the lips are closed. The plinth is of modern origin.
cee9abc9-7697-5210-9e9a-510d6ec672a0.short_description: The small sculpture without a colour setting was originally used as a model for an assistant figure on an altar. Despite the small size of the figure its impression is astonishingly monumental.

cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.name: Cup
cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.description: A tin cup decorated with a representation of St. Joseph, the patron saint of carpenters and a carpenter himself. In the course of the 19th century, craftsmen entered into different guilds to protect their professional rights. Membership to a professional guild was regulated in all details, which created a very particular way of life and work in Hungary that continued up until the end of 19th century. In Hungary as elsewhere in Europe, in order to enter a guild the candidate was obliged to fulfil a “wandering year”, a statutory trip that involved travelling sometimes far afield in order to learn and practice different techniques, after which the practioner had to accomplish a masterpiece. From this journey potential guild members made a “book of wandering” where they wrote about their journey,  noted all importants events, the names of the masters with whom they worked, the cities they visited and the pieces they made. Naturally, in this book the owner would write their name and where they were from, which meant that the book of wandering served as both a personal document and passport. On the basis of all this the guild decided whether to accept the candidate as a guild member or not. Activity of the guilds in Pest-Buda ended in 1872. This cup is an example of an object with religious imagery used in a non-religious setting.
cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.short_description: A ceremonial object belonging to the Guild of Carpenters in the city of Buda. It is an early example of guild history in the city.
cf4c5cb6-fba8-5008-a74f-32d21004ada0.method_for_datation: Historical documents and by analysis of the decoration and style.

cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.name: Head of St. Philip Neri
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.description:
This head modelled in wax is considered a replica of a bronze in the collection of the Rhode Island School of Design in Providence, made by Alessandro Algardi around 1640. Another bronze version is in the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica in Rome. These bronzes were made a few years before the artist was charged with the statue in marble of St. Philip Neri for the sacristy of Santa Maria in Vallicella, in Rome (1635–38). For this commission Algardi carefully studied the death mask of the saint, dead in 1595 and sanctified in 1622. The saint's face is strained by old age and suffering but shows deep humanity, humility and the extraordinary strength of a man near to God. Its classicising features make it similar to an antique portrait.  
Algardi, a pupil of Ludovico Carracci's, began a career as a sculptor and in 1625 moved to Rome where he spent nearly all his artistic life.
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.short_description: This wax head is thought to be a replica of two bronze ones portraying the same saint, made by Alessandro Algardi around 1640. The sculptor previously carved a marble statue of St. Philip with an angel for the sacristy of Santa Maria in Vallicella in Rome (1635-38). In these head portraits which are strictly devotional, he deepens his analysis of the facial features, emphasising the strong humanity of the saint and his strong moral and spiritual strength.
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.holder: Museo di Arte Industriale e Galleria Davia Bargellini
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.method_for_datation: The bronze head in Providence is nearly identical to the wax one, which bears a date. Critics think that heads like this were commissioned to sculptors after the success of the marble statue with St. Philip Neri and the angel for S. Maria in Vallicella, finished in 1638.
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.obtention: The work was probably purchased at the beginning of the twentieth-century; no documentation survives.

d0575561-8c84-58c7-8351-14e3712f07f9.name: National Pantheon and Church of St. Engrácia
d0575561-8c84-58c7-8351-14e3712f07f9.description:
The National Pantheon, also known as the Church of St. Engrácia, rises magnificently above the River Tagus overlooking one of the city's oldest quarters, Alfama. One of the most beautiful examples of Portuguese Baroque, the undulating exterior elevations give the building grace and movement, while inside, the contrast between the polychrome marble and white stone creates a unique game of light and shadow.  
The National Pantheon was inaugurated on 7 December 1966 and houses the tombs of some of the most outstanding Portuguese Presidents of the Republic, writers, artists and politicians.
d0575561-8c84-58c7-8351-14e3712f07f9.short_description:
The National Pantheon, also known as the Church of St. Engrácia, is set high above the city's historic quarter and the River Tagus. Serving as a reference point to the city's image, it is one of the most beautiful testimonies to the Baroque period in Portugal. Foundation of the church dates to the early 17th century and the present structure was completed in the mid-20th century. This long and troubled 400-year construction history is tellingly apparent in the popular expression “\[like\] the works of Santa Engrácia!” said in reply to the mention of a project that is running late or unlikely ever to be completed. Despite this, the Church of St. Engrácia has retained the initial 17th-century Baroque vision.  
Since 1966 the church has paid homage to and accommodated the tombs of some prominent figures of recent Portuguese history.
d0575561-8c84-58c7-8351-14e3712f07f9.method_for_datation: Historical documents, other evidence and stylistic analysis
d0575561-8c84-58c7-8351-14e3712f07f9.bibliography:
Carvalho, A., *As Obras de Santa Engrácia e os seus* artistas, Lisbon, 1971.  
Ataide, M. M., *Monumentos e Edifícios Notáveis do Distrito de Lisboa*. Junta Distrital de Lisbon, 1975.  
Gomes, P. V., *O Essencial sobre a Arquitectura barroca em Portugal, INCM, Lisbon, 1987.*  
Birg, M., *João Antunes Arquitecto*, Lisbon, 1988.  
Mantas, H., *O Panteão Nacional, Memória e afirmação de um ideário de decadência. A intervenção da DGEMN na Igreja de Santa Engrácia*, Tese de Mestrado, FLUL, Lisbon, 2002.
d0575561-8c84-58c7-8351-14e3712f07f9.history:
The original Church of St. Engrácia was founded at the beginning of the 17th century to satisfy the wishes of Princess Maria, an outstanding figure of Portuguese Humanism and the daughter of King Manuel I. Built by the architect Nicolau de Frias and possibly his son, Teodósio de Frias, nothing remains of this original construction which was robbed and defaced in 1630. Following this, the architects Mateus do Couto (uncle and nephew) conducted reconstruction works in the chancel, but the church was ruined again as a result of a storm in 1681.  
Nobles and other prominent aristocratic figures then formed the Brotherhood of the Holy Sacrament Slaves and decided to construct a new and more sumptuous church on the same site.  
A public tender of 1681 was awarded to the architect João Antunes, who was responsible for the first-stage construction of 1682, and to which ceremonial opening Prince Regent D. Pedro (future King Pedro II) presided.  
João Antunes took full advantage of the location overlooking the river Tagus, designing the first clearly Baroque structure in Portuguese architecture: a large, central-plan church that forms a Greek cross and with four turrets. A majestic dome, rising almost 80 metres above the ground, crowns the monument.

keywords: Greek cross, central plan church, early Baroque period in Portugal, inlaid marble, João Antunes

d061ab3f-c31d-523f-8665-b8b2bb273788.name: St. Anne’s Column
d061ab3f-c31d-523f-8665-b8b2bb273788.description: The Corinthian column fashioned from red Kramsach marble is the work of the sculptor Cristoforo Benedetti from Trentino. The column is crowned with a Mary Immaculata, below which, on the cross shaped pedestal, are saintly figures at each point of the compass: To the north St. Anne, Mother of Mary, to the west, Cassian, the patron saint of the diocese of Brixen, to the east Vigilius, the patron saint of the diocese of Trent, and to the south, St. George with the dragon and the lance, the patron saint of the province. The plinth relief features putti with inscriptions. All figures and reliefs were executed in white marble; some of the saintly attributes are highlighted with gilding.
d061ab3f-c31d-523f-8665-b8b2bb273788.short_description: St. Anne’s Column is the most important example of a religious votive monument in Tyrol. It is a memorial to the liberation of Tyrol from the troops of the Bavarian Elector Max Emanuel in the War of the Spanish Succession who were repelled on the Feast of St. Anne. The column, crowned by a figure of the Virgin Mary on the crescent moon, together with the Mary Help Church, was an important centre for the public veneration of the Virgin Mary, initiated by the Estates of the Province of Innsbruck.
d061ab3f-c31d-523f-8665-b8b2bb273788.history: The erection of St. Anne’s Column goes back to the liberation of Tyrol from the invading Bavarian and French troops, the so called “Bavarian Rummel” in the War of the Spanish Succession. On 26 July 1703, on the Feast of St. Anne, Tyrol was liberated from foreign rule. On 15 March 1704, the Estates of the Province of Tyrol vowed to erect St. Anne’s Column and commissioned the sculptor Cristoforo Benedetti. The inauguration took place on 26 July 1706.
d061ab3f-c31d-523f-8665-b8b2bb273788.patrons: Estates of the Province of Tyrol
keywords: Votive monument; veneration of the Virgin Mary; public monument
d061ab3f-c31d-523f-8665-b8b2bb273788.author: Frank Purrmann

d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.name: Former residence of the painter family Zeiller
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.description: The paintings adorning the Zeiller House, in which Johann Jakob Zeiller had his home and workshop, are closer stylistically to the work of his cousin Franz Anton which is why they are usually attributed to the latter. It is an especially rich example of the “Lüftlmalerei” common in Außenfern. As Außenfern belonged to the diocese of Augsburg, the stylistic sources as well as pictorial models are primarily to be sought there. The special features of the paintings on the Zeiller House are their virtuoso composition featuring religious and profane motifs and exoticisms.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.short_description: The most famous of the numerous residential houses with façade paintings in Lechtal, Tyrol, was the home of the famous family of painters Zeiller. The façades of the elongated house are decorated on three sides with “Lüftlmalerei” (outside paintings), with the especially richly decorated gable end with bay window forming the main visible face. A very pretty example of the artistic self-presentation of this period.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.dates: The house with a gable-end façade was built in the 16th century and subsequently altered numerous times. The Late Rococo façade paintings originate from the period around 1770/75.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.bibliography: Baur-Heinhold, *Margarete, Süddeutsche Fassadenmalerei vom Mittelalter bis zur Gegenwart*, Munich 1952, pp. 114–18.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.history: The Zeiller House, also called “Schönes Haus”, was erected in the 16th century. It is situated in the north of Reutte on the so-called “Untermarkt” (Lower Market). It survived the major fires of 1703/04. Paul Zeiller (1658–1738), the father of Johann Jakob and founder of the Außerfern school of painting had his workshop here. On the south side of the building fragments of paintings are preserved which date from around 1600. The façade paintings on the other sides originate from around 1770/75 and are either the work of Johann Jakob or his nephew Franz Anton Zeiller.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.architects: Façade paintings, attributed to: Franz Anton Zeiller (1716–1794) or Johann Jakob Zeiller (1708–1783)
keywords: Façade paintings; Lüftlmalerei; fresco paintings; secular building; residential house; family of artists
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.author: Frank Purrmann

d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.name: St. Vitus Cathedral, Rijeka
d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.description:
The basic characteristic of the Church of St. Vitus is its centralisation, expressed both in the spatial proportions and in the way the architectural units interconnect. The central octagonal space under the dome opens up with arcades towards lower, oval domed chapels, those serving the chancel distinguished by only slightly greater depth. The enduring Renaissance-informed static concept is apparent in the articulation of dark-marble Tuscan pillars and arches that continue along all eight sides of the central space. According to the still-extant Briano plan, an evenly lit space required a coffered dome with a lantern, however, in the building, not only was the lighting enhanced but the plastic articulation of the exterior elaborated with freestanding Tuscan pillars at the central entrance projection. Furthermore, there was another step towards the introduction of the Baroque by way of the gallery extension, characteristic of the 18th century, and, in addition, the exterior received a new vertical accent in the shape of a high tambour and a dome encompassed by a conical roof.  
The architectural quality seen in St. Vitus Church (today St. Vitus Cathedral) was never repeated in the Bay of Kvaerner area. This unique building with its parallel in the contemporary Santa Maria della Salute in Venice originates, via Sebastiano Serli, with the Brunelleschi-prototype octagonal Church of Santa Maria degli Angeli in Florence. All these influences might be a direct reflection – not only within architecture – of the international religious sensibility of the time, as shown, for example, in the never-realised plan for a central Jesuit church in Dubrovnik.
d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.short_description: Today the Cathedral, once the Jesuit Church of St. Vitus in Rijeka, is the only Baroque Jesuit central-plan church in Croatia. Its spatial organisation, accomplished in 1638, is characterised by a regular octagon originally surmounted by a high dome and surrounded with oval chapels, an architectural solution influenced by the famous Italian architects, Andrea Palladio and Baldassare Longhena. The entire oeuvre of the designer Giacomo Briano, however, suggests even older origins related to his work in the framework of Renaissance Florence, suggested by the two colours used in the articulation of the interior: dark-grey marble pillars and arches in front of white walls. The church obtained its Baroque stamp only with the building of the gallery above the chapels in 1725, and with the execution of a new dome at a higher level.
d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.type: Religious architecture, an Early Baroque central octagonal church with side chapels and dome
d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.method_for_datation: Dated on the basis of documents, the Briano plan and later architectural drawings, and stylistic features.
d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.bibliography:
Fučić, B., *Sveti Vid*, Rijeka, 1994.  
Kudiš, N., “Projekt Giacoma Briana za isusovačku crkvu sv. Vida u Rijeci” in *Prilozi povijesti umjetnosti u Dalmaciji*, 34, 1994, pp. 269–283.  
Matejčić, R., *Crvka svetog* Vida, Rijeka, 1994.
d0a91bc9-fefd-595c-930b-f16dbb5f6b97.history: The Jesuits arrived in Rijeka in 1626 prompted by Archduke Ferdinand II. According to the original plans, the intention was a large church with a nave and two-aisles, built alongside city walls on the sea (1633). However, because of groundwater, they opted for a dominant position alongside the *castello* (1636), which led in turn not only to the church having a central ground plan – not at all typical of the Jesuits – but for defensive reasons, a limitation on the height also. Giacomo Briano of Modena drew up both plans. Although the foundation stone was laid in 1638, construction continued into the 17th century (it was not until 1659 that the church was consecrated). In the 18th century, some adjustments to the original plans saw a gallery extension and a new dome, this time according to plans by the Friulian builder, Bernardino Martinuzzi.

d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.name: *An Aristocratic Couple as Adam and Eve*
d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.description:
*An Aristocratic Couple as Adam and Eve* is a very unusual, bizarre picture of the genre; an allegorical portrait that allowed the artist to ignore the formalities of traditional portraiture. The couple, wearing white wigs and sitting in the garden of Eden among tame wild animals obviously commissioned the painting, but their identities are still unknown. Because of the boldness of the portrayal it is very likely that the painting was the result of an established friendship between the artist and the commissioner, particularly as this kind of portrayal is unparalleled in Millitz's oeuvre as he painted mainly traditional, representative half-length portraits.  
As we know little about Millitz's genre or group portraits and still less about his portraits with landscape elements, this allegorical portrait implies an unusual and new venture for the painter. The basis for the faces was probably traditional portraiture, but for the other parts of the composition the painter in all likelihood used a French sample picture, perhaps suggested by his commissioner. A composition of Adam and Eve by Jean Francois Troy (1679–1752) painted in 1730 is a case in point. This work shows the moment of the Fall of Adam and Eve in a style similar to the Rococo genre but with real emotion. Regards the content of this painting, it portrays the travesty of the biblical scene from the perspective of the Age of Enlightenment. As to its philosophical background, the scene is an enlightened transformation of the free will of the first human couple who acted independently of God's wish.  
Millitz was Martin van Meytens' pupil at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. He lived and worked in Vienna from 1749 and then worked in Pozsony (Bratislava) between 1778 and 1784. He executed several commissions for mainly Hungarian aristocratic families.
d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.short_description: An unusual representation by the master of Pozsony (Bratislava) painted while Millitz was studying in Vienna: the double nude composition was born under the influence of the new philosophical ideas of the Age of Enlightenment.
d1d2c280-9bfc-5ff6-9d5a-7ba47f268569.obtention: Purchased from a private owner in 1980.

d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.name: Petar Zrinski  (Vrbovec, Croatia, 6.6.1621–Wiener Neustadt, 30.4.1671)
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.description:
A descendant of a noble and distinguished Croatian family, Count Petar Zrinski excelled in battles against the Turks. After the death of his elder brother Nikola (d. 1664) – Croatian *ban* (viceroy) and a most prominent Hungarian poet of his time – Petar became *ban* from 1665 to 1671. He translated – from Hungarian to Croatian – Nikola's poem *Adrianskoga mora Syrena* (The Siren of the Adriatic Sea). He was married to Ana Katarina Frankopan (d. 1673) with whom he had a son, Ivan Antun, and three daughters: Judita Petronila and Veronika who became nuns, and Jelena (1643–1693), who married first Franjo Rákóczy and later Emerik Tököly.  
Petar Zrinski along with other distinguished noblemen – his brother-in-law Franjo Krsto Frankopan, Franjo Nadasdy and Erasmus Tattenbach – were accused and tried for conspiracy against the Absolutist rule of Emperor Leopold I Habsburg. Found guilty, execution of the conspirators took place at Wiener Neustadt on 30 April 1671. On the eve of his death, Petar wrote a famous goodbye letter in Croatian to his wife Katarina, beginning with the words “My dear heart …” After his death the huge Zrinski estates in Croatia were confiscated and plundered.  
The portrait shows Petar Zrinski dressed as a wealthy nobleman, with the Zrinski coat of arms in the upper left-hand corner. Painted for the monastery in Svetice near Karlovac, Croatia, this portrait together with the portrait of Emperor Leopold I, are by an unknown Pauline artist. Pairing up the two portraits – *Petar Zrinski* and *Emperor Leopold I* – suggests that both were produced before the conspiracy and trial, some time before 1670.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.short_description: A portrait of the Croat nobleman, Count Petar Zrinski, who excelled in battles against the Turks and was executed for treason by Emperor Leopold I.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.initial_owner: Gallery of Donors, Pauline monastery in Svetice
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.method_for_datation: A painted inscription at the bottom of the work states “*Monastery Szveticzensis fundationem 1627. factam, Comes / Petrus Zrinius ratificat 1640. 19 Iuny. Eidémq(ue) forum Ecclesiae / Vicinum imperpetuat 1646*”, indicating that the painting was for the Pauline monastery in Svetice, Croatia. Further confirmation of the date and origin of the work relies on documentation in the Museum inventory.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.obtention: Bought for the Museum from a private owner in 1964.

d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.name: Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, Pauline Chapel
d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.description:
The chapel has a Greek cross floorplan and a dome, similar to its 25 years older "twin", the Sistine Chapel. The iconographic program was ideated by the Oratorian Cesare Baronio, who readapted many early Christian and martyrial Roman churches according to the Counter-Reformation’s precepts. Entirely covered with precious marble slabs and columns, with stucco, fresco and marble decorations, the chapel saw the participation of the major protagonists of the Roman art scene between Mannerism and Baroque.  
Above the altar of the sacred icon, Stefano Maderno sculpted the bas-relief with Pope Liberius tracing the perimeter of the Marian basilica in the snow. The lunette above the altar was frescoed by Cavalier d’Arpino and depicts, on one side, St. Gregory Thaumaturgus’s vision of the Virgin and St. John the Evangelist, and on the other a crowd bitten by the serpent of heresy, the temple of God and His believers.  
The dome hosts the Assumption of the Virgin, a fresco by Ludovico Cardi, known as Cigoli. The moon placed under the feet of the Madonna was painted with great scientific accuracy on the basis of the telescope images provided by Galileo Galilei, a friend of the painter.  
In the lower circle, overlooked by the Virgin, the Apostles are visible, while in the upper circle there are angelic hosts playing musical instruments, singing and strewing flowers.  
At the top of the small roof lantern God is depicted, ready to welcome the Virgin into heaven.  
The pendentives of the dome were frescoed by Cavalier d’Arpino and show the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel. He also painted the altar arch with the holy bishops Ignatius, Theophilus, Irenaeus and Cyprian.  
On the sides of the chapel there are two funeral monuments: on the right that of Pope Clement VIII Aldobrandini, and on the left, that of Paul V. Both of them were sculpted by Silla da Viggiù.  
The side arches were frescoed by Guido Reni. Among the several saints that Reni painted, St. Dominic and St. Francis stand out for their dramatic force. Above the funeral monument to Paul V, Guido Reni painted the Eternal Father, too. The chapel’s exuberant decorations somewhat conceal the architectural structure designed by Flaminio Ponzio, thus becoming one of the first examples, together with the Sistine Chapel, of Baroque *horror vacui*.
d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.short_description: Dedicated by Paul V to the Assumption of the Virgin. The iconographical program was drawn up by the Oratorian Cesare Baronio. Example of interaction of the arts and application of the Counterreformation’s rules.
d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.bibliography: Barroero, L., “La basilica dal Cinquecento all'Ottocento”, in C. Pietrangeli (ed), *Santa Maria Maggiore a Roma,* Rome: Nardini, 1988.
d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.history:
Commissioned by Paul V immediately after his election, the chapel was created to offer a sumptuous architectural frame to the venerated, miraculous Marian icon known as *Salus Populi Romani,* which was, according to the tradition, painted by St. Luke the Evangelist, while probably a work of the early Christian age instead, and repainted around the 13th century.  
The Pauline Chapel, which mirrors the architecture of the opposite Sistine chapel, which had been commissioned by Sixtus V, cost about 230 *scudi,* an astronomical price for the time, which had to cover, in addition to the salaries of the several artistic workshops, also the purchase of the finest marbles, as well as expensive lapis lazuli used to frame the Marian icon. The consecration of the chapel took place in 1613, but the decoration was fully completed only in the following years.
d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.architects: Flaminio Ponzio (architect); Stefano Maderno; Silla da Viggiù; Giuseppe Cesari known as Cavalier d’Arpino; Guido Reni; Ludovico Cardi known as il Cigoli
d31c9a9c-95c3-5ec3-a947-b575b33572c7.author: Pier Paolo Racioppi

d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.name: *Anna Maria Victoria Jabornigg-Gamseneck*
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.description:
A portrait of a finely dressed and learned noblewoman in an ermine pelisse, she sits on a chair by a table on which are geometrical implements, several books and some sheets of paper.  
The painting is thought to be a portrait of Maria Victoria Jabornigg Gamsenegg, the first wife of Josip Ignac Sigismund Hilleprand-Prandau, son of Petar II Anton.  
Attributed to Ephraim Hochhauser who studied at the Vienna Academy and made his name painting portraits of the aristocracy, perhaps the identity of the sitter in this case is less important than the context. The woman holding compasses in her hand sits in front of sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and protractor. At the time, geometry was an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and seen as part of a good education. With a little freedom of thought, we might link these items with the laying out of the Baroque *parterre* garden in front of Valpovo Manor.  
The History Gallery of the Hungarian National Museum in Budapest has an identical portrait, which according to researchers represents Maria Christina the beloved daughter of Empress Maria Theresia, and attributed to the court painter Martin van Meytens who was a great favourite of the Empress. Since Petar II Hilleprand-Prandau was in the diplomatic service of the Austrian Court, it is possible that a portrait of the Empress's daughter found its way to Valpovo Manor.
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.short_description:
A portrait of a finely dressed and learned noblewoman, which according to the Prandau family archive, is a portrait of Anna Maria Victoria – the first wife of Josip Ignac – son of Petar II Anton.  
There is an identical portrait in the History Gallery of the Hungarian National Museum by Martin van Meytens, which according to researchers shows Maria Christina, daughter of Empress Maria Theresia.  
Perhaps the identity of the sitter in this case is less important than the context, for the woman holding compasses in her hand sits amidst sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and protractor. At the time, geometry was an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and seen as part of a good education. With a little freedom of thought, we might link these items with the laying out of the Baroque *parterre* garden in front of Valpovo Manor.
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.initial_owner: Valpovo, family of Baron Hilleprand-Prandau later of Count Normann-Ehrenfels
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.dates: Third quarter of the 18th century; about 1770

d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.name: *Portrait of Domenico Scarlatti*
d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.description:
Court Maestro to the exiled Polish queen Maria Kazimiera, and responsible for the Vatican's *Capella Giulia*, Domenico Scarlatti (1685–1757) was hired in 1714 as *Kappelmeister* by the Marquis of Fontes, Ambassador to King D. João V, at the Court of Pope Clement XI.  
Scarlatti's arrival in Portugal was a result of the high praise he had received from the King of Portugal's brother, Prince D. António who had attended one of his concerts in Rome. Scarlatti arrived in Portugal in around 1720 to become Princess Maria Barbara and Prince D. Jose's music teacher. Meanwhile the Pope had consented to the upgrade of the Royal Chapel to a Patriarchal Chapel and Scarlatti was invited to become *Kappelmeister* of the orchestra and choir of the Patriarchal Seminar Chapel.  
The Neapolitan Scarlatti's contribution to the Portuguese music scene was immense, he introduced Italian Opera, and the new musical and artistic patterns in vogue all over Europe at the time.  
In 1729 Scarlatti moved to Madrid to become once again Princess Maria Bárbara's music master, who by this time had married the Prince of Asturias, son of King Philip V and future King Philip VI of Spain. He remained in Spain until his death in 1757.  
Under the patronage of King D. João V, Domenico Scarlatti lived with his family in Spain where he enjoyed all the preconditions necessary to enhance his musical career and ensure his notoriety grew among his European musical peers.  
The art of portraiture peaked in the 18th century, fuelled by commissions from the European monarchs. Artists such as Louis Michel Van Loo, court painter to King Philip V of Spain (grandson of Louis XIV) between 1738 and 1752, or Jean Ranc (1674–1735) gained notoriety. The latter also painted the Portuguese Royal family following H. Rigaud.  
So it was that the Spanish artist Domingos António Velasco painted this portrait of Scarlatti in the Van Loo style in around 1739. Velasco depicts the maestro standing in front of an opulently painted curtain, his body twisted to the right and his hand resting on a wooden box. The light falls on the musician's face and hands, and he is dressed in a golden yellow and grey-blue ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious St James, a cognizance bestowed upon him one year previously by King D. João V, Grand-Master of the Order.
d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.short_description: *Kappelmeister* of the Patriarchal orchestra and choir, and music master to Princess Maria Barbara the daughter of the King D. João V and the Queen of Spain, this portrait of Domenico Scarlatti is by the Spanish painter Domingos António Velasco. The artist depicts Scarlatti dressed in a ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious Order of St. James, a cognizance bestowed upon him one year previously by King D. João V, Grand-Master of the Order.

d450789d-d8de-5381-91d6-952696e07e5e.name: *St. Catherine*
d450789d-d8de-5381-91d6-952696e07e5e.description:
This altarpiece painting represents a young St. Catherine half-kneeling on clouds and wearing a yellow and white dress with a red cloak. She has a crown on her head and holds a lily in her right hand. Beside her are some books and in front of her left knee is a sword. While the clouds surround her, angel heads look out from behind the clouds above her. The composition follows the traditional iconography of the subject.  
Xaver Ferenc (Francis) Falconer was one of the best known members of the Falconer family of artists, which according to tradition, originated from Scotland and settled in Buda at the end of the 18th century. Xaver Ferenc Falconer studied with his grandfather and another painter named Schultz, and became an independent master in 1761. After the early death of his father, the painter Polykarp Falconer, he studied painting with his stepfather János (John) Schultz, a painter from Brandenburg. In 1761 Falconer enrolled at Vienna's Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture (Academy of Fine Arts, Vienna). He was made a citizen of Buda in 1761, and in 1765 – along with his spouse (whom he married in 1763) – he bought a modest bourgeois house in the castle district of Buda. In 1794, their heirs sold the house and established a shop on the ground floor. Today this house is in the possession of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and serves as a guesthouse. From the altarpieces Falconer executed, only one is still *in situ* in Hungary, Szécsény. In the 1770s Falconer produced some signed altarpiece paintings for the cloisters of the Franciscan order in Croatia.
d450789d-d8de-5381-91d6-952696e07e5e.short_description: A Baroque altarpiece painting of St. Catherine from the Parish Church of the Viziváros (Watertown) in the district of Buda.

d4b21bad-0844-5f2e-b159-aec16bf2fb08.name: Palazzo Chigi
d4b21bad-0844-5f2e-b159-aec16bf2fb08.description:
Renovation of Palazzo Chigi was commissioned by the Chigi family following their acquisition of it in 1661. During renovation, the original fortified-palace aspect with repeating angular towers on all four sides was retained, while the façade connected to the Porta Napoletana on Via Appia remained simple, despite the addition of the portal and balustrade balcony.  
The interior is an almost unique example in the region of an ancient residence whose fixtures and fittings have been retained in full: the decorative frescos in the halls along with the extensive collection of paintings that include portraits, landscapes and allegories that represent many of the genres typical of country residences of the period. Gilt-leather wall hangings still adorn the walls, as does the sanguine used on the walls by Bernini to decorate the chapel; marble and terracotta busts of family members, the series of portraits of “Beautiful Women” and the cabinets designed for the pharmacy, are all still in situ. In recent years the top storey of the palace has been home to the interesting Roman Baroque Museum established by means of significant donations from the Lemme, Fagiolo and Laschena collections, and providing an exhaustive overview of Roman painting from 1600 to 1700, with masterpieces by Mattia Preti, Pietro da Cortona, Giacinto Brandi, Sebastiano Conca, Corrado Giaquinto, Pompeo Batoni, Domenico Corvi and many others. To the rear, the beautiful park leading to the shores of Lake Nemi—full of holm oak, ash and Turkey oak—is still inhabited by animals that constituted the family’s private hunting reserve, as was customary at the time.  
The palace was deliberately linked to the Church (see IT1 26) as the main defining element of the Piazza di Corte, an urban development intended by the Chigi family as the fulcrum of the routes through the residence—originally entirely in the lower part and therefore completely and symbolically dominated by the structure of the square—and between this and the surrounding area, crossed by the ancient Via Appia linking Rome and Naples. Today, both the monumental bridge built by Pius IX between 1846 and 1854 and the expansion of the town have, unfortunately, obscured the symbolic and dimensional links of palace and square, which was designed almost as a terrace for the palace, facing the town.
d4b21bad-0844-5f2e-b159-aec16bf2fb08.short_description: The palace is an almost unique example in the region of an ancient residence whose fixtures and fittings have been retained in full: the decorative frescos in the halls; the extensive collection of paintings; the gilt-leather wall hangings and the sanguine used on the walls by Bernini to decorate the chapel; the marble and terracotta busts of family members; the series of portraits of “Beautiful Women” and the cabinets designed for the pharmacy. Consequently, it was chosen by Luchino Visconti as the setting for his famous film *The Leopard*.

d4b21bad-0844-5f2e-b159-aec16bf2fb08.history: The palace was the stronghold of the Savelli family who converted it into a family residence. It was then acquired in 1661 during the papacy of Alexander VII Chigi (1655–67) by the Chigi family, an aristocratic family from Siena that moved to Rome in the 15th century. Among the Chigi family was Agostino Chigi, a banker and treasurer to the Church. It was the Chigi family that commissioned the renovation work presumably from Bernini and others. Palazzo Chigi remained in the Chigi family until 1998 when it was acquired by Ariccia Town Council and converted into a cultural centre and museum.

d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.name: Parish Church of St. Gordian and Epimachus
d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.description: The traditional spacious hall church is extended into a cross shape by two side chapels, the left side of which had already been attached to the previous building in 1719 along with the altar of the Cross. The altar of the Virgin Mary on the opposite side also originates from this setting, so that these two pieces, still architecturally designed late-Baroque examples, drastically contrast the heavily ornamentalised Rococo altars on the sides of the chancel arch in a stylistic way. Instead of stucco decoration, ceiling frescoes of illusory architecture seamlessly cover the vaults of the nave and chancel.
d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.short_description: In the Swabian village of Stöttwang, a highly educated parish priest, as the patron of a new parish church, carried out himself a programme of interior features. This is ambitious not only in its theological content but also in its medial arrangement, and therefore is extraordinary for a rural parish church. The impressive ceiling frescoes, with their eye-deceiving illusory architecture reveal above all an orientation towards Roman sacral Baroque.
d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.method_for_datation: Archival documents; Chronogram above the chancel arch from the year 1745
d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.bibliography:
Anonymous, *Stöttwang, Pfarrkirche St. Gordian und Epimachus* (Kirchenführer), Schongau: no date.  
Breuer, T., *Stadt und Landkreis Kaufbeuren* (Bayerische Kunstdenkmale), Munich: Deutscher Kunstverlag, 1960: 185–188.

d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.history: The local parish priest and dean Johann Martin Klein, a man of outstanding theological education and to whom the parish of Stöttwang near Kaufbeuren had been transferred in 1730, had a new parish church erected in 1744. Because the parish was incorporated Kempten prince-abbey, its building manager Josef Galler designed the church building; in addition, its court painter Franz Georg Herrmann provided the painting. The altar furnishing, largely still missing at the time of the consecration on 11 September 1746, was acquired in stages. The close relationship between Stöttwang and Kempten prince-abbey is also reflected in the patrocinium of the church: relics of St. Gordian and Epimachus, who suffered martyrdom in the 4th century AD, were transferred from Rome to Kempten on the orders of Queen Hildegard, a legendary Swabian wife of Charlemagne. In Kempten over the centuries, they found local veneration as patron saints.
d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.patrons: Dean Johann Martin Klein, Parish Priest at Stöttwang (officiated 1730–80)
d570267c-e68a-50b4-829b-748f9236fdc9.author: Peter Heinrich Jahn, Hanna Böhm

d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.name: *The Concert*
d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.description:
The painting, which was probably kept by the painter's family, is one of a series of Flemish works acquired in 1783 by Marcantonio Borghese. Gerrit van Honthorst, better known in Italy as Gherardo delle Notti, fitted in perfectly with the followers of Caravaggio in Rome, who revisited and reworked Merisi's favourite subjects, especially the secular themes. This piece, which dates from 1626–1630, apparently shows a simple musical theme, although in fact the composition hides a moral meaning.  
Typical of the art of the Counter-Reformation and particularly esteemed in the culture of the Netherlands, the artist's homeland, are themes related to allegories intended to express moral meanings. In this case, music, an excellent, virtuous, but also ephemeral art, is represented by an old woman who, in pointing to her toothless mouth, appears to be warning the three youths playing a concert of the fleetingness of youth and beauty.  
The subject also reveals the trick being played on the young man who, intent on singing, fails to realise that the maiden is taking his earring, with the complicity of the old woman, who is ready to slip it into her pocket. The theme of the trick is related to the allegorical evocation of the five senses: hearing through music, sight in expressive looks, taste through wine and food, touch by the gesture of the seductress, and smell through the nose, which the old woman appears to be pointing to. Special attention is paid to the table, where a basket of fruit is clearly visible. This element combines with the others in a sort of pastiche, the figurative motifs borrowed from famous Caravaggesque works, which also influenced the neutral choice of background.
d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.short_description: Gerrit Van Honthorst, called Gherardo delle Notti, absorbed the influence of Caravaggio during his stay in Italy (1610–1620). The subject, the composition, the still life on the table, the light falling on the left, all are quotations from Caravaggio's works.
d59e62bc-4bc3-5e41-b150-7cce9eb386c9.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

d6242828-53d8-51c8-a66d-cb1f54b10ff7.name: Ratkaj Palace
d6242828-53d8-51c8-a66d-cb1f54b10ff7.description: Inside the two-winged, two-storey palace, the lower, two-winged ground-floor buildings enclose the inner courtyard. The oldest part of the palace is the rear wing, constructed in the 16th century as a fortified grange. Renaissance features are still extant, manifested in the shape of the courtyard passage, which opens up on both floors with arcades; a similar model was repeated for the side-wing extension in the 17th century. The facade of the two-wing palace was painted with what at the time was a characteristic dark-grey graphite colour with white and yellow accents along the apertures, pillars and arcades and, as an expression of an increasingly high standard of living at the beginning of the 18th century, along the external façade of the side-wing. The addition of annexes for the sanitary facilities improves the architectural projection, articulated with dynamic stucco decorations. The last important architectural development was the addition of a ground-floor wing at the front. Opened up with a grand, central portal surmounted by a small turret, in a formal sense it marked the achievement of the Baroque aspiration for emphasising the central axis and the formation of deep spatial effects.
d6242828-53d8-51c8-a66d-cb1f54b10ff7.short_description: The Ratkaj complex in Miljana is one of the best preserved examples of a Baroque palace in northwest Croatia. It is a historically stratified complex, composed of a two-winged, two-storey building that closes-off a courtyard. The Baroque fondness for the scenic manifests in the disposition of the higher residential wings with porticoes, which open up with arcades and lower floor utility buildings accented with a tower. The main value of the palace consists in the Early Baroque paintings on the façade and the Rococo frescoes of the interior.
d6242828-53d8-51c8-a66d-cb1f54b10ff7.bibliography:

d6242828-53d8-51c8-a66d-cb1f54b10ff7.history: The palace, of which the first building phase dates from the 16th and 17th centuries, was owned by the noble Ratkaj family until the end of the 18th century (1793), during which time the owners undertook several important reconstructions and enlargements of the complex and through which the current spatial organisation took shape.
d6242828-53d8-51c8-a66d-cb1f54b10ff7.architects: Architect unknown; painter: Anton Joseph (Jožef) Lerchinger (Lerhinger) (c. 1720–after 1787)

d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.name: *Judith and Holofernes*
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.description:
This carved panel depicting *Judith and Holofernes* in high relief is part of pair, the other panel is an image of *Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well*.  
During the Baroque era, Northern Europe experienced a revival of collecting precious ivory objects. The anonymous artist is very skilled in ivory carving technique and shows a deep knowledge of Italian classicism and baroque sculpture. The scene is well planned showing Judith with the sword in her hand, the beheaded body of Holofernes and an old servant holding the head of Holofernes. An angel is in the background holding a curtain. Clarity, narrative, theatricality and elegance join together to form a high quality work of art. These two bas-relieves have been frequently attributed to the French sculptor Pierre Puget; if this is correct, these panels are the only surviving ivory works of his.
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.short_description:
This carved panel depicting *Judith and Holofernes* in high relief is part of a pair, its pendant showing *Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well*.  
In the seventeenth-century there was a revival in collecting precious carved ivory objects, especially in northern Europe. Clear and efficacious narrative, theatricality and elegance combine in this high quality piece which has all the main features of late seventeenth-century art.
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.dates: Third quarter of the seventeenth century
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.method_for_datation: The carving is dated to around the second half of the seventeenth-century due to stylistic evidence.
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.obtention: Petronio Matteucci, a professor of astronomy in Bologna University and assistant to the Specola donated both panels to the University Collections in 1740. With the creation of the Museo Civico di Bologna (1871), the two panels were given to the Municipality and exhibited in room XV in the new museum. In 1985 they became part of the ivory collection of the Museo Civico Medievale.

d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.name: *The Gourmet*
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.description:
Jacob van Schuppen studied painting with his father – Pierre Louis van Schuppen a painter and engraver in Antwerp – and his uncle, Nicolas Largillière, one of the period's most respected portrait painters. This beginning determined both his career and his preferred genre. Van Schuppen worked both in Paris and at the Lorraine princely court in Luneville as a portrait painter. In 1705, he became a member of the Paris Academy, arriving in Vienna in 1716 as a successful and notable portraitist in the service of Prince Eugene of Savoy. Having been settled in the imperial city for only a short time, he became court painter in 1723. In 1725, he approached the emperor with a plan for a French-style art academy, which he directed from 1726. Vienna's Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture (Academy of Fine Arts Vienna) was unprecedented in Central Europe and remained the most important institution of its kind in the German-speaking territories. As a painter, van Schuppen was primarily an excellent portraitist. His large-size portraits, representing the aristocracy and contemporary writers and artists, effectively reflect the personality and character of the sitters.  
*The Gourmet*, although for a long time registered as a work of a German master, is an excellent example of van Schuppen's art, holding the characteristic features of his work. Like his other paintings, the motifs of both genre painting and still life are present.  
The objective approach of Dutch and Flemish art, fine colouring and French elegance come together in this painting; the basic motif – a man uplifting his glass to demonstrate his aspirations in seeking happiness in drinking and smoking: the minor pleasures of life – is a favourite and frequent characteristic of 17th-century painters. Although known primarily as a portraitist, van Schuppen nevertheless approached genre painting in a similar way, as can be seen in this painting and others in Hungarian collections.
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.short_description: Jacob van Schuppen, from the Netherlands, was a pupil of his uncle Nicolas Largilliere. From 1716 he lived in Vienna, and from 1726 directed the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, breathing new life into the institution, which was renamed the Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture. *The Gourmet*, showing a man enjoying the finer things of life, is both a portrait and a genre painting.
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.obtention: Initially from the Esterházy Collection in Pottendorf, in 1867 Endre Pánthy acquired the painting. From 1906, it was in the Lyceum school’s substantial collection in Eger as part of the Endre Pánthy legacy. It was then transferred to the Dobó István Castle Museum in Eger.

d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.name: *Ships in a Harbour*
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.description: A finely executed Baroque painting of a harbour with ships and throngs of people on the shore. The composition is a rare example of a small size genre piece, which may have been part of a series. The execution of the painting is finely detailed, and contrary to its small size, the work is of high quality. This is an unusual representation within the iconography of this type of picture. Scenes of everyday life became common in the 17th and 18th centuries, and depictions of the “low-life” of peasants and the “high-life” of the aristocracy, featuring fashionably dressed figures in different scenes were also common. The popularity of seascapes and maritime pictures spread to Hungary by way of Flemish and Dutch painting. Small seascapes (*zeekens*) were a very popular theme representing – like this painting – imaginary views of exotic ports.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.short_description: A finely executed Baroque genre painting of a harbour with ships and throngs of people on the shore. Because of these and other features, the painting represents a rare example among Baroque seascapes.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.obtention: From the bequest of Count Jenő Zichy in 1903.

d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.name: *The Hunt of Diana*
d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.description:
The work was commissioned from Domenichino by his patron, Cardinal Pietro Aldrobrandini. However, it came into the possession of Cardinal Scipione Borghese when he took it by force from the artist's study, depriving the original client, a nephew of Clement VIII (1592–1605), his traditional rival. The subject is inspired by a passage from Virgil's *Aeneid* (canto V) that describes the archery competition between Aeneas' friends: aiming at a dove tied to a post, the first archer hits the post; the second cuts the ribbon holding the bird; the third misses and the fourth shoots regardless to demonstrate his skill, and his arrow bursts into flames and ends up in the clouds. The sequence is transposed into the domain of nymph disciples of Diana, the goddess of hunting, an idyllic and luminous environment that represents the mythical Arcadia. The literary metaphors derive from the cultured Domenichino's involvement with G. B. Agucchi, secretary to the cardinal and adviser to the painter in the conception of the work.  
In the representation of the nymphs' play, the painter is attempting to paint the poetic and chronological narration of the facts, lifting pictorial art above poetic art and, in general dissolving the limit traditionally placed on different art forms; a topic that was widely discussed in the Baroque period.  
The pose and the expression of the “affections” (feelings) on the faces help to explain the succession of events, while the unbridled play is contained in a classical equilibrium. The nymph holding the greyhound shows us what will happen to the two male figures hidden amongst the bushes on the right-hand side of the canvas.  
According to the myth, Diana's terrible rage was unleashed against the hunter Actaeon who, having seen her bathing, was turned into a stag and devoured by his own dogs. One of the nymphs immersed in the water, tender and sensual, gazes at the viewer and links the internal and external spaces of the painting; another attempt to overcome limitations, in this instance spatial, that is typical of Baroque art.
d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.short_description:
The canvas was painted for Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, nephew of the preceding Pope Clement VIII, who had a strong dislike for the Borghese family. However, Cardinal Scipione wanted the painting for himself and had it forcibly removed from the artist's studio, imprisoning the artist for several days.  
In this painting Domenichino synthesises the colour of Bolognese painting, Roman drawings and Leonardo's theories on aerial perspective.
d774f40f-b0fd-5b12-b1f9-f0ce525c936c.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.name: *Feast at the House of Simon the Pharisee*
d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.description:
The work was initially attributed to Veronese, a hypothesis that, although incorrect, successfully identifies the inspirations of the artist, who, in his early twenties trained in Venice.  
In the lagoon city, the painter was able to study the work of Tiziano, Veronese and Tintoretto, as well as Bassano and Schiavone, reworking the characters of Venetian painting through his strictly Ferraran training.  
The scene develops within an open loggia framed by columns, two of which appear to be inspired by the columns of Trajan and Antoninus. The representation shows a well known story from the Gospel of St. Luke (7, 36–50) which tells of a feast at the house of Simon, a Pharisee, who believed that he had fulfilled all his duties to God and that, therefore, he had the right to a tranquil, comfortable life. The feast is interrupted by the sinner Magdalene, who shocks those present by kissing Christ's feet, washing them with her tears and sprinkling them with precious scented oils.  
The episode highlights divine mercy for sinners who demonstrate humble and sincere penitence. Arranged diagonally around the table, the figures are grouped into small genre scenes characterised by lively expressions, inspired by the style of Bassano. The sky in the background, crossed by intense strips of green, fades into the distant landscape. The fulcrum of the scene has been shifted to the left-hand side of the painting where Magdalene, the jar of ointment at her feet and her hair untied, turns her head in a silent dialogue with Christ.  
The intense colours, lively gestures and unusual perspective are indicative of the taste that precluded the scenic representations of the Baroque period.
d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.short_description: The historical reference refers to the Gospel of St. Luke: Mary Magdalene who was in the house of Simon during a banquet. Kneeling at the feet of Christ with her usual attribute, a jar of ointment, she washes His feet and dries them with her long hair. The protagonists of the scene are not in the central part of the composition, but on the left-hand side that becomes the fulcrum for the narrative.
d78b8b3a-ee36-596b-9334-2db393fb9dc7.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

d7b85ecb-f845-5c61-ae6f-c9b3b77e3a2c.name: Church of São Roque
d7b85ecb-f845-5c61-ae6f-c9b3b77e3a2c.description:
The church, a simple and sober construction in the mannerist style, complies with the doctrines of the Society of Jesus. The interior comprises a nave and eight side chapels, the decoration of which took place between the second half of the 16th century and the first half of the 18th century. Worth noting is the amazing contrast between the Mannerist style and the more elaborate decoration of the Baroque period. The main façade of the church is very sober: symmetrical, it has two floors, the lower one with three doors, the lateral ones surmounted by two small windows, and the upper floor with three windows. A triangular pediment with an eye-window completes the top of the façade as a result of some works that were partially undertaken after the earthquake of 1755.  
The Chapel of Our Lady of the Doctrine is a typical example of Portuguese Baroque decoration, the ceiling and side walls covered with gilt woodwork. The side walls hold some relics offered to the church by D. João de Borja – an ambassador of King Filipe II at the Imperial Court of Rudolf II in Prague – in 1588. Most of the relics are kept inside two altars situated on either side of the main chapel; it is a most remarkable collection second only to that at the Escorial in Spain.  
The most imposing of all chapels, however, is the one dedicated to St. John the Baptist. It was commissioned from Rome by King João V in 1740. Construction began in 1742, carried out by a team of high profile artists under the supervision of the architects, Luigi Vanvitelli and Nicola Salvi. An important collection of liturgical objects was produced at the same time as the interior decoration: gold-embroidered vestments, several metal objects – candleholders, reliquaries and crucifixes – and also books for the Mass. The painted ceilings of the church and the sacristy are also remarkable.
d7b85ecb-f845-5c61-ae6f-c9b3b77e3a2c.short_description: The church, a simple and sober construction in the Mannerist style, complies with the doctrines of the Society of Jesus. The interior comprises a nave and eight side chapels, which were decorated between the second half of the 16th century and the first half of the 18th century. A keynote feature is the amazing contrast between the Mannerist style and the more elaborate decoration of the Baroque period. The main façade of the church is very sober. A triangular pediment with an eye-window completes the top of the façade as a result of some works that were partially undertaken after the earthquake of 1755, and again at the beginning of the 20th century. The painted ceiling of the church, dating to the 16th and 17th centuries, is also notable. Lastly, in the sacristy, there is a large chest of drawers from the 17th century. On its wooden backboard are 20 paintings relating to the Life of St. Francis Xavier.
d7b85ecb-f845-5c61-ae6f-c9b3b77e3a2c.method_for_datation: Historical documents, inscriptions and stylistic analysis.

d7b85ecb-f845-5c61-ae6f-c9b3b77e3a2c.history:
The Church of São Roque was built in the second half of the 16th century to meet the demands of priests of the Society of Jesus who in 1540 (during the reign of João III; King of Portugal 1521–1557) arrived in Lisbon to preach. A chapel dedicated to the devotion of São Roque formerly stood on the site. This chapel had been commissioned by King Manuel I (1495–1521) to house a relic of the saint, protector of sufferers of the plague. The Society of Jesus received the chapel in 1553, and the first enlargement of the building was undertaken in 1555.  
João III had initially intended to build a monumental building with three naves but the Society of Jesus opposed the design in accordance with the principles of the Catholic Refor­mation, which emphasised both simplicity and functionality in church layouts. The new design changed the orientation of the building from east-west to north-south, and increased its length. In 1565 the church was enlarged for a second time according to plans brought from Rome. These plans maintained the principle of a single nave. The completion of the church took place during the reign of Philip I of Portugal (Philip II of Spain; 1580–1598). After the expulsion of the Jesuits from Portugal in 1759, São Roque Church and annexed residences were given to the Santa Casa da Misericórdia de Lisboa by a Royal Charter issued on 8 February 1768.

d84145a7-19e4-5c52-b07d-7b34e48ec61a.name: Benedictine Abbey Church of St. Dionysius and Juliana, former Premonstratensian abbey church
d84145a7-19e4-5c52-b07d-7b34e48ec61a.description: The abbey church is integrated co-axially into the symmetrically designed monastery complex. Its simple appearance gives no indication of the magnificent Rococo interior furnishings and decorations . The single nave of the wall-pillar church is rhythmised by a large centralised bay and two connecting bays facing east and west respectively. The staggered arrangement of the bays creates a different weight of the spatial sections according to their liturgical function; as well as a stage-like scenography that funnels the eye towards the choir. These features are not a given in accordance with a wall-pillar church. Johann Baptist Zimmermann’s soulfully accentuated stucco of rocaille ornaments and strapwork displays a subtle colouring and is limited to the vaults, just like the frescoes. The ceiling frescoes depict the glorification of the founder of the order, Norbert von Xanten, and also the founding of Schäftlarn. The collaboration of prominent Munich court artists created a consistently elegant, courtly influenced overall impression that distinguishes the Abbey Church of Schäftlarn from other Baroque ecclesiastical buildings from the 18th century in Bavaria.
d84145a7-19e4-5c52-b07d-7b34e48ec61a.short_description: The church of the former Premonstratensian Abbey in Schäftlarn is situated beautifully in the Isar Valley and is one of the most outstanding abbey churches of the Late Baroque in Bavaria. A vast number of famous artists in the vicinity of the Munich Court contributed to the planning, building, and interior design of the scenographically configured ecclesiastical building. The elegant courtly embellishments of the church interior, with the stucco work of court stuccoer, Johann Baptist Zimmermann, and the work of court sculptor, Johann Baptist Straub, are some of the most remarkable achievements of their time.

d84145a7-19e4-5c52-b07d-7b34e48ec61a.history: Founded in 762 by Benedictine monks, the monastery was taken over by the Premonstratensian Order between 1140 and 1806. Today, the abbey is once again administered by the Benedictine Order. In 1702, Giovanni Antonio Viscardi received the order to build a new monastery complex that should include the old Gothic church. In this process, the old steeple that had collapsed in 1710 was rebuilt. Because of the dilapidation of the old abbey church, construction of a new one began in 1733 under the supervision of the Munich Court Architect, François de Cuvilliés the Elder. After the construction was halted for a time, Johann Baptist Gunetzrhainer and Johann Michael Fischer continued the building in 1751. Stucco and frescoes were designed by court stuccoer, Johann Baptist Zimmermann, between 1754–56; whereas the altars, chancel, and sculptural work — including the bench end  carvings — were crafted by court sculptor Johann Baptist Straub between 1755–64.

da7ffcbe-213c-5a62-86d2-2fcfc157d79f.name: Ráday Mansion
da7ffcbe-213c-5a62-86d2-2fcfc157d79f.description:
Today the mansion is a two-storey U-shaped building, the side-wings of which surround a small courtyard. During alterations carried out under the auspices of Gedeon Ráday, parts of the old building were re-used. The central risalit of the main façade stands out emphasised by two alettes, an embossed gable and the cupola. The gate is framed by four pillars, above which the beautiful wrought-iron balcony is shouldered by corbels decorated with volutes. The side risalits only stand proud of the wall to a slight degree, completed with triangular tympana, which probably in the past bore coats of arms.  
There are significant sequences of wall paintings in two rooms on the ground floor. The main library is divided by four red marble columns into nine bays, on which painted allegorical figures of the Sciences appear. Pallas Athene and the Triumph of Science can be seen in the middle, surrounded by History, Philosophy, Mathematics, Theology, Law, Medicine, Grammar, Poetics and Rhetoric. On the vault of the small library the Dionysiac Poet, Arion, appears riding a dolphin and playing the lute. This composition reflects an engraving from Bernard Pickart's *Le Temple des Muses* (Amsterdam, 1733). The side-wall pictures also portray the power of Music and Poetry represented by scenes from the Life of Orpheus.  
Besides the main library, the 12,000–15,000-volume book collection (that consisted of 6,500 literary works) of Gedeon Ráday, filled more than five rooms in the mansion. The collection, and the policy by which Count Ráday selected books for it, was unique in the era: encyclopaedic in its remit, it aimed to own works from all branches of the natural sciences, humanities and literature. It included works in Hungarian, French literature of the Enlightenment and Protestant theology. With the systematisation of the collection based on the expertise of Count Ráday, the collection emerged as one of the most important and unique in Hungary; in all of Europe among private libraries.        
The wall paintings in the ceremonial hall on the upper floor (1766) follow a unique iconographic programme mentioned both by Kazinczy and Gedeon Ráday in the journal entitled *Orpheus* of 1790. The pictures were modelled on Pickart's aforementioned work and Ovid's *Metamorphoses* (Amsterdam, 1732) illustrated by Pickart and Philipp v. Gunst.  
The ceiling fresco in the ceremonial hall, which was ruined in 1825, illustrated the Fall of Phaeton; thematically linked are two of the *grisaille* paintings on the side walls depicting two scenes from the Life and Death of Phaeton. These pictures, along with the other *grisaille*s depicting scenes from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* completed with Gedeon Ráday's own Hungarian hexametric commentaries, transmit a homogeneous pictorial message of the idea of Gedeon Ráday.  
In the “picture room facing the courtyard” immediately next to the ceremonial hall, images of Habsburg monarchs copied from coins reveal their patron's taste. **The Hercules Room in the west wing is also worthy of mention, where wall paintings illustrating the Labours of Hercules can be seen, again based on Pickart's engravings.**
da7ffcbe-213c-5a62-86d2-2fcfc157d79f.short_description: Ráday Mansion in Pécel is a fine example of Hungarian 18th-century gentry-class architecture. Its significance lays not so much in the architectural form of the building – which mirrors the owner's social status – but in the unique intellectual character of the Protestant Ráday family that is revealed in the interior decoration. The extensive library of Gedeon Ráday I, the son of Pál Gedeon I, was extraordinary for its time, yet he coupled his learnedness with artistic sensitivity; for instance he applied his own poems to certain murals in the mansion. The mansion of the “holy old man”, as Hungarian language-reformer Ferenc Kazinczy called him, was the apogee of the cultural taste of the day.
da7ffcbe-213c-5a62-86d2-2fcfc157d79f.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual resources, as well as stylistic and wall investigations and research and archaeological excavations.

Garas, K., *Magyarországi festészet a 18. században (Painting in Hungary in the 18th century)*, Budapest, 1955, pp. 126–127.

Segesváry, V., *The History of a Private Library in 18th Century Hungary*, Budapest, 2007.
da7ffcbe-213c-5a62-86d2-2fcfc157d79f.history:
The first multi-winged mansion in Pécel was built by Pál Ráday I between 1722 and 1730. The alterations that led to the mansion's present form (1755–66; 1766–1774) are associated with his son, Gedeon Ráday I, and were inspired by the “*Grassalkovich* style” of Gödöllő Palace.  Apart from stylistic similarities, these two buildings are also connected through their architects: András Mayerhoffer designed Gödöllő Palace, while his son, János Mayerhoffer, is thought to have designed Pécel Mansion possibly with his father's help. The murals in the two libraries were painted by Mátyás Schervitz between 1763 and 1766; Schervitz was still working there in 1770, probably in one of the larger rooms. However, the decayed ceiling mural, as well as the *grisaille* pictures (of which there were originally 16), are the works of an unknown artist from Pozsony (Bratislava). The Czech painter, Johann Nepomuk Schöpf, was also known to have worked in Pécel. Several stoves, made by local and foreign craftsmen, were set on the premises.  
The bookshelves were a unique part of the interior decoration, as was the Ráday Gallery with its well-known collection of Hungarian portraits, which was destroyed by fire in 1825. The Ráday family's collection of paintings, built up in the 18th century, was sold by the family to Count Antal Brunswick and was auctioned in Wien, together with other precious works of art belonging to the Brunsvik family, in 1902.  
After many attempts to sell the contents of the library following the death of Count Gedeon Ráday the library's founder, the family successfully sold the contents of the library and some paintings to the Danubian District of the Hungarian Reformed Church in 1861. The Ráday Collections of the Danubian District of The Hungarian Reformed Church contains three departments: the Library, Archive and Museum, which today, with their continuously growing collection from 1861, is open for research and public visits.  
Today Ráday Mansion is managed by the National Trust of Monuments for Hungary.
