f3e4d209-2bec-5851-8ab2-7247da1e8c09.name: *Sepolcro del Giovedì Santo*
f3e4d209-2bec-5851-8ab2-7247da1e8c09.description: This etching documents the main installation created by the sculptors Angelo and Domenico Piò in the church of the Holy Saviour in Bologna. Antonio Cartolari drew the engines, Petronio Nanni built them, Angelo Sarti was the painter and Marco Montanari the scenographer. It was a tradition to keep a drawn memory of ephemera built during the Holy Week in one of the three churches chosen each year among the 60 selected in the diocese of Bologna for this celebration This was a practice created by cardinal Gabriele Paleotti, that took shape in the eighteenth-century, with sumptuous and solemn liturgies. On the Holy Thursday the Catholic Church celebrated the institution of the Eucharist with the Last supper. The host was taken from the tabernacle and put in the Repository, called the Sepulchre, to commemorate the death of Christ. The repository was an installation built to emphasise the tabernacle holding the holy Eucharist. This etching was part of a booklet, helping the faithful to meditate over the Passion and Resurrection of Christ. The analytical description of the sumptuous installation involving the whole church was made in order to preserve the memory of a work created to last only few days.  The work was made to touch the faithful hearts and at the same time to instruct them about the core of the Catholic faith, thus helping them to follow in the right behaviour preached by the Church. On the altar stand the allegories of Holy Grace, Religion, Faith and Fortitude, defeating the devil. On the cartouche we read the words of St. Paul: “Gratia Dei Salvatoris nostri” “Thanks to the Lord our Saviour” (Tit. II. 11). The rest of the church was uniform, thanks to six installations like this one. All the figures were painted in white to convey the idea of marble, while the architectural details, standing inside niches covered with red and gold material, were made to look like travertine. The spirit animating the whole installation reflected the rhetoric and the ostentation of the age.
f3e4d209-2bec-5851-8ab2-7247da1e8c09.short_description: Among the most significant documented ephemera built in the baroque age are the so-called sepolcri (“sepulchres”). This is an effective example. A group of sculptors, scenographers, sceneshifters, architects and painters erected them in churches during the three days before Easter.
f3e4d209-2bec-5851-8ab2-7247da1e8c09.provenance: This print is part of the booklet *Explanation of the Holy Sepulchre of the Redeemer exposed to the faithfuls piety...*, In Bologna, printing house of St. Thomas Aquinas, 1764

f4070107-bd84-5299-8132-72ae7c8a76e8.name: *Portrait of Felice Zacchia Rondanini*
f4070107-bd84-5299-8132-72ae7c8a76e8.description:
Domenico Guidi, nephew of the sculptor Giuliano Finelli, with whom he worked in Naples (1639–49), moved to the workshops of Algardi in Rome in 1649. He stayed there until the death of his master, from whom he learned the classicism that is a fundamental part of his style, although he was not as skilled in its execution.  
The bust was acquired by the Italian state from an antique market in 1907. It was initially attributed to the Berninian school on account of the elliptical shape enclosing the female figure and the “unfinished” back, a trait peculiar to Bernini on unseen surfaces. It was later attributed to 17th- and 18th-century sculptors (such as Bracci on account of the stylistic analogies with the sculptor's bust of Clement XII in the Borghese collection). It was finally attributed to Guidi, who was summoned by Bernini in 1668 to decorate the Ponte Sant'Angelo, although his style was more classical and less elaborate in form.  
The woman is probably Felice Zacchia Rondanini, daughter of Laudivio Zacchia who, once widowed, gave his life to religion and was made a cardinal in 1626. Algardi made a portrait of the father, having already made several busts for the Rondanini family. For his part, Guidi was responsible for the Rondanini tomb in S. Maria del Popolo, Rome in 1657. In 1683, in the same church, he sculpted the funerary monument to Vincenza Danesi, who some scholars connect to the Borghese portrait, although there is no documentation to support the theory. A ring is fixed under the cloak, which suggests it was originally intended to be placed in a niche, and the measurements coincide with the anchor points of the Danesi monument.  
The old lady wears a large veil forming a convex shape, on which shadows accentuate the face in the foreground, which is struck by light. The detail on the face is particularly interesting, especially the deep lines on the face and neck and the wart on the right cheek, emphasising the realism of the portrait.  
Guidi was so well regarded by the French for his classicism that by the end of his career he was a synonym for French taste. Nonetheless, a sculptural group made for Louis XIV failed to please the king and it ended up in the same place as Bernini's: the gardens of Versailles.
f4070107-bd84-5299-8132-72ae7c8a76e8.short_description:
A portrait of an old lady who wears a veil. The detail on the face is particularly interesting, especially the deep lines on the face and neck and the wart on the right cheek, emphasising the realism of the portrait.  
Guidi produced a few works for Bernini (such as the *Angel with a Lance* on Ponte Sant'Angelo) most of his collaborative work was, however, with Algardi.

f44c2151-d639-5889-a76b-b8712c9107ad.name: Palazzo Marchi Codronchi
f44c2151-d639-5889-a76b-b8712c9107ad.description: The building, with its imposing façade on via San Pier Grisologo, looks as continual and compact whole framing the austere doorway. Note the entablature with its horsehead corbels. To late to take the picture In the 18th century the great Renaissance rooms were subdivided into smaller ones. The Main Hall on the first floor is celebrated for its monumental fireplace and ceiling decoration in a great oval framing.
f44c2151-d639-5889-a76b-b8712c9107ad.short_description: Palazzo Codronchi Marchi is an imposing sixteenth-century building in the town centre. The vault of the hall of honour on the first floor is decorated with a mythological fresco. This decoration reminds the fresco by Canuti in the hall of honour of Palazzo Pepoli Campogrande in Bologna where he painted the same subject.
f44c2151-d639-5889-a76b-b8712c9107ad.bibliography: Guadalupi, G., Buscaroli, B. and Varni, A., *Imola, nella storia, nell'arte, nel lavoro*, Villanova di Castenaso (BO), 2006, p. 30
f44c2151-d639-5889-a76b-b8712c9107ad.history: The building dates to the 16th century but in the following years the inside was heavily refurbished. Today Palazzo Codronchi houses offices and private apartements and is sometimes used for ceremonies and rehersals.

f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.name: *Martyrdom of St. Januarius* (?)
f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.description:
The canvas was acquired by Camillo Borghese in 1818. Critics do not agree on the attribution, although it is acknowledged as clearly belonging to the culture of Southern Italian Baroque. The painting has been attributed to Cesare Fracanzano, a Puglian artist who first trained with Ribera and was later influenced by the artistic currents inspired by Van Dyke. Other scholars have suggested that the work is by a follower of Francesco Fracanzano, the brother of Cesare.  
Even the identity of the subject, who is undoubtedly a martyr, is not known for certain. Some scholars see the bishop-saint, one of the Fathers of the Church, as Ignatius of Antioch, the third largest and important city in the Mediterranean. The martyr was imprisoned by Emperor Trajan (96–117), who took him to Rome and had him killed by wild animals. In his “Letters”, he was the first person to use the adjective “Catholic” or “Universal” regarding the Church.  
The iconography of the saint killed by wild animals is also consistent with the hagiographic account of St. Januarius, Bishop of Benevento, who during the reign of Diocletian (284–305) was condemned to death and tortured on several occasions. Although he escaped unharmed from the wild animals, he was finally decapitated at Solfatara.  
The work is characterised by very dramatic gestures, accompanied by the piteous face of the saint. The artist took care to render in minute detail the lines of the face, the hands marked with age, and the emaciated body rent by the teeth of the wild beasts. The dappled fur and facial features of the animals are picked out in an almost exotic style. The colour of the fine cape, now in shreds, is striking and the elegance of the cloth of blue silk and gold is sumptuously rendered.
f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.short_description: Ignatius of Antioch – who inspired another Ignatius, the founder of the Jesuits – is perhaps portrayed here at the time of his martyrdom, killed by wild animals. Ignatius, one of the Fathers of the Church wrote seven “Letters” for the first time in which appear the terms “Catholic Church” and “Christianity”. It could also be the iconography of St. Januarius who was similarly killed by wild animals. The painting is characterised by an extreme theatricality of gestures.
f4692372-1200-55f7-94fd-a3eb2c1d5192.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.name: *Conversion of St. Paul* Altarpiece
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.description:
A Rococo type of *reredos* (retable) with ornamental pilasters instead of columns, and a wealth of Rococo ornamentation in compact form. At the centre is the *Conversion of St. Paul*, flanked by two female saints without attributes. Two angels kneel at the corners of the cornice. The central, upper section of the altarpiece holds the coat of arms of the Halper-Sigetski family.  
Initially, the altarpiece stood in St. Mark's Church in Zagreb, near the triumphal arch. Like most altarpieces in the church, this one was commissioned by a particular guild, the boot-makers' guild. Its production was part funded by a donation from Anna Gerlichich in 1760, as an inscription on the altarpiece details.  
The altarpiece is by an accomplished master, showing a high level of design and technical skill. The influence of Vid Königer (one of the greatest Styrian sculptors of the second half of the 18th century) is apparent, seen in the female saints in particular.  
During restoration of St Mark's at the end of the 19th century, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, at that time owned by Baron Halper-Sigetski, who placed his baronial arms on it.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.short_description:
A richly carved Rococo altarpiece: two saints stand either side of twisted pilasters and two angels decorate the attic, while the central scene of the *Conversion of St Paul* is in high relief.  
Commissioned for St Mark's Church by the boot-makers' guild in 1760, it was part-funded by a donation from Anna Gerlichich, as an inscription on the altarpiece details.  
During restoration of the church at the end of the 19th century, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, at that time owned by Baron Halper-Sigetski, who placed his baronial arms on it.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.dimensions: H: 226 cm; w: 258 cm; depth 70 cm
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.method_for_datation:
By stylistic analysis and research.  
During restoration and conservation work an older painted layer was discovered under the coat of arms revealing letters next to the frame and the year: "S. D. M. ANNA SAN(C) NATA DE GERLICHISCH 1760". Anna Gerličić, whose name appears on the coat of arms, probably sponsored some of the work for this altarpiece, such as the gilding.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.provenance: Boot-Makers’ Guild altarpiece, Church of St. Mark, Zagreb
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.obtention: During restoration of St. Mark’s Church by architects Schmidt and Bollé (1876–1882), in 1880, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of the former Patačić Manor in Zajezda. It is probable that the coat of arms of the Halper-Sigetski family was applied to the altarpiece while at Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, from where it was transferred to Zagreb.

f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.name: *Two Bookcase Doors Depicting Shelves with Music Books*
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.description: This extraordinary still life is formed by two paintings depicting the shelves of a bookcase. Music books are casually displayed vertically and horizontally. The books are depicted tidy and dense on the upper level and on the lower levels they are untidy, including books laying down. On the lower shelves there are several writing devices: two pen dryers, an inkstand, a bottle of ink, and a bunch of goose-quills. The original provenance of this painting is uncertain: the first documented information is in 1801 when it was moved from the monastery of St Francis to the Liceo Musicale. For a long time, Father Giovanni Battista Martini was thought to be the patron of this painting. He was a great scholar, specialist in contrappunto, and one of the most significant personalities of XVIII century music. Recent studies (A. Mazza in *Le stanze della Musica*) show that the paintings were probably intended as a present for Father Martini, who was younger than the painter. From a careful analysis the inscriptions on the book bindings appear to be posterior to the date attributed to the painting, perhaps to adapt it to the musical culture of a new owner.
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.short_description: This extraordinary still life is formed by two paintings depicting the shelves of a bookcase with music books casually displayed vertically and horizontally. The books are tidy and dense on the upper level, untidy, and in some cases lying down on the lower shelves. On the lower shelves there are several writing devices: two pen dryers, an inkstand, a bottle of ink, and a bunch of goose-quills.
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.holder: Museo Internazionale e Biblioteca della Musica
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.dimensions: Left door 165,5 x 78 cm; right door 165,5 x 75,5 cm
f60adefb-a63f-5390-8b0c-fc7edae265bc.obtention: The painting was part of the collection of Father Martini. It was moved along with his books after the death of his successor, Father Mattei, who saved this precious heritage from the Napoleonic confiscations. In 1801 the collections – donated to the municipality of Bologna – were moved to the suppressed monastery of St. James the Great. From 1804, this was the new Liceo Musicale of Bologna.

f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.name: *Apotheosis of King Saint Ladislaus*
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.alternate_name: Oil sketch for the high altar in the Primatial Palace at Pozsony (Bratislava)
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.description:
This sketch (*bozzetto*) in oil on copperplate was made for the high altar in the chapel of the archbishop's palace in Pozsony (Bratislava), built by Melchior Hefele. The chapel constitutes the last remaining example of fine Late Baroque art associated with the cult of St. Ladislaus in Hungary. The dome fresco, painted in the same year by Franz Anton Maulbertsch, represents the king striking water out of rock. The artist's intention was to revive the memory of the ruler who alleviated the thirst of his people by performing a miracle. The fresco shows the king on horseback as he performs the miracle, while in the altarpiece painting he is ascending to heaven. According to a legend current at the time, the king arranged for a portrait of Our Lady of Hungary, the Virgin Mary, *Patrona Hungariae*, to be painted on his battle flags. Thus, the white flag unfurling above his head bears the inscription “*S. Maria Mater Patrona Regni*” with an image of the Virgin and the Infant Jesus, much as if the flag was intended as a substitute for a more traditional celestial appearance. In other parts of the painting, St. Ladislaus is offering his crown together with the coronation regalia and the battleaxe, the latter being the king's usual attribute.  
Adreas Zallinger worked in Pozsony (Bratislava) from the 1770s; he was a pupil and a follower of Maulbertsch, sometimes assisting him in the execution of his work. The sketch illustrated here shows the influence of the Master's late style, his clear colours, silvery light and realistic representation of historic costumes and objects, all of which gradually dominated his work as his earlier passion and artistic inspiration began to leave him.
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.short_description: Andreas Zallinger was a member of Franz Anton Maulbertsch’s studio and worked on the decoration of the high altar in the Primatial Palace, Pozsony (Bratislava). This painting of the Hungarian Holy King is devoid of the Baroque vision.
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.initial_owner: Andrea Zallinger (the artist) or József Batthyány (the Archbishop of Esztergom)
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.method_for_datation: By analogy and a signature on the high altar in Bratislava (Pozsony)
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.provenance: The artist or the Archbishop of Esztergom
f6ca901f-3bd3-50dc-a127-e4b8b089187b.obtention: Purchased at an auction of BÁV (Hungarian Commission) in Budapest in 1974.

f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.name: *Moses Striking the Rock*
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.description:
*Moses Striking Water From the Rock* was a production of the workshop of the Neapolitan painter, Francesco Solimena. Solimena was taught painting initially by his father, the Mannerist painter, Angelo, and was later a pupil of Francesco di Mario of Naples. The well-known artists, Pietro da Cortona and Luca Giordano also influenced Solimena's style. Although he painted mainly decorative, religious and mythological subjects, he also undertook decorative frescos and portraits. His work, representative of the Late-Baroque painting of Naples, reveals Rococo elements, as seen in this religious composition. Solimena ran his own celebrated art school where numerous familiar names of Neapolitan painting were educated. He also designed his own villa and palace.  
This painting holds many features typical of Solimena: the dynamism of the composition, the multitude of intermingled bodies within which he manages to show the marked elegance of individual figures who are strikingly illuminated against their brownish shadows to come out of the depths of the composition. The painting depicts the Biblical story of Moses leading the people of Israel through the wilderness to the Promised Land. When they arrive at a high rock – which symbolises Christ – the prophet strikes the top of the rock with his staff, and water pours from it. The thirsty people climb the rock to drink the water, in fact, an allegory of the faith and mercy of God. The water here prefigures the “blood and water” that poured from the wounded side of Christ, and refers to the Baptism. In the centre of the composition, Moses stands alongside the rock, water running down to the base. Above, in the clouds, God the Father hovers surrounded by angels. Together they create the culmination of this dynamic composition. The individual figures of men and women of all ages climbing up the steep rock with vessels in their hands are, on the whole, painted from behind and from underneath. The remainder of a somewhat distant landscape is discernable; on the left, an oasis with palm trees and tents, while to the right a few figures running towards the rock against the sky. Although painted in the academic manner, the colours are lively and intense and the figures are individualised and well painted. Solimena spent the whole of his working life in Naples and was one of the most prolific painters of the Late Baroque. This painting, probably produced in his workshop, may be a prototype for a larger fresco or altarpiece.
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.short_description:
Francesco Solimena's work, representative of the late Neapolitan Baroque, reveals traces of the Rococo. His father, Angelo, gave him his first painting lessons, and he was later a pupil of Francesco di Mario of Naples. The well-known artists, Pietro da Cortona and Luca Giordano also influenced Solimena's style. He was a prolific painter, creating altarpieces, painting frescos in churches and palaces, mythological compositions and portraits. He designed his own villa and palace and had his own celebrated school of art in Naples.  
*Moses Striking Water From the Rock* takes a low angle, depicting the many figures climbing the high rock out of which Moses struck water. The Bible relates how Moses led his people through the desert to the Promised Land. On the way, they stopped alongside a high rock above which, in the clouds, God the Father hovered. Moses quenching the thirst of the people is symbolic of Christ and religion: the thirsty people climbing the rock are bearing vessels to fill with the water of life. This painting bears all the features typical of Solimena's work. Probably created in his workshop, it was perhaps a prototype for a larger composition.
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.method_for_datation: Study of the literature, stylistic analysis and comparative material and consultations with eminent art historians.
f6f8d8d6-b9c8-5b6c-870e-0ef02019a256.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.

f7b5eed2-bad6-5128-931e-3d1c1d65061e.name: Church of São João Evangelista
f7b5eed2-bad6-5128-931e-3d1c1d65061e.description: The Church of São João Evangelista has a Mannerist façade that is typical of Iberian models of the Jesuit Order. Sculptures of *St. Ignatius of Loyola*, *St. Francis Xavier*, *St. Stanislas* and *St. Francis of Borja* decorate the façade. The interior is dominated by a large nave with eight lateral open-vaulted chapels, an illusionary transept and a main chapel, all of which accord with the Jesuit model. On the walls of the nave, frescoes represent the Evangelists, scenes from the lives of several Jesuits and architectural and vegetal motifs. The wooden ceiling, with a *trompe l'oeil* vault and foliate paintings, is framed by two domes with allegories and *quadratura* compositions that align with the central axe. In the centre there is a panel with the Jesuit insignia “IHS”. The simplicity of the Mannerist architectural outline is combined with the richness of Baroque ornamentation, in line with the principles of the Counter-Reformation.
f7b5eed2-bad6-5128-931e-3d1c1d65061e.short_description: The Church of São João Evangelista is one of the best examples in Madeira of the integration of the Baroque with the Mannerist style. Decorated after 1647, the interior combines gilded wood carved retables, patterned and figurative *azulejos*, *trompe l´oeil* ceiling painting and frescoes on the walls of the nave and sacristy.

f7b5eed2-bad6-5128-931e-3d1c1d65061e.history:
The church of São João Evangelista with its mannerist outline was built in 1629 by the Jesuits who established themselves in Madeira some time after 1570. The church was already built by 1647, but due to its monumental character and exuberance, works continued until the beginning of the 18th century. In fact, the Baroque style took over from the original Mannerist composition, and in meeting with the ideas of the Counter-Reformation, it called Christians to glorious salvation and elevated them in its artistic glory.  
With the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1760 the church was closed until 1846 at which time, aware of the monument's valuable heritage, the Civil Governor, José Silvestre Ribeiro, undertook important renovation works and returned the church to the Bishropic thereby making it once again available for religious services.

f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.name: Wilten Basilica (Parish Church of the Immaculate Conception)
f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.alternate_name: Our Lady Under the Four Columns
f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.description: The architectural character of Wilten parish church is a typical work of Penz, with a clear and simple ground plan, balanced proportions and a harmonious spatial arrangement, all carefully calculated to generate a pleasing prospect. The further development of the scheme of the Innsbruck city parish church resulted in a unification of the spatial image, which in Innsbruck was more clearly characterised by the sequence of bays with cupola-like vaults. While Penz supplied ideas and acted as construction supervisor, the plans originate from the sculptor Joseph Stapf from the Füssen school. The building work was carried out by Matthias and Johann Michael Umhauser.
f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.short_description: Wilten Basilica is considered the most important Rococo ecclesiastical building in North Tyrol, and alongside Gossensaß, the most accomplished of Franz de Paula Penz’s works. The plain building, a two-bay pilaster church with a barely retracted choir surprises with a magnificent prospect composed of finely coordinated architecture, ornamentation and sculptures of great stylistic unity.
f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.type: Ecclesiastical architecture (parish church, papal basilica and pilgrimage church)
f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.method_for_datation: Archives, choir arch cartouche with chronogram, “1755”

f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.history: According to the founding legend even Roman legionnaires in Wilten worshipped an image of the Virgin Mary “Under the Four Columns”, and according to records it served as a site of pilgrimage as early as the 13th century. Excavations revealed an original building dating from the early Christian period, a consecration was held in 1311, and in the late 15th century a Gothic vault was inserted. Up until 1643 the building also served as the parish church of Innsbruck. In 1728 the church was refurbished in the Baroque style. Following building damage in 1750 a new building was erected between 1751 and 1756. Interior work was carried out up until the late 18th century.
f7e4c02e-6b61-5d4c-85bf-101b2a06a6b8.patrons: Wilten Foundation (under Abbot Norbert I. Bußjäger)

f811818c-63f6-5385-94c0-2eb1a870aecb.name: Chapel of the Rosary, basilica di San Domenico, Bologna
f811818c-63f6-5385-94c0-2eb1a870aecb.description: The complex painted decoration of Mitelli and Colonna involves four pilasters, two archivolts, the walls and the vaults of the whole chapel. The painters were helped by the sculptor Domenico Ottani, who made the stucco decorations, the capitals and the elegant friezes, and the gilders Alessandro Miselli and Carlo Veronese. The abundant use of gold leaf for the decorations gives the chapel its typical baroque sumptuousness and contributes to the diffusion of light. Mitelli and Colonna started working in February 1655, completing the painting in May 1657. The subject chosen was the glorification of the Blessed Virgin of the Rosary. The dome is decorated with a beautiful sky wherein the Madonna is carried up by the angels and crowned. In the roundels at the base of the dome are represented the merits of the Rosary handed by the Virgin to St. Dominic in order to defeat the plague of 1630. Putti, angels and Virtues celebrate the glory of the Virgin among flowers, in one of the most impressive scenes of Emilian baroque. The altar is framed by illusionistic architecture on the apse and crowned by two choirs of angels holding crowns, one of flowers and one of stars thus following the motto “*Dat flores tellus, coelum dat sidera sertis*”. Three great ovals frame episodes from the life of the Virgin (the *Birth of Mary*, *Mary presented to the temple* and the *Marriage of the Virgin*). This extraordinary fresco decoration ideally faces the *Glorification of St. Dominic* painted by Guido Reni in the chapel dedicated to the saint, just across the nave.
f811818c-63f6-5385-94c0-2eb1a870aecb.short_description:
The Chapel of the Rosary was created in 1589 when the Brotherhood of the Rosary refurbished the medieval chapel held by the Guidotti family.  
Particularly striking is the altar framing the statue of the Madonna of the Rosary, surrounded by 15 small pictures with the mysteries of the Rosary, work of many celebrated Bolognese painters.  
In the second half of the seventeenth-century the interior of the chapel was rebuilt with a new dome and a new apse, while the exterior held the polygonal late Gothic features. Between 1655 and 1657 the whole chapel was decorated by the painters Angelo Michele Colonna and Agostino Mitelli, who made the present rich scenographic decoration, glorifying the Blessed Virgin of the Rosary.

f811818c-63f6-5385-94c0-2eb1a870aecb.history: In 1460 Giovanni Guidotti asked the mason Giovanni del Lago di Como to build a chapel in the church of San Domenico imitating that dedicated to St. Thomas, in Gothic style. The chapel was named the Guidotti chapel. In 1575, with the Guidotti's permission, the confraternity of the Rosary started to use the chapel for its meetings and in 1589 paid for its total refurbishment. Among the most significant works of art of this period stand the sumptuous altar dedicated to the Virgin and the decoration of the vault. In 1601 the most celebrated workshops in Bologna commissioned 15 paintings that now surround the statue of the Virgin and represent the Mysteries of the Rosary. They are representative of Bolognese contemporary painting style. After the plague of 1630 the Madonna of the Rosary became the focus of a rejuvenated religious zeal. Many gifts were presented to the chapel from the people who had survived the epidemic. In 1654 the master Francesco Dotti and the architect Francesco Martini modified the whole structure by building a deep apse and a square antechamber with a decorated vault and a dome. The painters Mitelli and Colonna were asked to decorate the chapel; they finished the work in 1657. During Dotti's refurbishing of the whole church (1727–1737) the chapel was partially changed, mainly in the liturgical apparel.

f88a365b-0b19-5fa2-8be0-31a30d035b7c.name: Breakfast Set
f88a365b-0b19-5fa2-8be0-31a30d035b7c.description: The breakfast set consists of a triangular tray, a sugar bowl, teapot, milk jug, high and low cups with saucers and porcelain teaspoons. The tray has rounded corners and a bevelled, scalloped rim. The teapot is potbellied with a curving handle and a tubular spout. The milk jug has a potbellied body on three short legs imitating twigs, a curved handle and short lip. The cups and the sugar bowl are simple in shape, on a low round base, and without handles. All parts of the set have gilt, lacy decorative edges. The knobs of the lids are in the shape of a rose. Each item of the set depicts a different war scene whose actors are Croatian border troops and the Pandurs of Baron Franjo Trenk, shown at moments of rest and while in action. Some of the scenes on the pieces are after Martin Engelbrecht’s prints. All items show the mark of the Meissen manufactory: crossed swords and a star, or a dot below and the impressed mark: X, P, 60, 64.
f88a365b-0b19-5fa2-8be0-31a30d035b7c.short_description: Adorning each item of the breakfast set are polychrome painted scenes of warfare with the soldiers of the Croatian border troops and the Pandurs of Baron Franjo Trenk.

f8d10a9b-dcff-531e-85e8-7c328a035d3e.name: Villa Sora, fresco decoration of the main hall
f8d10a9b-dcff-531e-85e8-7c328a035d3e.description:
The decoration is split into two registers: the lower register showing the standing *Liberal Arts* and *Intellectual Activities* (arithmetic, comedy, tragedy, heroic poetry, lyrical poetry, philosophy, geometry, rhetoric, astrology and dance) as if supporting the entire decoration, between windows decorated with grotesques; the upper register, *Landscapes*, designed as mock tapestries possibly by Vespasiano Strada, which alternate with seated allegorical figures representing the *Nine Muses* (Clio, Euterpe, Thalia, Melpomene, Polyhymnia, Erato, Terpsichore, Urania and Calliope) *and Mnemosyne* (Memory) Mother of the Muses, in accordance with the dictates of Cesar Ripa's *Iconologia.* Between the two parts, garlands of flowers and fruit with heraldic animals (lion and dragon) held up by *putti* link together a series of monochrome medallions with busts of *Illustrious Men* from antiquity. In the centre of the long sides of the hall stand two prominent coats of arms, combining the heraldic symbols of the Boncompagni (dragon) and Sforza di Santa Fiora (lion rampant) families, to which the wife of Giacomo Boncompagni, Costanza, belonged. The hall is completed by a contemporary painted ceiling.  
This is an interesting example of a secular decorative theme following the Counter-Reformation: it is dominated by moral, allegorical subjects through the use of illustrious men and the essential protective role of the intellectual activities exercised by a noble family linked to the papacy, which is naturally, albeit indirectly, celebrated thus. The rich and complex decoration, which lends itself to different levels of interpretation, combines mythological, historical and naturalistic references—all alluding to different commemorative intentions nonetheless harmoniously combined by a single plan—and represents well the moment of transition from the austere spirit at the height of the Counter-Reformation to the more animated, albeit still strictly divided, spirit of early 17th-century Rome; a moment of transition recorded in numerous decorative works undertaken by the school of Cavalier d'Arpino, a genuine artistic entrepreneur in Rome during those years, who was able to call upon a considerable group of pupils from different backgrounds to help him carry out his work.
f8d10a9b-dcff-531e-85e8-7c328a035d3e.short_description: The decoration is split into two registers: the lower register, showing the standing *Liberal Arts* and *Intellectual Activities* as if supporting the entire decoration, in between windows decorated with grotesques; the upper register, *Landscapes*, designed as mock tapestries, which alternate with seated allegorical figures representing the *Nine Muses and Mnemosyne* (Memory) Mother of the Muses.
f8d10a9b-dcff-531e-85e8-7c328a035d3e.method_for_datation: Guerrieri Borsoi, M. B., *Villa Sora a Frascati*, Rome 2000.
f8d10a9b-dcff-531e-85e8-7c328a035d3e.bibliography:
Tantillo, A. M., "Villa Sora", *I principi della chiesa*, Milan 1998, p. 101.  
Guerrieri Borsoi, M. B., *Villa Sora a Frascati*, Rome 2000.
f8d10a9b-dcff-531e-85e8-7c328a035d3e.history: The villa, located on Via Tuscolana just before the town, was built in the mid-16th century by Cardinal Giovanni Moroni who was an influential prelate of the Council of Trent. Built in a style of a city villa, it has a central courtyard, a covered roof-terrace and arched belvedere tower. In 1600 it was bought by Giacomo Boncompagni, natural son of Gregory XIII (1572–85), who commissioned Giuseppe Cesari (also known as Cavalier d’Arpino) and his studio to decorate the “main hall” with frescos, which was carried out in the first decade of the 17th century. At the end of the 19th century, the villa passed to Tommaso Saulini, who sold it to the Salesiana family, who are the current owners.

f8dc2654-17a7-5060-9ab1-d36689f94609.name: San Salvatore, Chiesa del Santissimo Salvatore
f8dc2654-17a7-5060-9ab1-d36689f94609.description:
The ancient abbot church with the nearby monastery of the Lateran Congregation of the Holy Saviour, also called Renian, was rebuilt in 1473–78. Between 1605 and 1623 a new plan by the Barnabite Milanese architect Giovanni Ambrogio Mazenta was built by Tommaso Martelli who is described in the documents as the “architect of our church”. The stucco statues and capitals were moulded by Giovanni Tedeschi, while Orazio Provaglia is the author of the bronze statues of the façade.  
The church bears a typical Counterreformation plan with some new ideas, referencing the Roman Jesuit church of the Gesù. The balanced longitudinal nave with its width double its height, has three chapels on both sides; the transept is crowned by a dome hidden outside by an octagonal tiburium. The apse is semi-circular inside and polygonal outside. The two tall symmetrical volumes, corresponding with the transept and central section, are easily recognizable from the outside as they are separated from the smaller volumes of the other two sections. The two sections have lateral chapels with palladian windows alternating with double, rectangular false windows, following the binary sequence of lesene and the wall design. The eight beautiful free standing columns, instead of the more common lesene or half columns, mark the progression of the nave.  
The exterior with its complex articulated prospect on the side of the church, facing via IV Novembre, is also particularly interesting.  
The interior houses memories and works of art coming from the former church. The iconographic and symbolic plan guiding the 17th century renovation culminates in the altarpiece of the high altar, representing the *Holy Saviour* by Guido Reni and Francesco Gessi (1620). This is surrounded by paintings by Giacomo Cavedoni (1622) hanging on the apse walls and representing the *Story of the Beirut Crucifix*, also the subject of one of the side chapels altarpieces, painted in late 16th century by the Florentine painter Jacopo Coppi. In the left transept stands the monumental *Sacred Family* by Alessandro Tiarini (1623). In the lateral central chapels, the *Resurrection of Christ* by Mastelletta faces *The Ascension of Christ* by Carlo Bononi. *The Ascension of the Virgin* by Agostino Carracci (now in the Pinacoteca Nazionale) hung in the third chapel on the left. In this church is buried Giovan Francesco Barbieri, known as il Guercino. He is memorialized by the slab in the middle of the main nave floor.  
After the suppressions the Napoleonic Age and of 1866, the monastery became property of the Italian government and the church is today part of the Fondo degli Edifici di Culto.
f8dc2654-17a7-5060-9ab1-d36689f94609.short_description: This church is a significant example of the architecture of the age of the Counterreformation. The façade is composed of two architectonical orders connected by volutes and is reminiscent of the Roman Jesuit church of the Gesù. The interior, wide and imposing, is a typical example of architectural classicism. Note the use of freestanding columns.
f8dc2654-17a7-5060-9ab1-d36689f94609.dates: Started in 1605, the church was completed in 1623 by different architects

f8dc2654-17a7-5060-9ab1-d36689f94609.history:
Work was started in 1605, interrupted in 1607, started again in 1613, and completed in 1623. This church perfectly exemplifies the debate about the doubled axis plan and the use of the free standing column employed by Magenta. While often criticized and opposed by his detractors it anticipates many future developments in architecture.  
In order to make the new church more impressive and imposing, between 1618 and 1622 some houses owned by the Lateran Canons and leaning against the side of the building were pulled down. This created an opening on the church-square, thus emphasizing the façade, standing on a high base. In 1624, in the outer corner of this church-square was built a votive column: the square and the column were both removed during the XIX century.  
Many cultivated tourists, especially foreigners, celebrated the church. Jean Mabillon, visited Bologna in May 1686 and described it as “a beautiful basilica, of modern architecture”. Montesquieu, in Bologna in 1729, wrote that “considering modern architecture, the Holy Saviour is one of most magnificent churches of Bologna”. Charles De Brosses, a passionate lover of Roman architecture, in Bologna in September 1739, described it without hesitation as the most beautiful church in town, comparing it to ancient Greek and Roman architecture.  
The roof was damaged on the 15th of June 1758 when it was struck by lightning. The church had to be restored and at that time its interior was embellished (1759-60).

f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.name: *Joseph and Potiphar’s Wife*
f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.description:
The painting is a variation of the fresco painted by the artist in the Palazzo Mattei in Rome in 1615. Unlike that work, the figure of Potiphar's Wife is naked and the colours are based on tones of red and ochre. The different hypotheses advanced by scholars include the possibility that it is an approximate replica of the Mettei fresco completed for Scipione Borghese. During the pontificate of Paul V, the artist received a series of extraordinary commissions, including the decoration of the Loggia delle Benedizioni in the Vatican Basilica, and part of the frescos in the Sala Regia in the Quirinal. These were followed by commissions from Cardinal Scipione himself, such as the decoration and fresco at Villa Mondragone in Frascati near Rome, and the vault of the loggia at Villa Borghese.  
The canvas shows a well-known episode from the Old Testament (Genesis, 39, 7–18) extolling the chastity of Joseph, courted by the wife of Potiphar, the head of the Pharaoh's guards. The woman, offended by Joseph's rejection, is left holding his tunic in her hands when he escapes; she accuses him unjustly and has him thrown into gaol. During his imprisonment, Joseph becomes known for his ability to interpret dreams and is freed immediately.  
The highly contrasting *chiaroscuro* and the Caravaggesque ascending layering of colour, associate the painting with the work of the painter Simon Vouet in the 1630s.  
Joseph's almost running pose and the foreshortening of the raised right hand are particularly noteworthy. A contrasting sense of movement is provided by the body of the woman, who will not release him and is pulling in the opposite direction. She is fully illuminated by a beam of light that leaves Joseph's face almost in shadow. Skilful compositional knowledge is evident in the essential nature of the elements, which emerge from the darkness in a notably theatrical style.
f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.short_description: It is Lanfranco who carries out one of the first examples of Baroque painting in Rome for Cardinal Scipione: *The Council of the Gods* in the loggia of Villa Borghese. The biblical theme represented in this painting celebrates the virtue of chastity. The canvas, a replica of the fresco in Palazzo Mattei in Rome, is a play of light with, clearly, theatrical inspiration.
f915f9d0-bd72-560a-a96c-be1703627823.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

f98fab12-852d-5d5d-9ded-f7b91c8f9481.name: Premonstratensian Monastery, Hradisko u Olomouce
f98fab12-852d-5d5d-9ded-f7b91c8f9481.description: The monastery, on a quadratic ground plan, with buildings constructed along an axis dictated by the church, its corner towers endowing it with a stronghold character, embodies an “infirmary of God”. A display of spiritual and secular power, the site’s fame and the virtues of its patrons are expressed through the monastery’s design, embracing a host of elements characterising secular residences: an impressive entrance; a spectacular staircase; a hall in the front and a system of anterooms and side rooms. The monastery buildings and the church lie in the second tract. The canonry complex also comprises farmyards, residences for individual demesnes (Šebetov, Vresovice and Konice), ornamental gardens, statues in the landscape and the Sv. Kopecek pilgrimage site.
f98fab12-852d-5d5d-9ded-f7b91c8f9481.short_description: A display of spiritual and secular power, the site’s fame and the virtues of its patrons are expressed through the monastery design. The extent of building activity, patronage and political influence rivalled those of the bishop, and surpassed those of the aristocracy. Leading Viennese and Olomouc artists joined forces in the interior decoration. The main subjects include allegories of the virtues and an apotheosis of the founder of the Premonstratensian order. The canonry complex also comprises farmyards, residences and the Sv. Kopecek pilgrimage site.
f98fab12-852d-5d5d-9ded-f7b91c8f9481.method_for_datation: Left of the entrance is a plaque with the year 1786, relating to the establishment of the new monastery. Contracts and correspondence for a large proportion of the work and art have survived. The progress of the work and significant visitors to the monastery are recorded in the monastery chronicles. These also mention some artefacts that once complemented the iconography of the monastery such as a fountain in the courtyard known from old pictures which have not survived.

f98fab12-852d-5d5d-9ded-f7b91c8f9481.history: The Premonstratensian order acquired the site, once a Benedictine monastery, in 1151. The monastery became a burial site for the appanage princes of the Przemyslid dynasty. The monastery was plundered by the Swedish army when it took Olomouc. It was subsequently rebuilt and a new church erected. The church was steadily supplemented with further canonry buildings, designed by G. P. Tencalla and M. A. Lublinský. The extensive building activities, patronage and political influence of the monastery rivalled those of the bishop, and surpassed the activities of the aristocracy. A major celebration, commemorating the 600th anniversary of the arrival of the Premonstratensian order in Hradisko, was held there in 1751. The monastery sustained damage during the Prussian siege in 1758 and in 1784 was converted into a military hospital.

fa49e731-54fb-5135-9928-fa56c209c110.name: Bishop’s Palace, Szombathely
fa49e731-54fb-5135-9928-fa56c209c110.description:
The U-shape layout of the Palace is an enduring feature of Baroque palace architecture in Europe and in Hungary. The *cour d'honneur*, however, does not open out onto the street, as local tradition required, but onto the garden instead. The row of most representative rooms is located on the first floor, the so-called *piano nobile*. According to local tradition a corridor runs in front of the rooms facing the courtyard. The main entrance opens onto a vaulted driveway. Walking away from the driveway, the entrance hall and *sala terrena* are on the right; to the left is the main stairway that leads to the first floor. The Baroque enfilade runs behind the main facade, and the Ceremonial Hall is located centrally in the building. Above the *piano nobile* there is a lower mezzanine floor.  
The facade reflects the characteristics of Viennese palace architecture. The arrangement of the axes follows a 4-3-4 pattern; the central risalit is only slightly projected, and a balcony in front of it rests on columns. The ground floor, which rather resembles a footing, ends in a string-course and then continues with the high windows of the *piano nobile* and the lower windows of the second floor. The first floor is articulated by monumental pilasters. On the façade are festoon decorations typical of the era. On the mid-section gable, the coat of arms of the patron can be seen. The articulation and decorations are simple, showing the calm linearity of the Late Baroque style, but also Neo-Classical features. The *sala terrana* is embellished with pictures of Rome, based on the engravings of Giovanni Battista Piranesi, and Roman woodcarvings exhibited there are also illustrated. The fresco in the Ceremonial Hall depicts the Allegory of Divine Providence, and on the walls are scenes from the history of ancient Savaria: *Tiberius Claudius founds Savaria*; *Septimius Severus becomes Emperor*; *Constantinus Chlorus becomes Legislator* and, finally, *Attila Defeats the Romans*. In the palace there are several oil sketches for the cathedral frescoes and altarpieces.
fa49e731-54fb-5135-9928-fa56c209c110.short_description: The Bishop's Palace in Szombathely is an outstanding example in Hungary of the so-called Late Baroque style with Neo-Classical features. Queen Maria Theresia (1740–1780) founded a new diocese in 1777 and appointed János Szily (1777–1799) as Bishop. Szily constructed the Bishop's Palace, the Seminary and the Cathedral. Of this building complex, the construction of the Bishop's Palace was completed first (1778–1783). Its cultural and historical value lies also in the fact that it was the first museum in Hungary, founded by Szily. The museum, on the ground floor of the palace (in the so called *sala terrena*), comprised of stone carvings excavated in the ancient Roman city of Savaria, which lay beneath Szombathely.
fa49e731-54fb-5135-9928-fa56c209c110.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources.

fa49e731-54fb-5135-9928-fa56c209c110.history:
Due to the oversized character of Hungarian dioceses, Queen Maria Theresia (1740–1780) decided to found new ones, including that of Szombathely, in 1777. She appointed János Szily (1777–1799) as the first bishop. After the diocese was founded, Szombathely required new public buildings to reflect the town's new-found status. Szily erected a building complex: first the Bishop's Palace, then the Seminary and lastly the Cathedral (1791–1814). The architect of the cathedral was Melchior Hefele, one of the most significant masters of his time.  
The ground plan of the basement, ground and first floors of the palace is still extant, and the original painting of the facade is recorded in a copy. In 1784, on the ground floor of the palace (in the so called *sala terrena*), Szily founded a museum comprised of stone carvings excavated in Savaria, the ancient Roman city that lay beneath Szombathely.  
The palace interior was decorated with frescoes by Stephan Dorffmeister. The bishop entrusted Franz Anton Maulbertsch, the most significant painter of the era, to paint the Central Hall with frescoes that would illustrate the glory of the diocese and the ancient history of the city.

fac6052d-8778-5973-8864-63b61123c63f.name: *Portrait of Baroness Erzsébet Haller*
fac6052d-8778-5973-8864-63b61123c63f.description:
*Portrait of Baroness Erzsébet Haller* depicts the daughter of Field Marshal Baron Sámuel Haller holding a brush and palette and beside her on a table with a marble top there is a small paint box. Between 1756 and 1767, Dániel Schmiddely painted a series of 14 portraits of which this is one. Today 12 are extant but the whereabouts of the other two is unknown. All of similar dimensions and compositional organisation, the paintings represent aristocratic young women and recognise contemporary requirements of high society manners and etiquette. The girls are depicted painting, drawing, playing the piano, standing by a globe or arranging a bouquet in a Rococo vase. These portraits, while seen as examples of a new representative genre, also bear witness to the artistic and intellectual education aristocratic society required from young aristocratic women at the time, hence they are depicted in the process of appropriating this education. The series, produced for the Convent of the Sisters of Notre Dame in Pozsony (Bratislava), represents the school's pupils in blue uniform. The religious order of Lorraine, under which this school operated, began its activity in the area in 1748 under temporary conditions. Schmiddely's paintings probably furnished the college and school that was finally built in 1754.  
Schmiddely studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. He then lived and worked in Pozsony (Bratislava) where he also undertook official commissions, and according to records, he was a professor of drawing at a college there. In view of this series of paintings, the college he worked at was that of the Sisters of Notre Dame.
fac6052d-8778-5973-8864-63b61123c63f.short_description: Schmiddely was a tutor in painting and drawing in Pozsony (Bratislava). The Portrait *of Baroness Erzsébet Haller* is part of a series of 14 portraits, others of which are in Slovakia and Bohemia. The paintings, depicting young women dressed in blue uniforms, refer to different aspects of a good education.

fafb3812-1969-5e3a-b9d0-22446066efee.name: Chest for a Portable Altar
fafb3812-1969-5e3a-b9d0-22446066efee.description:
Portable altars in the form of chests were an element of religious furniture, epitomising Portuguese maritime travel to different parts of the world.  
This type of furniture developed from the 16th century onwards as Portuguese maritime voyages, in particular to India and China, increased.  
These voyages often involved both regular and secular clergymen embarking on missionary activities, aristocratic families, the backbone of the administration in the Portuguese empire, or those who set out for diverse corners of the world in the quest for new commercial markets.  
The need to reduce the volume and weight of the cargo transported on these voyages resulted in the construction of furniture that was light and easy to handle and store.  
This piece of furniture is built of wood and covered with black-painted leather. It is adorned with engraved plant motifs and a pattern made out of tacks. On the outside it is fairly plain. The exuberance of the piece is revealed after it is opened and assembled. The internal lining in red silk is further embellished by gold trimming. The fittings that frame the lid were inspired by incised motifs, a decorative mode that flourished during the period.  
The liturgical implements (chalice, crucifix, pyx, cruet, paten and bell), all of which were necessary to celebrate mass, were stored in a drawer below the altar table, in customised, made-to-measure indentations.  
Many masses were celebrated aboard the carracks on altars such as this one, as well as on land, at sites that did not have suitable facilities for religious worship.  
Mass could only be celebrated on altars that contained an altar-stone – a stone that had been blessed – upon which was placed the chalice and the host. In this altar, the altar-stone is found in a concave indentation within the table.  
During voyages, priests were obliged to celebrate mass every Sunday and on holy days. A particular feature of masses celebrated on board ship was that they did not have the consecration and consequently did not have communion. They were thus called “dry masses”.  
In his work, *As* *Cartas Ânuas da China: 1636, 1643 a 1649,* a compilation of letters from China written to the Jesuit General in Rome annually, the Jesuit priest António de Gouveia described the presence of altars in the houses of Portuguese settlers. He relates that it was a common practice to “assemble the altar” in the largest room so that mass could be held.
fafb3812-1969-5e3a-b9d0-22446066efee.short_description: A chest containing a portable altar, it was designed to be transported long distance on Portuguese maritime voyages to enable those on board to celebrate Mass both while on board the ship and, on arrival, in foreign lands.

fb4db280-b1e8-5792-9924-ea1569ecf8e4.name: *Petar II Anton Hilleprand-Prandau*
fb4db280-b1e8-5792-9924-ea1569ecf8e4.description:
Baron Petar II Anton Hilleprand-Prandau stands at the centre of the painting finely dressed and wearing a long wig. His left arm rests on a marble-topped table, while his right arm points to the manor house he had built in the background. The family crest is in the right upper corner.  
Petar II was one of the most respected members of this distinguished family originally from Tyrol. He was born in Bozen, studied law in Ingolstadt and served with the Austrian Court. Granted the Valpovo estate in Slavonia in 1721, he died in Vienna in 1771.  
Commissioned to mark a double jubilee, the painting celebrates the Baron's 75th birthday, and commemorates the right of the female line of the family to inherit the Valpovo estate.  
Although much about the life and work of Hochhauser remains a mystery, we do know that he studied at the Vienna Academy under Jacob van Schuppen. We know that the court painter and favourite of Empress Maria Theresia, Martin van Meytens, was a great influence on him, and that he was well trained and kept to the best portrait traditions of the time, relying on the generally accepted and acknowledged conventions of Baroque portrait painting.
fb4db280-b1e8-5792-9924-ea1569ecf8e4.short_description: A portrait of Baron Petar II Anton Hilleprand-Prandau, painted by Ephraim Hochhauser who studied painting at the Vienna Academy under Jacob van Schuppen. In his portraits, Hochhauser relies on the generally accepted and recognised conventions of Baroque portrait painting. Influenced by Martin van Meytens, court painter and favourite of Empress Maria Theresia.
fb4db280-b1e8-5792-9924-ea1569ecf8e4.initial_owner: Valpovo, family of Baron Hilleprand-Prandau, later of Count Normann-Ehrenfels
fb4db280-b1e8-5792-9924-ea1569ecf8e4.method_for_datation: From the signature and family archives.
fb4db280-b1e8-5792-9924-ea1569ecf8e4.obtention: Confiscated after the Second World War.

fc45efc5-13ac-52a6-acca-d9f0c752a728.name: Episcopal residence, Kroměříž
fc45efc5-13ac-52a6-acca-d9f0c752a728.alternate_name: Kremsier, known as the Athens of the Haná region
fc45efc5-13ac-52a6-acca-d9f0c752a728.description: This residential complex for the bishops of Olomouc consists of a chateau with a lower garden and a floral garden. Canonical homes line the street leading to the Church of St. Mauritz, which contains a chapel in which bishops were interred. The chateau, with a closed central courtyard, is a free-standing building with four wings and two floors on a trapezoid ground plan.
fc45efc5-13ac-52a6-acca-d9f0c752a728.short_description: Originally a market village, Kroměříž grew up around the crossroads of major European trade routes. Moravian bishops purchased the demesne in 1107. The residential complex consists of a chateau with a lower garden, floral garden and canonical homes lining the street leading to the Church of St. Mauritz. A fresco by F. A. Maulbertsch in the Feudal Hall is considered the most impressive of its kind in Central Europe. In 1998 the Kroměříž gardens and chateau were included on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
fc45efc5-13ac-52a6-acca-d9f0c752a728.method_for_datation: A number of receipts, contracts and correspondence associated with the monument have survived. Additional information for the dating of individual stages is provided by historical events and biographies of the bishops.

fc45efc5-13ac-52a6-acca-d9f0c752a728.history: Originally a market village, Kroměříž grew up around the crossroads of the Amber and Salt Trails, two major European trade routes. Moravian bishops purchased the demesne in 1107. Bruno of Schaumburk (d.1281) built a Gothic castle and established the Chapter of St. Mauritz. In 1290 Kroměříž was granted town status. Under Stanislav Thurzo (d.1540), a man of humanist leanings, the castle was converted into a Renaissance chateau and a summer residence. In 1643 the town was plundered by the Swedes and burnt down during the Wallachian uprising of 1821. The famous picture gallery, now containing work by L. Cranach and one of Titian’s last paintings, was built around the end of the 17th century.

fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.name: *Triumphal Procession of Charles V Duke of Lorraine*
fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.description:
The signature on this work is of an unknown artist. The composition is similar to that on a series of tapestries in Nancy, France, depicting the recapture of Buda, which saw an end not only to 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary but also to a long period of anti-Ottoman fighting. The event was represented in a series of contemporary graphic works, tapestries and paintings, but the painting illustrated here is a lesser known work.  
This allegorical painting represents the fictitious triumphal entry into Buda of Charles Duke V of Lorraine (1643—1690). Set against representations of Hungarian towns that played an important role in the anti-Ottoman campaigns, the triumphal coach of the duke, who was held up as a hero for his recapture of Buda from the Turks in 1686, is surrounded by flags. Also around the coach are allegorical female figures, and on the triumphal arch are statues of the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I and Pope Innocent XI.
fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.short_description: This allegorical painting depicts a fictitious triumphal procession of Charles Duke V of Lorraine into Buda. Lorraine was held up as a hero for his recapture of Buda from the Turks in 1686. The painting makes use of antique imagery and iconography.
fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.method_for_datation: On the basis of historical data
fc9b70c5-0250-5dad-903a-92b40e149fb7.obtention: Purchased from an art dealer in Budapest between the two world wars.

fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.name: Tureen with tray and spoon
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.alternate_name: Count of Aveiras’ Tureen with tray and spoon
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.description:
The import of luxury objects from France enshrines the Portuguese external relations on the XVIII century. The then wealthy and prosperous Kingdom of Portugal elected Paris as the main purveyor of “wonders”, precious fabrics, cabinetry or golden jewelry. King João V was instrumental in the process and the patronage offered to artists, namely the goldsmith Thomas Germain, was maintained by his son and successor, King. José I. Nobles and diplomats accompanied the royal preference and ordered an extraordinary array of French artworks to decorate their palaces and castles.  
The round tureen, more accurately called *pot-à-oille* style, was commissioned in Paris by the Count of Aveiras, D. Francisco da Silva Telo e Menezes. A product of the Charles Spire's workshop, was made circa 1752-3, one of an identical pair.  
It's a superb *rocaille* silver piece, profusely decorated with floral motifs, *rocaille* shells and spirals, also present in the circular tray's rim. The cover depicts a hunting scene.  
The shell shaped spoon is another perfect example of silver carving, with a branch-shaped shaft covered by spiraling foliage and ending in a richly chased bowl.
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.short_description: Round tureen, with four supporting feet, profusely decorated with extremely ornate *rocaille* shell, spiral and floral motifs. The center bears the arms of the Aveiras family, which also appear on the circular tray supporting the tureen and on the large spoon.
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.initial_owner: D. Francisco da Silva Telo e Menezes, Count of Aveiras

fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.name: Church of St. Francis, Oporto
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.alternate_name: Igreja Monumento de São Francisco, Oporto
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.description: A Gothic mendicant church with three aisles, covered with gilded carving and Baroque imagery. In the main body of the church the gradual installation of various altars and retables culminate in blanketing it entirely and changing it completely, giving it a totally Baroque décor. The carving and gilding awaken the senses; not even the ceiling veins can be seen as they are covered by rich carved ornamentation. This is due in part to a well-known characteristically Baroque programmatic principle: if the outside of the building corresponds to the body, the inside is the expression of the soul enriched by God's gifts.
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.short_description: A Gothic church, of the “mendicant” type that was commissioned by the order of St. Francis. It was built during the 13th and14th centuries and entirely covered in gilt carving in several stages throughout the 17th and 18th centuries.
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.location: Parish of St. Nicolau, Oporto, Porto
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.bibliography:
Smith, R. C., *A talha em Portugal*, Lisbon, 1963.  
Chicó, M. T., *A Arquitectura Gótica em Portugal*, Lisbon, 1981.  
Borges, N. C., *História da Arte em Portugal. Do barroco ao rococó*, vol. 9, Lisbon, 1987.  
Alves, N. M. F., “De arquitecto a entalhador. Itinerário de um artista nos séculos XVII e XVIII”, *Actas do I Congresso Internacional do Barroco*, Vol. 1, Porto, 1991, pp. 355–369.  
Dias, P., *A Arquitectura Gótica Portuguesa*, Lisbon, 1994.  
Quaresma, M. C. De carvalho, *Inventário Artístico de Portugal, Cidade do Porto*, Lisbon, 1995.
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.history: Installation of the altarpieces and the carving in general began in the 17th century and lasted until the end of the 18th. The presence of several period altarpieces and carving, mostly of the Baroque style from the first half of the 18th-century culminate in a harmonious visual impact. This variety  was caused by an  increase of orders because Oporto had a vibrant and wealthy bourgeoisie, organized in several brotherhoods, willing to  finance art works in this period. The Church of St Francis stands nowadays as a museum of northern carving. In the 19th century with the extinction of the religious orders and after a violent fire in 1833, right after the siege of Oporto, the convent started to decline, was burnt down and the church was used for instance as a Customs warehouse. The Church of St. Francis was classified as a National Monument in 1910, being now part of the Historic Centre of Oporto. It became an Unesco World Heritage in 1996 .
fcff82c9-8279-56b7-a30f-66d4a410e5f6.patrons: Order of St. Francis, the third order of the St. Francis Brotherhood from Oporto

fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.name: Church of the Paulistas
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.alternate_name: Igreja de Santa Catarina; Igreja dos Eremitas de S. Paulo da Serra d’Ossa
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.description: An urban church of considerable dimensions and flanked by other convent buildings. The façade has two symmetrical towers and a great receding pediment in the Late Baroque style. Three great stone arches give access to a large vaulted porch. The plan is based on a Latin cross with a single nave and side chapels, transept and a chancel. The altars are decorated in carved and gilded woodwork. Despite rebuilding, the church is mainly a synthesis of Baroque and Rocaille features, although during reconstruction in 1763, Neo-Classical elements were introduced. The church houses a collection of Baroque paintings by André Gonçalves. The richly decorated high altar was one of the first to be built during the reign of King João V. Designed by the master carver Santos Pacheco in 1728 its monumental wooden structure is flanked by two Italian-inspired Solomon columns, and a Churrigueresque column adorned with angels. The Solomon columns resonate theatrically with the great sculptural work in the pediment. Together these features mark the transition of a new taste in gilt wood carvings that witnessed great thrones and frontispieces inspired by Bernini and Andrea Pozzo.
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.short_description: The Church was part of a convent founded in 1647 for the Order of The Eremites of St. Paulo da Serra de Ossa, known as the Paulistas. The plan, based on a Latin cross, incorporates a deep chancel and side chapels. The interior decoration is well known for the carved and gilded woodwork of the altarpieces and the stucco ceiling.
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.bibliography:
Santos, R. dos, *Oito Séculos de Arte Portuguesa*, Vol. II, Lisbon, \[n.d.\].  
Neves, E. A. da Silva, “A Igreja de Santa Catarina”, *Olisipo*, No. 115/116, Lisbon, 1966.  
Berger, F. J. G., *Lisboa e os Arquitectos de D. João V*, Lisbon, 1994.
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.history: In 1647, under the initiative of Father Diogo da Ponte, the Church of the Paulistas was founded as part of a convent for the Order of the Eremits of St. Paulo da Serra d' Ossa (Paulistas). It was built on the site of the former Church of Santa Catarina dos Livreiros. Building began in 1654 but the structure was seriously damaged in the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, and building was resumed with a new façade and vaults of the nave. Even so, parts of the original church were preserved and incorporated into the newly built church.
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.patrons: Padre Mestre Fr. Diogo da Ponte (1647)
fd20a177-01af-5d2e-a2a9-299fd1d42188.architects: Architect unknown; woodcarver: Santos Pacheco de Lima (active 1728); stucco ceiling: António Pimenta Rolim (c. 1759/1851); stucco work: João Grossi  [n.d.], Toscanelli [n.d.]; painters: André Gonçalves (1685–1762), Francisco Vieira de Matos (known as Vieira Lusitano 1699–1783).

fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.name: Benedictine Abbey of St. Theodor and St. Alexander
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.description: The monastery complex designed by Father Christoph Vogt is not built facing east as is common, but rather, appears as a rectangle stretched from south to north and is divided in the same direction by a middle axis. In this way the combination of a Benedictine abbey cloister and a sovereign imperial foundation is given a special architectonic expression. The duality shown with the eastern half as a monastery divided by the library wing into two equal courtyards, and the western half surrounding a single courtyard with an outward projecting main facade as a secular, princely residence building, simultaneously appears included and preserved due to the framing effect of the quadrant construction. The abbey church stands alone in front of the north wing and the choir connects to the monastery complex. Its facade with pompous columns and high towers is intended to be viewed from afar. Inside, the colossal columns and pillars intensify the perspective view, the focus of which is the high altar.
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.short_description: The Benedictine Abbey Ottobeuren, dominated by its massive Late Baroque church with delicate Rococo interior, belongs to the largest and most marvellous Baroque monastery complex of southern Germany. The former imperial abbey, often called the “Swabian Escorial”, has always been a centre of science and culture culminating in its representative Imperial Hall, which lives up to expectations, with an amazing display of splendour.
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.dates: 1711–1731: monastery building; 1717–1724: economy building; 1737–1766: church; 1739–1740: government building
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.method_for_datation: Archival documents, among which the diary of the 52nd abbot of Ottobeuren, Rupert Ness.
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.bibliography:
Jahn, P. H., “Wenigst habe in Wien und Rom davon alle Ehr. Die 'kaiserliche' Phase in der Baupolitik des Reichsstiftes Ottobeuren”, *Zeitschrift für Kunstgeschicht*e, 67: 2, 2004, pp. 183–200.  
Hofer, S., *Studien zur Stuckausstattung im frühen 18. Jahrhundert. Modi und ihre Funktion in der Herrschaftsarchitektur am Beispiel Ottobeuren* (Kunstwissenschaftliche Studien 56), Munich/Berlin 1987.  
Schnell, H., *Ottobeuren. Kloster und Kirche* (Große Kunstführer 2, 7th revised and enlarged edition), Regensburg 1979.  
Wagner, H., *Barocke Festsäle in bayerischen Klöstern und Schlössern*, Munich 1974, pp. 112–6.  
Hitchcock, H.-R., *Rococo Architecture in Southern Germany*, London/New York 1968, pp. 198–201.
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.history: Founded in 764 by a count of the name Silach an important historical turning point for the Lower Swabian Benedictine Monastery Ottobeuren was the appointment to a sovereign Imperial Abbey in the 13th century. The land over which this rule extended included a multitude of villages, which later would be the financial basis for the economic and cultural expansion that the monastery experienced during the first half of the 18th century under the active Abbot Rupert Ness. Addressed as the “Hereditary Imperial Chaplain”, Abbot Rupert attempted to express his political closeness to the imperial court in Vienna with an enormous residence-like monastery. This expensive complex, on which a legion of local and trans-local artists worked, was such a strain on the finances of the abbey that the church building had to be delayed. Shortly before his death, Abbot Rupert commissioned the Swabian master builder Simpert Kramer for the construction of the church; however, in 1743, his successor transferred this responsibility to the famous architect Johann Michael Fischer from Munich, who was able to complete the prestigious building in 1766.
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.patrons: Abbots Rupert II Ness (gov. 1710–1740), Anselm Erb (gov. 1740–1767)
fd47a768-1c13-5b0f-82f0-572eb14c0584.architects:
Monastery complex (selection), architecture: Father Christoph Vogt OSB (1648–1725), Simpert Kramer (1675–1753), Andrea Maini (b. 1683); stucco, among others: Johann Baptist Zimmermann (1680–1758), Andrea Maini (b. 1683), Cristoforo Volpini (d. 1733); frescos in the Imperial Hall, its forecourt and south stairwell: Karl Jakob Stauder (1694–1751/56); frescoes of the Theatre Hall and north stairwell of the Imperial Hall: Franz Josef Spiegler (1691–1757); ceiling paintings of the Benedictus Chapel, the Winter Abbey and the Prince’s Rooms: Jacopo Amigoni (1682–1752)  
Abbey church (selection), architecture: Simpert Kramer (1675–1753), Johann Michael Fischer (1692–1766); frescoes: Johann Jakob (1708–1783), Franz Anton Zeiller (1716–83/94); stucco and altar architecture: Johann Michael Feichtmayr (1696–1772); sculpture and design of the choir stalls: Johann Joseph Christian (1706–1777); joinery of choir stalls and confessionals: Martin Hörmann (1688–1782)

fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.name: Tomb
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.description:
The tomb, which is made of gilded silver shaped like a reliquary, holds a casket within which a figurine of Christ lies. Resting upon a trilateral base and supported on the backs of three ivory dragons, the tomb is decorated with embossed and chased foliate and *rocaille* ornaments and jewels. Enamel tablets hold within them scenes from the Life of Christ. From the base, a halo rises surrounded by a border of double rays. Attached to the base are allegorical figures of Faith, Hope and Love, flanked by St. Peter and St. Paul, and above them the figures of the Fathers of the Church Saints Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory. The centre of the sunburst halo holds an enamelled painting of the Virgin and Child in a jewelled frame. It is decorated with foliate and *rocaille* ornaments, supported by two gilded angels. Above the frame is a splendid jewelled crown with a pendant pearl, flanked by two small ivory angels.  
Made in Augsburg and bought for the treasury with money bequeathed by Cardinal Juraj Haulik (the first Archbishop of Zagreb enthroned in 1853) a great patron of the arts and patriot whose ideas reflected the Enlightenment spirit.
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.short_description: A gilded silver tomb shaped like a reliquary, which holds a casket within which a figurine of Christ lies. It rests upon a trilateral base supported on the backs of three ivory dragons. The tomb is decorated with embossed and chased foliate and *rocaille* ornaments and jewels. Enamelled tablets hold within them scenes from the Life of Christ.
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.dimensions: H: 38.7 cm; w: 23 cm: base h: 13.7 cm; w: 31 cm; d: 35.5 cm
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.method_for_datation: The tomb has the hallmark of Augsburg from 1739–1741 and the master’s initials “GDW” in a heart-shaped shield.
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.obtention: Funded by a bequest of Zagreb Archbishop and Cardinal, Juraj Haulik.

fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.name: *Trompe l’œil* with Pious Pictures of *St. Philipp* and the *Virgin Mary*
fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.description:
Elias Mögel was active in Pozsony (Bratislava). His family background is unknown; the first piece of information about him is his wedding in 1751. His last will and testament was written in 1779 and announced on 12 June 1786. His earliest, signed, still life dates from 1760, the latest from 1784. Mögel would have known the Swiss branch of *trompe l'œil* painting through the circle of Johann Gaspar Füssli (1706–1782). The Quodlibets of the writer and professor of drawing in Zürich already carry an unmistakable intention of a popular and artistic education; all that might be of interest to one wanting to appreciate art seems to be present in this picture and its pair: etchings and engravings of all possible techniques, paintings, different types of paper and materials find their place on a trimmed piece of illusionistically painted wood.  
Mögel's paintings served in the improvement of general taste while also evoking a pious disposition. The illusory painting creates a milieu for the depiction of the saints and thus the printed pious paper-pictures, having been popular since the Middle Ages, were advanced here to works of art while at the same time they continue a century-long tradition of religious still life painting. The pair of this painting, conserved in the Bishop's Palace in Vác, is a *trompe l'œil* with engraved pictures of *St. Barbara* and *Salvator Mundi* (after Piazzetta) fixed with an iron nail, and accompanied by a paper with text referring to the Saint.  
Mögel also painted profane *trompe l'œil* pictures and imitated the Dutch genre painters as well. His signed picture kept in the Xantus János Museum in Győr was inspired by Rembrandt's pupil, Frans Bol; his two small genre scenes in Sopron were modelled on Gottfried Schalcken's works. The scenes of the Card players and Pipe smokers in Andrássy Castle in Krasznahorka (Krásna Hôrka) are reminiscent of Adriaen Brower's pictures. A series of six character-head studies, also kept there, may be attributed to him conditionally, as can the *trompe l'œil* of a collector's cabinet in the Museum of Červený Kameň.
fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.short_description: Mögel, who worked in Pozsony (Bratislava), was a master of *trompe l'œil*. This work together with its pair imitated engravings representing pious paper-pictures that had been popular since the Middle Ages.
fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.holder: Bishop’s Palace (Museum of the Diocese) in Vác
fd93f758-39d0-53bd-b0d1-b105ee918d94.method_for_datation: Signed lower right: Elias Mögel pinxit 1773
